## DIY Lawn Care vs. Hiring a Pro in St. Louis: What the Science Says Revised July 27, 2026 Should I do my own lawn care in St. Louis? ⭐ MU Extension on spring seeding, verbatim: **“In some cases, complete failure should be expected.”** The real window is **Aug 25 – Oct 10**, Labor Day best. Rates: **7 lb** tall fescue per 1,000 sq ft in fall vs **10 lb** in spring (40% more seed, worse result). September is the most important fertilization: 1–1½ lb N per 1,000 sq ft. Best grass = turf-type tall fescue (90/10 with Kentucky bluegrass); zoysia is the warm-season option but goes straw-colored mid-fall to mid-spring; **bermuda is NOT recommended** in our transition zone. ⚠️ **Never add sand to clay** — MU says it sets up “bricklike” below 75% sand by volume; use compost, and topdressing only works combined with core aeration. ⚖️ You need NO license to treat your OWN lawn with general-use products, but applying pesticide on someone else’s land for money legally requires a **certified commercial applicator’s license** ($65/yr, Category 3). University of Missouri Extension has a sentence about seeding a lawn in spring that ought to be printed on every bag of grass seed sold in this state: **“In some cases, complete failure should be expected.”** That is a land-grant university telling you that the seed everyone buys in April is largely money in the trash. Timing, not effort and not equipment, is what separates a good St. Louis lawn from a bad one — and it’s also what decides whether you should be doing this yourself. ## Should I do my own lawn care in St. Louis? Mostly yes, with two exceptions. Missouri law lets you apply any general-use product to **your own** lawn with no license, and the highest-value task — seeding in the **August 25 to October 10 window** — requires timing rather than skill. Hire out **core aeration**, where renting the machine barely beats the roughly $107–$202 a service charges, and hire out anything on a *neighbor’s* property, because applying pesticide on someone else’s land for money legally requires a certified commercial applicator’s license. ## Why nothing quite works here St. Louis sits in what turf scientists call the **Transition Zone** — and MU Extension defines it exactly as bluntly as it deserves: an area “where neither warm- nor cool-season grass species are completely adapted.” There is no perfect grass for this city. There are only trade-offs, and picking one means choosing which season you’re willing to lose. **Cool-season grasses** grow best between 60 and 75 degrees — spring and fall — and struggle through a St. Louis August. **Warm-season grasses** want 80 to 95 degrees and go dormant in the cold. MU’s recommendation for Missouri lawns has been the same for decades: **turf-type tall fescue**, ideally as a mix of 90% tall fescue and 10% Kentucky bluegrass. It has a deep root system and handles heat and drought better than other cool-season options. It is green in April and green in November and it suffers in high summer. **Zoysia** is the other legitimate choice, adapted to the southern two-thirds of Missouri. It is genuinely tough — durable, weed-resistant, heat- and drought-tolerant, easy to mow. The price is that it goes **straw-colored from mid-fall to mid-spring**. Roughly half the year, your lawn is brown while your neighbor’s is green. Neither is wrong. But **bermudagrass is**, at least here — MU says flatly that it is “not recommended for lawns in Transition Zone,” and is best adapted to the southern third of the state. One number worth having if you pay a water bill: properly managed, tall fescue needs about **25% less water** and zoysia about **50% less** than Kentucky bluegrass to stay green and growing here. ## The three weeks that decide your year If you take one thing from this article, take this. For cool-season grass in Missouri, the seeding window is **August 25 to October 10**, and lawns seeded around **Labor Day** outperform ones seeded in October. Spring seeding fails because spring moisture feeds weeds that outcompete your seedlings, and then summer heat kills whatever survived. Fall works because the soil is still warm enough for fast germination while the air is cooling, rain is more regular, and weed pressure has dropped. The seeding rates make the point by themselves. MU specifies **7 pounds of tall fescue per 1,000 square feet in fall — and 10 pounds in spring.** Forty percent more seed, for a result the same publication says may fail completely. And here is what makes that window so efficient: **the three highest-value jobs of the entire lawn year all land in it.** Aeration is best in early fall. Seeding runs August 25 to October 10. And September is, in MU’s words, **the most important time to fertilize** — 1 to 1½ pounds of nitrogen per 1,000 square feet. Done as one operation, the sequence is: **mow low, aerate, seed, lightly rake in, fertilize, water.** One weekend in early September does more for your lawn than everything you will do in April, May and June combined. ## The rest of the calendar For **tall fescue**: half a pound to a pound of slow-release nitrogen in early-to-mid April, the big feeding in September, and a moderate application in late October or November once temperatures drop below 50 degrees to push root growth. # DIY Lawn Care vs. Hiring a Pro in St. Louis: What the Science Says Revised July 27, 2026 Should I do my own lawn care in St. Louis? ⭐ MU Extension on spring seeding, verbatim: **“In some cases, complete failure should be expected.”** The real window is **Aug 25 – Oct 10**, Labor Day best. Rates: **7 lb** tall fescue per 1,000 sq ft in fall vs **10 lb** in spring (40% more seed, worse result). September is the most important fertilization: 1–1½ lb N per 1,000 sq ft. Best grass = turf-type tall fescue (90/10 with Kentucky bluegrass); zoysia is the warm-season option but goes straw-colored mid-fall to mid-spring; **bermuda is NOT recommended** in our transition zone. ⚠️ **Never add sand to clay** — MU says it sets up “bricklike” below 75% sand by volume; use compost, and topdressing only works combined with core aeration. ⚖️ You need NO license to treat your OWN lawn with general-use products, but applying pesticide on someone else’s land for money legally requires a **certified commercial applicator’s license** ($65/yr, Category 3). University of Missouri Extension has a sentence about seeding a lawn in spring that ought to be printed on every bag of grass seed sold in this state: **“In some cases, complete failure should be expected.”** That is a land-grant university telling you that the seed everyone buys in April is largely money in the trash. Timing, not effort and not equipment, is what separates a good St. Louis lawn from a bad one — and it’s also what decides whether you should be doing this yourself. ## Should I do my own lawn care in St. Louis? Mostly yes, with two exceptions. Missouri law lets you apply any general-use product to **your own** lawn with no license, and the highest-value task — seeding in the **August 25 to October 10 window** — requires timing rather than skill. Hire out **core aeration**, where renting the machine barely beats the roughly $107–$202 a service charges, and hire out anything on a *neighbor’s* property, because applying pesticide on someone else’s land for money legally requires a certified commercial applicator’s license. ## Why nothing quite works here St. Louis sits in what turf scientists call the **Transition Zone** — and MU Extension defines it exactly as bluntly as it deserves: an area “where neither warm- nor cool-season grass species are completely adapted.” There is no perfect grass for this city. There are only trade-offs, and picking one means choosing which season you’re willing to lose. **Cool-season grasses** grow best between 60 and 75 degrees — spring and fall — and struggle through a St. Louis August. **Warm-season grasses** want 80 to 95 degrees and go dormant in the cold. MU’s recommendation for Missouri lawns has been the same for decades: **turf-type tall fescue**, ideally as a mix of 90% tall fescue and 10% Kentucky bluegrass. It has a deep root system and handles heat and drought better than other cool-season options. It is green in April and green in November and it suffers in high summer. **Zoysia** is the other legitimate choice, adapted to the southern two-thirds of Missouri. It is genuinely tough — durable, weed-resistant, heat- and drought-tolerant, easy to mow. The price is that it goes **straw-colored from mid-fall to mid-spring**. Roughly half the year, your lawn is brown while your neighbor’s is green. Neither is wrong. But **bermudagrass is**, at least here — MU says flatly that it is “not recommended for lawns in Transition Zone,” and is best adapted to the southern third of the state. ## The St. Louis Homeowner Starter Toolkit (and Knowing Your Limits) Revised July 23, 2026 What tools does every St. Louis homeowner need? The essential starter kit for a St. Louis home: a claw hammer, a screwdriver set or multi-bit driver, a retractable tape measure, a level, pliers, an adjustable wrench, a utility knife, a stud finder, and one cordless drill/driver — plus a plunger, a small drain auger, and, for our common plaster-and-lath walls, proper toggle or molly wall anchors. Buy quality on the few tools you’ll use most, and leave electrical, gas, and structural work to a licensed pro. Keep reading ↓There’s a small, specific pride in fixing something yourself. The picture finally hung straight. The kitchen drawer that glides again. The wobbly chair made solid. You don’t need to be handy by nature — you just need a handful of the right tools and the confidence to start. Whether you just bought your first bungalow in south city or you’ve rented the same place in Overland for years, a basic toolkit turns “I should call someone” into “I’ll just do it.” Here’s the honest starter kit — what actually earns its place in a St. Louis home, a couple of things our older houses specifically demand, the first projects to cut your teeth on, and, just as importantly, where to put the tools down and call a pro. ## The starter kit at a glance The honest starter kit is short: a claw hammer, a screwdriver set (or a multi-bit driver), a retractable tape measure, a level, pliers, an adjustable wrench, a utility knife, and a stud finder — plus one cordless drill/driver. That handful covers the overwhelming majority of everyday household fixes. What St. Louis adds to the standard list is **proper wall anchors for plaster**, because so much of our housing stock has plaster-and-lath walls rather than drywall. Buy quality on the few tools you’ll use most, and add the rest as real projects call for them. ## The core hand tools every homeowner should own - **Claw hammer**— comfortable grip, solid head. The workhorse; a 16-ounce is the do-everything size. - **Screwdriver set**— a range of flathead and Phillips sizes, or a good multi-bit driver that stores the tips in the handle. - **Tape measure**— retractable, with a lock. “Measure twice” is real, and a 25-foot tape reaches across a room. - **Level**— so shelves and pictures are actually straight, not just close. A torpedo level fits a drawer; a longer one is better for shelving. - **Pliers**— needle-nose for fiddly work, standard for gripping, and a pair of channel-locks once you start on plumbing fixtures. - **Adjustable wrench**— for the nut the pliers keep slipping off. - **Utility knife**— with spare blades; a sharp blade is safer than a dull one you have to force. - **Stud finder**— cheap, and it saves you from anchoring a heavy shelf into thin air. Round it out with the small consumables that live in the same box: a tape measure’s useless without a pencil, and a starter assortment of screws, nails, and wall anchors, a roll of painter’s tape, and a tube of caulk will handle half the little jobs a house throws at you. None of it is expensive, and buying it once means you’re never stuck mid-project driving to the hardware store. ## The two power tools to add first You don’t need a garage full of machines. Start with a **cordless drill/driver** and a set of bits — it drills holes and drives screws and will earn its keep the first weekend. Look for one with two batteries so you’re never waiting on a charge. When your projects grow, a **circular or reciprocating saw** covers most cutting and light demolition. Add tools as real projects call for them, not before — a tool you bought for one job and never touch again is just clutter with a cord. When a project’s bigger than the toolbox, St Louis Near Me Directory is where you find the right person fast — browse local handymen and licensed trades across the metro, compare reviews, and reach out. Keeping the car in shape too? See our St. Louis car care guide. And if you’re the neighbor who’s *always* the one with the drill, that skill can be a side business. Listing it is how those neighbors find you on purpose — it takes only a few minutes. ## What a St. Louis old house specifically demands Here’s the local twist most tool lists miss. A huge share of our housing stock — the brick bungalows, two-families, and century homes — has **plaster-and-lath walls, not modern drywall.** Plaster is brittle and behaves differently: a standard drywall anchor can crack it, and screws don’t bite the same way. So stock **proper wall anchors** (toggle or molly bolts for heavy items), use that stud finder, and drill a pilot hole rather than muscling a screw in. Get that right and you’ll hang a heavy mirror on 1920s plaster with total confidence. Two more worth having in our climate: a **plunger and a basic drain auger** for the inevitable clog, and, if you’ve got the kind of basement a lot of St. Louis homes have, a **wet/dry shop vac** is a genuine hero after a heavy rain. Older homes here also tend to have quirks worth a few dollars of prevention — ...

## How to Choose an Interior Painter in St. Louis (Cost & Checklist) Revised July 13, 2026 What is the average cost to paint an interior room? Professional interior painting runs about $300 to $1,000 per room, with a national average around $624 for a standard 12×12 room (most land $400 to $950). By area, painters charge $2 to $6 per square foot for walls alone, or about $4.70 to $6.75 with ceilings and trim included. Tall ceilings, heavy prep, and premium paint push a room toward the high end. Keep reading ↓You’ve been staring at that room for a year. The color’s dated, there’s a scuff by the light switch you’ve stopped seeing, and every time you say “we should repaint” you picture the version that goes wrong — drips on the trim, crooked cut-in lines, tape that peels the paint right off with it. A good interior paint job is one of the highest-return, most satisfying things you can do to a home. A bad one you look at every single day. Whether your place is in Webster Groves, Florissant, or a loft downtown, choosing the right painter is the whole ballgame. This guide covers what interior painting actually costs in 2026 — by room and by whole house — whether the season matters, the one certification most St. Louis homeowners forget to ask about, and the checks that separate a pro who’ll make you happy from one who’ll make you repaint. ## What Is the Average Cost to Paint an Interior Room? For a direct answer: professional interior painting runs about **$300 to $1,000 per room**, with a national average around **$624 for a standard 12×12 room** — most 12×12 rooms land between **$400 and $950**. Priced by area, painters generally charge **$2 to $6 per square foot** for walls alone, or roughly **$4.70 to $6.75 per square foot** when ceilings and trim are included. What moves a room toward the high end: tall or vaulted ceilings, heavy prep (patching, sanding, priming bare or damaged walls), trim and doors, dark-to-light color changes needing extra coats, and premium paint. Remember that **labor is 70 to 85 percent** of the total — which is exactly why the prep and skill you’re paying for matter more than the paint on the shelf. ## How Much Does It Cost to Paint a Full House Interior? Painting a whole home’s interior ranges widely — roughly **$1,800 to $12,000** — because it depends entirely on square footage, how many rooms, ceiling height, and how much trim and prep are involved. For a typical **2,000-square-foot home**, most homeowners spend around **$4,200 to $9,500** for a full interior repaint including walls, ceilings, and trim. Doing the whole house at once usually earns a better per-room price than one room at a time, since the crew mobilizes, masks, and sets up only once. If you’re on a budget, a good painter can help you phase it — the main living areas now, bedrooms later — or focus on the walls and skip the ceilings where they’re still in good shape. ## How Much Does It Cost to Repaint a 3-Bedroom House? A three-bedroom home is right in that typical-house range. Depending on size and scope, repainting the interior of a three-bedroom house generally falls somewhere around **$4,000 to $9,500** for a full, professional walls-ceilings-and-trim job — less if you’re doing walls only or a lighter refresh, more for a large home with lots of trim, tall ceilings, or extensive prep. Individual bedrooms typically run **$350 to $850** each (a large primary bedroom can reach **$650 to $1,400**), while a small bathroom might be as little as **$150 to $350**. The single biggest cost lever is prep and condition — smooth, sound walls paint fast; cracked plaster and heavy patching add labor. ## Can I Paint My House in October? Yes — and for interior painting, fall is actually one of the *best* times. Because you’re painting inside, you control the temperature and humidity year-round, so you’re not at the mercy of the weather the way exterior painting is. October in St. Louis brings mild temperatures and lower humidity than our sticky summers, which helps paint dry and cure well, and you can crack windows for ventilation without the swampy air or deep freeze that summer and winter bring. It’s also often a slightly quieter season for painters than the spring-and-summer rush, which can mean better availability. The only real rule for any season is **ventilation and reasonable indoor temperatures** while painting and drying — conditions a good pro manages regardless of the month. ## EPA Lead-Safe Certification — Critical in St. Louis This is the check most homeowners don’t know to ask about, and it matters enormously here because so many of our homes are old. Under federal law, any paid firm disturbing paint in a home built **before 1978** must be an **EPA Lead-Safe Certified** firm and follow lead-safe work practices — because sanding or scraping old lead paint releases dust that’s genuinely dangerous, especially to kids and pregnant women. Given how much of St. Louis’s housing stock predates 1978, this is not a technicality. If your home is that old, **ask the painter directly whether they’re Lead-Safe Certified** and how they contain the dust. A real pro says yes and explains their process; anyone who waves the question off is a company to avoid. ...

## Dog Boarding and Daycare in St. Louis: Real Prices, and How to Check a Kennel Revised July 27, 2026 How much does dog boarding cost in St. Louis? Published St. Louis rates: standard boarding **$34–$60/night**, suites **$54.50–$86.50**, full-day daycare **$21–$48**. Cheapest published is **Muttropolitan** (5280 Fyler Ave) at $34/night, $21 daycare. Also publishing: Creve Coeur Animal Hospital ($40–$53.50 by weight), Silver Maple ($44–$54.50), WestInn ($45), The Watering Bowl ($53), Petropolis ($53–$73), Dogtopia Ellisville ($58), Sled & Breakfast ($60). ⭐ **Missouri LICENSES and INSPECTS boarding kennels** — unannounced, at least yearly — and reports are public, but there is NO searchable database: call (573) 751-3076. Rabies + DHPP + bordetella are near-universal; only Silver Maple REQUIRES canine influenza. ⚠️ North county has just 2 verified facilities and Jefferson County none. Missouri licenses and inspects dog boarding kennels. The inspections are **unannounced**, they happen at least once a year, and the reports are public records. Almost nobody knows this, because there is no website to search. You have to ask the state for the file. Every “best boarding in St. Louis” list ranks by star rating. None of them mention the inspection reports. Here’s how to actually check a kennel, what boarding really costs here based only on facilities that publish their rates, and the one vaccine question that separates them. ## How much does dog boarding cost in St. Louis? Based only on metro facilities that publish rates on their own websites, standard overnight boarding for one dog runs about **$34 to $60 a night**, with suites and luxury rooms from about **$54.50 to $86.50**. Full-day daycare runs about **$21 to $48**, dropping toward $17 a day with an unlimited membership. The cheapest published boarding we found is Muttropolitan at $34; the low end for daycare is also Muttropolitan at $21. Holiday surcharges are common, typically around $10 a night where they’re disclosed. ## The thing nobody tells you: the state inspects these Under Missouri’s Animal Care Facilities Act, a boarding kennel must hold a state license — a separate one for each physical location. Licenses run annually, and the law covers boarding operations regardless of what they call themselves. The Missouri Department of Agriculture states that routine inspections happen **at least once yearly**, that they are **unannounced**, and that they occur between 7am and 7pm on weekdays. Complaint-driven and follow-up inspections happen on top of that. Inspection reports, complaints and investigative reports are all obtainable — the Department says so plainly — through a Missouri Sunshine Law records request. **But there is no public database.** You cannot type a kennel’s name into a state website and see its record. You have to submit a records request, or call the Animal Care Facilities Program at **(573) 751-3076** or email **acfa@mda.mo.gov**. That friction is the whole reason this matters. The reports exist, they’re legally yours, and essentially nobody asks — so a facility’s inspection history plays no part in the reviews you read. The program has teeth, too. In 2025 the state **denied a license to St. Louis County’s own animal shelter** in Olivette after three failed inspections that documented undersized kennels, expired medications, and insects in food storage. That’s a county shelter rather than a private boarding kennel — different kind of facility, same licensing program — but it shows the inspections are real. ## One honest caveat about daycare We want to be precise here, because this is where other write-ups would overreach. Overnight boarding clearly requires a license. The Department’s own guidance frames the trigger as animals being cared for *overnight* away from the owner’s home for consideration. It also says training and grooming on their own are not regulated in Missouri — only if the animals stay overnight. What the guidance never addresses is a **daycare-only** facility where no dog stays the night. The underlying regulation is worded broadly enough that it might apply; the Department’s published FAQ doesn’t say. So we’re not going to tell you every dog daycare in St. Louis is inspected, because that isn’t established. If it matters to you, ask the Department directly about that specific facility. ## What the metro actually charges Ten facilities publish rates openly. # Dog Boarding and Daycare in St. Louis: Real Prices, and How to Check a Kennel Revised July 27, 2026 How much does dog boarding cost in St. Louis? Published St. Louis rates: standard boarding **$34–$60/night**, suites **$54.50–$86.50**, full-day daycare **$21–$48**. Cheapest published is **Muttropolitan** (5280 Fyler Ave) at $34/night, $21 daycare. Also publishing: Creve Coeur Animal Hospital ($40–$53.50 by weight), Silver Maple ($44–$54.50), WestInn ($45), The Watering Bowl ($53), Petropolis ($53–$73), Dogtopia Ellisville ($58), Sled & Breakfast ($60). ⭐ **Missouri LICENSES and INSPECTS boarding kennels** — unannounced, at least yearly — and reports are public, but there is NO searchable database: call (573) 751-3076. Rabies + DHPP + bordetella are near-universal; only Silver Maple REQUIRES canine influenza. ⚠️ North county has just 2 verified facilities and Jefferson County none. Missouri licenses and inspects dog boarding kennels. The inspections are **unannounced**, they happen at least once a year, and the reports are public records. Almost nobody knows this, because there is no website to search. You have to ask the state for the file. Every “best boarding in St. Louis” list ranks by star rating. None of them mention the inspection reports. Here’s how to actually check a kennel, what boarding really costs here based only on facilities that publish their rates, and the one vaccine question that separates them. ## How much does dog boarding cost in St. Louis? Based only on metro facilities that publish rates on their own websites, standard overnight boarding for one dog runs about **$34 to $60 a night**, with suites and luxury rooms from about **$54.50 to $86.50**. Full-day daycare runs about **$21 to $48**, dropping toward $17 a day with an unlimited membership. The cheapest published boarding we found is Muttropolitan at $34; the low end for daycare is also Muttropolitan at $21. Holiday surcharges are common, typically around $10 a night where they’re disclosed. ## The thing nobody tells you: the state inspects these Under Missouri’s Animal Care Facilities Act, a boarding kennel must hold a state license — a separate one for each physical location. Licenses run annually, and the law covers boarding operations regardless of what they call themselves. The Missouri Department of Agriculture states that routine inspections happen **at least once yearly**, that they are **unannounced**, and that they occur between 7am and 7pm on weekdays. Complaint-driven and follow-up inspections happen on top of that. Inspection reports, complaints and investigative reports are all obtainable — the Department says so plainly — through a Missouri Sunshine Law records request. **But there is no public database.** You cannot type a kennel’s name into a state website and see its record. You have to submit a records request, or call the Animal Care Facilities Program at **(573) 751-3076** or email **acfa@mda.mo.gov**. That friction is the whole reason this matters. The reports exist, they’re legally yours, and essentially nobody asks — so a facility’s inspection history plays no part in the reviews you read. The program has teeth, too. In 2025 the state **denied a license to St. Louis County’s own animal shelter** in Olivette after three failed inspections that documented undersized kennels, expired medications, and insects in food storage. That’s a county shelter rather than a private boarding kennel — different kind of facility, same licensing program — but it shows the inspections are real. ## One honest caveat about daycare We want to be precise here, because this is where other write-ups would overreach. Overnight boarding clearly requires a license. The Department’s own guidance frames the trigger as animals being cared for *overnight* away from the owner’s home for consideration. It also says training and grooming on their own are not regulated in Missouri — only if the animals stay overnight. What the guidance never addresses is a **daycare-only** facility where no dog stays the night. The underlying regulation is worded broadly enough that it might apply; the Department’s published FAQ doesn’t say. So we’re not going to tell you every dog daycare in St. Louis is inspected, because that isn’t established. If it matters to you, ask the Department directly about that specific facility. ## What the metro actually charges Ten facilities publish rates openly. That is genuinely useful, and it is also a decent proxy for how a business treats customers. **Muttropolitan**, 5280 Fyler Ave in south city — $34 a night, $62 for two dogs, $96 for three; daycare $21 full day, $16 half. The lowest published rates we found. **Creve Coeur Animal Hospital**, 12550 Olive Blvd — priced by weight, from $40 for a dog under 20 pounds up to $53.50 for one near 88 pounds, with suites to $71. Vet-attached boarding, which is worth considering for a senior dog or one on medication. **Silver Maple Pet Center**, 2014 N Ballas Rd in Des Peres — $44 small, $49.50 medium, $54.50 large, villas $78. **WestInn Kennels**, in Wentzville and Dardenne Prairie — $45 a night, with 10% off for three or more pets. **The Watering Bowl**, with locations in Brentwood, on Manchester in the city, and in St. Peters — $53 standard, $59.50 suite, plus $10 on holidays; daycare $37 full day, and multi-day packages down to $30 a day. **Petropolis**, in Chesterfield and St. Charles — $53 to $73 by room size, with daycare at $48 and a 30-day package at $1,258.20. **Dogtopia of Ellisville**, 15400 Manchester Rd — $58 a night if you’re on ...

## How to Choose a Roofing Contractor in St. Louis (Homeowner Guide) Revised July 23, 2026 How do you pick a good roofer? Hire a licensed, insured, established local roofer with strong verifiable reviews and a detailed written estimate — and never sign under pressure. The most important filter is local track record: a contractor with a real St. Louis address and years of history has a reputation to protect and will be around for future repairs. Verify credentials, compare a few detailed bids, and be wary of storm-chasers who demand cash up front. Keep reading ↓Imagine it’s the morning after one of those violent St. Louis storms — the kind that rolls through in spring with hail the size of marbles — and you spot a dark stain spreading across your bedroom ceiling. Your stomach drops. You need a roofer, fast, and within a day there’s a truck in your driveway and a stranger on your roof telling you it all needs to be replaced. How do you know if he’s honest, skilled, and going to be around next year if something goes wrong? Choosing a roofing contractor is one of the highest-stakes hiring decisions a homeowner makes — it’s expensive, it protects everything under it, and the St. Louis area is a magnet for out-of-town “storm chasers” after big weather. This guide walks through exactly how to pick a good roofer here: the signs of a reputable one, the questions to ask, the red flags that should send you running, and the best time to get the work done. ## How Do You Pick a Good Roofer in St. Louis? The short answer: hire a licensed, insured, established *local* roofer with strong reviews and a detailed written estimate — and never sign under pressure. The single most important filter is local track record. A contractor with a real St. Louis address, years of history here, and a trail of verifiable reviews has a reputation to protect and will still be around if a repair is needed years down the line. A crew that showed up from three states away after a hailstorm has neither. Beyond that, it comes down to verifying credentials, comparing a few detailed bids, and trusting your gut if something feels off. The rest of this guide is how to do each of those well. ## Signs a Roofer Is Reputable A trustworthy roofing contractor checks a consistent set of boxes. They’re **properly licensed and insured** — both liability and workers’ compensation — and will hand you proof without hesitation (if a worker is hurt on your property and the roofer isn’t insured, you can be on the hook). They’re **established and local**, with a physical St. Louis-area address and a real history, not a magnetic sign and an out-of-state plate. They have a **solid, verifiable reputation** — recent reviews, references you can actually call, and a rating that holds up across sources. They provide a **detailed written estimate** that spells out materials, scope, timeline, and cost, rather than a number scribbled on a business card. They offer a clear **warranty** on both materials and workmanship. And they communicate professionally from the first contact. When a roofer hits all of these, you’re almost certainly in good hands. ## What Questions Should You Ask a Roofing Contractor? Before you sign anything, get clear answers to these. *Are you licensed and insured, and can I see proof?* *How long have you been in business in the St. Louis area, and do you have a local address?* *Can you provide recent local references?* *Is this estimate detailed and in writing, with materials and scope spelled out?* *What warranty do you offer on materials and on your workmanship?* *Who exactly will do the work — your own crew or subcontractors?* *How will you protect my property and handle cleanup?* And, if it’s storm damage, *how do you handle the insurance claim process?* A reputable roofer answers all of these calmly and clearly. Hesitation, vague answers, or irritation at being asked are themselves useful information. ## Red Flags: What to Watch Out For With Roofers Certain behaviors should end the conversation. Be very wary of the **door-knocking storm chaser** who appears right after bad weather, pressures you to sign immediately, and can’t point to a local address or history. Run from anyone who **demands large payment up front** or wants cash before any work is done — a reasonable deposit is normal, but paying in full before the job is not. Watch for **no written contract**, a **bid dramatically lower than everyone else’s** (often a sign of cut corners or a coming bait-and-switch), **no verifiable license or insurance**, high-pressure “today only” deadlines, and offers to **“waive your deductible”** on an insurance job, which is insurance fraud you don’t want to be party to. St. Louis’s heavy storm season makes it prime territory for these operators, so slow down and verify — a real roof is worth a few days of due diligence. ## When Is the Cheapest — and Best — Time for a New Roof? Timing can save you money and hassle. Roofers are busiest right after storm season and in the peak of summer and early fall, so demand — and often pricing — runs highest then. The quieter stretches, typically **late winter and early spring** before the storm rush, can mean better availability and more competitive bids, ...

## How to Find a Good Handyman in St. Louis (Homeowner Guide) Revised July 22, 2026 What is the best way to find a good handyman? Find a good handyman by combining reputation with verification: start with a referral or a well-reviewed local pro, then confirm with recent reviews, references, and a clear talk about your jobs. Because a handyman works in your home with little oversight, reliability and trustworthiness matter as much as skill. Bundle several small jobs into one visit to lower the per-task cost, and favor someone who knows when a job needs a licensed specialist. Keep reading ↓Every home has a running list of them: the leaky faucet, the door that won’t latch, the ceiling fan still in its box, the fence board that’s been loose since spring. Individually they’re small; together they’re the low hum of a to-do list that never ends — and none of them is big enough to justify calling a specialized contractor. What you need is a good handyman: a skilled, reliable jack-of-all-trades who can knock out a dozen small jobs in an afternoon and actually show up when they say they will. The catch is that “handyman” covers everyone from a true craftsman to a guy with a truck and a Facebook post, and telling them apart before you hand over your list (and your key) isn’t easy. This guide walks through how to find a good handyman in St. Louis: the best way to find one, what they typically charge, the red flags to avoid, what they can and can’t legally do, and how to hire someone you’ll want to call again. ## What Is the Best Way to Find a Good Handyman? The best handyman is usually found through a combination of **reputation and verification**: strong reviews or a personal referral, confirmed by a quick check of their work and reliability. Start with recommendations — a neighbor’s trusted handyman or a well-reviewed local pro is worth far more than a random ad — then verify with recent reviews, references, and a clear conversation about your specific jobs. The qualities that separate a great handyman from a frustrating one are consistency and communication as much as skill: someone who returns calls, shows up on time, quotes fairly, and does tidy work you don’t have to redo. Because a handyman often works inside your home with little oversight, trustworthiness matters enormously, so favor established local people with a track record over the cheapest unknown quote. ## What Do Most Handymen Charge? Handyman pricing varies by region, experience, and the job, so focus on understanding *how* they charge rather than hunting one magic rate. Many handymen bill **by the hour**, often with a minimum (a first hour or a service-call fee) since small jobs still require showing up and setup. Others quote a **flat rate per job** for well-defined tasks. A more experienced handyman may charge a higher hourly rate but work faster and better, which is often the better deal. The smart approach: describe your full list up front and get an estimate, because bundling several small jobs into one visit almost always lowers the per-task cost versus calling multiple times. Ask what’s included, whether materials are separate, and whether there’s a minimum — then compare a couple of quotes on value, not just the lowest hourly figure. ## What Is the Most Requested Handyman Service? Handymen handle an enormous range of small jobs, and a few come up constantly. The most-requested tend to be the everyday fixes and installs most homeowners can’t or don’t want to do themselves: **minor plumbing** (leaky faucets, running toilets, new fixtures), **drywall repair and painting** (patching holes, touch-ups), **furniture and fixture assembly and mounting** (TVs, shelves, ceiling fans, blinds), **door and window fixes** (sticking doors, broken latches, weatherstripping), **general carpentry** (trim, decking boards, small repairs), and a long tail of odd jobs from caulking to gutter cleaning to hanging pictures. A good handyman is essentially a one-stop solution for the pile of small tasks that don’t each warrant a specialist — which is exactly why having a reliable one on speed dial is such a relief. When you call, share the whole list; you’ll often be surprised how much they can knock out in a single visit, and how much cheaper it is than tackling each job separately. ## What Are Red Flags When Hiring a Handyman? Because the field is unregulated compared to licensed trades, vetting matters. Watch for a handyman who **demands full payment upfront** (a reasonable deposit for materials is fine; paying in full before work is done is not), has **no reviews or references** you can check, **won’t put the scope or price in writing**, gives a quote **far below everyone else**, is **vague about their experience** with your type of job, or has poor communication from the start (missed calls, no-shows for the estimate — it only gets worse once you’ve paid). Another important one: a handyman who’s willing to take on **work that legally requires a licensed pro** — major electrical, gas, or structural work — is a red flag, because a good handyman knows the limits of what they should do and refers you out when a job needs a licensed electrician or plumber. Reliability and honesty about scope are the real tells. ## What a Handyman Can — and Can’t — Legally Do This is worth ...

## How to Choose a Landscaping Company in St. Louis (Guide) Revised July 12, 2026 How do you pick a good landscaper? First match the type of company to your project — maintenance, design/install, or hardscape are different skill sets. Then vet for a real portfolio, strong local reviews, appropriate licensing and insurance, a clear written estimate, and knowledge of plants that thrive in St. Louis’s clay soil and climate. A great landscaper listens, gives honest guidance about your space and budget, and designs for how it will look years from now. Keep reading ↓You look out at the yard and picture what it could be — a real patio for summer evenings, beds that actually bloom, a lawn that isn’t half weeds, maybe a retaining wall to tame that awkward slope. Or maybe you’re just tired of fighting the mowing and mulching every weekend and want someone reliable to keep it looking sharp. Either way, the right landscaper can transform both how your St. Louis home looks and how much you enjoy being outside — and the wrong one can waste a lot of money on plants that die and work that doesn’t last. “Landscaping” spans everything from weekly mowing to full design-and-build projects, and the companies range from a teenager with a mower to full-service design firms. Knowing how to choose the right one for your project is what separates a yard you love from an expensive disappointment. This guide covers how to pick a good landscaper in St. Louis: what it costs, the common mistakes to avoid, the elements of good design, the red flags, and how to find a pro near you. ## How Do You Pick a Good Landscaper? Start by matching the *type* of company to your project, then vet for quality. A weekly **lawn-maintenance** service, a **landscape designer/installer** for new beds and plantings, and a **hardscape** specialist for patios, walls, and walkways are different skill sets — so first get clear on whether you need ongoing maintenance, a design-and-install project, or hardscaping. From there, the markers of a good landscaper are consistent: a **portfolio** of real past work you can look at, **strong local reviews and references**, appropriate **licensing and insurance** (especially for bigger installs and hardscape), a **clear written estimate and plan**, and knowledge of **plants that actually thrive in the St. Louis climate**. A great landscaper listens to what you want, offers honest guidance about what will work in your space and budget, and puts it in writing — rather than just quoting a number and disappearing. ## What Does a Landscaper Cost? Landscaping costs vary enormously by the service, so think in terms of the type of work rather than one hourly rate. **Routine maintenance** (mowing, trimming, cleanup) is typically priced per visit or as a seasonal contract and is the most affordable tier. **Design and installation** (new beds, plantings, sod) is a bigger, project-based investment that depends on scope and materials. **Hardscaping** (patios, retaining walls, walkways) is the most expensive because of materials and labor-intensive work. For hourly work, rates vary by region and the crew’s expertise, and a more experienced designer or crew costs more but often delivers results that last far longer. The reliable approach: define your project clearly, get two or three detailed estimates for the same scope, and understand exactly what’s included — materials, labor, cleanup, and any guarantee on plantings — so you’re comparing apples to apples rather than chasing the lowest bid. ## What Are Common Landscaping Mistakes to Avoid? Knowing the pitfalls helps you (and your landscaper) avoid wasting money. The classics: **choosing the wrong plants for the spot** — sun-lovers in shade, or thirsty plants in dry areas — which leads to a slow, expensive die-off; **ignoring how big plants get**, so they crowd the house or each other in a few years; **poor drainage and grading**, a real issue on St. Louis’s clay soil, which can send water toward your foundation; **planting without a plan**, resulting in a patchwork that never looks cohesive; **neglecting soil prep**, since even great plants struggle in poor soil; and **overlooking maintenance needs** — designing something beautiful that you have no time to keep up. A good landscaper steers you away from all of these, recommending plants suited to your specific light, soil, and climate, and designing for how the space will look and function years from now, not just on planting day. ## What Are the Basic Elements of Good Landscape Design? Understanding a few design fundamentals helps you talk to a landscaper and judge their work. Classic landscape design balances several elements: **unity** (a cohesive look, so the yard feels intentional rather than random), **balance and proportion** (sizing plants and features to the space and the house), **color** (thoughtful combinations, and often year-round interest rather than one big spring show), **line and form** (the shapes of beds, paths, and plantings that guide the eye), and **focal points** (a feature tree, a water element, a patio that anchors the design). A related idea landscapers often use is the “rule of three” — grouping plants in odd numbers like threes for a more natural, pleasing look. You don’t need to master this yourself; the point is that a skilled landscaper is thinking about these principles, and a good design feels harmonious and purposeful rather than a scattered collection of plants thrown into the ground. ## ...

# How to Choose a Landscaping Company in St. Louis (Guide) Revised July 12, 2026 How do you pick a good landscaper? First match the type of company to your project — maintenance, design/install, or hardscape are different skill sets. Then vet for a real portfolio, strong local reviews, appropriate licensing and insurance, a clear written estimate, and knowledge of plants that thrive in St. Louis’s clay soil and climate. A great landscaper listens, gives honest guidance about your space and budget, and designs for how it will look years from now. Keep reading ↓You look out at the yard and picture what it could be — a real patio for summer evenings, beds that actually bloom, a lawn that isn’t half weeds, maybe a retaining wall to tame that awkward slope. Or maybe you’re just tired of fighting the mowing and mulching every weekend and want someone reliable to keep it looking sharp. Either way, the right landscaper can transform both how your St. Louis home looks and how much you enjoy being outside — and the wrong one can waste a lot of money on plants that die and work that doesn’t last. “Landscaping” spans everything from weekly mowing to full design-and-build projects, and the companies range from a teenager with a mower to full-service design firms. Knowing how to choose the right one for your project is what separates a yard you love from an expensive disappointment. This guide covers how to pick a good landscaper in St. Louis: what it costs, the common mistakes to avoid, the elements of good design, the red flags, and how to find a pro near you. ## How Do You Pick a Good Landscaper? Start by matching the *type* of company to your project, then vet for quality. A weekly **lawn-maintenance** service, a **landscape designer/installer** for new beds and plantings, and a **hardscape** specialist for patios, walls, and walkways are different skill sets — so first get clear on whether you need ongoing maintenance, a design-and-install project, or hardscaping. From there, the markers of a good landscaper are consistent: a **portfolio** of real past work you can look at, **strong local reviews and references**, appropriate **licensing and insurance** (especially for bigger installs and hardscape), a **clear written estimate and plan**, and knowledge of **plants that actually thrive in the St. Louis climate**. A great landscaper listens to what you want, offers honest guidance about what will work in your space and budget, and puts it in writing — rather than just quoting a number and disappearing. ## What Does a Landscaper Cost? Landscaping costs vary enormously by the service, so think in terms of the type of work rather than one hourly rate. **Routine maintenance** (mowing, trimming, cleanup) is typically priced per visit or as a seasonal contract and is the most affordable tier. **Design and installation** (new beds, plantings, sod) is a bigger, project-based investment that depends on scope and materials. **Hardscaping** (patios, retaining walls, walkways) is the most expensive because of materials and labor-intensive work. For hourly work, rates vary by region and the crew’s expertise, and a more experienced designer or crew costs more but often delivers results that last far longer. The reliable approach: define your project clearly, get two or three detailed estimates for the same scope, and understand exactly what’s included — materials, labor, cleanup, and any guarantee on plantings — so you’re comparing apples to apples rather than chasing the lowest bid. ## What Are Common Landscaping Mistakes to Avoid? Knowing the pitfalls helps you (and your landscaper) avoid wasting money. The classics: **choosing the wrong plants for the spot** — sun-lovers in shade, or thirsty plants in dry areas — which leads to a slow, expensive die-off; **ignoring how big plants get**, so they crowd the house or each other in a few years; **poor drainage and grading**, a real issue on St. Louis’s clay soil, which can send water toward your foundation; **planting without a plan**, resulting in a patchwork that never looks cohesive; **neglecting soil prep**, since even great plants struggle in poor soil; and **overlooking maintenance needs** — designing something beautiful that you have no time to keep up. A good landscaper steers you away from all of these, recommending plants suited to your specific light, soil, and climate, and designing for how the space will look and function years from now, not just on planting day. ## What Are the Basic Elements of Good Landscape Design? Understanding a few design fundamentals helps you talk to a landscaper and judge their work. Classic landscape design balances several elements: **unity** (a cohesive look, so the yard feels intentional rather than random), **balance and proportion** (sizing plants and features to the space and the house), **color** (thoughtful combinations, and often year-round interest rather than one big spring show), **line and form** (the shapes of beds, paths, and plantings that guide the eye), and **focal points** (a feature tree, a water element, a patio that anchors the design). A related idea landscapers often use is the “rule of three” — grouping plants in odd numbers like threes for a more natural, pleasing look. You don’t need to master this yourself; the point is that a skilled landscaper is thinking about these principles, and a good design feels harmonious and purposeful rather than a scattered collection of plants thrown into the ground. ## ...

## How to Choose a Carpet Cleaner in St. Louis (Homeowner Guide) Revised July 28, 2026 How do you choose a good carpet cleaner? Hire an experienced, well-reviewed, insured carpet cleaner who gives an honest, upfront price and uses the right method for your carpet — and be skeptical of suspiciously cheap ads. The biggest tell of a good one is transparent pricing based on your actual space, with no surprise add-ons once they’re inside. Hot water extraction (steam) deep-cleans best for most homes; look for strong reviews, a real business history, and a guarantee. Keep reading ↓You’ve been staring at it for weeks: the traffic path worn gray down the hallway, the mystery stain by the couch, the faint pet smell that no amount of vacuuming touches. Carpet takes a beating — especially in a busy St. Louis home with kids, pets, and muddy shoes tracking in the seasons — and every so often it needs a real professional cleaning that a rented machine just can’t match. So you start searching, and immediately hit a wall of “$29 whole-house special!” ads that sound too good to be true (because they usually are). Choosing a good carpet cleaner is trickier than it looks: the industry is full of bargain-bait pricing, and the difference between a quality job and a cheap one shows up in whether your carpets actually come clean, dry properly, and stay fresh. This guide walks through how to choose a carpet cleaner in St. Louis: the cleaning methods and which to pick, what it really costs, how often to clean, the classic bait-and-switch to avoid, and how to find a trustworthy pro near you. ## How Do You Choose a Good Carpet Cleaner? The essentials: hire an **experienced, well-reviewed, insured** carpet cleaner who gives you an **honest, upfront price** and uses the right method for your carpet — and treat suspiciously-cheap ads with real skepticism. The single biggest tell of a good carpet cleaner is transparent pricing: a reputable company quotes based on the actual square footage and condition, explains what’s included, and doesn’t bait you with a rock-bottom number and then pile on charges once they’re in your home. Beyond that, look for strong local reviews, a company that’s been around, insurance (in case something’s damaged), and clear answers about their process, drying time, and any guarantee. A good carpet cleaner also tailors the approach to your carpet type and problem — heavy stains and pet odor need more than a quick surface pass. ## Steam Cleaning vs. Dry Cleaning: Which Method? Understanding the two main methods helps you ask the right questions. **Hot water extraction** — commonly called steam cleaning — sprays hot water and cleaning solution deep into the carpet and immediately extracts it along with the dirt. It’s the method most manufacturers recommend and the most thorough for deep cleaning and lifting stubborn dirt and allergens; the tradeoff is longer drying time (often several hours). **Low-moisture or “dry” cleaning** uses much less water with specialized compounds or pads, so carpets dry fast — convenient for quick turnarounds or moisture-sensitive situations — but it’s generally less deep than hot water extraction. For most homes wanting a genuine deep clean, hot water extraction is the go-to; low-moisture shines when speed matters. A good cleaner will recommend the right method for your carpet and situation rather than pushing a one-size-fits-all process, and will be able to explain why. ## What Does Carpet Cleaning Cost? Costs depend on the square footage, the number of rooms, the carpet’s condition, and any add-ons like heavy stain treatment, pet-odor removal, or protectant, so ignore the flashy flat-rate ads and get a real quote. Reputable cleaners typically price by the room or by the square foot, and will give you an honest estimate up front — often after asking about your space or seeing it. The classic warning sign is the **absurdly low advertised price** that exists only to get a technician in your door, after which the “real” price for anything beyond a token surface pass appears. As with any home service, get two or three clear quotes for the same scope, ask exactly what’s included (pre-treatment, spot treatment, moving furniture, drying), and choose on value and trust rather than the lowest headline number. A fair, honest price for quality work beats a bait price every single time. ## How Often Should You Have Carpets Cleaned? A good rule of thumb is a professional cleaning about **once a year** for most homes, and more often — every six months or so — for households with **pets, kids, allergies, or heavy foot traffic**. Regular professional cleaning does more than freshen the look: it removes the deep-set dirt, allergens, and dust mites that regular vacuuming can’t reach, which matters for indoor air quality, and it genuinely extends the life of your carpet by preventing abrasive grit from wearing down the fibers. Many carpet warranties even require periodic professional cleaning to stay valid, so it can protect your investment in more ways than one. Between professional visits, vacuum regularly and treat spills quickly — the faster a spill is addressed, the less likely it becomes a permanent stain. Think of professional cleaning as maintenance that pays for itself in longer-lasting, healthier carpet. ## Red Flags: The Bait-and-Switch and Other Warning Signs The carpet-cleaning industry has a well-known bad-actor problem, so vet carefully. ## How to Choose a Pest Control Company in St. Louis (Guide) Revised July 13, 2026 What should I look for when choosing a pest control company? Choose a licensed and insured pest control company with experience treating your specific pest, a strong local reputation, a clear written plan, transparency about the products they use and how they protect kids and pets, and a guarantee. Favor companies that emphasize prevention and sealing entry points — not just spraying. In termite-prone, humid St. Louis, a knowledgeable local pro (and a termite specialist when needed) makes a real difference. Keep reading ↓It usually starts small. A trail of ants marching across the kitchen counter. A mouse dropping behind the pantry. A wasp nest going up under the eaves, or — the one that makes every St. Louis homeowner shudder — the first sign of termites in a region where they thrive. Whatever the pest, the reaction is the same: you want it gone, safely, and you want to be sure it stays gone. So you start searching for a pest control company, and immediately face a flood of options all promising to solve your problem. Choosing the right one matters more than most people think — the difference between a good exterminator and a bad one is the difference between a solved problem and a recurring nightmare (plus chemicals sprayed around your family and pets). This guide walks through how to choose a pest control company in St. Louis: what to look for, the types of pest control, which pests are genuinely hard to beat, the red flags to avoid, and how to find a trustworthy local pro. ## What Should You Look for When Choosing a Pest Control Company? The essentials come down to a short, non-negotiable list. Look for a company that’s **licensed and insured** — pest control involves regulated chemicals, and a licensed operator is trained to apply them safely and legally (ask to see proof). Look for **experience with your specific pest**, since treating termites, bed bugs, and mice each require different expertise. Check for a **strong local reputation** in recent reviews and references. Insist on a **clear plan and written estimate** that explains what they’ll treat, how, what it costs, and what happens if the pests come back. Ask about their approach to **safety** — the products they use and how they protect children and pets. And favor a company that offers a **guarantee or warranty** and stands behind its work. A pest company that checks these boxes will solve the problem rather than just spraying and leaving. ## What Are the Types of Pest Control? Knowing the main approaches helps you understand what a good company is actually offering. The broad categories: **chemical control** (the pesticides and baits most people picture); **biological control** (using natural predators or organisms to manage pests, more common in gardens and agriculture); **physical or mechanical control** (traps, barriers, exclusion — sealing the gaps pests use to get in); and **cultural or preventive control** (removing the food, water, and shelter that attract pests in the first place). The best modern pest companies practice **Integrated Pest Management (IPM)**, which combines these thoughtfully — identifying the pest, using the least-toxic effective method, sealing entry points, and preventing recurrence — rather than defaulting to blasting everything with chemicals. When a company talks about prevention and exclusion, not just spraying, that’s a good sign you’ve found a real professional. ## What Is the Hardest Pest to Get Rid Of? Some pests are simply tougher, and knowing which ones sets your expectations. **Bed bugs** are notoriously difficult — they hide in tiny cracks, resist many treatments, and usually require specialized, repeated effort. **Termites** are both hard to eliminate and genuinely destructive, which is why they demand a specialist and why prevention matters so much in the St. Louis area. **Cockroaches**, especially German cockroaches, breed fast and develop resistance, making full eradication a persistent job. And **rodents** can keep returning if the entry points aren’t sealed. The lesson: for these tough pests especially, a cheap one-time spray rarely works — you want a company with specific expertise, a thorough plan, and a willingness to follow up. If a company promises to wipe out bed bugs or termites in a single quick visit for a bargain price, be skeptical. ## What Are the 3 C’s of Pest Control? A useful way to think about effective pest control is the “three C’s”: **Control** (dealing with the active infestation you have now), **Correction** (fixing the underlying conditions — the gaps, moisture, and food sources — that let the pests in), and **Continuity** (ongoing monitoring and prevention so they don’t come back). A good pest company works all three, not just the first. Anyone can spray to knock down what you can see; the professionals also find how the pests got in and make it harder for the next wave. When you’re evaluating companies, ask not just how they’ll kill the current pests, but how they’ll keep them out — the ones with a real answer to that are the ones worth hiring. ## Red Flags When Hiring a Pest Control Company Watch for warning signs before you let anyone spray around your home. Be wary of a company that’s **not licensed or insured** or won’t show proof; one that **pressures you to sign a long contract** on the spot; a **price ...

## How to Find a Plumber in St. Louis You Can Actually Trust (Cost Guide) Revised July 13, 2026 How much do plumbers charge per hour in St. Louis? St. Louis plumbers generally charge about $75 to $140 per hour for standard service and roughly $135 to $275 for emergency or after-hours calls; a master plumber runs about $80 to $200 an hour. Local pricing tends to sit a bit below national averages. Many plumbers price bigger jobs as a flat rate instead of hourly — either way, get the number in writing before work starts. Keep reading ↓Picture it: you pad into the basement in your socks one January morning and step into cold water. Somewhere behind the wall, a pipe let go overnight. Or maybe it’s subtler — a faint sewage smell in the laundry room, a toilet that gurgles every time the washing machine drains, a water bill that jumped for no reason you can see. Maybe you’ve lived it, whether it was your parents’ place in Kirkwood, a rental you manage in Florissant, or your own house out in St. Charles. Plumbing trouble has a way of turning calm people into panicked, 2 a.m. Googlers. The water is spreading, you’re not sure where the shutoff is, and the first name that pops up is quoting a number that feels invented. Two questions actually matter in that moment: *is this an emergency — and who do I call who’ll fix it right without gouging me?* This is a plain-English guide to answering both, with the St. Louis-specific details generic advice tends to skip — including what plumbers really charge here. ## How Much Do Plumbers Charge Per Hour in St. Louis? For a straight answer: plumbers in the St. Louis area generally charge about **$75 to $140 per hour** for standard service, rising to roughly **$135 to $275 per hour for emergency or after-hours calls**. A **master plumber** typically runs **$80 to $200 an hour** depending on the job’s complexity. The good news is that St. Louis pricing tends to sit a bit *below* national averages thanks to our lower cost of living and a competitive local market. That said, many plumbers price bigger jobs as a **flat rate** rather than hourly — a set price for, say, a water-heater swap or a toilet replacement — which protects you from a slow clock. What matters most isn’t the raw rate but getting the number **in writing before work starts**. ## What Is the Average Call-Out Charge for a Plumber? Most plumbers charge a **service-call (or “call-out”) fee** just to come diagnose the problem — in St. Louis that typically runs **$65 to $300**, and it often *covers the first hour* of work rather than being a pure trip charge. Many companies will also credit that fee toward the repair if you approve the work on the spot. For a genuine after-hours emergency, expect to pay more — the average emergency plumber visit here lands around **$162**, with the range depending on the hour and severity. When you call, ask two things directly: *what’s the service-call fee, and is it applied to the repair if I move forward?* A straight answer is itself a good sign. ## What Are the Three Types of Plumbers? Knowing who does what helps you hire the right person. Broadly, plumbers specialize in three areas: **residential** plumbers handle homes — the leaks, clogs, fixtures, water heaters, and repipes most homeowners need; **commercial** plumbers work on businesses and larger buildings with bigger, more complex systems; and **service-and-repair** plumbers focus on diagnosing and fixing problems (versus new-construction plumbers who install systems in buildings going up). For your house, you want a residential service-and-repair plumber. You’ll also hear skill *levels* — apprentice, journeyman, and master — which describe training and licensing rather than specialty. Matching both the specialty and an appropriate skill level to your job is half of hiring well. ## What Is the Highest Level of a Plumber? The highest level is a **master plumber**. It’s a real, earned credential — not a business-card title. In St. Louis County, a master plumber licensed through the **Board of Plumber & Drainlayer Examiners** has to document at least two years of experience as a licensed journeyman and pass a master exam. A master plumber can pull permits, design systems, and oversee other plumbers. Below that, a **journeyman** is fully qualified to do most plumbing work independently, and an **apprentice** is still training under supervision. For a complex job — a repipe, a sewer line, anything touching gas — you want a master plumber or a company that employs one; for a routine fixture repair, a good journeyman is perfectly appropriate. ## What “Licensed Plumber” Actually Means in St. Louis Here’s a local wrinkle that matters: Missouri has **no statewide plumbing license**. There’s no single “Missouri plumber’s license” good everywhere — it’s handled locally. **St. Louis City and St. Louis County each license plumbers separately**, and a legitimate plumber holds the license for the jurisdiction they’re working in. Bigger jobs — a water-heater swap, a repipe, sewer work, anything touching a gas line — require a **permit and an inspection**, which is really a free second set of expert eyes confirming the work is safe. So “licensed and insured” isn’t filler here; it’s a checkable bar. Ask which **City or County license** they hold and confirm they ...

The good news is that St. Louis pricing tends to sit a bit *below* national averages thanks to our lower cost of living and a competitive local market. That said, many plumbers price bigger jobs as a **flat rate** rather than hourly — a set price for, say, a water-heater swap or a toilet replacement — which protects you from a slow clock. What matters most isn’t the raw rate but getting the number **in writing before work starts**. ## What Is the Average Call-Out Charge for a Plumber? Most plumbers charge a **service-call (or “call-out”) fee** just to come diagnose the problem — in St. Louis that typically runs **$65 to $300**, and it often *covers the first hour* of work rather than being a pure trip charge. Many companies will also credit that fee toward the repair if you approve the work on the spot. For a genuine after-hours emergency, expect to pay more — the average emergency plumber visit here lands around **$162**, with the range depending on the hour and severity. When you call, ask two things directly: *what’s the service-call fee, and is it applied to the repair if I move forward?* A straight answer is itself a good sign. ## What Are the Three Types of Plumbers? Knowing who does what helps you hire the right person. Broadly, plumbers specialize in three areas: **residential** plumbers handle homes — the leaks, clogs, fixtures, water heaters, and repipes most homeowners need; **commercial** plumbers work on businesses and larger buildings with bigger, more complex systems; and **service-and-repair** plumbers focus on diagnosing and fixing problems (versus new-construction plumbers who install systems in buildings going up). For your house, you want a residential service-and-repair plumber. You’ll also hear skill *levels* — apprentice, journeyman, and master — which describe training and licensing rather than specialty. Matching both the specialty and an appropriate skill level to your job is half of hiring well. ## What Is the Highest Level of a Plumber? The highest level is a **master plumber**. It’s a real, earned credential — not a business-card title. In St. Louis County, a master plumber licensed through the **Board of Plumber & Drainlayer Examiners** has to document at least two years of experience as a licensed journeyman and pass a master exam. A master plumber can pull permits, design systems, and oversee other plumbers. Below that, a **journeyman** is fully qualified to do most plumbing work independently, and an **apprentice** is still training under supervision. For a complex job — a repipe, a sewer line, anything touching gas — you want a master plumber or a company that employs one; for a routine fixture repair, a good journeyman is perfectly appropriate. ## What “Licensed Plumber” Actually Means in St. Louis Here’s a local wrinkle that matters: Missouri has **no statewide plumbing license**. There’s no single “Missouri plumber’s license” good everywhere — it’s handled locally. **St. Louis City and St. Louis County each license plumbers separately**, and a legitimate plumber holds the license for the jurisdiction they’re working in. Bigger jobs — a water-heater swap, a repipe, sewer work, anything touching a gas line — require a **permit and an inspection**, which is really a free second set of expert eyes confirming the work is safe. So “licensed and insured” isn’t filler here; it’s a checkable bar. Ask which **City or County license** they hold and confirm they ...

## St. Louis: Where Flavor Tells a Story Revised July 24, 2026 What is St. Louis food culture known for? St. Louis food culture is a story of immigrant kitchens and longtime institutions: farm-to-table Vicia, James Beard-winning Balkan Treat Box (Bosnian), Ethiopian Meskerem, Korean-Mexican Seoul Taco, Italian Zia’s on The Hill, plus century-old Crown Candy Kitchen, pioneering Vietnamese Mai Lee, Pappy’s barbecue, and Nick Bognar’s Indo. Neighborhoods each tell a culinary story — South Grand, The Hill, Cherokee Street, and the Bevo Mill “Little Bosnia” — so you can take a world tour of flavors without leaving the city. Keep reading ↓Beyond its iconic Gateway Arch, St. Louis boasts a thriving restaurant scene that hums with the city’s dynamism. Forget generic chain fare. Here, restaurants are lively social spaces where stories are woven into every dish. From trendy cafes with meticulously brewed coffee to innovative fine-dining establishments crafting seasonal masterpieces, St. Louis’s culinary landscape is a testament to the city’s rich history and ever-evolving spirit. ## Culinary Renaissance in St. Louis In recent years, St. Louis has undergone a culinary renaissance, shedding its past image as a meat-and-potatoes town. A wave of passionate chefs and restaurateurs has opened their doors, introducing a diverse array of cuisines that tantalize the taste buds. Farm-to-table havens like Vicia, with its commitment to farm-fresh bounty and ever-changing seasonal menus, have become culinary darlings. Here, diners can witness the city’s agricultural bounty transformed into plates bursting with freshness and flavor. But the culinary journey doesn’t stop there. Balkan Treat Box in Webster Groves transports you to Eastern Europe with its cevapčići (grilled sausages) and pide (boat-shaped flatbreads), each bite a testament to the city’s vibrant immigrant heritage — and chef Loryn Nalić’s cooking there earned her the 2026 James Beard Award for Best Chef: Midwest. This explosion of flavors reflects a growing appreciation for quality, locally-sourced ingredients and innovative techniques. St. Louis chefs are no longer afraid to experiment, pushing boundaries and creating dishes that are as unique as the city itself. The city’s commitment to fostering a robust culinary ecosystem is evident in the numerous incubators and community kitchens that support emerging talent. These spaces provide not only the physical resources but also mentorship and networking opportunities, ensuring a continuous influx of fresh ideas and culinary innovation. This dedication to nurturing talent is a key driver behind the city’s dynamic food scene, making it a place where both established chefs and aspiring culinary artists can thrive and contribute to its ever-growing reputation. ## Experience Global Cuisine on Your Plate In St. Louis St. Louis’s immigrant heritage is another vital thread woven into its rich culinary tapestry. Take a walk down Cherokee Street, a true melting pot of Latino shops, taquerias, and artists, and you can eat and drink your way around the world within a few blocks. Head south to the Bevo Mill area — St. Louis’s “Little Bosnia,” home to one of the largest Bosnian communities outside Bosnia — and sip strong, thick Bosnian coffee at Berix Coffeehouse on Lemay Ferry Road, or settle in for ćevapi at Lemmons by Grbic, where a Bosnian refugee family reinvented an old Gravois dive into a beloved neighborhood restaurant. Or venture deeper into the city to savor the delectable Ethiopian delights at Meskerem Restaurant, where fragrant stews and injera flatbread create a flavorful journey. St. Louis is a haven for adventurous eaters, offering a taste of the world without ever leaving the city limits. From the sizzling grills of Seoul Taco where Korean and Mexican flavors come together to authentic Italian fare at Zia’s on The Hill, there’s a global culinary adventure waiting around every corner. The city’s diverse neighborhoods each offer a unique culinary narrative. For instance, the vibrant South City area, with its eclectic mix of shops and eateries, showcases a remarkable array of international flavors. Exploring areas like The Hill, renowned for its Italian heritage, or the burgeoning international districts in South City reveals a culinary landscape that is as diverse as the people who call St. Louis home. This geographical diversity in culinary offerings means that a world tour of flavors is accessible right within the city limits, from the spicy curries of India to the delicate pastries of France, all prepared with local flair and ingredients. ## More Than Just a Meal: A Community Connection St. Louis’s dining scene isn’t just about satisfying your appetite — it’s where the city gathers. Artisan coffee shops like Sump Coffee and Blueprint Coffee have become integral parts of the city’s social fabric. These cozy havens, filled with the aroma of freshly roasted beans, serve as community hubs. Here, students huddle over laptops, friends catch up over steaming lattes, and locals gather to discuss everything from the Cardinals’ latest win to the blossoming art scene. The emphasis on community extends beyond coffee shops. Many restaurants actively engage with local charities and community events, further solidifying their role as neighborhood cornerstones. Neighborhood food crawls, farmers markets, and street festivals bring together local chefs and vendors, celebrating the city’s culinary talent and knitting the community together. These gatherings are not just about enjoying delicious food; they are about strengthening the bonds that tie the community together, creating a vibrant and supportive environment for both businesses and residents alike.
