## Streamline Your Life: Master St. Louis Services in One Place Revised July 23, 2026 How do I keep track of all my household services? One page with four columns: your vetted pros (who), when each service last happened and is next due, model numbers and install dates for your big equipment, and where the paperwork lives. Pair it with a St. Louis seasonal rhythm — AC checkup in spring, furnace in fall, gutters twice a year, sump pump test before storm season — and put the recurring items in the calendar you already use daily. Keep reading ↓Imagine it’s a Tuesday night in Webster Groves, or Florissant, or out in O’Fallon. Somewhere on your kitchen counter there’s a sticky note that says “call gutter guy.” It has said that for three weeks now, quietly judging you. Your phone holds a screenshot of a dog groomer a friend recommended in April, a reminder to find a new dentist that you’ve snoozed eleven times, and a photo of the water heater’s serial number you took “just in case” — though you no longer remember in case of what. None of these things are hard. That’s the maddening part. Each one is a ten-minute task. But they live in six different places — a note here, a screenshot there, a vague intention everywhere — and so the mental load of running a household ends up heavier than any single job on the list. Somebody in every house is carrying that invisible clipboard, and somehow it never quite gets any shorter. This guide is about putting the clipboard down. Not with an app subscription or a productivity system you’ll abandon by August like the last three — just a seasonal rhythm that matches how St. Louis actually works, one page that holds your people, and one place to look when you need someone new. ## The St. Louis household service calendar The single best trick for streamlining services is to stop treating them as surprises. Most of what a metro home needs follows the seasons here, and the seasons are predictable: - **Spring:**Air conditioning checkup- *before*the first 90-degree week, when every HVAC company’s phone melts. Gutter cleaning after the maple seeds drop. A slow walk around your foundation to spot what winter’s freeze-thaw opened up — clay soil moves in this region, and small cracks are cheaper conversations than big ones, every single time. Storm season also starts: if your trees haven’t been assessed in a few years, our tree storm-proofing guide is the place to start. - **Summer:**Exterior work season — painting, decks, concrete, roofing. The good crews book out, so summer projects are really late-spring phone calls. It’s also peak season for discovering your AC’s limits; if it’s struggling, the AC repair guide covers repair-or-replace honestly. - **Fall:**Furnace checkup before the first cold snap (same phone-melting rule as spring, in reverse). Gutters again once the leaves finish. Chimney sweep if you burn wood. Fall is also the sweet spot for interior projects — painters and remodelers often have more room in the calendar before the holidays. - **Winter:**Planning season. Get estimates for next year’s big project while contractors have time to talk, watch for basement dampness during the January thaw (our waterproofing guide explains what’s normal and what isn’t), and keep an eye on ice dams after heavy snow. Put those eight-or-so recurring items on your actual calendar — the one that already runs your life — and half the sticky notes never get written in the first place. ## One page that holds your people Here’s the lowest-tech system that actually survives contact with real life: a single page — a note on your phone, a doc, a sheet of paper on the fridge, it genuinely doesn’t matter — with four columns: - **Who:**Your vetted pros. One plumber, one electrician, one HVAC company, one handyman, plus the household regulars — dentist, vet, groomer, hair stylist, mechanic. - **When:**The last time each one came, and roughly when they’re due again. - **What:**Model numbers and install dates for the big stuff — furnace, AC, water heater, roof. (That mystery screenshot of the water heater serial finally has a home.) - **Paper:**Where the warranties and receipts live — a folder, a drawer, an email label. One answer, not four. Building the “who” column is the real work, and it’s worth doing before anything breaks. Our step-by-step guide to hiring home repair pros walks the full vetting process — insurance certificates, three estimates, red flags — and it works for every trade on your list. ## Beyond the house: the whole-life version The same system runs the rest of your life’s services, and it’s arguably more valuable there — because nobody sends you a reminder that the dog is overdue for the groomer. - **The people services:**dentist, doctor, hair stylist, barber. Most run on six-month or six-week rhythms; book the next visit before you leave the current one and the slot problem disappears — it’s the single highest-leverage habit on this whole page. (Choosing well is its own skill — our personal care guide covers how to pick salons, spas, and stylists you’ll keep.) - **The pet services:**vet, groomer, boarding. Boarding especially rewards planning — the good kennels fill up for holidays months out, and the scramble always lands the week before Thanksgiving. A standing row on your page — vet in spring, boarding ...

## How to Check If a Contractor Is Licensed in Missouri (the Answer Surprises People) Revised July 28, 2026 How do you check if a contractor is licensed in Missouri? **You can’t — there is no state database to check.** **Missouri issues no statewide license for general contractors, plumbers, or HVAC contractors**, so the standard advice to “look them up on the state board” describes something that doesn’t exist here. Licensing happens at the **city level** instead, and St. Louis County alone holds 80+ municipalities with separate rules. To verify someone: find which city governs your address, call that permit office, and ask whether the company is current. ⚠️ Then ask **who pulls the permit** — if they want you to pull it as the homeowner, that usually means they can’t. ## How do you check if a contractor is licensed in Missouri? Search that question and you will get a wall of official-looking answers, nearly all of them useless to you. We pulled the live results for this exact phrase from a Missouri location, and page one was **nine different state license lookup portals** — California, Washington, Florida, South Carolina, New Jersey, Tennessee, Virginia, Minnesota, North Carolina. Missouri was not among them. Not lower down, not on page two. **Missouri has no statewide licensing board for general contractors, plumbers, or HVAC contractors**, so there is no state database to search. The advice everyone gives — “just check the state license board” — describes a thing that does not exist here. That is not a loophole or an oversight anyone is hiding. Bills to create statewide contractor licensing have been introduced in Jefferson City repeatedly and have not passed. So the verification job falls to you, and it works differently than it does almost anywhere else. ## What Missouri does license, and what it doesn’t The distinction matters, because “unlicensed” sounds alarming until you understand it is often just how the state is organized. **The state does license** a long list of professions through its Division of Professional Registration — electricians in some contexts, elevator mechanics, engineers and architects, cosmetologists, and many health professions. If your project needs a licensed design professional, there is a state record to check. **The state does not license** general contractors, remodelers, plumbers, HVAC contractors, roofers, painters, or handymen. There is no state exam, no state number, no state complaint history. Home inspectors are not licensed by the state either — a fact worth knowing before you rely on an inspection report. So when a roofer tells you they are “fully licensed,” the honest follow-up is: *licensed by whom?* The answer should be a city. If they cannot name one, that is your first real signal. ## Where the license actually lives: your city hall Missouri pushes this work down to local government, and in the St. Louis metro that means it is fragmented to an unusual degree. The **City of St. Louis** licenses contractors directly through its License Collector, with its own application and its own requirements. If work is happening inside the city limits, that is where the record is. **St. Louis County is not one jurisdiction.** It holds more than eighty separate incorporated municipalities — the published count runs 84 or 88 depending on whether villages are counted — plus unincorporated territory. Kirkwood, Clayton, Florissant, Webster Groves, Chesterfield and the rest each write their own contractor rules. Some require a bonded registration or a master’s card. Some require little. The practical consequence: **a contractor can be perfectly licensed for the job they did last week and not licensed for yours**, purely because your house sits in a different municipality. This is not misconduct. It is the structure. It also means the only license that matters to you is the one valid where *your* address is. ## How to actually verify a contractor here Since there is no portal, the sequence is manual. It takes about twenty minutes and it works. **1. Find out which city governs your address.** Do not assume. A “St. Louis, MO” mailing address frequently sits in a county municipality with entirely separate rules. Get this right first or every other step points at the wrong office. **2. Call that city’s permit or building office and ask two questions.** Does this trade require a license or registration here? And is this specific company current? Permit desks answer this routinely — it is not an unusual request, and they will tell you. **3. Ask who is pulling the permit.** This is the highest-value question on this page. A licensed contractor pulls the permit in their own name. If they suggest *you* pull it as the homeowner, understand what that means: liability shifts to you, inspections become your responsibility, and the arrangement is frequently a sign the contractor cannot pull one. Occasionally there are legitimate reasons. Usually there are not. **4. Verify insurance directly with the insurer, not the contractor.** Ask for the certificate, then call the number on it. A certificate is a PDF; anyone can edit a PDF. The insurer will confirm the policy is active in about a minute. Ask for general liability and, if they have employees, workers’ compensation — without the latter, an injury on your property can become your problem. **5. Check the paper trail that does exist.** No state board does not mean no record. Look at Better Business Bureau complaint history, Missouri Attorney ...

The practical consequence: **a contractor can be perfectly licensed for the job they did last week and not licensed for yours**, purely because your house sits in a different municipality. This is not misconduct. It is the structure. It also means the only license that matters to you is the one valid where *your* address is. ## How to actually verify a contractor here Since there is no portal, the sequence is manual. It takes about twenty minutes and it works. **1. Find out which city governs your address.** Do not assume. A “St. Louis, MO” mailing address frequently sits in a county municipality with entirely separate rules. Get this right first or every other step points at the wrong office. **2. Call that city’s permit or building office and ask two questions.** Does this trade require a license or registration here? And is this specific company current? Permit desks answer this routinely — it is not an unusual request, and they will tell you. **3. Ask who is pulling the permit.** This is the highest-value question on this page. A licensed contractor pulls the permit in their own name. If they suggest *you* pull it as the homeowner, understand what that means: liability shifts to you, inspections become your responsibility, and the arrangement is frequently a sign the contractor cannot pull one. Occasionally there are legitimate reasons. Usually there are not. **4. Verify insurance directly with the insurer, not the contractor.** Ask for the certificate, then call the number on it. A certificate is a PDF; anyone can edit a PDF. The insurer will confirm the policy is active in about a minute. Ask for general liability and, if they have employees, workers’ compensation — without the latter, an injury on your property can become your problem. **5. Check the paper trail that does exist.** No state board does not mean no record. Look at Better Business Bureau complaint history, Missouri Attorney ...

## Master Home Repair in St. Louis: A Step-by-Step Guide to Hiring the Right Pro Revised July 24, 2026 How do I find a trustworthy home repair contractor in St. Louis? Eight steps: name the job precisely, ask neighbors who they’d use again, check recent reviews, verify licensing and — critically — liability insurance and workers’ compensation (ask for the certificate), get three written estimates and compare scope not just price, test how they communicate before they have your money, get the warranty in a signed agreement, and trust your gut. In St. Louis specifically, watch for clay-soil foundation issues, old-brick tuckpointing, aging wiring in pre-1950s homes, and post-storm door-knockers. Keep reading ↓*Updated June 21, 2026.* Imagine the water heater goes out on a Sunday, or a storm leaves a branch through the gutter, or that “I’ll get to it” repair finally can’t wait. Now you’re staring at your phone, about to hand a stranger your house, your money, and your trust — and hoping you pick a good one. Whether you’re in a century-old brick two-family in the city or a newer build out in the county, here’s a step-by-step way to find a home repair pro in St. Louis you can actually count on — and to spot the ones you can’t. ## 1. Get clear on what you need Before you call anyone, name the job: plumbing, electrical, roofing, HVAC, drywall, general handyman work. The clearer you are, the easier it is to find a specialist instead of a jack-of-all-trades who dabbles — and the more accurate your quotes will be. ## 2. Ask the people you trust A neighbor who just had the same work done is worth more than any ad — they’ve seen the crew’s punctuality, the cleanup, and the final invoice. Ask friends, family, and your neighborhood Facebook group who they’d use again — and, just as useful, who they’d warn you away from. ## 3. Do a little homework online Look the company up: their website, recent reviews across Google and other sites, and a local directory listing. You’re looking for a real, consistent track record — and *recent* reviews, since a company can change a lot in a year. ## 4. Check the credentials that protect you This is the step that saves people thousands. Confirm the company is **licensed for the work** (and that any required St. Louis city or county permits will be pulled), and — this is the big one — that they carry **liability insurance and workers’ compensation**. Ask for a certificate of insurance. If an uninsured worker is hurt on your property, you don’t want to be the one holding that bill. ## 5. Get at least three written estimates Don’t take the first number. Get three, in writing, and read them closely — the cheapest bid often leaves something out, while a higher one may include better materials or a step the others skipped. Price is one factor; understanding *exactly* what each includes is the real goal. Be especially wary of a quote that’s dramatically lower than the rest. ## 6. Test how they communicate Call the office. Does a real person answer, or does it ring out? How quickly do they call back? The way a company communicates *before* they have your money is a pretty good preview of how they’ll treat you *after*. Prompt, clear, patient communication is a green flag. ## 7. Ask about warranties — and get it in writing A confident pro stands behind their work with a warranty on parts and labor. Ask what’s covered and for how long, and make sure the scope, price, timeline, and warranty all land in a signed written agreement before work starts. ## 8. Trust your gut You’ll know. The right pro listens, answers your questions in plain English without hiding behind jargon, doesn’t pressure you, and makes you feel like a customer rather than a transaction. If something feels off, keep looking — there are plenty of good ones in this town. One quiet tell: look at how a company keeps its online presence and directory profile. A business that takes the time to maintain a complete, professional profile tends to bring that same care to the work itself. ## Reading three estimates side by side Once the three written quotes are in hand, don’t just compare the bottom lines — compare what each one actually commits to: - **Scope:**Does each bid describe the same job? A cheaper bid that quietly omits haul-away, patching, or a code-required upgrade isn’t cheaper — it’s incomplete. - **Materials:**Brand and grade matter. “Water heater” tells you nothing; a specific model with a specific warranty tells you plenty. - **Allowances and exclusions:**The fine print where surprises live. What happens if they open the wall and find rot, old wiring, or a surprise from a previous owner’s handiwork? A good estimate says how change orders get priced and approved. - **Timeline and payment schedule:**Start date, duration, and payments tied to completed milestones — not the calendar. If a bid is dramatically lower than the other two, ask the contractor to walk you through it line by line. Sometimes there’s an honest reason — lighter overhead, a slower season, a simpler approach. Often, though, the walkthrough answers the question for you: something was missing, and you’d have paid for it later as a change order. ## The St. Louis ...

## Home Inspections in St. Louis: What They Miss, and Why It Matters Here Revised July 28, 2026 What does a home inspection cover in St. Louis? ⚠️ **Missouri does NOT license home inspectors** — no exam, no registration, no state board to complain to. (Bills to create licensing were introduced in 2011, 2013 and 2019 and none passed.) Worse: both national standards of practice — InterNACHI and ASHI — **explicitly exclude radon, lead paint, asbestos, mold, pests, and anything underground**, which is every hazard old St. Louis housing is known for. Order separately: a **sewer scope** (the highest-value add-on here), a termite/WDO inspection, and a **FREE radon kit from Missouri DHSS** (coupon code MO TESTING). 📍 St. Louis City and County are EPA radon **Zone 2**, not Zone 1 as some local content claims — but 1 in 3 Missouri homes tested still exceeded the action level. Note the occupancy permit (City $120) is a code-minimum check, NOT a home inspection. Missouri does not license home inspectors. No exam, no state registration, no required insurance, no board to complain to. The legislature has been asked to change this at least three times and has declined every time. Anyone in this state can print a business card tomorrow and inspect the largest purchase of your life. Then there’s the second half, which is worse: the inspection you *do* get is contractually excused from looking at almost everything that’s actually wrong with old St. Louis houses. ## What does a home inspection cover in St. Louis? A standard inspection is a **visual, non-invasive** examination of accessible areas — roof, foundation, structure, plumbing, electrical, heating and cooling, and visible components on the day of the inspection. Under both major national standards, it explicitly does **not** include radon, lead paint, asbestos, mold, termites, anything underground, remaining life expectancy of any system, repair costs, or code compliance. In a metro where the median city home was built in 1938, those exclusions cover most of what you actually need to know — which means the specialty tests have to be ordered separately. ## Nobody licensed the person inspecting your house This surprises almost everyone, so here is how it checks out. “Home inspector” does not appear anywhere on the Missouri Division of Professional Registration’s list of licensed professions — a list that runs to 57 occupations and includes barbers, cosmetologists, tattoo artists, private investigators and real estate appraisers. And Chapter 339 of the Missouri statutes, which licenses real estate professionals, contains no home inspector provisions at all. Sit with the comparison for a second. **The person selling you the house is licensed and can be disciplined by a state commission. The person inspecting it is not regulated at all.** One caution while we’re here, because we nearly got this wrong ourselves: you may find claims online that Missouri created a home inspector registration board. Those cite statute numbers that come from a *bill* introduced in 2019 that never passed. It isn’t law. Similar bills failed in 2011 and 2013. ## What to check instead of a license Since the state isn’t vetting anyone, the private certifications carry the weight. Two matter, and they are not equivalent. **ASHI Certified Inspector (ACI)** is the higher experience bar. It requires passing the National Home Inspector Examination and completing a **minimum of 250 fee-paid inspections**, with a sample of reports reviewed and verified by ASHI, plus 20 hours of continuing education a year. **InterNACHI Certified Professional Inspector (CPI)** requires passing an exam, completing ethics and standards courses, and **submitting four mock inspection reports** — then 24 hours of continuing education annually and **re-passing the exam every three years** at 80% or better. Both impose a code of ethics and continuing education that Missouri law does not. Neither, as far as we could verify, requires errors and omissions insurance — so ask whether they carry it and ask to see the certificate. Ask for a sample report too. A good one runs to dozens of photographed pages; a bad one is a checklist. ## The exclusion list is the whole story Here is where this gets specific to St. Louis, and where most buyers get hurt. Both national standards of practice state plainly that an inspection is not technically exhaustive and will not identify concealed or latent defects. Then they list what the inspector is **not required to determine.** Among the items on those lists: the presence of **pests, mold or fungus**; airborne hazards **including radon**; environmental hazards **including lead paint and asbestos**; the remaining life expectancy of anything; the cause of any condition; the cost of any correction; compliance with codes; and anything **underground**. Now line that up against what defines housing here. Radon. Lead paint in a city where most homes predate 1978 by forty years. Asbestos. Termites. The sewer lateral and the water service line, both underground. **Every hazard St. Louis is known for is on the excluded list.** That isn’t a criticism of inspectors — it’s their published rulebook, and a general inspection was never meant to do those jobs. But a buyer who orders “a home inspection” and assumes it covered them is wrong, and will find out later. ## Radon: everyone gets the zone wrong You will read locally that St. Louis sits in EPA Radon Zone 1, the highest-risk category. We checked EPA’s own map of Missouri. **St. Louis City and St. Louis ...

## How to Choose a Home Repair Company in St. Louis (Without Getting Burned) Revised July 23, 2026 How do I choose a home repair company in St. Louis? Vet a home-repair contractor by knowing exactly what you need, checking license and insurance (Missouri licenses plumbers, contractors, and most electricians locally, not statewide), reading reviews across platforms, and getting two or three written itemized estimates. Watch for red flags: large cash payments up front, high-pressure tactics, no written contract, and no verifiable address or reviews. Get scope, price, and warranty in writing before work starts. Keep reading ↓Picture a Saturday morning gone wrong: a ceiling stain spreading in Webster Groves, a furnace that won’t light in Florissant, a deck board that finally gave way in St. Charles. You need someone good, you need them soon, and the internet coughs up fifty names with no obvious way to tell the pros from the problems. Hiring the wrong contractor can cost you far more than the repair itself — in money, in do-overs, and in stress. This is an honest, St. Louis-specific guide to choosing a home-repair company you can actually trust: what to check, which credentials matter here in Missouri (and across the river in Illinois), the red flags that should end a conversation, and the questions that separate a real pro from a smooth talker. The good news is that vetting a contractor isn’t complicated — it’s a short, repeatable set of checks, and the small amount of time it takes is the cheapest insurance you’ll ever buy on a home project. It matters more here than a lot of homeowners realize. The St. Louis metro’s housing skews older — century-old brick in the city, mid-century ranches across the county — and older homes hide more surprises, which means the gap between a careful pro and a careless one shows up fast. Add our clay soil, hard water, and freeze-thaw winters, and the quality of the work you hire genuinely determines whether a repair holds for a decade or fails by next season. ## Start by knowing exactly what you need Before you call anyone, get clear on the job. Is it plumbing, electrical, roofing, HVAC, or general handyman work? The clearer you are, the better your quotes will be and the harder it is for anyone to pad the scope. A specialist in the exact problem — a roofer for a roof, not a general contractor who “does roofs too” — usually does better work at a fairer price, and can spot the underlying cause a generalist might miss. Write down what you’re seeing (the symptom, when it started, any photos) so you can describe it consistently to everyone you call and get comparable quotes back. If you’re not sure whether a job needs a licensed trade or a handyman, our home-services hiring guide breaks the trades down. ## The credential check — and how licensing actually works here This is where St. Louis homeowners get tripped up, because Missouri’s licensing is local, not statewide. A few honest facts to arm you: - **Missouri has no statewide general contractor license,**and plumbers and general contractors are licensed at the- *city or county*level. Most electricians are too (there’s an optional statewide electrical contractor license). So “licensed” means licensed- *where your job is*— ask which municipality issued the license and confirm it with that city or county building department. - **Illinois (the Metro East) is stricter on paper.**Under the Illinois Home Repair and Remodeling Act, contractors must carry public liability and property-damage insurance, and jobs over a set dollar amount require a written contract. If you’re in Belleville, Edwardsville, or O’Fallon IL, hold them to it. - **Insurance is non-negotiable everywhere.**Ask for a current certificate of liability insurance, and workers’ comp if they bring a crew. If a worker is hurt on your property or your home is damaged and there’s no coverage, the exposure can land on you. A legitimate contractor hands over license and insurance details without flinching. Hesitation, excuses, or “I’ll get that to you later” when you ask for basic license and insurance proof is your first real red flag, and one worth taking seriously no matter how good the rest of the pitch sounds. Ready to find someone? Run a home-repair business? A complete, well-maintained directory profile is how careful homeowners find you — and the same attention to detail that fills out a good profile is what signals you’ll bring that care to their home. ## Do your homework: reviews, references, and real work Reputation is the best predictor you have. Work three angles: - **Read reviews across platforms,**not just the star average. Look at how the company responds to criticism — a gracious, specific reply to a bad review tells you more than a wall of five stars. Check Google, and directories that show real local businesses. - **Ask for local references and call them.**A reputable pro will gladly share recent nearby clients. Ask those homeowners the real questions: did the work hold up, did they stick to the quote, would you hire them again? - **See comparable work.**Photos are fine; a similar job you can actually look ...

## Summer Jobs in St. Louis for Students: Where to Look and What They Pay Revised July 27, 2026 Where can students find summer jobs in St. Louis? ## Top 10 Companies in St. Louis: The Giants That Call the Metro Home Revised July 23, 2026 What are the biggest companies in St. Louis? The metro’s giants: Centene (Fortune 500 #23), Enterprise Mobility, Edward Jones, World Wide Technology (~$20B revenue, Maryland Heights), Anheuser-Busch, BJC Health System (Missouri’s largest private employer, ~47,000 people), Emerson (#238), Nestlé Purina, Reinsurance Group of America (#196), and Bunge (~$53B, headquartered here since 2019). Greater St. Louis, Inc. counts seventeen Fortune 1000 headquarters in the region. Keep reading ↓Here’s a bar-trivia question that stumps people who’ve lived here their whole lives: how many Fortune 1000 companies are headquartered in greater St. Louis? Most folks guess four or five — the beer, the brokerage, maybe the pet food. The actual answer, last time the count was published by Greater St. Louis, Inc., is seventeen and growing — and that count doesn’t even include the privately held giants that never appear on Fortune’s revenue-ranked lists at all. Whether you’re a job seeker sizing up the market, a business owner wondering who anchors the local economy, or just someone who likes knowing what’s behind the logos on the highway, this is the honest tour: the ten biggest corporate names that call the metro home, what each actually does, and why they matter to the rest of us. Every fact here traces to the companies themselves or to Greater St. Louis, Inc.’s headquarters data — no padding, no guesswork, and no ranking anyone paid for. ## 1. Centene The biggest company most St. Louisans have never bought anything from. Centene is a healthcare insurance giant — managed care, government health programs — and at **#23 on the Fortune 500**, it’s the highest-ranked company headquartered in the metro. Its Clayton campus reshaped that suburb’s skyline, and its scale makes it one of the region’s most consequential employers for healthcare, technology, and corporate roles alike — when Centene sneezes, Clayton commercial real estate catches a cold. ## 2. Enterprise Mobility You know it as the rental counter, but Enterprise is quietly one of the largest privately held companies in America — which is why it never shows up on the Fortune 500 despite belonging in any conversation about it. Founded here and still family-owned and headquartered in the metro, Enterprise runs a global mobility business from St. Louis, and its name is on the Blues’ arena downtown. ## 3. Edward Jones The investment firm built on the one-broker-office model — there’s probably a branch in a strip mall near you, and that’s the point. A Fortune 500 firm headquartered in the metro, Edward Jones runs one of the region’s largest corporate campuses and hires steadily across finance, technology, and operations. For St. Louis job seekers in financial services, it’s the anchor tenant of the whole local industry — and its steady hiring across technology and operations surprises people who only picture brokers. ## 4. World Wide Technology The metro’s great under-the-radar success story. WWT is a technology solutions company — enterprise IT, cloud, AI infrastructure — with roughly **$20 billion in revenue** and a global headquarters at Westport Plaza in Maryland Heights (WWT). Privately held, founded here, and one of the largest Black-founded companies in the country, WWT is the biggest reason “St. Louis tech” is a serious phrase rather than a hopeful one. ## 5. Anheuser-Busch The one everybody knows. The historic Soulard brewery complex has anchored the city since the 1850s, and it remains the U.S. brewing headquarters — One Busch Place, where the Budweiser Clydesdales still live part of the year and the brewery lights still draw crowds every December. Whatever has changed about global ownership, the brewing, the jobs, and the civic identity are still very much here — ask anyone who’s taken the brewery tour, or anyone whose grandfather worked the bottling line. ## 6. BJC Health System Not a household “brand” so much as the place half the metro was born, treated, or employed. BJC — anchored by Barnes-Jewish Hospital and its Washington University medical partnership — is **the largest private employer in Missouri**, with a workforce around 47,000 after its merger with Kansas City’s Saint Luke’s (BJC). If employment is the measure, this is the biggest name on the list — and its hiring reach runs from surgeons to schedulers to software teams. ## 7. Emerson A St. Louis industrial institution since 1890. Emerson builds automation technology and software for industries worldwide, sits at **#238 on the Fortune 500**, and runs its global operations from its longtime campus in the metro. It’s the classic quiet giant: little consumer visibility, enormous engineering payroll — and a name on more automation systems worldwide than most people will ever notice. ## 8. Nestlé Purina PetCare If you have a dog or cat, Purina is probably in your pantry right now. The pet care giant’s North American headquarters sits at 800 Chouteau Avenue downtown — Purina has been a St. Louis company since its Ralston Purina days more than a century ago, and its checkerboard logo is as local as the Arch. It remains one of downtown’s largest corporate anchors and a major employer in marketing, R&D, and operations. ## 9. Reinsurance Group of America (RGA) The metro’s most invisible giant: RGA sells reinsurance — insurance for insurance companies — from its Chesterfield headquarters, and at **#196 on the Fortune 500** it outranks almost everything on this ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/top-10-company-st-louis-picks-for-2025

## What It Actually Costs to Start a Business in St. Louis (Missouri vs. Illinois) Revised July 28, 2026 What does it actually cost to start a business in the St. Louis metro? Far less than most people expect on the Missouri side. A **Missouri LLC is $50 online** ($105 by mail) and then **nothing again — no annual report, no annual fee** (Missouri is one of only four states with none). An **Illinois LLC is $150** plus **$75 every year**. Add a free federal EIN, a **$7** fictitious-name filing if you use a trade name, and a **$200** business license inside St. Louis city limits — roughly **$250 total** to exist legally. 💡 The cheap part is becoming legal. The expensive part is becoming findable. ## What does it actually cost to start a business in the St. Louis metro? Less than almost anyone expects on the Missouri side, and the gap between the two states is bigger than most people in this metro realize. A Missouri LLC costs **$50 to file online** ($105 by mail), and then Missouri asks for nothing again — **no annual report, no annual fee**. Across the river, an Illinois LLC runs **$150 to form** and **$75 every single year** after that. Same metro, same drive to work, three times the setup cost and a recurring bill that never appears in Missouri. Add a free federal EIN and, if you are inside St. Louis city limits, a $200 business license, and a genuinely lean Missouri startup can be legally standing for well under $300. ## The state filing, side by side Run that forward. Five years in, the Missouri LLC has paid $50 total. The Illinois LLC has paid $525. Neither number is large in the scheme of a business, but the structural difference is worth knowing before you assume the states are interchangeable — particularly if you are choosing where to register a business that could sit on either side. To be clear about what that does *not* mean: you do not get to form in Missouri to dodge Illinois obligations for an Illinois business. Where you actually operate drives what you owe. But for a genuinely mobile or online business, it is a real consideration. ## The thing Missouri quietly gets right The no-annual-report rule deserves its own moment, because it removes an entire failure mode. In most states, the way small LLCs die is not dramatic. The owner forgets an annual filing, the fee goes unpaid, late penalties stack, and the entity is administratively dissolved — often discovered months later when a bank or a client asks for proof of good standing. **Missouri does not require LLCs to file an annual report, and does not impose a franchise tax on them**, which puts it among only four states with no recurring annual LLC fee at all. So the single most common paperwork trap in American small business simply does not apply to a Missouri LLC. That is worth more than the $50 saved. Corporations and other structures have their own requirements, and this is one of the few places where twenty minutes with an accountant genuinely pays for itself. But for the ordinary one-or-two-person LLC, Missouri is about as low-maintenance as it gets. ## What you do not have to pay for A large share of what people spend forming a business is optional, and the upsells are aggressive because the margins are good. **You do not need a formation service.** Filing directly with the Secretary of State is the same filing. Services are a convenience purchase, not a legal requirement, and the “$0 + state fees” offers typically recover their margin on the registered agent renewal. **You may not need a paid registered agent.** You can generally serve as your own if you have a physical address in the state and are available during business hours. The real reasons to pay for one are privacy — your address becomes public record — or not having a reliable street address. Those are legitimate. “It is required” is not. **You do not need to buy a “business license package.”** There is a whole industry selling Missouri business licenses. Missouri does not issue a general statewide business license, so what these products actually do is fill out local forms you could file yourself. Our guide to what licensing you actually need in St. Louis covers which office to go to and what each one charges. **You almost certainly do not need a trademark on day one.** Worth doing eventually if the brand matters. Not a startup cost. ## The local layer, which is where it gets uneven The state fee is the predictable part. Local licensing is where two identical businesses pay different amounts for no reason other than geography. Inside the **City of St. Louis**, a Graduated Business License runs **$200** to start — or $100 if you begin between January 1 and May 31 — and renews from $200 a year for a business with up to two city employees, on a license year running June 1 to May 31. In **St. Louis County**, there is no single county-wide equivalent. The county holds more than eighty separate municipalities, each with its own rules and its own fees. Two competitors five miles apart can face entirely different requirements. Budget for this rather than being surprised by it, and find out which municipality ...

## The Heart of Community: Why Local Matters Revised July 28, 2026 Why is shopping locally important? When you spend with a St. Louis-owned business, more of that dollar stays in the neighborhood — paying local staff, funding local causes, and keeping storefronts alive. Local owners answer to their neighbors, not a distant corporate office, so quality and care stay personal. That circulation of money, trust, and familiar faces is what keeps a community feeling like one. Keep reading ↓Sit with me for a moment. Picture lunchtime on a Saturday: the sun soft on the corner of Main Street, the warm smell of fresh barbecue drifting from a small café or food truck, and you hear the low, satisfied rumble of a lawn mower being tuned at a family-run garage down the block. That feeling — of places that know your name, of streets threaded together by familiar faces and dependable services — is what the St. Louis Near Me spirit is about. This is not a sales pitch; it's an invitation to hold a door open for neighbors and friends, to make daily life a little easier for the people who make our neighborhood, city, and region hum. ## Why Choosing Local Is an Act of Community When you choose a local barbecue restaurant instead of a chain, you're doing more than buying a sandwich. You're making possible the sound of the smoker timer, the restaurant or food truck owner's family who remembers your order, and the teenager saving for college who works the register. Have you patronized a business like this? That single, small act ripples: dollars that stay close by, jobs that support families, and the authentic character of neighborhoods from Warrenton to Highland and from Bonne Terre to Jerseyville. The human economy is woven from these small local choices we make to support our friends and neighbors. Think about the sensory memory of a place you love: the softness of a storefront's worn wooden sign and the creak in the store's old wooden floors, the spicy tang of a food truck's simmering sauce that you remember from your last visit, the distant rhythm of a band tuning up at a town festival that you've been looking forward to for weeks. Those layers — sight, smell, sound, texture, taste — are the town's real capital. It's where life is made and experiences are photographed, and those photos are sent to friends and remembered forever. You're not just shopping or buying a barbecue sandwich; you're supporting local businesses, which keeps those delicate layers of interaction alive. Those businesses train the younger generation and teach the skills that are necessary to lead a long, productive, and happy life right here in our community. Whether those businesses support a single mother, an older couple, or a larger business with many employees, you know that all of us are in this community together and that we need to continue to support each other. St Louis Near Me Directory is the connector — pointing neighbors to the businesses that serve them, and businesses to the neighbors looking for exactly what they do. Let's call it a hyperlocal collaboration, or more simply call it helping each other. Sound good? ## The Directory as More Than a List — A Quietly Humming Community There's a difference between a directory and a community. A directory can be a database; a community is a conversation. On our pages, you'll find more than phone numbers — you'll find voices. People leave notes about a florist's careful arrangements in Ferguson, praise for a mechanic's honest assessment in Millstadt, or a tip about the best late-night sandwich in Sappington. These small, human insights turn discovery into trust. When you talk to a friend about an experience with a business and they use words like "reliable," "friendly," "on time," that language is a kind of local shorthand. It tells you who to trust without a hard sell. The St Louis Near Me Directory amplifies those real conversations so neighbors can make better choices faster. ## How Supporting Local Businesses Strengthens Our Regional Fabric Dollars spent locally recirculate. A resident or business that hires a gardener or landscaper from the neighborhood spends more locally on supplies; a plumber who hires an apprentice keeps wages within the community. It means the person who fixes your roof might also be the one coaching at the local youth league in the evening. This kind of local recirculation builds an economic web that's resilient — and intimately affects each one of us. Beyond economics, local businesses hold the civic memory of a place. The mural outside a family shop in Dupo, IL, the annual block party in Bellefontaine Neighbors, MO, the outdoor farmers' table on a Saturday in Columbia, IL — these are the textures that make our towns distinct. (New to the metro, or showing it off to visitors? Start with our guide to exploring St. Louis.) When you use the directory to choose local, you're participating in preserving those textures. ## For Business Owners: How the Directory Helps You Be Found and Chosen If you own a shop, a studio, or a service business, the St Louis Near Me Directory is designed to be practical: it helps customers find you, understand what you do, and decide to reach out. A clear headline, a few clean photos, and a short descriptive note about what ...

## Part-Time Jobs in St. Louis: A Local Guide Revised July 28, 2026 What are the best part-time jobs in St. Louis? Part-time jobs in St. Louis span retail and food service, warehouse and delivery, gig work (Amazon Flex, Instacart), healthcare support and patient services, substitute teaching, and seasonal guest-services roles at places like the Saint Louis Zoo. As of 2026, Missouri’s minimum wage is $15.00/hour, so legitimate W-2 jobs should start at or above that (gig roles are contractor work with variable pay before expenses). Find roles with the part-time filter on Indeed and Snagajob, on employer career pages, through the free Missouri Job Centers (jobs.mo.gov), and on the local St. Louis Jobs Board. Keep reading ↓Maybe you’re a student trying to cover rent without wrecking your class schedule. Maybe you’re a parent who needs work that fits around school pickup, or a retiree who misses having somewhere to be a few mornings a week, or you’re just trying to close the gap between what you earn and what everything costs now. Whatever brought you here, a good part-time job in St. Louis can do more than pad a paycheck — it can give your week some shape, your budget some breathing room, and sometimes a foot in the door of something bigger. Here’s an honest local guide to where the part-time work actually is in the metro, what it really pays, and how to find a role that fits your life instead of fighting it. ## Who part-time work fits Part-time jobs aren’t one thing, and the “right” one depends entirely on why you’re looking. **Students** usually want flexibility and something near campus or transit. **Parents** often want daytime or weekend hours that line up with childcare. **Retirees** tend to want something low-stress and social that uses the experience they already have. **Career-changers** use a part-time role to test an industry before jumping in. And plenty of people simply want a **second income** layered on top of a full-time job. None of those searches look the same — so start from your own constraints (hours, commute, energy) rather than chasing whatever pays the most on paper. ## Where the part-time jobs actually are in St. Louis A handful of categories drive most of the metro’s part-time hiring: - **Retail:**the most flexible on-ramp — national chains and locally owned shops both lean on part-timers, and hiring spikes hard around the holidays. - **Food service:**restaurants, coffee shops, and fast-casual spots across the metro hire part-time constantly, often with same-week starts and tips on top of wages. - **Warehouse & delivery:**St. Louis is a logistics hub, so package handling, sorting, and delivery roles are plentiful and frequently offer evening and weekend shifts. - **Gig & rideshare:**the most schedule-in-your-own-hands option (more on the trade-offs below). - **Healthcare support:**the region’s hospitals hire part-time patient-services, transport, and aide roles — steady, benefit-adjacent work. - **Education:**substitute teaching and tutoring are a natural fit for anyone with weekday daytime availability. - **Seasonal & guest services:**the Zoo, museums, stadiums, and event venues staff up part-time around their busy seasons. ## Seven part-time roles worth a look These are real, currently-hiring kinds of part-time work in St. Louis, spanning gig, institutional, and seasonal: - **Amazon Flex delivery**— deliver packages on blocks you choose through the Amazon Flex app. You need to be 21+, have a reliable vehicle, and pass a background check. Be skeptical of a posting advertising less. The big exception is **gig work** — Amazon Flex, Instacart, rideshare and the like are *independent-contractor* roles, which means no hourly floor, no benefits, and pay that’s quoted before you subtract gas, vehicle wear, and self-employment taxes. ## Spa Services Near Me: Your Complete Guide to Massage, Medical Spas, and Wellness Retreats Revised July 22, 2026 What is the difference between a medical spa and a regular spa? A regular (day) spa focuses on relaxation and beauty — massage, facials, body treatments, manicures, and pedicures — with no medical supervision required. A medical spa (med spa) operates under a licensed physician and offers medical-grade treatments like Botox, dermal fillers, laser hair removal, chemical peels, and microneedling. A day spa is about unwinding; a med spa delivers clinical cosmetic results. Many St. Louis wellness centers blend both under one roof. Today's spa services encompass everything from traditional Swedish therapeutic massage to advanced medical treatments like laser therapy and injectable cosmetics. Modern spas recognize that wellness is deeply personal and varies significantly between individuals. Men increasingly seek spa services for stress relief, athletic recovery, and grooming, while women continue to embrace both traditional beauty treatments and innovative wellness therapies. This shift has created a more inclusive spa environment where everyone can find their perfect wellness match. ### Types of Spa Services Available The spa services landscape can be broadly categorized into several distinct types, each serving unique purposes and clientele: - **Day Spa:**focus on relaxation and beauty treatments that can be completed in a single visit. ## EZlocal Business Listing: How to Add Your Business (and Is It Worth It?) Revised July 28, 2026 Is EZlocal legit? An EZlocal business listing is a legitimate but minor citation source. Claiming a free, accurate one is fine — it’s one more consistent mention of your business — but on its own it won’t bring customers. Don’t pay much for it, and never let it introduce an inconsistent phone number or address. Keep reading ↓You searched “EZlocal” because someone suggested listing your business there, or you saw it on a list of “directories every business needs.” Fair enough — so let’s do two things in order. First, the practical part you came for: exactly what EZlocal is and how to get your business listed on it in about ten minutes. Then the honest part most guides skip: whether it will actually bring you customers, and where it fits in a real St. Louis growth plan. **Short version: an EZlocal listing is a legitimate, free citation worth claiming — it’s a genuine business directory that also pushes your info out to other sites. But on its own it won’t move the needle. The mistake is treating it (or any single general directory) as a growth strategy instead of what it is: one small consistency signal.** Claim it, keep it accurate, and don’t stop there. Here’s how. ## What EZlocal Is EZlocal is a general online business directory and citation service — one of many sites that list your business name, address, phone, and category. Its useful twist is distribution: EZlocal is a recognized U.S. citation source that can push your listing out to a wide network of other directories and data platforms (Google, Bing, Yahoo, Apple Maps, MapQuest, and Waze among them) from one submission. Being listed there creates a **citation** — a mention of your business details on another site. Citations still play a role in local SEO, but their weight has declined, and consistency now matters far more than raw count (Whitespark, 2026). So the value of EZlocal isn’t traffic from EZlocal itself — it’s one more accurate, consistent mention of your business in the wider ecosystem. ## How to List Your Business on EZlocal (Step by Step) This is the part you came for, and the good news is it’s quick and free. Here’s the process: - **Go to EZlocal and start a free listing.**On ezlocal.com, look for “Claim Your Free Listing” (or the free business-listing page) and enter your business phone number. EZlocal checks whether your business is already in its system. - **Claim or create.**If your business already appears (many do, pulled from existing data), claim it so you control the information. If it doesn’t appear, create a new listing. - **Enter your core NAP exactly.**Business- **name, address, and phone number**must match — character for character — how they appear on your website and your Google Business Profile. This consistency is the whole point; a mismatch here does more harm than good. - **Complete the full profile.**Add your website URL, email, hours of operation, primary and secondary categories, a clear business description, your logo, and a few real photos. A complete listing is worth far more than a bare-bones one. - **Add extras if offered.**EZlocal lets you post coupons, links, and additional details on a free profile — reasonable to fill in, but don’t overthink it. - **Verify and save.**Confirm ownership if prompted, then save. Note the login so you can update it later — an out-of-date listing (old address, disconnected phone) is worse than none. EZlocal also sells premium marketing plans (starting around $95/month). For nearly every small business, the **free listing captures essentially all of the value** — skip the paid upsell unless you have a specific reason. ## Where EZlocal Sends Your Listing Part of EZlocal’s pitch is reach: submit once, and your business data can be syndicated out to a broad network of search engines, maps, and directory partners. In practice that means the accurate name, address, phone, and category you enter can help feed the platforms people actually use to find local businesses — the big search and maps players, plus smaller directories that pull from shared data. That syndication is the real reason a citation source like EZlocal is worth ten minutes: not because customers browse EZlocal, but because it helps keep your information *consistent* across a lot of places at once. The flip side is the same coin: if you enter the wrong details, you’ve now syndicated an *error* to a lot of places at once. That’s why the “enter your NAP exactly” step matters more than any other — garbage in, garbage everywhere. ## The Honest Verdict, at a Glance ## Is It Worth It? The Honest Take If you can claim a free, accurate EZlocal listing in a few minutes, do it — a consistent citation never hurts, and the one-click distribution is a small bonus. But be realistic about two things. First, general directories like this send **very little direct traffic**; an analysis of 5,000+ sites found that being in hundreds of directories barely out-performed being in none (Near Media). Second, **don’t pay much for it**, and never let it introduce inconsistent information — a wrong phone number on EZlocal is worse than no listing at all, because it pollutes the very consistency you’re trying to build. “A general directory listing is a consistency signal, ...

## Essential Legal Pages for a Small Business Website: An Honest Missouri Guide Revised July 23, 2026 What legal pages does a small business website need? For most small B2C websites: a Privacy Policy, Terms of Service, and a Return & Refund Policy at minimum, plus a Shipping Policy if you ship goods. Add situational pages (warranty, subscription disclosures, accessibility statement) based on what you sell. Missouri doesn’t legally require a privacy policy — it has no comprehensive privacy law as of 2026 — but customers now expect one, and other states’ laws (like California’s) can apply if you sell to their residents. Keep reading ↓This article is general information for St. Louis-area business owners, not legal advice. Laws change and vary by industry — for anything specific to your business, talk to a Missouri attorney. It’s late on a Sunday. Your small St. Louis shop — maybe you sell handmade goods online from Maplewood, run a service business out of St. Charles, or ship products from a spare room in Florissant — is quiet. A notification pings: another online order. By Tuesday, that same customer has filed a chargeback with their bank, insisting the package never arrived. What happens next depends less on your memory of the transaction and more on what your website actually said at checkout. If your terms spelled out shipping and delivery, if your return policy laid out timelines, you have a clear, documented answer. If they didn’t, you’re arguing from scratch — on the bank’s timeline, not yours. That’s the real reason a small business needs a handful of legal pages: not to look corporate, but to protect you when something goes sideways and to build enough trust that fewer things go sideways in the first place. Here’s an honest, Missouri-grounded guide to which pages actually matter, what they do, and how much to worry about the alphabet soup of privacy laws. ## First, the good news for Missouri owners If you’ve read scary articles about privacy fines, take a breath. As of 2026, about 20 U.S. states have passed comprehensive consumer-privacy laws — and **Missouri is not one of them.** There is no Missouri law requiring your website to have a privacy policy, and no Missouri “comprehensive privacy law” hanging over a local shop. So why bother? Two honest reasons. First, the laws that *can* reach you are other states’ and countries’ laws, which apply based on *who your customers are*, not where you’re located — more on that below. Second, and more practically: privacy and terms pages have become the baseline convention customers expect. A site without them reads as amateur or sketchy, whether or not any law is involved. You want these pages the way you want a clean storefront — because trust converts. One thing Missouri *does* have is the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act, the state’s consumer-protection law. It bans deception, false promises, and unfair practices in selling or advertising. In plain terms: whatever your website claims — about pricing, refunds, results — needs to be truthful. That’s the local rule most likely to matter to an honest small business, and the good news is that honesty is the entire compliance strategy. ## The legal pages a small B2C site actually needs You don’t need all fourteen pages a big-box e-commerce operation might carry. For most local businesses selling to consumers, this short list covers the real bases: ### 1. Privacy Policy What personal information you collect (names, emails, addresses, payment info handled by your processor, analytics/cookie data), why you collect it, who you share it with, and how customers can reach you about it. Even though Missouri doesn’t require one, it’s the single most expected page — and if you use Google Analytics, run ads, or take payments, you’re collecting data worth being transparent about. If you ever sell to California residents, this is also where their rights live (see below). ### 2. Terms of Service (a.k.a. Terms & Conditions) The rulebook for using your site and buying from you: acceptable use, your intellectual-property rights, payment terms, and limits on your liability. For it to actually hold up, customers should have to *agree* to it — a checkbox at checkout (“I agree to the Terms”) is far stronger than a link quietly sitting in your footer. If you can, keep a simple record of who agreed and when. ### 3. Return & Refund Policy Your eligibility window, item conditions, who pays return shipping, and any exclusions (final-sale items, perishables, custom orders). This is the page that resolves the chargeback story above. Put a one-line summary near the buy button and the full policy at checkout — clarity here measurably reduces disputes and refund fights. ### 4. Shipping Policy (if you ship) Processing times, carriers, tracking, and what happens if a package is delayed, lost, or stolen. Spelling out delivery expectations up front heads off a surprising share of “where’s my order” complaints before they start. ### 5. A cookie/tracking note and consent (situational) If you serve customers in the EU or UK, you need genuine cookie consent before non-essential tracking fires. For a purely local St. Louis audience, a simple, honest note about the analytics and cookies you use is good practice rather than a strict legal must. Don’t bolt on an aggressive EU-style consent banner you don’t need — match the tool to your actual customers. Solid legal ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/essential-legal-pages-for-b2c-websites-compliance-trust-protection

## The St. Louis Service Guide: Finding a Pro & Starting Your Own Revised July 23, 2026 How do I find or start a service business in St. Louis? To find a trusted local service pro, check licensing and insurance, get written estimates from two or three providers, read reviews across platforms, and get the scope and price in writing. To start one in Missouri: form an LLC with the Secretary of State, get an EIN, register for any required taxes, and get the right local license — Missouri has no statewide general business license, so requirements depend on your city or county. Some trades need a state professional license; many (plumbers, electricians, contractors) are licensed locally. Keep reading ↓Imagine two people on the same Tuesday night in the St. Louis metro. In Kirkwood, a homeowner is staring at a water stain spreading across the ceiling, phone in hand, typing “plumber near me” and hoping the first name that comes up is one they can trust. Twenty miles away in St. Charles, a talented handyman who’s been doing side jobs for friends is wondering whether he could finally turn it into a real business — and where on earth he’d even start. Those two people are the whole St. Louis service economy in miniature: someone who needs good work done, and someone capable of doing it, trying to find each other. This guide is honestly written for both of them. If you’re hiring, you’ll get a clear way to find and vet a local pro. If you’re building a service business across the metro — from Florissant to Chesterfield to O’Fallon to the Metro East towns of Belleville and Edwardsville — you’ll get the real, unglamorous steps to do it right in Missouri. No hype, no invented statistics, and no pretending it’s easier than it is. Just what actually matters on both sides of the handshake — because the St. Louis metro, with roughly 2.8 million people spread across Missouri and Illinois, runs on exactly these small, local, person-to-person transactions. ## If you’re hiring: how to find a service pro you can trust The hard part of hiring locally isn’t finding *a* provider — it’s finding one you won’t regret. A short, honest checklist does most of the work: - **Check licensing where it applies.**Some trades need a license (more on which ones below). For those, ask for the number and verify it. For a licensed profession, “trust me” isn’t enough. - **Confirm insurance.**Ask for proof of liability insurance — and workers’ comp if they bring a crew. If someone’s hurt on your property or your home is damaged, this is what stands between you and a nightmare. - **Get written estimates from more than one.**Itemized, in writing, from at least two or three providers. Be wary of anyone demanding a large cash payment up front or pressuring you to decide on the spot. - **Read reviews across platforms, not just the star average.**Look at how a business- *responds*to criticism, not only how many stars it has. According to BrightLocal’s 2026 consumer survey, the vast majority of consumers read reviews before choosing a local business — 97% read them, with about 71% reading regularly. Patterns matter more than any single glowing or angry review. - **Ask for local references and recent work.**A good pro can point to similar jobs nearby. A vague answer is an answer. - **Get it in writing.**Scope, price, timeline, payment schedule, and any warranty — on paper before work starts. Run that list and you’ve filtered out most of the risk. The point of a good local directory is to make the first few steps faster: see a business’s services, service area, and reviews together, so you’re comparing real information instead of gambling on whoever bought the top ad. It’s the difference between an informed hire and a hopeful one — and with the bigger jobs (a re-pipe, a roof, a full clean-out), that difference is measured in thousands of dollars and a lot of stress. Looking for a trusted local pro — a plumber in Florissant, a cleaner in Chesterfield, a stylist in St. Charles? ## Transforming St. Louis: A Comprehensive City Cleanliness Program Revised July 23, 2026 How can illegal dumping be prevented? Illegal dumping is prevented best by pairing deterrence with easy alternatives: camera surveillance (St. Louis runs about 275 anti-dumping cameras), cleaning up existing messes fast (people dump where it’s already dirty), convenient free bulk-disposal so the legal option beats the alley, and community and corporate cleanup partnerships — like the $1 million Boeing grant that cleared Kinloch. Enforcement alone rarely holds; deterrence plus easy disposal and local pride does. Keep reading ↓Drive down the wrong alley in parts of St. Louis on a Tuesday morning and you’ll see it before you smell it: a mattress slumped against a fence, a busted TV, bags that split open in the last rain. Ride down a main drag — Gravois, Kingshighway, West Florissant — and you’ll watch a fast-food bag sail out of a car window at 40 miles an hour. Chicken bones. A diaper. We wish we were exaggerating. We’re not. Those of us who have lived in the city 20-plus years know the reputation, because St. Louis earned it honestly. “Trashy” is a word this town has worn for a long time. But here is the part we hesitate to say out loud, because it sounds too much like a sales pitch: over the last few years, it has gotten *noticeably* better. Not fixed — certain pockets are still magnets for illegal dumping, and litter still blows across every ZIP code — but better. Cleaner blocks. Fewer tires in the creeks. More people who seem to actually care. This is the honest story of how St. Louis got dirty, who is quietly cleaning it up right now — from a $1 million Boeing grant in Kinloch to the volunteers who have shown up for Brightside since 1982 — what has actually worked in other cities that turned the corner, and how you can be part of it, whether you own a business here or just love the place. ## Why does St. Louis have a reputation for being dirty? The short answer: St. Louis is a big city that lost most of its people. The population peaked around 856,000 in 1950 and sits closer to 280,000 today — inside a metro of roughly 2.8 million. When more than half a city moves away over a few decades, it leaves behind something specific: vacant lots, empty buildings, and long stretches where nobody is watching. The city’s land bank, the Land Reutilization Authority, holds thousands of those vacant parcels. An empty lot with no owner around is exactly where a contractor with a truck full of demolition debris dumps it at 2 a.m. rather than pay the landfill fee. So the trash breaks into two different problems, and it matters that we don’t blur them. **Illegal dumping** — the mattresses, the tires, the truckloads of construction waste — concentrates heavily in North City’s alleys and vacant lots, where the dumper counts on nobody looking. **Litter** — the bottles, the bags, the car-window stuff — is genuinely citywide, South City to North, Dogtown to Baden. Most neighborhoods deal mostly with litter and the occasional dumped couch; the heavy, organized dumping is a North City burden the rest of the city rarely sees. Here is the part most people never think about, and it’s the reason litter is more than an eyesore. That plastic bottle in the gutter doesn’t just sit there. The next hard rain washes it into a storm drain, and St. Louis storm drains run to the River Des Peres, then the Mississippi. The bag that blew out of a car in Affton can end up wrapped around a turtle downstream, or broken into microplastics in the water a city pulls its drinking supply from. Litter is a water-pollution problem wearing a disguise. And it costs money — real money, your money. Every hour a city crew spends hauling an illegally dumped pile of shingles is an hour not spent fixing a park, and every dollar spent chasing dumpers is a dollar not spent on a rec center or a streetlight. A dirty city taxes itself twice: once in what the mess does to property values and business, and again in what it costs to clean up. ## Is St. Louis actually getting cleaner? Honestly? Yes — slowly, unevenly, and mostly in effort rather than in a tidy statistic you can frame. We want to be straight with you here, because the whole point of this piece is trust: the same police unit that runs the cameras will tell you the problem is far from solved. What has changed is that the city stopped treating dumping as background noise and started treating it as a crime with a badge behind it. The St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department’s Environmental Investigations Unit now monitors roughly **275 surveillance cameras** trained on the alleys and vacant lots that dumpers favor, funded in part with federal American Rescue Plan money, and it has issued a record number of citations for illegal dumping. The Citizens’ Service Bureau — the city’s 311 line, at 314-622-4800 — takes dumping reports, and the city offers a reward of up to $100 for a tip that leads to a conviction. Is it enough? No. But a dumper who used to face zero odds of getting caught now faces a camera and a fine, ...

## When a Contractor Won't Finish the Job (Missouri vs. Illinois Rules) Revised July 28, 2026 What do you do when a contractor takes your money and disappears? It depends which side of the river your house is on. In **Missouri** there is **no state contractor licensing board** — no agency can suspend a license or order your money back, so your leverage is a **credit card chargeback** (fastest), a certified demand letter, and **small claims up to $5,000** (RSMo 482.305). In **Illinois** you have more: work over **$1,000 requires a written contract** plus the state consumer-rights pamphlet *before* you sign, and **roofers must hold a state license and surety bond**. ⚠️ In both states, an unpaid subcontractor can lien your house **even if you already paid the contractor**. ## What do you do when a contractor takes your money and disappears? Search that and you will be sent to a licensing board. Which board depends on the day: we pulled the live results from a Missouri location and page one was California’s CSLB, Arizona’s Registrar of Contractors, Tennessee, Florida, Massachusetts, North Dakota, Maryland, Louisiana. Not one of them has any authority over a contractor in Missouri. **Missouri has no statewide contractor licensing board**, which means there is no state agency that can suspend a license, order restitution, or make anyone come back and finish your kitchen. The complaint form everyone tells you to file does not exist here. That is genuinely worse for homeowners than it is in most states, and it is worth knowing before you hire rather than after. But “no board” does not mean no recourse. It means your leverage is in different places, and the order you use them in matters. ## First: stop and write things down Before you make a single angry phone call, spend twenty minutes building a record. Everything below depends on it, and it gets harder to reconstruct the longer you wait. - **The contract**, plus any change orders, texts, and emails where scope or timing was discussed. Texts count. - **Every payment**— amount, date, method. Cancelled checks and card statements are stronger than memory. - **Dated photographs**of the current state of the work. Take more than you think you need. - **A timeline**: promised dates, actual visits, when contact stopped. - **The permit status.**Call your municipality and ask whether a permit was pulled, in whose name, and whether any inspections passed. That last one is often the moment things become clear. A contractor who never pulled the permit has usually left you with unpermitted work as well as unfinished work — and that is a problem that resurfaces years later when you sell. ## Second: send a written demand, and send it properly A phone call is not a record. A letter is. Send a short, unemotional written demand that states what was agreed, what was paid, what is incomplete, exactly what you want done, and a specific deadline. Send it by certified mail with return receipt, and email a copy. This is not a formality and it is not about being polite. Every step after this one goes better when you can show a judge that you asked plainly and gave them a chance. Some contractors also simply reappear at this point, because a certified letter reads differently than a voicemail. Keep it factual. Do not threaten things you are not going to do, and do not describe your feelings about the situation. Dates, dollars, deliverables. ## Third: the leverage Missouri actually gives you With no licensing board in the picture, these are the levers that exist: ### Small claims court — up to $5,000 Missouri’s small claims division handles civil claims where the amount in controversy does not exceed **$5,000**, under RSMo 482.305. It is designed to be used without a lawyer, and for a deposit that vanished or a job abandoned partway, it is frequently the right tool. One useful wrinkle: if your damages exceed $5,000, **you can choose to waive the excess** and stay in small claims for the speed and the simplicity. You give up the difference permanently, so it is a real trade — but for a $6,500 loss, many people decide that recovering $5,000 in a few months beats chasing $6,500 for a year. ### Associate circuit court, above that Larger claims move up to associate circuit court, where the process is more formal and a lawyer starts to make sense. If the number is big enough that you are weighing this, talk to a construction attorney before filing anything — the strategy differs and the deadlines are real. ### The Missouri Attorney General’s consumer complaint The Attorney General accepts consumer complaints, and filing one is worth doing. Be clear-eyed about what it is, though: it builds a public record and can contribute to a pattern that draws enforcement attention. It is not a mechanism that gets your money back, and no one should wait on it instead of filing suit. ### Your municipality’s permit office Underused, and in Missouri it is closer to a regulator than anything the state offers. If the contractor is registered in that city, the city has a relationship with them and an interest in how they behave. If the work was done without a required permit, the city wants to know that too. Call and describe what happened. ### The Better Business Bureau No legal power, ...
