## Charlie Gitto’s on The Hill: A St. Louis Italian Institution Revised July 23, 2026 What is Charlie Gitto’s on The Hill known for? Charlie Gitto’s on The Hill (5226 Shaw Ave, St. Louis) is a traditional Italian fine-dining institution open since 1981, famous for toasted ravioli, handmade pastas, veal, and seafood. It occupies the former Angelo’s, one of the most commonly cited birthplaces of St. Louis toasted ravioli, though the dish’s origin is disputed. It’s a special-occasion, reservation-recommended, dinner-only restaurant; call (314) 772-8898. Keep reading ↓Some restaurants are just dinner; a few are institutions. On The Hill — St. Louis’s historic Italian neighborhood, all brick bungalows and fire-hydrants painted red, white, and green — Charlie Gitto’s has spent more than four decades earning the second title. It’s the kind of place St. Louisans take out-of-town guests to prove a point about their city, and where a lot of families have marked anniversaries, graduations, and the occasional splurge just because. This is an honest look at Charlie Gitto’s on The Hill: what it is, its place in the city’s most famous food story, what to order, and how to plan a visit. One quick note up front — this is specifically the Shaw Avenue location on The Hill, the original fine-dining room, not the separate Gitto’s spots elsewhere in the metro. ## A genuine St. Louis institution Charlie Gitto’s on The Hill sits at **5226 Shaw Avenue** in the heart of the neighborhood, and it has been serving traditional Italian fine dining there since **1981**, when Charlie Gitto Jr. bought the restaurant that previously occupied the space and put his name on it. The Gitto family has deep St. Louis restaurant roots stretching back decades, and Charlie Gitto Jr. still owns and runs the Hill room today. That kind of continuity — the same family, the same corner, for over 40 years — is rare, and it’s a big part of why the place feels like the real thing rather than a theme. It’s a proper white-tablecloth Italian restaurant — a special-occasion room where the service is polished and the food is classic rather than trend-chasing. The reviews back up the reputation: it holds strong ratings, generally in the range of 4.3 to 4.7 stars across the major platforms, each with well over a thousand reviews. That’s the kind of deep, consistent record a restaurant only earns by getting it right, night after night, for a very long time. Trends come and go; a place that’s still packing its dining room after four decades is telling you something no marketing can. In a restaurant landscape where the average spot doesn’t survive its first few years, that kind of longevity is its own recommendation. ## The Hill: the neighborhood that made it To understand Charlie Gitto’s, it helps to understand The Hill. This compact St. Louis neighborhood was settled by Italian immigrants — many from northern Italy and Sicily — who came to work the area’s clay mines in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Generations later, it remains one of the most authentically intact Italian-American neighborhoods in the United States: rows of tidy brick shotgun houses, family-run bakeries and delis, bocce courts, and the famous fire hydrants painted in the Italian tricolor. It’s the childhood home of baseball legends Yogi Berra and Joe Garagiola, and it wears its heritage without a trace of theme-park artificiality. Restaurants like Charlie Gitto’s aren’t transplants dropped into this neighborhood — they grew out of it, run by families who are part of its fabric. That’s the difference between eating “Italian food” and eating *on The Hill*: here, the tradition is lived, not performed. When you sit down at Gitto’s, you’re eating in the middle of a genuine cultural neighborhood that has kept its identity for more than a century, which is a rare and increasingly precious thing in American cities. ## The toasted-ravioli story You can’t talk about Charlie Gitto’s without the toasted ravioli — the breaded, deep-fried, marinara-dunked appetizer that’s practically the official starter of St. Louis. Here’s the honest version of the lore, because it’s more interesting than the tidy myth: Gitto’s occupies the former home of Angelo’s, and the widely-told legend is that a chef there, back in the 1940s, accidentally dropped a ravioli into hot oil instead of water — and a St. Louis icon was born. Charlie Gitto’s is one of the most commonly cited birthplaces of the dish, thanks to that lineage. It’s worth being straight, though: the true origin is genuinely disputed, with a few Hill restaurants each laying claim, so the fairest thing to say is that Gitto’s is part of the dish’s founding story rather than its sole inventor. Either way, ordering toasted ravioli here — at a place woven into its history — is about as St. Louis as a meal gets, a small edible piece of the city’s history. If you’ve never tried the dish, this is the place to have your first: crisp, golden pillows of breaded pasta, hot from the fryer, with a bowl of marinara for dunking. It’s simple, a little indulgent, and completely beloved for good reason. Order a plate to share and you’ll understand instantly why St. Louis claims it so fiercely. Making a night of it on The Hill? ## How to Remove a Google Review (Mostly You Can't - Here's What Works) Revised July 28, 2026 Can you actually remove a Google review? **Almost never, if you’re the business.** Only two parties can remove a review: the person who wrote it, and Google. An owner can **report** a review for breaking Google’s content policies — spam, conflict of interest, off-topic, harassment, impersonation — but a review that’s merely *negative or unfair* will not come down. ⚠️ And since **October 21, 2024** the FTC’s consumer reviews rule bans **review suppression**, fake reviews, buying positive OR negative reviews, and undisclosed insider reviews — with penalties up to **$51,744 per violation**. Reporting a genuine policy breach is fine; pressuring a reviewer is not. 💡 Your public reply is read by future customers, not the reviewer — that’s where the value is. ## Can you actually remove a Google review? Almost never, if you are the business. That is the honest answer, and it is not the one most of page one is selling. **A business owner cannot delete a customer’s review.** There is no button, no account level, no support tier that grants it. You can *report* a review to Google for violating its content policies, and Google decides. Only two parties can actually remove a review: the person who wrote it, and Google. Search the question and you will find the flag-button instructions repeated a dozen ways, alongside companies promising permanent removal on a no-win-no-fee basis. What none of page one mentions is that **this whole area became federally regulated in October 2024**, and some of what gets sold as review management is now the kind of conduct the FTC can fine you for. So this page covers three things in order: what genuinely works, what the new rule changed, and the thing that outperforms removal anyway. ## What actually gets a review taken down Google removes reviews that break its content policies — not reviews that are unfair, wrong, or written by someone having a bad day. That distinction is the whole game, and it is why most reports fail. **Reportable**, broadly: spam and fake engagement, content posted by someone with a conflict of interest, off-topic content that is not about a customer experience, profanity and harassment, impersonation, and personal information. A competitor review-bombing you, a review that is plainly about a different business, an ex-employee’s rant, five one-star ratings from accounts created the same afternoon — those are policy arguments and worth making. **Not reportable**: “this is unfair,” “they misremembered,” “we did nothing wrong,” or a one-star rating with no text. A negative opinion from a real customer is exactly what the platform is for, and no amount of escalating gets it removed. To report one: open your Google Business Profile, go to reviews, find it, use the three-dot menu, choose to report it, and pick the policy it violates. Then screenshot everything — the review, the profile of who wrote it, the date — because if you escalate later, the review may already be edited. Pick the *specific* policy, not the closest emotional match. “This review is spam because the account has posted identical text on four unrelated businesses today” is a reviewable claim. “This review is unfair” is not. ## What changed in October 2024, and why it matters more than the flag button The FTC’s **Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials took effect on October 21, 2024**, passed on a 5–0 vote. It is the first time the agency has had civil penalty authority here, and the numbers are not symbolic: **up to $51,744 per violation** for knowing violators, plus consumer restitution. What it prohibits, in plain terms: - **Fake reviews and testimonials**— written by people who never used the business, or by AI, presented as genuine. - **Buying reviews, positive or negative.**Both directions. Paying for a rival’s bad reviews is squarely covered. - **Incentivizing reviews that express a particular sentiment**— conditioning a reward on the review being positive. - **Undisclosed insider reviews**, including from officers and managers, that do not clearly and conspicuously disclose the connection. Your manager reviewing your business without saying so is now a rule problem, not just bad taste. - **Review suppression**— using unfounded legal threats, intimidation, or similar pressure to force a review down, or presenting your displayed reviews as if they were all the reviews when negative ones have been withheld. Read that last one against how review removal is often sold. A service promising that bad reviews will “disappear in seven days” is either flagging genuine policy violations, which you can do yourself for free, or doing something else. If the something else involves pressuring reviewers, you are the client whose name is on it. To be clear, because the opposite reading would be worse: **reporting a review that genuinely violates Google’s policies is completely legitimate.** Nothing in the rule discourages that. The line is between contesting content on the platform and leaning on a human being to retract it. ## When the reviewer was never a customer This is the most common version of the problem for small businesses, and it is genuinely maddening: reviews from people who were never there. Sometimes it is mistaken identity — two businesses with similar names in the metro, and the reviewer picked the wrong pin. Sometimes it is a competitor. Sometimes it is one person with ...

## St. Louis Hotels with Indoor Pools: The Verified List by Area Revised July 28, 2026 Which St. Louis hotels have an indoor pool? St. Louis hotels with confirmed year-round indoor pools include the Drury Plaza at the Arch and Hilton at the Ballpark (downtown), the Drury Inn and Hampton Inn & Suites at Forest Park (near the Zoo), the Clayton Plaza Hotel, Drury and Hyatt Place in Chesterfield, and Embassy Suites at the airport and in St. Charles. Drury and Embassy Suites are the most reliable bets for an indoor pool. Keep reading ↓Picture a gray St. Louis Saturday in February. The kids are bouncing off the walls, the forecast is hopeless, and everyone needs to burn energy somewhere warm. Or maybe it’s a July scorcher and the last thing anyone wants is a sun-baked outdoor deck. Either way, the answer is the same: a hotel with a real, heated, **indoor** pool — open year-round, weather be damned, and ready whether it’s a snow day or a heat wave outside. An indoor pool is quietly one of the most useful things a hotel can offer a family. It turns a rained-out afternoon into the highlight of the trip, tires the kids out before bed, and gives everyone a reason to stay put after a long day of sightseeing. It’s also a genuine year-round amenity in a city that swings from icy Januaries to swampy Julys — the water’s the same perfect temperature either way. The catch is that plenty of hotel listings blur “pool” and “indoor pool,” and a family can arrive to find a seasonal outdoor deck that’s closed for the season. So here’s a local’s guide to St. Louis-metro hotels with **confirmed year-round indoor pools**, sorted by area, plus a quick honest list of popular hotels whose pools are *outdoor-only* — so you book the right one the first time. ## St. Louis Hotels With Confirmed Indoor Pools, by Area ## Downtown: Pool Plus Everything Within Walking Distance If you want a swim *and* the Arch, the ballpark, and City Museum on foot, downtown delivers. The **Drury Plaza Hotel St. Louis at the Arch** has a year-round indoor pool plus two whirlpools, and it stacks Drury’s trademark free hot breakfast and free evening food and drinks on top — a genuinely good family value a short walk from Busch Stadium and the Gateway Arch. Nearby, the **Hilton St. Louis at the Ballpark** keeps a climate-controlled indoor pool in a glass atrium, with views toward the Arch and the ballpark, right across from Ballpark Village. One important correction for downtown: the **St. Louis Union Station Hotel** is a wonderful, historic place to stay, but its pool is a *seasonal outdoor* one, not an indoor pool — so if a winter swim is the goal, steer to the Drury or the Hilton instead. ## Forest Park: Pool After the Zoo and the Museums The Forest Park area is the sweet spot for families, because you can pair the free Saint Louis Zoo, Science Center, and Art Museum with an indoor pool for the after-nap wind-down. The **Drury Inn & Suites St. Louis Forest Park** has a heated year-round indoor/outdoor pool and a hot tub, plus the usual free Drury extras. And the **Hampton Inn & Suites St. Louis at Forest Park** — the closest hotel to the zoo with an indoor pool — adds a hot tub and free hot breakfast. Both put you minutes from the park, so the kids can chase penguins in the morning and cannonball in the afternoon — the ideal family one-two punch. ## Clayton: A Quieter, Upscale Home Base For a calmer, more upscale base a few miles west, the **Clayton Plaza Hotel & Extended Stay** runs a year-round heated pool and offers extended-stay suites — handy for longer trips or families who want a bit more room and a kitchen. Clayton itself is a walkable district of restaurants and shops, and you’re a short drive from Forest Park and the zoo. (Note: some older listings still show a “Sheraton” or “Crowne Plaza” name for this property; the current brand is the independent Clayton Plaza Hotel & Extended Stay.) ## West County: Chesterfield and Creve Coeur Out in West County, indoor-pool options are plentiful. The **Drury Plaza Hotel St. Louis Chesterfield** has a heated year-round indoor/outdoor pool; **Hyatt Place St. Louis/Chesterfield** keeps an indoor pool open daily; and the **Drury Inn & Suites St. Louis Creve Coeur** offers a heated indoor pool and a large jacuzzi. This area is convenient to Chesterfield’s shopping and the Creve Coeur/Maryland Heights corridor — a good pick if your trip centers on the west side of the metro rather than downtown. (One to skip if you need indoor: Homewood Suites Chesterfield’s pool is outdoor and seasonal.) ## By the Airport: Easy Flights, Warm Water If you’re flying in and out, or just want an easy in-and-out stay, the airport cluster in Bridgeton has solid indoor pools. The **Embassy Suites by Hilton St. Louis Airport** has an indoor pool, all-suite rooms, free made-to-order breakfast, and a free airport shuttle; the **Renaissance St. Louis Airport Hotel** offers a year-round indoor/outdoor pool and its own free shuttle. In a stretch of the metro dominated by familiar franchise signs, that’s worth knowing about, because the independent, family-run places are usually the ones actually worth the drive. ## What Chimi’s Fresh-Mex actually is Chimi’s Fresh-Mex is a St. Louis-area **family-owned local chain** — run by the Casillas family — serving fresh, made-to-order Mexican food. That “Fresh-Mex” label is the key: this is fresh, from-the-kitchen Mexican rather than heavy, gloppy Tex-Mex. The Wentzville location is one of several across the metro, from St. Charles County out into St. Louis County, and each carries the same menu and the same family standards. ## Indoor Things to Do in St. Louis: The Best Rainy-Day Attractions Revised July 12, 2026 What are the best indoor things to do in St. Louis? St. Louis is stacked with indoor options for any weather: the free Saint Louis Science Center, Art Museum, and Missouri History Museum; the climb-through City Museum; the Magic House children’s museum in Kirkwood; and the Saint Louis Aquarium and the St. Louis Wheel at Union Station. Several of the best are completely free. Keep reading ↓Every St. Louisan knows the feeling. The forecast flips to all-day rain, or the July heat index hits triple digits, and suddenly the zoo-and-park plan is out the window. The kids still have energy to burn, or you’ve got out-of-town guests and a day to fill — and you need somewhere good, indoors, that won’t break the bank. Good news: St. Louis is loaded with world-class indoor attractions, and several of the very best are completely **free**. This is genuinely one of the city’s superpowers — a rainy or brutally hot day, which would blow up a trip in a lot of places, is barely an inconvenience here. Here’s a local’s guide to the best indoor things to do in St. Louis when the weather won’t cooperate — from a museum you can literally climb through, to free art and science, to warm-weather escapes under glass. ## St. Louis Indoor Attractions at a Glance ## The Free Big Three: World-Class and $0 Here’s the local secret that makes a rainy St. Louis day so cheap: three of the city’s major museums have **free general admission** every day, thanks to a regional cultural tax district. The **Saint Louis Science Center** is a hands-on wonderland of experiments, dinosaurs, and a planetarium (the Omnimax and some simulators are paid add-ons; note it’s typically closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays). The **Saint Louis Art Museum**, up on Art Hill in Forest Park, spans thousands of years of art for free. And the **Missouri History Museum**, also in Forest Park, tells the city’s story — from the 1904 World’s Fair to Chuck Berry — at no charge. Three world-class institutions, zero admission. You can add a fourth free stop: the **Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis** in Grand Center is always free, with rotating modern and experimental exhibitions. Together, these make a rainy day in St. Louis one of the best cultural bargains in the country. It’s a genuinely unusual perk — most big cities charge $20 or more per person at their flagship museums, while a St. Louis family can spend a full day at three world-class institutions and pay nothing but parking. If you’re showing the city off to visitors, this is the trump card: world-class culture, zero admission, all indoors when the weather turns. ## City Museum: The Indoor Wonderland If you do one paid indoor thing in St. Louis, make it the **City Museum**. Housed in a 600,000-square-foot former shoe warehouse and dreamed up by the late artist Bob Cassilly, it’s part museum, part playground, part fever dream — caves and tunnels, multi-story slides, a rooftop school bus hanging off the edge, and endless salvaged-material art to climb through. It’s genuinely as fun for adults as for kids (wear clothes you can crawl in). On a miserable-weather day, you can lose three or four hours here without noticing. A tip from locals: it’s busiest on weekend afternoons, so go at opening or on a weekday if you can, and know that much of the fun is physical — this is a climb-crawl-slide kind of place, not a look-with-your-eyes museum. There’s even a pinball and arcade room tucked inside if your crew needs a breather from the tunnels. ## For the Kids: Aquariums, Wheels, and Hands-On Fun Families have easy wins downtown. The **St. Louis Aquarium at Union Station** brings touch pools and a shark tank under one roof, and the **St. Louis Wheel** right outside is a climate-controlled, 200-foot observation wheel that runs year-round — a fun, dry way to see the skyline even in a downpour. Out in Kirkwood, **The Magic House** (the St. Louis Children’s Museum) is a beloved hands-on playground for younger kids, and in Chesterfield, the **Sophia M. Sachs Butterfly House** is a warm indoor tropical conservatory with roughly 2,000 free-flying butterflies — a genuine mood-lifter on a gray day. Little kids tend to love it: butterflies land right on you, it’s warm and calm, and it’s an easy hour that doesn’t require a nap-time meltdown recovery afterward. ## Rainy-Day Ideas for Grown-Ups, Too Indoor doesn’t have to mean kid-focused. The **Missouri Botanical Garden’s Climatron** — a geodesic-dome rainforest conservatory — is a lush, humid escape when it’s cold and gray outside (and St. Louis city and county residents get in free on Wednesday and Saturday mornings). **City Foundry STL** in Midtown packs a food hall, the Alamo Drafthouse cinema, Puttshack’s high-tech mini golf, and more under one roof — a whole indoor date without moving your car. And for a classic grown-up rainy afternoon, the free Art Museum plus a long lunch is hard to beat. Grand Center, the arts district around the Contemporary Art Museum, is also home to theaters, jazz at the Dark Room, and the Fabulous Fox — so a gray day can easily turn into a culture-packed evening if you let it. ## Indoor Mini Golf, Bowling, and Other Rainy-Day Standbys When you ...

## Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill: Mexican Favorites in St. Charles County Revised July 23, 2026 Where is Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill and what does it serve? Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill is a family-run Mexican restaurant with two St. Charles County locations: the Winghaven area of O’Fallon (905 Caledonia Dr) and the original in Warrenton (1000 Warrenton Outlet Ctr, Ste 14). It serves street tacos, sizzling fajitas, carne asada, chunky guacamole, its signature Trash Can Nachos, and a deep list of margaritas and tequilas. It also runs a food truck for private events. Keep reading ↓Imagine a Friday night in St. Charles County. Someone in the group wants tacos, someone else wants a margarita the size of their face, and nobody wants to drive downtown for either. Casa Tequila has built the kind of loyal following — hundreds of four-and-five-star reviews across two locations, holding right around a 4.5-star average — that only comes from feeding people well, again and again. Here’s an honest look at what it is, what to order, and where to find it. ## Two locations, one family First, a point the internet often muddles: Casa Tequila Cantina & Grill is **one restaurant with two locations**, both in St. Charles County’s western reaches. The original is in **Warrenton**, inside the Warrenton outlet center; the second, in the **Winghaven** development in **O’Fallon**, opened a couple of years later. “Winghaven” isn’t a separate place — it’s just the name of the O’Fallon store’s neighborhood. Both are run by the same husband-and-wife team, Leo and Jessenia Lopez, and that family ownership shows. This is a from-scratch, hands-on operation, not a franchise following a corporate playbook — the kind of independent local restaurant that a chain-heavy stretch of suburbia is lucky to have. When the same family has its name over two doors, the recipes and the standards travel between them, which is why regulars trust either location to deliver the same plate. ## What to order The menu is classic Mexican done with care, and a few things earn their reputation: - **Street tacos**— carne asada, al pastor, barbacoa, shrimp — the everyday workhorse and a great first order. - **Sizzling fajitas**— steak or chicken, arriving loud and fragrant, built for sharing. - **The Trash Can Nachos**— a signature, and exactly as over-the-top and shareable as the name promises. - **Carne asada and chunky guacamole**— the fundamentals, done right, which is the real test of any Mexican kitchen. - **The margaritas**— genuinely a draw here, backed by a deep tequila selection numbering in the hundreds. Regulars call them out by name. Portions run generous, which is part of the value equation — you tend to leave full and carrying a box. Menus evolve, so if you have a specific craving, glance at the current menu online or just ask — the staff are happy to point you to what’s good tonight. Reviewers across Google and the delivery apps routinely rank it among the better Mexican food in the area, and the consistency — the same quality on a random Tuesday as on a packed Saturday — is exactly what turns a first-time visitor into a monthly regular. If you’re eating at home, both locations are set up for takeout, and the food travels well — tacos and fajitas hold up on the drive across O’Fallon or Warrenton better than most. It makes a solid weeknight option when nobody wants to cook but everyone’s tired of the usual pizza rotation, and it delivers through the major apps for the nights when even leaving the house feels like too much. Yes — Satchmo’s Bar & Grill (13375 Olive Blvd, Chesterfield, MO 63017; (314) 392-9401; satchmosgrill.com) is open under new ownership since mid-2024. The new team remodeled it into a more polished American neighborhood bar and grill and reworked the menu. Signature dishes include the Smokehouse Burger (cheddar, bacon, BBQ sauce, hand-battered onion rings on brioche), shrimp and grits with andouille, and loaded nachos. Keep reading ↓Imagine it’s a Thursday evening in Chesterfield and you don’t want a big production — no white tablecloths, no forty-minute wait, no chain off the highway that could be anywhere in America. You want a comfortable room, a genuinely good burger, a cold draft at a fair price, and maybe a game on. That’s the exact itch a good neighborhood bar and grill scratches, and in west St. Louis County, Satchmo’s Bar & Grill has settled back into that role. Here’s an honest look at what Satchmo’s is today — because it changed hands recently and the menu changed with it — what’s actually worth ordering, and why it’s a solid pick for a low-key night out in Chesterfield. ## What Satchmo’s is today Satchmo’s Bar & Grill sits at **13375 Olive Boulevard in Chesterfield, MO 63017**, phone **(314) 392-9401** (the current official site is **satchmosgrill.com**). It’s an American neighborhood bar and grill — burgers, sandwiches, salads, a few heartier entrees, a full bar, and TVs for the game. The name is a nod to Louis Armstrong, whose nickname was “Satchmo,” but don’t come expecting a jazz theme or Cajun cooking; the concept is straightforward, well-executed American pub fare. The important recent news: Satchmo’s came under **new ownership in mid-2024**, and the new team — led by a longtime restaurant operator with decades in the business — put it through several months of remodeling before reopening as a more polished, upscale-leaning bar and grill. If you visited years ago and remember it one way, it’s worth a fresh look; the room, the service, and the menu all got a reset. ## What to order The menu is focused rather than sprawling, which is usually a good sign — it means the kitchen is cooking a tight list well rather than reheating a phone book. A few things stand out: - **The Smokehouse Burger.**This is the one to beat — a burger topped with cheddar, bacon, tangy BBQ sauce, and hand-battered onion rings on a brioche bun, with fries. It’s the signature for a reason: rich, messy in the best way, and built for a hungry night. - **Shrimp & Grits.**A genuinely more ambitious plate than you expect from a bar menu — grilled shrimp and andouille sausage in a bouillabaisse-style sauce over cheesy grits. It’s the dish that shows the new kitchen has range beyond burgers and wings. - **The nachos.**A proper shareable starter — house tortilla chips loaded with cheese sauce, tomatoes, jalapeños, and black olives. Good for the table while you figure out the rest of the order. - **A salad done right.**There’s a real lineup here — a House, a Caesar, a Steakhouse, and a Baja Explosion — so the lighter eater in your group isn’t stuck with an afterthought. Save room if you can: the dessert list keeps it local and comforting, with St. Louis-style gooey butter cake, key lime pie, and handmade donuts. It’s the kind of short, well-chosen menu where it’s hard to order badly — start with the Smokehouse Burger on a first visit and branch out from there. ## Old St. Louis Chop Suey & the St. Paul Sandwich: A Hometown Tradition Worth Tasting Revised July 12, 2026 What type of cuisine was Old St. Louis Chop Suey known for? “St. Louis chop suey” means the tradition of small Chinese-American carry-out restaurants across the city, and their signature is the St. Paul sandwich: an egg foo young patty on white bread with mayo, pickle, lettuce, and tomato. Get a great one at Park Chop Suey, Mai Lee, Chinese Express, or Bo Fung. Keep reading ↓Maybe you grew up with it. A little corner carry-out with a glowing “CHOP SUEY” sign, a bulletproof lazy-susan window, and a paper sack that came back warm with something you’d never find on a menu anywhere else in the country. Or maybe you’ve lived in St. Louis for years and never once ordered the one sandwich that’s pure hometown. Either way, the old St. Louis chop-suey house — and its signature, the St. Paul sandwich — is one of the most quietly St. Louis things you can eat. It’s cheap, it’s a little strange to outsiders, and it carries a century of city history in a couple slices of white bread. Here’s what it actually is, where it came from, and where you can still get one today — because once you understand the story behind it, that strange little sandwich starts to taste like the city itself. ## Where to Get One, at a Glance ## What the St. Paul Sandwich Actually Is If you’ve never had one: the St. Paul sandwich is a hot **egg foo young patty** — egg, bean sprouts, and minced onion, bound with a little flour and fried — served between two slices of plain white bread with **mayonnaise, dill pickle, lettuce, and tomato**. That’s the classic build. Order it “with meat” and you can add chicken, pork, shrimp, or beef mixed into the patty; a “Special” usually piles on a combination. It sounds odd written out — a fried egg patty on cold white bread with mayo and pickle — and that’s exactly the point. It’s comfort food invented at the intersection of a Chinese-American kitchen and a Midwestern lunch counter, and it tastes like nowhere else because it exists almost nowhere else. How you eat one is part of the ritual. It comes wrapped in paper, warm and a little messy, best eaten in the car or straight out of the sack. The contrast is the whole appeal: the hot, savory, fried egg patty against cool mayo, crisp lettuce, and the sharp bite of dill pickle. Most shops let you customize — extra meat, no tomato, hot mustard or soy on the side — and each carry-out’s version is a little different, which is exactly why St. Louisans argue about whose is best. ## The name: fact, legend, and a little mystery Nobody can prove where the “St. Paul” name truly came from, and that’s part of its charm. The most-repeated story ties it to Steven Yuen and his Minnesota hometown. Food writers have floated other ideas over the years — including that the sandwich is a cousin of the egg-based “Denver” or “Western” sandwich, which some historians believe Chinese cooks helped create from egg foo young. There’s even a bit of folklore about a cook aboard a Mississippi steamboat named the St. Paul. Treat all of it as the kind of tale that grows up around a beloved local food: fun to trade, impossible to nail down, and beside the point once the sandwich is in your hands. ## A Taste With Deep St. Louis Roots To understand the St. Paul sandwich, you have to know a little about **Hop Alley** — St. Louis’s original Chinatown. It sat downtown, roughly bounded by Seventh, Tenth, Walnut, and Chestnut streets. The city’s first Chinese resident, a man recorded as Alla Lee, arrived in 1857, and the community really took shape after 1869, when a wave of roughly 250 immigrants came seeking factory work. By 1900 the neighborhood was home to several hundred people, with laundries, groceries, restaurants, and shops. Hop Alley didn’t survive the twentieth century. Between the late 1950s and the mid-1960s it was condemned and cleared in the name of urban renewal — the ground was needed for **Busch Memorial Stadium**, which opened in 1966. The heart of St. Louis’s first Chinatown literally became a stadium and its parking. But the city’s Chinese-American families and their restaurants didn’t disappear; they scattered and put down new roots across the metro, and the neighborhood carry-out — the “chop suey” — became a fixture in working-class neighborhoods all over town. Over the following decades, the community’s new center of gravity shifted west, to the stretch of Olive Boulevard in University City that St. Louisans now call the “unofficial Chinatown” — today lined with dumpling houses, Cantonese barbecue, and Asian groceries. So the story runs in a straight line: a downtown Chinatown razed for a ballpark, families rebuilding across the region, and a humble egg-foo-young sandwich carrying a piece of that history forward on every corner-store menu. When you bite into a St. Paul, you’re tasting the legacy of a neighborhood that no longer exists. The sandwich itself came later than Hop Alley. As local legend has it, the St. Paul was created in the early 1940s by a cook named Steven Yuen, who is said to have ...

## The St. Louis Halloween Guide: Haunts, Family Fun & Pumpkin Patches Revised July 23, 2026 What Halloween events happen in St. Louis every year? St. Louis has a deep bench of annual Halloween traditions. For scares: The Darkness and Creepyworld (Scarefest) and Six Flags Fright Fest in Eureka. For families: Boo at the Zoo at the Saint Louis Zoo, Halloween Nights at Grant’s Farm, and Trick or Train at Union Station. For pumpkin patches and harvest fun: Eckert’s in Belleville, plus Thies Farm’s Pumpkinland, Stuckmeyer’s, and Rombachs. Most run from late September through late October or early November — check each venue’s calendar for exact dates. Keep reading ↓There’s a particular week in October when the whole St. Louis metro seems to lean into the season at once — the corn mazes open, the haunted houses fire up their fog machines, and every farm stand out toward the county line turns into a pumpkin patch. Whether you’ve got little kids who want a friendly not-scary night, teenagers hunting the most terrifying haunt in the region, or you just want to pick a pumpkin and drink something warm, the area delivers. Here’s an evergreen guide to the Halloween traditions that come back every year around St. Louis — sorted by how spooky they are, so you can match the outing to your crew. Exact dates shift each season, so check each venue’s official calendar before you go; the events themselves are annual fixtures you can count on. ## The Halloween season at a glance St. Louis has a deep bench of annual Halloween traditions. For scares, **The Darkness** and **Creepyworld** (plus the **Lemp Haunted House**) and **Six Flags Fright Fest** lead the region. For families, **Boo at the Zoo** at the Saint Louis Zoo, **Halloween Nights at Grant’s Farm**, and **Trick or Train at Union Station** are the go-tos. And for pumpkin-patch and harvest fun, **Eckert’s**, **Thies Farm’s Pumpkinland**, **Stuckmeyer’s**, and **Rombachs** anchor the season. Most run from late September through late October or early November. ## For the fearless: haunted houses and scream parks If your idea of Halloween is a genuine adrenaline rush, St. Louis is a serious haunt town — and its flagship is a legend. **The Darkness**, in the Soulard area near Ballpark Village, has been terrifying visitors for more than three decades and is regularly ranked among the best haunted houses in the country. Its detailed sets and monsters set the bar. A short distance away, the same company’s **Lemp Haunted House** on Lemp Avenue leans into the neighborhood’s real haunted lore for a second, distinct scare. For a bigger, outdoor-heavy experience, **Creepyworld** in Fenton (off Highway 141) is a sprawling “scream park” with multiple attractions including a haunted hayride — a full night out rather than a single walk-through. And for scares wrapped inside a theme park, **Fright Fest at Six Flags St. Louis** in Eureka overlays the whole park with haunted mazes and scare zones after dark while the coasters keep running. These ramp up from weekend nights in late September to nightly as Halloween approaches, so buy timed tickets ahead and expect lines on the closest weekends. Planning the rest of the season? Our guides to the best St. Louis Christmas lights and exploring St. Louis year-round round out the calendar with more local traditions worth the trip. Run a seasonal attraction, farm, or event in the St. Louis area? This is how families find you when they search “Halloween events near me.” Listing it keeps your dates, hours, and reviews in front of local parents planning the season. ## For families: not-scary Halloween fun Plenty of the best local Halloween is built for little ones, with costumes encouraged and the scares dialed all the way down. The classic is **Boo at the Zoo**, the Saint Louis Zoo’s after-hours family event in Forest Park — a festive, friendly evening (note it’s a themed experience rather than a trick-or-treat event, and older kids are asked to skip the truly scary costumes). It runs select evenings in the back half of October and is a beloved rite of the season for St. Louis families. **Halloween Nights at Grant’s Farm** in Grantwood Village is another family favorite — an after-dark experience with a haunted tram ride (watch for the headless horseman), decor, and shows, plus a daytime **Fall Fest** at the Clydesdale stables for the younger set. Downtown, **St. Louis Union Station** runs its **Trick or Train** walk-through of Halloween-themed railcars, lights up the St. Louis Wheel, and the **St. Louis Aquarium’s Pirates & Pumpkins** adds underwater pumpkin carving to the mix. Purina Farms out in Gray Summit has also long run a not-so-scary kids’ Halloween event — confirm the current year’s dates with the venue before making the drive. ## For the harvest crowd: pumpkin patches and farms Some of the most reliable fall fun around St. Louis has nothing to do with fright — it’s hayrides, corn mazes, and the annual hunt for the perfect pumpkin. The regional heavyweight is **Eckert’s** in Belleville, Illinois (about 25 minutes east of downtown), a seventh-generation farm with pick-your-own pumpkins and “Ecktoberfest” festival weekends; its newer **Jack’s Lighted Trail**, a walkable illuminated pumpkin path, has become a fresh evening draw. On the Missouri side, **Thies Farm & Market’s Pumpkinland** brings a straw castle, corn maze, and rides; **Stuckmeyer’s Farm** in Fenton (near the junction of Highways 141 ...

## The Best Fishing Spots in St. Louis: A Local Guide to Free Public Water Revised July 23, 2026 Where can I go fishing in St. Louis? St. Louis has excellent free public fishing — local lakes and ponds in county and state parks (like Creve Coeur Lake and the lakes in Forest Park), Missouri Department of Conservation areas, and the Missouri and Mississippi rivers. Many spots are free and open year-round; you’ll need a Missouri fishing license if you’re between 16 and 64. Check the MDC site for stocked lakes and access points near you. Keep reading ↓Close your eyes and you can probably still feel it. A Saturday morning that started too early. A styrofoam cup of nightcrawlers sweating in the cupholder. A cheap rod — maybe your dad’s, maybe a garage-sale special — and a bobber sitting dead-still on flat water until, out of nowhere, it twitched, then plunged, and your whole small world narrowed to that one red-and-white dot. Maybe it was a grandpa in Affton who taught you. Maybe an uncle out past St. Charles. Maybe it’s a memory you’ve been meaning to hand down to a kid of your own. Here’s the good news, and it surprises people: you don’t need a bass boat, a lake-house membership, or a tackle box the size of a suitcase to go fishing in St. Louis. You need a rod, a few bucks of bait, and a spot — and this metro is quietly loaded with free, public, genuinely good ones. Whether you’re in Florissant, south county, Valley Park, or the city itself, there’s honest fishing water within about fifteen minutes of your front door. This is the guide to all of it: where to actually go, what you’ll catch, the one permit rule that trips people up, and a St. Louis secret most folks don’t know — you can catch *trout* here, in the city, in the dead of winter. **The best public fishing spots in the St. Louis area include Creve Coeur Lake (the largest natural lake in Missouri), the 32 lakes of the August A. Busch Conservation Area near Weldon Spring, Simpson Lake in Valley Park, Bee Tree and Suson Parks in south county, and Jefferson Lake in Forest Park — all free and public. Anglers ages 16 to 64 need an inexpensive Missouri fishing permit; kids 15 and under and residents 65 and up fish free.** ## First, the One Rule Everyone Trips On: Your Fishing Permit Let’s clear this up before you load the car, because it’s the single most common St. Louis fishing question. In Missouri, anyone **ages 16 through 64 needs a valid fishing permit** to fish public water. The good news: it’s cheap — a resident annual permit runs around $14 — and you can buy it in minutes online through the Missouri Department of Conservation, in the MDC app, or at nearly any Walmart, Bass Pro, or bait shop in the region. Two exemptions worth knowing: **kids 15 and under fish free**, and so do **Missouri residents 65 and older** — which makes this a genuinely cheap outing for a grandparent taking the grandkids. One catch: if you want to *keep* trout (outside a designated trout park), you need a separate trout permit. For a full day of catch-and-release bluegill with the kids, the basic permit is all you’ll ever touch. When in doubt, the MDC website spells out current rules and prices — check it before your first trip of the year. ## The St. Louis Secret: You Can Catch Trout in the City in January Here’s the thing almost nobody outside serious anglers knows about. The MDC runs a **St. Louis Urban Fishing Program** that stocks a handful of city and county lakes with fish all year — channel catfish through the warm months (roughly March to September), hybrid sunfish, and, best of all, **rainbow trout in the winter**. That’s right: while everyone else is inside complaining about the cold, you can be standing at a lake in the city limits reeling in trout, a fish most people assume you have to drive to the Ozarks to catch. Only a few local lakes get the winter trout treatment — the Boathouse Lake in Carondelet Park is one of the standouts — and MDC even runs a fish-stocking hotline and online schedule so you can time your trip to a fresh stocking. It turns the deadest, grayest part of the St. Louis calendar into fishing season. Pack gloves, bring a thermos, and go. ## Where to Fish in St. Louis, by Where You Live St. Louis fishing spreads across the whole metro, so the smartest move is usually the closest good water to you. Here’s the honest rundown, grouped by area, with what each is known for. ### West County & St. Charles: The Big Water If you want room to spread out, head northwest. **Creve Coeur Lake** in Maryland Heights is the headliner — at roughly 320 acres it’s the largest natural lake in Missouri, ringed by a county park with trails and boat rentals. You’ll find crappie, bass, channel catfish, and even gar; it’s electric-motor only and there’s no swimming, which keeps it calm and fishable. A little farther out, the **August A. Busch Memorial Conservation Area** near Weldon Spring is the region’s crown jewel for variety: roughly 7,000 acres holding *32* fishable lakes, stocked by ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-the-best-good-fishing-spots-in-st-louis

One catch: if you want to *keep* trout (outside a designated trout park), you need a separate trout permit. For a full day of catch-and-release bluegill with the kids, the basic permit is all you’ll ever touch. When in doubt, the MDC website spells out current rules and prices — check it before your first trip of the year. ## The St. Louis Secret: You Can Catch Trout in the City in January Here’s the thing almost nobody outside serious anglers knows about. The MDC runs a **St. Louis Urban Fishing Program** that stocks a handful of city and county lakes with fish all year — channel catfish through the warm months (roughly March to September), hybrid sunfish, and, best of all, **rainbow trout in the winter**. That’s right: while everyone else is inside complaining about the cold, you can be standing at a lake in the city limits reeling in trout, a fish most people assume you have to drive to the Ozarks to catch. Only a few local lakes get the winter trout treatment — the Boathouse Lake in Carondelet Park is one of the standouts — and MDC even runs a fish-stocking hotline and online schedule so you can time your trip to a fresh stocking. It turns the deadest, grayest part of the St. Louis calendar into fishing season. Pack gloves, bring a thermos, and go. ## Where to Fish in St. Louis, by Where You Live St. Louis fishing spreads across the whole metro, so the smartest move is usually the closest good water to you. Here’s the honest rundown, grouped by area, with what each is known for. ### West County & St. Charles: The Big Water If you want room to spread out, head northwest. **Creve Coeur Lake** in Maryland Heights is the headliner — at roughly 320 acres it’s the largest natural lake in Missouri, ringed by a county park with trails and boat rentals. You’ll find crappie, bass, channel catfish, and even gar; it’s electric-motor only and there’s no swimming, which keeps it calm and fishable. A little farther out, the **August A. Busch Memorial Conservation Area** near Weldon Spring is the region’s crown jewel for variety: roughly 7,000 acres holding *32* fishable lakes, stocked by ...

## Finding Low Income Apartments in St. Louis: Your Guide to Affordable Housing Revised July 28, 2026 What salary do you need to afford $1200 rent? A common rule is that rent should be about 30% of your gross income, so a $1,200 apartment points to roughly $48,000 a year (about $4,000 a month). Many St. Louis renters stretch beyond that, but a better move is to look for income-restricted or affordable units that set rent based on what you earn. Use price filters on Apartments.com and Zillow, and check income-based options if $1,200 strains your budget. Keep reading ↓Looking for a place to live in St. Louis that won't break the bank? Finding affordable housing can feel like a big task, but it's totally doable. This guide is here to help you find low income apartments in St. Louis. We'll walk you through where to look, what you'll need, and how to make the process smoother. Let's get started on your search for a comfortable and affordable home. ### Key Takeaways - Understand what makes housing qualify as low income and the advantages of opting for affordable places. - Explore various online platforms, local housing authorities, and community groups that list low income apartments in St. Louis. - Prepare for the application process by gathering necessary documents and understanding income verification. - Learn about government programs like Section 8 vouchers that can help cover rent costs. - Get tips on finding suitable neighborhoods and what to expect when viewing apartments. **📌 Found this helpful? That’s exactly why we made it.** ## Understanding Low Income Apartments in St. Louis Finding a place to live in St. Louis that fits your budget can feel like a puzzle, especially when you're looking for affordable options. Let's break down what makes housing ## Resources for Finding Low Income Apartments ### Online Listing Platforms for Affordable Rentals Looking for a place to live can feel like a big task, especially when you're trying to find something affordable. Luckily, the internet has made it a lot easier to find listings. There are websites specifically designed to help people find low-income housing. These sites often have filters so you can narrow down your search by location, price, and even specific programs like Section 8. **You can often create an account to save your favorite listings and get alerts when new places become available.** It's a good idea to check these sites regularly because affordable apartments can get snapped up quickly. Some popular platforms include: - AffordableHousing.com - Rent.com (look for their affordable housing section) - Apartments.com (use their filters for income-restricted units) ### Local Housing Authorities and Agencies Your local government plays a big role in affordable housing. In St. Louis, the St. Louis Housing Authority (SLHA) is a key resource. They manage public housing and administer programs like the Housing Choice Voucher program (often called Section 8). These agencies often have their own lists of available properties or can guide you on how to apply for their programs. It's worth visiting their website or giving them a call to see what they offer. They can also tell you about other local initiatives that might not be advertised on general listing sites. ### Community Organizations and Non-profits Beyond official government agencies, many non-profit groups and community organizations in St. Louis are dedicated to helping people find housing. These groups might offer services like: - Housing counseling to help you understand your options. - Assistance with filling out applications. - Information on local resources and support services. - Sometimes, they even have their own housing developments. These organizations often have a deep connection to the community and can provide personalized support. A quick search for "St. Louis housing non-profits" should give you a starting point for finding these helpful groups. **Helping People Find Housing** ## Eligibility and Application Process Getting approved for a low-income apartment involves a few steps, and understanding them beforehand can make the whole thing smoother. It's not just about finding a place; it's about showing you meet the requirements and then getting your application in. ### Income Verification Requirements Landlords and housing programs need to confirm your income to make sure you qualify for affordable housing. This usually means providing proof of what you earn. **This is often the most important part of the application.** Here's what you might need to show: - **Pay stubs:**Recent ones, usually from the last 30-60 days. - **Tax returns:**Your most recent federal tax return. - **Benefit statements:**If you receive Social Security, disability, or unemployment benefits, you'll need official award letters. - **Bank statements:**These can show regular income deposits. - **Letter of employment:**From your employer, stating your position and salary. Sometimes, there are limits on how much you can earn to qualify for certain programs. These limits are often based on a percentage of the Area Median Income (AMI) for St. Louis. For example, you might see terms like "30% AMI" or "50% AMI," meaning your rent should be no more than 30% or 50% of that median income. ### Completing Rental Applications Once you've gathered your income documents, you'll ...

## Millwoods Sports Bar & Grill, Maryland Heights: What to Order & Know Before You Go Revised July 22, 2026 What is Millwoods Sports Bar and Grill known for? Millwoods Sports Bar & Grill is a casual American sports bar at 12068 Dorsett Rd in Maryland Heights — roughly 40 TVs, pool tables, a patio, and pub food done without fuss. Order the fish tacos or the double smash burger, and come back Wednesday for bingo. Closed Mondays; about 4 stars. Keep reading ↓It’s a Friday night in Maryland Heights, the game’s about to start, and you want the kind of place where the wings are hot, the beer’s cold, the TVs are everywhere, and nobody’s going to rush you out. Maybe you’re coming off a shift, maybe you’re meeting friends before a show at the amphitheater, maybe you just don’t feel like cooking. Either way, a good neighborhood sports bar is exactly the right answer. Millwoods Sports Bar & Grill has quietly become one of those answers on the west side of the metro — a two-level spot with a full menu, a downstairs taproom, and a calendar of bingo, DJs, and live music. Here’s what to order, what to know before you go, and how to build a whole Maryland Heights night around it. ## At a Glance: What to Order ## What Millwoods Actually Is Millwoods is a full-on sports bar and grill in Maryland Heights — think roughly forty TVs, pool tables, darts, Golden Tee, and a downstairs taproom that essentially makes it two bars in one. It’s the kind of place built for a game day: plenty of screens, a big menu of shareable bar food, and enough going on that a group can settle in for hours. It’s a locals’ spot rather than a polished chain, and that’s the appeal — a genuine neighborhood bar with room to spread out. The Maryland Heights location is actually the second Millwoods, an expansion of the original, which tells you the formula works: give people good bar food, a wall of screens, cheap ways to have fun, and a reason to come back on a Tuesday, and they will. It draws a solid, mixed rating across review sites — roughly in the 3.7-to-4.0-star range depending on the platform — with regulars praising the food and the atmosphere, and the occasional note about service on a busy night. For a neighborhood sports bar, that’s a dependable sign: people come for the wings, the screens, and the events, and they keep coming back. ## The Vibe: Two Bars in One Part of what sets Millwoods apart from a generic wings-and-TVs joint is the layout. Upstairs is the main sports bar — the screens, the tables, the game-day energy. Downstairs is a separate taproom, which effectively gives the place two personalities under one roof: the loud, everyone-watching-the-game space, and a slightly more laid-back bar below. On a packed Saturday, that second room is a lifesaver; when the upstairs is elbow-to-elbow for a Cardinals or Blues game, you can slip downstairs and still catch the action without fighting for a stool. Scattered around are the things that keep a group entertained between innings: pool tables, darts, and Golden Tee for the golf crowd. It’s the sort of place you can walk into alone and end up in a conversation, or bring a group of ten and nobody feels crammed. That unpretentious, settle-in-for-the-night feel is exactly what people mean when they call a place a good neighborhood bar — and it’s why Millwoods has built a regular crowd on the west side. On a big game night, the mix of the upstairs roar and the downstairs hum is the whole point — there’s a spot for the die-hards glued to every play and a spot for the folks who mostly came to hang out. ## What to Order at Millwoods Start with the **wings** — traditional or boneless, sold by the pound, with a long list of house sauces from Buffalo and Honey BBQ to Sriracha Lime, Hot Honey, Garlic Parm, and a dry rub. They’re the classic sports-bar order and Millwoods does them right. The **double smash burger** (two patties, your choice of cheese) is the go-to if you want a proper burger, and the **Prime Dip** — a prime rib French dip — is the signature sandwich worth trying at least once. For the table, the **Southern fried pickle chips** with house cayenne sauce and the **breaded mushrooms** (with ranch or horsey sauce) are the crowd-pleasing starters, and the **Macho Nachos** come piled on house-made chips. Other menu highlights include the **buffalo chicken wrap** (crispy fried chicken, buffalo, bacon, cheddar, ranch), **Millwood’s Pork Sticks**, and **smothered chicken**. There’s also a lunch buffet and daily specials if you’re coming midday. It’s hearty, shareable, sports-bar comfort food — exactly what you want with a pitcher and a game. A tip for first-timers: this is a menu built for the table, not for going solo on a single plate. Order a pound of wings in a couple of different sauces, add the fried pickle chips and a round of Macho Nachos to share, and let everyone graze while the game’s on. If you’re there for lunch, the buffet and daily specials are the value play. And because there’s a full bar plus the downstairs taproom, the drink list keeps pace with the food ...

## Hotels Near Busch Stadium: Where to Stay for a St. Louis Cardinals Game Revised July 12, 2026 What hotel is walking distance from Busch Stadium? The closest hotels to Busch Stadium are the Hilton St. Louis at the Ballpark (about two blocks), Live! by Loews (directly across the street in Ballpark Village), and the Drury Plaza Hotel at the Arch (about two blocks), with several more a short walk away. Book early for Cardinals home stands — downtown fills up fast. Keep reading ↓Picture the perfect Cardinals day. You roll out of bed, grab coffee, and you can already hear the buzz building outside — because your hotel is close enough that “getting to the game” means a short walk, not a parking nightmare. After the ninth inning, you’re back in your room in ten minutes instead of sitting in a garage line with 40,000 other people. That’s the whole case for staying near Busch Stadium — the walk to the ballpark becomes part of the fun instead of a logistics headache. Whether you’re driving in from Columbia or Cape Girardeau, flying in for a weekend series, or making a birthday out of a single game, where you stay decides how good the day feels. Here’s a local’s guide to the hotels closest to the ballpark, ranked by how far you’ll actually have to walk, plus the game-day booking tips that save you money and hassle. ## At a Glance: Closest Hotels to Busch Stadium ## Right Across the Street: Ballpark Village If you want to fall out of bed and into your seat, **Live! by Loews — St. Louis** is the answer. It sits inside **Ballpark Village**, the dining-and-entertainment district directly across from Busch Stadium, roughly a tenth of a mile from the gates. It’s Cardinals-themed by design; many suites face the stadium, and the hotel’s terrace even carries a live video feed from inside Busch. On a game day, you simply cannot stay closer to the action — which is exactly why it books up first. Ballpark Village itself is worth knowing about even if you stay elsewhere: developed by the Cardinals and The Cordish Companies next to the stadium, it’s packed with bars, restaurants, and the Cardinals Nation venue, and it’s where the pre- and post-game crowd gathers. Staying here means the party is downstairs. ## A Few Blocks Away: The Reliable Big-Brand Picks Just west of the stadium, in the historic Cupples Station district, **The Westin St. Louis** is an upscale option a couple of blocks from the gates — close enough that the hotel calls itself steps from Busch and Ballpark Village. A short walk north, the **Hilton St. Louis at the Ballpark** (about 0.3 mile, roughly two blocks) is a Cardinals preferred hotel partner, with the popular Three Sixty rooftop bar looking out over the field — a genuine game-day amenity. Both are dependable, full-service downtown hotels that put you within an easy stroll of first pitch. ## The Arch District: A Short, Scenic Walk A few blocks east toward the Gateway Arch, two more hotels put you within a comfortable walk of the ballpark and the riverfront at once. The **Drury Plaza Hotel St. Louis at the Arch** (about 0.3 mile) is a local favorite for its free extras — the Drury chain is known for free hot breakfast and evening drinks — and, handy for families, it has an indoor pool. Nearby, the **Hyatt Regency St. Louis at The Arch** (about 0.4 mile) is a large hotel steps from Gateway Arch National Park, an easy walk to both the game and the Arch grounds. *One heads-up:* the old Millennium Hotel on the riverfront is **closed and being demolished** as part of a major redevelopment — don’t confuse it with the fully-operating Hyatt Regency, which is a separate building. If an old listing points you to the Millennium, skip it. ## A Little Farther, Still Walkable If the closest hotels are booked or your budget wants options, several more sit within about a 10-to-15-minute walk along the Washington Avenue corridor. The **Magnolia Hotel St. Louis**, a Tribute Portfolio hotel (about 0.5 mile), is a stylish boutique choice; the **Embassy Suites by Hilton St. Louis Downtown** (about 0.6 mile) offers all-suite rooms with free breakfast; the **Courtyard by Marriott Downtown/Convention Center** (about 0.9 mile) is a solid mid-range pick; and the **Marriott St. Louis Grand** (about 0.9 mile), housed in the historic former Statler hotel, is a grand old downtown landmark. All keep you downtown and walkable to the ballpark, the Arch, and the convention center. ## Getting to the Game (and Skipping the Parking Mess) Here’s the underrated reason to stay close: parking. On a Cardinals home date, downtown garages and lots fill up and prices spike, and the post-game exit crawl can eat 30 to 45 minutes before you even reach a highway. Stay within a few blocks of Busch and that whole problem disappears — you walk to the gate, and you walk home. If you’re driving in for the day instead, plan to park once, early, and treat the ballpark district as a walkable zone; many visitors leave the car at the hotel entirely. The MetroLink light rail also has a stop right at the stadium (Stadium Station), which is handy if you’re staying near a line or coming from the airport. ## Budget, Mid-Range, or Splurge The ballpark ...

## Active Indoor Things to Do in St. Louis: Escape Rooms, Climbing, VR & Barcades Revised July 12, 2026 What are fun indoor activities in St. Louis? The best indoor activities in St. Louis to beat the boredom — especially for adults and couples — include escape rooms (St. Louis Escape in Soulard, Escape the Room STL downtown), indoor rock climbing at Upper Limits, retro bowling at Pin-Up Bowl, games at Main Event, free-roam VR at Sandbox VR, and barcades like Up-Down STL. Keep reading ↓Some days you don’t want to look at things in a museum — you want to *do* something. Maybe it’s a first date that needs a spark, a group of friends who can never agree on a plan, a birthday, or just a restless Saturday when the weather won’t let you outside. You want to move, compete, and laugh a little. Good news: St. Louis has a deep bench of active indoor entertainment — escape rooms, rock climbing, virtual reality, retro barcades, bowling, and axe throwing — all under a roof and open whatever the sky is doing. Here’s a local’s guide to the best active indoor things to do in St. Louis, sorted by the vibe you’re after. Think of it less as a list of places and more as a menu of moods: some nights call for a puzzle and a team, some for a wall to climb, some for a cocktail and a pinball machine. St. Louis can cover all of them within a short drive. ## St. Louis Active-Indoor Spots at a Glance ## Escape Rooms: Turn a Night Into a Team Sport Escape rooms are the perfect active indoor plan for a date or a small group — an hour of puzzles, teamwork, and a ticking clock. **St. Louis Escape** in Soulard runs eight themed rooms and even adds blacklight 3D mini golf and a pinball arcade if you want to make a night of it. Downtown in the Loft District, **Escape the Room STL** offers several themed rooms for around $35 a person. Both are ideal for four-to-eight people who want to laugh, argue about clues, and (maybe) beat the clock together. They’re also a great equalizer for mixed groups — there’s a job for the detail-spotter, the big-picture thinker, and the person who just enjoys yelling “try that key in that lock.” Book a slot ahead, show up a few minutes early, and plan to grab food or drinks afterward to rehash how you did. ## Indoor Rock Climbing: Surprise Yourself You don’t need to be an athlete to have fun on a climbing wall — the good gyms are built for beginners. **Upper Limits** in Maryland Heights is a big, well-equipped gym with 45-foot walls and auto-belays, so you can climb even without a partner. **Climb So iLL** runs a dramatic downtown location inside a former power plant (plus a St. Charles gym), pairing climbing with yoga and fitness. Rent shoes, take the intro, and you’ll be surprised how quickly a rainy afternoon turns into a real workout you actually enjoyed. Climbing is also a sneaky-great date or group activity: you’re cheering each other up the wall, there’s a built-in sense of accomplishment, and no experience is required to have a genuinely good time. ## Barcades: Beer, Quarters, and Zero Boredom For grown-ups, St. Louis’s barcades are some of the best nights out in the city. **Up-Down STL** in the Central West End is the flagship — more than 60 retro arcade games, pinball, skee-ball, and console classics, with a rooftop bar (it’s 21+ in the evenings, with family hours during the day). Over in The Grove, **Purple Quarters** is a newer cocktail-and-arcade bar from a well-loved local team, with comedy and karaoke nights mixed in. Both nail the same trick: cheap games, good drinks, and the instant nostalgia of a machine you haven’t touched since childhood. ## Bowling and Games, Grown-Up Edition Bowling never goes out of style, and St. Louis does it with character. **Pin-Up Bowl** in the Delmar Loop pairs retro lanes with a full cocktail lounge and runs late into the night — a great low-key date or group hang. For a bigger, do-it-all option, **Main Event** in Chesterfield stacks bowling, multi-story laser tag, and 100-plus arcade games under one roof, open late daily — ideal for families or big groups who want variety without venue-hopping. ## Virtual Reality: The Group Adrenaline Hit VR has grown up, and St. Louis has real options now. **Sandbox VR**, which opened inside City Foundry in late 2025, is the premium pick — full-body motion capture and haptics that drop your group into a shared virtual world (zombies, space, the works). In south county, **STL Virtual Reality** in Oakville is an all-ages spot where up to six players can team up or compete across co-op, competitive, and escape-style games. Either way, it’s a genuinely modern, high-energy activity that groups and older kids love. ## Axe Throwing and Other Ways to Blow Off Steam If your idea of active indoor fun involves throwing something, St. Louis has you covered. **Top Notch Axe Throwing** runs locations in St. Louis and St. Charles where a coach gets you sticking axes into a target in minutes — a surprisingly fun group or date activity. **Amp Up Action Park** combines an axe range with other action attractions under one roof. It’s the ...

## Cate Zone Chesterfield: Authentic Northeastern Chinese in West County Revised July 23, 2026 Is there a Cate Zone in Chesterfield, and what does it serve? Yes — Cate Zone opened a second location at 24 Four Seasons Shopping Center in Chesterfield, MO (314-392-9624) in February 2024; the original University City cafe is still open too. It serves authentic Northeastern Chinese (Dongbei) food from Liaoning province — dumplings, cumin lamb with cilantro, hot crispy fish, sweet and sour pork — in generous, shareable portions. Closed Mondays; call ahead. Keep reading ↓For years, if you wanted the real thing — authentic Northeastern Chinese cooking, not the Americanized takeout most of the metro grew up on — you drove to a small, perpetually-packed cafe in University City and waited for a table. Cate Zone earned that kind of devotion. So when the family behind it opened a second, roomier location in Chesterfield, west-county food lovers took notice. This is an honest look at Cate Zone Chesterfield: what it is, what to order, and why it’s worth the trip — and why, if you’ve only ever eaten the strip-mall-takeout version of Chinese food, it might just change your mind about the whole cuisine. The good news for the west side of the metro: you no longer have to drive across town for this food. Cate Zone brought its Dongbei-style cooking to the Four Seasons Shopping Center, in a bigger, more modern room built for exactly the kind of big, shared, family-style meals this cuisine is made for. It’s the same food that built the reputation, now with elbow room — a rare case where a beloved spot expands without watering down what made it special. ## A real second location — and the original is still going Let’s clear up the geography first, because it matters. Cate Zone Chesterfield is a genuine **second location**, opened in February 2024 — not a relocation. The beloved **original in University City is still open and running**, so you can visit either. Co-owner Daniel Ma runs the Chesterfield restaurant, while his partner stayed on at the University City cafe, keeping both kitchens in the same family’s hands. You’ll find the Chesterfield location at **24 Four Seasons Shopping Center, Chesterfield, MO 63017**, phone **(314) 392-9624**. The owners hail from Liaoning province in Northeastern China, and the whole concept is built around sharing: as Daniel Ma has put it, in China you share food and bring the family, and the bigger Chesterfield dining room was designed to let more people do exactly that. It’s a place that makes the most sense with a crowd, a lazy Susan turning, and a dozen dishes in the middle of the table. ## What is Northeastern Chinese food? This is the part worth understanding, because it’s what makes Cate Zone special. “Dongbei” cuisine comes from Northeastern China — a cold, hearty region — and it tastes noticeably different from the Cantonese-derived American-Chinese takeout most people know. Expect bold, savory, generously spiced dishes: hand-crafted dumplings, cumin-scented lamb, chili-oil-slicked fish, and rich, comforting braises. It’s food built for a table full of people sharing plates, not a single takeout carton. The region borders Korea and Russia and has a distinct culinary identity: heavy on wheat rather than only rice, big on dumplings and hearty stews, and unafraid of cumin, chili, and bold, layered flavors. If you’ve traveled in China or have friends from the north, this will taste like home; if you haven’t, it’s a delicious education. For a lot of St. Louis diners, Cate Zone was their first taste of this regional style, and it’s converted plenty of skeptics who thought they knew what “Chinese food” meant. If your idea of the cuisine stops at sweet-and-sour and fried rice, this is a genuinely eye-opening upgrade. Love real regional Chinese food? Cate Zone’s original University City location put Northeastern Chinese cooking on the St. Louis map — and our guide to the best Chinese food in St. Louis rounds up more across the metro. Run a restaurant in the St. Louis area? This is how diners find you when they search “Chinese food near me” or ask an AI assistant where to eat. Listing your restaurant keeps your menu, hours, and reviews in front of hungry locals. ## The cafe that started it Cate Zone’s story is a good one. It began in University City in 2016 as a small cafe that quickly became a favorite of international students and adventurous local eaters — a word-of-mouth phenomenon that ran on the strength of genuinely authentic cooking rather than any marketing. The owners, from Liaoning in Northeastern China, were serving the food they grew up on, and St. Louis diners who’d never tasted real Dongbei cuisine found themselves hooked. The original became known for long waits and a devoted following, the surest sign a restaurant is doing something right — the kind of place people drive out of their way for and then tell everyone they know about. The Chesterfield location grew directly out of that success. Demand outstripped the little cafe, and west-county fans were tired of the drive, so the family opened a larger, more comfortable room to serve them — and to give everyone the space to do the big, shared, celebratory meals this cuisine is built around. It’s a genuinely heartening arc: an immigrant family’s honest cooking earning enough love to expand ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/cate-zone-chesterfield-a-culinary-gem-you-can-t-miss

## America's Center Convention Complex: A Hub for Innovation and Events Revised July 23, 2026 What is America’s Center in St. Louis? The America’s Center Convention Complex is downtown St. Louis’s largest event venue — about 2.2 million square feet including the 574,000-square-foot Cervantes Convention Center, a ballroom, the Ferrara Theatre, and the 67,000-seat Dome at America’s Center, home of the St. Louis Battlehawks. It’s operated by Explore St. Louis at 701 Convention Plaza. Keep reading ↓If you’ve ever felt a building shake, it was probably a Saturday at The Dome. When the St. Louis Battlehawks are home and 40,000 fans throw up the “caw” at once, the loudest venue in the UFL earns the name. But that same downtown complex is quiet-busy the other six days a week too — hosting the conventions, trade shows, and graduations that quietly pump hundreds of millions of dollars into the city. That’s the America’s Center Convention Complex: part stadium, part convention hall, part downtown anchor. Whether you’re coming for a Battlehawks game, a concert, a trade show, or your niece’s college graduation, it helps to know what’s actually under that roof — and how to get in and out without stress. This guide covers what the complex is, the story behind The Dome, what’s new after its big 2024 expansion, and everything you need to plan a visit — verified against Explore St. Louis’s current information for 2026. **Heading downtown for an event? Bookmark this page and share it with whoever you’re going with.** ## What is the America’s Center Convention Complex? The America’s Center Convention Complex is downtown St. Louis’s largest event venue — about **2.2 million square feet** at 701 Convention Plaza, managed by **Explore St. Louis**, the region’s convention and visitors organization. It’s really four venues under one umbrella: - **The Cervantes Convention Center**—- **574,000 square feet**of contiguous exhibit space across seven halls, plus- **95 meeting rooms**. - **The America’s Ballroom**— a 28,000-square-foot ballroom for galas and large banquets. - **The Ferrara Theatre**— an intimate theater seating about 1,400. - **The Dome at America’s Center**— the 67,000-seat domed stadium most St. Louisans just call “The Dome.” Put together, it’s the engine room for St. Louis’s biggest gatherings, hosting more than 350 events and around 1.8 million attendees in a single year. Here’s the complex at a glance: ## The Dome at America’s Center: from the Rams to the Battlehawks The Dome has worn a few names. It opened in 1995 as the **Trans World Dome** (TWA Dome), became the **Edward Jones Dome** in 2002, and is now simply **The Dome at America’s Center**. For two decades it was the home of the NFL’s St. Louis Rams, who played there from 1995 until the franchise left for Los Angeles after the 2015 season — a wound St. Louis football fans still feel. But the story didn’t end there. The Dome found a new heartbeat with the **St. Louis Battlehawks**, whose electric, sold-out crowds turned it into a genuine phenomenon. The Battlehawks are back at The Dome for the 2026 UFL season, with a home opener on **March 28, 2026**. Beyond football, the venue hosts concerts, motocross and monster-truck rallies, large graduations, and convention overflow — a flexible big-room that keeps downtown busy year-round. ## What’s new: the AC Next Gen expansion In 2024, America’s Center completed its first major expansion in more than 30 years — the roughly **$240 million AC Next Gen project**. It was a real modernization, not a coat of paint: - A brand-new **72,000-square-foot exhibit hall**, expanding total exhibit space to 574,000 square feet. - The **28,000-square-foot America’s Ballroom**. - More than double the enclosed **loading docks**(a big deal for the trade shows that live and die by move-in logistics). - An on-site **culinary garden**, refreshed restrooms, and a refurbished Washington Avenue entrance. The upgrade keeps St. Louis competitive for the national conventions that shop cities against each other — and those events are what fill downtown hotels and restaurants. ## What happens at America’s Center? On any given week the complex might host a medical convention in the exhibit halls, a corporate meeting in the conference center, a touring concert in The Dome, and a wedding reception in the ballroom — all at once. The regular lineup includes: - **Conventions, trade shows, and conferences**— the core business, from national association meetings to regional expos. - **Battlehawks UFL football**— spring Saturdays at The Dome. - **Concerts and touring shows**, motocross, and monster-truck events. - **Graduations and community events**for the region’s schools and universities. What ties it all together is flexibility. A single week can pair a 20,000-person medical convention in the exhibit halls with a sold-out concert at The Dome and a black-tie gala in the ballroom — each running independently, none in the other’s way. That range is exactly what lets St. Louis compete for national events while still hosting hometown graduations and community gatherings; the complex is built to do both at once. ## Game day at The Dome If your trip is for a Battlehawks game, know that you’re walking into one of the best atmospheres in pro football. The team’s rabid fan base — and the signature “**Battlehawks**” caw that rolls around the bowl — regularly draws crowds north of 35,000, remarkable for a spring league. It’s an affordable, family-friendly day out compared to an NFL ticket, and the indoor Dome means ...

Osteria Forto is named for chef Fortunato Pietoso, who grew up in Aversa, Italy, and cooked for decades at St. Louis institutions including John Mineo’s, Giovanni’s on the Hill, and Café Napoli. Co-owned by Dominic and Liz Pietoso, the O’Fallon, Missouri dinner house opened in December 2023 and makes its pasta from scratch daily. Keep reading ↓Planning a visit to Osteria Forto soon?
