Let's take a look at what makes their food and drinks so good. ### Key Takeaways - You can try signature dishes like scallops with shiitake mushrooms, pork rib chop saltimbocca, and the Tre Amici cake. - The menu focuses on making pasta from scratch and using fresh, quality ingredients for authentic Italian tastes. - They have a nice selection of drinks, including Italian Spritz, the Bourbon Millionaire cocktail, and a good wine list. - The restaurant offers a cozy atmosphere and great service, making for a top-notch dining experience. - You can find seasonal specials, off-menu options, and vegan choices when you explore the menu. ## Discover Osteria Forto's Signature Dishes When you visit Osteria Forto, you'll want to make sure you try some of their standout plates. These are the dishes that really capture the essence of what they do here, the ones people talk about long after they've left. ### Scallops with Shiitake Mushrooms and Sundried Tomatoes This dish is a real winner. You get these perfectly cooked scallops, tender and sweet, paired with earthy shiitake mushrooms and the intense, sweet-tart flavor of sundried tomatoes. It’s a combination that just works, hitting all the right notes. It’s a great example of how they balance flavors and textures. ### Pork Rib Chop Saltimbocca If you're looking for something hearty and classic, the Pork Rib Chop Saltimbocca is the way to go. It’s a substantial chop, cooked just right, and topped with prosciutto and sage, just like traditional saltimbocca. It’s savory, a little salty from the prosciutto, and has that wonderful aroma from the sage. This is Italian comfort food done right. ### Tre Amici Cake Don't even think about skipping dessert. The Tre Amici Cake is something special. It’s a multi-layered creation featuring peanut butter cream, rich chocolate ganache, and a salted caramel sauce. - Peanut Butter Cream: Adds a nutty, smooth layer. - Chocolate Ganache: For that deep, decadent chocolate hit. - Salted Caramel Sauce: A touch of sweetness with a hint of salt to balance everything. Each plate tells a story of quality ingredients and careful preparation. ## A Taste of Authentic Italian Cuisine When you step into Osteria Forto, you're not just walking into a restaurant; you’re stepping into an evening that feels like Italy. The chefs here are serious about bringing you the real deal, the kind of food that makes you feel like you're sitting at a table in a bustling piazza. It’s all about honoring tradition and using the best ingredients they can find. ### The Art of Pasta Making Forget those boxed noodles you might have at home. At Osteria Forto, pasta is treated like the art form it is. They put a lot of care into making their pasta fresh, right there in the kitchen. You can see it in the way the dough is rolled and cut, each shape perfect for holding just the right amount of sauce. It’s a slow, deliberate process, and you can really taste the difference. - **Handmade Daily:**Every strand of pasta is crafted fresh each day. - **Traditional Techniques:**They use time-honored methods passed down through generations. - **Perfect Pairings:**Each pasta shape is thoughtfully matched with its ideal sauce. ### Fresh, Quality Ingredients What’s the secret to truly great Italian food? It’s simple: start with amazing ingredients. Osteria Forto is all about sourcing the freshest produce, the finest meats, and the best seafood. They believe that when you begin with first-rate components, the food just speaks for itself. You won't find any shortcuts here; it's all about quality from start to finish. This commitment is why dishes like their Margherita Pizza are so memorable. ### Traditional Italian Flavors This is where the heart of Italian cooking truly shines. Osteria Forto focuses on classic flavor combinations that have been loved for centuries. Think rich tomato sauces, fragrant basil, garlic that’s just right, and olive oil that adds a smooth finish. They aren't trying to reinvent the wheel; they're perfecting it. It’s about comfort, warmth, and that unmistakable taste of Italy that feels like coming home. The focus is on letting the natural flavors of the ingredients shine through, creating dishes that are both simple and deeply satisfying. It’s a philosophy that respects the heritage of Italian cooking. ## Osteria Forto's Exquisite Drink Selection Beyond the incredible food, Osteria Forto really knows how to quench your thirst. ## Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe: Valley Park’s Thai Dessert Gem Revised July 23, 2026 What is Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe known for? Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe (2961 Dougherty Ferry Rd, Valley Park, MO 63122; (636) 529-8690) is a family-owned, Lao-influenced Thai restaurant that opened in 2019, famous for its namesake Thai dessert cups — layered fruit, jelly, coconut milk, syrup, and shaved ice. On the savory side, the pad kee mao (drunken noodles) is the most-praised dish, and the Thai iced tea and fruit shakes are essential drinks. It shares the 63122 ZIP with Kirkwood but is a single location in Valley Park; closed Mondays. Keep reading ↓Some restaurants win you over with one thing you can’t get anywhere else. For Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe, tucked into a west St. Louis County shopping center, that thing is dessert — the namesake Thai “sweetie cups” of fruit, jelly, coconut milk, and shaved ice that the whole place is named for. But it would be a mistake to file it away as just a sweets stop. This is a genuine, family-owned Thai kitchen with real Lao roots, and it’s worth the drive whether you come for the drunken noodles or the dessert. Here’s an honest look at what Sweetie Cup is, where to find it, and what to order on a first visit. ## What Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe is Sweetie Cup Thai Cafe sits at **2961 Dougherty Ferry Road in Valley Park, MO 63122** — in the Shoppes at Seven Oaks, next to Tavern Kitchen & Bar — phone **(636) 529-8690**. (A quick note for your GPS: the 63122 ZIP is shared with Kirkwood, so some listings say Kirkwood or even just “St. Louis,” but the restaurant is in Valley Park.) It’s a sit-down Thai restaurant that opened in the spring of 2019, family-owned and run, and it’s built a loyal following in the years since. The story behind it is part of the charm. Co-owner Saengchan Inthichak was born in Laos and moved to northern Thailand as a child, and that background gives the kitchen a Lao accent alongside the Thai menu — the cooking comes from real memory and heritage rather than a corporate template. The name, meanwhile, comes from the restaurant’s signature: the Thai dessert cups that are its calling card. It’s a Thai street-food-and-dessert spot with a personality all its own. ## What to order Start with the savory food, because it’s genuinely good. The dish that gets the most love is the **pad kee mao — drunken noodles** — wide rice noodles stir-fried with holy basil, a plate that’s equal parts comforting and punchy. It’s the one to order if you want to understand why regulars keep coming back for more than the sweets. Then, of course, the reason for the name. The **Sweetie Cup dessert cups** are layered creations of fruit, jelly, coconut milk, syrup, and shaved ice, with several varieties on the menu. The owners’ standout is the **Lod Chong Singapore** — green tapioca noodles in coconut milk with fragrant pandan syrup and jackfruit. Other Thai desserts round it out: **Tub Tim Grob** (water chestnuts in sweet coconut milk over ice), **bua loi** (glutinous rice balls in coconut milk), and more coconut-milk classics. To drink, the **Thai iced tea** is the essential order — strong black tea with condensed milk over crushed ice — and there’s a lineup of fruit and tea shakes (mango, honeydew, strawberry, green tea) plus bubble tea if you want the boba experience. A good first-visit strategy: order a savory dish like the drunken noodles, a Thai iced tea, and at least one sweetie cup to share — that trio shows off exactly what makes the place special. The menu covers the wider range of Thai standards too, but the noodles, the desserts, and the drinks are the signatures worth building an order around. Hungry for more of the metro’s independent kitchens? Our roundup of St. Louis restaurants locals actually love spans barbecue, burgers, ramen, and more — real places, real reviews. Run a restaurant in the St. Louis area? This is how diners find you when they search “Thai food near me” or ask an AI assistant where to eat. Listing your restaurant keeps your menu, hours, and reviews in front of hungry locals. ## The desserts, explained If Thai desserts are new to you, they’re worth the small leap of faith — they’re unlike the heavy, sugary desserts a lot of American menus default to. The through-line is coconut milk: subtly sweet, a little savory, cool and refreshing rather than cloying. Add chewy textures (tapioca, jelly, water chestnut, glutinous rice) and fresh fruit, pile it over shaved ice, and you get something that feels light even when it’s indulgent. On a hot, humid St. Louis afternoon, a sweetie cup is close to the perfect thing. It’s also a genuinely fun order for a group or a family — the cups are colorful, a little theatrical, and easy to pass around and compare. For anyone who’s only ever thought of Thai food as pad thai and curry, the dessert side is a whole world, and Sweetie Cup is one of the few places in the metro that treats it as the main event rather than an afterthought. ## Why it’s worth the trip West county isn’t always where people think to look for authentic, owner-run ethnic food — the ...

## Beyond the Arch: Unique & Offbeat Things to Do in St. Louis Revised July 12, 2026 What are some unique things to do in St. Louis? The best unique things to do in St. Louis for adults include City Museum (a surreal warehouse playground with a rooftop bar), the free World Chess Hall of Fame and its giant chess piece, the Budweiser Brewery Experience, the City Foundry entertainment hall, antique-lined Cherokee Street, and the Delmar Loop — plus the ancient Monks Mound at Cahokia Mounds across the river. Keep reading ↓Everyone who visits St. Louis sees the Arch, and they should — it’s magnificent. But the Arch is the beginning of what makes this city interesting, not the end of it. Scratch the surface and St. Louis turns out to be one of the quirkiest, most surprising cities in the country: a place where you can climb through a ten-story art playground, stand next to the world’s largest chess piece, and eat frozen custard so thick they hand it to you upside down. Whether you’re a visitor who wants more than the postcard or a local looking to rediscover your own city, here’s a guide to the most unique and offbeat things to do in St. Louis — the “wait, that’s here?” stuff that sticks with you. These are the places locals bring out-of-town guests to show off — the spots that turn a skeptical visitor into someone who suddenly gets why people love this underrated city. ## City Museum: Not Just for Kids (Especially at Night) Start with the strangest, best thing in the city. The **City Museum** is a 600,000-square-foot former shoe warehouse that the late sculptor Bob Cassilly turned into a climbable, crawlable fever dream — caves, tunnels, ten-story slides, a rooftop school bus dangling over the edge, and salvaged-material art everywhere you look. It opened in 1997 and still feels like nothing else on earth. Come during the day with kids, or come on a weekend night when it’s open late and 21+ energy takes over — either way, wear clothes you can crawl in. ## Pop’s Kitchen Maryland Heights: Fried Catfish, Jack Salmon & Wings Worth the Trip Revised July 12, 2026 What is Pop’s Kitchen in Maryland Heights known for? Pop’s Kitchen is a takeout-only fish-and-chicken shop in the Dorsett Village plaza in Maryland Heights, known for fried catfish, jack salmon, wings, and a loaded Philly cheesesteak — generous portions at fair prices, around 4.4 to 4.5 stars. Open Monday through Saturday, closed Sundays; no dine-in, so order ahead. Keep reading ↓It’s Friday, you’re wiped, and the last thing you want to do is cook. What you actually want is a paper bag going translucent at the bottom, still warm, packed with something fried that was worth the drive home. Maybe you’re headed back toward Bridgeton, maybe out to Creve Coeur, maybe you just need to feed a hungry house without spending an hour at the stove. In Maryland Heights, a small counter-service spot tucked into the Dorsett Village plaza has quietly built a reputation for exactly that. No dining room, no frills — just made-to-order fish, chicken, and sandwiches that come out fast and come out big. That’s Pop’s Kitchen. Here’s what to order, what to know before you go, and the family story behind the counter. ## At a Glance: What to Order ## What Pop’s Kitchen Actually Is Pop’s Kitchen is a fast, order-at-the-counter comfort-food shop — fried fish, fried chicken, and grilled sandwiches, made to order. There’s no dine-in room; this is a pick-up spot, so you order ahead or wait a few minutes and carry it home. What keeps people coming back isn’t ambiance — it’s that the portions are huge, the food is flavorful, and the price is fair. It’s also a genuine family business. Pop’s is run by the Qasem family, who came to St. Louis from Palestine — founder Mohammed Qasem immigrated in 1997, opened the original shop on St. Charles Rock Road in 2013, and grew it into a second Maryland Heights location in 2021, where his brother Fayez runs the counter. That’s the “Pop” energy people feel here: a spot built by one family, one fryer basket at a time, feeding their corner of the metro. It’s a very St. Louis story, when you think about it — a family that crossed an ocean and built something real out of a strip-mall storefront, serving the fried catfish and wings their neighbors grew up on. There’s no corporate playbook behind the counter, no test kitchen deciding the recipes. Because everything is cooked to order rather than sitting under a heat lamp, what you carry out is genuinely fresh from the fryer — the trade-off being that you wait a few minutes, which is exactly why calling ahead is the regular’s move. That combination — family-run, made-to-order, big portions, fair prices — is why a small counter with no dining room has earned the loyalty it has. ## A St. Louis kind of shop If you’re not from here, the fried-fish-and-chicken counter might need a little explaining — because in St. Louis, it’s practically its own food group. All over the metro you’ll find small, independent shops doing exactly this: catfish and whiting in the fryer, wings tossed to order, and, more often than not, a Philly cheesesteak on the same menu. Longtime institutions like King Edward’s Chicken & Fish have been working this template since 1966. Pop’s sits squarely in that tradition — the neighborhood fry counter where dinner comes in a paper bag and nobody leaves hungry. It’s the kind of food that shows up at St. Louis fish fries and Friday-night dinner tables year-round — fried fish is close to a regional love language here — and a shop like Pop’s turns it into a weeknight option you don’t have to cook yourself. Pairing a Philly cheesesteak with a catfish dinner might sound odd on paper, but in St. Louis it’s a familiar combination: the neighborhood fry counter is where a lot of these menus grew up, adding hot sandwiches and wings until there was something for everybody in the car. Pop’s carries that tradition forward without overthinking it — the point isn’t novelty, it’s a hot, generous meal handed across the counter in a couple of minutes. ## Fried fish is a St. Louis love language To really understand a place like Pop’s, it helps to know how seriously St. Louis takes fried fish. For generations, the **Friday fish fry** has been a regional institution — rooted in the Catholic tradition of skipping meat on Fridays, especially during Lent, and turned into a community event in church basements and social halls across the metro. Some have been running for decades; the fish fry at St. Ferdinand in Florissant has been going since 1953. Learning to love a paper plate of fried cod or catfish is, only half-jokingly, part of becoming a true St. Louisan. A shop like Pop’s takes that seasonal, once-a-week ritual and puts it on the menu six days a week. You don’t have to wait for Lent or a parish calendar — the fryer’s already going. ## What to Order at Pop’s Kitchen **The fried catfish** is the headliner — crisp cornmeal crust, moist inside, the plate people make the drive for. You can get it as a fillet, or go for catfish nuggets if you want all crunch. Right next to it, order the **jack salmon** (more ...

## Explore the Cosmos at the McDonnell Planetarium in St. Louis Revised July 23, 2026 What is the planetarium at the Saint Louis Science Center? The James S. McDonnell Planetarium is the iconic, hyperboloid-shaped planetarium at the Saint Louis Science Center in Forest Park (5050 Oakland Ave). Opened in 1963 and designed by architect Gyo Obata, it reopened in July 2026 after a major renovation with a new GOTO star projector and a Cosm Digistar full-dome system. The Science Center itself is free to enter; the immersive star shows in the StarBay Theater are ticketed. It’s regularly ranked among the best planetariums in the country. Keep reading ↓Look up almost anywhere in Forest Park and you’ll spot it: a great white hourglass of a building, curving up against the sky like something that landed rather than was built. That’s the James S. McDonnell Planetarium, one of St. Louis’s most beloved landmarks — and after a major upgrade, it’s better than ever. This is your honest guide to exploring the cosmos right here in St. Louis: what it is, what you’ll see, and how to plan a visit. The timing couldn’t be better. The planetarium reopened in July 2026 after a nearly six-month renovation, emerging with cutting-edge technology that has it billed as one of the most advanced hybrid planetariums in the country. If you haven’t been in a while — or ever — now is the moment. The upgrade was significant enough to make national news, and locals who grew up with the old star projector are discovering a genuinely transformed experience under the same iconic roof. ## A St. Louis icon, reborn The McDonnell Planetarium is part of the **Saint Louis Science Center** in Forest Park, and it’s been the city’s home for all things space for more than 60 years. It first beamed a star show on April 16, 1963, and its unmistakable shape — a thin-shell concrete hyperboloid designed by celebrated St. Louis architect Gyo Obata of HOK — has been a landmark on the Forest Park skyline ever since. It’s named for aviation pioneer James Smith McDonnell, whose aerospace legacy is woven through the whole building and, in a real sense, through the whole city. For generations of St. Louisans, a trip here was a childhood rite of passage — the school field trip where space suddenly felt close enough to touch. The reopening gives a whole new generation that same first moment of looking up in the dark and feeling small in the best possible way. What makes the reopening a genuine event is what’s now inside. The renovation installed a first-of-its-kind-in-the-U.S. hybrid star projector paired with a state-of-the-art full-dome digital system, letting the theater fly you through more than 100 million stars in immersive, 360-degree detail under what the Science Center calls the largest artificial sky in the Western Hemisphere. It’s a serious leap, and it earned national recognition even before the upgrade — the McDonnell Planetarium was named the best planetarium in the country in a recent USA TODAY 10Best Readers’ Choice poll. Planning a St. Louis day around the planetarium? Pair it with the rest of Forest Park — the free Zoo, Art Museum, and History Museum are all a short walk away. Our guide to exploring St. Louis maps a full day out. Run a St. Louis business families would love to find? A directory listing puts you in front of people searching “things to do near me” and planning their next outing. ## Six decades of looking up The planetarium’s history is a real part of its charm. When it opened in 1963, its space-age silhouette felt like a promise about the future — fitting, in a city that built the Mercury and Gemini capsules that carried the first Americans into orbit. That aerospace heritage isn’t decoration here; it’s local history. James McDonnell’s company put St. Louis at the center of the space race, and the planetarium that bears his name has spent generations turning that legacy into wonder for kids and adults alike. Gyo Obata’s hyperboloid design — that graceful, curving concrete shell — has aged into one of the most recognizable pieces of mid-century architecture in the region. It’s the kind of building that makes an impression before you ever walk inside, and it’s been a fixture in the memories of St. Louisans who came here on childhood field trips and now bring their own kids. Few attractions manage to be both a genuine scientific institution and a nostalgic landmark; this one has been both for over 60 years. ## What you’ll experience The heart of a visit is a live or immersive show in the **Bill and Laura Orthwein StarBay Theater**, under the big dome. Current programs cover a real range: - **The Sky Tonight**— a live, educator-guided tour of the current night sky, so you’ll actually know what you’re looking at when you step outside. - **The Earth Today: A Changing Planet**— a striking look at our own world using real-time geospatial data. - **The Little Star That Could 360**— a gentle, immersive show made for younger kids and families, and a great first planetarium experience for the smallest visitors. Because programming rotates and new shows debut over time, it’s worth checking the current lineup before you visit — there’s usually something for both the serious space enthusiast and the kid who just wants to see ...

## Hiring a Personal Injury Lawyer in St. Louis: Deadlines, Fees and the State Line Revised July 27, 2026 How long do I have to file an injury claim in St. Louis? **Which side of the river decides your case.** Missouri: **5 years** for personal injury, 3 for wrongful death (from death), 2 for med-mal. Illinois: **2 years** for injury and wrongful death, and only **1 year** against a local public entity. Shorter deadlines override: **30 days** written notice to your employer for a work injury, **90 days** written notice to the mayor for a City of St. Louis street/sidewalk defect. ⚖️ **Fault works oppositely:** Missouri is PURE comparative fault, Illinois bars recovery above 50%. At 60% at fault on $100,000 — **Missouri pays $40,000, Illinois pays $0**. 💰 Missouri’s rules require your contingency agreement to state whether expenses come off BEFORE or AFTER the fee — on a $100K settlement that one sentence is worth $3,333. Provider liens are capped at 50% of NET (after fees and costs). 🚫 A lawyer phoning or approaching you after a crash is prohibited outright; written solicitation is barred for 30 days. Two cars crash the same way on the same afternoon. One wreck happens on Kingshighway, the other on a street in Belleville, twenty minutes east. The Missouri driver has **five years** to file. The Illinois driver has **two**. And if a jury later decides each driver was 60% at fault, the Missouri driver still collects a substantial check while the Illinois driver collects **nothing at all.** St. Louis straddles a state line, which means the single most important fact about an injury claim here is one almost nobody explains: *which side of the river it happened on.* ## How long do I have to file an injury claim in St. Louis? In **Missouri**, generally **five years** for personal injury, **three years** for wrongful death from the date of death, and **two years** for medical malpractice. In **Illinois**, it’s **two years** for personal injury and wrongful death, and only **one year** for a claim against a local public entity. If your claim is against the City of St. Louis for a street or sidewalk defect, written notice must reach the mayor within **90 days**. And a work injury must be reported to your employer in writing within **30 days**. Which deadline applies is a legal question — don’t self-diagnose it. ## Missouri’s five years is a trap Missouri’s general five-year window is unusually generous, and that generosity is exactly what hurts people. Someone hears “five years,” relaxes, and blows through every shorter deadline that actually governs their case. Because the five years is the *exception* in this list, not the rule: **Wrongful death: three years** from the date of death, not from the injury. **Medical malpractice: two years** from the act, with a ten-year outer limit. **A work injury: 30 days** to notify your employer in writing. **Street or sidewalk defect in the City of St. Louis: 90 days** written notice to the mayor. **Anything that happened in Illinois: two years** — or one year against a municipality. One more that surprises people: for a minor, the Missouri clock is paused until the disability is removed — and the statute sets that at age **twenty-one**, not eighteen. Medical malpractice has its own separate rule for minors. ## The 90-day rule almost nobody knows If you were hurt by a defect in a street, sidewalk, bridge, boulevard or thoroughfare in a Missouri city of 100,000 or more — which in this metro essentially means the City of St. Louis — you must give **written notice to the mayor within 90 days** of the occurrence. The notice has to state the place, the time, the character and circumstances of the injury, and that you will claim damages. Two limits worth being precise about, because they get blurred constantly. It applies only to **cities** over 100,000 — St. Louis County is a county, not a city, so this particular provision doesn’t reach it. And it applies only to **those specific kinds of defects**, not to every claim against a city. Suing a public entity is harder in another way, too. Missouri governments are generally immune, with narrow exceptions — principally the negligent operation of a motor vehicle by a public employee on the job, and injuries caused by a dangerous condition of public property. Outside those windows the claim often does not exist at all. Where immunity is waived, damages are capped, and the cap is adjusted for inflation every year. For **2026** the Department of Commerce and Insurance publishes it at **$532,148** for any one person and **$3,547,658** for all claims from a single occurrence. Those numbers change every January 1 — if you see them quoted without a year attached, they’re probably stale. ## Partly your fault? It depends which state This is the single biggest practical difference across the river, and it’s the reason people who assume they have no case sometimes do. **Missouri uses pure comparative fault.** There is no cutoff. Your recovery is reduced by your share of the blame, and that’s all. (Worth noting for accuracy: for ordinary negligence this comes from a 1983 Missouri Supreme Court decision rather than a statute, so anyone citing “the Missouri comparative fault statute” for a car wreck is misinformed.) **Illinois uses modified comparative negligence with a bar.** If you are found *more ...

# Hiring a Personal Injury Lawyer in St. Louis: Deadlines, Fees and the State Line Revised July 27, 2026 How long do I have to file an injury claim in St. Louis? **Which side of the river decides your case.** Missouri: **5 years** for personal injury, 3 for wrongful death (from death), 2 for med-mal. Illinois: **2 years** for injury and wrongful death, and only **1 year** against a local public entity. Shorter deadlines override: **30 days** written notice to your employer for a work injury, **90 days** written notice to the mayor for a City of St. Louis street/sidewalk defect. ⚖️ **Fault works oppositely:** Missouri is PURE comparative fault, Illinois bars recovery above 50%. At 60% at fault on $100,000 — **Missouri pays $40,000, Illinois pays $0**. 💰 Missouri’s rules require your contingency agreement to state whether expenses come off BEFORE or AFTER the fee — on a $100K settlement that one sentence is worth $3,333. Provider liens are capped at 50% of NET (after fees and costs). 🚫 A lawyer phoning or approaching you after a crash is prohibited outright; written solicitation is barred for 30 days. Two cars crash the same way on the same afternoon. One wreck happens on Kingshighway, the other on a street in Belleville, twenty minutes east. The Missouri driver has **five years** to file. The Illinois driver has **two**. And if a jury later decides each driver was 60% at fault, the Missouri driver still collects a substantial check while the Illinois driver collects **nothing at all.** St. Louis straddles a state line, which means the single most important fact about an injury claim here is one almost nobody explains: *which side of the river it happened on.* ## How long do I have to file an injury claim in St. Louis? In **Missouri**, generally **five years** for personal injury, **three years** for wrongful death from the date of death, and **two years** for medical malpractice. ## The Best Dance Clubs in St. Louis: Where to Go Out Revised July 23, 2026 What are the best places to go dancing in St. Louis? St. Louis nightlife clusters in a few walkable districts: Washington Avenue downtown for big clubs, The Grove for LGBTQ+-friendly and eclectic spots, Soulard for bars and live music, and the Delmar Loop for a mixed crowd. Whether you want a DJ-driven dance floor, Latin night, or a live band, these entertainment districts are where the scene lives — check each venue’s nights and age policy before you head out. Keep reading ↓You know the itch. It’s Friday, the group chat is lighting up, and somebody finally says it out loud: *let’s go dancing.* Not a quiet wine bar. Not a booth where you have to lean in and shout. You want the real thing — a floor, a good DJ, bass you feel in your chest, and a couple of hours where the only decision is whether to stay for one more song. Whether you’re getting ready in Florissant, pre-gaming in Soulard, or piling into a rideshare from St. Charles, the night starts with the same question: *where do we actually go?* Here’s the honest truth about dancing in St. Louis — the scene is genuinely good, but it’s scattered across a half-dozen neighborhoods, and it changes fast. Clubs open, close, and rebrand; the hot spot from three years ago might be a food hall now. So this is the current, on-the-ground guide: where to dance right now, sorted by vibe and neighborhood, plus the one local quirk that quietly decides how your whole night ends. **The best places to go dancing in St. Louis span a few districts: Washington Avenue downtown (EDM and hip-hop at Europe, dressy dancing at Pepper Lounge), The Grove (the heart of LGBTQ+ nightlife and Latin nights), Soulard’s DJ bars, Latin dancing at Club Viva, country line-dancing at PBR in Ballpark Village, and true after-hours clubs across the river in Sauget, Illinois. Most are 21+.** ## The Local Quirk That Shapes Your Whole Night: Last Call by Zone Before you pick a spot, know this — it’s the single most useful thing about St. Louis nightlife. **When the music stops depends entirely on which side of which line you’re standing on.** Across most of the Missouri metro, last call is 1:30am. But qualifying high-volume venues in the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County can serve until 3am, which is why the downtown and Grove spots keep going after the suburbs have gone dark. And if you’re still not ready to quit? Cross the Mississippi into Sauget, Illinois, where the clubs run until 5 or 6am — and one legendary spot never closes at all. So the shape of your night is really a choice: a normal-hours neighborhood bar, a 3am downtown club, or a dawn-patrol run across the river. Plan the finish before you plan the start, and line up your rides accordingly. ## Downtown & Washington Avenue: The Club District Washington Avenue was St. Louis’s marquee club strip for years, and while it’s thinned out, its anchor is still standing and still packed. **Europe Night Club** (710 N 15th St) is the survivor — a proper nightclub running house, techno, bass, hip-hop, and Latin nights, open late Thursday through Saturday, and big enough to land touring names when the trance and EDM crowd comes to town. It inherited the crowds from the downtown clubs that have closed around it, which is exactly why it still feels alive on a Saturday at midnight. For something a little dressier, **Pepper Lounge** brings an all-night dance floor with hip-hop, R&B, house, and EDM and a cocktail-and-heels crowd — a good pick if you want to dance but also want the night to feel like an occasion. Over at Ballpark Village, **Tin Roof** mixes live bands and DJs for a rowdier, no-pretense party, and right next door sits the metro’s wildest curveball (more on that below). ## The Grove: St. Louis’s Nightlife Heart (and LGBTQ+ Home Base) If you want the densest concentration of dance floors in one walkable stretch, go to The Grove on Manchester Avenue — the center of St. Louis’s LGBTQ+ nightlife and one of the most welcoming, high-energy scenes in the region for absolutely everyone. **Just John Nightclub** (4112 Manchester) is the flagship: a real dance floor, a stage, a patio, rotating DJs and theme parties, and drag bingo early in the week. A few doors down, the bike-themed **HandleBar** is a two-story party with open-format DJ sets, karaoke, drag, and a monthly Latin dance night (salsa, bachata, cumbia) that’s become a metro favorite. Round out the Grove crawl with **Rehab Bar & Grill** (drag shows, patio, DJ nights), the long-running neighborhood staple **Attitudes**, and **Bar:PM**, with spacious dance floors and regular events. One geography note so you find it: the beloved **Grey Fox Pub** — a gay pub and drag venue going strong since 1988 — is just south in Tower Grove South, not in the Grove proper, but it’s well worth the short hop. ## Soulard: Where the DJ Sets Sneak Up on You Soulard is famous for its bar-crawl energy, and several of its spots turn into genuine dance parties after dark. **Social Bar & Grill** on South 7th throws a bass-heavy EDM night on Thursdays and an industry party on Sundays. ...

## Local SEO for Contractors in St. Louis: What Google Actually Says Revised July 27, 2026 How does local search ranking actually work? ⭐ Google’s own words: **“There’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.”** Ranking is relevance + distance + prominence — and you cannot influence distance. **Service-area rules:** up to 20 service areas (cities/ZIPs, NOT a radius), ~2 hours max driving time, remove your address if customers don’t visit, and **never create a separate listing per suburb** — Google prohibits it and it’s the top cause of suspension. Virtual offices and PO boxes are ineligible. ⚠️ **Missouri does NOT license HVAC/mechanical, plumbing or general contractors statewide** — despite what several sites claim. That bill has FAILED in six sessions. Electrical contractors are the only construction trade licensed by the state, it’s optional, and municipalities must recognize it in lieu of a local license. 🚫 Reviews: Google publishes NO threshold; incentivized reviews (even a discount) are explicitly prohibited and can get existing reviews unpublished. Google publishes a sentence that most of the marketing industry would rather you didn’t read: **“There’s no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.”** That is Google’s own help documentation, not our opinion. And it is worth starting there, because if you search the question this article answers, *every single result on the first page is written by someone selling the service.* Including a block of ads for SEO agencies. We sell directory listings, so we have our own interest — and we’ll be upfront about where it shows up. But most of what follows is Google telling you how this works, and Missouri law telling you something about your license that a lot of websites are getting flatly wrong. ## How does local search ranking actually work? Google says local results are ranked on three things. **Relevance** is “how well a Business Profile matches what someone is searching for.” **Distance** is “how far each business is from the customer who’s searching.” **Prominence** is “how well-known a business is.” You can influence relevance and prominence. You cannot influence distance, and you cannot buy position — Google states plainly there is no way to request or pay for better local ranking. ## The thing about being a service-area business Most trades don’t have a shop customers walk into. You drive to them. Google calls that a service-area business, and the rules are specific, published, and routinely violated by people trying to game them. You can list **up to 20 service areas**, defined by city, postal code, or similar. You **cannot set a radius** — “thirty miles around Kirkwood” is not an option; you name places. Google says your service area should not exceed **about two hours of driving time** from your base, which in this metro means the whole thing, Illinois included, is fair game. If customers don’t come to you, Google says to **remove your address from your profile**. If you have a showroom and also go out, you can run as a hybrid and keep the address visible. Now the rules that get businesses penalized, all in Google’s own words: **“Do not create more than one page for each location of your business.”** That kills the scheme somebody will eventually pitch you — a separate listing for Ballwin, one for Florissant, one for O’Fallon. It is against the rules, in writing, and it is the most common reason a trade business gets its profile suspended. A rented mailing address you don’t operate from — a virtual office — **“isn’t eligible for a Business Profile.”** Neither are P.O. boxes or remote mailboxes. And your business name has to be your actual business name, “as used consistently on your storefront, website, stationery, and as known to customers.” Not *Smith Plumbing — Emergency Plumber St. Louis Ballwin Kirkwood*. ## The uncomfortable math nobody selling you services will explain Put those three facts together and you get a conclusion worth sitting with. Distance from the searcher is a confirmed ranking factor. A service-area business has to hide its address. And you are allowed exactly one listing. Which means **you cannot rank equally across the whole St. Louis metro, and no amount of money changes that.** A plumber based in Affton will have a harder time surfacing for someone searching in St. Peters than a plumber based in St. Peters will — not because of effort or budget, but because of geometry. That is not a reason to do nothing. It is a reason to be skeptical of anyone promising metro-wide dominance, and a reason to think hard about which twenty areas you actually name. ## The Missouri license thing that half the internet gets wrong If you have searched for what license you need in Missouri, you may have read that the state has a statewide HVAC or mechanical contractor license, and possibly that it took effect in early 2026. **That is not true.** The Missouri Statewide Mechanical Contractors Licensing Act has been introduced *and has failed* in at least six sessions — 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2025, and the current one, where it sits in committee. Bills carry conditional effective dates, and websites keep mistaking those for law. Here is what Missouri actually licenses at the state level, per the Division of Professional Registration’s own list of professions: **Electrical contractors:** yes — and it’s the only ...

## How to Choose a Real Estate Agent in St. Louis (After the 2024 Rule Change) Revised July 27, 2026 How do you choose a real estate agent in St. Louis? Verify the license first — Missouri’s free lookup is at **mopro.mo.gov/license/s/license-search**, and disciplinary actions since 2011 are posted separately at **pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp**. Since **August 17, 2024** (the *Burnett v. NAR* settlement, decided in a Missouri federal court), buyer-agent compensation no longer appears on the MLS and buyers must sign a written agreement BEFORE touring a home — and that agreement’s compensation must be “objectively ascertainable” and “not open-ended,” so a blank or “standard rate” does not qualify. ⚠️ Commissions did NOT fall: Redfin tracked 2.36% (Q3 2024) → 2.42% (Q3 2025), and homes under $500K average **2.52%** — the highest tier, where nearly all St. Louis sales sit. Only 27.2% of buyers negotiate. Watch the geography on any median quoted: City ~$261K vs County ~$325K vs MSA list price ~$290K (June 2026). The rules for hiring a real estate agent changed in August 2024, and the lawsuit that changed them was decided in a Missouri federal courtroom — the Western District, in Kansas City. If you are buying a house in St. Louis right now, you will be asked to sign something before you are allowed to walk through your first front door. Most people sign it without reading it. Here is what actually changed, what didn’t, and the specific things worth checking before you pick anyone. ## How do you choose a real estate agent in St. Louis? Start by verifying the license. Missouri’s public lookup is at **mopro.mo.gov**, and disciplinary actions since 2011 are posted separately at **pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp** — both free, both take a minute. Then interview at least three, and before signing anything, get the compensation figure written as an actual number. Since August 2024 a buyer must sign a written agreement before touring a home, and that agreement’s compensation term must be, in the National Association of Realtors’ own words, “objectively ascertainable” and “not open-ended.” A blank, or “standard rate,” or “whatever the seller offers” does not meet that standard. ## What actually changed in 2024 The case was *Burnett v. National Association of Realtors*. NAR agreed to pay $418 million, and a judge granted final approval in November 2024. The practice changes took effect on August 17, 2024. Two of them matter to you. **One: offers of buyer-agent compensation came off the MLS.** This is the change that gets described wrong more than any other. Compensation was *not* banned. Sellers can still offer to pay a buyer’s agent — it just can’t be advertised through the multiple listing service anymore. Seller concessions toward your closing costs can still appear there. **Two: you sign before you tour.** An agent working with you must have a signed written agreement in place before showing you a home. There are exceptions — an open house hosted by the seller’s agent doesn’t require one, and neither does a showing where you’re unrepresented. What did **not** change: commissions were always negotiable. The settlement didn’t create that, cap anything, or set a rate. NAR now requires agents to conspicuously disclose that compensation “is not set by law and is fully negotiable” — which was true before, and is now something they have to say out loud. ## Commissions did not go down You will read that the settlement drove commissions down. The data doesn’t support it, and you should know that before you sit across from anyone. Redfin’s research tracked the average buyer’s-agent commission at **2.38% in the second quarter of 2024**, dipping to **2.36% in the third quarter** as the rules took effect — and back to **2.42% by the third quarter of 2025**. Slightly higher than before the change. A separate analysis by AccountTECH, covering more than 224,000 closed transactions across roughly 1,300 offices, found the same shape: a real dip in late 2024 that round-tripped within about five months. Two independent datasets, same conclusion. Anyone telling you the market has settled this for you is wrong. And there’s a detail in that data that lands directly on St. Louis. Broken out by price, the average buyer-agent commission in the third quarter of 2025 ran **2.52% on homes under $500,000**, 2.32% between $500,000 and $999,000, and 2.22% above a million. The cheaper the house, the higher the percentage. # How to Choose a Real Estate Agent in St. Louis (After the 2024 Rule Change) Revised July 27, 2026 How do you choose a real estate agent in St. Louis? Verify the license first — Missouri’s free lookup is at **mopro.mo.gov/license/s/license-search**, and disciplinary actions since 2011 are posted separately at **pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp**. Since **August 17, 2024** (the *Burnett v. NAR* settlement, decided in a Missouri federal court), buyer-agent compensation no longer appears on the MLS and buyers must sign a written agreement BEFORE touring a home — and that agreement’s compensation must be “objectively ascertainable” and “not open-ended,” so a blank or “standard rate” does not qualify. ⚠️ Commissions did NOT fall: Redfin tracked 2.36% (Q3 2024) → 2.42% (Q3 2025), and homes under $500K average **2.52%** — the highest tier, where nearly all St. Louis sales sit. Only 27.2% of buyers negotiate. Watch the geography on any median quoted: City ~$261K vs County ~$325K vs MSA list price ~$290K (June 2026). The rules for hiring a real estate agent changed in August 2024, and the lawsuit that changed them was decided in a Missouri federal courtroom — the Western District, in Kansas City. If you are buying a house in St. Louis right now, you will be asked to sign something before you are allowed to walk through your first front door. Most people sign it without reading it. Here is what actually changed, what didn’t, and the specific things worth checking before you pick anyone. ## How do you choose a real estate agent in St. Louis? Start by verifying the license. Missouri’s public lookup is at **mopro.mo.gov**, and disciplinary actions since 2011 are posted separately at **pr.mo.gov/realestate-disciplines.asp** — both free, both take a minute. Then interview at least three, and before signing anything, get the compensation figure written as an actual number. Since August 2024 a buyer must sign a written agreement before touring a home, and that agreement’s compensation term must be, in the National Association of Realtors’ own words, “objectively ascertainable” and “not open-ended.” A blank, or “standard rate,” or “whatever the seller offers” does not meet that standard. ## What actually changed in 2024 The case was *Burnett v. National Association of Realtors*. NAR agreed to pay $418 million, and a judge granted final approval in November 2024. The practice changes took effect on August 17, 2024. Two of them matter to you. **One: offers of buyer-agent compensation came off the MLS.** This is the change that gets described wrong more than any other. Compensation was *not* banned. Sellers can still offer to pay a buyer’s agent — it just can’t be advertised through the multiple listing service anymore. Seller concessions toward your closing costs can still appear there. **Two: you sign before you tour.** An agent working with you must have a signed written agreement in place before showing you a home. There are exceptions — an open house hosted by the seller’s agent doesn’t require one, and neither does a showing where you’re unrepresented. What did **not** change: commissions were always negotiable. The settlement didn’t create that, cap anything, or set a rate. NAR now requires agents to conspicuously disclose that compensation “is not set by law and is fully negotiable” — which was true before, and is now something they have to say out loud. ## Commissions did not go down You will read that the settlement drove commissions down. The data doesn’t support it, and you should know that before you sit across from anyone. Redfin’s research tracked the average buyer’s-agent commission at **2.38% in the second quarter of 2024**, dipping to **2.36% in the third quarter** as the rules took effect — and back to **2.42% by the third quarter of 2025**. Slightly higher than before the change. A separate analysis by AccountTECH, covering more than 224,000 closed transactions across roughly 1,300 offices, found the same shape: a real dip in late 2024 that round-tripped within about five months. Two independent datasets, same conclusion. Anyone telling you the market has settled this for you is wrong. And there’s a detail in that data that lands directly on St. Louis. Broken out by price, the average buyer-agent commission in the third quarter of 2025 ran **2.52% on homes under $500,000**, 2.32% between $500,000 and $999,000, and 2.22% above a million. The cheaper the house, the higher the percentage. Nearly every St. Louis transaction sits in that first tier — so buyers and sellers here are in the segment paying the *most*, proportionally, and have the most to gain from asking. Which almost nobody does. A survey conducted by Ipsos for Redfin in spring 2025 found **37.4% of sellers** negotiated or tried to negotiate commission — against just **27.2% of buyers.** Buyers are leaving the most on the table, in the tier where the percentage is highest. ## Verify the license in about a minute Two free public tools, and almost nobody uses either. **License status:** the Missouri Division of Professional Registration portal at **mopro.mo.gov/license/s/license-search**. You can confirm the license is real, active, and whether the person is a salesperson or a broker. ## Old-House Wiring in St. Louis: Knob-and-Tube, Aluminum, and Your Panel Revised July 28, 2026 What is knob-and-tube wiring, and is it dangerous? The median home in the **City of St. Louis was built in 1938** and 57.9% predate 1940 (Census ACS 2020–2024); **St. Louis County’s median is 1969** with ~34% built 1960–1979. That means two different problems: the city is **knob-and-tube** country, the county is **aluminum branch wiring** (1965–73) and questionable-panel country. Existing knob-and-tube is legal and grandfathered — the real hazard is **insulation covering it**, which the electrical code prohibits, because it was designed to shed heat into open air. CPSC: pre-1972 aluminum-wired homes are **55× more likely** to reach “Fire Hazard Conditions” (cover-plate screws at 300°F). ⚠️ CPSC closed its Federal Pacific investigation in 1983 *without* a conclusion either way. 100 amps is the code MINIMUM, not a deficiency — a load calculation decides. In the City you may NOT pull your own permit for a rewire or service change. The median house in the City of St. Louis was built in **1938**. Nearly **58%** of the city’s housing went up in 1939 or earlier, per the Census Bureau’s five-year American Community Survey estimates. In St. Louis County the median is **1969**, and about a third of the housing stock was built between 1960 and 1979. Those two numbers, both from the Census Bureau, mean the city and the county have *completely different* electrical problems hiding in their walls. City houses are knob-and-tube country. County houses are aluminum-wiring and questionable-panel country. Here’s how to tell what you have, what actually matters, and what you can ignore. ## What is knob-and-tube wiring, and is it dangerous? Knob-and-tube was the standard wiring method from roughly the 1880s through the 1940s — two separate conductors run several inches apart, supported by white porcelain knobs and passing through porcelain tubes where they cross framing. It has no ground wire, and its cloth-and-rubber insulation gets brittle with age. But the single biggest hazard isn’t age at all: **it was engineered to shed heat into open air, so burying it in insulation is what makes it dangerous.** The National Electrical Code prohibits concealed knob-and-tube in spaces filled with loose, rolled or foamed-in insulation for exactly that reason. ## The city problem: knob-and-tube A 1938 median puts the typical city house dead in the middle of the knob-and-tube era. If you own a brick house in south city, Tower Grove, Dutchtown, Baden or the north side, there is a genuine chance some original wiring is still in service somewhere in it. **Go look, and don’t touch anything.** In an unfinished basement or attic you’re looking for white porcelain spools nailed to the joists with a single wire running through each, porcelain tubes where wire passes through wood, and — the giveaway — two separate wires running parallel several inches apart instead of one modern cable. The sheathing is cloth or rubber, often cracked. The thing you are actually hunting for is **knob-and-tube buried under or inside blown-in insulation.** That is the combination the Code specifically bans, and it is the realistic fire scenario. It usually happens innocently: somebody insulated the attic decades after the wiring went in and had no idea it mattered. Two more clues that you’re on an ungrounded system: two-prong outlets throughout the house, and no third slot anywhere. ## So is it legal? Yes. Existing knob-and-tube is generally grandfathered — the electrical code is not retroactive, and neither Missouri nor the federal government bans living with it. You are not breaking a law by owning it. Where it bites is the moment you *touch* it. The Code permits knob-and-tube only as an extension of an existing installation, typically with the local inspector’s approval, and new installation isn’t allowed at all. Insulating over it is prohibited outright. The City of St. Louis enforces the 2017 edition of the National Electrical Code; St. Louis County runs on its own adopted edition, so confirm with the County before planning work out there. ## The county problem: aluminum branch wiring If your house went up in the late sixties or early seventies — which describes about a third of St. Louis County — your risk is different and better documented. Between roughly **1965 and 1973**, a copper shortage pushed builders to aluminum branch circuit wiring. The Consumer Product Safety Commission estimates about **two million homes** got it. And the CPSC finding is blunt: homes built before 1972 wired with aluminum are **55 times more likely** to have one or more connections at outlets reach what the agency calls “Fire Hazard Conditions.” That phrase has an actual definition, which almost nobody quoting the statistic bothers to include. It means the cover plate screws on a receptacle reaching **300°F**, or sparks coming out of the receptacle, or the material around it charring. The important nuance: **the danger is at the connections, not in the wire itself.** Aluminum expands, contracts and oxidizes where it terminates at a switch or outlet, and those spots turn into high-resistance hot spots over decades. To spot it, look at the cable sheathing in your basement or at the panel for printed **“AL”** or **“ALUMINUM,”** and at conductor color — dull silver rather than copper. CPSC accepts two permanent repairs short of a full copper rewire: **COPALUM** crimp connectors and **AlumiConn** connectors. What it does *not* accept as a permanent fix is ...

## Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine: A Hazelwood Middle Eastern Favorite Revised July 23, 2026 What kind of food does Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine serve? It serves Levantine classics — chicken and beef shawarma, lamb shish kebab, kefta, and a mixed grill, plus mezze like hummus, baba ganoush, fattoush, falafel, and stuffed grape leaves, with baklava for dessert. It first opened in Florissant around 2013 before moving to its longtime Hazelwood home. In north St. Louis County, Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine is exactly that spot. This is an honest look at what it is, what to order, and why it’s spent more than a decade earning a loyal Hazelwood following. If you’ve driven North Lindbergh and never stopped, you’ve been missing some of the best Middle Eastern food on the north side — shawarma, kebabs, hummus, and mezze made from scratch by a family that’s been doing it right for years. It’s the sort of place that doesn’t advertise much because it doesn’t have to; word of mouth and a loyal regular base keep it going, which is usually the best possible sign about a restaurant. ## What Kaslik is Kaslik Mediterranean Cuisine sits at **7847 North Lindbergh Boulevard in Hazelwood, MO 63042**, phone **(314) 972-8282**. It’s a family-owned Mediterranean and Middle Eastern restaurant serving Levantine classics — the shawarma, kebabs, and mezze of the eastern Mediterranean. It first opened in Florissant around 2013 and moved to its Hazelwood home a couple of years later, and it’s been a north-county fixture ever since. A note on the name and the food, because it’s a nice story: “Kaslik” is a town in Lebanon, and the menu draws on that whole Levantine tradition — but the family behind the restaurant is Palestinian, having come to St. Louis from the West Bank. The result is honest, home-style Middle Eastern cooking rooted in real heritage rather than a corporate concept, which is exactly why it tastes the way it does. ## What to order The menu covers the Levantine greatest hits, and a few dishes anchor any good order: - **Shawarma**— chicken or beef, sliced from the spit, wrapped or over rice. The gateway dish and a reliable favorite. - **Kebabs and grilled meats**— lamb shish kebab, chicken kabob, kefta, and a mixed grill platter for the table that wants a bit of everything off the fire. - **The mezze**— hummus, baba ganoush, fattoush, and stuffed grape leaves. Order a few to share; they turn a sandwich run into a proper spread. - **Falafel and vegetarian options**— crisp, herby falafel and a genuinely good veggie platter make this an easy call for meatless eaters. - **Baklava**— the classic sweet, flaky finish. Save room. The kebabs and the hummus are the fundamentals that tell you whether a Middle Eastern kitchen is the real deal, and Kaslik passes the test — the grilled meats come off the fire juicy and well-seasoned, and the dips taste made-that-day because they are. If you’re new to the cuisine, a mixed grill with a couple of mezze and warm pita is the perfect introduction. It’s the kind of food that tends to surprise skeptics: fresh, satisfying, and far more interesting than the fast-casual chain versions of “Mediterranean bowls” that have popped up everywhere. The Levantine tradition — the cooking of the eastern Mediterranean, from Lebanon and Syria through Palestine and Jordan — is built on fresh, bright, generous flavors: grilled meats seasoned simply and well, fresh herbs, lemon and garlic, olive oil, and a whole family of dips and salads meant for sharing with warm bread. It’s food that feels both healthy and deeply comforting, which is a rare combination — you can eat well here without the heavy, over-full feeling a lot of restaurant meals leave you with, and still walk out satisfied. It’s also a cuisine built for the table, not the individual plate. A proper Middle Eastern meal is a spread — several mezze in the middle, a platter of grilled meats, a stack of pita, everyone reaching and passing. That communal, unhurried style is part of what makes a place like Kaslik feel welcoming, and it’s why it works so well for a group. ## Candicci’s: A 40-Year St. Louis Italian Favorite, Reinvented Revised July 23, 2026 Is Candicci’s still open, and what does it serve now? Yes, but in a new form. The full-service Candicci’s restaurant closed in 2024 and reopened as Candicci’s Catering & Express at 14870 Clayton Road on the Chesterfield/Ballwin border, (636) 220-8989. It focuses on takeout, delivery, and catering — St. Louis-style thin-crust pizza, toasted ravioli, pastas, Italian-American entrees, family specials, and catering trays — rather than sit-down dining. Keep reading ↓If you’ve been ordering from Candicci’s for years — a family pizza night, a toasted-ravioli fix, a catered office lunch — here’s the news that matters: the beloved St. Louis Italian institution is still very much alive, but it has changed shape. This is an honest, up-to-date look at what Candicci’s is *now*, so you know exactly what to expect before you call. The short version: after more than 40 years as a full-service restaurant, Candicci’s closed its longtime Ballwin dining room in 2024 and reopened as **Candicci’s Catering & Express** — a takeout-and-catering operation built around the pizzas, pastas, and family favorites that made its name. If you’re picturing the old white-tablecloth veal-and-seafood dining room with its patio and sit-down service, gently update that picture; the format is different now, but the pizzas, pastas, and toasted ravioli you love are still here, just served a new way. ## What Candicci’s is today Candicci’s Catering & Express operates from **14870 Clayton Road**, on the Chesterfield/Ballwin border in west St. Louis County (ZIP 63017), phone **(636) 220-8989**. It moved here in 2024 into the former Chirco’s Pizza space at Clayton and Baxter — not in Old Town Chesterfield or the Valley, but along the Clayton Road corridor between the two communities. The concept shifted from sit-down dining to **takeout, delivery, and catering**. Owner Bob Candice has been candid in local coverage about why: staff shortages, rising lease costs, and food-cost pressure made the full-service model untenable, so the family reinvented the business around what it does best rather than closing the doors for good. It’s a genuinely admirable pivot — keeping a 40-year name alive by changing the format instead of giving up, and a reminder that the restaurants worth rooting for are often the ones that find a way to keep going when the easy choice would be to walk away. ## The food: St. Louis Italian, built for takeout The menu centers on the crowd-pleasers that travel well: - **St. Louis-style thin-crust pizza**— the local classic, cut into squares — alongside a New York hand-tossed option for a different mood. - **Toasted ravioli**— the quintessential St. Louis appetizer, and a Candicci’s staple. - **Pastas and Italian-American entrees**— think pasta con broccoli, pasta primavera, spaghetti and meatballs, lasagna, eggplant Parmesan, and chicken Marsala. - **Starters and salads**— spinach-artichoke dip, mozzarella sticks, house salad. - **Family specials and a kids’ menu**— built to feed a household without a big-night-out bill. - **Catering trays**— the same favorites scaled up for a crowd, from pastas to pizzas to sliced-meat spreads. It’s an Italian-American menu in the truest, most comforting sense — not chasing trends, just doing the classics well. You price the flight, then the hotel, then the “resort fee” nobody warned you about, then the $18 airport beer — and somewhere around the third browser tab you quietly close the whole thing and tell yourself maybe next year. Here’s the thing most St. Louisans forget: you don’t have to get on a plane to have that night. Twenty minutes from wherever you’re sitting — south county, St. Charles, the Metro East — there’s a real casino floor humming with the same slot chimes, the same green felt, the same “maybe this hand” feeling. And when it’s over, you sleep in your own bed instead of a $300 room at altitude. So before you daydream your way to McCarran again, let’s talk about what’s right here — all six St. Louis casinos, what each one is actually like, and why staying home might be the smartest bet you make all weekend. **There are six casinos in the greater St. Louis area: four in Missouri — Hollywood Casino (Maryland Heights), River City Casino (Lemay), Horseshoe St. Louis (downtown, formerly Lumière Place), and Ameristar (St. Charles) — plus two in Illinois, DraftKings at Casino Queen (East St. Louis) and Argosy Casino Alton. You can play blackjack two blocks from the Gateway Arch, then walk out into a real downtown. You can turn a Cardinals afternoon at Busch into a casino evening without ever moving your car out of a walkable radius. You can win a little, lose a little, and still make it home for a plate of toasted ravioli. Try doing *that* from a hotel tower on the Strip. Then there’s the small stuff that adds up: Midwest dealers who’ll actually talk to you, free parking instead of a $25 garage, and rooms — when you do want to stay over — that cost a fraction of a comparable Vegas weekend, right down to a downtown Four Seasons attached to the casino. The trip you keep not taking? A better version of it is a short drive away. ## Six Casinos, Two States, One River St. Louisans search for “St. Louis casinos” roughly 12,100 times a month, and the area rewards the curiosity: six operating gaming floors inside about a 40-minute drive of downtown, four in Missouri and two across the river in Illinois. That state line matters more than you’d guess, and it’s tangled up in one of the best pieces of local trivia going. Every Missouri casino is, technically, a **floating** casino. State law requires gaming to sit on or right beside the Mississippi or Missouri River, so even the sleek, land-style rooms like Hollywood and Ameristar are actually built atop enormous concrete barges set in water basins. You’d never feel it on the floor — it plays like any Vegas room — but that quirk is why every one of them hugs the riverfront. Illinois plays it more literally still: up in Alton sits an honest-to-goodness riverboat. ## St. Louis Casinos at a Glance ## Hollywood Casino & Hotel — The Biggest Night Out (Maryland Heights) If you want the works — a giant floor, a hotel, a real night — Hollywood in Maryland Heights is the metro’s heavyweight. Around 2,100 slots and video poker machines, 70-plus tables, a 502-room hotel, roughly seven restaurants, and a weekend dance club that leans hard into ’70s and ’80s music. There’s a fitness center, valet, and a free airport shuttle, which makes it the natural landing pad for out-of-towners flying into Lambert. **Best for:** the biggest slot selection, a hotel-and-nightlife weekend, and groups who want everything under one roof. ## River City Casino & Hotel — The South County Favorite (Lemay) Down in Lemay, right on the Mississippi in south county, River City is the pick for anyone on the south ...

## 9 St. Louis Restaurants Locals Actually Love (Not the Chains) Revised July 23, 2026 What are St. Louis’s most iconic restaurants? St. Louis’s most beloved independent restaurants span every price point: Pappy’s Smokehouse for Memphis-style barbecue, Hi-Pointe Drive-In and Stacked STL for standout burgers, The Frisco Barroom in Webster Groves for elevated tavern food, Havana’s Cuisine in the Central West End for a real Cuban sandwich, Menya Rui for Tokyo-style shoyu ramen, The Golden Hoosier for sandwiches with quirky decor, and, for something more refined, Acero in Maplewood and Peppe’s Apt. 2 in Kirkwood. None are chains — that’s the point. Keep reading ↓Picture a Friday night when nobody at the table wants a drive-thru. Maybe you’re showing an out-of-town friend around, or you’re just tired of the same three chains off the highway in Chesterfield, Kirkwood, or Florissant. You want somewhere that actually tastes like St. Louis — a place a local would send you, not a logo you could find in any city in America. This is that list. A quick honesty note first: despite how it sometimes gets labeled, none of these are “fast food” in the drive-thru sense. They run the range from order-at-the-counter barbecue to sit-down, special-occasion kitchens — the common thread is that they’re independent, they’re beloved, and they’re the opposite of an interchangeable chain. Here are nine St. Louis spots worth going out of your way for. ## Nine St. Louis restaurants worth the drive St. Louis’s most beloved local restaurants span every price point and craving: **Pappy’s Smokehouse** for Memphis-style barbecue, **Hi-Pointe Drive-In** and **Stacked STL** for standout burgers, **The Frisco Barroom** in Webster Groves for elevated tavern food, **Havana’s Cuisine** in the Central West End for a real Cuban sandwich, **Menya Rui** for Tokyo-style shoyu ramen, **The Golden Hoosier** for sandwiches with a side of taxidermy, and, when you want something more refined, **Acero** in Maplewood and **Peppe’s Apt. 2** in Kirkwood. Below is what to order at each. ## 1. Pappy’s Smokehouse If you only eat at one place on this list, make it Pappy’s. This is the St. Louis barbecue institution — old-school, Memphis-style, and worth every minute of the line that regularly forms out the door. The dry-rubbed ribs are the headliner: smoked low and slow, tender without turning to mush, with that deep bark that tells you someone who cares was tending the pit. Don’t stop at ribs, though. The brisket comes off moist and thinly sliced, the pulled pork is smoky and piled high, and the sides pull their weight — rich baked beans, sweet potato fries, and applesauce that tastes homemade. Go early; the most popular cuts sell out, and when the meat’s gone for the day, they close. It’s casual, family-friendly, and about as St. Louis as a plate of food gets. ## 2. Hi-Pointe Drive-In Part burger joint, part retro movie set, Hi-Pointe Drive-In leans into a fun, nostalgic vibe — pop-culture touches everywhere and a menu built around genuinely excellent burgers. You can build your own or order one of the signature creations, and the staff are happy to walk a first-timer through it. A few crowd favorites to point you in the right direction: the **Frisco Melt**, a rich, melty burger on sourdough; the **Arch D-Lux**, a stacked, bold-flavored classic; the **Taco Burger** for something crunchy and a little different; and the **Cowboy Burger** loaded with fixings. Add a thick shake — the flavors get creative — and you’ve got the whole experience. It’s a burger a step above the usual, in a room that makes you smile. ## 3. Stacked STL Stacked STL is for the person who wants their burger built exactly their way. You pick the patty — beef, pork, turkey, or a beef-pork blend — then the bun (brioche, pretzel, gluten-free, or a lettuce wrap), the cheese, the sauces, and a genuinely long list of toppings. If decision fatigue sets in, there’s a lineup of a dozen signature burgers ready to go. People rave about the juicy patties and the crispy fries, and the vibe is laid-back and friendly, with customer artwork on the walls. It gets busy at peak hours and parking can take a lap or two, but for a burger made precisely to your spec, that’s a small price. Not in the mood to go out? It’s an easy one to get delivered. ## 4. The Frisco Barroom Over in Webster Groves, on Big Bend Boulevard near Webster University, The Frisco Barroom does elevated tavern food in a warm, rustic room — and its upstairs patio is one of the better places in the area to lose an afternoon. There are heaters up there, so it works well past the first cold snap, too. The kitchen keeps it fresh and consistent: the burgers get real praise (the double cheeseburger with horseradish cheese has a following), the salads are surprisingly good, and they turn out solid pierogies and kielbasa when you want something heartier. There’s a deep whiskey list with generous pours, and live music turns up now and then. It’s the kind of place you settle into for a few hours. Hungry for more? ## Discover Unique Finds: Your Guide to St. Louis Union Station Shopping Revised July 23, 2026 What shopping is at St. Louis Union Station? St. Louis Union Station is more experience than traditional mall now — the old shops gave way to attractions like the aquarium, the St. Louis Wheel, and mini-golf, alongside gift shops, candy and sweets stores, and boutiques inside the historic 1894 train shed. Expect souvenirs and local treats rather than a full retail mall, plus restaurants, hotels, and the nightly fire-and-light show. Keep reading ↓If you grew up around St. Louis in the ‘80s or ‘90s, “Union Station” probably means one thing: the mall. The Disney Store, the Fudgery pulling taffy in the window, the food court, that whole festival-marketplace buzz under the old train shed. So it’s a fair question when you’re planning a visit today — *can I still go shopping at Union Station?* The honest answer is that Union Station isn’t the shopping mall it used to be. But it turned into something arguably better: one of St. Louis’s top family destinations, where the “shopping” is now charming gift shops and sweet treats woven through a whole complex of attractions, restaurants, and a landmark hotel. Here’s the straight story on what happened to the mall, what shopping and gifts you’ll actually find at Union Station today, and how to make a great visit out of it — verified against Union Station’s current information for 2026. **Bookmark this before you go — and set your expectations right: Union Station is a play-and-dine destination now, not a mall.** ## Is there still a mall at Union Station in St. Louis? **No — the traditional shopping mall at Union Station is gone.** The 1980s festival marketplace, with its dozens of stores, declined through the 2000s and eventually closed. In a fitting twist, the **St. Louis Aquarium literally took over the old interior mall space** when Union Station was redeveloped into an entertainment destination. So if you’re picturing a day of retail browsing, that’s not what Union Station offers anymore. What replaced it is, for most visitors, a lot more fun: an aquarium, a 200-foot observation wheel, a ropes course, mini golf, a mirror maze, nightly light and fire shows, a slate of restaurants, and a beautifully restored historic hotel. The “shopping” today is the gift-shop-and-treats kind — a nice add-on to a day of attractions rather than the main event. ## What shopping and gifts you’ll find at Union Station today Set your expectations for **specialty gift shops and sweets**, not department stores, and you’ll have a great time. Here’s what’s actually there: - **The St. Louis Aquarium gift shop**— the biggest “store” at Union Station, packed with plush sharks and otters, toys, apparel, and souvenirs. You don’t always need an aquarium ticket to browse it, and it’s the go-to for a kid’s keepsake. - **Cookies and Cupcakes**— a bakery for a sweet grab-and-go treat. - **The Soda Fountain**— part restaurant, part candy-and-sweets shop, famous for over-the-top “Freak Shakes” and old-fashioned confections. - **Attraction shops and kiosks**— small gift and photo stands tied to the Wheel and the other attractions, good for souvenirs and mementos. The story is a St. Louis landmark’s reinvention. **Union Station opened in 1894** as the largest and busiest railroad terminal in the world, serving 22 railroads beneath its jaw-dropping Grand Hall. In 1985 it reopened as a **festival marketplace mall** — the era most St. Louisans remember, full of shops and restaurants. That format thrived for a while, then slowly declined as retail changed, until the stores emptied out. Rather than let a National Historic Landmark fade, developers reimagined it: beginning around 2018–2019, Union Station was **redeveloped into a family entertainment and hospitality destination**, anchored by the new St. Louis Aquarium (opened Christmas Day 2019) and the St. Louis Wheel. The Grand Hall became the centerpiece for a spectacular free 3D light show. The building was saved — just with a new job. It’s a history worth appreciating while you’re there. At its opening, Union Station was the largest and busiest passenger terminal in the world, and generations of travelers — soldiers heading off to war, families heading West, dignitaries and everyday St. Louisans — passed beneath that Grand Hall ceiling.
