## Cate Zone Chinese Cafe: The University City Spot for Real Northeastern Chinese Revised July 23, 2026 What’s the best Chinese restaurant in St. Louis? Cate Zone Chinese Cafe, at 8148 Olive Blvd in University City, is one of St. Louis’s most-loved authentic Chinese restaurants — a Northeastern (Dongbei) kitchen, not Sichuan. Order the hot crispy fish, the sweet and sour pork, and the housemade dumplings. Closed Mondays; an Ian Froeb STL 100 honoree. Keep reading ↓You know the difference. There’s the Chinese takeout you order on autopilot — the same crab rangoon, the same neon sweet-and-sour — and then there’s the real thing, the food someone’s grandmother would actually recognize. If you’ve been craving the second kind, and you’re willing to point the car toward Olive Boulevard, there’s a small storefront in University City that has built a devoted following doing exactly that. Cate Zone Chinese Cafe isn’t trying to be everything to everyone. It’s rooted in Northeastern Chinese cooking — hearty, homestyle food from the Dongbei region up near the Russian and Korean borders — and it does it well enough to keep landing on the city’s best-restaurant lists. Here’s what it is, what to order, and what to know before you go. ## At a Glance: What to Order ## What Cate Zone Actually Is This is Northeastern Chinese food — a point of confusion worth clearing up, because plenty of listings mislabel it as Sichuan. It isn’t. Dongbei cooking is heartier and homier than the mouth-numbing spice most Americans associate with Sichuan, and the menu here first attracted notice for that Northeastern focus, even if it also reaches into other regions with dishes like Yangzhou fried rice and spicy Chengdu chicken. The restaurant is owned by Daniel Ma and Quincy Lin, and it has quietly become one of St. Louis’s most respected authentic Chinese kitchens — a longtime pick on Ian Froeb’s STL 100 list of the region’s best restaurants (named in 2018, 2019, 2020, and 2023), and the subject of a glowing Riverfront Times review that singled out its hot crisp fish as the dish it’s best known for. It’s the kind of unassuming strip-mall spot that food-obsessed St. Louisans send their out-of-town friends to. Don’t let the modest storefront fool you — some of the best food in any American city hides in exactly these rooms. Cate Zone isn’t chasing trends or plating for photos; it’s cooking the food of a specific place and doing it with care. That focus is the whole appeal. When a menu commits to one regional tradition instead of trying to please everyone, you get dishes with real point of view, and Cate Zone has built its reputation on precisely that. ## A quick primer on Northeastern (Dongbei) Chinese food If “Dongbei” is new to you, here’s the short version. Dongbei means China’s northeast — the provinces of Heilongjiang, Jilin, and Liaoning, up against the Russian and North Korean borders. It’s a cold-winter region with a short growing season, so the cooking leans on preserved and pickled vegetables, wheat as much as rice, and pork as the favorite meat. The result is hearty, savory, generous food built on a few bold flavors rather than delicate ones. The region’s history shows up on the plate: Dongbei cooking carries influences from neighboring Russian, Mongolian, and Korean kitchens, and it grew out of the older Shandong and Manchu traditions. Cold-weather staples — wheat-flour breads and dumplings, crocks of fermented cabbage, big braises — make sense the moment you picture the winters they were built for. A few dishes tell the whole story. **Guo bao rou** — crispy fried pork in a bright sweet-and-sour sauce — is the Northeastern original that the gloopy American-Chinese “sweet and sour pork” was loosely descended from; tasting the real one is a small revelation. **Suan cai**, fermented sour cabbage, gets stewed with fatty pork belly into something deeply comforting. **Di san xian** braises potato, eggplant, and green pepper into a savory, glossy classic. And dumplings — thick-skinned, pan-fried or boiled — are the heart of the table, often served with chilled noodles alongside. Compared with fiery Sichuan or light, seafood-forward Cantonese cooking, Dongbei food is the rustic, warming, pickle-and-pork cousin — less about shock-and-awe spice, more about deep, satisfying, cold-night flavor. ## What to Order at Cate Zone Start with the **hot crisp fish** — the dish Cate Zone is best known for, lightly battered and fried with a Sichuan-pepper kick that sneaks up on you. The **guo bao rou** (sweet and sour pork) is the Northeastern version done right: crisp pork cutlets in a light, ginger-snapped sauce, nothing like the neon takeout goo you’re picturing. The **housemade dumplings** are a must — hand-folded in-house, thick-skinned and satisfying, and a specialty the second location leaned into even harder. From there, don’t skip the **sour cabbage with pork belly**, a true Dongbei signature where fermented cabbage and fatty pork stew into something warming and a little tangy, and the **cumin lamb**, fragrant with toasted cumin, a little heat, and fresh cilantro. If your table is adventurous, ask what’s good that day — the kitchen’s homestyle Northeastern dishes are where it shines. Everything is meant to be shared family-style, so bring people and order across the menu; portions are generous and half the fun is passing plates around. ## Before You Go: Hours & Tips Cate Zone Chinese Cafe ...

## The Best Coffee Shops in Wentzville, MO: A Local’s Guide Revised July 12, 2026 What are the best coffee shops in Wentzville, MO? The best coffee in Wentzville: Flower Coffee Collective (a cafe built inside a restored 1960s camper) and Ellbee’s General Store (a historic downtown shop and cafe) lead the independents, with Ziggi’s a specialty drive-thru — plus 7 Brew and Starbucks when you just need it fast. Keep reading ↓Wentzville runs on coffee — it just about has to. This is one of the fastest-growing cities in Missouri, a place where half the town seems to be commuting east on I-70 or wrangling kids to a Saturday soccer game, and everyone needs a good cup somewhere along the way. Whether you want a two-minute drive-thru fix, a laptop-friendly table, or a genuinely only-in-Wentzville spot worth the detour, the town delivers. Here’s a local’s guide to the best coffee shops in and around Wentzville — the quirky independents, the reliable drive-thrus, and one lavender-farm café just up the road that’s worth the short drive. ## The Coffee Shops at a Glance ## The Independent Standouts Start with the one you’ll tell people about. **Flower Coffee Collective** serves espresso out of a lovingly restored **1960s Nomad camper trailer** — you can drive up or park and sit at the outdoor tables. It was started by a young local, Faith McDonald, who opened it at nineteen, and it pours **locally roasted coffee** (the beans come from a small Missouri roaster) with homemade cold foam and salted-caramel lattes that have a real following. It’s the kind of place that gives a growing suburb some soul, and it’s the single best “only in Wentzville” coffee stop. Downtown on Main Street, **Ellbee’s General Store** is the sit-down-and-linger pick. Part old-fashioned general store, part café, it does espresso drinks, frappes, milkshakes, and ice cream alongside candy and sandwiches — a nostalgic, charming spot to actually stay a while rather than grab and run. Between the two, Wentzville’s independent scene punches above its weight. What makes both worth seeking out is the thing the chains can’t bottle: a sense of place. Flower Coffee Collective feels like a Wentzville story — a young local betting on her hometown, roasting-partner beans from just up the river, a camper that people now plan their morning around. Ellbee’s leans the other direction, into old-fashioned Americana, the kind of counter where you might actually strike up a conversation. In a town that’s adding rooftops and strip malls by the month, these are the spots that still feel like *Wentzville*, not Anywhere, USA. If you only have time for one independent stop, make it the camper — but locals rotate through both. ## The Reliable Drive-Thrus Sometimes you just need caffeine, fast. **7 Brew Coffee** on Wentzville Parkway is the speed champion — a drive-thru-only stand known for fast, customizable orders, infused energy drinks, Italian sodas, and shakes, open early morning to late at night. ## Tasty Bowl in Fairview Heights: Sushi, Ramen & Robot-Cooked Stir-Fry Revised July 23, 2026 What kind of food does Tasty Bowl in Fairview Heights serve? Tasty Bowl in Fairview Heights, IL (51 Lincoln Highway, (618) 206-6123) is a modern Asian-fusion restaurant serving hand-rolled sushi, ramen, and build-your-own stir-fry bowls cooked in automated robotic stir-fry barrels, plus bubble tea and a bar. Despite the generic name, it’s not a poke bar, Vietnamese spot, or Chinese buffet — the robot-cooked, customizable stir-fry is its signature. Keep reading ↓Picture this: you build your own stir-fry bowl — pick a base, a protein, your vegetables, your sauce — hand it off, and a *robot* cooks it in a spinning barrel, hot and fresh, right in front of you. That’s not a gimmick someone dreamed up for this article; it’s the actual draw at Tasty Bowl, a genuinely different Asian-fusion spot that opened in Fairview Heights, Illinois. In a Metro East dining scene full of familiar options, it stands out for a reason. This is an honest look at what Tasty Bowl actually is, what to order, and where to find it — because the name alone doesn’t begin to tell you what’s going on inside, and more than one online write-up has gotten the basics (including the city) wrong. ## What Tasty Bowl actually is Despite a name that could belong to any generic takeout spot, Tasty Bowl is a modern **Asian-fusion restaurant** built around three things: hand-rolled **sushi**, **ramen**, and its signature **build-your-own, robot-cooked stir-fry bowls**. Add **bubble tea** and a bar to the mix, and you’ve got a spot that covers a lot of cravings under one roof. It’s not a poke bar, not a Vietnamese restaurant, and not a Chinese buffet — it’s its own thing, and that’s the fun of it. It’s located at **51 Lincoln Highway in Fairview Heights, Illinois** (that’s the “51” in its web address), phone **(618) 206-6123**. One quick clarification, since some early write-ups got it wrong: the restaurant is in **Fairview Heights**, not O’Fallon — a labeling mix-up that floated around when it opened. Fairview Heights is the right spot to point your GPS. ## The robot stir-fry, explained The signature experience is worth walking through, because it’s genuinely novel and a little bit of dinner-and-a-show. You start by choosing your ingredients cafeteria-style — a base like rice or noodles, a protein, vegetables, and a sauce. Then, instead of a line cook at a wok, your bowl goes into an automated **robotic stir-fry barrel** that tumbles and cooks it to order at high heat. A few minutes later, it comes out hot, evenly cooked, and made exactly the way you built it. The whole thing is oddly satisfying to watch, and it’s a natural conversation-starter — the kind of small novelty that makes a meal feel like a little outing rather than just refueling. The appeal is real: total customization (great for picky eaters, big appetites, and dietary needs alike), consistent cooking every time, and a bit of novelty that makes it a fun stop with kids or friends. It’s the kind of thing you try once out of curiosity and come back to because it actually works — a fresh, fast, made-your-way meal. Exploring the Metro East food scene? Listing your restaurant keeps your menu, hours, and photos in front of hungry locals — especially valuable when you’re new in town. ## Why build-your-own works so well Beyond the novelty, there’s a real practical case for the build-your-own bowl. If you eat gluten-free, avoid certain proteins, keep it vegetarian, or just have a kid who won’t touch anything green, a customizable stir-fry solves the problem that trips up a lot of restaurant meals: you control exactly what goes in. Nobody has to send a dish back or pick around ingredients — you simply didn’t add them in the first place. The robotic cooking adds a second, quieter benefit: consistency. A human wok cook has good nights and rushed nights; an automated barrel cooks your bowl the same way every time, at the right heat, without the guesswork. For a fast, fresh, made-to-order meal, that reliability is genuinely useful — you know what you’re getting, and you built it yourself. It also tends to be quick, which makes Tasty Bowl a solid option for a weeknight dinner when you want something fresher than fast food but faster than a sit-down. ## Beyond the bowls: sushi, ramen, and bubble tea The stir-fry gets the attention, but Tasty Bowl is a full Asian-fusion menu: - **Sushi and sashimi**— hand-rolled to order, a proper sit-down-and-share option rather than a grab-and-go afterthought. - **Ramen**— warming, brothy bowls loaded with toppings for when the stir-fry mood isn’t calling and you want something to curl up with. - **Build-your-own stir-fry**— the robot-cooked signature, endlessly customizable from base to sauce. - **Appetizers and bubble tea**— starters to share and the sweet, chewy-pearled tea in a range of flavors that rounds out the meal or stands in for dessert. - **A bar**— drinks to go with dinner, which not every Asian-fusion ...

## St. Louis Annual Events: A Season-by-Season Guide to the City's Best Festivals Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best annual events and festivals in St. Louis? St. Louis marks its seasons with mostly-free annual festivals: Soulard Mardi Gras (late winter); the Downtown and Dogtown St. Patrick’s Day parades (March); Shakespeare in the Park and PrideFest (late spring/June); the Fourth of July on the Gateway Arch grounds; Festival of Nations, the Japanese Festival, and Big Muddy Blues (late summer); the Saint Louis Art Fair and Great Forest Park Balloon Race (September); Soulard Oktoberfest (October); and the Ameren Thanks-For-Giving Parade (late November), which bridges into the winter holidays. Confirm each year’s exact date before you go. Keep reading ↓Have you ever moved to a new city and felt like everyone else already knew the rhythm of the year — when the parades roll, when the balloons go up, when the whole town seems to spill outdoors at once? St. Louis runs on exactly that kind of calendar. From the first beads of a late-winter Mardi Gras to the smell of bratwurst at an October Oktoberfest, the city marks its seasons with festivals that are, more often than not, free and open to anyone who shows up. Here is a season-by-season guide to the annual events St. Louis throws every single year — the traditions worth building a weekend around, whether you’ve lived here for decades or just unpacked the last box. Dates shift a little year to year, so treat this as the shape of the calendar and confirm the exact weekend before you go. ## Late winter: Mardi Gras season St. Louis takes Mardi Gras seriously — fittingly, for a city with French roots. The heart of it is **Soulard Mardi Gras**, one of the largest Mardi Gras celebrations in the country, unfolding over several weeks in the historic Soulard neighborhood and peaking with a massive Grand Parade the Saturday before Fat Tuesday. There are family-friendly events earlier in the season and a rowdier street party on parade day; either way, it’s the city’s first big outdoor gathering of the year and a genuine only-in-St.-Louis experience. Bundle up, get there early for parking, and let the beads fly. ## Spring: parades and green rivers of people March belongs to St. Patrick. St. Louis runs **two** beloved St. Patrick’s Day parades, and locals have strong opinions about them. The **Downtown St. Patrick’s Day Parade** is the big, decades-old civic one along Market Street, with floats, bands, and a run to match. Out in **Dogtown** — the historically Irish neighborhood near Forest Park — the **Ancient Order of Hibernians parade on March 17** is the neighborhood-party version, a wall-to-wall street celebration that’s as much block party as parade. Pick your style, wear green, and plan your ride: both draw enormous crowds. ## Late spring and early summer: culture in the park As the weather turns, St. Louis heads to Forest Park and downtown. The **St. Louis Shakespeare Festival’s “Shakespeare in the Park”** stages a free, professional production in Forest Park’s Shakespeare Glen across late May and June — bring a blanket, a picnic, and a bottle of wine. In late June, **PrideFest**, the region’s largest Pride celebration, fills downtown with a parade and festival. It’s a stretch of the calendar defined by long evenings, free entertainment, and the city rediscovering its outdoor self. ## Summer: fireworks over the Arch The Fourth of July is a marquee event here. The annual **Fourth of July celebration on the Gateway Arch grounds** (the long-running successor to Fair Saint Louis) packs the riverfront and downtown with live music, an air show, and one of the biggest fireworks displays in the Midwest, framed by the Arch itself. It’s hot, it’s crowded, and it’s worth it — stake out a spot early, hydrate, and enjoy a genuinely spectacular backdrop. Smaller municipal fireworks light up communities all across the metro the same week if downtown feels like too much. ## Late summer: the world comes to St. Louis Late August and early September are the city’s most gloriously international stretch. The **Festival of Nations** in Tower Grove Park — a free, decades-old celebration put on by the International Institute — gathers dozens of cultures for food stalls, music, and dance, and it is a food-lover’s dream. Over Labor Day weekend, the **Japanese Festival** at the Missouri Botanical Garden (running since the 1970s) turns the world-class Japanese Garden into a showcase of taiko drumming, tea ceremonies, and lantern-lit evenings, while the **Big Muddy Blues Festival** brings free live blues to Laclede’s Landing. Between them, you could eat and listen your way around the globe without leaving town. ## Early fall: art, balloons, and beer September and October are arguably peak festival season. The **Saint Louis Art Fair** transforms downtown Clayton into one of the top-ranked juried art fairs in the country, free to browse. Nearby, the **Great Forest Park Balloon Race** — and its can’t-miss Friday-night **Balloon Glow**, when the balloons light up after dark — is a free, decades-old St. Louis tradition that draws a hundred thousand people to Forest Park. Then the season turns to beer: **Soulard Oktoberfest** brings German food, music, and steins to Soulard Market Park, one of several Oktoberfests across the metro. Cooler air, big crowds, and a lot to do outdoors before winter. ## Late fall: the bridge to the holidays As the ...

## Golden Chicken: A Beloved St. Peters Mediterranean Eatery Revised July 23, 2026 What kind of food does Golden Chicken in St. Peters serve? Golden Chicken at 632 Jungermann Rd in St. Peters serves Mediterranean and Middle Eastern halal food — rotisserie chicken, shawarma, kebabs, gyros, falafel, and wings, plus mezze like hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, and fattoush. Despite the name it is not a Southern or fried-chicken spot; the ‘golden’ refers to its rotisserie chicken. It holds 4.7 stars across 1,000+ Google reviews, is closed Thursdays, and offers dine-in, takeout, catering, and delivery. Keep reading ↓Picture a Friday evening in St. Peters — Friday, because on Thursdays this particular kitchen goes dark, and more than one hopeful diner has learned that the hard way. The light is going amber over Jungermann Road, everyone in the car is tired of the same three dinners on rotation, and someone votes for “something different, but not a whole production.” A few minutes later you’re unwrapping a warm shawarma, the garlic sauce doing exactly what garlic sauce is supposed to do, and the car has gone quiet in that good way. Maybe you’ve driven past the little storefront in the Spencer Creek Shopping Center a hundred times on your way through St. Charles County and never stopped. Maybe a coworker in O’Fallon swears by the falafel, or a neighbor in Cottleville keeps bringing it to gatherings. However you get there, Golden Chicken has a way of turning first-timers into regulars — which is roughly what a thousand-plus reviews will tell you before you ever taste a bite. The word-of-mouth in this corner of the metro does a lot of the restaurant’s advertising for it, and once you’ve been, you understand why people bother to tell their neighbors. This is an honest look at what the place actually is, what to order, and why a small, family-owned spot on Jungermann Road has quietly become one of the St. Peters area’s most beloved kitchens. ## What Golden Chicken actually is (and isn’t) Let’s clear up the name first, because it fools people. Golden Chicken is not a fried-chicken chain and not a Southern-food joint. It’s an independent, family-owned **Mediterranean and Middle Eastern** restaurant serving **halal** food — shawarma, kebabs, gyros, falafel, and the from-scratch **rotisserie chicken** that gives the place its name. Feast Magazine described it simply as a spot cooking “classic Middle Eastern fare,” and the St. Louis Post-Dispatch summed up the signature dish as chicken that “spins delight from the rotisserie.” That’s the truest picture you’ll find. It sits at 632 Jungermann Rd, St. Peters, MO 63376, a modest storefront that TripAdvisor reviewers lovingly call “small, unassuming… with world-class food.” That gap — humble room, serious kitchen — is a big part of the charm. Open since around 2021 and family-run the whole way, it’s the kind of independent spot a chain-heavy stretch of suburbia badly needs more of. You are not paying for chandeliers here. You are paying for the food. ## What to order the first time If you’re new, a few dishes do the introducing better than others: - **Rotisserie chicken**— the “golden” in the name. Whole or half, juicy under a burnished skin, with garlic sauce and warm pita that disappears fast. - **Shawarma**— chicken or beef, sliced from the vertical spit, wrapped or served over rice. The gateway dish, and for good reason. - **Kebabs**— grilled, generous, and the move when you want a proper plate rather than a handheld. - **Falafel**— the reliable test of any Mediterranean kitchen: crisp outside, green and herby inside. Regulars order it on repeat. - **The mezze and salads**— hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, fattoush, tahini. Order a couple to share; they turn a sandwich run into an actual spread. Save room for baklava. The wings deserve a mention too — done in a few styles for the table that can’t agree. One honest note on the menu: it evolves, and the kitchen leans on doing things fresh rather than pinning down a hundred fixed items. If you have a specific craving, the safest move is to glance at the current menu at goldenchicken-stpeters.com or simply ask when you order — and yes, there is no such thing as too much garlic sauce. Hungry now? Golden Chicken is at 632 Jungermann Rd in St. Peters. It's a fantastic choice! This guide is here to help you get organized so you can focus on enjoying the Gateway City. We'll cover the best times to visit, how the city is laid out, and some smart ways to save money. ### Best Times To Visit St. Louis When you decide to visit St. Louis can really shape your experience. The weather is generally pleasant in the spring and fall, making these popular times for a reason. Spring brings blooming flowers and comfortable temperatures, perfect for exploring parks and outdoor attractions. Fall offers crisp air and a vibrant foliage display, plus it's festival season! Think food fairs, art shows, and the famous Great Forest Park Balloon Race. Summer can be quite warm and humid, but it's also when many outdoor events and activities are in full swing. If you're looking to save a bit, consider visiting during the shoulder seasons or even the winter. While it can be cold, you'll often find fewer crowds and lower prices on accommodations. Here's a quick look at what weather to expect: - **Spring (April-May):**Mild temperatures, blooming gardens, and outdoor activities begin. Great for sightseeing. - **Summer (June-August):**Hot and humid, but lots of festivals and events. Ideal for riverfront activities. - **Fall (September-October):**Cooler, pleasant weather, beautiful foliage, and peak festival season. - **Winter (November-March):**Cold, but fewer crowds and potentially lower prices. Good for indoor attractions. ### Understanding St. Louis's Layout St. Louis is pretty spread out, but understanding its general layout can make getting around much easier. The city is bisected by the Mississippi River, with downtown on the west bank. Many of the major attractions, like the Gateway Arch, are located downtown or nearby in Forest Park. The neighborhoods radiate outwards from the city center. Knowing this helps you group activities by area, saving you travel time. For instance, if you're visiting the Arch, you might want to explore the nearby riverfront and downtown attractions on the same day. If you plan to visit the Missouri Botanical Garden, you can group that with other attractions in the southern part of the city. It's helpful to think of the city in terms of these general zones. Planning your itinerary around these key areas will help you make the most of your time and minimize unnecessary travel. ### Budget-Friendly Travel Tips St. Louis can be surprisingly affordable if you plan smart. One of the easiest ways to save is by visiting during the off-season when hotel rates tend to drop. Look for deals and packages, especially if you're a member of travel clubs. Eating like a local can also cut costs; instead of always opting for sit-down restaurants, try grabbing a bite from a food truck or a casual eatery. Many of the city's best attractions are free, like exploring Forest Park or visiting the grounds of the Gateway Arch. Consider purchasing a city pass if you plan on visiting multiple paid attractions, as this can offer significant savings. Also, keep an eye out for local events and festivals, which often provide free entertainment and a chance to experience the city's culture without breaking the bank. You might even find some great local businesses listed on a local directory if you're looking for specific services or shops. ## Game Day After Heritage: The Best Sports Bars in the Metro East Revised July 23, 2026 What happened to Heritage Sports Bar & Grill in Collinsville? Heritage Sports Bar & Grill at 118 E. Keep reading ↓Imagine it’s a Saturday in Collinsville and your group text is already going: kickoff’s at noon, who’s got a table? Somebody suggests Heritage on Main Street — and somebody else has to break the news. Heritage Sports Bar & Grill closed its doors in July 2026, without public notice or explanation. No farewell post, no final send-off — one week it was hosting watch parties and fundraisers, the next the lights were off. This page used to be our guide to game day at Heritage, and we’re not going to pretend otherwise. The bar had only opened in mid-2025, built a real following for live games and community events, and its sudden closing left regulars — and employees — without answers. We don’t know why it closed, so we won’t speculate. What we can do is answer the question the group text actually needs answered: **where does the Metro East watch the game now?** From Collinsville’s own Main Street to Edwardsville’s bar row, from Troy to Belleville to Granite City, the Illinois side of the metro still has plenty of rooms where the sound is up, the wings are hot, and somebody at the bar will argue the call with you. Here’s the town-by-town tour, verified and current. Every spot below was verified open as of this writing — recent reviews, active kitchens, current listings. (One local bar we considered including turned out to have gone quiet since 2023; it didn’t make the list. That’s the whole point of checking.) One honest note before you go: hours shift, especially on holidays and during slow seasons, so give any of these a quick call before you load up the car. ## What Game Day Actually Means in the Metro East Part of what made Heritage work — and what makes every bar on this list work — is that the Metro East’s sports calendar never really stops. Summer belongs to the Cardinals, and a bar with the radio call on the patio is its own kind of church. Fall splits the room: this is Illini country on paper, but Mizzou flags fly on half the blocks, and the SEC-versus-Big-Ten needling is a local sport in itself. Winter brings the Blues, spring brings the Battlehawks packing the Dome across the river, and Friday nights year-round belong to high school football and basketball — several of these bars are where the postgame crowds land, win or lose. ## The Best Outdoor Activities in St. Louis: Parks, Trails & Day Trips Revised July 22, 2026 What are the best outdoor things to do in St. Louis? The best outdoor activities in St. Louis range from easy strolls to real hikes: Forest Park, the Gateway Arch grounds, the Missouri Botanical Garden, and Tower Grove Park for an easy day; the free Saint Louis Zoo and Grant’s Farm for families; and Castlewood State Park, Cliff Cave Park, and the Katy Trail when you want a real hike or bike ride. Many are free. Keep reading ↓Picture a bright St. Louis Saturday with nothing on the calendar. Maybe you’re a family looking to wear the kids out, a couple after a cheap and pretty date, or a transplant who keeps hearing the metro has more green space than you’d expect. The good news: St. Louis is quietly one of the best outdoor cities in the Midwest, and a huge amount of it is free. From a park bigger than Central Park to a 240-mile bike trail to genuine bluff hikes twenty minutes from downtown, here’s a local’s guide to the best outdoor activities in St. Louis — sorted by the kind of day you’re after, with what’s free, what’s worth the drive, and what to know before you go. ## St. Louis Outdoors at a Glance ## Easy Does It: Strolls, Gardens, and Icons Start with the crown jewel. **Forest Park** is about 1,300 acres — larger than New York’s Central Park — and it’s the beating heart of outdoor St. Louis, with paved paths for walking and biking, boating on the Grand Basin, and four free attractions (the Zoo, the Saint Louis Art Museum, the Saint Louis Science Center, and the Missouri History Museum) scattered across it. You could spend a dozen weekends here and not repeat yourself. Downtown, the grounds of **Gateway Arch National Park** are free to roam, with riverside paths beneath the country’s tallest monument (the tram to the top is ticketed, the walk around is not). And in the city’s south side, **Tower Grove Park** — a 289-acre Victorian gem next to the Missouri Botanical Garden — is a favorite for a farmers-market morning or a shady picnic. For manicured beauty, the **Missouri Botanical Garden** (paid admission) is one of the oldest botanical gardens in the country, and **Laumeier Sculpture Park** pairs 105 free acres with more than 60 large outdoor sculptures — it’s celebrating its 50th year in 2026. *Tower Grove Park’s West Gatehouse at the Kingshighway entrance — look for the “TGP” worked into the slate roof. (Photo: Lane Forman)* ## Bring the Kids: Animals and Wide-Open Space Few cities make family days this affordable. The **Saint Louis Zoo** is consistently ranked among the country’s best — and general admission is **free**. **Grant’s Farm**, the Busch family’s historic animal preserve, is also free to enter (you just pay for parking), with a tram ride past roaming deer and bison, a goat corral, and the famous Clydesdales. For a quieter outing, **Suson Park** in south county has a small working farm with animals kids can meet, and **Creve Coeur Lake Memorial Park** — the largest lake in St. Louis County — offers flat trails, sailing and rowing, and plenty of room to run. ## Real Adventure: Bluffs, Trails, and a River Think St. Louis is all flat? The bluffs will fix that. **Castlewood State Park**, about twenty minutes west, is the local hiker’s favorite, with switchback trails up to dramatic overlooks above the Meramec River. **Cliff Cave Park** in south county offers rugged riverbluff trails (the cave itself is usually closed, and trails occasionally close after flooding, so check the county’s status first). For a woodsy, wildflower-filled ramble, **Shaw Nature Reserve** in Gray Summit protects 2,400+ acres of Ozark-border landscape with miles of trails. ## On Two Wheels: The Trails St. Louis is a genuinely great trail city. The **Katy Trail** is the longest developed rails-to-trails path in the country — about 240 crushed-limestone miles running from near Kansas City to the St. Louis suburbs — and the stretch through the Missouri River wine country near Augusta is a bucket-list ride. Closer in, the **Great Rivers Greenway** network links more than 140 miles of paved greenways across the region, and the **Old Chain of Rocks Bridge** carries walkers and cyclists across the Mississippi on a historic Route 66 span with skyline views. Rent a bike or lace up your shoes; the mileage is there. And you don’t have to be a serious cyclist to enjoy it — the crushed-limestone Katy Trail and the paved greenways are flat, shaded, and beginner-friendly, so a casual family ride is just as doable as a long training day. Several outfitters near the trails rent bikes by the hour if you don’t have your own. ## Want to Get Out of Town? Easy Day Trips When you’ve got a full day, a few destinations are worth the drive. Just across the river in Illinois, **Cahokia Mounds** is a UNESCO World Heritage Site — the largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, where you can climb **Monks Mound**, the biggest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. (Note: the site’s Interpretive Center is currently closed for renovation, but the grounds, mounds, and trails remain open.) South of the city, **Elephant Rocks State Park** lets you scramble over billion-year-old granite boulders the size of small ...

## Explore St. Louis: A Local’s Guide to the Must-See Attractions Revised July 24, 2026 What are the must-see attractions in St. Louis? St. Louis’s must-see attractions include the Gateway Arch, the City Museum, and Forest Park — home to the free Saint Louis Zoo, Saint Louis Art Museum, Missouri History Museum, and Science Center. Add the Missouri Botanical Garden, the Cathedral Basilica, the Fabulous Fox Theatre, and a Cardinals game at Busch Stadium. Many of the best stops are free, making St. Louis one of the best big U.S. cities for a full day out on a budget. Keep reading ↓Maybe you’ve got a long weekend and out-of-town family to entertain. Maybe you’ve lived in the metro for years and realized you’ve never actually gone up in the Arch. Either way, St. Louis rewards the person who goes looking — it’s a city of world-class institutions hiding in plain sight, many of them free, most of them within a short drive of each other. This is a local’s overview of how to explore St. Louis: the landmarks worth your time, the neighborhoods worth wandering, and the outdoor spaces that surprise first-time visitors. Think of it as the map; the deeper neighborhood and restaurant guides linked throughout are the turn-by-turn directions once you pick a direction. ## The landmarks you actually have to see ### Gateway Arch National Park Start with the obvious, because the obvious earns it. The 630-foot Gateway Arch is the tallest man-made monument in the country and the symbol of St. Louis’s role in westward expansion. Take the tram to the top for a view stretching across the Mississippi and deep into Illinois — book tickets ahead in busy seasons, because the small pods fill up. Underneath sits a genuinely excellent (and free-to-enter) museum on the pioneers and the monument’s construction, and the riverfront walk gives you the Arch from below, framing the river. ### City Museum Forget every museum you’ve been dragged through. The City Museum, built inside a former shoe factory downtown, is a giant hand-built playground of repurposed industrial salvage — caves, slides, a rooftop Ferris wheel, aircraft you can climb into, a multi-story slide. It’s beloved by kids and, honestly, more so by adults who forgot they were allowed to climb things. Wear clothes you don’t mind scuffing. It consistently ranks among the most original attractions in the country for a reason. ### Forest Park Larger than New York’s Central Park, Forest Park is the beating cultural heart of the city and home to a remarkable cluster of institutions — most of them free. You could spend a whole day here without repeating yourself: - **Saint Louis Zoo**— consistently ranked among the nation’s best, with free general admission. - **Saint Louis Art Museum**— a world-class collection from ancient artifacts to modern masters, also free to enter. - **Missouri History Museum**and the- **Saint Louis Science Center**— both free, both excellent for families. That so much of this is free is not a small thing — St. Louis is genuinely one of the best big cities in America for a rich day out on almost no budget. Don’t miss the James S. McDonnell Planetarium at the Saint Louis Science Center. Planning where to eat between stops? The St Louis Near Me Directory keeps local restaurants, shops, and things to do in one place — start with our local guide to the best restaurants in St. Louis. And if you run a St. Louis business that visitors and locals should be finding — a shop, a restaurant, a tour, an attraction — listing it in the directory puts you in front of the people searching “things to do near me” and asking AI assistants where to go. ## Arts, culture, and the grand old rooms Beyond Forest Park, the culture keeps going. The Fabulous Fox Theatre is a jaw-dropping 1929 movie palace — a “Siamese-Byzantine” fantasy of gold leaf and grand staircases — that now hosts Broadway tours and concerts; walking into the lobby is genuinely half the show, and the Fox even runs tours of the building on non-performance days for anyone who wants to gawk in daylight. The Cathedral Basilica of St. Louis holds one of the largest mosaic collections in the world — a quietly stunning, free stop that first-timers rarely expect. For contemporary work and local artists, the galleries clustered around Grand Center and the Central West End rotate often enough that there’s always something new. Downtown adds more: Citygarden’s free sculpture park, where kids splash in the fountains in summer; the historic Old Courthouse, where the Dred Scott case was first heard; and the growing entertainment around Ballpark Village next to Busch Stadium. Union Station, the grand former train depot, now holds an aquarium, a giant Ferris wheel, a nightly light-and-fountain show, and a mini-golf course — a full evening in one place, especially with kids. It’s all an easy area to explore on foot between other stops. A little further out, two stops reward the curious. Grant’s Farm — the ancestral home of the Busch family, on land once farmed by Ulysses S. Grant — offers a free tram tour past free-roaming animals and is a longtime family favorite. And the Anheuser-Busch brewery, a working National Historic Landmark, runs tours through its cathedral-like brew houses and Clydesdale stables. Both are quintessentially St. Louis in a way no museum quite ...

## The Best Christmas Lights in St. Louis: A Local’s Guide Revised July 23, 2026 What are the best Christmas lights in St. Louis? Top St. Louis Christmas light displays include Garden Glow at the Missouri Botanical Garden and Brewery Lights at Anheuser-Busch (walk-through), Winter Wonderland at Tilles Park in Ladue and Santa’s Magical Kingdom in Eureka (drive-through), Wild Lights at the Saint Louis Zoo, WonderLight’s Christmas at World Wide Technology Raceway, Holiday Lights at Grant’s Farm, and the free Candy Cane Lane in St. Louis Hills. Dates shift yearly, so check each display’s official page. Keep reading ↓There’s a particular kind of magic to a St. Louis December evening: the car warm, cocoa in the cupholders, someone in the back seat gasping as a whole hillside or historic building suddenly blazes to life in color. Whether you like to cruise slowly through a dazzling drive-thru or bundle up and walk beneath a canopy of a million bulbs, the metro goes genuinely all out for the holidays, from grand institutions to entire neighborhoods that band together to light up a street. This is a local’s guide to the best Christmas light displays across St. Louis and the surrounding communities — the long-running traditions, the huge drive-thru spectacles, and a free neighborhood gem or two. We’ve split them into walk-through and drive-through so you can pick based on the weather, the kids, and how much you feel like leaving the car. Since dates and hours shift a little each year, treat this as your map and check each display’s official page or call ahead for this season’s exact schedule before you head out — a thirty-second check saves a disappointed carload. ## The big walk-through spectacles ### Garden Glow at the Missouri Botanical Garden A St. Louis holiday centerpiece. The Missouri Botanical Garden transforms after dark into a wonderland of more than two million lights strung along a roughly mile-long path, with the bulbs shimmering off the water features and illuminating the Rose Garden, the Japanese Garden, and other iconic spots you know by day but have never seen glowing after dark. Expect immersive themed areas, plenty of photo-worthy moments, and festive refreshments like hot cocoa and s’mores along the way. It’s self-paced, so give yourself a relaxed hour or more, and buy tickets online ahead of time — this one genuinely sells out on the busiest nights. It’s the walk-through most locals name first when someone asks where to take out-of-town guests, and the garden setting makes it feel a cut above a parking-lot light show. ### Brewery Lights at the Anheuser-Busch Brewery You can’t talk St. Louis holiday lights without the Anheuser-Busch Brewery, a 40-plus-year tradition. Stroll Pestalozzi Street beneath over a million lights that make the historic Germanic-Romanesque buildings glow, catch the nightly parade with vintage trucks, floats, and the famous Budweiser Clydesdales, and — for guests 21 and up — enjoy a complimentary beer. You can gather around a private fire pit with friends and there’s festive food and drink throughout the grounds. It’s equal parts holiday cheer and local history, and it’s free to walk the grounds — a genuinely generous tradition in a season that can get expensive fast. Arrive a little before the nightly parade if you want a good spot, and give yourself time to wander; the historic buildings under a million lights are worth lingering over. ### Wild Lights at the Saint Louis Zoo The Zoo lights up after hours with Wild Lights, a walk-through of glowing, themed areas — think Frosted Forest, Butterfly Grove, Toy Town, Arctic Alley, and a towering 40-foot lighted tree — perfect for photos and little ones. The animals are mostly tucked in for the night; the dazzling light installations are the star. It runs select nights, often with a sensory-friendly evening for families who need a calmer experience, so grab tickets in advance and check the schedule. Being in the heart of Forest Park, it pairs naturally with the free museums nearby if you’re building a whole day out of it, and the walk itself is stroller- and grandparent-friendly. Want to stay in the warmth of the car? We have a dedicated guide to the metro’s best drive-through Christmas light displays, plus more seasonal ideas in the St Louis Near Me Directory events listings. Run a St. Louis business with a holiday event, popup, or seasonal special? Listing it in the directory puts it in front of families out looking for exactly that — the same neighbors driving around hunting for lights. ## The great drive-through shows ### Winter Wonderland at Tilles Park (Ladue) A cherished St. Louis tradition since the 1980s, Winter Wonderland at Tilles Park — the larger park in Ladue, in St. Louis County — strings up over a million lights across roughly 75 acres, with more than a hundred festive scenes and a glittering canopy overhead. You can drive through (the classic, cozy option), walk it, or splurge on a horse-drawn carriage ride for something romantic. It’s a beloved local ritual generations of families return to year after year, and for many St. Louisans it simply *is* the start of the holiday season — the night you finally feel it’s December. Note it’s the larger Tilles Park in Ladue you want, not the smaller city park of the same name in St. Louis Hills. ### Santa’s Magical Kingdom (Eureka) Out at Jellystone ...

## The Best Arcades in St. Louis: Barcades, Pinball & Family Fun Revised July 12, 2026 What are the best arcades in St. Louis? St. Louis arcades split into two camps: 21+ barcades like Up-Down STL (Central West End), Purple Quarters (The Grove), and the pinball-only Silver Ballroom — and all-ages family centers like Dave & Buster’s (Maryland Heights), Main Event (Chesterfield), and Swing-A-Round Fun Town (Fenton). There’s also a deep pinball scene, from the Lazarus Pinball Museum in Fenton to Atomic Pinball across the river. Keep reading ↓There’s something universal about the pull of an arcade — the beep and clatter, the glow of a hundred screens, the muscle memory of a game you haven’t touched since you were twelve. Maybe you want a date night with a drink in one hand and a joystick in the other, a rainy afternoon that wears the kids out, or a serious pinball session with people who take flippers as seriously as you do. Whatever your speed, St. Louis has become a genuinely great arcade town. Here’s a local’s guide to the best arcades in St. Louis and across the metro — sorted by the two questions that actually matter: are you bringing kids or a cocktail, and how deep is your pinball obsession? ## The Two Kinds of Arcade Night St. Louis arcades really split into two camps. There are the **21+ barcades** — grown-up bars stuffed with retro cabinets and pinball, where the games are cheap and the drinks are the point — and the **all-ages family entertainment centers**, the big rooms with redemption games, laser tag, and prize counters for a kid’s birthday. Then there’s a passionate third lane running through both: **pinball**, which has a devoted St. Louis scene all its own. Know which one you want, and the choice gets easy. The good news is you’re rarely far from one: the metro has barcades in its trendy neighborhoods, family centers in the suburbs, pinball bars tucked into corners you’d never expect, and a whole second cluster across the river in the Metro East. Whatever mood and age group you’re working with, there’s a room full of games nearby. ## The Barcades: Beer, Nostalgia, and 25-Cent Classics For adults, the barcade is the perfect low-stakes night out. **Up-Down STL** in the Central West End is the flagship — more than 60 retro arcade games, pinball, skee-ball, console classics, and a rooftop bar. It’s 21+ in the evenings (with daytime family hours), and it nails the nostalgia-plus-cocktails formula. Over in The Grove, **Purple Quarters** is a newer cocktail-and-arcade bar from a beloved local team, mixing games with comedy and karaoke nights. And out in St. Charles, **Two Plumbers Brewery + Arcade** pairs house-brewed beer with free-play cabinets — a genuinely fun combination. A couple of newer St. Charles spots, including **Rec Hall** and the recently opened **Rec Haus**, round out a growing west-of-the-river barcade scene. What makes barcades such an easy win is the low pressure. You don’t need a reservation, you don’t need to be good at anything, and you don’t need to commit to a whole evening — you can drop in for one drink and a round of Mario Kart or stay till close working the pinball. They’re also a rare night-out option that’s genuinely fun sober or not: the games carry the evening either way. For a first date, a small group, or a “we don’t know what we want to do” night, a barcade almost never misses. ## The St. Louis Pinball Trail If pinball is your thing, St. Louis over-delivers. The legendary **Silver Ballroom** in the Bevo neighborhood — a punk-rock bar in a former bowling alley — keeps dozens of machines and a fierce local following. **Murphy’s On 21** in south county and the **Benton Parkade** in Benton Park are favorites for league players, and **Red Fish Blue Fish** in St. Charles keeps a solid bank of tables. For an all-ages pinball fix, the **Lazarus Pinball Museum** in Fenton is a dedicated collection you can play, and there’s even a pinball-and-arcade room tucked inside the **City Museum**. St. Louis runs real pinball leagues, so if you catch the bug, there’s a whole community waiting. The scene stretches into the Metro East too, where **Atomic Pinball Arcade** and the **Pump House** in Wood River keep dozens of machines for Illinois-side players. What’s great about the pinball trail is how welcoming it is to newcomers. You don’t need to be good — most of these spots keep older, easier tables alongside the brutal modern ones, and the regulars are usually happy to show a first-timer the ropes. Drop a few dollars in, learn to nudge without tilting, and you’ll understand why pinball, of all things, became one of the city’s most durable nightlife hobbies. ## Family Game Centers: Bring the Kids When the point is to wear kids out (and win a plastic prize), the big all-ages centers deliver. **Dave & Buster’s** in Maryland Heights is the reliable classic — a wall of games, sports on the screens, and a full menu. **Main Event** in Chesterfield stacks bowling, multi-story laser tag, and 100-plus arcade games under one roof, and **Swing-A-Round Fun Town** in Fenton adds go-karts and mini golf to its 80-game arcade. For the youngest kids, **Chuck E. Cheese** has several metro locations with the tokens-and-tickets formula that never dies. And on the ...

Keep reading ↓There’s something universal about the pull of an arcade — the beep and clatter, the glow of a hundred screens, the muscle memory of a game you haven’t touched since you were twelve. Maybe you want a date night with a drink in one hand and a joystick in the other, a rainy afternoon that wears the kids out, or a serious pinball session with people who take flippers as seriously as you do. Whatever your speed, St. Louis has become a genuinely great arcade town. Here’s a local’s guide to the best arcades in St. Louis and across the metro — sorted by the two questions that actually matter: are you bringing kids or a cocktail, and how deep is your pinball obsession? ## The Two Kinds of Arcade Night St. Louis arcades really split into two camps. There are the **21+ barcades** — grown-up bars stuffed with retro cabinets and pinball, where the games are cheap and the drinks are the point — and the **all-ages family entertainment centers**, the big rooms with redemption games, laser tag, and prize counters for a kid’s birthday. Then there’s a passionate third lane running through both: **pinball**, which has a devoted St. Louis scene all its own. Know which one you want, and the choice gets easy. The good news is you’re rarely far from one: the metro has barcades in its trendy neighborhoods, family centers in the suburbs, pinball bars tucked into corners you’d never expect, and a whole second cluster across the river in the Metro East. Whatever mood and age group you’re working with, there’s a room full of games nearby. ## The Barcades: Beer, Nostalgia, and 25-Cent Classics For adults, the barcade is the perfect low-stakes night out. **Up-Down STL** in the Central West End is the flagship — more than 60 retro arcade games, pinball, skee-ball, console classics, and a rooftop bar. It’s 21+ in the evenings (with daytime family hours), and it nails the nostalgia-plus-cocktails formula. Over in The Grove, **Purple Quarters** is a newer cocktail-and-arcade bar from a beloved local team, mixing games with comedy and karaoke nights. And out in St. Charles, **Two Plumbers Brewery + Arcade** pairs house-brewed beer with free-play cabinets — a genuinely fun combination. A couple of newer St. Charles spots, including **Rec Hall** and the recently opened **Rec Haus**, round out a growing west-of-the-river barcade scene. What makes barcades such an easy win is the low pressure. You don’t need a reservation, you don’t need to be good at anything, and you don’t need to commit to a whole evening — you can drop in for one drink and a round of Mario Kart or stay till close working the pinball. They’re also a rare night-out option that’s genuinely fun sober or not: the games carry the evening either way. For a first date, a small group, or a “we don’t know what we want to do” night, a barcade almost never misses. ## The St. Louis Pinball Trail If pinball is your thing, St. Louis over-delivers. The legendary **Silver Ballroom** in the Bevo neighborhood — a punk-rock bar in a former bowling alley — keeps dozens of machines and a fierce local following. **Murphy’s On 21** in south county and the **Benton Parkade** in Benton Park are favorites for league players, and **Red Fish Blue Fish** in St. Charles keeps a solid bank of tables. For an all-ages pinball fix, the **Lazarus Pinball Museum** in Fenton is a dedicated collection you can play, and there’s even a pinball-and-arcade room tucked inside the **City Museum**. St. Louis runs real pinball leagues, so if you catch the bug, there’s a whole community waiting. The scene stretches into the Metro East too, where **Atomic Pinball Arcade** and the **Pump House** in Wood River keep dozens of machines for Illinois-side players. What’s great about the pinball trail is how welcoming it is to newcomers. You don’t need to be good — most of these spots keep older, easier tables alongside the brutal modern ones, and the regulars are usually happy to show a first-timer the ropes. Drop a few dollars in, learn to nudge without tilting, and you’ll understand why pinball, of all things, became one of the city’s most durable nightlife hobbies. ## Family Game Centers: Bring the Kids When the point is to wear kids out (and win a plastic prize), the big all-ages centers deliver. **Dave & Buster’s** in Maryland Heights is the reliable classic — a wall of games, sports on the screens, and a full menu. **Main Event** in Chesterfield stacks bowling, multi-story laser tag, and 100-plus arcade games under one roof, and **Swing-A-Round Fun Town** in Fenton adds go-karts and mini golf to its 80-game arcade. ## How Much Does a Bookkeeper Cost? (And Why Missouri Licenses None of Them) Revised July 28, 2026 How much does a bookkeeper cost? Roughly **$200–$400 a month** for straightforward monthly bookkeeping, rising toward **$1,500+** as scope grows. Hourly, the reported median is about **$24**; freelancers commonly quote **$25–$50**. ⚠️ Treat those loosely — almost every page publishing bookkeeping rates is published by an outsourced bookkeeping company. Price tracks **transaction volume and number of accounts**, not your revenue. 💡 And the part nobody mentions: **Missouri doesn’t license bookkeepers at all** — no exam, no registry, no board. Anyone may use the title. **“CPA” is protected**; bookkeeper isn’t, so look for AIPB or NACPB certification and professional liability insurance instead. ## How much does a bookkeeper cost? For most small businesses, somewhere between **$200 and $400 a month** for straightforward monthly bookkeeping, rising toward **$1,500 or more** as the work gets more involved. Hourly, the reported median sits around **$24**, with freelancers commonly quoting **$25 to $50**. A word on those numbers before you rely on them. Almost every page publishing bookkeeping rates is published *by an outsourced bookkeeping company*, and their in-house-versus-outsourced comparisons are marketing. The ranges above appear consistently enough across sources to be useful as a sanity check. Treat any single figure — including a quote you are given — as a starting point rather than a market rate. What actually drives your price is not your revenue. It is **transaction volume, number of accounts, and how bad the shoebox is.** A consultant billing four invoices a month is cheap to keep straight. A restaurant with daily deposits, tips, vendor accounts and a payroll run is not, at any revenue level. ## The thing nobody tells you: anyone can call themselves a bookkeeper This is the part worth knowing before you hand someone your bank logins. **Missouri does not license bookkeepers.** There is no state exam, no registry, no board, and no complaint process. The title is unregulated, and a person who took a weekend course and a person with twenty years in the trade may describe themselves identically. **“CPA” is different.** Certified Public Accountant is a protected title in Missouri — only licensees may use it, or any designation implying it. That protection is what makes the letters meaningful, and it is why the distinction matters when you are comparing quotes. Worth being precise about what that protection does and does not do, because the internet gets this wrong in both directions: a non-licensee may still perform a great deal of legitimate accounting work, including preparing tax returns, advisory work, and preparing non-attest financial statements. The restriction is on *calling yourself a CPA*, not on doing bookkeeping. If this pattern feels familiar, it should — it is the same structure as the trades here. Missouri does not license contractors either, which is why verifying a contractor works differently in this state. In both cases the vetting is yours to do. ### What to look for instead of a license Since there is no state credential, these carry the weight: - **Voluntary certification.**The AIPB Certified Bookkeeper and NACPB Certified Public Bookkeeper credentials are the recognized ones. Neither is required, which is rather the point — someone who obtained one chose to be tested. - **Professional liability insurance.**Ask directly. Someone touching your financial records without it is asking you to carry the risk. - **References from businesses like yours.**Restaurant books and contractor books are different animals; experience in one does not transfer cleanly. - **A named CPA they work with.**Good bookkeepers usually have one, and are quick to say where their scope ends. ## Bookkeeper, accountant, CPA — what you are actually buying These get used interchangeably and they are not the same purchase. **A bookkeeper** handles the ongoing record: categorizing transactions, reconciling accounts, chasing invoices, producing monthly statements. This is the recurring work, and it is what most small businesses are actually short of. **An accountant** works on what the records mean — financial statements, tax planning, structure. Often seasonal or periodic rather than monthly. **A CPA** is a licensed accountant, and the license matters most where independence and attestation are required — audits, reviewed statements, representation before tax authorities. Most small businesses need the first regularly and the second occasionally. Paying CPA rates for monthly transaction categorization is a common and expensive mistake; so is having nobody look at the year until March. ## In-house, freelance, or a service **A service or a freelancer** is where nearly every small business should start. You pay for the hours the work takes, not for a person’s day, and you can leave. **A full-time in-house bookkeeper** reportedly runs roughly $45,000 to $60,000 in salary before benefits and overhead, which is commonly estimated to add another 25% to 40%. That is a real employer decision — and if you are contemplating it, note that the obligations attach the moment you hire anyone. We covered them in hiring your first employee in Missouri. The honest test is not cost, it is volume. If the work genuinely fills a week, hire. If it fills two afternoons a month, hiring for it is expensive in a way the salary figure understates. ## How do you know when it is time? Most owners do their own books at the start, and that is usually correct. The question is not whether you *can* keep doing it ...

## Find Quality Roof Tiles Near Me: A St. Louis Buyer's Guide Revised July 23, 2026 How much does a tile roof cost in St. Louis? Installed costs run roughly to 5 per square foot depending on the material — composite at the lower end, slate at the top — which puts many home roofs in the tens of thousands. Three things push the number up: roof complexity, structural reinforcement (many older St. Louis homes were framed for lighter asphalt), and tear-off of the old roof. Get itemized local bids, and in this hail region, ask about impact ratings and how each material affects your insurance before choosing. Keep reading ↓*Updated June 21, 2026.* Imagine standing at the curb looking up at your roof, knowing it’s on borrowed time. You’ve seen tile roofs — the kind that make a house look like it belongs in a magazine spread — and you’re wondering if that’s the move. It’s a big decision, and an expensive one — likely among the largest single purchases your house will ever ask of you — so it’s worth understanding what you’re getting into before you call anyone. Here’s an honest, St. Louis-minded guide to roof tiles: the types, what they really cost, how to find someone who can install them right, and what our Midwest weather means for the decision. ## First, an honest word about tile in St. Louis Tile roofs are everywhere in the Southwest and Florida, but they’re less common here — most St. Louis homes wear asphalt shingles, with slate and clay showing up mainly on historic and higher-end houses. That doesn’t make tile a bad choice; it means two things matter more locally: **weight** (many of our older homes weren’t framed for heavy tile and may need structural reinforcement) and **freeze-thaw durability** (our winters cross above and below freezing constantly, so you want a tile rated to handle it). A good local installer will steer you right on both — and a bad one will skip the conversation entirely, which is itself the tell. ## Your roof tile options The main players, each with its own look, weight, and price: - **Concrete**— the workhorse: tough, versatile, can mimic clay or slate, and the most budget-friendly tile. Heavy, though. - **Clay / terracotta**— classic, warm, and long-lasting, with that Mediterranean charm. A bit more fragile and pricier. - **Slate**— the premium, natural look that can last a century. Beautiful, very heavy, and the most expensive. - **Composite**— made from recycled materials, lighter and more impact-resistant; a great way to get the slate look without the weight. - **Metal**— lightweight and durable, and it can be shaped to resemble tiles or shakes. - **Solar tiles**— generate electricity while protecting the home; a big investment with long-term energy payback. ## The St. Louis look: matching tile to the house you actually own Tile reads differently on different St. Louis housing. On the metro’s historic stock — the grand homes of Compton Heights and the Central West End, the century-old brick throughout the city — slate and clay are period-correct: that’s what many of those roofs wore originally, and restoring the look adds real character value that appraisers and future buyers both notice. On mid-century ranches across the county, a heavy Mediterranean profile can look borrowed from another climate — flatter concrete or composite profiles usually sit more naturally. And on newer builds out in St. Charles County or the Metro East, composite “slate-look” tile delivers the upscale effect without the framing drama. Two practical notes before you fall in love with a photo: drive your own neighborhood and see what tile actually looks like on homes shaped like yours, and if you’re in a historic district or an HOA, check approval requirements before ordering samples — some districts care a great deal about roof materials, and finding out after the deposit is the expensive way to learn. Ten minutes with your municipality or HOA board now saves a standoff later. ## What tile actually costs Tile is a premium roof, and the price reflects it. Installed costs vary widely by material, and the figures below are *national ballpark ranges* — your real St. Louis quote will depend on your roof’s size, pitch, and complexity, so treat these as a starting point and get real local bids: - Concrete: roughly $11–$28 per square foot installed - Clay / terracotta: roughly $9–$26 - Slate: roughly $8–$35 - Composite: roughly $8–$15 - Solar tile: roughly $21–$25 Three things push the number up: **roof complexity** (lots of valleys, dormers, and steep pitches mean more cuts, waste, and labor), **structural support** (heavy tile may require reinforcing the framing), and **tear-off and disposal** of your old roof. Ask for an itemized estimate so you can see exactly what’s included — and what conveniently isn’t. ## Tile versus the alternatives, honestly Tile isn’t automatically the right answer, and a guide that pretends otherwise isn’t helping you. The honest comparison: - **Asphalt shingles**cost a fraction of tile up front and install on any framing — which is why most of the metro wears them. Their trade-off is lifespan: decades shorter than tile, meaning you (or the next owner) buy the roof again. If you plan to move within ten years, asphalt’s economics usually win. - **Metal roofing**splits the difference: lighter than tile, longer-lived than asphalt, excellent in storms. It’s tile’s real competitor ...

## Credit Card Processing Fees: What Missouri Businesses Actually Pay Revised July 28, 2026 What do credit card processing fees actually cost a small business? **1.5% to 3.5% per transaction** — in person about 1.8–2.6% + 8–15¢, online or keyed about 2.25–3.5% + 25–30¢, debit 0.5–1.5%. Your rate is **three stacked fees**: interchange (goes to your customer’s bank), assessments (the network), and the processor’s markup — and **only the markup is negotiable**. 💡 **Missouri has no surcharge ban**, so you may legally pass the fee on, subject to card-network caps around 3–4% and advance disclosure. ⚠️ Avoid **tiered** pricing, and judge any offer on your **effective rate** — total monthly fees ÷ total card volume — not the quoted number. ## What do credit card processing fees actually cost a small business? Between **1.5% and 3.5%** of each transaction, and where you land inside that range depends less on luck than most owners think. That range is the one point everyone agrees on — NerdWallet, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and OnDeck all publish the same figures independently. Roughly: - **In person**, tapped or swiped — about 1.8% to 2.6%, plus 8 to 15 cents - **Online or manually keyed**— about 2.25% to 3.5%, plus 25 to 30 cents - **Debit**— about 0.5% to 1.5%, lower because debit interchange is regulated So the same $100 sale costs you roughly $2 across the counter and closer to $3.50 typed into a form. If a meaningful share of your work is invoiced or taken over the phone, that difference is not rounding — it is a line item worth managing. And the question almost everyone is really asking: **in Missouri, you are allowed to pass it on.** More on that below, because it is the part page one does not answer. ## Where the money actually goes Your rate is not one fee. It is three, stacked, and only one of them is negotiable — which is the single most useful thing to understand before any sales call. **Interchange.** The largest slice, and it goes to the bank that *issued your customer’s card* — not to your processor. It is set by the card networks, it is the same for everyone, and nobody can discount it for you. Rewards cards carry higher interchange, which is why the customer paying with a premium travel card costs you more than the one with a plain debit card. **Assessments.** A small cut to the network itself — Visa, Mastercard, and so on. Also fixed, also not negotiable. **The processor’s markup.** This is the only part that is actually up for discussion, and it is the entire basis of every competing quote you will ever receive. When a salesperson promises to “beat your rate,” they are talking about that third layer. Anyone claiming they can cut the first two is either confused or counting on you being. ## The three pricing models, and the one to avoid **Flat rate.** One blended percentage for everything — the Square and Stripe model. You pay the same whether the customer used a debit card or a premium rewards card. It is simple, predictable, requires no negotiation, and for low volume it is genuinely hard to beat on total cost once you account for your own time. Published rates as of this writing: **Square** 2.6% + $0.15 in person on the free plan, 3.3% + $0.30 for online and invoices, 3.5% + $0.15 keyed. **Stripe** 2.9% + $0.30 for standard online domestic cards. Both change their pricing periodically, so check current rates rather than trusting any article, including this one. **Interchange-plus.** You pay the real interchange, whatever it happens to be for that card, plus a stated markup. A competitive markup for a small or mid-sized merchant runs roughly **0.20% to 0.50% plus 10 to 20 cents**. It is the transparent option — you can see exactly what the processor is making — and as volume grows it usually wins. It also requires you to read a statement. **Tiered.** Your transactions get sorted into vague buckets labeled something like “qualified,” “mid-qualified” and “non-qualified.” The advertised rate is the qualified one. A great deal of your volume will mysteriously not qualify. **Avoid tiered.** The structure exists to make comparison impossible, and the headline number it advertises is the one you will rarely pay. ## Can you charge customers the fee? In Missouri, yes. This is the most-asked question on the topic and the least well answered, because the answer genuinely depends on your state — and nearly every guide ranking for it is written for nobody in particular. **Missouri has no state law prohibiting or regulating credit card surcharging.** A Missouri business may add a surcharge to credit card transactions. You are still bound by the card networks’ own rules, which generally cap surcharges in the region of 3–4%, require advance disclosure, and require that you register the practice with the networks. For context on why this varies at all: in *Expressions Hair Design v. Schneiderman*, the Supreme Court held unanimously that surcharge bans regulate *speech* rather than conduct — they govern how a business is allowed to describe its prices. That reasoning dismantled outright bans in states that had them. Missouri never had one to dismantle. ### Surcharge or cash discount? They sound like the same thing and they are not, legally or in how customers receive them. A **surcharge** ...

## Missouri Baking Co Menu: What to Order at The Hill’s Legendary Bakery Revised July 12, 2026 What are some customer favorites at Missouri Baking Co? Missouri Baking Co is a family-owned Italian bakery on The Hill, open since 1924 and rated the #1 bakery in St. Louis. What to order: the cannoli, a slice of gooey butter cake, and a mixed box from the cookie case — sold by the pound — plus fresh bread. It’s cash-first and closed Sundays and Mondays. Keep reading ↓Picture a Saturday morning. You’ve got family coming over — maybe driving in from Kirkwood, maybe from as far as St. Charles — and you promised you’d handle dessert. Not the grocery-store kind. The real thing. The kind that makes your aunt go quiet for a second after the first bite. So where do you go? If you’ve lived around St. Louis long enough, you already know the answer, and you already know there’s going to be a line. On a plain corner on The Hill, behind a storefront that hasn’t needed to change in a hundred years, sits Missouri Baking Company — and the crowd out the door on a weekend morning tells you everything before you even walk in. This is a local’s guide to what’s actually worth ordering, what to know before you go, and why a bakery that opened in 1924 is still the one St. Louis argues about most — more than a century later. ## At a Glance: What to Order ## What Missouri Baking Co Actually Is Missouri Baking Company is a family-owned Italian bakery at 2027 Edwards Street, right in the heart of The Hill — the historic Italian neighborhood that’s been feeding St. Louis fresh bread and red sauce for generations. It was founded in 1924 by Stefano Gambaro, a baker from Genoa in northern Italy, and it has stayed in the family for a full century. That century wasn’t without drama. After a two-year ownership dispute among the third generation, a St. Louis court in January 2026 placed the bakery entirely in the hands of Camille “Mimi” Lordo — a granddaughter of the founder — keeping the 100-year-old institution family-run and intact. So when you walk in today, you’re buying cannoli from a business that has survived a full century, a changing city, and a family fight to stay exactly what it always was: a neighborhood Italian bakery that refuses to modernize the things that matter. There’s something fitting about that. A place this old has watched The Hill change around it, watched grocery-store bakeries and national chains come and go, and simply kept doing the same thing at the same corner. The recent court battle could easily have ended with the doors closing or the recipes sold off; instead, it stayed in the founder’s family and stayed open. For a lot of longtime customers, that outcome was a small relief — proof that at least one St. Louis institution can make it to a second century intact. ## Why a 100-year-old bakery still matters It would be easy to dismiss the hype — every city has an “oldest bakery.” But Missouri Baking has earned its standing the hard way, and the accolades are real: it was named best bakery in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch’s 2024 “Headliners,” and it’s a fixture on food critic Ian Froeb’s STL 100 list of the region’s best restaurants. What those honors are really recognizing is consistency — the same recipes, the same hand-work, the same cash-only counter, decade after decade. That’s the rare thing here. In an era when most bakeries chase trends, Missouri Baking has spent a century doing a handful of Italian classics extraordinarily well and refusing to cut corners on any of them. When people say a place is “worth the line,” this is the kind of spot they mean. ## What to Order From the Missouri Baking Co Menu The case is long and the line moves fast, so it helps to walk in with a plan. Here’s what locals reach for. ### The Cannoli Start here. Missouri Baking’s cannoli are filled to order, so the shell stays crisp against the sweet, faintly citrus-and-chocolate ricotta cream — the way a cannoli is supposed to be, and the opposite of the soggy pre-filled versions sitting in a grocery case. That fill-to-order detail is the tell of a serious bakery: they won’t let a shell go soft just to save thirty seconds at the counter. It’s the single most-recommended thing in the shop, and for good reason — order a few, because one is never enough once the box is open. ### Gooey Butter Cake Gooey butter cake is a St. Louis original — dense, buttery, sugar-dusted, more “why is this so good” than elegant — and Missouri Baking’s is a benchmark version. Legend holds the cake itself was a happy St. Louis baking accident generations ago, and eating a great one is a small rite of passage here. If you’re introducing an out-of-towner to exactly one St. Louis dessert, this is a strong pick — buy an extra piece for the car, because it rarely makes it home intact. ### Chocolate Drops & the Cookie Case, By the Pound The cookie case is where Missouri Baking earns its arguments. Their **chocolate drops** — a rich, chocolate-coated house specialty — are a top seller and a local ...
