## The Best Independent Gyms and Studios in St. Louis Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best independent gyms in St. Louis? St. Louis has a deep bench of independent, locally owned gyms and studios: Climb So iLL and Upper Limits for climbing; CrossFit boxes like Gambit, Two Six, and Blues City Athletics; StrongHer Everyday for women’s strength; yoga at Urban Breath and Southtown; The Boxing Gym STL for boxing; and TruFusion for mixed boutique classes. To pick one, take a free trial class, watch how coaches treat regulars, check the drive, and read the contract before you sign. Keep reading ↓Every January the parking lots at the big-box chains overflow with resolution crowds. By March, half those cars are gone. If you have ever signed a year-long contract under humming fluorescent lights, wandered a sea of identical treadmills, and left twelve months later without a single staff member ever learning your name, you already know the problem. St. Louis is quietly full of a better answer: small, locally owned gyms and boutique studios where the person coaching your first class is often the person who owns the place. These are the spots where community is the product, not an upsell. From a climbing gym built inside a century-old power plant to a CrossFit box that has held the same Soulard block since 2009, here are the independent St. Louis gyms worth your membership dollars. What ties them together isn’t a category — it’s that a real person, often the owner, is invested in whether you come back. That’s the thing a fluorescent-lit warehouse of machines can’t sell you, and it’s the reason people who find the right small gym tend to stay for years. ## Climbing: Climb So iLL Drive near Lafayette Square and you cannot miss it: an enormous brick building studded with climbing holds. That is the Power Plant, the flagship home of **Climb So iLL**, an indoor rock climbing gym that opened in 2012 inside a genuinely historic former power station at 1419 Carroll Street. The company grew out of a De Soto, Missouri climbing-gear maker, so the people running it actually live and climb here. Beyond the towering walls, the St. Louis location adds yoga and fitness classes, which makes it a real option even if heights make you nervous. There is a second location too, the Steel Shop, in the Frenchtown area of St. Charles. Climbing turns out to be one of the friendliest ways to get fit, because the regulars genuinely want you to send that route — expect to get cheered on by strangers inside your first hour. ## CrossFit boxes with real coaching CrossFit has a reputation for intensity, but a good locally owned box is one of the most beginner-friendly rooms you can walk into, precisely because a coach watches every rep. St. Louis has several worth knowing. **Gambit Fitness** (also known as CrossFit Gambit) has been in Soulard since 2009, at 2322 S Seventh Street. It runs group CrossFit, personal training, weightlifting courses, nutrition coaching, and a Masters program for members 55 and up. That range tells you the coaching is built around real people, not just the 25-year-old crowd. **Two Six Fitness** (formerly CrossFit 26) has served St. Louis since 2010, now at 3120 S Big Bend Boulevard in Maplewood, right where Big Bend meets Sutton. Owner Kim Yawitz is a registered dietitian who is quoted nationally on nutrition, so your training and your eating can finally line up under one roof. Members describe the place as family, and it leans genuinely beginner-friendly. **Blues City Athletics** sits at 8500 Manchester Road in Brentwood and focuses on CrossFit, strength training, and HYROX-style functional fitness. It is locally owned, well-equipped, and known for coaches who modify each workout to your ability instead of throwing everyone into the same grinder. ## Boutique and specialty studios If group barbell work is not your thing, St. Louis has independent studios built around one specific experience. **StrongHer Everyday**, co-founded by St. Louis mom Katy Ferguson, runs functional fitness and strength classes for women out of a Maplewood studio on Sutton Boulevard, with some outdoor sessions in the warmer months. It started in 2018 for one reason: to take the intimidation out of lifting weights. Your first class is free. If you have ever felt like the odd one out in a weight room, this one was built for you. **TruFusion** at The Foundry in Midtown (3730 Foundry Way) is technically a franchise, but the St. Louis location is locally owned and operated. It stacks yoga, barre, cycling, Pilates, strength, and boxing into heated and non-heated studios under one roof — a strong fit if you want variety without juggling five different memberships. ## More independent studios worth knowing The list above leans toward climbing and CrossFit, but St. Louis’s independent scene runs deeper — especially for yoga, a second climbing option, and combat sports. **Upper Limits** is the metro’s veteran climbing brand, with gyms in **Maryland Heights and Chesterfield** (its downtown location has closed, so aim for the two suburban spots). It’s a great complement or alternative to Climb So iLL if you’re on the west side. For yoga, **Urban Breath Yoga** has been independently owned since 2005 with studios in **The Grove and Maplewood** and a reputation for accessible, welcoming classes (including scholarship options). On the south side, **Southtown Yoga** is a ...

## St. Louis Dive Bars Worth Pulling Up a Stool For Revised July 13, 2026 What are the best dive bars in St. Louis? The best dive bars in St. Louis include The Venice Cafe (an art-covered dive in Benton Park), Tick Tock Tavern and Riley’s Pub in Tower Grove, CBGB on South Grand, The Silver Ballroom in Bevo (pinball), Nick’s Pub and Pat Connolly Tavern in Dogtown, Pop’s Blue Moon near the Hill, The Heavy Anchor in Dutchtown, and the cash-only Iowa Buffet. Keep reading ↓Picture a Thursday night when you don’t want a $16 cocktail or a bar with a name you can’t pronounce. You want a cold beer, a worn-in stool, a bartender who calls you “hon,” and a jukebox that hasn’t been updated since the Clinton administration. Maybe you’re coming off a long week in Dogtown, maybe you’re showing an out-of-town friend the St. Louis that doesn’t make the tourism brochures. Either way, what you’re after is a dive. The good news: St. Louis is a dive-bar town down to its bones. This is a place built by brewery workers and factory shifts, and a lot of the corner taverns that served them are still pouring, still cheap, and still gloriously unbothered by whatever’s trending. Some are grimy in the best way; some are just old and honest; one or two are secretly works of art. All of them are the kind of place where you can walk in a stranger and leave with a story. Here’s a local’s guide to the St. Louis dive bars worth pulling up a stool for — where to find them, what makes each one worth the trip, and how to be the kind of regular these places are built for. ## What Makes a St. Louis Dive a Dive A real dive isn’t about being dirty — it’s about being unpretentious. The drinks are cheap and poured strong. The decor is accidental, accumulated over decades rather than chosen by a designer. There’s usually cash-only or a suspiciously old card reader, a bartender who’s seen everything, and a crowd that mixes neighborhood regulars with whoever wandered in. You come for the beer and the price, but you stay for the characters. St. Louis has its own flavor of dive. Many of these bars sit in the old working-class neighborhoods — Benton Park, Bevo, Dutchtown, Dogtown, Tower Grove — where corner taverns once served the brewery and factory crews within walking distance. That history is baked into the buildings and, often, into the regulars whose families have been drinking there for generations. Here are the ones locals send you to. ## The St. Louis Legends **The Venice Cafe** (1903 Pestalozzi, Benton Park) is the one that breaks the rules — it’s a dive in spirit and price but a jaw-dropping outsider-art wonderland in practice. Every inch of the place, inside and out onto one of the best patios in the city, is covered in mosaic, found objects, and decades of accumulated weirdness. Cheap drinks, live music, and an atmosphere you simply cannot get anywhere else. If you take one out-of-towner to one bar, make it this one. **Tick Tock Tavern** (3459 Magnolia, Tower Grove East) is the platonic ideal of a neighborhood dive done right: stiff drinks, a great jukebox, a photo booth, pinball, and a crowd that’s equal parts old-timers and Tower Grove twenty-somethings. It’s dark, it’s friendly, and it does the impossible trick of feeling like a genuine dive while actually being well-run. A perfect first stop on a Tower Grove crawl. ## South City Corner Bars **CBGB** (3163 South Grand, Tower Grove South) — not the New York punk club, but a beloved little South Grand dive with a punk heart, cheap cans, a patio, and a genuinely welcoming vibe. It’s the kind of place that anchors a neighborhood: unpretentious, friendly to newcomers, and a reliable landing spot on the South Grand strip after dinner up the block. **The Silver Ballroom** (4701 Morgan Ford, Bevo) is a pinball-lover’s dive — a wall of machines, horror-movie decor, cheap drinks, and a punk-and-metal soul. It’s one of the best places in the city to sink quarters into pinball while you drink, and it draws a loyal, friendly crew. Come for the games, stay for the beer, and don’t be surprised if you close the place out. **The Heavy Anchor** (5226 Gravois, Dutchtown) splits the difference between dive bar and music venue: a comfortable, unfussy front bar with cheap drinks and a back room that hosts live bands, comedy, and trivia. It’s the kind of spot where you can have a quiet pint on a slow night or catch a sweaty local show on a busy one — a true neighborhood workhorse on Gravois. ## Dogtown’s Old Guard **Nick’s Pub** (6001 Manchester, Dogtown) is a Dogtown institution — an old-school Irish neighborhood bar with cheap drinks, live music, and a fierce local loyalty, especially around St. Patrick’s Day when Dogtown becomes the center of the St. Louis Irish universe. It’s not fancy and doesn’t want to be. It’s where the neighborhood actually drinks. **Pat Connolly Tavern** (6400 Oakland, Dogtown) is a half-step up from a pure dive — a historic, family-run Irish tavern that’s been serving Dogtown for generations. It’s known as much for its food (that toasted ravioli and a serious burger) as its beer, but it keeps the warm, ...

## Great River Road: Best Stops from Alton to Grafton Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best stops on the Great River Road from Alton to Grafton? The Great River Road from Alton to Grafton, Illinois is one of the best day trips near St. Louis. Start in Alton with Fast Eddie’s, the free National Great Rivers Museum, and winter bald-eagle watching, then see the Piasa Bird and the historic village of Elsah. In Grafton, ride the SkyTour to Aerie’s, hit the wineries and The Loading Dock, take the free Brussels Ferry, and finish at Pere Marquette State Park. Most stops are free, and you can do it in a day. Keep reading ↓There is a stretch of road about a half hour northeast of St. Louis where the city falls away and limestone bluffs rise straight up out of the Mississippi. The Great River Road from Alton to Grafton, Illinois hugs the water the whole way, with the bluffs on one side and the river on the other. In winter, bald eagles hang in the bare trees overhead. In summer, the wineries fill their terraces and the river towns hum. It is one of the easiest big-payoff day trips in the region, and you can do the whole thing on a tank of gas and a free afternoon. Here is how to drive it, stop by stop, heading upriver from Alton to Grafton with a worthwhile detour into the bluffs at the end. ## Start in Alton Alton is the gateway. It is a river town with a long history, antique shops, and one bar that has become a regional institution: **Fast Eddie's Bon Air**. Open since the 1930s, Fast Eddie's is cash-friendly, loud, and famous for cheap food and a packed calendar of live music. It is not fancy, and that is the point. Get there early on a weekend if you want a seat. Before you leave the Alton area, swing by the **National Great Rivers Museum** at the Melvin Price Locks and Dam in East Alton. Admission is free, the museum is open daily, and the interactive exhibits walk you through how the Mississippi shapes everything around here. They also run free guided tours of the working locks and dam most days, where you can watch barges actually lock through. It is a genuinely good stop for kids and adults alike, and the price is right. A mile or so up the road, keep an eye on the bluff face for the **Piasa Bird** — a huge, brightly painted recreation of a Native American legend that stares out over the river from the rock. There’s a small pull-off where you can stop for a photo; it’s free, always visible, and one of the most striking sights on the whole drive. ## Watch for eagles (especially in winter) If you are driving this route between December and February, slow down and look up. The Alton-to-Grafton corridor hosts one of the largest wintering bald eagle populations in North America. Eagles gather near the open water below the dams to fish, and you can spot them perched in trees right along the byway. Across the river in West Alton, the **Audubon Center at Riverlands Migratory Bird Sanctuary** is a prime viewing spot and hosts an annual Eagle Days event in early February with spotting scopes and live raptor programs. Bring binoculars and a thermos. ## Detour into Elsah Between Alton and Grafton, watch for the small turnoff into **Elsah**. This tiny village tucked into a gap in the bluffs was one of the first places in the country added to the National Register of Historic Places in its entirety. Walk the quiet streets past preserved 19th-century stone cottages, poke into a shop or two, and enjoy the fact that almost nothing here has changed in over a century. It takes maybe twenty minutes to stroll, and it is the kind of place that makes you want to move slower. ## Spend the afternoon in Grafton Grafton sits where the Illinois River meets the Mississippi, and it is the heart of the trip. The town has reinvented itself around the water, with wineries up on the bluffs and patios down on the riverfront. For the best view, ride the **Grafton SkyTour** up to **Aerie's Resort**. The SkyTour is an open chairlift (with enclosed gondola cars available) that carries you 300 feet up the bluff to a winery terrace overlooking the river confluence. Aerie's has an award-winning winery, a restaurant, lodging, a zipline, and an alpine coaster if you are bringing thrill-seekers. The view from the top alone is worth the ticket. Down in town, the **Grafton Winery** pours local wines, and its riverside Brewhaus on West Main is an easy place to land. If you want your drink with your toes practically in the river, head to **The Loading Dock** on Front Street — an open-air bar and grill built on the old Grafton Boatworks site, with weekend live music, casual food, and tropical drinks served right at the water's edge. # Great River Road: Best Stops from Alton to Grafton Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best stops on the Great River Road from Alton to Grafton? The Great River Road from Alton to Grafton, Illinois is one of the best day trips near St. Louis. Start in Alton with Fast Eddie’s, the free National Great Rivers Museum, and winter bald-eagle watching, then see the Piasa Bird and the historic village of Elsah. In Grafton, ride the SkyTour to Aerie’s, hit the wineries and The Loading Dock, take the free Brussels Ferry, and finish at Pere Marquette State Park. Most stops are free, and you can do it in a day. Keep reading ↓There is a stretch of road about a half hour northeast of St. Louis where the city falls away and limestone bluffs rise straight up out of the Mississippi. The Great River Road from Alton to Grafton, Illinois hugs the water the whole way, with the bluffs on one side and the river on the other. In winter, bald eagles hang in the bare trees overhead. In summer, the wineries fill their terraces and the river towns hum. It is one of the easiest big-payoff day trips in the region, and you can do the whole thing on a tank of gas and a free afternoon. Here is how to drive it, stop by stop, heading upriver from Alton to Grafton with a worthwhile detour into the bluffs at the end. ## Start in Alton Alton is the gateway. It is a river town with a long history, antique shops, and one bar that has become a regional institution: **Fast Eddie's Bon Air**. Open since the 1930s, Fast Eddie's is cash-friendly, loud, and famous for cheap food and a packed calendar of live music. It is not fancy, and that is the point. Get there early on a weekend if you want a seat. Before you leave the Alton area, swing by the **National Great Rivers Museum** at the Melvin Price Locks and Dam in East Alton. Admission is free, the museum is open daily, and the interactive exhibits walk you through how the Mississippi shapes everything around here. They also run free guided tours of the working locks and dam most days, where you can watch barges actually lock through. It is a genuinely good stop for kids and adults alike, and the price is right. A mile or so up the road, keep an eye on the bluff face for the **Piasa Bird** — a huge, brightly painted recreation of a Native American legend that stares out over the river from the rock. There’s a small pull-off where you can stop for a photo; it’s free, always visible, and one of the most striking sights on the whole drive. ## Watch for eagles (especially in winter) If you are driving this route between December and February, slow down and look up. The Alton-to-Grafton corridor hosts one of the largest wintering bald eagle populations in North America. Eagles gather near the open water below the dams to fish, and you can spot them perched in trees right along the byway. Across the river in West Alton, the **Audubon Center at Riverlands Migratory Bird Sanctuary** is a prime viewing spot and hosts an annual Eagle Days event in early February with spotting scopes and live raptor programs. Bring binoculars and a thermos. ## Detour into Elsah Between Alton and Grafton, watch for the small turnoff into **Elsah**. This tiny village tucked into a gap in the bluffs was one of the first places in the country added to the National Register of Historic Places in its entirety. Walk the quiet streets past preserved 19th-century stone cottages, poke into a shop or two, and enjoy the fact that almost nothing here has changed in over a century. It takes maybe twenty minutes to stroll, and it is the kind of place that makes you want to move slower. ## Spend the afternoon in Grafton Grafton sits where the Illinois River meets the Mississippi, and it is the heart of the trip. The town has reinvented itself around the water, with wineries up on the bluffs and patios down on the riverfront. For the best view, ride the **Grafton SkyTour** up to **Aerie's Resort**. The SkyTour is an open chairlift (with enclosed gondola cars available) that carries you 300 feet up the bluff to a winery terrace overlooking the river confluence. Aerie's has an award-winning winery, a restaurant, lodging, a zipline, and an alpine coaster if you are bringing thrill-seekers. The view from the top alone is worth the ticket. Down in town, the **Grafton Winery** pours local wines, and its riverside Brewhaus on West Main is an easy place to land. If you want your drink with your toes practically in the river, head to **The Loading Dock** on Front Street — an open-air bar and grill built on the old Grafton Boatworks site, with weekend live music, casual food, and tropical drinks served right at the water's edge. Traveling with kids in summer? Just outside Grafton, **Raging Rivers WaterPark** is a seasonal water park (open roughly Memorial Day through Labor Day) with slides, a wave pool, and a lazy river tucked against the bluffs — an easy way to turn the drive into a full family day when it’s hot. ## Cross on the free ferry ...

## Best Family Fun Centers Across the St. Louis Suburbs Revised July 24, 2026 What are the best family fun centers near St. Louis? The best family fun centers around St. Louis are spread across the suburbs and Metro-East: Kokomo Joe’s in St. Peters and The Edge in Belleville do a bit of everything; Amp Up in Town and Country and Swing-A-Round in Fenton cover go-karts; Tropicana Lanes is the big bowling pick; Urban Air handles trampolines; and Main Event, Dave & Buster’s, Topgolf, and Edison’s round out the list. Many use pay-as-you-play pricing, and birthday packages are usually the best value. Keep reading ↓It is 2 p.m. on a gray Saturday, the kids have already asked “what are we doing today” four times, and nobody wants another afternoon staring at a screen. Anyone raising a family around St. Louis knows the feeling. The good news: you do not have to drive downtown or wait for summer at Six Flags to wear everybody out. Some of the best family fun centers in the metro are tucked into the suburbs and across the river in the Metro-East — bowling, trampolines, go-karts, laser tag, mini golf, and arcades, often all under one roof. Here are real spots worth the drive, spread from St. Charles County to the Illinois side, with a little about what makes each one click for families. A quick note on how to read this list: it is organized by area, from St. Charles County through West and South County and over to the Illinois Metro-East, so you can start with whatever is closest and work outward. Most of these places are indoors or have a solid indoor core, which makes them just as useful on a rainy spring Saturday as on a blazing July afternoon. And because they range from a quiet weekday bowling outing to a full-blown, everything-under-one-roof extravaganza, there is a right answer here for a low-key two hours and for a marathon birthday party alike. ## St. Charles County: where the big indoor centers live ### Kokomo Joe's — St. Peters If you want one place that does almost everything, Kokomo Joe's on N. Cloverleaf Drive is hard to beat. The locally owned center packs 12 full-size bowling lanes, laser tag and a laser maze, bumper cars, escape rooms, and a big arcade into one building. It runs on a pay-as-you-play game card, so you are not forced into an all-day pass if you only have a couple of hours. ### Urban Air Adventure Park — Cottleville For families with kids who simply need to *jump*, the Urban Air on Mid Rivers Mall Drive in Cottleville (just outside O'Fallon, Missouri) is built for it. Trampolines, climbing walls, obstacle courses, and indoor adventure zones give younger and older kids different ways to burn energy. It is a chain, but it is a verified suburban location and a reliable rainy-day release valve for St. Charles County parents. ## West County: racing and bowling traditions ### Amp Up Action Park — Town and Country This one is for the speed crowd. Amp Up on Manchester Road runs European-style electric go-karts on an indoor track where drivers can hit 40 to 45 miles per hour on the straightaway. There is no admission charge — you pay only for what you do — and beyond karting they offer axe throwing, laser tag, a high-ropes ninja course, and patio games. Junior karts keep the younger drivers (ages 7 to 11) in the action, so it is not just a teenagers-and-up spot. ### Tropicana Lanes — Richmond Heights Sometimes you just want to bowl. Tropicana Lanes on Clayton Road has been a St. Louis bowling tradition since 1960 and is the largest bowling center in Missouri, with 52 lanes plus arcade games, billiards, and party rooms. Bumpers and assist ramps are available, which makes it genuinely workable with little kids who would otherwise gutter every ball. It is an easy, no-fuss outing close to the center of the county. ## South County and Jefferson County: the classic fun-town feel ### Swing-A-Round Fun Town — Fenton Swing-A-Round on Skinker Lane in Fenton has been entertaining St. Louis families for more than 30 years, and it leans into the old-school outdoor fun center vibe. The Fenton location has go-karts with Honda engines, three nine-hole mini golf courses laid out around ponds and waterfalls, batting cages (they bill theirs as St. Louis' largest), bumper boats, bumper cars, an indoor playground, and an 80-game arcade. Fun passes come in one-hour, two-hour, and all-day flavors, so you can match the visit to your kids' stamina. ## Illinois Metro-East: two heavyweight centers across the river ### The Edge — Belleville Do not skip the Illinois side. The Edge on S. Belt West in Belleville is an 82,000-square-foot complex that genuinely has it all: go-karts, six lanes of black-light bowling, bumper cars, virtual reality attractions, multiple video arcades, and what they call the world's largest laser tag arena — a 14,000-plus-square-foot space that can run up to 60 players at once across five different game modes. For a group of mixed ages or a big birthday crowd, it is tough to outgrow. ### Edison's Entertainment Complex — Edwardsville A little north in Edwardsville, Edison's on S. State Route 157 brings a more polished, boutique feel. Think 12 lanes of upscale bowling with blacklight at night, a 4,000-square-foot laser tag ...

## Best Tutoring and Learning Centers Across the St. Louis Metro Revised July 24, 2026 Where are the best tutoring and learning centers in the St. Louis metro? St. Louis has strong tutoring across the metro: math-focused Mathnasium (St. Charles, St. Peters, Des Peres) and worksheet-based Kumon (Chesterfield, Wildwood, Ballwin, Clayton); multi-subject Sylvan (Ballwin, Chesterfield, O’Fallon IL); local independent Mackler Associates in Frontenac and the Huntington chain for diagnostic test prep; and Brain Balance for focus and attention. Match the program to the actual problem, take the free assessment, mind the drive, and check free options first — library homework help, National Honor Society peer tutoring, and Khan Academy. Keep reading ↓Report cards come home, and suddenly the kitchen table turns into a battleground. Maybe it is fractions in third grade, or chemistry that stopped making sense in October, or the looming ACT that decides which scholarships your high schooler qualifies for. If you have ever Googled “math help near me” at 9 p.m. on a Sunday, you are in very good company across the St. Louis metro. The good news: the region is loaded with quality tutoring and learning centers, and they are spread out from St. Charles County to the Illinois Metro-East. You do not have to drive downtown or settle for whoever a neighbor happened to mention. Here is a practical look at where to find help, how to choose, and what it actually costs. ## When it is time to get a tutor A rough patch on one quiz is normal. The signs that point toward outside help are more persistent: grades sliding two quarters in a row, homework that triggers tears or shutdowns, a kid who says “I am just bad at math” (a confidence problem, not an ability one), or a standardized test on the calendar with real stakes attached. Tutoring is not a punishment or an admission of failure. It is the same logic as hiring a swim coach. Some skills are easier to build with a trained outside eye. The other common trigger is timing. Reading and math gaps compound. A second grader who never locked in place value will struggle with long division in fourth grade and algebra in eighth. Catching it early is almost always cheaper and faster than catching it late. ## The national learning centers, town by town The familiar chains run on proven systems, and the St. Louis suburbs have plenty of them. What matters is finding the specific location near you, because quality and hours vary by franchise owner. **Mathnasium** focuses purely on math, K-12 through pre-calculus, with a free assessment that maps a student's exact gaps before any lessons begin. You will find centers in **St. Charles**, **St. Peters** (the St. Peters North location on Mexico Road), and **Kirkwood** (technically on Manchester Road in Des Peres, serving Kirkwood and Webster Groves families). Across the river, **Mathnasium of O'Fallon, Illinois** serves the Metro-East including Belleville families. **Kumon** takes a different angle: a worksheet-based, self-paced method in both math and reading that builds independent study habits over the long haul. Metro centers include **Chesterfield** (on Olive Boulevard), **Wildwood**, **Manchester** (located in Ballwin on Manchester Road), and **Clayton** (on Ladue Road). Kumon tends to reward consistency. It is a marathon, not a quick fix. **Sylvan Learning** covers the widest subject range: math, reading, writing, science, and ACT/SAT prep, with personalized plans tied to local school curriculum. The **Ballwin** center serves Ballwin, Chesterfield, and Kirkwood, there is a dedicated **Chesterfield** location, and **Sylvan of O'Fallon, Illinois** serves the Metro-East. Sylvan is a strong pick when a student needs help across several subjects rather than just one. ## Local independents and specialized programs The national chains aren’t the whole picture. St. Louis has homegrown independents and specialty programs that fill gaps the big brands don’t. **Mackler Associates** in Frontenac is a longtime local name in academic tutoring and ACT/SAT prep, the kind of established, one-location practice families pass along by word of mouth. **Huntington Learning Center**, another established brand with metro locations, runs K-12 tutoring and intensive, diagnostic-driven test prep, and is often a fit when a student needs a structured, results-focused plan rather than casual help. A different category worth knowing: **Brain Balance**, which has a presence in the metro, is not subject tutoring at all — it’s a drug-free program aimed at focus, attention, and behavior for kids who struggle to sit still and absorb material in the first place. If the real obstacle is attention rather than the algebra itself, a focus-and-executive-function program can matter more than another hour of math. Beyond any brand, plenty of independent one-on-one tutors — retired teachers, graduate students, and subject specialists — work across the metro, and they often cost less and flex around your schedule. ## Match the help to the subject The best choice depends on what’s actually hard. For **reading struggles or dyslexia**, look specifically for a tutor or center trained in a structured, multisensory method like Orton-Gillingham — it’s the researched approach for stubborn reading gaps, and not every general tutor offers it. For **math**, a diagnostic center that pinpoints the exact missing building block usually beats generic homework help. For **writing**, you want someone who’ll coach the process, not just fix a paper the night before it’s due. And for **ACT and SAT prep**, ask about real practice tests, score tracking, and whether the tutor knows ...

## The Best Local Credit Unions in the St. Louis Metro Revised July 13, 2026 What are the best credit unions in the St. Louis area? The St. Louis metro has strong member-owned credit unions on both sides of the river. St. Louis–headquartered options include First Community (the largest, about $4.78 billion in assets), Together (formerly the Anheuser-Busch Employees’ Credit Union), Vantage, Neighbors, Alliance, West Community, Alltru, and the community-focused St. Louis Community Credit Union; Scott and 1st MidAmerica anchor the Illinois Metro East. Most now let anyone who lives or works in the area join, and members typically get better loan and savings rates than at a bank. Keep reading ↓Imagine it’s a Saturday morning and you’re finally staring down the bank statement you’ve been avoiding — a $12 “maintenance” fee here, an ATM charge there, a savings rate that rounds to nothing. Maybe a neighbor in Florissant just financed a car and mentioned the rate she got through her credit union, and it was a full point lower than what your big bank quoted. You start to wonder if you’ve been leaving money on the table for years. If that sounds familiar, you’re in one of the best metros in the country to do something about it. St. Louis — on both sides of the river — is thick with strong, member-owned credit unions, several of them founded right here for local workers and neighborhoods. This guide walks through the best local credit unions across the metro, who’s allowed to join each one, and why so many St. Louisans quietly bank this way. ## What Makes a Credit Union Different From a Bank The short version: a credit union is a not-for-profit financial cooperative that’s owned by its members, not by outside shareholders. When you open an account, you become a part-owner with a vote. Because there are no stockholders to pay, the money a credit union earns flows back to members as lower loan rates, higher savings rates, and fewer fees. A bank, by contrast, answers to investors who expect a profit. That difference shows up in real numbers. According to the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), the federal regulator, credit unions nationally averaged a 6.27% rate on a 60-month new-car loan versus 7.50% at banks, and paid 3.26% on a one-year $10,000 CD versus 2.41% at banks (NCUA, 2025). On a car loan or a mortgage, a point or more adds up to real money over the life of the loan. And your money is just as safe. Deposits at federally insured credit unions are protected up to $250,000 by the NCUA — the credit-union equivalent of FDIC insurance, backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. The coverage amount is identical to a bank’s; only the insuring agency’s name changes. ## The St. Louis–Headquartered Credit Unions These are the home-grown institutions — founded and headquartered in the St. Louis area, most now open to anyone who lives or works in the metro. **First Community Credit Union** (Chesterfield) is the largest credit union headquartered in St. Louis — roughly $4.78 billion in assets, more than 408,000 members, and about 42 branches. It celebrated its 90th anniversary in 2024, and its community charter covers St. Louis City plus a wide sweep of Missouri and Illinois counties, so most metro residents can join. **Together Credit Union** (St. Louis) began in 1939 as the Anheuser-Busch Employees’ Credit Union — a beer-industry credit union that grew into a roughly $2.64-billion institution with about 145,000 members and 26 branches. It rebranded to Together in 2020 and is now a founding and official banking partner of St. Louis CITY SC. Membership is open to people who live or work across the core metro counties, plus employees of partners like Anheuser-Busch, Nestlé Purina, and BJC, and their families. **Vantage Credit Union** (Bridgeton) runs about 14 metro branches and has one of the friendliest community charters around: you can join if you live, work, *worship, or attend school* in St. Louis, St. Charles, Jefferson, or Franklin counties in Missouri, or St. Clair or Madison counties in Illinois. **Neighbors Credit Union** (St. Louis), with about 8 branches, leans on a “once a member, always a member” promise and serves the core Missouri and Illinois metro counties, plus select employer groups like Costco and Bi-State/Metro. **Alliance Credit Union** (Fenton) was founded in 1948 and carries deep labor-union and skilled-trades roots — its field of membership includes dozens of employer groups and several labor organizations alongside the usual live-or-work-here counties on both sides of the river. ## A Metro That Keeps Growing: Recent Mergers The St. Louis credit-union map has shifted recently, and it’s worth knowing so you don’t go looking for a branch that’s changed its sign. **West Community Credit Union** (O’Fallon, MO) completed a legal merger with Gateway Metro Federal Credit Union on April 7, 2026, creating a roughly $670-million credit union with 43,000-plus members and about 16 branches under the West Community name. **Alltru Credit Union** (Wentzville) is another rebrand to know: it was 1st Financial Federal Credit Union until late 2020, and it started life in 1968 as the McDonnell Douglas Credit Union — a nod to St. Louis’s aerospace heritage. Alltru is a certified Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) serving St. Louis City, St. Louis County, and St. Charles County. And there’s a big new entrant: **CommunityAmerica Credit Union**, ...

# The Best Local Credit Unions in the St. Louis Metro Revised July 13, 2026 What are the best credit unions in the St. Louis area? The St. Louis metro has strong member-owned credit unions on both sides of the river. St. Louis–headquartered options include First Community (the largest, about $4.78 billion in assets), Together (formerly the Anheuser-Busch Employees’ Credit Union), Vantage, Neighbors, Alliance, West Community, Alltru, and the community-focused St. Louis Community Credit Union; Scott and 1st MidAmerica anchor the Illinois Metro East. Most now let anyone who lives or works in the area join, and members typically get better loan and savings rates than at a bank. Keep reading ↓Imagine it’s a Saturday morning and you’re finally staring down the bank statement you’ve been avoiding — a $12 “maintenance” fee here, an ATM charge there, a savings rate that rounds to nothing. Maybe a neighbor in Florissant just financed a car and mentioned the rate she got through her credit union, and it was a full point lower than what your big bank quoted. You start to wonder if you’ve been leaving money on the table for years. If that sounds familiar, you’re in one of the best metros in the country to do something about it. St. Louis — on both sides of the river — is thick with strong, member-owned credit unions, several of them founded right here for local workers and neighborhoods. This guide walks through the best local credit unions across the metro, who’s allowed to join each one, and why so many St. Louisans quietly bank this way. ## What Makes a Credit Union Different From a Bank The short version: a credit union is a not-for-profit financial cooperative that’s owned by its members, not by outside shareholders. When you open an account, you become a part-owner with a vote. Because there are no stockholders to pay, the money a credit union earns flows back to members as lower loan rates, higher savings rates, and fewer fees. A bank, by contrast, answers to investors who expect a profit. That difference shows up in real numbers. According to the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), the federal regulator, credit unions nationally averaged a 6.27% rate on a 60-month new-car loan versus 7.50% at banks, and paid 3.26% on a one-year $10,000 CD versus 2.41% at banks (NCUA, 2025). On a car loan or a mortgage, a point or more adds up to real money over the life of the loan. And your money is just as safe. Deposits at federally insured credit unions are protected up to $250,000 by the NCUA — the credit-union equivalent of FDIC insurance, backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. The coverage amount is identical to a bank’s; only the insuring agency’s name changes. ## The St. Louis–Headquartered Credit Unions These are the home-grown institutions — founded and headquartered in the St. Louis area, most now open to anyone who lives or works in the metro. **First Community Credit Union** (Chesterfield) is the largest credit union headquartered in St. Louis — roughly $4.78 billion in assets, more than 408,000 members, and about 42 branches. It celebrated its 90th anniversary in 2024, and its community charter covers St. Louis City plus a wide sweep of Missouri and Illinois counties, so most metro residents can join. **Together Credit Union** (St. Louis) began in 1939 as the Anheuser-Busch Employees’ Credit Union — a beer-industry credit union that grew into a roughly $2.64-billion institution with about 145,000 members and 26 branches. It rebranded to Together in 2020 and is now a founding and official banking partner of St. Louis CITY SC. Membership is open to people who live or work across the core metro counties, plus employees of partners like Anheuser-Busch, Nestlé Purina, and BJC, and their families. **Vantage Credit Union** (Bridgeton) runs about 14 metro branches and has one of the friendliest community charters around: you can join if you live, work, *worship, or attend school* in St. Louis, St. Charles, Jefferson, or Franklin counties in Missouri, or St. Clair or Madison counties in Illinois. **Neighbors Credit Union** (St. Louis), with about 8 branches, leans on a “once a member, always a member” promise and serves the core Missouri and Illinois metro counties, plus select employer groups like Costco and Bi-State/Metro. **Alliance Credit Union** (Fenton) was founded in 1948 and carries deep labor-union and skilled-trades roots — its field of membership includes dozens of employer groups and several labor organizations alongside the usual live-or-work-here counties on both sides of the river. ## A Metro That Keeps Growing: Recent Mergers The St. Louis credit-union map has shifted recently, and it’s worth knowing so you don’t go looking for a branch that’s changed its sign. **West Community Credit Union** (O’Fallon, MO) completed a legal merger with Gateway Metro Federal Credit Union on April 7, 2026, creating a roughly $670-million credit union with 43,000-plus members and about 16 branches under the West Community name. **Alltru Credit Union** (Wentzville) is another rebrand to know: it was 1st Financial Federal Credit Union until late 2020, and it started life in 1968 as the McDonnell Douglas Credit Union — a nod to St. Louis’s aerospace heritage. Alltru is a certified Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) serving St. Louis City, St. Louis County, and St. Charles County. ## Best Wedding & Event Caterers Across the St. Louis Metro Revised July 13, 2026 Who are the best wedding caterers in St. Louis? St. Louis has excellent caterers for every style and budget. Full-service wedding houses include Butler’s Pantry (since 1966), Ces & Judy’s, Russo’s, Catering St. Louis Events, and Callier’s. For barbecue and comfort food, Salt + Smoke, Grace, Championship Catering, and Pasta House stand out, while SqWires, Herbie’s, and Kakao cover boutique and dessert needs. Cygan-Delaney and Bella Milano anchor the Metro East. The best choice depends on your venue, style, and budget. Keep reading ↓Picture the moment the guest list finally comes together — 130 people, a venue booked for a Saturday next fall, and the sudden realization that you now have to feed all of them. Maybe it’s a wedding in Kirkwood, a milestone anniversary in St. Charles, or a company party in the Metro East. Whatever it is, the food is the part guests will actually remember, and it’s usually the single biggest line on the budget. No pressure. The good news: St. Louis has a deep, genuinely excellent catering scene, from white-glove wedding houses that have been at it for half a century to barbecue teams turning brisket into burnt-end toasted ravioli. This guide walks through the best wedding and event caterers across the metro — on both sides of the river — plus what catering actually costs here and the questions that save you from an expensive surprise. ## What Wedding & Event Catering Costs in St. Louis Catering is almost always the largest single expense at a wedding, so it helps to walk in with real numbers. Nationally, the average wedding ran about $34,200 in The Knot’s 2026 Real Weddings Study, but Missouri comes in well below that — a median closer to $17,470 — and St. Louis is one of the more affordable major metros for a celebration. For catering specifically, budget expectations vary widely by service style. At the low end, drop-off or prepared-food-only catering can run roughly $15 to $18 per person (Thumbtack). Full-service wedding catering — with staff, plated or attended-buffet service, and bar — is more commonly planned around $225 to $325 per guest once you add service and beverages, and independent estimates put the St. Louis average near $263 to $292 per guest (wedding.report). Local venue guides peg a typical 75-to-125-guest St. Louis wedding at roughly $18,000 to $35,000 all-in, with catering the biggest slice. Treat these as planning ranges, not quotes — your number depends on menu, guest count, and bar. A few things move that number the most: service style (plated dinners cost more than buffets, which cost more than drop-off), whether you add a hosted bar, your guest count, and the season — peak spring and fall dates command premium pricing and book out first. Rentals like linens, china, and glassware, plus staffing and the service charge, can add 20% to 30% on top of the food itself, which is exactly why an itemized quote matters so much when you’re comparing caterers side by side. ## Full-Service vs. Drop-Off: Know What You’re Buying Before you compare caterers, get clear on the two main models, because a “cheap” quote and an “expensive” one often aren’t the same product. **Full-service** catering means the team handles it all: setup, plated or attended-buffet service, bartending, and teardown and cleanup at the end of the night. It’s the widest menu range and the least work for you. **Drop-off** catering means the caterer cooks, delivers, and sets out ready-to-serve trays — then you and your people handle serving and cleanup. It’s meaningfully cheaper and perfect for casual events, but it’s not the same as having a staffed reception. ## The Full-Service Wedding Heavyweights These are the established, staff-everything wedding houses St. Louis couples have trusted for decades. **Butler’s Pantry** (Lafayette Square) has catered St. Louis weddings and events since 1966. It’s the exclusive caterer at venues like The Coronado, 18Rails, and The Reverie, and a preferred caterer at 40-plus more — the Missouri History Museum, The Muny, and Third Degree Glass among them. If your venue has a caterer list, Butler’s Pantry is often on it. **Ces & Judy’s Catering** (Frontenac) has been an elegant-wedding mainstay for 40-plus years and runs its own exclusive venue, The Venue at Maison du Lac. **Russo’s Catering** (St. Louis) brings roughly 60 years of experience and all-inclusive bridal packages, comfortably scaling from an intimate dinner to a 10,000-guest event. **Catering St. Louis Events** is chef-owned and has been since 1980, pairing full-service catering with 14 boutique event venues — a one-stop option if you still need a space. And **Callier’s Catering** (Warson Woods/Ballwin), family-owned since 1983, spans everything from plated weddings to drop-off and BBQ, handling events from 15 to 2,000-plus. ## Barbecue, Comfort Food & Crowd-Pleasers Not every great St. Louis reception is black-tie. Some of the most-loved catering in town comes off a smoker. **Salt + Smoke** (University City and beyond) caters weddings and corporate events with post-oak-smoked brisket and a signature only St. Louis could invent: burnt-end toasted ravioli. Food service starts around $15 per person, with vegan, vegetarian, and gluten-free options and a 4.9-star WeddingWire rating. **Grace Meat + Three** (The Grove) caters Southern comfort food from chef Rick Lewis, a James Beard Rising Star Chef semifinalist known for some of the city’s best fried chicken. **Championship Catering** ...

## What to Do After a Car Accident in St. Louis Revised July 24, 2026 What should I do after a car accident in St. Louis? After a car accident in St. Louis, first get to safety and call 911 if anyone is hurt. Call the police for any injury, death, or more than $500 in property damage, document the scene with photos, and exchange information — without admitting fault. See a doctor even if you feel fine, then notify your own insurer. Missouri is an at-fault, pure-comparative-negligence state, requires at least 25/50/25 liability plus uninsured-motorist coverage, and gives you five years to file most injury claims (RSMo 516.120). Keep reading ↓One second you are merging onto I-64 thinking about lunch. The next, there is a crunch, your heart is pounding, and a stranger is walking toward your window. The minutes right after a crash are loud, confusing, and easy to fumble — and what you do in them can shape the weeks that follow. Whether your fender-bender happened downtown, out in St. Charles County, across the river in the Metro-East, or on a quiet road in Jefferson County, the same calm checklist applies. The goal in those first minutes is simple: keep everyone safe, capture what happened while it’s fresh, and avoid the handful of mistakes that make the aftermath harder than it needs to be. Do that, and you’ll be in a far stronger position whether the whole thing wraps up with a quick insurance claim or turns into something more complicated. This is general information to help you stay organized after a wreck. It is not legal advice, and every accident is different. For guidance on your specific situation, talk with a licensed Missouri attorney. ## First, Get Safe Before anything else, check yourself and your passengers for injuries. If anyone is hurt, call 911 right away. If the cars are drivable and blocking traffic, move them to the shoulder or a nearby lot so you are not sitting in a live lane — St. Louis interstates do not slow down for a stopped car. Turn on your hazard lights. If you cannot move the vehicle safely, leave it, get yourself to a safe spot away from traffic, and wait. ## When to Call the Police Call the police for any crash involving an injury, a death, or noticeable property damage. In Missouri you must report a crash that causes injury, death, or more than $500 in property damage, and you may also need to file a written accident report with the Missouri Department of Revenue within 30 days. A police report gives you an official, neutral record of what happened. Even for a minor bump, a report is worth having. If officers respond, ask how to get a copy of the report and write down the report number. If police do not come to the scene — which happens with smaller crashes — you can still document everything yourself. ## Document the Scene Your phone is your best tool here. Take wide shots and close-ups of: - Damage to every vehicle involved, from several angles - License plates - The position of the cars before anyone moves them, if it is safe to photograph - Skid marks, debris, traffic signals, and street signs - Any visible injuries - The overall scene, so the road and weather conditions are clear If there are witnesses, politely ask for their names and phone numbers. A neutral bystander who saw the whole thing can matter a great deal later. ## Exchange Information — Carefully Swap names, phone numbers, addresses, driver’s license numbers, license plate numbers, and insurance details with the other driver. Stay civil, but keep it factual. This is the moment people often slip up: do not apologize, do not say “it was my fault,” and do not argue about who caused it. You may be rattled and not have the full picture yet. Stick to exchanging information and let the facts come out later. ## See a Doctor, Even If You Feel Fine Adrenaline is a powerful painkiller. Plenty of people walk away from a crash feeling okay, only to wake up the next morning with a stiff neck, a pounding headache, or back pain that will not quit. Whiplash and concussions often show up hours or days after impact. Getting checked out by a doctor — even a visit to urgent care or your primary care office — protects your health and creates a medical record that ties any injuries to the accident. If you skip care and symptoms appear later, an insurer may argue your injury had nothing to do with the crash. ## Report It to Your Insurance Notify your own insurance company promptly, even if the other driver was clearly at fault. Most policies require you to report accidents within a reasonable time, and reporting does not mean you are admitting blame. Give your insurer the facts you have. Be honest, but you do not need to volunteer guesses or speculate about fault. If the other driver’s insurance company calls and asks for a recorded statement, you are allowed to slow down, ask questions, and get advice before agreeing to one. ## How Fault Works in Missouri Missouri is an at-fault state, which means the driver responsible for a crash (and their insurer) is generally on the hook for the resulting damages. Missouri also ...

## St. Louis Suburbs Compared: Find the Right Town for You Revised July 24, 2026 Which St. Louis suburb is right for me? St. Louis suburbs group by region. West County (Kirkwood, Webster Groves, Chesterfield, Ballwin) is established, leafy, and pricier; Mid County (Clayton, Ladue, Maplewood, U. City) is close-in and walkable; St. Charles County (O’Fallon, St. Peters, Wentzville) is newer and growing; South and Jefferson counties are more affordable; North County offers real value; and the Illinois Metro-East (Edwardsville, Belleville) often gives you more house for the money. Compare the specific school district, commute, and total monthly cost — including taxes — not just the town name. Keep reading ↓At some point in every St. Louis house hunt, a quiet question shows up at the kitchen table: where should we actually live? You can love this region and still feel stuck, because the metro is a patchwork of small towns and school districts, each with its own personality, price level, and commute. The good news is that the differences are real and knowable. Once you understand how the suburbs group together, the map gets a lot less intimidating. The single biggest mistake newcomers make is shopping by town name alone — two houses a mile apart can sit in different school districts, different tax rates, and wildly different commutes. So treat this as a starting framework, then verify the details for the exact street you’re considering. A weekend spent actually driving the neighborhoods, at the times you’d really be on the road, is worth more than any list. This guide walks through the major regions, with an honest, specific note on each town. We have grouped them by area so you can compare apples to apples. A quick reminder before you start: O'Fallon, Troy, and Washington each exist in both Missouri and Illinois, so always confirm the state when you search a listing. ## West County: established, leafy, and pricier West County is the part of St. Louis County most people picture when they think suburbs — bigger lots, strong schools, and home prices that sit toward the top of the metro. - **Kirkwood and Webster Groves**are the walkable-downtown stars. Both have lively, historic main streets you can stroll for dinner, and both school districts are highly regarded — Kirkwood and Webster Groves consistently rank among the best in Missouri. You pay for that combination of charm and schools. - **Chesterfield, Town and Country, Wildwood, and Des Peres**lean more spread-out and newer, with larger homes and a higher price point. Chesterfield has major shopping and the Valley as an employment center; Wildwood is greener and more rural in feel. - **Ballwin and Ellisville**are the more attainable West County options — solid, family-friendly, and generally a step more affordable than Town and Country or Chesterfield while keeping access to the same well-regarded districts. - **Eureka and Manchester**stretch the West County dollar a little further — Eureka is more rural and newer out toward Six Flags with Rockwood schools, and Manchester is a solid mid-priced pick between Ballwin and Kirkwood with Parkway and Rockwood access, minus the Town and Country premium. ## Mid County: close-in, walkable, and varied Mid County sits between the city and West County. It trades big lots for shorter commutes and more walkable, character-rich neighborhoods. - **Clayton**is the metro's marquee address — the county seat, a true walkable downtown, and one of the very top school districts in Missouri (Ladue and Clayton routinely trade the number-one and number-two spots). It is also one of the most expensive places to live in the area, so it fits buyers prioritizing schools and walkability over square footage. - **Ladue, Frontenac, and Huntleigh**are the prestige addresses — estate-scale lots, the highest household incomes in the metro, and, in Ladue’s case, the top-ranked school district in Missouri for several years running. This is close-in luxury: big, private, and expensive, for buyers who want space without leaving Mid County. - **Maplewood and Brentwood**are compact, older streetcar suburbs with revitalized, walkable main streets full of independent restaurants and shops. They are popular with people who want city energy and a short commute without leaving the county. - **University City, Richmond Heights, Creve Coeur, and Maryland Heights**round out the area — U. City has the Loop and a diverse, urban feel; Creve Coeur skews more upscale and corporate; Maryland Heights is convenient to the airport and Westport. ## St. Charles County: newer, growing, and family-focused Across the Missouri River, St. Charles County is where much of the metro's new construction and population growth has gone. Expect newer subdivisions, newer schools, and a longer-but-manageable commute to downtown. - **St. Charles**itself anchors the county with its historic brick Main Street along the riverfront. - **O'Fallon (Missouri), St. Peters, Wentzville, Lake St. Louis, Cottleville, and Dardenne Prairie**are the growth engines. Wentzville has been among the fastest-growing school districts in the entire state. Lake St. Louis is built around its lakes; Cottleville and Dardenne Prairie are smaller and newer. If you want a newer home and a yard for a more reasonable price than West County, this county is usually the first place to look — just budget for the extra drive time. ## South County and Jefferson County: practical and affordable South St. Louis County offers steady, established neighborhoods at gentler prices than West County. - **Oakville, Mehlville, Affton, and Sunset Hills**are dependable, family-oriented communities. Sunset Hills sits ...

You can love this region and still feel stuck, because the metro is a patchwork of small towns and school districts, each with its own personality, price level, and commute. The good news is that the differences are real and knowable. Once you understand how the suburbs group together, the map gets a lot less intimidating. The single biggest mistake newcomers make is shopping by town name alone — two houses a mile apart can sit in different school districts, different tax rates, and wildly different commutes. So treat this as a starting framework, then verify the details for the exact street you’re considering. A weekend spent actually driving the neighborhoods, at the times you’d really be on the road, is worth more than any list. This guide walks through the major regions, with an honest, specific note on each town. We have grouped them by area so you can compare apples to apples. A quick reminder before you start: O'Fallon, Troy, and Washington each exist in both Missouri and Illinois, so always confirm the state when you search a listing. ## West County: established, leafy, and pricier West County is the part of St. Louis County most people picture when they think suburbs — bigger lots, strong schools, and home prices that sit toward the top of the metro. - **Kirkwood and Webster Groves**are the walkable-downtown stars. Both have lively, historic main streets you can stroll for dinner, and both school districts are highly regarded — Kirkwood and Webster Groves consistently rank among the best in Missouri. You pay for that combination of charm and schools. - **Chesterfield, Town and Country, Wildwood, and Des Peres**lean more spread-out and newer, with larger homes and a higher price point. Chesterfield has major shopping and the Valley as an employment center; Wildwood is greener and more rural in feel. - **Ballwin and Ellisville**are the more attainable West County options — solid, family-friendly, and generally a step more affordable than Town and Country or Chesterfield while keeping access to the same well-regarded districts. - **Eureka and Manchester**stretch the West County dollar a little further — Eureka is more rural and newer out toward Six Flags with Rockwood schools, and Manchester is a solid mid-priced pick between Ballwin and Kirkwood with Parkway and Rockwood access, minus the Town and Country premium. ## Mid County: close-in, walkable, and varied Mid County sits between the city and West County. It trades big lots for shorter commutes and more walkable, character-rich neighborhoods. - **Clayton**is the metro's marquee address — the county seat, a true walkable downtown, and one of the very top school districts in Missouri (Ladue and Clayton routinely trade the number-one and number-two spots). It is also one of the most expensive places to live in the area, so it fits buyers prioritizing schools and walkability over square footage. - **Ladue, Frontenac, and Huntleigh**are the prestige addresses — estate-scale lots, the highest household incomes in the metro, and, in Ladue’s case, the top-ranked school district in Missouri for several years running. This is close-in luxury: big, private, and expensive, for buyers who want space without leaving Mid County. - **Maplewood and Brentwood**are compact, older streetcar suburbs with revitalized, walkable main streets full of independent restaurants and shops. They are popular with people who want city energy and a short commute without leaving the county. - **University City, Richmond Heights, Creve Coeur, and Maryland Heights**round out the area — U. City has the Loop and a diverse, urban feel; Creve Coeur skews more upscale and corporate; Maryland Heights is convenient to the airport and Westport. ## St. Charles County: newer, growing, and family-focused Across the Missouri River, St. Charles County is where much of the metro's new construction and population growth has gone. Expect newer subdivisions, newer schools, and a longer-but-manageable commute to downtown. - **St. Charles**itself anchors the county with its historic brick Main Street along the riverfront. - **O'Fallon (Missouri), St. Peters, Wentzville, Lake St. Louis, Cottleville, and Dardenne Prairie**are the growth engines. Wentzville has been among the fastest-growing school districts in the entire state. Lake St. Louis is built around its lakes; Cottleville and Dardenne Prairie are smaller and newer. If you want a newer home and a yard for a more reasonable price than West County, this county is usually the first place to look — just budget for the extra drive time. ## South County and Jefferson County: practical and affordable South St. Louis County offers steady, established neighborhoods at gentler prices than West County. - **Oakville, Mehlville, Affton, and Sunset Hills**are dependable, family-oriented communities. ## A Guide to St. Louis Metro Farmers Markets by Town Revised July 24, 2026 Where are the farmers markets in the St. Louis metro? Nearly every St. Louis-area town has a farmers market. Year-round, head to Soulard near downtown; suburban markets like Kirkwood (most of the year), Ferguson, Wildwood, St. Charles, Lake St. Louis, and SOL Food in Maplewood mostly run Saturday or weekday mornings from roughly April through October. On the Illinois side, try O’Fallon’s Vine Street Market, Edwardsville, Alton, and Belleville. Markets are seasonal, so check the current schedule, go early for the best produce, and bring small bills. Keep reading ↓There is a particular kind of Saturday morning that makes summer in the St. Louis area feel worth it. You are up a little earlier than you wanted to be, there is coffee in a paper cup, and you are walking past a folding table piled with tomatoes still warm from someone’s field that morning. A grower hands you a peach. Somewhere a band is tuning up. This is farmers market season, and the good news is that you do not have to drive into the city to find it. From Kirkwood to Edwardsville, nearly every town in the metro has its own market, each with its own personality. There’s a real payoff to shopping this way beyond the freshness. Your money stays with a neighbor instead of a distant supply chain, the produce was usually picked within a day so it lasts longer in your fridge, and you get to actually talk to the person who grew it — which is how you end up trying a vegetable you’d never have picked up under fluorescent lights. For families, it’s a cheap, screen-free Saturday outing; for cooks, it’s the best way to let the season decide dinner. Once you find your regular market, it tends to become a weekly habit rather than a chore. The vendors start to recognize you, they set aside the thing you always buy, and a routine grocery errand quietly turns into the best part of the weekend. Here is a by-town guide to where you can find fresh local produce across the suburbs and the Illinois Metro-East. Markets are seasonal and schedules shift year to year, so always check the current schedule before you go. ## Mid-County and South County, Missouri **Kirkwood.** The Kirkwood Farmers’ Market on East Argonne is one of the oldest in the region and runs most of the year, with peak local-grower season in the warmer months. Unlike weekend-only markets, it keeps daily hours, which makes it an easy weekday stop. Saturday mornings are busiest, so arrive early if you want first pick of the produce. **Maplewood.** The market formerly sponsored by Schlafly now runs as the **SOL Food Farmers Market** on Sutton Boulevard in downtown Maplewood. It is a producer-only, vendor-owned market on Wednesday evenings during the growing season, which means the people behind the tables actually grew or made what they are selling. Expect pastured meats and eggs, mushrooms, honey, preserves, and seasonal produce. ## North County, Missouri **Ferguson.** The **Ferguson Farmers Market** at the Plaza at 501 on South Florissant is a Saturday-morning staple that serves the whole North County area, including nearby Florissant. Produce here is often picked within a day of the market. One standout: Ferguson participates in **SNAP and Double Up Food Bucks**, a program that matches what you spend with your EBT card on fruits and vegetables, dollar for dollar up to a limit. It is a quiet way to stretch a grocery budget while eating better. Check the current schedule for token details. ## West County and Far West, Missouri **Wildwood.** The Wildwood Farmers Market on Plaza Drive opens later in the spring, usually around late May, and runs Saturday mornings through early fall. It pairs fresh produce, eggs, and meats with handmade soaps, honey, and crafts. **Lake St. Louis.** The **Lake Saint Louis Farmers & Artists Market** at The Meadows shopping center runs Saturday mornings across a long season, rain or shine, and leans into both local growers and local artisans. Vendors are drawn from within roughly 100 miles, so what you buy is genuinely regional. **St. Charles.** The Saint Charles Market on Historic Main Street is one of the longer-running seasons in the metro, stretching well into late fall on Saturday mornings. With farmers, bakers, crafters, and artisans together on a brick-lined street, it doubles as a morning out. ## Illinois Metro-East **O’Fallon, Illinois.** Note the state — there is an O’Fallon in Missouri too. The **Vine Street Market** at O’Fallon Station has become one of the most popular markets in the Metro-East, with 60-plus vendors at peak, live music, and food trucks. It focuses on food grown or made within about 100 miles and runs roughly May through October. **Edwardsville.** The **Land of Goshen Community Market** is a beloved Saturday-morning fixture. For the 2026 season it temporarily moved to City Park while its usual downtown home is rebuilt as a new park, so confirm the current location before you go. It is large, lively, and worth the drive. **Alton.** The **Alton Farmers’ & Artisans’ Market**, organized by Alton Main Street, runs Saturday mornings near the downtown historic district from late spring into mid-fall. Expect locally grown fruits and vegetables alongside handmade crafts, specialty foods, and even pet goods. **Belleville.** Belleville’s Old Town area hosts a long-running ...

## St. Louis Chambers of Commerce and Networking, by Suburb Revised July 24, 2026 Which chamber of commerce or networking group should my St. Louis business join? St. Louis has an active chamber in nearly every suburb. Key ones: the St. Charles Regional, O’Fallon (MO), and Western St. Charles County chambers out west; Chesterfield Regional and West St. Louis County (Ellisville) in West County; Kirkwood-Des Peres, Mid County (Maplewood), Clayton, and the rebranded Quad Chamber (Webster Groves/Shrewsbury/Rock Hill/Brentwood) close in; Greater North County (Florissant) up north; and Edwardsville/Glen Carbon, Belleville, O’Fallon-Shiloh, Collinsville, and the RiverBend Growth Association in the Illinois Metro-East. BNI runs weekly referral groups metro-wide, and Greater St. Louis, Inc. is the regional organization. Join by where your customers are, visit before you pay, and show up consistently. Keep reading ↓Running a small business can feel like a solo sport. You handle the work, the invoicing, the marketing, and the slow weeks — usually alone. One of the oldest fixes for that isolation still works: get in a room with other local owners. Across the St. Louis metro, on both the Missouri and Illinois sides, that room usually has a name. It is your local chamber of commerce, a referral group, or a small-business network. Here is who does what, where they meet, and how to get real value without wasting money. ## What a chamber of commerce actually does A chamber of commerce is a membership organization of local businesses in a defined area — a city, a cluster of towns, or a county. You pay annual dues, and in return you get a mix of the following: networking events where you meet other owners, a public member directory that links to your website, ribbon cuttings and grand-opening support, referrals when residents call asking who to hire, advocacy with city hall on issues that affect business, and educational workshops on things like taxes, hiring, and marketing. The honest truth is that a chamber gives back what you put in. Owners who show up to a few events a year, introduce themselves, and follow up tend to win work. Owners who pay dues and never attend tend to shrug and not renew. Membership is a tool, not a magic switch. ## Chamber vs. referral group vs. industry association These three get mixed up, so here is the plain difference: - **A chamber of commerce**is broad and local. Any kind of business in the area can join — a plumber, a bakery, a law firm, a nonprofit. The point is community connection across industries. - **A referral group**(sometimes called a leads group) is small, structured, and built to pass business directly. The best-known is- **BNI**, which runs chapters around St. Louis. Most groups allow only one person per profession — one realtor, one electrician, one insurance agent — so members refer work to each other without competing. Meetings are usually weekly and attendance is expected. - **An industry association**is national or regional and tied to one trade — restaurants, home builders, accountants. You join for industry training, standards, and contacts in your own field, not for local cross-referrals. Many owners belong to more than one. A common combo is one chamber for community visibility plus one referral group for steady leads. ## Chambers in St. Charles County (Missouri) The fast-growing western side of the metro has several active chambers. The **St. Charles Regional Chamber** in St. Peters serves the St. Charles County region and is part of the Missouri Chamber Federation. The **O'Fallon Chamber of Commerce and Industries** covers O'Fallon, Missouri (not the Illinois O'Fallon — both exist). Out west, the **Western St. Charles County Chamber of Commerce** serves Wentzville and the growing communities around it. These are good first stops if your customers live in St. Charles, St. Peters, O'Fallon (MO), or Wentzville. ## Chambers in West and Mid St. Louis County If you work the western suburbs, the **Chesterfield Regional Chamber** is one of the larger chambers in the region and covers the Chesterfield business corridor. Further along Manchester Road, the **West St. Louis County Chamber of Commerce** in Ellisville serves Ballwin, Ellisville, Manchester, Wildwood, Valley Park, and several neighboring towns — a strong choice for home-service pros and retail owners across far West County. Closer in, the **Kirkwood-Des Peres Area Chamber of Commerce** serves Kirkwood, Des Peres, Warson Woods, Glendale, and Oakland, and has been around since the 1940s. The **Mid County Chamber of Commerce**, based in Maplewood, covers the Maplewood and Richmond Heights area, which is a busy small-business and restaurant pocket. And in the region’s business hub, the **Clayton Chamber of Commerce** serves downtown Clayton — the county seat, packed with law firms, agencies, and finance offices — a strong fit if your clients are professional-services businesses. ## Chambers in South County and the Webster Groves area The **Quad Chamber of Commerce** — the rebranded name for the longtime Webster Groves, Shrewsbury, Rock Hill and Brentwood chamber — covers that string of inner-ring suburbs (“the Quad”) along the south-central corridor. Head into Jefferson County and the **Arnold Chamber of Commerce** serves Arnold and the surrounding Jeffco communities. Both are practical fits for trades, shops, and service businesses that draw from those neighborhoods. ## Chambers in North County (Missouri) In North St. Louis County, the **Greater North County Chamber of Commerce**, based in Florissant, serves Florissant, Hazelwood, Black Jack, Spanish Lake, and the wider north-county ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/st-louis-chambers-of-commerce-and-networking-by-suburb

## Basement Waterproofing in St. Louis: A Homeowner’s Guide Revised July 13, 2026 Why do St. Louis basements leak? St. Louis basements leak mainly because of expansive clay soil, which swells when wet and shrinks when dry — pressing on foundation walls and channeling water against them (the “clay bowl effect,” where loose backfill holds water and builds hydrostatic pressure). Heavy spring rains, freeze-thaw, and older foundations make leaks common. Start with gutters, downspout extensions, and grading before bigger fixes. Keep reading ↓You go downstairs after a hard St. Louis spring rain and there it is again — that dark, damp line where the wall meets the floor, or a puddle spreading across the concrete, or just the musty smell that tells you water got in somewhere. If you own a home here long enough, a wet basement stops being an if and becomes a when. It’s not your imagination, and it’s usually not your fault. St. Louis is unusually hard on basements for reasons baked into the ground itself. The good news: most basement water problems are fixable, some of the fixes are cheap and DIY, and knowing the difference between a real problem and a cosmetic one can save you thousands. Here’s a homeowner’s guide to why St. Louis basements leak, how water actually gets stopped, and how to hire the right help without getting scared into overpaying. Because that last part is real: basement waterproofing is an industry that runs on fear, and an informed homeowner is a lot harder to oversell than a panicked one. ## Why St. Louis Basements Leak So Often The main culprit is under your feet: **expansive clay soil**. Clay absorbs water and swells — expansions of ten percent or more are common — then shrinks as it dries. That endless swell-and-shrink does two things to a foundation. It presses inward on basement walls with real force, and it opens gaps and fissures around the foundation that channel water straight down against it. Add the region’s heavy spring rains, freeze-thaw cycles, and a lot of older homes with aging foundations, and you get basements that weep. There’s a name for the classic version: the **“clay bowl effect.”** When your house was built, the hole around the foundation was backfilled with loosened soil that drains differently than the packed earth around it — so it acts like a bowl that collects water against your walls. Under enough saturation, that water creates **hydrostatic pressure** — the sheer weight of waterlogged soil pushing on the foundation — and forces its way through pores, cracks, and the cove joint where the wall meets the floor. Expansive soils, for the record, cause more property damage across the U.S. each year than earthquakes, floods, hurricanes, and tornadoes combined — you’re not fighting a small thing. ## A Real Problem Versus Minor Seepage Before you spend a dime, figure out what you’re actually dealing with — because not all basement moisture is a leak. In St. Louis’s humid summers, warm outside air hits cool basement walls and pipes and **condenses**, making surfaces damp with no leak at all. Homeowners routinely misdiagnose condensation as wall leakage and spend money on the wrong fix. Here’s the tell: **condensation** is seasonal, forms an even film on cold surfaces, and wipes away; true **water intrusion** tracks rainfall and snowmelt, comes from a source point, leaves staining, and gets worse over time. A simple test recommended by university extension experts: tape a piece of plastic tightly to the wall for a day — if moisture forms on the *room* side, it’s condensation (run a dehumidifier); if it forms *behind* the plastic, water is coming through the wall. Signs that you have a genuine, escalating problem include **efflorescence** (white mineral residue), a persistent musty or moldy smell, water stains, peeling paint, and — most seriously — **bowing or bulging walls**. ## How Water Actually Gets Stopped Real fixes fall into two camps, plus a cheap first line of defense. **Start outside, for free or cheap.** Before any big system, manage the surface water, which is the strongest, best-documented advice there is: clean the gutters so they don’t overflow onto the foundation, **extend downspouts** to discharge at least 4 to 10 feet from the house, and **regrade** so the soil slopes away — about an inch per foot for the first several feet. A few inches of rain on a roof is thousands of gallons of water; sending it away from the foundation solves a surprising number of “leaks” on its own. **Interior systems** manage water that still gets in: an **interior drain tile** (a perforated pipe in the footing) feeding a **sump pump** captures rising groundwater and relieves hydrostatic pressure; **crack injection** seals individual foundation cracks (flexible polyurethane for active, wet leaks); and vapor barriers manage dampness. Interior work is cheaper, doesn’t tear up the yard, and can be done year-round. **Exterior waterproofing** is the most thorough and the most expensive: excavating down to the footing, applying a waterproof membrane or coating, and installing footing drains so water never reaches the wall. It disrupts landscaping and costs more, but it stops the problem at the source. Which system is right depends on your specific basement: many St. Louis homes do well with an interior drain-tile-and-sump approach because it’s effective, affordable, and doesn’t require tearing up mature landscaping — but a home with severe exterior water ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/basement-waterproofing-in-st-louis-a-homeowners-guide
