This guide walks the Loop end to end: the institutions, the international row, sushi and hot pot, and the coffee-and-donut stops, plus an honest note on what’s closed. As always in a district that turns over, **a quick call to confirm hours before you go is smart**. Come hungry and plan to wander. **📌 Love the Loop? Keep this — and share it.** Bookmark this guide and send it to the friend headed to a show at the Pageant, the group doing a Loop food crawl, or the visitor who wants the real St. Louis eclectic-street experience. **Every share points one more hungry person to a great meal on Delmar. That’s the whole idea.** ## The Iconic Institutions Start with the anchors that built the Loop. **Blueberry Hill** ($$) is Joe Edwards’ 1972 landmark — the “Famous Burger,” walls of pop-culture memorabilia, and the Duck Room where Chuck Berry played for decades. **Fitz’s** ($$) bottles its root beer on-site behind a glass wall and serves burgers and famous floats — a family and tourist favorite. **Three Kings Public House** ($$) is the craft-beer gastropub with a big patio, rebuilt bigger after a 2023 fire. And **Salt + Smoke** ($$) brings St. Louis-style BBQ right by the Chuck Berry statue. These are the timeless Loop stops. ## The International Row The Loop’s signature is its density of independent global kitchens. For Korean-Mexican fusion, **Seoul Taco** ($) got its start here, with **K-Bop** ($) nearby for Korean rice bowls and **Kimchi Guys** ($$) for Korean fried chicken on the west edge. For ramen and pho, **Nudo House** ($$); for hand-pulled noodles and soup dumplings, **Corner 17** ($$); and for a newer Chinese noodle spot, **Noodle Story** ($$). Add Thai (**Fork & Stix**, Thai Gai Yang), Vietnamese banh mi (**Paris Banh Mi**), Lebanese-Syrian mezze at **Ranoush** ($$), 40-year-old Greek gyros at **Gyro House** ($), Filipino street food at **Guerrilla Street Food**, plus Indian (Gokul, Turmeric) and African (Africana). You could eat a different country every night for two weeks. ## Sushi, Ramen & Japanese The Loop has become a genuine Japanese-dining destination. **Nobu’s** ($$$) does multi-course omakase (reservations via Tock) — the Loop’s date-night splurge. For fun, **Sakatanoya** ($$) is St. Louis’s first double-tier conveyor-belt sushi bar (plus ramen), and **Katsuya** ($$) does Japanese katsu in tidy bento-style presentations. Whether you want a chef’s tasting or a plate gliding to you on a conveyor, the Loop delivers. It’s a remarkable range for one short strip — and part of the international-row energy that makes the neighborhood so fun to graze. ## Hot Pot & Interactive A fast-growing Loop niche is the cook-it-yourself meal. **Umami Seasons Hotpot** ($$), across from Blueberry Hill, does Taiwanese tabletop hot pot, and **Movoc** ($$) offers DIY individual hot pots and malatang. Gather a group, pick your broth, and cook your way through the meal — it’s a social, interactive night out that fits the Loop’s playful spirit. Along with the conveyor sushi and the noodle shops, it’s proof the Loop has quietly become one of the metro’s best strips for adventurous, hands-on Asian dining. ## Coffee, Donuts & Ice Cream The Loop is great for a sweet or caffeinated stop, too. **Blueprint Coffee** ($) is a beloved third-wave roaster (try the gooey-butter latte), the longtime **Meshuggah Cafe** ($) keeps the bohemian coffeehouse tradition alive, and **Strange Donuts** ($) does creative St. Louis-born donuts. Just east in the Delmar Maker District, the vintage-style **Fountain on Delmar** ($$) serves soda-fountain ice cream, floats, and cocktails. Between a proper cup of coffee, a wild donut, and an old-fashioned float, the Loop covers the sweet side as well as it does the savory. ## More Than Food: The Loop Experience Eating on the Loop comes with a built-in show. ## Where to Eat in Lafayette Square: A Local's Guide to St Louis's Most Romantic Neighborhood Revised July 17, 2026 Where should you eat in Lafayette Square? Lafayette Square is St. Louis’s most romantic dining neighborhood. The anchors: Eleven Eleven Mississippi (Tuscan), SqWires (New American), The Bellwether (contemporary American with rooftops), and Polite Society (gastropub). For steaks and a raw bar, Hamilton’s and the new Extra Wavy. For drinks, 33 Wine Shop, Planter’s House (cocktails), and Square One Brewery. And for St. Louis-pride sweets, Park Avenue Coffee (gooey butter cake), Clementine’s ice cream, and Baileys’ Chocolate Bar — all around historic Lafayette Park. Keep reading ↓If St. Louis has a neighborhood built for romance, it’s Lafayette Square. Wrapped around Lafayette Park — generally cited as the oldest park west of the Mississippi — this compact, walkable district is the city’s showcase of restored Victorian mansions and townhomes, all brick sidewalks, wrought iron, and gaslit-feeling streets. And the dining matches the setting: candlelit rooms in old brick warehouses, a chocolate-and-cocktails lounge, wine bars steps from the park’s bandstand. This is where St. Louis comes for anniversaries, date nights, and long, lingering brunches. The restaurant density per block is remarkable, and it leans distinctly special-occasion — but there’s also gooey butter cake, boozy ice cream, and a neighborhood brewpub to keep things grounded. This guide walks you through the best of the Square — the romantic anchors, the brunch spots, the sweets, and the wine-and-cocktail bars — plus an honest note on a couple of places that have closed. Keep this — and share it.** Bookmark this guide and send it to the partner you’re planning a date with, the friend celebrating an anniversary, or anyone who loves a beautiful historic neighborhood with great food. **Every share helps one more couple find their perfect table. That’s the whole idea.** ## The Romantic Anchors Start with the Square’s special-occasion heavyweights. **Eleven Eleven Mississippi** ($$$) is the neighborhood anchor — Tuscan and Northern-California cooking with a strong wine list in a restored brick warehouse. **SqWires** ($$-$$$) is a women-owned New American landmark since 2001, set in a converted 19th-century factory. **The Bellwether** ($$$) does contemporary American with seasonal small plates, fresh pasta, and two rooftop patios. And **Polite Society** ($$-$$$) is the beloved New American gastropub (try the Jimmy Burger). Any of these makes a memorable dinner — book ahead on weekends. ## Steaks, Raw Bar & What’s New The Square’s edges (along Chouteau) have added serious firepower. **Hamilton’s Urban Steakhouse & Bourbon Bar** ($$$) does heritage Black Angus steaks and a big bourbon list, with an on-site hydroponic greenhouse. And the buzzy newcomer **Extra Wavy** ($$$), open since late 2025 from the Yellowbelly team, brings a coastal raw bar and inventive tropical cocktails to the former PW Pizza space. For a fresh, of-the-moment date, these two are the talk of the neighborhood right now. They round out a lineup that spans classic romance and modern buzz. ## Weekend Brunch Lafayette Square does a proper weekend brunch. **SqWires** runs an extensive Saturday-and-Sunday spread, **The Bellwether** does a lovely Sunday brunch indoors or on the patio, **Polite Society** serves weekend brunch with its signature gastropub polish, and **Eleven Eleven Mississippi** adds a Saturday brunch seating. A leisurely brunch followed by a stroll around Lafayette Park is one of the great low-key luxuries of a St. Louis weekend — and the district’s walkability makes it easy to wander off the meal. ## Sweets & St. Louis Pride Save room, because the Square’s dessert game is distinctive. **Park Avenue Coffee** is a must — the St. Louis original serves **gooey butter cake in some 75 flavors** alongside house-roasted coffee. Just up the way, **Clementine’s Naughty & Nice Creamery** ($) does boozy and vegan microcreamery ice cream (including a gooey-butter-cake flavor — peak St. Louis). And for the most romantic finish in the city, **Baileys’ Chocolate Bar** ($$) pairs desserts and chocolate cocktails with cheese boards in a candlelit room. Gooey butter cake two ways plus a chocolate lounge — that’s a St. Louis sweet tooth’s dream block. ## Wine & Cocktails The Square is one of the best drinking neighborhoods in the city. **33 Wine Shop & Bar** is a 25-year institution with 500-plus labels and an expanded small-plates menu. **Planter’s House** is a nationally regarded craft-cocktail bar with an intimate upstairs room (the Bullock Room) and food to match. **Winnie’s Wine Bar** pours flights in a retro-aviation setting near Hamilton’s. And **Square One Brewery & Distillery** keeps it casual as the neighborhood brewpub (and Missouri’s first post-Prohibition microdistillery). Whether you want a rare bottle, a perfect cocktail, or a house-brewed pint, the Square has your pre- or post-dinner drink. ## Casual & Local Not every meal here is a splurge. **Mayo Ketchup** ($-$$) does fast-casual Puerto Rican, Dominican, and Cuban food — empanadas, plantains, and mofongo from chef Mandy Estrella (the “Plantain Girl”). And **Vicini Pastaria** ($$) is a handmade-pasta shop, cafe, and market rolled into one (open Friday through Sunday). These are the everyday, come-as-you-are spots that balance out the district’s special-occasion reputation — proof that Lafayette Square is a real neighborhood, not just a date-night stage set. ## The Historic District: More ...

## Where to Eat in The Grove: A Local's Guide to St Louis's Liveliest Food & Nightlife District Revised July 17, 2026 Where should you eat in The Grove? The Grove is St. Louis’s liveliest food-and-nightlife strip on Manchester Avenue. Acclaimed picks: Grace Meat + Three (Southern), Sultan Mediterranean (Kurdish), Sameem (Afghan), and Fordo’s pizza inside Urban Chestnut’s bierhall. International: Chao Baan (Thai), Seoul Taco, Everest (Nepali), and La Calle (Mexican). Breweries and bars: Urban Chestnut, Rockwell, HandleBar, and whiskey den The Vandy. It’s the heart of the city’s LGBTQ nightlife (Just John, Rehab, Prism), with late-night eats at Little Lucy and Pie Guy. Keep reading ↓The Grove — officially Forest Park Southeast — is St. Louis’s most concentrated food-and-nightlife strip, a stretch of Manchester Avenue splashed with colorful murals, neon, and energy. It’s the beating heart of the city’s LGBTQ nightlife, a craft-brewery hub, and home to some genuinely acclaimed chef-driven kitchens and a deep bench of international independents. Few places in the metro pack this much personality into a few blocks. This is a neighborhood where you can eat refined Southern fried chicken, authentic Kurdish food, and Afghan kabobs; drink at a 400-seat German bierhall or a whiskey den; catch a drag show; and grab a late-night vegan cheeseburger — all on foot, all past midnight if you like. It’s artsy, inclusive, and a little wild, in the best way. This guide walks you through the best of The Grove: the acclaimed spots, the international kitchens, the breweries and bars, the LGBTQ nightlife, and the late-night eats. As always in a fast-moving district, **a quick call to confirm hours before you go is smart**. Come ready for a good time. **📌 Love The Grove? Keep this — and share it.** Bookmark this guide and send it to the friend planning a night out, the group doing a Grove bar crawl, or anyone who loves an artsy, inclusive, food-and-drink neighborhood. **Every share points one more person to a great night in The Grove. That’s the whole idea.** ## Acclaimed & Chef-Driven The Grove’s food ambition is real. **Grace Meat + Three** ($$) is the anchor — Rick Lewis’s refined Southern fried chicken and a rotating “meat-and-three” of sides, one of the metro’s most beloved restaurants. **Fordo’s Killer Pizza** ($$), from Gerard Craft’s Niche Food Group, does wood-fired sourdough pizza inside Urban Chestnut’s bierhall. **Sultan Mediterranean** ($$) is a family-owned, critically praised **Kurdish** kitchen. And for fine dining, **Aperi** ($$$), an amaro bar with Italian small plates, and seafood-forward **Lucy Quinn** ($$$) round out a surprisingly high-end lineup. This is destination eating. ## International Flavors The Grove’s international row is deep. **Sameem** ($$) is Missouri’s original Afghan restaurant (kabobs, bolani, stews). **Chao Baan** ($$) does regional Thai from the family behind King & I. **Everest Cafe** ($$) covers Nepalese and Indian, **La Calle** ($$) does Mexican with a patio, **Seoul Taco** ($) brings its Korean-Mexican fusion, and **Creole With a Splash of Soul** ($$) serves po’boys and gumbo. From Kabul to Bangkok to New Orleans, the Grove lets you travel the world in a couple of blocks — all independent, all distinctive. ## Casual, Comfort & Late-Night The Grove is a champion of casual and after-hours eats. **Good Company** ($$) is a cocktail bar with burgers and inventive mains (in the former Layla space), **The Gramophone** ($) does sandwiches and mac and cheese with live music, and **Songbird** ($$) covers locally sourced breakfast and lunch. For late-night, **Little Lucy** ($) serves creative fare and vegan cheeseburgers to midnight, and **Pie Guy** ($) slings New York-style sourdough slices to 1am. # Where to Eat in The Grove: A Local's Guide to St Louis's Liveliest Food & Nightlife District Revised July 17, 2026 Where should you eat in The Grove? The Grove is St. Louis’s liveliest food-and-nightlife strip on Manchester Avenue. Few places in the metro pack this much personality into a few blocks. This is a neighborhood where you can eat refined Southern fried chicken, authentic Kurdish food, and Afghan kabobs; drink at a 400-seat German bierhall or a whiskey den; catch a drag show; and grab a late-night vegan cheeseburger — all on foot, all past midnight if you like. ## Best Restaurants in Belleville, IL: A Local's Guide to the Metro East Revised July 23, 2026 Where are the best restaurants in Belleville, IL? Founded in 1814 and settled heavily by German immigrants (by 1870, roughly 90% of residents were German-born or descended), Belleville wears its history well. Today its downtown Main Street district mixes cozy taverns, wine bars, pizza pubs, and cafes among the old brick storefronts, while the real destination draw — Beast Craft BBQ — pulls hungry St. Louisans across the river. Casual, fun, and full of personality — that’s the Belleville pizza vibe. ## International Flavors The international bench is solid across Belleville and its neighbors. For Thai, **Sala Thai** ($$) and the west-side **Banana Leaf** ($$) both do authentic, customizable-spice cooking. And across in Swansea, **India’s Oven** ($$) covers Indian with butter chicken, tandoori, and fresh naan. It’s a well-rounded global lineup for the area. ## Cafes, Breakfast & a Famous Orchard Belleville does mornings and casual well. And don’t miss **Eckert’s Country Restaurant** ($$) — the restaurant at what’s billed as the largest pick-your-own orchard in the country, famous for fried chicken, a hearty farm breakfast, and seasonal fun. It’s a destination in its own right, especially in apple season. ## Bars & Brewpubs For a drink, downtown Belleville has independent options. **Shoehorn Brewing** ($) is a veteran-and-homebrewer-owned taproom on Main (bring your own food, stay for trivia), and **4204 Main Street Brewing Co.** ($$) is an established brewpub pairing food with house beer. ## Best Restaurants in South County: A Local's Guide to South St Louis County Revised July 24, 2026 Where are the best restaurants in South County? South County’s strength is long-tenured family independents. The institutions: Tucker’s Place South (steakhouse), Bartolino’s South (Italian and seafood, special occasion), Helen Fitzgerald’s (Irish pub), and Crusoe’s (Oakville). The standout angle is Bosnian food — Berix and Taste of Bosnia for ćevapi and burek. Plus La Oaxaqueña (Oaxacan, Mehlville), Thai Racha (Telegraph), Breakfast and Burgers (Affton diner), and 9 Mile Garden’s food-truck garden. Unpretentious, great-value spots spread along Lindbergh, Gravois, and Telegraph. Keep reading ↓South County — the sprawling southern half of St. Louis County, covering Affton, Mehlville, Oakville, Lemay, Concord, Sunset Hills, and Crestwood — isn’t a trendy, walkable dining district. It’s a big, friendly, car-dependent suburb where the best food lives in strip malls and along the arterials: Lindbergh, Gravois, Telegraph, and Lemay Ferry. And that’s exactly its charm. South County’s strength is **unpretentious, long-tenured family independents** — steakhouses and Irish pubs that have fed neighborhood families for decades — plus a genuinely notable **Bosnian food scene**, thanks to St. Louis’s large Bosnian community, whose home cooking spills south from Bevo Mill into Affton and beyond. These are trusted neighborhood spots, not Instagram bait, and locals are fiercely loyal to them. This guide rounds up the best independent restaurants across South County: the family institutions, the Bosnian kitchens, the international favorites, and the diners. As always, **a quick call to confirm hours before you go is smart**. Skip the chains and eat where South County actually eats. **📌 South County local? Keep this — and share it.** Bookmark this guide and send it to the neighbor who always defaults to a chain, the friend who’s never tried Bosnian food, or the family looking for a new regular spot down south. **Every share points one more hungry person to a great local meal. That’s the whole idea.** ## Local Institutions & Family Classics South County runs on beloved, decades-old family spots. **Tucker’s Place South** ($$) has been the area’s go-to steakhouse since 1982 — a genuine institution off South Lindbergh. **Helen Fitzgerald’s** ($$) is a sprawling Irish grill and pub with a huge patio and live music, a Lindbergh landmark since 1992. And **Crusoe’s** ($$) is the family-owned Oakville favorite (with an attached sports bar) doing a big, reliable American menu. These are the trusted, come-back-often spots that define eating in South County — no pretense, just good food and regulars who’ve been coming for years. ## For a Special Night When the occasion calls for white tablecloths, **Bartolino’s South** ($$$) is South County’s special-occasion staple — classic Italian and fresh seafood served since 1982 on South Lindbergh. It’s the spot for an anniversary, a birthday, or a nice dinner out that doesn’t require driving into the city. Pair it with Tucker’s for steaks, and South County covers the special-night bases without you ever crossing into St. Louis proper. Both prove the area’s independents can do a genuine occasion, not just a weeknight. ## The Bosnian Story Here’s South County’s standout angle: St. Louis has one of the largest Bosnian diasporas outside Bosnia, and its food is a real local treasure. The historic heart is Bevo Mill in South City, but the community and its cooking spill directly into Affton and South County. The living South County anchors are **Berix** ($) on Lemay Ferry Road — a longtime kitchen famed for **ćevapi** (grilled minced-meat sausages) and doner — and **Taste of Bosnia** ($) on Union Road, a warm counter-service spot doing fresh ćevapi, **burek** (flaky filled pastry), and musaka. If you’ve never had Bosnian food, this is your chance — hearty, savory, and unlike anything else in the metro. (An honest note: two names people ask about, Grbic and Bosna Grill, are no longer sit-down restaurants, so head to Berix or Taste of Bosnia.) ## Mexican, Oaxacan & Thai The international bench is strong. In Mehlville, **La Oaxaqueña** ($$) is a standout for authentic Oaxacan cooking — tlayudas and mezcal margaritas from an Oaxaca native — and **Tequila** ($) is the neighborhood Mexican spot in Oakville. For Thai, **Thai Racha** ($) on Telegraph is a genuine hidden gem, doing panang, pad thai, and tom yum from a Thai-migrant owner. These are the small, family-run international kitchens that reward anyone willing to look past the strip-mall exterior. ## Diners, Breakfast & Something Different For a hearty morning, **Breakfast and Burgers** ($) is a veteran- and family-owned Affton diner doing generous home cooking, and **Dave’s Diner** ($) is the no-frills South County spot for slingers and daily specials (worth confirming its hours before a late-night run). And for something genuinely different, **9 Mile Garden** ($-$$) in Affton is Missouri’s first food-truck garden — rotating local trucks, live music, and a family-friendly scene. It’s a fun, low-key way to sample several kitchens in one visit, and a real community gathering spot. ## What About BBQ? South County has its smoke spots too. Local favorites like **Nubby’s** ($$) in Oakville and **Sharpshooter Pit & Grill** ($$) in Affton have real neighborhood followings for from-scratch smoked meats (both are worth a quick call to confirm current hours). Just over the county line in Arnold, **Smokee Mo’s** ($$) is a well-regarded scratch smokehouse if you’re heading a little further south. ## Coffee Shops in Maplewood, MO: A Local Guide Revised July 27, 2026 What are the best coffee shops in Maplewood, MO? Maplewood’s coffee splits by what you want. **La Cosecha Coffee Roasters** (7360 Manchester Rd) is the established roaster, sourcing and roasting since 2006. **Kentzo Koffee** (2500 Sutton Blvd) air-roasts its own and opened July 2025. **Maplewood Deli & Coffeehouse** (7298 Manchester Rd, formerly Foundation Grounds) adds a full deli menu and an L-shaped patio. **Living Room** (2808 Sutton) is a solar-powered cart partnered with Bridges Community Support Services, and **Mauhaus Cat Cafe** (3101 Sutton) pairs a cafe with an adoptable-cat lounge. All five sit within a short walk of the Manchester and Sutton intersection. Note: Stone Spiral, Looking Meadow and C Oliver all closed and still appear in older guides. Maplewood is barely two square miles, and you can walk most of its coffee in an afternoon. That’s unusual. Most of this metro makes you drive between good cafes; here they’re stacked along Manchester and Sutton within a few blocks of each other. It also means the neighborhood turns over. One storefront on Sutton has held three different coffee shops in a decade — which is worth knowing before you drive out on the strength of a list somebody wrote in 2021. Here’s what’s actually open, and what each one is for. ## What are the best coffee shops in Maplewood, MO? Maplewood’s coffee splits neatly by what you want. **La Cosecha Coffee Roasters** on Manchester is the serious roaster — they’ve been sourcing and roasting since 2006. **Kentzo Koffee** on Sutton is the newest, air-roasting its own since July 2025. **Maplewood Deli & Coffeehouse** is the one with a real food menu and a patio. **Living Room** is a solar-powered cart with a community mission, and **Mauhaus Cat Cafe** is exactly what it sounds like. ## La Cosecha Coffee Roasters 7360 Manchester Rd. The anchor. La Cosecha has been roasting since 2006 with relationship-based sourcing, meaning they buy from farms and cooperatives they have ongoing relationships with rather than through anonymous commodity channels. Their house roast is called City Limits. If you want to understand what Maplewood coffee is, start here and ask what they’re excited about that week. Roasters generally like being asked. ## Kentzo Koffee 2500 Sutton Blvd. Brothers John and Hunter Iffland opened in July 2025, air-roasting their own beans. They also run something called the Kentzo Clean Up Project, which is the kind of thing a neighborhood shop does and a chain doesn’t. That Sutton address carries some history. It held Stone Spiral Coffee & Curios for about fifteen years until it closed in 2022, then Looking Meadow Cafe, which also closed. Kentzo is the current occupant, and by all appearances a well-loved one. If you find an older Maplewood coffee guide naming either of the previous two, that’s how you know it hasn’t been updated. ## Maplewood Deli & Coffeehouse 7298 Manchester Rd. This one confuses people, because for years it was **Foundation Grounds** and a lot of the internet still calls it that. Same location, new identity, deli menu attached. There’s an L-shaped patio, which matters in a neighborhood where outdoor seating is the difference between a quick stop and an actual afternoon. This is the Maplewood option when someone in your group wants lunch and someone else wants a flat white. ## Living Room 2808 Sutton Blvd. A solar-powered coffee cart that partners with Bridges Community Support Services. Small operation, genuine mission, and a good reminder that a coffee business doesn’t have to be a build-out with a hundred seats to be worth your money. ## Mauhaus Cat Cafe & Lounge 3101 Sutton Blvd. A cat cafe, so let’s be precise about what that means: there’s a cafe side and a separate lounge where the cats live, and the cats are adoptable. It is not primarily a coffee destination and shouldn’t be judged as one. It is an extremely good place to take a kid, a date who likes animals, or yourself on a bad week. ## Which one for which occasion Five shops in a few blocks means you can actually choose based on the situation rather than proximity. **You want the best cup in the neighborhood.** La Cosecha. They roast it, they source it, and the counter staff can tell you where it came from. **You’re meeting someone for lunch and coffee.** Maplewood Deli & Coffeehouse. It’s the only one on the strip with a proper food menu attached, and the patio absorbs a group better than the smaller rooms. **You want to try something new.** Kentzo. Newest arrival, air-roasting, and still in the phase where the owners are experimenting. **You have a kid, or you’ve had a rough week.** Mauhaus. There is no version of a bad afternoon that isn’t improved by a room full of cats who are all available for adoption. **You want to support something small.** Living Room. A solar-powered cart partnered with a community services organization is about as close to direct as local spending gets. ## Why Maplewood ended up with this much coffee Two square miles shouldn’t support five coffee businesses. Maplewood does it because the business district was built for walking before that was a planning fashion — a continuous run of small storefronts on Manchester and Sutton, most of them narrow, most of them cheap enough historically that an ...

## African Hair Braiding & Natural Hair Salons in St. Louis Revised July 27, 2026 Where can I get African hair braiding in St. Louis? St. Louis braiding and natural hair shops cluster in two areas. **Walk-in African braiding storefronts** line St. Charles Rock Rd, Chambers Rd, W. Florissant and Olive Blvd — Amy (St. Ann), Abi and Jumelle (Chambers Rd), Claire (Olive Blvd), 3 in 1 (Florissant), Sabou’s (Gravois Ave). **Appointment-based loc and natural hair specialists** sit mostly in the city: Locs of Glory (5886 Delmar), The Loc Loft STL (Goodfellow), KEKE CREATEZ (5455 Delmar), ResilienceHD (Fox Park). Sory African Hair Braiding in Belleville is the confirmed Metro East option. Typical STL prices: box braids ~$150-250, knotless $100-300, cornrows $55-65, silk press $80-100, loc retwist ~$100 — always ask whether the hair is included. Missouri law (RSMo 329.275) requires braiders to register with the state Board and post the certificate at the shop. Finding a braider you trust is not like finding a restaurant. You are handing someone six hours and your hair, and the difference between a good chair and a bad one shows up months later at your hairline. Most guides to this skip everything that matters. They list shop names and stop — nothing on what a style should cost here, how long to block out, what a tight braid is actually doing to your scalp, or the fact that Missouri law requires your braider to have something posted on the wall. This covers all of it, for the St. Louis metro specifically. ## Where can I get my hair braided in St. Louis? The metro’s braiding and natural hair shops cluster in two places: the city corridor and North County. Storefront African braiding shops that take walk-ins are concentrated along **St. Charles Rock Rd, Chambers Rd, W. Florissant** and **Olive Blvd**. Appointment-based loc and natural-hair specialists sit mostly in the city — the Delmar/West End area and South City. There’s one confirmed option across the river in Belleville. That distribution is worth saying out loud, because it means South County, West County and St. Charles County residents are generally driving in. That’s not a gap in this guide — it’s the actual shape of the market. ## Appointment-based: locs, natural hair, silk press These all run live online booking, which is the strongest sign a shop is actively taking clients. **Locs of Glory** — 5886 Delmar Blvd. Sisterlocks, microlocs, starter locs, retwists, and loc repair and restoration, plus color. Open Monday through Saturday with Sunday hours as well, which is unusual. **The Loc Loft STL** — 4829 Goodfellow Blvd. Locs, retwists and natural hair care, with their own product line. **KEKE CREATEZ** — 5455 Delmar Blvd, inside STL Hair Cafe. Starter locs, loc retwist and style, silk press, and detox treatments. **ResilienceHD by T.Denise** — 2903 S. Jefferson Ave in Fox Park. Box braids, cornrows, loc retwist, silk press, and — usefully — takedown and detangling as separate bookable services. **Jess On The Press** — South City. Silk press, natural styles, protective styling, color and cuts, Tuesday through Saturday. Their listed address has a zip code that doesn’t match the street, so confirm the location when you book. **Gokor Xclusive** — 110 N. 17th St downtown. Small and medium knotless, box braids, and men’s cornrows. **_Thebraidfairy_** — 5400 Page Blvd. Knotless in large and medium, and box braids. **beautyxbraids** — 10501 Lilac Ave in North County. Small and medium knotless. Their small knotless is booked as an eight-hour appointment, which tells you something honest about what that style actually takes. ## Walk-in African braiding shops These are storefront shops in the traditional model — generally walk-in friendly, though calling ahead is always smarter. **Sabou’s African Hair Braiding** — 3802 Gravois Ave, Gravois Park. Box braids, cornrows, twists, extensions and kids’ styles. Walk-ins welcome but appointments preferred. **Amy African Hair Braiding** — 10007 St Charles Rock Rd, St. Ann. Full range including Senegalese twists and children’s styles. Ignore the “open 24 hours” you’ll see on one listing — that’s a data artifact, not a promise. **Abi African Hair Braiding** — 701 Chambers Rd, Moline Acres. Open early, Monday through Saturday. **Claire African Hair Braiding** — 8512 Olive Blvd near the Olivette and University City line. **Jumelle African Braiding** — 2164 Chambers Rd. Open seven days. **3 in 1 African Hair Braiding** — 11724 W. Florissant Ave, Florissant. **Natural Inner Beauty & Barbershop** — 12522 Lusher Rd, Spanish Lake. Multi-stylist shop covering braids, locs and faux locs, silk press, crochet, updos and cuts. Pricing varies by stylist, so ask when you book. **Sory African Hair Braiding** — 1205 N. Illinois St, Belleville. The one confirmed Metro East option, open late seven days a week. ## What it costs in St. Louis These are advertised starting prices pulled from live St. Louis booking listings in July 2026. Length, braid size and whether hair is included all move them. **Box braids:** roughly $85 to $344, with most landing between $150 and $250. **Knotless braids:** about $100 for large, up to $300 for small; medium tends to run $175 to $180. **Cornrows:** roughly $20 to $75, commonly $55 to $65. **Silk press:** roughly $42 to $140. **Loc retwist:** roughly $50 to $125. **Starter locs:** around $130. **Braid takedown:** $30 to $75, and often billed separately. Notice the spread on box braids — the cheapest and most expensive advertised prices in ...

## Coffee Shops in Kirkwood and Webster Groves: A Local Guide Revised July 27, 2026 What are the best coffee shops in Kirkwood and Webster Groves? In **Kirkwood**: **Kaldi’s Coffee** (120 S. Kirkwood Rd), the town anchor since 2005 with a large patio and free garage parking behind, and **Teleo Coffee** (132 W. Monroe Ave), the independent, sourcing from socially-conscious suppliers with a charitable model. In **Webster Groves**: **Maypop Coffee & Garden Shop** (803 Marshall Ave) inside a working greenhouse; **The Clover and the Bee** (100 W. Lockwood) for cinnamon rolls, grits and a late walk-up window; **The Annex Coffee & Foods** (8122 Big Bend) part market, cafe and bar with a covered patio; **23 West Coffee** (23 W. Lockwood); and the **Webster Groves Garden Cafe** (117 E. Lockwood), whose owners perform music in the room. Both downtowns are walkable and only minutes apart. Kirkwood and Webster Groves sit next to each other, look similar from the road, and have completely different coffee. Kirkwood’s is built around two solid anchors near the train station. Webster’s is spread across Lockwood and Big Bend in five distinct places, one of which is inside a greenhouse. If you live in one, you probably drive past better options in the other. Here’s the whole picture — both towns, everything verified open, and what each place is actually for. ## What are the best coffee shops in Kirkwood and Webster Groves? In **Kirkwood**, it’s **Kaldi’s Coffee** on S. Kirkwood Rd — a fixture since 2005 with a big patio — and **Teleo Coffee** on W. Monroe, which runs a charitable sourcing model. In **Webster Groves**, **Maypop Coffee & Garden Shop** operates inside a working garden center, **The Clover and the Bee** on W. Lockwood is the food-forward one, **The Annex Coffee & Foods** on Big Bend is part market and part bar, **23 West Coffee** is the small roaster-minded option, and the **Webster Groves Garden Cafe** has owners who perform music in the room. ## Kirkwood: two anchors, both worth it **Kaldi’s Coffee**, 120 S. Kirkwood Rd. Kirkwood’s default since 2005, and deservedly. There’s a large patio and free garage parking behind the building, which in downtown Kirkwood is worth more than it sounds. Regulars mention the avocado toast and the outdoor seating as often as the espresso. Worth being straight about: Kaldi’s is now more than a dozen cafes across the metro. It’s St. Louis-born and roasts its own, but it isn’t a small independent anymore. That doesn’t make the coffee worse — it just means if “support the little guy” is the goal, Teleo is the one. **Teleo Coffee**, 132 W. Monroe Ave. Sources from socially-conscious suppliers and runs a charitable model, and it earns unusually warm reviews for a shop its size. The honey bear latte comes up constantly. This is the Kirkwood option when you want the independent. ## Webster Groves: five, and none of them redundant Webster is the deeper bench, and the shops genuinely don’t overlap. **Maypop Coffee & Garden Shop**, 803 Marshall Ave. A coffee shop inside a working garden center and greenhouse, with house-made syrups and vegan and gluten-free pastries that are actually good rather than merely available. In February this is the most pleasant room in either town. **The Clover and the Bee**, 100 W. Lockwood Ave. The food-forward one — cinnamon rolls, grits, a Banana Walnut Dutch Baby, and a late walk-up window. If someone in your group wants a real breakfast, this is the stop. **The Annex Coffee & Foods**, 8122 Big Bend Blvd. Part market, part cafe, part bar, and there’s ice cream. Covered patio. The most flexible option if you don’t know yet whether the visit is a coffee, a lunch or a drink. **23 West Coffee**, 23 W. Lockwood Ave. Founded by an attorney who left law for coffee, working with the First Crack roastery. Small and focused. **Webster Groves Garden Cafe**, 117 E. Lockwood Ave. Owners Gary and Mandy Schoenberger are musicians and perform in the room. That’s either exactly what you want from a neighborhood cafe or exactly what you don’t, and you probably know which. ## What regulars actually order Menus tell you what a shop sells. Reviews tell you what people come back for, and the two aren’t always the same. At **Kaldi’s Kirkwood**, the avocado toast comes up nearly as often as the espresso — it functions as much as a light-breakfast stop as a coffee one. At **Teleo**, the honey bear latte is the drink people name unprompted, and the lattes generally are what the shop is known for rather than straight espresso. At **The Clover and the Bee**, it’s the cinnamon roll and the grits, which tells you plainly that this is a breakfast place that happens to make good coffee rather than the reverse. The Banana Walnut Dutch Baby is the order for anyone who wants the visit to feel like an occasion. At **Maypop**, the house-made syrups are the differentiator — a seasonal syrup on a simple latte is a better test of the kitchen than anything else on the board. And the vegan and gluten-free pastries are worth ordering on their merits, not as a substitution. ## Which town, and when A practical way to choose. **You need parking and a fast, reliable cup.** Kaldi’s Kirkwood, with the garage behind it. **You want breakfast, not just coffee.** The Clover and the ...

Lockwood Ave. Owners Gary and Mandy Schoenberger are musicians and perform in the room. That’s either exactly what you want from a neighborhood cafe or exactly what you don’t, and you probably know which. ## What regulars actually order Menus tell you what a shop sells. Reviews tell you what people come back for, and the two aren’t always the same. At **Kaldi’s Kirkwood**, the avocado toast comes up nearly as often as the espresso — it functions as much as a light-breakfast stop as a coffee one. At **Teleo**, the honey bear latte is the drink people name unprompted, and the lattes generally are what the shop is known for rather than straight espresso. At **The Clover and the Bee**, it’s the cinnamon roll and the grits, which tells you plainly that this is a breakfast place that happens to make good coffee rather than the reverse. The Banana Walnut Dutch Baby is the order for anyone who wants the visit to feel like an occasion. At **Maypop**, the house-made syrups are the differentiator — a seasonal syrup on a simple latte is a better test of the kitchen than anything else on the board. And the vegan and gluten-free pastries are worth ordering on their merits, not as a substitution. ## Which town, and when A practical way to choose. **You need parking and a fast, reliable cup.** Kaldi’s Kirkwood, with the garage behind it. **You want breakfast, not just coffee.** The Clover and the ...

In the **Central West End**: **Northwest Coffee Roasting Company** (4251 Laclede Ave), the metro’s flagship Black-owned roaster, hand-roasting low and slow and open until 7 p.m. daily — unusually late for good coffee here; **Shortwave Coffee** (33 N. None of that is really anyone’s fault — coffee guides get written once and rarely revisited. ## Coffee Shops in St. Charles, MO: 18 Independents, Checked One by One Revised July 28, 2026 What is the best coffee shop in St. Charles, MO? Eighteen independent coffee shops are open in St. Charles County, each verified against its own website. **The three that roast their own beans:** Mocha Point (343 N Main St, Yemeni single-origin, roasted in-house), Course Coffee Roasters (1218 N 2nd St, Frenchtown) and Upshot Coffee (roasts at 45 Jason Ct on a 10kg Mill City roaster; cafes in Cottleville and at 816 N Kingshighway). **On Historic Main Street:** Picasso’s (101 N Main, since 2003), Frontier Perk (108 S Main), Saint Charles Coffee & Creperie (336 S Main). **Earliest:** Crooked Tree, 6am weekdays. **Latest:** Lydia’s, 11pm Fri–Sat. ⚠️ Peace Love Coffee (524 S Main), Tex-Mo and Alpha & Omega (both 111 N Main, O’Fallon) have CLOSED but are still listed as open elsewhere. No verifiable independent remains in O’Fallon, Weldon Spring or Dardenne Prairie. Someone in the St. Charles Facebook group asked for a coffee shop that wasn’t a chain, was locally owned, and made its own food. The thread ran to more than 370 comments. That’s the whole problem in one number. There are plenty of recommendations. What’s missing is any list that’s been checked recently — three of the shops still being recommended on live, indexed pages right now have closed. So we checked all of them, one at a time, against each shop’s own website. Eighteen independents are open in St. Charles County. Here they are, sorted by what you actually want out of a morning. ## What is the best coffee shop in St. Charles, MO? For coffee itself, the three roasters: **Mocha Point** (343 N Main St) roasts in-house and pours Yemeni single-origin; **Course Coffee Roasters** (1218 N 2nd St) roasts in Frenchtown; **Upshot Coffee** roasts on a 10kg Mill City roaster and pours it at the Brake Shop, 816 N Kingshighway. For the setting, **Bike Stop Cafe** at 701 S Riverside sits across from the riverfront with its own bakery. For early, **Crooked Tree** (559 First Capitol) opens at 6am weekdays. For late, **Lydia’s** (1735 S River Rd) runs to 11pm Friday and Saturday. ## The three that actually roast Most coffee shops buy their beans from somebody else. That’s not a knock — Picasso’s buys from St. Louis-area micro-roasters and does well by them. But if you want coffee roasted in the county you’re standing in, there are three. **Mocha Point Yemeni Coffee Co.**, 343 N Main St. Sources directly from small farms and roasts in-house. Yemeni coffee is a genuinely different cup from the Latin American beans most American shops pour — older varietals, usually processed dry, and it tends to land somewhere spiced and winey rather than bright. Worth ordering black once before you decide what you think. **Course Coffee Roasters**, 1218 N 2nd St in Frenchtown. Bags start around $20. Check the day before you drive over — they’re closed Mondays and close at noon on Tuesdays. **Upshot Coffee** roasts at 45 Jason Ct on a 10kg Mill City roaster and serves it at two county cafes: the flagship at 5326 Highway N in historic Cottleville, open since 2019, and the Brake Shop at 816 N Kingshighway, which occupies a 1950s service station with the garage doors still in place. Four cafes total, all local. ## Historic Main Street, and what’s actually on it The original brick paving on North Main, still in service. Photographed by Lane Forman, July 26, 2026. Main Street is the reason most people come to St. Charles, and it’s where the coffee-shop question usually starts. Four independents are on the street itself. **Picasso’s Coffee House**, 101 N Main St, has been there since 2003 — the default answer to this question for two decades, and the one that turns up first on nearly every ranking. It runs late: 7:30am to 9pm Thursday through Saturday. There’s a second location at 1650 Beale St. **Frontier Perk Cafe**, 108 S Main St, is open Wednesday through Sunday, 8 to 3, with a view toward the Missouri River. Their own site is inconsistent about the street number — the contact page says 108, an older page header says 336 — so call if you’re meeting someone there. **Saint Charles Coffee & Creperie**, 336 S Main St, does what the name says and takes orders online. **Mocha Point** is at 343 N Main. One block off, at 701 S Riverside Dr, **Bike Stop Cafe** is the most useful building on this list. It’s a coffee shop, a bike shop and a bakery — the bakery is up at 1312 N 2nd St — and it rents bikes and runs shuttles for the Katy Trail, which passes directly outside. Open at 6am Mondays and until 9pm Friday and Saturday. If you have out-of-town guests and one free morning, this is the plan. Also walkable: **Sucrose** at 700 S Fifth St, a scratch European and German bakery that keeps short hours (Tuesday to Friday 7 to 3, Saturday 8 to 3), and **Crooked Tree Coffee House** at 559 First Capitol Dr, which sells beans by the pound and opens earlier than anyone else here. ## Early birds and night owls If you need coffee before 7am, the county gives you three real options. **Crooked Tree** opens at 6am Monday through Friday and 7am on weekends, closing at ...

## Coffee Shops Open Late in St. Louis: Only Six, and None in the City Revised July 27, 2026 Where can I get coffee late at night in St. Louis? Only six independent coffee shops in the entire St. Louis metro close at 8pm or later, and **none of them are in the city**. Latest: **Qahwatea Coffee** (15957 Manchester Rd, Ellisville) and **Mocha Point** (343 N Main St, St. Charles), both Yemeni coffeehouses reported open to midnight Fri–Sat. Most reliably verified: **The Annex** (8122 Big Bend Blvd, Webster Groves) to 9pm Mon–Sat. Also **The Wolf Cafe** (Ballwin) 9pm Tue–Fri, **La Bonne Bouchée** (Creve Coeur) 8:30pm Tue–Sat, and **Corner Cafe** (Chesterfield) 8:30pm most nights plus a Saturday 10:30pm–midnight window. ⚠️ There is no 24-hour coffeehouse — Coffee Cartel closed in 2018. MoKaBe’s now closes at 3pm; Meshuggah early afternoon. Earliest opens are 6am; nobody opens sooner. St. Louis used to have a 24-hour coffeehouse. Coffee Cartel sat at 2 Maryland Plaza in the Central West End for twenty-two years, and it closed in 2018. Nothing in the city replaced it. Not one thing. We checked every independent coffee shop in the metro we could verify. Six are open past 8pm. Only two run past 10pm — and both of those are Yemeni coffeehouses in the outer suburbs, not in the city. That’s the actual state of late-night coffee here, and it’s a more interesting story than a list. ## Where can I get coffee late at night in St. Louis? The latest verified independent options are **Qahwatea Coffee** in Ellisville (15957 Manchester Rd), reported open to 10pm on weeknights and midnight Friday and Saturday, and **Mocha Point** on Main Street in St. Charles, listed with similar hours. In St. Louis County proper, **The Annex Coffee & Foods** at 8122 Big Bend Blvd in Webster Groves closes at 9pm Monday through Saturday and is the most reliably verified late option. **The Wolf Cafe** in Ballwin runs to 9pm Tuesday through Friday. Inside the city limits, there is currently no independent coffeehouse open past 8pm. ## The six that are actually open late These are the only independents we could verify closing at 8pm or later anywhere in the metro. **Qahwatea Coffee**, 15957 Manchester Rd, Ellisville. A Yemeni coffeehouse built deliberately as an alcohol-free late-night alternative — hand-stitched Yemeni wicker chairs, cushion seating, carved Moroccan wood panels, murals. Reported hours are 10pm Monday through Thursday, midnight Friday and Saturday. Two cautions: the business has no website at all, so those hours come from a magazine feature and listings rather than the owners, and the Sunday hours conflict between sources. Call. **Mocha Point Yemeni Coffee Co.**, 343 N Main St, St. Charles. Roasts its own beans, pours Yemeni single-origin, family-owned since 2023. Listed at 10pm weeknights and midnight on weekends — but its own website publishes no hours, and third-party listings disagree. Treat as promising, not certain. **The Annex Coffee & Foods**, 8122 Big Bend Blvd, Webster Groves. Open to 9pm Monday through Saturday and 8pm Sunday, with the hours published on their own site — the most trustworthy entry on this list. Heated, covered patio; cocktails; a Half Pint ice cream counter under the same roof. In the Old Orchard district, so there’s somewhere to walk afterward. **The Wolf Cafe**, 15480 Clayton Rd, Suite 210, Ballwin. Open to 9pm — but only Tuesday through Friday. Saturday it closes at 3pm, and it’s shut Sunday and Monday. Check the day. **La Bonne Bouchée**, 12344 Olive Blvd, Creve Coeur. A French patisserie open since 1981. The bakery and café run to 8:30pm Tuesday through Saturday; the restaurant side closes at 2:30pm. Two different schedules in one building — don’t confuse them. **Corner Cafe at Greentrails**, 14276 Ladue Rd, Chesterfield, has the most unusual schedule in the metro and it’s worth understanding rather than just reading. It’s certified Kosher by the Vaad, so the week is shaped around Shabbat: open until 8:30pm Sunday through Thursday, closing early at 5pm Friday, and then **opening at 10:30pm on Saturday night and running to midnight**. If you want coffee at 11pm on a Saturday in west county, this is a genuine and slightly wonderful option. ## What happened to the city’s late-night coffee If you’ve lived here a while, the names on that list are all wrong. The late-night coffee places were in the city. **Coffee Cartel** in the Central West End was open twenty-four hours and lasted twenty-two years before closing in 2018. **Café Ventana** on West Pine has closed. **Harvey’s Coffee & Cocktails** on Olive has closed. The two survivors changed. **MoKaBe’s** on Arsenal, a Tower Grove institution and once a reliable late hang, now closes at 3pm and is shut Mondays. **Meshuggah** on Delmar, the other name everyone remembers, now closes in the early afternoon. Older articles still list all of these as late-night options. They are not. If you see a St. Louis coffee guide recommending Coffee Cartel, you’ve found a page nobody has checked since roughly 2017. So the honest summary: the metro’s late-night coffee scene didn’t shrink so much as it **relocated to the outer ring and changed nationality.** The two latest-closing coffeehouses in the region are both Yemeni, both opened recently, and both sit well outside the city — in Ellisville and on Main Street in St. Charles. That’s a real shift in where this city drinks coffee after dark, and almost ...

Saturday it closes at 3pm, and it’s shut Sunday and Monday. Check the day. **La Bonne Bouchée**, 12344 Olive Blvd, Creve Coeur. A French patisserie open since 1981. The bakery and café run to 8:30pm Tuesday through Saturday; the restaurant side closes at 2:30pm. Two different schedules in one building — don’t confuse them. **Corner Cafe at Greentrails**, 14276 Ladue Rd, Chesterfield, has the most unusual schedule in the metro and it’s worth understanding rather than just reading. It’s certified Kosher by the Vaad, so the week is shaped around Shabbat: open until 8:30pm Sunday through Thursday, closing early at 5pm Friday, and then **opening at 10:30pm on Saturday night and running to midnight**. If you want coffee at 11pm on a Saturday in west county, this is a genuine and slightly wonderful option. ## What happened to the city’s late-night coffee If you’ve lived here a while, the names on that list are all wrong. The late-night coffee places were in the city. **Coffee Cartel** in the Central West End was open twenty-four hours and lasted twenty-two years before closing in 2018. **Café Ventana** on West Pine has closed. **Harvey’s Coffee & Cocktails** on Olive has closed. The two survivors changed. **MoKaBe’s** on Arsenal, a Tower Grove institution and once a reliable late hang, now closes at 3pm and is shut Mondays. **Meshuggah** on Delmar, the other name everyone remembers, now closes in the early afternoon. Older articles still list all of these as late-night options. They are not. If you see a St. Louis coffee guide recommending Coffee Cartel, you’ve found a page nobody has checked since roughly 2017. So the honest summary: the metro’s late-night coffee scene didn’t shrink so much as it **relocated to the outer ring and changed nationality.** The two latest-closing coffeehouses in the region are both Yemeni, both opened recently, and both sit well outside the city — in Ellisville and on Main Street in St. Charles. That’s a real shift in where this city drinks coffee after dark, and almost ...

## What Junk Removal Actually Costs in St. Louis (Check Your City First) Revised July 28, 2026 How much does junk removal actually cost? **Most households land between $150 and $400** — but the number turns on two things nobody explains: it is priced by **volume** (a fraction of a truck), not weight or hours, and the advertised low price is a **minimum charge** that almost nothing fits inside. ⚠️ Before booking, check your own city — this metro is ~90 municipalities and many include bulk-item pickup in the trash service you already pay for. 💡 No national pricing page mentions that, because every one of them is lead-gen for haulers. The couch has been in the garage for four months. The old treadmill is holding coats. There is a dead water heater behind the shed that you have stopped seeing. At some point you search what it costs to make it all go away, and the answers come back $99, $210, $400, $950. All for the same job, apparently. ## How much does junk removal actually cost? Most households land somewhere between **$150 and $400**. But the number you get depends almost entirely on two things nobody explains up front: - **It is priced by volume, not weight or time.**You are buying a fraction of a truck — an eighth, a quarter, a half. Not an hour of labor. - **The advertised low price is a minimum charge.**The $99 headline exists to get the truck to your driveway. Very little actually fits inside it. And before you book anything: **in a lot of this metro, your own municipality will haul bulk items for free or close to it.** That option is invisible on every pricing page you will find, for reasons worth understanding. ## Why every site gives you a different number Line up the results and the spread stops looking random. Each source is describing a different business, and none of them mentions it: - A **storage company**says $75 to $800. - A **national booking platform**says $150 to $350, national average $210. - A **moving-comparison site**says $100 to $400. - A **regional hauler**publishes $100–$199 for an eighth of a truck and $700–$950 for a full one. - An **operator in another state**prices it at $0.85 per cubic foot. The last two are the honest ones, because they are quoting the unit the industry actually uses. The middle ones are averages across job sizes that have nothing to do with each other — a single mattress and a full basement cleanout are both “junk removal.” The most useful number on that whole page comes from a forum, where somebody reported what they were actually billed: charged by the truckload, told their load was three-eighths of a truck, about $260. That is what this looks like in practice. ## How the pricing actually works Almost every full-service hauler charges by how much of the truck bed your stuff fills. The crew looks at the pile, quotes a fraction, and that is the price. Roughly what the fractions mean in real objects: **an eighth** is a couple of large items — a mattress and a chair. **A quarter** is a small room’s worth, or a bedroom set. **A half** is a garage’s worth of accumulated things. **A full truck** is a basement, an estate cleanout, or a whole apartment. Two things break that model and cost extra, so ask about them by name: - **Heavy material.**Concrete, dirt, brick, roofing tear-off and tile are priced by weight, not volume, because the truck hits its weight limit long before it fills up. A small pile of concrete can cost more than a truckload of furniture. - **Items with disposal fees.**Appliances with refrigerant, televisions and monitors, mattresses, tires and paint carry per-item charges at the transfer station, and those get passed to you. Labor is usually included, but stairs, long carries and anything requiring disassembly can add to the quote. Say up front that the couch is in a walk-out basement. ## Check your city first Here is the option the pricing pages cannot mention, because all of them make money sending you to a hauler. The St. Louis metro is not one city. It is roughly ninety municipalities on the Missouri side alone, plus the Metro East, and **many of them include bulk-item pickup in the trash service you already pay for.** Some run it on a schedule, some on request, some a set number of times a year. For a couch, a mattress or a grill, that is frequently the entire answer — at no additional cost. Because the rules genuinely differ from one municipality to the next, the only reliable move is to check your own. Search your city name plus “bulk pickup” or call the number on your trash bill, and ask four things: - Is bulk pickup included, and how often? - Do I need to schedule it, or is there a set week? - What is excluded — appliances, electronics, tires, construction debris? - Is there an item limit per pickup? That call takes five minutes and regularly saves a couple hundred dollars. Where it does not work: exclusions are common for the exact items you most want gone, volume limits are real, and if you are on a deadline — a closing, a move-out, a landlord — a scheduled municipal pickup three weeks out is no help. ...

## Repair It or Replace It? An Honest Guide to St. Louis Appliance Repair Revised July 28, 2026 Is it worth repairing, or should you replace it? **Two rules settle most of it.** The **50% rule**: if the repair costs more than about half a comparable new unit, replace it. The **age rule**: if it is past roughly three-quarters of its expected life, replace it even if the fix is cheap. ⚠️ Ask before anyone comes out — **is the diagnostic fee credited toward the repair?** Many credit it, some do not, and that is the difference between paying once and paying twice to hear bad news. 💡 Under five years old, repair nearly always wins. The dryer is making a noise. Not a dramatic noise — a rhythmic one, the kind you can talk yourself into ignoring for a week. Then it stops heating, and you are standing in the basement with wet towels doing math you have no basis for. Is this a $200 fix or a $900 mistake? ## Is it worth repairing, or should you replace it? Two rules settle most of these, and between them they cover almost every appliance in the house: - **The 50% rule.**If the repair costs more than about half the price of a comparable new unit, replace it. - **The age rule.**If the appliance is past roughly three-quarters of its expected life, replace it — even if the repair is cheap. You are about to meet the next failure. And the question to ask before anyone comes out: **is the diagnostic fee credited toward the repair if I go ahead?** Many companies credit it. Some do not. That single answer is the difference between paying once and paying twice to be told bad news. ## The diagnostic fee, and why it feels like a trap Nearly every repair company charges a call-out or diagnostic fee. That is legitimate — someone drove to your house with a van full of parts and spent time working out what is wrong. What makes it feel unfair is the sequence. You pay the fee, the technician tells you the control board is dead and the part costs most of what a new machine costs, and you have now spent money to be told to buy a different thing entirely. You cannot avoid the fee, but you can avoid the sting. Ask three things when you book: - **Is the fee credited toward the repair if I approve the work?**Frequently yes, and it should be stated plainly. - **Will you quote the full repair before starting?**You want the total — parts and labor — not a running clock. - **Do you service this brand, and can you get parts for it?**This is the one people skip, and it is the most common reason a repair stalls. Describe the symptom precisely when you call. “It runs but does not heat” and “it will not turn on” are different problems, and a good dispatcher can sometimes tell you on the phone that it is not worth the visit. ## What actually drives the price Repair quotes vary far more than people expect, and it is not arbitrary. **Which part failed.** This is most of it. A thermostat, igniter, belt, valve or heating element is usually a modest repair. A control board, compressor, sealed refrigeration system or transmission is usually the one that ends the conversation. **Whether the part still exists.** Manufacturers stop making parts. On older or discontinued models the part may be unavailable, back-ordered for weeks, or only available refurbished — and a two-week wait for a refrigerator part is its own kind of expensive. **How the machine is built.** Some units require pulling the whole appliance apart to reach a cheap component. The part is $40 and the labor is three hours. **Whether it is a sealed system.** Refrigerant work on refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners requires certification and specialized recovery equipment, which is why those repairs sit in a higher bracket than anything mechanical. ## Rough lifespans, and where yours sits The age rule needs a denominator. These are the widely published general ranges — treat them as orientation, not prophecy, because usage matters enormously. A washer running two loads a day in a house of six is not on the same clock as one running twice a week. - **Refrigerators:**commonly cited around 10 to 15 years, with the compressor the usual terminal failure. - **Washers and dryers:**commonly around 10 to 13 years. Dryers often outlast washers because they do less mechanical work. - **Dishwashers:**commonly around 9 to 12 years. - **Ranges and ovens:**often the longest-lived in the house, particularly gas, which has fewer electronics to fail. - **Microwaves:**commonly under 10 years, and rarely economical to repair. Find the model number — usually on a plate inside the door, behind the kick panel, or on the back — and look up its manufacture date. Knowing whether the machine is six years old or fourteen changes the whole calculation, and most people genuinely do not know. ## When repair is clearly the right call Fix it, without much agonizing, when: - **The appliance is young.**Under about five years, repair almost always wins. - **It is a known consumable.**Belts, igniters, thermostats, door seals, filters and heating elements are wear items, not death sentences. - **It is a high-end unit.**On a built-in or professional-grade appliance, a repair ...

Dryers often outlast washers because they do less mechanical work. - **Dishwashers:**commonly around 9 to 12 years. - **Ranges and ovens:**often the longest-lived in the house, particularly gas, which has fewer electronics to fail. - **Microwaves:**commonly under 10 years, and rarely economical to repair. Find the model number — usually on a plate inside the door, behind the kick panel, or on the back — and look up its manufacture date. Knowing whether the machine is six years old or fourteen changes the whole calculation, and most people genuinely do not know. ## When repair is clearly the right call Fix it, without much agonizing, when: - **The appliance is young.**Under about five years, repair almost always wins. - **It is a known consumable.**Belts, igniters, thermostats, door seals, filters and heating elements are wear items, not death sentences. - **It is a high-end unit.**On a built-in or professional-grade appliance, a repair ...

## Hardwood, Laminate or Vinyl? Start by Looking Under Your Carpet Revised July 28, 2026 Hardwood or laminate — which should you actually put down? **The room decides it more than taste does.** **Hardwood** for main living areas above grade, especially in an older home. **Laminate or luxury vinyl** for basements, heavy traffic, rentals and big dogs. **Engineered wood** for real wood over a concrete slab. ⚠️ Solid hardwood does not belong below grade — that is moisture physics, not preference. 💡 Before pricing anything, pull up a corner of carpet in a closet: a lot of houses here have original hardwood underneath, and refinishing usually costs less than replacing. The carpet in the back bedroom has to go. That much is settled. What replaces it is less settled, and an hour of reading turns up confident people telling you hardwood is the only real answer, laminate is a scam, vinyl plank has solved everything, and engineered wood is either the smart compromise or a marketing exercise. ## Hardwood or laminate — which should you actually put down? It depends far less on taste than the comparison articles suggest, and far more on three questions: - **What room is it, and is it below grade?**Solid hardwood does not belong in a basement. That is not a preference, it is moisture physics. - **What is already under the carpet?**In a lot of houses around here, the answer is original hardwood — and refinishing beats buying. - **Who lives there?**Large dogs, small children and heavy traffic push the answer toward wear resistance over authenticity. The short version: **hardwood** for main living areas above grade, especially in an older home. **Laminate or luxury vinyl** for basements, high-traffic rooms, rentals, and houses with big dogs. **Engineered wood** when you want real wood over a concrete slab or in a room with some humidity swing. ## Look under the carpet first Before you price a single square foot, pull up a corner in a closet. This metro is full of houses built long before wall-to-wall carpet existed, and a great many of them have original hardwood underneath — oak, usually, installed when the house was built and covered over sometime in the second half of the last century. If your house predates the carpet by decades, there is a genuine chance the floor you want is already in the room. Refinishing existing hardwood is usually cheaper than buying and installing new flooring, and the material is frequently better than what you would buy today: old-growth, tighter grain, and thick enough to sand more than once. It also keeps the house consistent with itself, which matters in a period home more than people expect. What to check when you look: whether the boards are actually wood rather than a thin veneer; how much thickness is left above the tongue, since that determines whether it can be sanded at all; whether there is water staining, cupping or crowning; and how much damage the carpet tack strips and staples did around the perimeter. A flooring contractor will tell you in one visit whether it is refinishable, and that visit is worth more than any amount of online comparison. If you have recently worked out that your house is older than the listing claimed, this is the practical payoff — that age makes it much more likely there is something worth uncovering. ## The basement rule This is the one place where the choice is not really a choice. Basements are below grade, which means the slab passes moisture upward continuously, humidity swings hard by season, and the risk of standing water is never zero. Solid hardwood in that environment cups, gaps and eventually fails — not because it is poor quality, but because wood moves with moisture and a basement never stops supplying it. What works below grade is waterproof by construction rather than by finish: luxury vinyl plank, tile, or sealed concrete. Laminate is a middle case — better than hardwood, but its core is wood-based, and a genuine water event will swell it permanently unless it is a specifically waterproof product. And the sequencing point that saves people the most money: **fix the water before you buy the floor.** A finished basement floor installed over an unresolved moisture problem is a floor you will pay for twice. If the space has ever taken water, deal with that first. ## What each material is actually good at **Solid hardwood.** Real wood, sandable several times over a lifetime, and the only option that genuinely adds to a period home rather than sitting inside it. Weaknesses: moisture, scratching, and cost. It should stay above grade. **Engineered wood.** A real wood veneer over a dimensionally stable core. It handles humidity swings better than solid, can go over concrete, and looks identical because the surface *is* wood. The catch is the veneer thickness — a thick wear layer can be refinished once or twice, a thin one never can. Ask for that number before buying anything. **Laminate.** A photographic layer under a hard wear surface. Modern laminate is genuinely scratch-resistant — often more so than real wood — and inexpensive. Weaknesses: it cannot be refinished, ever, and water at the seams is its failure mode. It also sounds different underfoot, which some people never stop noticing. **Luxury vinyl plank.** Fully waterproof, quiet, comfortable underfoot, and the most forgiving of everything the ...

## Your Auto Body Estimate Will Probably Change. Here Is Why That Is Normal Revised July 28, 2026 How does an auto body repair estimate actually work? **The first estimate is written from damage somebody can see — it is a starting position, not a final price.** Once the vehicle is taken apart, hidden damage may or may not turn up; if it does, the shop writes a **supplement** and negotiates it directly with your carrier. ⚠️ “Get three estimates” is the wrong instruction when insurance is paying — comparing prices works for the carrier, not for you. 💡 Interview three or more shops instead, then tell your carrier which one you want and expect them to work with it. Almost every detail here depends on your specific policy and your state. The estimate lands in your inbox and the number looks oddly specific. Then the shop calls two weeks later with a second number, and the specificity starts to feel like a magic trick. Nothing has gone wrong. That is close to how the process is built to work — but almost nothing you will find online explains it, because most of what ranks for this question is a form pretending to be a calculator. ## How does an auto body repair estimate actually work? The first estimate is written from **damage somebody can see**. It is a starting position, not a final price. Once the vehicle is disassembled — the bumper cover comes off, the fender liner comes out — hidden damage may or may not turn up. If it does, the shop writes a **supplement**: a revised estimate for what was not visible the first time. That is normal, and it is why the number moves. Three things follow from that, and they are the whole article: - **The shop negotiates the supplement with the carrier, not you.**That is in your favor, and it is the opposite of what most advice suggests. - **“Get three estimates” is the wrong instruction when insurance is paying.**Interview shops instead. You are choosing a contractor, not shopping a price. - **Almost every answer here depends on your specific policy**, on which state you are in, and on case law that can shift quickly. Anyone giving you a flat answer is guessing. ## Why the shop should do the negotiating When a supplement is needed, the body shop or mechanic takes it directly to the carrier. Left alone, that arrangement works better for you than getting in the middle of it. Consider what the negotiation is actually about. Whether a particular bracket is compromised. Whether a sensor housing behind the bumper still meets spec. Whether a panel can be repaired or has to be replaced. Most vehicle owners do not know what those parts are or how they are supposed to function, and there is no reason they should — they want the vehicle fixed correctly and returned. The shop, meanwhile, has a powerful reason to fight for the right repair: **it does not want liability for workmanship that could contribute to a future accident.** A shop that lets a carrier talk it into a cheaper repair it does not believe in is the shop holding the risk afterward. So the incentives line up. Your interest and a good shop's interest point the same direction, and the shop speaks the language. ## What “advocate for yourself” should actually mean The advice is not wrong, it is aimed at the wrong target. The chain runs **owner to shop, then shop to carrier** — not owner to carrier. Here is what that looks like. The carrier authorizes repainting the two front fenders and the hood. The work is done and the paint does not match the rest of the car, because paint ages and fresh paint on three panels of an older finish is visibly newer. The thing to say is simple, and you say it to your shop: *this car did not have two-tone paint before the accident, and I do not accept it now.* Then the shop takes that to the carrier and argues for the money to blend adjacent panels and do it properly. The standard underneath that argument is **pre-loss condition** — the idea that a settlement should restore you to roughly the condition you were in before the damage. That is what it means to indemnify a claim. A mismatched paint job plainly falls short of it, and that is an argument worth making through someone who makes it every week. ## Why “get three estimates” is the wrong instruction Collecting three prices is comparison shopping. That is exactly right when you are buying a vacuum cleaner, or when you are paying for the repair yourself. When the carrier is paying, price comparison is not working for you. It is working for them. None of that requires believing carriers are villains. It is arithmetic. An insurer settling on the order of a hundred thousand claims a year, saving two dollars per claim, has covered the annual salaries of several full-time employees. At that scale, small per-claim savings are a genuine business line rather than a conspiracy. Anyone would run it that way. Which tells you what your job is. You already know who is paying. Your job is deciding **who they pay**. So **interview and research** three or more shops rather than collecting three numbers from them. Ask how ...

## How to Choose an Electrician in St. Louis (Homeowner Guide) Revised July 12, 2026 How do you pick a good electrician? Hire a licensed and insured electrician with strong reviews, experience relevant to your job, and a clear written estimate — and never cut corners to save money on work that can cause a fire. Licensing is non-negotiable: it means they’ve met training standards and know the codes. For older St. Louis homes, look for experience with aging wiring and panels. Get a couple of detailed quotes for the same scope and prioritize safety over the lowest price. Keep reading ↓Picture a flickering light that won’t quit, an outlet that’s warm to the touch, or a breaker that keeps tripping every time you run the microwave and the coffee maker together. Maybe you’re renovating a kitchen, or you just moved into one of those beautiful century-old St. Louis brick homes and discovered the wiring is older than your grandparents. Electrical work isn’t something to gamble on — get it wrong and you’re risking fire, injury, and failed inspections — so finding a genuinely good electrician matters more than almost any other home hire. The challenge is that most homeowners have no idea how to tell a great electrician from a mediocre or unlicensed one until it’s too late. This guide fixes that: how to pick a good electrician in St. Louis, how to know if they’re actually skilled, what they typically charge, the different types of electricians, the red flags to avoid, and how to find a trustworthy one near you. ## How Do You Pick a Good Electrician? The short version: hire a **licensed and insured** electrician with strong reviews, relevant experience for your specific job, and a clear written estimate — and never cut corners to save a few dollars on something that can burn your house down. Licensing is non-negotiable with electrical work; a licensed electrician has met training and testing standards and knows the codes that keep your home safe and your work able to pass inspection. Beyond the license, you want someone with a solid local reputation, experience with your type of project, and the professionalism to explain the work and put it in writing. Verify credentials, get a couple of estimates, and prioritize safety and skill over the lowest price every single time. ## How Do You Know If an Electrician Is Good? A good electrician shows it in consistent ways. They’re **properly licensed and insured** and will show proof without hesitation. They have **relevant experience** — residential work, and ideally experience with older St. Louis homes if that’s what you have, since knob-and-tube and outdated panels need someone who’s seen them. They carry a **strong, verifiable reputation** in recent reviews and references. They provide a **detailed written estimate** and explain the work in plain language rather than talking down to you. They’re **professional and communicative** — on time, responsive, tidy. And critically, they **pull permits and follow code** when a job requires it, rather than doing quiet under-the-table work that fails inspection or voids your insurance. An electrician who does all this is one you can trust with your home’s safety. ## What Are the Types of Electricians? It helps to know who does what, so you hire the right specialist. Electricians generally fall into a few categories: **residential** electricians handle homes — wiring, panels, outlets, lighting, and the everyday repairs and upgrades most homeowners need; **commercial** electricians work on businesses and larger systems; **industrial** electricians handle factories and heavy equipment; and some do **specialized** work like low-voltage, data, solar, or generators. For your house, you want a residential electrician, and for a specific job — say a generator install or a panel upgrade — one with experience in exactly that. You’ll also hear about apprentice, journeyman, and master electricians, which describe skill and licensing level; a master electrician has the highest credential and often oversees larger or more complex work. Match the type and level to your job rather than assuming any electrician does everything. ## What Do Electricians Charge? Costs vary widely by the job, the region, and the electrician’s experience, so rather than fixate on a single hourly figure, focus on getting clear, itemized estimates. Electricians may charge by the hour, by the job (a flat rate for a defined task like installing a ceiling fan or an outlet), or with a service-call minimum that covers coming out plus an initial period of work. A more experienced or master electrician typically costs more per hour but often works faster and gets it right the first time, which can make them the better value on complex jobs. The key isn’t chasing the lowest rate — it’s getting two or three detailed quotes for the same scope, understanding exactly what’s included (parts, permits, labor), and choosing based on value and trust. On electrical work especially, a cheap bid that cuts corners is the most expensive kind. ## Red Flags When Hiring an Electrician Some warning signs should stop you cold. Walk away from anyone who **isn’t licensed or insured** or won’t provide proof — with electrical work this is simply not negotiable. Be wary of a bid **dramatically lower than the others** (often a sign of an unlicensed “handyman’s cousin” who’ll leave you with a code violation), **no written estimate or contract**, **demands for large upfront cash**, unwillingness to pull permits ...
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/discover-st-louis-best-electricians-your-easy-guide
