Local St. Louis neighborhood guides, researched and maintained ## Patch Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Patch, St. Louis

Patch serves as the southernmost neighborhood of the City of St. Louis — the riverfront tip of historic Carondelet anchored by St. Boniface Catholic Church (now the Ivory Theatre), Doering’s Carondelet Bakery (in business since 1875), and three National Register historic districts — offering custom manufacturing, B2B consulting, coworking, event services, and small-business support for residents and businesses across the south St. Louis riverfront.

Patch sits at **38.5715° N, 90.2398° W** in zip code 63111, occupying the southernmost tip of the City of St. Louis along the Mississippi River. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are **Robert Avenue** on the north, the **City Limits** on the south, the **Mississippi River** on the east, and **Alabama Avenue** on the west. City planning descriptions trace the northern boundary across Robert Avenue, Virginia Avenue, South Broadway, and East Nagel Avenue, accounting for Patch’s slightly irregular shape. Covering approximately 0.9 square miles, Patch is one of the smallest of the city’s 79 official neighborhoods, with a 2020 population of 2,842 — a 5% increase from 2010 and one of the few St. Louis neighborhoods to gain residents during that decade. The neighborhood forms the southern tip of historic Carondelet, and many residents and visitors still consider the two as one community.

The land that became Patch was originally part of **Carondelet Village**, founded in 1767 by French settler **Clément Delor de Treget** on a 6,000-acre Spanish land grant. Originally called Louisbourg in honor of King Louis XVI and nicknamed **“Vide Poche”** (folk-translated “empty pocket,” reflecting the friendly poverty of its early inhabitants), the village was renamed Carondelet in 1794 to honor Baron de Carondelet, governor-general of Spanish Louisiana. Patch itself sat within **Carondelet Commons North** — a tract of shared grazing land north of the River des Peres set aside for the use of all villagers. After the Louisiana Purchase brought the village into American hands in 1803, Carondelet was incorporated as a town in 1832, became a city in 1851, and was annexed by St. Louis in 1870. Patch was carved out as a distinct neighborhood within Carondelet’s southern tip and now stands on its own among the 79 official neighborhoods of the City of St. Louis.

German immigration transformed the area beginning in the 1840s. In 1843, German immigrant **Joseph Stein** acquired a lot at what is now the corner of Steins and Reilly Streets and built a large stone house that same year — a structure still standing and listed as a St. Louis City Landmark. Stein was so impressed with the land that he convinced many other Germans to settle in the area, and his surname now graces **Steins Street**, joined by other German-derived street names like **Koeln, Espenschied, Schirmer, and Polk**. The Irish followed in the 1850s and settled in what became known as the Patch, working in the riverfront industries. By the late 19th century, the neighborhood’s identity was deeply tied to its German Catholic and Irish immigrant working-class roots, the riverfront economy, and the Carondelet shipyards.

During the Civil War, Patch’s riverfront position gave it national significance. At the **Union Marine Works shipyards** near the confluence of the Mississippi and River des Peres — owned by engineer **James Buchanan Eads** — 32 ironclad gunboats were built for the Union Army and Navy. Among them was the **USS Carondelet**, launched in 1862, which became one of the most-engaged Union ironclads of the war. Several Civil War-era stone houses still stand in Patch today, including the **Henry Zeiss houses on Vulcan Street** (built in the 1850s by German stonemasons known as “Steins”) and the **Anton Schmitt House** from 1859, since relocated for preservation.

Patch contains **three National Register Historic Districts**, each documenting a different chapter of the neighborhood’s story. The **Steins Street District** (designated 1980) showcases the 1851 Steins Street Row Houses and other early German stone construction. The **St. Boniface District** (designated 2002, bounded by Koeln, Tesson, Broadway, and Alabama) is anchored by **St. Boniface Catholic Church** — a Romanesque Revival church built by German Catholics beginning in the early 1860s and completed in 1890 with the addition of its final tower. The parish closed in 2005, and the restored church now serves as the **Ivory Theatre**, the neighborhood’s primary cultural venue. The **Central Carondelet District** (designated 2006, expanded 2007 and 2009; bounded by Koeln, Loughborough, Broadway, and Alabama) ties together the heart of the old village. Together, these three districts preserve more than 150 years of layered building history.

Patch’s civic and cultural landmarks include the **Joseph Otzenberger House** (1858, at Reilly and Primm Streets), the **Carlin Rathgerber-Krauss House** (1848), **Firehouse No. 34** (1895, one of the oldest fire houses in St. Louis), and the **Carondelet School** (1877, restored and now home to Grace Hill Head Start). **Doering’s Carondelet Bakery** has operated continuously on Schirmer Street since 1875 — one of the oldest continuously operating bakeries in St. Louis. **Ivory Triangle Park**, the small green wedge where horses were once tied while their owners shopped at Ivory and Schirmer Street stores, now features a bronze bust of longtime Alderman **Albert “Red” Villa** sculpted by **Bob Cassilly** (founder of the City Museum), and an old horse watering trough has been converted into a fountain. **South Public Park** and **Patch Park** provide neighborhood green space, and the **Sisters of St. Joseph of Carondelet** — whose 1836 founding in Carondelet seeded institutions including Fontbonne University, St. Joseph Institute for the Deaf, and St. Joseph’s Academy — still maintain their international headquarters at the historic Carondelet motherhouse just to the north.

Beyond its boundary streets, the Patch street network includes familiar south St. Louis routes such as **South Broadway, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Steins, Davis, Marceau, Vulcan, Reilly, Schirmer, and Primm**. Most of the neighborhood’s housing dates from the mid-19th to early 20th centuries: an eclectic mix of stone houses, brick rowhomes, modest bungalows, and occasional larger residences laid out in a traditional grid pattern. The neighborhood divides naturally into a residential western half and a heavily industrial eastern half along the Mississippi River, where the former **Carondelet Coke plant** site has been repurposed as the **River City Business Park**, and Anheuser-Busch beer kegs have historically been moved through the riverfront industrial corridor.

Today, Patch retains a strong south-side identity even as it slowly reinvests. Public neighborhood guides describe a mix of homes roughly a century old alongside signs of renovation and newer business activity in recent years. Long-time residents remain a defining part of the neighborhood’s character while newer homeowners and small businesses gradually reshape its blocks. Patch’s riverfront position, three historic districts, German-stone-masonry heritage, and Civil War shipbuilding history together give it one of the deepest and most distinctive identities of any St. Louis neighborhood — one whose name remains uniquely its own among the city’s 79 official neighborhoods.

Image: Streetscape view in the Patch neighborhood, south St. Louis — photo by Onegentlemanofverona — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

Patch sits at the southernmost edge of St. Louis where the Mississippi River meets the city limits, with the four-season Midwest climate shaping the rhythm of the neighborhood’s residential blocks and riverfront industry. Hot, humid summers with highs in the upper 80s°F bring peak activity to Ivory Triangle Park, South Public Park, and the patios along South Broadway. Cool springs and falls are the busiest seasons for Ivory Theatre performances, Doering’s Carondelet Bakery’s 150-year holiday baking tradition, and the historic-district walking tours that connect Patch with greater Carondelet. Cold winters with periodic snow shift commerce indoors to the bakery, the Ivory Theatre, and the small storefronts along South Broadway. Because the neighborhood hugs the Mississippi River, residents and businesses also remain attentive to spring high-water levels, with portions of the riverfront industrial corridor occasionally affected during major flood years like 2019.

## Peabody Darst Webbe Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Peabody Darst Webbe, St. Louis

Peabody Darst Webbe serves as a compact “Near Southside” neighborhood of St. Louis — anchored by The Georgian Condominiums at the historic City Hospital site, the A.T. Still University Missouri School of Dentistry & Oral Health, and the 350-unit Clinton-Peabody mixed-income redevelopment — offering B2B marketing, beverage distribution, historic condominium living, affordable housing, and professional services for residents and businesses across the south St. Louis corridor.

Peabody Darst Webbe sits just south of downtown St. Louis at **38.6065° N, 90.2073° W** in zip code 63104. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are **Chouteau Avenue** on the north, **South Tucker Boulevard / 12th Street** on the east, the **I-55 / I-44 interchange** on the south, and **Dolman Street** on the west. Also known historically as the **Near Southside**, the neighborhood is hemmed in by Lafayette Square to the west, LaSalle Park to the east, Downtown West to the north, and Soulard and McKinley Heights to the south. As of the 2020 Census, the neighborhood’s racial makeup was 79.7% Black, 15.3% White, 3.6% two or more races, 0.8% Asian, and 1.6% Hispanic or Latino — reflecting a 65-resident gain and a substantial 52-unit drop in vacancy since 2010, when the population had already grown 61 percent from the 2000 count.

The neighborhood’s identity is inseparable from three mid-20th-century public housing projects whose names it still bears. **Clinton-Peabody**, built in 1942 under the New Deal Housing Act of 1937, was the first generation of St. Louis public housing — a low-rise development that opened as the segregated white-tenant sibling to **Carr Square Village** on the Near North Side, which was built for Black families. The **Joseph M. Darst Apartments** followed in 1956 (four nine-story towers, 645 units), named for Mayor Joseph Darst (1949–1953), the same St. Louis mayor whose urban-renewal vision also produced the infamous Pruitt-Igoe. The **Anthony M. Webbe Apartments** opened in 1961 (two nine-story towers, one twelve-story, one eight-story, 578 units). Designed by the famed firm of **Leinweber, Yamasaki & Hellmuth** — led by architect Minoru Yamasaki, who would later design Pruitt-Igoe and the original World Trade Center — the Darst-Webbe complex was built on the grounds of a 1940s-cleared near-south neighborhood between Soulard and Lafayette Square.

Like Pruitt-Igoe, Darst-Webbe declined quickly under chronic underfunding by the St. Louis Housing Authority — elevators failed, sanitation lapsed, and by the 1990s the high-rises were widely regarded as failures of mid-century housing policy. **The Darst-Webbe apartments were demolished in 1999**, and the site was replaced with the current two-story, mixed-income brick properties — designed to echo the older brick rowhomes of Soulard and Lafayette Square — that define the neighborhood’s residential streets today. The neighborhood also contains a small number of Italianate-style rowhomes (some dating to the turn of the 20th century, others recent infill) plus a corridor along Park Avenue that has seen new construction in the years since the demolitions.

The redevelopment story continues today with the **Clinton-Peabody Apartments** — St. Louis City’s oldest public housing development, built in 1942. In 2023, residents voted overwhelmingly to demolish the existing buildings and replace them with a **$150 million POAH-led redevelopment** creating 350 new mixed-income apartments and affordable homes, centered around a reconfigured street grid, a renovated community center, and a new central park. Demolition began in 2025; current residents were relocated to refreshed on-site units in 2023 and 2024; and the first wave of new units broke ground in early 2026. The 10-year project is expected to fundamentally reshape the western half of the neighborhood through the early 2030s.

Anchoring the eastern side of the neighborhood is the **City Hospital Historic District**, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2001. The site has served continuously as a public-health landmark since the city built its first hospital here in 1846, in response to a cholera outbreak. The original wooden complex was destroyed by fire in 1856; rebuilt the next year; then leveled by the “Great Cyclone” tornado of 1896 — the third-deadliest tornado in U.S. history. The current **Georgian Revival complex**, designed by famed St. Louis architect **Albert B. Groves** of Grable, Weber & Groves, was completed in 1912 on the same 10-acre site at 1515 Lafayette Avenue. Under Dr. Max C. Starkloff — the St. Louis City Health Commissioner whose 1918–19 Spanish flu protocols are still studied today — the hospital became a state-of-the-art institution and was renamed the Max Starkloff Memorial Hospital after his death. The complex grew to 18 buildings, included a power plant and laundry building, and operated continuously until it closed in 1985.

After two decades of abandonment, the City Hospital site was successfully redeveloped. In 2006, the 1912 Administration Building reopened as **The Georgian Condominiums** — 102 loft-style residences with high ceilings, hardwood floors, gas fireplaces, walk-in closets, and 360-degree views of downtown St. Louis. The old **Power Plant** became Climb So iLL, an indoor climbing gym; the **Laundry Building** (a 1940 Public Works Administration project) became Palladium St. Louis, a private event space. In 2014, **A.T. Still University’s Missouri School of Dentistry & Oral Health** broke ground on the former Malcolm Bliss Psychopathological Institute site — a 79,000-square-foot dental school that opened in 2013 and now serves as ATSU’s third campus after Kirksville, Missouri, and Mesa, Arizona. By 2018, redevelopment had moved on to the remaining vacant buildings — the Commissioner’s Building (1907), Commissary (1940), Ambulance Garage (1921), and Clinic Building (1921) — under Pearl Companies of Indianapolis with design by Trivers Associates.

The neighborhood’s civic infrastructure includes **Peabody Academy** (built 1957 on 14th Street, the St. Louis Public Schools system’s only school in the neighborhood, serving Kindergarten through 8th grade), the **Al Chappelle Community Center** (a St. Louis Housing Authority operation with public meeting rooms), **Mestres Park** (a 3-acre linear park parallel to the neighborhood), and the adjacent **Ray Leisure Park** with its **12th & Park Recreation Center** (gymnasium, multipurpose courts, and indoor pool). The neighborhood’s most visible amenity remains the proximity to **Lafayette Park** — established in 1851 as the city’s first public park — just to the west, with its biweekly summer concert series, fall festival, and historic Victorian-era surroundings.

Today Peabody Darst Webbe sits at one of the most strategic transit positions in St. Louis: surrounded by I-44, I-55, and I-64, two miles east of SSM Health Saint Louis University Hospital, and 16 miles south of Lambert St. Louis International Airport. The neighborhood’s mix of historic condominium living, ongoing affordable-housing redevelopment, brick infill homes, and B2B professional services makes it a uniquely transitional district — one whose blocks reflect every major chapter of 20th- and 21st-century St. Louis housing policy, from the New Deal’s first public housing experiments to today’s mixed-income reinvestment.

Image: City Hospital Historic District (now The Georgian Condominiums), 1515 Lafayette Avenue, Peabody Darst Webbe, St. Louis — designed by Albert B. Groves, completed 1912 — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

Local St. Louis neighborhood guides, researched and maintained ## Penrose Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Penrose, St. Louis

Penrose serves as a stable residential and small-business neighborhood on the Near North Side of St. Louis — anchored by the 51.22-acre Penrose Park, the historic Penrose Park Velodrome (one of only 27 in the United States), and the Heartland St. Louis Black Chamber of Commerce at the North Spring Empowerment Center — offering chamber advocacy, telecom infrastructure, general contracting, mold remediation, screen printing manufacturing, industrial packaging, chemical distribution, and wholesale tire supply for residents, contractors, and Near North Side businesses across the metro.

Penrose sits on the north side of St. Louis at **38.6815° N, 90.2578° W** in zip code 63115, just south of I-70 and west of O’Fallon Park. The neighborhood’s official boundaries are **Florissant Avenue and I-70** on the north, **Natural Bridge Avenue** on the south, **North Newstead and Pope Avenues** on the east, and **Kingshighway Boulevard** on the west. The neighborhood is split between the city’s 21st Ward and 1st Ward, and as of the 2020 Census, Penrose had 5,243 residents — 95.3% Black, 0.9% White, 2.8% two or more races, with 0.8% Hispanic or Latino origin. Familiar residential streets like **Penrose, Euclid, Shreve, Lee, Margaretta, and Steinlage Drive** tie the area together, with Natural Bridge, West Florissant, and Kingshighway carrying most of the commercial activity.

Penrose’s name comes not from a settler but from a speculator: in the early 19th century, the area was characterized more by land speculation than actual settlement. The neighborhood takes its name from **Clement B. Penrose**, whom **Thomas Jefferson** appointed land commissioner in 1805 to settle disputed Louisiana Purchase land claims. Penrose lived on a nearby estate and was one of the region’s prime land investors. Another early landowner was the Kentucky statesman **Henry Clay**, a shaper of the Missouri Compromise of 1820 — making the Penrose ground one of the few St. Louis neighborhoods to claim a direct connection to two major figures of the early American republic.

Penrose did not take on the contours of a community until the late 1880s, when **farmers and dairymen, most of German heritage**, moved their families into the area. By 1900, the community — though still rural — was sufficiently settled to boast two German churches: **St. Engelbert’s Catholic Church** and **Salem German Evangelical Church**. The 1920s brought commercial development and transit lines, raising land values around the northern edges of the city, and most of Penrose’s subdivisions date from that era when single-family brick homes sprang up along Euclid, Shreve, and Lee Avenues. Some subdivisions were the work of outside investors; others were developed by long-time residents — a prime example being the area around **Steinlage Drive**, a street named for a local German family in the dairy business whose properties were subdivided for housing.

The early 1960s were years of transition for Penrose. As older residents moved out, **middle- and upper-income African-American families** moved in. The well-constructed brick houses were ideal for moderate-sized families, offering many their first opportunity for home ownership. Teachers, nurses, and city and government employees made Penrose their new home — a significant number coming from **The Ville**, located to the southeast and long the city’s premier African-American neighborhood. As Penrose’s African-American population grew from 33 percent in 1960 to 95 percent in 1970, African-American institutions helped solidify the neighborhood: **St. Peter’s A.M.E. Church**, a historic African Methodist Episcopal congregation, relocated to the corner of Shreve and Margaretta in 1962, and in 1974 the **Julia Davis Branch Library** — named to honor the well-known St. Louis educator — opened on Natural Bridge Avenue. Penrose developed into a stable African-American middle-class neighborhood, though residents were long subjected to **redlining** by financial institutions because of the neighborhood’s location north of Delmar.

One of the standout features of Penrose is the **51.22-acre Penrose Park**, proposed in the city’s landmark 1907 comprehensive plan by the “Inner and Outer Parks Committee” — whose members included George Kessler and Julius Pitzman, the same Forest Park master planner who would later plat the Central West End’s Westmoreland and Portland Places. Established in 1910, the park is bisected by North Bircher and Kingshighway Boulevards and east-west oriented train tracks. Its amenities include ball fields, basketball and handball courts, a softball field, tennis court, playground, pavilions with BBQ grills, a jogging path with fitness stations — and the centerpiece, the **Penrose Park Velodrome**: a banked outdoor cycling track measuring 1/5 of a mile long with a 28-degree bank, one of only 27 velodromes in the United States and the only one in Missouri.

The Penrose Park Velodrome has a remarkable origin story. When highway officials announced in 1958 that they would expand U.S. Highway 40 along the southern edge of Forest Park — razing the city’s 1930s-built Forest Park bicycle track in the process — the City of St. Louis donated land adjacent to Penrose Park for a replacement velodrome. Built in 1962 and designed by **Olympic cyclist and Schwinn Bicycle Company designer Frank Burlando**, the new Penrose Park Velodrome hosted the prestigious **U.S. National Track Cycling Championships** in its inaugural year. A sewer collapse in the 1970s left the track with the affectionate nickname “**Mr. Bumpy Face**”; resurfacings in 1984 and 2005 followed, and in 2019 the track was rebuilt with a brand-new concrete surface that restored it to championship caliber. Open dawn to dusk, 365 days a year, the velodrome remains a regional cycling destination and a defining feature of Penrose.

Beyond Penrose Park, the neighborhood’s civic infrastructure includes the **St. Elizabeth Mother of John the Baptist Catholic Church** on Shreve Avenue (operated by the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of St. Louis), the historic **St. Peter’s A.M.E. Church** on Margaretta Avenue, the **Julia Davis Branch Library** on Natural Bridge, and the small neighborhood park **Eugene “Tink” Bradley Park** (3.18 acres, established 1958). The neighborhood’s housing stock remains predominantly classic North St. Louis brick — many homes built during the 1920s boom on Euclid, Shreve, Lee, and surrounding side streets — with deep front yards, front porches, and mature street trees that give Penrose a traditional St. Louis feel. Economically, Penrose is largely residential but closely tied to the broader north-city business network along I-70, Natural Bridge, and West Florissant, giving many residents short commutes to industrial, logistics, health care, and public sector jobs.

Image: Residential Modern Infill, North Newstead Avenue, St. Louis — photo by Paul Sableman — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

Penrose sits on the level upland of the Near North Side, where the four-season Midwest climate shapes the rhythm of the neighborhood’s residential blocks and small commercial corridors. Hot, humid summers with highs in the upper 80s°F bring peak activity to Penrose Park — the velodrome’s Thursday-night racing series runs from May through August, and the ball fields, handball courts, and pavilions stay busy with church picnics, family reunions, and youth leagues. Cool springs and falls are the best seasons for biking, fitness-station walking, and the neighborhood-organization meetings that have defined Penrose’s civic life since the early 1970s. Winters are chilly with occasional light snow that dusts the brick rooftops and the velodrome berms, shifting commerce indoors to the chambers of commerce, churches, and small storefronts along Natural Bridge, West Florissant, and Kingshighway. Residents are used to quick weather swings, from pop-up thunderstorms in growing season to the occasional snow squall.

Local St. Louis neighborhood guides, researched and maintained ## Princeton Heights Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Princeton Heights, St. Louis

Princeton Heights is a quiet, walkable south St. Louis neighborhood of early-1900s brick bungalows, anchored by the lively Macklind Avenue Business District and bordered by Hampton, Eichelberger, Christy, and Gravois.

Princeton Heights sits in south St. Louis, bounded by **Hampton Avenue** on the west, **Eichelberger Street** on the north, **Christy Boulevard** on the east, and **Gravois Avenue** on the south. It covers roughly **0.83 square miles** and falls within the city’s Wards 2 and 5.

Long before the brick streets arrived, this was rural farmland known as **Gardenville**, and one 1860s Moellenhoff-family farmhouse still stands on Loughborough as a reminder of those days. The neighborhood name has two roots: the historic **Princeton Creamery** that once operated on Kingshighway near Gravois, and the **“Princeton Place” subdivision platted in 1906** — the “Heights” nodding to the gentle rise up from the River Des Peres.

**Gravois Road was the first road paved by the State of Missouri**, and streetcar lines soon followed it south. By around 1920, nearly all of the old farms had been developed, with the main buildout coming in the **1920s and 1930s**. Many of the earliest homeowners were **German** families, and a number of street names were later Anglicized after the World Wars.

The housing stock is the defining feature of Princeton Heights. Block after block is lined with **1920s and 1930s brick Craftsman bungalows, “storybook” gingerbread houses, and American Foursquares** — the kind of sturdy, gabled brick homes that give south city its character. The resident-run **Princeton Heights Neighborhood Association (PHNA)**, a 501(c)(3) **incorporated in 1976**, helps look after those streets, organizes the neighborhood, and keeps residents connected.

Daily life centers on the **Macklind Avenue Business District**, a compact, walkable strip of locally owned restaurants, cafés, and shops that promotes the Southampton and Princeton Heights area together. Just off the southeast edge sits **Christy Park**, a roughly 16-acre city park founded in 1910 and named for brick-industry businessman William Tandy Christy; its **Christy Greenway** connects toward Carondelet Park. Along the south and southwest edge, the **River Des Peres Greenway and Christy Greenway** (part of Great Rivers Greenway) offer adjacent trails for walking and biking.

The Laundry Basket, a neighborhood laundromat on Macklind Avenue — the kind of locally owned, everyday business that gives the Macklind corridor its character. Photo by Lane Forman, July 2026.

A few landmarks border the neighborhood without sitting squarely inside it. **Our Lady of Sorrows** parish, at the Kingshighway edge, was founded in 1907 with a school that opened in 1908 — a longtime heritage anchor, though the **parish closed in 2023**. Just northwest, across Hampton Avenue, lie **St. Louis Hills and Francis Park**, popular adjacent destinations that many Princeton Heights residents treat as part of their extended backyard.

Princeton Heights is known for its early-1900s brick ‘gabled’ bungalows on quiet, tree-lined streets. Photo: “Princeton Heights” by Paul Sableman, licensed under CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Fine Art Deco stonework crowns the windows of an unassuming brick building on January Avenue in Princeton Heights — one of the small architectural surprises tucked into this 1920s–30s south-city neighborhood. Photo by Lane Forman, July 2026.

Princeton Heights shares St. Louis’s humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa), which means warm, sticky summers and cool, changeable winters. The average July high runs about 89.6°F while the average January high sits near 40.4°F, and the area sees roughly 41.7 inches of rain and about 16.6 inches of snow in a typical year. With around 48 thunderstorm days annually and a spot inside Tornado Alley, spring can bring active severe weather, so local homes and businesses keep an eye on the forecast. 

What residents notice day to day is the mature tree canopy arching over the brick-lined streets, which softens the summer heat and turns the neighborhood gold and red each fall. Those big shade trees, paired with the solid brick housing stock, give Princeton Heights a comfortable, lived-in feel through every season — from leafy summer evenings on the porch to crisp, quiet winter mornings.

By **Lane Forman**, Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory

Local St. Louis neighborhood guides, researched and maintained ## Riverview Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Riverview, St. Louis

Riverview is a far-north St. Louis riverfront area strung along Riverview Drive at the Chain of Rocks, where the Mississippi bends past historic water-intake towers and the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge — a stretch of the city defined by its river, its 19th-century waterworks, and a working corridor of independent businesses.

This guide covers primarily the City of St. Louis “Riverview” neighborhood, which sits at the far-northern edge of the city along Riverview Drive near the Chain of Rocks. For accuracy, note that there is also a separately incorporated Village of Riverview just to the north in St. Louis County — a distinct community of roughly 2,397 residents that was incorporated in 1950 and voted in November 2023 to become a fourth-class city. This is not the same as Riverview Gardens, a different area nearby. The city neighborhood itself is small, with about 242 residents recorded in the 2020 census and a population that is roughly 70 percent Black.

The story of the area begins with **Riverview Drive** itself. Around 1830 it took shape as the “Columbia Bottoms road,” a farm-to-market route that ran through north St. Louis County and down through Baden to the city market. Residential building along its southern end began in the early 1870s and picked up again in the early 1890s, a wave that coincided with construction of the new Chain of Rocks waterworks. That road, now lined with shops, distributors, and small industrial firms, is still the spine of the neighborhood today.

Water shaped Riverview as much as the road did. The **Chain of Rocks site** was chosen for the St. Louis waterworks in 1865; construction began in 1887, and the plant went into service in 1894. A 1915 filter-plant addition was, at the time, the largest in the world, and the facility is still operational today — recognized as a historic civil-engineering landmark by the American Society of Civil Engineers. Out in the Mississippi, the castle-like **Chain of Rocks water intake towers** still stand; Tower #1, built in 1894 in a Romanesque Revival style, remains in use by the St. Louis Water Works. The connected **Chain of Rocks Water Treatment Plant**, established in 1894, is known for award-winning tap water drawn from the river.

The neighborhood’s most famous landmark is the **Old Chain of Rocks Bridge**. Opened in 1929 and stretching about 5,353 feet across the Mississippi, it once carried Bypass Route 66 and is known for the dramatic 22-degree bend at its middle, where the span turns mid-river. It closed to car traffic on February 25, 1970, and reopened in 1998 as a pedestrian and bicycle bridge. Today it serves as the northern point of the **Mississippi Greenway / Riverfront Trail**, a riverside path that runs about 12 miles toward downtown St. Louis.

The riverfront has seen new investment as well. **Chain of Rocks Park**, a 16-acre park at roughly 10840 Riverview Drive, reopened in April 2024 through Great Rivers Greenway. It offers a river overlook with access to the bridge, a pavilion, and a restored prairie, giving residents and visitors a place to take in the Mississippi up close. The area also carries a lighter slice of local history: the former **Chain of Rocks Amusement Park** operated nearby from 1927 to 1978 and, though long gone, is still remembered as part of the neighborhood’s recreational past.

Taken together, these landmarks — the 1830s farm-to-market road, the historic bridge, the river intake towers, the working treatment plant, the new riverfront park, the long greenway trail, and the memory of the old amusement park — give Riverview a character rooted firmly in the Mississippi. The businesses listed below operate along this corridor, serving both the local residents and the regional clients who pass through this far-north stretch of St. Louis.

The historic Old Chain of Rocks Bridge spans the Mississippi at the northern edge of St. Louis, beside Riverview. Photo: “Chain of Rocks Bridge” by Marcin Wichary, licensed under CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

St. Louis sits in a humid climate zone (Köppen Cfa), and Riverview feels it fully. The average July high runs near 89.6°F while the average January high is about 40.4°F, with an annual average around 57°F. The metro typically sees roughly 41.7 inches of precipitation and about 16.6 inches of snow each year, along with some 48 thunderstorm days. Because Riverview sits directly on the Mississippi, summer humidity is amplified near the water, and the low riverfront ground faces periodic flooding — the Great Flood of 1993 remains the local benchmark for how high the river can rise. 

The wider region lies in Tornado Alley, so spring and summer bring frequent and sometimes severe storms. For homeowners and businesses along Riverview Drive, that means planning around the seasons: durable, water-resistant materials and storm-aware scheduling matter here more than in many inland neighborhoods. Mild, pleasant stretches in spring and fall are the sweet spot for outdoor work, river visits, and trips out onto the Old Chain of Rocks Bridge.

Local St. Louis neighborhood guides, researched and maintained ## Shaw Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

**Shaw, St. Louis**

Shaw is a near–South Side St. Louis neighborhood named for Henry Shaw, whose 1840 land purchase gave the city both the Missouri Botanical Garden and Tower Grove Park. A Certified Local Historic District since 1985, it is one of St. Louis's most architecturally intact neighborhoods — and its walkable pocket of cafés, wine shops, and ice cream along Shaw Boulevard and 39th Street keeps it lively today.

The land began as the French colonial Prairie des Noyers (“Meadows of the Walnut Trees,” 1769), narrow farm strips running west from Grand Boulevard. By the mid-1800s Henry Shaw and Mary L. Tyler dominated the area, and in 1857 the two agreed by deed to open Shaw, Flora, and Tower Grove Avenues with restrictions against “offensive factories” — conditions that produced one of the most consistent streetscapes in the city.

Henry Shaw arrived from England in 1819 as a young hardware merchant. By 1840 he had bought a 2,000-acre prairie tract, and in 1850 he built his Italianate villa, Tower Grove House, the first building of what became the Missouri Botanical Garden (1859, the oldest in the country). In 1868 he gave the city Tower Grove Park — 276 acres on the neighborhood's southern edge.

Designated a Certified Local Historic District in 1985, Shaw is prized for its Flora Place private boulevard (1897–1901), the 1878–1883 Shaw Place subdivision, and an 1890–1924 mix of Victorian, Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, American Foursquare, and Art Deco homes.

Shaw runs from Interstate 44 on the north to Magnolia Avenue and Tower Grove Park on the south, South Grand Boulevard on the east, and Tower Grove Avenue and the Botanical Garden on the west (ZIP 63110). It borders Botanical Heights and Tiffany to the north, Compton Heights to the east, Tower Grove South to the south, and Southwest Garden to the west; Shaw Boulevard and Flora Place are its main east–west spines.

Most of the neighborhood's businesses cluster on Shaw Boulevard and the walkable 39th Street node near Tower Grove Park — a patio-and-wine-bar row, a liquid-nitrogen ice cream shop, a wine-and-cheese provisioner, a Thai kitchen, and a vegetarian café — alongside a restored 1915 theatre now hosting weddings and a #1-ranked bed & breakfast across from the park.


A street in the Shaw neighborhood, St. Louis. Photo via Wikimedia Commons (CC).

Like the rest of St. Louis, Shaw has a humid subtropical climate with four distinct seasons. Summers are warm and humid, with July highs near 90°F and about 41.7 inches of rain across the year. Spring and early summer bring the region's severe-weather season, so local roofs, trees, and patios are built to weather sudden storms.

Winters are cold but rarely extreme, with January highs around 40°F and roughly 16.6 inches of snow in a typical year. That mix of stormy summers and icy winters shapes everyday life here — from the home-services calls Shaw businesses field to the seasonal rhythm of foot traffic along Shaw Boulevard and 39th Street.

By **Lane Forman**, Founder of St Louis Near Me Directory

Local St. Louis neighborhood guides, researched and maintained ## Skinker-DeBaliviere Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

 Skinker-DeBaliviere, St. Louis

Tucked into west-central St. Louis between Forest Park and the Delmar Loop, Skinker-DeBaliviere is a compact, leafy neighborhood of early-1900s homes that is best known for the deliberate way its neighbors kept it diverse and stable through decades when many nearby areas came apart.

The neighborhood takes its name from the two streets that bookend it: **Skinker Boulevard** on the west edge, near the City limits, and **DeBaliviere Avenue** on the east. **Delmar Boulevard** forms the northern edge, while **Forsyth and Lindell Boulevards** mark the south, where the neighborhood meets Forest Park. It is officially City Neighborhood #46, covers about 0.52 square miles, and sits within ZIP code 63112.

For most of the 1800s this was farmland. The land began as an eighteenth-century French colonial grant to Marie Louise Chouteau Papin and stayed largely in the Chouteau-Papin family into the late 19th century, kept rural in part because the unruly River Des Peres ran across it. That changed at the turn of the 20th century, when the **1904 World’s Fair** in adjacent Forest Park set off a streetcar-era building boom across the city’s west end.

The neighborhood is generally dated to 1908, and its private subdivisions went up in quick succession: **Parkview platted in 1905**, Washington Heights in 1907, and the Catlin Tract developed in 1909. Hamilton Elementary School opened in 1914, and three churches built in the 1910s — **Grace Methodist, New Cote Brilliante Baptist, and St. Roch Catholic** — still anchor the area today. The Parkview Historic District and the Catlin Tract preserve street after street of architecturally significant early-1900s houses, and Parkview is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

What put Skinker-DeBaliviere on the national map is its mid-1960s integration story. The neighborhood **became racially integrated in 1964**, and in **1966 residents formed the Skinker-DeBaliviere Community Council** to manage that transition on their own terms and resist the blockbusting and white flight that destabilized so many other St. Louis neighborhoods. The Council’s work is widely credited with keeping the area diverse and steady; the 2020 census still recorded a notably mixed community of about 3,899 residents. In **1978 the City designated the area a Local Historic District**.

The neighborhood’s edges are its biggest draw. **Forest Park** — the roughly 1,300-acre park that hosted the 1904 World’s Fair and is home to the St. Louis Zoo and the Art Museum — runs along the southern boundary, and **Washington University in St. Louis** and its Danforth Campus sit just southwest across the park. Along the northern Delmar Boulevard edge runs the **Delmar Loop**, one of the region’s liveliest dining, shopping, and live-music districts, which straddles the city and University City line.

Getting around is easy by St. Louis standards. Two MetroLink light-rail stations serve the area — the **Forest Park–DeBaliviere station** on the eastern side and the **Skinker station** on the west — putting downtown, the airport, and Washington University a short train ride away, while the Loop and the park are walkable from most blocks. The businesses below reflect that geography: a mix of long-running Loop venues and shops on Delmar, a few spots tucked strictly inside the neighborhood, and trusted service providers that serve residents here.

The Delmar Loop along the northern edge of Skinker-DeBaliviere. Photo: “Delmar Loop - Parkview Gardens Historic District” by Liezl Moss, licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Skinker-DeBaliviere shares the humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) of the wider St. Louis region. Summers are warm and humid, with average July highs near **89.6°F**, and the neighborhood’s mature tree canopy and the green expanse of neighboring Forest Park make the hot months noticeably more bearable. Spring and fall are mild and pleasant, though spring also brings the region’s severe-storm season, since the area sits within or near Tornado Alley and sees a real risk of thunderstorms and the occasional tornado. 

Winters are cold but generally manageable, with average January highs around **40.4°F** and roughly **16.6 inches** of snow a year against about **41.7 inches** of annual precipitation. The neighborhood’s solidly built early-1900s brick homes were made for this swing of seasons, and the local businesses below — from restaurants to salons to service providers — keep regular hours through summer heat and winter cold alike.

✓  Home to the 1779 Soulard Farmers Market — oldest west of the Mississippi ✓  St. Louis’s oldest neighborhood, NRHP-listed Soulard Historic District (1972) & Anheuser-Busch HQ ✓  Avg. rating: 4.8/5 across 10,202 reviews

## Soulard Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

Soulard, St. Louis

Soulard serves as St. Louis’s oldest neighborhood — founded in 1779 around the city’s third public marketplace, anchored by the Soulard Farmers Market (oldest west of the Mississippi, donated by Julia Cerré Soulard in 1841), the Anheuser-Busch Brewery (a National Historic Landmark since 1966), St. Vincent de Paul and St. John Nepomuk churches, and the Second Empire and Italianate “flounder house” row homes of the NRHP-listed Soulard Historic District — offering breweries, restaurants, blues bars, wedding venues, coffee, board games, and reputation management across the Russell, 12th, and 9th Street corridors.

Soulard is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods and one of **eight certified local historic districts** in the City of St. Louis, located at **38.6028° N, 90.2103° W** on the near south side of the city, just south of Downtown. The neighborhood’s triangular boundaries are defined by **Interstate 55** on the west and north, **7th Street** and **South Broadway** to the southeast, and the **Anheuser-Busch Brewery** complex extending south to Arsenal Street. Surrounding neighborhoods include **LaSalle Park** and **Lafayette Square** to the north (across I-55), **Benton Park West** to the west, and **Benton Park** and the Mississippi River to the south. The neighborhood sits within **ZIP code 63104**. Soulard is divided roughly by Lynch Street — north of which is mostly 19th-century brick row homes, Second Empire Victorians, Italianate town houses, Federal-style buildings, and the unique **“flounder houses”** (narrow homes built with only one slope to the roof) — while south of Lynch Street is largely the campus of **Anheuser-Busch** (the North American headquarters and St. Louis Brewery) and its surviving 19th-century brewery buildings.

The story of Soulard begins with the **founding of the Soulard Farmers Market in 1779** — a flat meadow where farmers from the surrounding French Creole village of St. Louis (founded 1764) came to sell fresh fruit, vegetables, dairy, and livestock. This was the **third public marketplace in St. Louis**, and the meadow lay on land that had been granted by the Spanish government to French merchant **Jean-Gabriel Cerré**. The neighborhood takes its name from Cerré’s son-in-law, **Antoine Pierre Soulard** — born in 1766 in Rochefort, France, a French aristocrat and former French naval officer who escaped the French Revolution and arrived in St. Louis around 1794. In **1795**, Antoine Soulard married **Julia Cerré**, and the couple received a **122-acre plot** of land that included the market grounds; additional land was given to Antoine by the Spanish colonial government as a gift for his service as **Surveyor of Upper Louisiana** under Governor Carlos de Hault de Lassus.

The **1803 Louisiana Purchase** threw the land grant into legal limbo, and following Antoine’s death in **1825**, his widow **Julia Cerré Soulard** fought a **thirty-year courtroom battle** to confirm the deed. She prevailed in **1836**, then began subdividing the land and selling lots — becoming the **first female real estate developer west of the Mississippi River**. Her most enduring gift came in **1841–1842**, when she donated **two city blocks** to the City of St. Louis with the stipulation that the land remain a public marketplace in perpetuity. Julia Soulard died in **1845**; the City formally acquired title in 1850. The first market building was constructed in **1843**, a one-story red brick structure; a second-story meeting hall was added in 1865. The original Soulard Market and many surrounding buildings were heavily damaged by the **Great St. Louis Tornado of May 27, 1896**. For more than three decades, vendors operated from temporary sheds and wagons until the **current Italian Renaissance Grand Hall** opened in **1929**, designed by City Architect **Albert E. Osburg** and modeled on Filippo Brunelleschi’s **Ospedale degli Innocenti** (Florentine Foundling Hospital, 1419).

During the mid-19th century, Soulard transformed from French Creole farmland into one of the most densely settled immigrant neighborhoods in St. Louis. The first wave was **French**; the much larger wave was **German** — particularly during the political upheavals of **1848** — followed by **Syrian, Hungarian, Croatian, Italian, Serbian, Irish, Slovak, and Czech** immigrants. The Eastern European population earned the area the nickname **“Bohemian Hill.”** The principal industry was **beer brewing**: Soulard hosted at least **half a dozen breweries**, including the **Green Tree Brewery** on Sidney Street, the **Excelsior Brewery** on Seventh Street, **Anthony & Kuhn’s Brewery** on Sidney Street, the **Lemp Brewery**, and **Eberhard Anheuser’s brewery** — which his son-in-law **Adolphus Busch** transformed into **Anheuser-Busch**. Most of these breweries sat atop a rumored cave system that runs along Sidney Street. By **Prohibition**, only Anheuser-Busch and Falstaff (formerly Lemp) survived. Notable 19th-century residents included **Max J. Feuerbacher**, **Dr. Franz Artzt**, **Thomas Allen**, **Adam Lemp**, and **Eberhard Anheuser**.

The **Anheuser-Busch Brewery** on Lynch Street, founded in the 1850s as Eberhard Anheuser’s Bavarian Brewery, transformed under **Adolphus Busch** from a small neighborhood brewery into a global icon. The campus — with its elaborate **red-brick German Romanesque buildings**, the original 1885 **Brew House**, the **Clydesdale Stables**, and the historic 19th-century buildings — was designated a **National Historic Landmark in 1966**. Today the brewery offers the **Budweiser Brewery Experience** with the Clydesdale VIP Experience, the Finisher Tour, and a 7-step brewing process tour. The famous **Clydesdale horses** — trademark of Anheuser-Busch since they were used to pull wagons of beer for Prohibition-repeal deliveries in 1933 — are regularly rotated in from the company’s farms near Grant’s Farm and Boonville. Beyond the brewery, the neighborhood is home to several **nineteenth-century church buildings**: **Saints Peter and Paul Catholic Church**, **St. Vincent de Paul Catholic Church** (built on land donated by Julia Soulard to Bishop Joseph Rosati), **St. John Nepomuk Czech Catholic Church** (the first Czech national church in the United States, founded 1854), and **Trinity Lutheran Church**.

In **1972**, the **Soulard Historic District** was placed on the **National Register of Historic Places** and became one of **eight certified local historic districts** in the City of St. Louis. The neighborhood is preserved by the **Soulard Restoration Group** and the **Soulard Business Association**, which publishes the neighborhood newspaper *The Soulard Renaissance*. The district is renowned for its surviving examples of **Greek Revival farmhouses**, **Federal Transitional**, **Federal**, **Italianate**, **Second Empire Victorian** (with characteristic **mansard roofs** inspired by 17th-century French architect François Mansart), and the uniquely St. Louis **flounder houses** — narrow brick homes with only one slope to the roof, built by working-class immigrants on long, narrow lots. The neighborhood is also known for its **Mardi Gras celebration**, the second-largest in the United States (behind New Orleans), the **world’s largest parade of costumed pets** (the Beggin’ Pet Parade), the annual **Oktoberfest**, and the blues / jazz scene that hosted barrelhouse blues piano player **James Crutchfield** from 1984 until his death in 2001.

Today, Soulard remains one of St. Louis’s most vibrant, walkable, and architecturally intact historic neighborhoods. The neighborhood’s key business anchors include the **Soulard Farmers Market** at 730 Carroll Street (140+ vendors, City Landmark 1971, open Wednesday through Saturday year-round), the **Budweiser Brewery Experience** at 1200 Lynch Street, the **Soulard Spice Shop** inside the market (Neighborhood Favorite 2023, 600–800 pounds of spices moved weekly), **Pieces Board Game Bar & Restaurant** at 2727 South 12th Street (1,200+ games), **Goshen Coffee Roasters** at 910 Geyer Avenue (Good Food Award winner), **The Franklin of Soulard** at 816 Allen Avenue (the 1905 wedding venue under Daniel and Christina Walsh), **Soulard Art Gallery** at 2028 South 12th Street (co-op under curator Earl Miller), **International Tap House** (iTap) at 1711 South 9th Street (40 beers on tap, 480+ bottles), **Soulard Market Lofts** at 1531 South 8th Street (managed by Sansone Group), **Unreview** at 1400 Russell Boulevard (reputation management SaaS), the **Pontiac Square Park** (1.50 acres, 1908), the **Soulard Market Park** (1.94 acres, 1908), and dozens of independent restaurants, blues bars, microbreweries, and boutiques.

Image: Soulard Farmers Market — the oldest farmers’ market west of the Mississippi River, founded 1779, donated to the City of St. Louis by Julia Cerré Soulard in 1841. The 1929 Italian Renaissance Grand Hall by City Architect Albert E. Osburg was modeled on Brunelleschi’s 1419 Ospedale degli Innocenti in Florence and designated a St. Louis City Landmark in 1971 — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA

Soulard sits one mile south of Downtown St. Louis at 38.6028° N along the Mississippi River, with seamless access to Interstate 55 (the western boundary), South Broadway (the eastern boundary along the river), the **Anheuser-Busch Brewery** complex (the southern boundary), Lafayette Square and LaSalle Park to the north, and Benton Park and Cherokee Street to the south. 

The neighborhood experiences St. Louis’s full humid continental climate: hot, humid summers, cold winters, and an active spring severe weather season — punctuated historically by the **Great St. Louis Tornado of May 27, 1896**. Peak outdoor activity falls during late winter, spring, summer, and fall, when the **Soulard Farmers Market** (open Wednesday through Saturday year-round, with Saturday morning crowds of 10,000+) draws shoppers from across the bi-state region; when the **Budweiser Brewery Experience** and **Clydesdale Stables** host daily tours; when **Pontiac Square Park** (1.50 acres, 1908), **Soulard Market Park** (1.94 acres, 1908), and the two neighborhood **dog parks** draw residents; when the annual **Mardi Gras** celebration (the second-largest in the United States with the Beggin’ Pet Parade) takes over the streets each February or March; when **Oktoberfest** arrives in autumn; and when the year-round blues / jazz scene fills the patios of **1860 Saloon**, **Molly’s in Soulard**, **The Shanti**, **Hammerstone’s**, and **McGurk’s**. 

Cool seasons drive intense indoor activity at **International Tap House** on South 9th, **Goshen Coffee Roasters** on Geyer, **Pieces Board Game Bar & Restaurant** on South 12th, **The Franklin of Soulard** on Allen, **Soulard Spice Shop**, **Soulard Art Gallery**, **Soulard Market Lofts**, **Unreview**, and the indoor venues of the 1929 Soulard Market Grand Hall, the Anheuser-Busch Brewery’s 19th-century buildings (including the 1885 Brew House), and the historic 19th-century churches (Saints Peter and Paul, St. Vincent de Paul, St. John Nepomuk, Trinity Lutheran). The neighborhood’s 1830s–1890s housing stock — Federal-style row homes, Greek Revival farmhouses, Italianate town houses, Second Empire Victorians with mansard roofs, and unique flounder houses — has weathered more than 180 years of Missouri climate with the durability of the French Creole, German, and Bohemian masons who built them.

Southampton Neighborhood Guide – St. Louis History & Businesses

Southampton serves as one of St. Louis's most architecturally distinctive 1905–1930s English-named streetcar subdivisions — anchored by the Macklind Avenue Business District, the 1939 Hampton Village shopping center (one of the first U.S. strip centers), St. Mary Magdalen Catholic Church (1927), and the "Hansel and Gretel," Neo-Tudor, and Arts & Crafts bungalows that define the "SoHa" skyline — offering custom apparel, candles, recording, wine, title insurance, and consulting across the Hampton and Macklind corridors.

Southampton Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

Southampton, St. Louis

Southampton serves as one of St. Louis’s most architecturally distinctive 1905–1930s English-named streetcar subdivisions — platted by an Anglophile developer who named the streets after Devonshire, Lansdowne, Nottingham, and Sutherland — anchored by the Macklind Avenue Business District, the 1939 Hampton Village shopping center, St. Mary Magdalen Catholic Church (1927), the Hope Lutheran Church, the Buder Branch Library, and the “Hansel and Gretel,” Neo-Tudor, Arts & Crafts, and American Foursquare bungalow homes that define the SoHa skyline — offering custom apparel, candles, recording, wine, title insurance, and community services across the Hampton, Chippewa, Macklind, and Kingshighway corridors.

Southampton is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at 38.5869° N, 90.2842° W in southwest St. Louis City. The neighborhood’s boundaries are Chippewa Street (Missouri Route 366, formerly U.S. Route 66) on the north, Hampton Avenue on the west, Eichelberger Street on the south, and South Kingshighway Boulevard on the east. The neighborhood occupies approximately 0.7 square miles and is home to roughly 6,647 residents (2020 census) in 3,718 housing units, making it one of the densest neighborhoods in the city at 9,500 people per square mile. Southampton sits within ZIP code 63109 in the 5th Ward of the City of St. Louis (currently represented by Alderman Matt Devoti). Surrounding neighborhoods include Lindenwood Park to the west across Hampton, St. Louis Hills to the south and southwest, Bevo Mill to the southeast across Kingshighway, Tower Grove South to the northeast, and Northampton to the north across Chippewa. The neighborhood is locally nicknamed “SoHa” (a portmanteau of South Hampton) and is one of the few St. Louis neighborhoods that gained population from 1990 to 2000.

The land that became Southampton was, through the 19th century, a mixture of farms and country estates that remained rural in character despite the conversion of the Christy Estate to the east into clay mines. Everard Horton’s farm occupied most of present-day Southampton, and Devonshire Avenue is named after his original hometown in England. Most of the remainder of the neighborhood was assembled from the Decker Farm, which was acquired and developed by the Mercantile Trust Company. The Mercantile Trust’s superintendent, identified in local histories as Mr. Sihrett, supervised the building of the subdivision and named it “Southampton” after a town in his native England. Many of Southampton’s streets were given the same English (and one Scottish) treatment: Nottingham, Hampton, Devonshire, Lansdowne, Murdoch, Sutherland, Brannon, and Macklind. Other streets carry names of local significance — Bancroft (for historian George Bancroft), Brannon (for landowners Thomas and Louisa Brannon), Delor (for Carondelet’s founder Clement Delor de Treget), and Wherry Avenue, which cuts the neighborhood diagonally on the former path of a creek of the same name.

Early Southampton residents carried water to their homes from a spring at Nottingham and Kingshighway until a water main was constructed. The neighborhood was actually one of several locations considered as a possible site for the 1904 World’s Fair, but it was determined to be almost impossible to run adequate transportation facilities to the Southampton area, and the fair was instead held at Forest Park. Residential development took off with the extension of the streetcar lines. The #50 Southampton streetcar line was established in 1889 as an east-west route between Third & Washington downtown and Macklind & Devonshire, and the #21 Tower Grove line began operating in 1890. The intersection of Macklind and Devonshire became the loop where the Southampton line terminated, and a small business strip and subdivision platting grew up around it. The first homes in the neighborhood were built around 1905–1915, but the great majority of Southampton’s housing stock was constructed in the 1920s and 1930s. Original residents reported that the typical brick Arts & Crafts home took about one year to build.

Southampton’s residential housing stock is one of the most architecturally distinctive collections in St. Louis, defined by brick and stone homes built in styles that include “Hansel and Gretel” Storybook cottages (with gingerbread trim and whimsical storybook detailing), Neo-Tudor revival cottages, Arts & Crafts bungalows, American Foursquare houses, and a small but distinctive collection of Prairie School and Colonial Revival homes. The neighborhood’s 1920s–1930s “Hansel and Gretel” houses, with their steeply pitched roofs, fairy-tale rooflines, and asymmetric stone-and-brick facades, are widely recognized as among the finest concentrations of Storybook-style residential architecture in the Midwest. Southampton also contains the only alley in the City of St. Louis divided by a median — running one block between Chippewa Street and Winona Avenue from Macklind to Brannon avenues, with the median once part of the track for a privately owned rail line.

The neighborhood was historically populated by German immigrants and their descendants in the early 20th century, and was traditionally home to a large number of St. Louis firefighters and police officers as a result of the city’s long-standing residency requirement for employees. Since the 1990s, a new generation of younger residents, artists, and craftsmen has moved into the neighborhood, helping drive a steady increase in property values after 2003. Southampton’s commercial life centers on three corridors: the Macklind Avenue Business District running through the heart of the neighborhood from Devonshire Avenue to Eichelberger Street (a streetcar-era walkable strip of restaurants, delis, bakeries, candle shops, recording studios, the SOHA Gallery, and the Southampton Community Garden); the perimeter Hampton Avenue commercial corridor on the west; the Chippewa Street corridor on the north (the historic Route 66); and the South Kingshighway Boulevard corridor on the east. The neighborhood’s post-war commercial centerpiece is Hampton Village, opened in 1939 at Hampton & Chippewa as one of the first dedicated strip shopping centers in the United States, with off-street parking and one-stop colonial-style retail buildings later expanded into today’s Hampton Village Plaza anchored by Schnucks.

Southampton’s religious life is anchored by several historic congregations: St. Mary Magdalen Catholic Church on South Kingshighway at Bancroft Avenue (the Romanesque Italian-basilica-style church at 5831 South Kingshighway designed by architect Adolph F. Stauder and dedicated February 12, 1927, with its narthex, clerestory, campanile, colonnaded front portico, mosaic altar, and dome, founded in 1919 from a portion of Our Lady of Sorrows parish by Father John J. Thompson to serve the rapidly growing Southampton area); Our Lady of Sorrows Catholic Church on Rhodes Avenue at South Kingshighway (whose parish boundaries cover the southeast portion of the neighborhood); Hope Lutheran Church on Neosho Street (founded 1907); and Kingshighway Baptist Church at South Kingshighway and Eichelberger. The public elementary school serving the neighborhood is Buder Elementary School, named for early-20th-century St. Louis attorney G. A. Buder, and the Buder Branch Library sits on Hampton just south of Chippewa. The Southampton Neighborhood Association (southamptonstl.org), a 501(c)(4) organization established in 1903, coordinates the neighborhood’s legislative advocacy, annual events, landscape committee, and the popular Macklind Days annual street festival.

Today, Southampton is a vibrant residential neighborhood of more than 6,600 residents, with its commercial life concentrated on the Macklind Avenue Business District (anchored by businesses including the Southampton Neighborhood Association headquarters at 5011–5099 Wherry Avenue, Sunburst Logo LLC at 5249 Neosho Street, the Urban Candle Company at 4920 Hampton Avenue, the Red Pill Recording Studio at 4710 Hampton Avenue, the Southampton Community Garden at 4915 Macklind Avenue next door to SOHA Gallery, the Spirit Wine & Craft bottle shop at 5760 Chippewa Street (the 40-year offshoot of The Wine & Cheese Place), Absolute Title Company at 4706 Hampton Avenue (50+ years), and the St. Louis Small Business Monthly publication serving the surrounding South City entrepreneurial community). With its dense walkable streetscape, the only median-divided alley in the city, the 1939 Hampton Village shopping center, the 1927 St. Mary Magdalen church, and the Macklind Days festival, Southampton remains one of the most desirable urban neighborhoods in southwest St. Louis.

Southampton sits about nine miles southwest of Downtown St. Louis at 38.5869° N along the Hampton / Chippewa / Kingshighway / Eichelberger corridor, with seamless access to Forest Park, the Missouri Botanical Garden, Grant’s Farm, Tower Grove Park, Carondelet Park, St. Louis Hills, Bevo Mill, and the broader southwest St. Louis market. The neighborhood experiences St. Louis’s full humid continental climate with hot, humid summers, cold winters, and an active spring severe weather season.

Peak outdoor activity falls during spring, summer, and fall, when the Macklind Avenue Business District hosts the annual Macklind Days street festival, the Southampton Community Garden at 4915 Macklind draws gardeners alongside SOHA Gallery First Fridays, the Southampton Neighborhood Association hosts events at Hope Lutheran, and Hampton Village handles peak retail traffic. Cool seasons drive intense indoor activity at Sunburst Logo LLC, Urban Candle Company, Red Pill Recording Studio, Spirit Wine & Craft, Absolute Title Company, Slalom Consulting in nearby Clayton, the Southwest Area Chamber of Commerce, the St. Louis Small Business Monthly, and the indoor venues of St. Mary Magdalen, Our Lady of Sorrows, Hope Lutheran, Kingshighway Baptist, the Buder Branch Library, and the restaurants and delis lining Macklind. The 1905–1930s housing stock — Storybook cottages, Neo-Tudor revivals, Arts & Crafts bungalows, American Foursquares, and brick-and-stone middle-class homes — has weathered more than a century of Missouri climate with the durability of the German immigrant masons who built them.

Southwest Garden Neighborhood Guide – St. Louis History & Businesses

Southwest Garden Businesses & Neighborhood Guide | St Louis Near Me Directory

Southwest Garden, St. Louis

Southwest Garden serves as one of St. Louis’s most architecturally rich neighborhoods — named for its proximity to Henry Shaw’s 1859-founded Missouri Botanical Garden, anchored by two National Register Historic Districts (Shaw’s Garden and Reber Place), the 1960 Climatron geodesic dome, Tower Grove Park, the 1869 William Rumbold-designed cast-iron-domed former St. Louis Lunatic Asylum, and Sublette Park — offering chamber-of-commerce networking, botanical research, gasket manufacturing, accounting, home decor, direct mail, and neighborhood-association services across the I-44, Kingshighway, and Shaw Boulevard corridors.

Southwest Garden is one of St. Louis’s 79 official neighborhoods, located at 38.6115° N, 90.2837° W in southwest St. Louis City and bisected by Kingshighway Boulevard, one of the city’s major arterial roads. The neighborhood’s boundaries follow the City of St. Louis Planning & Urban Design Agency map: I-44 (Interstate Highway 44) on the northeast, the Missouri Botanical Garden and Tower Grove Park on the east, Scanlan Avenue and Connecticut Street on the south, Hampton Avenue on the west, and a jagged northwestern boundary that follows Columbia Avenue, Southwest Avenue, and South Kingshighway. The neighborhood occupies approximately 0.86 square miles and is home to roughly 5,245 residents (2020 census) at a density of 6,100 people per square mile. Southwest Garden spans ZIP codes 63110 and 63139 and sits in the 5th Ward of the City of St. Louis (currently represented by Alderman Matt Devoti). Surrounding neighborhoods include The Hill and Forest Park Southeast to the north, the Missouri Botanical Garden and Tower Grove Park (and the Shaw neighborhood beyond them) to the east, Lindenwood Park and Clifton Heights to the west, and North Hampton to the south. Vandeventer and Southwest Avenues span the neighborhood and follow the route of Old Manchester Road — the first public road from St. Louis to Jefferson City and an extension of Market Street that was the only way west without crossing the Missouri or Meramec Rivers.

The land that became Southwest Garden was first divided into agricultural arpents in 1769 by Illinois Country French settlers, who established the Prairie des Noyers Commons — a large tract of communal agricultural land between Grand Avenue and Kingshighway Boulevard. Through the 18th and early 19th centuries, French farmers worked these arpents until advancing urbanization led to gradual sales of combined parcels to private landowners. One of these owners would profoundly shape the future of the neighborhood: Henry Shaw (1800–1889), an English-born St. Louis merchant who arrived in 1819 at age 19, made his fortune in hardware and real estate, and retired at age 39. On an 1851 journey to England, Shaw visited the impressive gardens of Chatsworth House in Derbyshire and returned to St. Louis determined to dedicate part of his land holdings to creating a garden worthy of the city’s future greatness. Shaw’s holdings eventually encompassed the modern-day Missouri Botanical Garden and most of the land between modern Tower Grove Park and Vandeventer Avenue.

The Missouri Botanical Garden — long known informally as “Shaw’s Garden” — opened to the public in 1859 at 4344 Shaw Boulevard, transforming a former treeless prairie into one of the great botanical institutions of the world. Shaw bequeathed the adjacent 289 acres of his prairie estate to the City of St. Louis in 1868 as Tower Grove Park, with the stipulation that it would forever remain a park — today the only municipal park in Missouri on the National Register of Historic Places, governed independently of the City Parks Department per Shaw’s will. The Garden bequest spurred the subdivision of nearby tracts, including Tower Grove Place between Kingshighway and Alfred Avenue in 1870, and the “Tower Grove Park Addition” developed slowly over the following three decades due to poor access to the streetcar system (the nearest line ran across Tower Grove Park on Arsenal Street). In 1897, the Missouri Street Railroad Company constructed a new streetcar line to Southampton extending down Vandeventer Avenue and Kingshighway, dramatically increasing the viability of residential development east of Kingshighway.

The neighborhood’s definitive period of architectural development came in the 1910s through the 1950s, under the visionary leadership of Missouri Botanical Garden director George T. Moore (appointed 1912) and chief landscape architect John Noyes (appointed 1915). Moore decided that rather than simply selling off the large land holdings bequeathed to the Garden by Henry Shaw to outside investors, the Garden itself would plat new subdivisions using Noyes’ landscape vision — ensuring that the surrounding neighborhoods would complement the Garden’s aesthetic and the new homes would enhance the Garden setting. The first plat, the “Shaw’s Vandeventer Avenue Addition” north of the Garden (along present-day Interstate 44), was completed in 1916. The larger trapezoidal tract west of the Garden required more substantial planning, and Noyes — following subdivision principles advanced by renowned landscape architect Henry Wright — designed a curved street grid that conformed to the tract’s irregular borders. The resulting “Shaw’s Garden Subdivision”, platted starting in 1922, was fully developed by third-party builders by the end of the 1920s and embodies progressive concepts in suburban planning rarely realized within the city limits of St. Louis. Two private places — Gurney Court and Heger Court — were established by independent developers in the early 1920s along Magnolia Avenue, each containing single-family homes centered around a landscaped court.

Southwest Garden contains two National Register Historic Districts that define its architectural character. The Shaw’s Garden Historic District, listed on February 22, 2012, encompasses approximately 18 city blocks roughly bounded by DeTonty Avenue, Tower Grove Avenue, Shaw Avenue, Alfred Avenue, Magnolia Avenue, Kingshighway Boulevard, and Vandeventer Avenue — built out largely between 1916 and 1955 as a cohesive streetcar-served neighborhood with an exceptionally intact collection of red-brick masonry duplexes and fourplexes from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, mature street trees, defined tree lawns, and landscaped front yards that visually extend the horticultural principles of the adjacent Missouri Botanical Garden and Tower Grove Park. The Reber Place Historic District, listed earlier the same year, sits directly west of Tower Grove Park and contains a diverse mix of frame homes, multifamily buildings, and bungalows from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Notable architectural styles across Southwest Garden include late 19th-century multifamily duplexes and fourplexes, 1920s American Movements-style duplexes along Shenandoah Avenue with Craftsman-influenced exposed rafters and built-in cabinetry, Queen Anne and Second Empire homes with asymmetrical facades and mansard roofs, Arts & Crafts bungalows, and shotgun houses.

West of Kingshighway, Southwest Garden has a history that closely parallels its neighbor The Hill. After the “Great Fire” of 1849 destroyed fifteen city blocks of St. Louis, a municipal ordinance banning frame construction put a premium on brick. The demand spurred the development of clay deposits discovered west of Kingshighway in the 1830s, including the nearby Russell and Christy coal and clay mines. As the mines attracted immigrant labor in the late 1800s, Italian workers settled in The Hill and German workers settled between The Hill and Arsenal Street, forming St. Aloysius Gonzaga parish in 1892 at Magnolia and January Avenues (razed 2006). This German community built the frame shotgun houses, flats, and block-wide masonry buildings around present-day Sublette Park. Sublette Park is set on the highest point of the City of St. Louis and offers views of the Downtown skyline; it includes a playground, a pavilion built by the Boy Scouts of America, tennis courts, and a soccer field. Also on the highest point of the city is the St. Louis Psychiatric Rehabilitation Center (formerly the St. Louis County Lunatic Asylum), a 196-bed psychiatric hospital on a 32-acre campus on Arsenal Street, including the William Rumbold-designed 1869 Romanesque Revival building topped by a prominent 200-foot cast iron dome visible from up to 30 miles away.

Today, Southwest Garden remains one of St. Louis’s most park-adjacent and architecturally distinctive neighborhoods. The Missouri Botanical Garden draws roughly a million visitors a year to its 79-acre grounds, 1960 Climatron geodesic dome (the world’s first completely air-conditioned greenhouse, designed by St. Louis architects Murphy and Mackey based on R. Buckminster Fuller’s principles, designated a National Historic Landmark in 1976), the Peter H. Raven Library (containing 85% of all literature ever published on systematic botany), the Japanese Garden, the Gladney and Lehmann Rose Gardens, the Tower Grove House, and the seasonal Garden Glow event. Local businesses in the neighborhood include the Southwest Area Chamber of Commerce, the Missouri Botanical Garden Library / Raven Library at 4500 Shaw Boulevard, the manufacturing firm Fairlane Industries Inc at 5033 Southwest Avenue, the long-standing accounting firm Mid-City Accounting Services, LLC at 5701 Southwest Avenue, the boutique Garden District STL, the 35-year direct-mail logistics firm Presort Inc. at 5051 Southwest Avenue, and the Southwest Garden Neighborhood Association at 4950 Southwest Avenue. With Sublette Park, the Kingshighway Branch Library on South Vandeventer Avenue, the South City YMCA, Central Visual and Performing Arts High School, and the Cleveland Naval Junior ROTC Academy serving residents, Southwest Garden offers a rare combination of cultural-landmark proximity and walkable streetcar-era residential character.

Southwest Garden sits about six miles southwest of Downtown St. Louis at 38.6115° N along the I-44 / Kingshighway / Hampton / Shaw Boulevard corridor, with seamless access to The Hill, Forest Park Southeast and Cortex (north), Forest Park (two miles north on Kingshighway), Tower Grove Park (east), and the Shaw, Tower Grove South, Lindenwood Park, Clifton Heights, Bevo Mill, Southampton, and North Hampton neighborhoods.

The neighborhood experiences St. Louis’s full humid continental climate with hot, humid summers, cold winters, and an active spring severe weather season. Peak outdoor activity falls during spring, summer, and fall, when the Missouri Botanical Garden draws its largest crowds for the Japanese Festival, Chinese Culture Days, and the autumn Garden Glow; when Tower Grove Park hosts the Festival of Nations and its weekly farmers market; when Sublette Park sees its peak playground, tennis, and soccer activity; and when the curving streets of the Shaw’s Garden Historic District fill with strollers and dog-walkers admiring the red-brick duplexes and fourplexes.

Cool seasons drive intense indoor activity at the Missouri Botanical Garden Climatron, the Raven Library at 4500 Shaw Boulevard, Mid-City Accounting Services at 5701 Southwest Avenue, Presort Inc. at 5051 Southwest Avenue, Fairlane Industries Inc at 5033 Southwest Avenue, Garden District STL at the City Foundry, the Southwest Area Chamber of Commerce, the Southwest Garden Neighborhood Association at 4950 Southwest Avenue, the Kingshighway Branch Library, the South City YMCA, Central Visual and Performing Arts High School, Cleveland NJROTC High School, and the dozens of restaurants and shops along the Southwest Avenue and Kingshighway corridors. The neighborhood’s 1869 William Rumbold cast-iron dome and 1960 Climatron geodesic dome — visible from up to 30 miles away — have weathered more than 150 years of Missouri climate.
