### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Where is the best place to buy auto parts?

A.  Depends on the part, not on loyalty. Chain counters win on common fast-movers, free testing and a warranty on file. Independent parts houses win on odd applications and professional-grade lines. Salvage yards win on panels, glass, trim, wheels and modules the aftermarket copies badly.

### Q. Where can I buy real OEM parts?

A.  A dealer parts counter sells the part the factory installed, often on a shorter warranty than people expect: 12 months on genuine Toyota, 24 on GM Genuine and ACDelco OE. A salvage yard sells the same factory stamping secondhand.

### Q. Do I get the core charge back if I throw the old part away?

A.  No. The deposit only comes back when you hand over a rebuildable core — same part type, reasonably complete, not cracked or crushed. NAPA lists 30 days as the standard window. Drain the fluids, put the old unit in the new one’s box, and bring the receipt. If a shop did the install, the core usually goes back with them.

### Q. Does using aftermarket parts void my car warranty?

A.  Not on its own. The federal Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act bars a manufacturer from voiding your warranty just because you used an aftermarket or recycled part. To deny a claim, they must show that the specific part caused the failure. The FTC enforced this in 2018 with warning letters to major automakers over warranty language implying otherwise.

### Q. Will an auto parts store clear my check engine light?

A.  Policies vary, and around St. Louis you may not want them to. Clearing codes wipes your readiness monitors, and vehicles registered in St. Louis City, St. Louis County, St. Charles County or Jefferson County are tested under the Gateway program. On 2001 and newer gas vehicles only one incomplete monitor is allowed, so a fresh clear can mean many miles of driving before you can pass.

### Q. Where can I find used auto parts in Saint Louis, Missouri?

A.  At licensed salvage yards on both sides of the metro. Call with the Hollander interchange number and ask for the ARA grade and damage code. Buy the cosmetic parts used; buy brake friction, airbags and seat belt components new.

### Q. Are there any junkyards in Missouri?

A.  Plenty, and the licensed ones are nothing like the word suggests — a modern yard runs a searchable, graded inventory. Missouri licenses used parts and salvage dealers through the Department of Revenue under RSMo 301.218; Illinois licenses recyclers through the Secretary of State.

### Q. Which lasts longer, a remanufactured alternator or a new aftermarket one?

A.  It depends on the process, not the label. A properly remanufactured unit is stripped, measured and rebuilt with every wear component replaced to meet or beat the original specification, which can outlast a budget new unit. A rebuilt part only gets its worn or broken pieces swapped. Ask which one you’re buying, then compare warranty terms.

### Q. Does my car need a safety inspection in Missouri or Illinois?

A.  Illinois has no safety inspection for passenger cars; parts of Madison, Monroe and St. Clair counties require an emissions test every two years by ZIP code. Missouri requires a biennial safety inspection once a vehicle passes ten model years old or 150,000 miles. In 2026 a 2016 is in its final exempt year and a 2015 is due.

### Q. Can I borrow tools instead of buying them?

A.  Yes, and it costs nothing if you return them. O’Reilly’s Loaner Tool Program covers over 80 specialty tools with a deposit equal to the tool’s value, refunded in full on return with no rental fee. AutoZone’s Loan-A-Tool runs the same way on a 90-day clock, after which the deposit becomes the purchase.

## What a Car Wash Costs in St. Louis, and When the Monthly Plan Pays Off
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/car-wash-cost-st-louis-monthly-membership

Imagine it’s the first Saturday in February and the sun finally shows up. You back down the driveway in Affton and there it is in the flat winter light — a chalky gray film up the rocker panels, salt packed into the wheel wells, paint that was navy in November and is now the color of a dirty nickel.

Maybe your version is a school run in Florissant, where the back doors have gone the shade of sidewalk concrete. Or a Belleville commute that left a tide line across the tailgate. Or a lot in St. Charles where you can read the exact height the slush reached.

Then the arithmetic starts. Twelve dollars right now? Twenty-five a month for as many washes as you want? Or wait for spring and hope whatever is happening underneath isn’t happening fast. That last one is the expensive answer, and the one most of us pick.

### What does a car wash cost in the St. Louis metro?

A single trip through an express exterior tunnel here generally runs about $10 to $20. Unlimited monthly plans posted by St. Louis-area operators in August 2026 ran from roughly $25 a month for a basic exterior plan up to about $45 for a top exterior tier, while full-service unlimited plans — the ones including a vacuum and interior wipe-down — ran about $55 to $75.

Three things move those numbers: vehicle size, tier, and whether a human touches the car. The top tier usually bundles a ceramic or graphene sealant, tire shine, and the underbody spray. Introductory pricing is everywhere — first-month rates in the high teens against a regular rate near $50 showed up on more than one metro price page this summer — so read what a plan renews at, not what it starts at.

### Are unlimited car wash plans worth it here?

Divide the monthly plan price by the single-wash price and you have your break-even. A $25 exterior plan against a $12 single wash pays off on wash number three. A $45 top-tier plan against a $20 single wash also pays off near the third visit. A $65 full-service plan needs four or five visits a month before it beats paying as you go.

The honest question isn’t how many washes you could take. It’s how many you actually take, and most people overestimate. Professional Carwashing & Detailing reported on March 30, 2026 that 2025 industry averages ran near 4.1% voluntary cancellations a month plus about 3.6% involuntary ones from failed cards — roughly 7.6% combined, which works out to an average member lasting 14 or 15 months.

Here is the local wrinkle. A St. Louis winter is when a plan earns its keep; summer is when it quietly doesn’t. Drive salted roads five days a week from December through March and four washes a month is realistic. Let the car sit in a Kirkwood driveway and you are paying for something you use twice. Some operators price-lock your rate while you stay enrolled, so canceling in June can cost you that rate in December. Ask before you sign.

### Is it good to get a car wash every month through a Missouri or Illinois winter?

Consumer Reports, in guidance updated February 13, 2026, advises a monthly car wash during snow season and more often when a vehicle is visibly coated in salt, and specifically recommends a touchless wash that includes the undercarriage. In the St. Louis metro, treat monthly as the floor rather than the target. Twice a month through an active stretch is closer to right.

The reason is the temperature pattern, not the snow total. St. Louis averages about 16.6 inches of snow a year at Lambert on the 1991 to 2020 normals. But the city sees roughly 85 days a year that drop to 32 degrees or below, and only about 19 that never climb back above freezing. Subtract, and you get about 66 days a winter when the car freezes overnight and thaws by afternoon. Dry salt on steel does very little; salt in solution, above freezing, in damp air is what eats brake lines and rocker panels.

The chloride volume is not small either. MoDOT keeps more than 30,000 tons of salt on hand for the St. Louis region, with over 200 plow trucks and more than 400 employees covering 6,400 lane miles of state routes. The City of St. Louis plans on 6,000 to 7,000 tons in an average winter and went through 12,000 tons in January 2025 alone. Across the river, IDOT entered the 2025-26 season with more than 542,000 tons stockpiled statewide and over 1,900 trucks for almost 45,000 lane miles, after spreading more than 312,000 tons the winter before.

The two states also treat roads differently. MoDOT and St. Louis County pretreat highways with brine ahead of a storm. IDOT deliberately does not pretreat in the Metro East, so its crews can run longer routes without stopping to reload chemicals, an operations engineer told St. Louis Public Radio in January 2026. A Chesterfield commuter drives on chloride before the first flake lands; a Belleville commuter picks it up during and after. Both of you carry it home.

Unrelated, obviously — a good hair salon is harder to find than clean paint.

### Is the undercarriage wash worth the upcharge?

Between December and March, yes. The underbody spray is the one add-on aimed at where the damage actually happens: frame rails, brake and fuel lines, exhaust hangers, suspension mounts. Consumer Reports calls it an added charge but a worthwhile upgrade for removing salt. Outside that window it’s optional unless you’ve been on gravel or through mud.

Two limits. A rinse is not rustproofing — it removes what it can reach and nothing else, and the magnesium and calcium chloride blends in modern road treatments mist upward under a vehicle and cling. Timing matters too: running the underbody spray at 20 degrees can leave water sitting in door seals, locks, and the parking brake cable. Wash on the thaw day, not during the storm.

Skip the driveway in winter. The Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District asks people to wash vehicles at a commercial facility that sends its water to treatment and to keep pavement wash water out of storm drain inlets. Their phrase is “only rain to the storm drain.”

### Touchless, soft-touch, or hand wash — what does each cost your paint?

Touchless washes cannot swirl your clear coat, because nothing physically contacts the paint. They compensate with stronger alkaline and acidic chemistry, and that chemistry strips wax and sealant faster. Soft-touch washes, using foam or cloth, pull road film off far better. Their swirl risk depends almost entirely on how well the operator cleans and rinses the material between cars.

The practical version is duller than the online argument. A well-kept soft-touch tunnel with fresh closed-cell foam and a working pre-soak arch is fine for a daily driver; a neglected one with grit trapped in the material is not. You can tell from the lot.

Hand washing is the gentlest method with two buckets and a grit guard, and the most damaging with one bucket and a sponge that hit the ground once. Dark paint on a car you love argues for touchless through winter and a careful hand wash in spring. A white crossover fighting construction traffic through Maryland Heights? Soft-touch every ten days is perfectly rational.

### What does a detail cost in St. Louis compared with a wash?

St. Louis detail shops publish full interior-and-exterior packages in the range of roughly $275 to $400 as of 2026, with interior-only packages commonly starting near $120 to $150 and exterior-only details around $125. A $25-a-month exterior wash plan costs $300 across a year. One detail and one year of washing land in about the same place.

They are not substitutes. Detailing corrects and protects: paint decontamination, machine polishing that removes swirls instead of hiding them, a sealant or coating, and an interior deep clean that lifts the white salt rings out of the carpet. Washing removes the material causing the damage. Wash steadily through salt season, then book one detail when spring settles in.

### What does skipping the wash actually cost?

AAA put the national bill at roughly $3 billion a year in rust repairs caused by road salt and de-icers — $15.4 billion over five years, at an average of about $490 per repair. Those figures date to 2017 and have not gotten cheaper. A single corroded brake line commonly runs $180 to $560 to replace; several corroded hard lines can run $700 to $1,500.

Missouri gives you one more reason to care. Once a vehicle passes its tenth model year or 150,000 miles, the state requires a safety inspection every two years, and the checklist covers brake lines and hoses, the exhaust system, and suspension components — the parts salt reaches first. The Missouri State Highway Patrol caps that inspection at $12. The Department of Revenue confirmed on January 6, 2026 that the requirement had not changed, after bad information circulated saying it was repealed.

Illinois works differently. There is no periodic safety inspection for ordinary passenger cars there; IDOT’s vehicle compliance program covers second-division vehicles, school buses, and heavy diesels. Metro East drivers in Madison, Monroe, and St. Clair counties get biennial emissions testing instead, and an emissions test never looks at a brake line. Live in Belleville or Edwardsville and nothing in the registration cycle catches corrosion for you.

### What this business looks like from the other side of the counter

An express tunnel is a capital business wearing a service business’s clothes. Industry feasibility work published in June 2026 puts a full project between $3.85 million and over $10 million, clustering around $5 to $7 million with land. Average ticket sits near $12 to $14, so a site lives or dies on volume — roughly 250 to 400 cars a day on a decent corridor. Labor and chemicals together eat about 28% of revenue, and a water reclaim system saves on the order of 75 cents a car, trivial until you multiply it by 100,000 cars. That math is why the trade moved to memberships: unlimited plans now make up 70% to 80% of wash sales at scaled operators, and the largest US chain reported 79% in the fourth quarter of 2025. Churn near 7.6% a month means refilling a twelfth of the member base forever. And a mild, dry winter is simply a bad year.

Which is where local search does real work: when somebody in Kirkwood or Granite City types a category and a town at 8 a.m., the operator whose hours, address, and services are filled in gets that visit, and being listed and complete is the cheap part of the equation.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much does a car wash cost in St. Louis?

A.  A single pass through an express exterior tunnel in the metro generally runs about $10 to $20, depending on the tier and the size of the vehicle. Self-serve bays cost less if you spend the time. Full-service washes with an interior vacuum cost more, and large trucks and SUVs usually carry a small surcharge.

### Q. Are unlimited car wash plans worth it?

A.  Divide the monthly price by the single-wash price. A $25 exterior plan against a $12 wash pays for itself on the third visit of the month. Metro exterior plans posted in August 2026 ran roughly $25 to $45, full-service plans roughly $55 to $75. Drive salted roads daily through winter and the math works easily.

### Q. Are unlimited car washes actually unlimited?

A.  The wash count generally is — that is what the plan sells. The price often isn’t. Introductory rates in the high teens against regular rates near $50 turned up on more than one metro price page this summer, so the number that matters is what a plan renews at, and some operators hold your rate only while you stay enrolled.

### Q. Is it good to get a car wash every month?

A.  Yes, and through a St. Louis winter monthly is the floor rather than the target. Consumer Reports advises at least monthly through snow season, more often when the car is visibly coated. St. Louis sees roughly 85 days a year at or below freezing but only about 19 that stay frozen all day, leaving about 66 thaw days — the wet, above-freezing conditions in which road salt corrodes fastest.

### Q. Does an undercarriage car wash really remove road salt?

A.  It removes a great deal of it, which is why it is the add-on worth paying for from December through March. It is not rustproofing. Underbody sprays reach frame rails, brake lines, and exhaust parts, but the chloride blends in modern road treatments mist upward and cling. Pick a day above freezing so nothing refreezes in the locks.

### Q. Is a touchless car wash better for my paint than a brush wash?

A.  Touchless cannot cause swirl marks, since nothing contacts the paint, but it compensates with harsher alkaline and acidic chemistry that strips wax and sealant faster. Soft-touch removes road film more effectively and is safe where the operator keeps the cloth clean and the pre-soak working. Poor maintenance causes swirls, not the method.

### Q. How much does a full car detail cost in St. Louis?

A.  St. Louis shops publish full interior-and-exterior detail packages roughly in the $275 to $400 range as of 2026. Interior-only packages commonly start around $120 to $150 and exterior-only details near $125. Price moves with vehicle size, pet hair, smoke odor, and how much paint correction the job needs.

### Q. Can I wash my car in my own driveway in St. Louis?

A.  Nothing stops you from rinsing a car at home, but the Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District asks residents to use a commercial facility that treats its wastewater and to keep pavement wash water out of storm drain inlets, which run untreated to local creeks and rivers. A driveway wash also uses roughly 80 to 140 gallons.

## How to Order Flowers From a Real St. Louis Florist, Not a Middleman
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/order-flowers-real-st-louis-florist

Imagine it’s a Wednesday morning in Maryland Heights and you remember, with a small jolt, that the thing you forgot was not the dry cleaning. You type flower delivery near me into your phone at a red light. The first result has St. Louis in the headline and promises delivery today.

So you order. Sixty-eight dollars, plus delivery, plus a service charge. The confirmation comes from a company you have never heard of. And somewhere in Affton or Florissant, a real flower shop gets a printout at 11 a.m. telling them to build an arrangement out of forty of your dollars.

What shows up is fine. It is not the photo, because the photo was never a picture of anything that shop makes. And a designer in Kirkwood, six minutes away, never knew you were looking. Is it better to order from a local florist or online? Plenty of real shops sell online — what matters is whether the site is the shop that will build it. Here is how to order so your money reaches the person cutting stems.

### How do you know you’re ordering from an actual local florist?

Check four things before you pay: a street address in the town the site claims to serve, a phone number a shop employee answers, photos of that shop’s own work and staff rather than stock images, and an active Google Business Profile with recent reviews. That is the checklist the Society of American Florists publishes for consumers.

The fastest test is a phone call. SAF puts the question in writing: “Is this the florist that will design and deliver my arrangement?” A shop with a cooler and a van answers in half a second. A call center pauses.

Search the address in Google Maps. Street View either shows a flower shop or an office park in another state.

Look for a shop name, not a keyword. Domains stitched from florist, flowers and a city name were built for search, not a storefront.

Watch the checkout. Every shop charges delivery. A separate service charge stacked on top of it is the line that pays a middleman.

Distrust the caller ID. SAF lists caller ID spoofing and impersonation calls among the tactics it tracks, so a local-looking number proves nothing.

### What is an order gatherer, and where does your money go?

An order gatherer is a website or call center that takes your order, keeps a cut, and passes the rest to a real florist to design and deliver. On a standard wire order the side taking the order typically keeps about 20 percent of the product and local delivery price, and the shop that builds it works with roughly 70 percent, minus a transmission fee of a dollar or two. That is why calling a local florist directly is cheaper where it counts: flower per dollar, not the total.

Passing orders between shops is legal, and useful when you are sending flowers to another city. The problem is misrepresentation. In a policy adopted in December 2019 and expanded into a public resource center on July 22, 2026, SAF names four deceptive practices: representing a business as local without a physical presence there, collecting undisclosed service fees, transmitting orders below stated retail prices and delivery fees, and misrepresenting business identity.

That third one explains the sad vase. An order transmitted below what you paid asks a designer to build a $68 arrangement on a $40 budget. Good designers do remarkable things with that. They cannot do the photo.

### What time do you have to order for same-day flower delivery in St. Louis?

Plan on noon. Checking published cutoffs at shops serving St. Louis and the Metro East in August 2026, same-day deadlines ran from 12 p.m. to 2 p.m. on weekdays, with 12 p.m. common on Saturdays, and many shops run no Sunday route. Noon works everywhere; confirm 2 p.m. by phone.

Three things move that deadline earlier, none of them the florist’s doing:

Funeral homes. The visitation time is the real deadline, almost always earlier than the shop’s cutoff. Call the funeral home first, then the florist.

Hospitals and care facilities. Front desks stop accepting deliveries at set times, and some units restrict fresh flowers. Thirty seconds with the nurses’ station saves a wasted run.

Distance. A south city shop can reach Webster Groves all afternoon. St. Charles, Wentzville or Waterloo is a route decision made that morning, so ask for a delivery window rather than a time.

### What should you tell a florist instead of picking a photo?

Give three things and stop: a dollar number, who it is for, and one boundary. “A hundred dollars, it’s for my mother’s birthday, she hates lilies” beats any picture on a website. Then let the designer pick the stems. That one habit buys more flower per dollar than anything else here.

The reason is supply. Nearly 80 percent of the cut flowers available in the US market are imported, according to a February 10, 2025 analysis by Gustavo Niño and Joe Janzen at the University of Illinois. Their figures put 2024 imports at a record $1.98 billion — $1.24 billion from Colombia and $491 million from Ecuador — against roughly $350 million grown domestically in 2023.

A chain that long means what is gorgeous this week can be scarce next week. A designer at the cooler knows which it is. A photo shot two years ago does not, and matching it costs money that could have been stem count. Florists are not offended by a budget. They are relieved by one.

Completely different errand — nail salons across the metro are worth comparing.

### What drives the cost of wedding flowers?

Labor and installation drive it, not the flowers. The Knot’s Real Weddings Study, built from 10,474 US couples married during 2025, puts average wedding flower spend at $2,800, with a lower quartile of $900, a median of $1,900 and an upper quartile of $4,800. That covers the bouquet, a boutonnière, wedding party flowers and centerpieces.

That spread is structural. Personal flowers are the cheap part. What escalates a quote is anything that has to be built, hung, hauled and taken down again:

Installations. An arch or hanging piece needs hardware, a crew and a ladder inside a two-hour setup window.

Guest count times centerpieces. Twenty tables is twenty arrangements, and that multiplies straight through.

Setup and strike. Somebody drives to Kirkwood at 9 a.m. and returns at midnight to pull it out. Both are billed hours.

Out-of-season stems. Peonies in October are a different transaction than peonies in May.

Rentals. Vessels, arbors and stands are line items you return or buy.

The most useful question at a consult is which pieces can be moved. Repurposing ceremony arrangements onto reception tables costs a labor hour and saves a second set of flowers.

### What are the unspoken rules for sending funeral flowers?

Get the visitation time and the funeral home’s delivery deadline before you call a florist, then name the piece you want. There are three, and they are not interchangeable: a casket spray, traditionally ordered by the immediate family; a standing easel spray, which is what friends, coworkers and organizations send; and a vase arrangement, which travels to a home afterward.

Price at that end is driven by structure and stem count. An easel spray needs a frame, foam, enough flowers to read from across a room, and a designer’s hour. A vase arrangement of the same value looks fuller up close because none of the budget went into architecture.

Check the obituary for a request for donations in lieu of flowers, and honor it. And consider sending something to the house two weeks later instead of a fifth easel spray on the day. That is when a delivery lands.

### Why do Valentine’s Day and Mother’s Day cost more?

Because a year’s demand lands in a 48-hour window on a product that cannot be stockpiled. The National Retail Federation’s 2026 survey put Valentine’s Day spending at a record $29.1 billion, averaging $199.78 per person, with 41 percent of consumers buying flowers and $3.1 billion going to flowers. Mother’s Day 2026 was bigger: a record $38 billion, $284.25 per person, $3.2 billion on flowers.

Set that against a supply chain where nearly 80 percent of cut flowers are flown in. Growers book those weeks months ahead, freight tightens, and every metro shop pays more per stem in early February than in March. Retail moves for the same reason airfare does at Thanksgiving.

Order five to seven days out. Shops buy to their order book, so early orders get built from product bought for you.

Skip red roses. They are the most bid-up item of the year. Tulips and garden-style mixes cost less and read as more thoughtful.

Take the day before or after. On February 14 the bottleneck is delivery capacity, not flowers.

Say designer’s choice. On a peak week that is the difference between a shop working around a photo and one working for you.

### Does it matter which side of the river your florist is on?

For sales tax, what matters is which shop took the order, not which one delivered it. Missouri’s rule, 12 CSR 10-103.620, provides that a Missouri florist who takes the original order and forwards it to another in-state or out-of-state florist is subject to sales tax on the transaction, while a Missouri florist merely filling an order taken out of state is not.

Illinois says the mirror image in 86 Ill. Adm. Code 130.1965, its florists and nurserymen regulation. Where an Illinois florist takes an order and instructs a florist outside Illinois to deliver, tax is owed on that Illinois florist’s receipts from the customer. Where an Illinois florist merely receives delivery instructions from another florist, it is not liable on those receipts.

The translation is short: tax, delivery fee and customer relationship all follow whoever took the order, so the shop that designed and drove your arrangement may not be the business that recorded the sale. Geography matters too. A Belleville shop delivering to St. Charles is a long, expensive stop.

### What this looks like from behind the counter

Ask a shop owner around here what they would change and the answer usually starts with the gathered order: roughly 70 percent of the ticket reaches the shop that builds and drives it, minus a transmission fee, while the customer’s expectations were set by a photo the designer has never seen. Add perishable inventory bought on a forecast, where every recipe has to carry a shrink rate, and margin thins fast. Two weeks — Valentine’s and Mother’s Day — carry a disproportionate share of the year, both 48-hour crushes needing temporary designers and extra drivers. Delivery is the quiet cost: a stop in Florissant followed by one in Fenton can eat an hour of a driver’s day. Weddings get quoted with setup, strike and rentals because that is where the labor lives. The shops that come out ahead are the ones people find directly, which is why a complete, current local listing earns its keep.

That covers bouquet, boutonnière, wedding party flowers and centerpieces. Installations, guest count, rentals and setup labor push a quote higher.

### Q. Do I pay sales tax if the florist is in Illinois and delivery is in Missouri?

A.  Tax follows the shop that took the order. Under 86 Ill. Adm. Code 130.1965, an Illinois florist who takes an order and has another florist deliver it owes tax on what it collects from you. Under 12 CSR 10-103.620, a Missouri florist who takes the original order is subject to Missouri sales tax even when another shop delivers.

None of this requires becoming a flower person. One phone call, one honest number, one shop near the person you are trying to reach. Do that on a Wednesday in Maryland Heights and the arrangement in Kirkwood shows up looking like somebody meant it.

## What Does a Photographer Cost in St. Louis? 2026 Prices and Permits
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/photographer-cost-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Thursday night in Affton. Your daughter starts her senior year in three weeks, you sit down to book the photos, and the first four quotes are $99, $350, $650 and $1,200. Same city. Same September light.

Or you got engaged on the Katy Trail outside St. Charles and three photographers have already sent numbers from $1,400 to $7,200. Or you’re an agent in Belleville with a listing going live Monday, staring at a $175 bid and a $450 one.

The spread is real, and nearly all of it is explainable. Here’s how much you should expect to pay for a photographer around St. Louis in 2026, what pushes the number up, and what you can skip.

### What is a reasonable price for a photographer in the St. Louis metro?

Plan on $150 to $350 an hour for portrait work, roughly $2,700 to $8,600 for full-day wedding coverage, $110 to $500 per listing for real estate, and about $150 to $350 for a headshot session. The Wedding Report’s 2026 St. Louis estimate puts the photographer line for a 75-guest wedding at $3,174 to $3,880.

The Knot’s 2026 Real Weddings Study, built from 10,474 US couples who married during 2025, puts the national average wedding photographer at $3,000 inside an average wedding of $34,200. Regionally it runs $3,800 in the Mid-Atlantic down to $2,600 in the Southwest. St. Louis sits near the middle.

### Why does one wedding quote say $1,400 and the next says $7,000?

Four things move it: hours of coverage, whether a second shooter is included, how much editing labor is priced in, and the date. Coverage is the biggest lever — four hours and ten hours are different jobs, and most of the gap is simply time on the clock.

The second shooter. Roughly a third of wedding photographers build one into the base package; the rest charge separately, and adding one typically runs $300 to $700, with some quoting $500 to $1,500. You’re buying simultaneous coverage — two getting-ready rooms, two ceremony angles — which matters as the guest list passes 100.

The editing. A full wedding day generates 3,000 to 6,000 raw frames and yields 500 to 800 finished images. Culling takes 3 to 5 hours; editing another 8 to 14. Post-production eats more than half of a working wedding photographer’s business hours. When a quote comes in cheap, that labor is what got cut.

The date. Fall is peak season. The Knot reports 35% of couples marry between September and November, and October alone accounted for 17% of US weddings in 2024. An October Saturday in Kirkwood is the hardest date in the metro to book and the least likely to be discounted.

### What do senior portraits, headshots and listing photos run here?

Family and senior sessions price at roughly $150 to $300 per hour of shoot time. St. Louis studio pricing pages in 2026 show session fees from under $100 up to about $650, with full collections landing between $650 and $1,200 once prints or an album are added.

Headshots average about $250 nationally, and most individual sessions fall between $150 and $350. Team shoots get priced per head at volume, roughly $30 to $80 a person on top of a day rate. Watch the add-ons: extra retouching, commercial usage rights and hair and makeup can push $250 past $400.

Real estate photography runs $110 to $500 per listing for a standard package in 2026, with premium HDR at the $300 to $500 end. Drone work prices separately — $75 to $200 as an add-on, $100 to $350 standalone. Anyone flying for a paid listing needs an FAA Part 107 certificate.

### Are you buying the copyright or just a print release?

A print release, almost always. Under US law the photographer owns the copyright the moment the shutter fires, and 17 U.S.C. §204(a) says a transfer of copyright ownership isn’t valid unless it is in writing and signed by the owner. Paying the invoice does not move the copyright.

The US Copyright Office states that a work is protected the moment it is created and fixed in tangible form. Handing over a file or an album transfers the object, not the rights. A full transfer leaves the photographer nothing — no portfolio use, no reprints — which is why it costs thousands more when it’s offered at all.

The practical questions are narrower. How many finished images, at what resolution? Does the release cover commercial use, which matters enormously for headshots and listing photos? How long does the gallery stay live? Put those answers in the contract, not a text thread.

### Is a photography retainer refundable if your date falls through?

Usually not, and the word in your contract is the reason. A retainer holds a specific date and is normally non-refundable. A deposit is an advance payment toward the work, and if the shoot never happens, it is far likelier to come back. Check which word appears before you sign.

The reasoning is opportunity cost: blocking your October Saturday means declining every other October Saturday, and that date can’t be resold in March. The flip side matters too. If the photographer breaches the contract, they generally owe back everything you paid, retainer included.

Ask what changes if you reschedule instead of cancel, whether there’s an illness clause, who shoots if your photographer goes down, and what happens if files are lost. Those four answers beat a discount.

Wildly off-topic — St. Louis-style pizza is its own argument entirely.

### Do St. Louis parks and gardens charge a photography permit fee?

It depends on who owns the ground, so check before you drive. Tower Grove Park states that photography permits are not needed in the park. The Missouri Botanical Garden requires a permit for formal photography — weddings, family sessions, prom, quinceañera — reserved 24 hours ahead.

The Garden’s conditions go past the permit: outdoor public areas only, no buildings, conservatories or Japanese Garden islands; no lighting or reflectors; props limited to one per person, no larger than two feet by two feet. Reservations aren’t accepted during Signature Events.

Gateway Arch National Park. Under the EXPLORE Act changes effective January 2025, still photography involving eight or fewer people needs no National Park Service permit, provided you stay in public areas, use hand-carried equipment, don’t require exclusive use of a spot, and don’t create added costs for the park.

Missouri conservation areas. The Missouri Department of Conservation dropped its paid commercial photography permit on July 1, 2023. A no-cost special use permit is still required if more than 10 people participate in a day, if you fly a drone, if props exceed what one person can carry, or for access outside open hours.

County and city ground. St. Charles County Parks requires professional photographers shooting portraits or group photos for profit to apply for authorization; the parks office is 636-949-7535. In Forest Park, flying a drone requires a City of St. Louis Board of Public Service permit plus a $1,000,000 certificate of insurance. The city Parks line is 314-289-5300.

The Illinois side. Metro East rules are published less uniformly, so call the site. At Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site, every activity requires an Activity Permit approved by the Illinois Department of Natural Resources, and photo sessions are arranged with staff in advance at 618-346-5160.

### Which line items are worth paying for, and which are padding?

Pay for the second shooter above 100 guests, pay for the engagement session, pay for the album only if you’ll print it. Skip the rush-delivery upgrade until you know the standard timeline. The Wedding Report’s 2026 St. Louis estimate prices an engagement session at $326 to $398 — cheap rehearsal for a day you can’t redo.

Turnaround. Four to eight weeks is the most commonly cited standard for a full wedding gallery, and some studios quote eight to twelve. A 2026 ShootProof report found 31% of clients expect the full gallery within 14 days. That gap is where the friction lives. Get the number in the contract.

Sales tax, which differs across the river. In Missouri, a separately stated sitting fee or hourly wedding rate isn’t subject to sales tax, finished prints and albums are, and electronic downloads aren’t — the framework set out in Missouri Department of Revenue Letter Ruling LR3714, issued April 4, 2007. Illinois runs it through its photoprocessing rule, 86 Ill. Admin. Code 130.2000, taxing 10% of a separately stated photoprocessing charge. Missouri’s state rate is 4.225%; Illinois’ is 6.25%. How the invoice is itemized changes what you owe.

### What questions separate a professional from someone with a good camera?

Five, and they take ten minutes. Are you insured, and can you send my venue a certificate? Do you shoot to two memory cards at once? Who actually shows up on the day? How many weeks until the full gallery? What happens if you’re sick? A vague answer is the answer.

Venues and corporate clients commonly require $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate in general liability coverage, with the venue named on the certificate for your date. A working photographer carries that year-round and can produce it in a day or two. Someone shopping for a policy after you ask has told you something.

Credentials are optional here but checkable. The Professional Photographers of America Certified Professional Photographer credential requires PPA membership, a $200 candidacy application good for two years, six exam modules and a Technical Image Evaluation. Plenty of excellent photographers skip it entirely.

### What the price looks like from behind the camera

If you shoot for a living here, the wedding itself is the small part. Eight hours on your feet becomes 3,000 to 6,000 raw frames, 3 to 5 hours of culling and 8 to 14 hours of editing — which is why post-production consumes over half the working hours, and why 44% of photographers report high burnout in peak season. Then the invisible costs: general liability at $1M/$2M because venues demand a certificate before you’re through the door, a second body because one can fail mid-ceremony, redundant storage, and a second shooter paid $200 to $600 a day out of your own fee. The retainer isn’t greed either — holding one October Saturday means declining every other one, in a month that was 17% of US weddings in 2024.

None of it fits in a quote, and none of it helps if the search that starts in Florissant at 10pm never reaches you — the whole argument for keeping a complete, current listing on St Louis Near Me Directory.

## Buying Building Supplies in St. Louis: Lumberyard, Big Box, or Salvage
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/buying-building-supplies-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Saturday morning in Kirkwood and the back deck has finally lost the argument. A board flexed under your heel last October and you let it go. Now there are two soft spots, a railing that moves, and a list on the back of an envelope.

Maybe your version is different. A basement in Florissant that needs framing before Thursday’s drywall crew. A garage in Belleville with a header gone soft under a leaky gutter. A fence in St. Charles that a June storm took down. A wall in Maryland Heights where the mortar falls out when you poke it.

The list is the easy part. Where you buy it decides what the job costs, how long you spend digging for boards that aren’t twisted, and whether anybody catches your math before you pay.

### Do lumber yards have better lumber than Home Depot?

Match the store to the job, not to habit. A big-box home center wins on hours, on small quantities, and on taking back the four boards you didn’t need. A lumberyard wins on grade selection, on stock somebody already pulled and stacked, on delivery that reaches a job site, and on a counter person who catches the wrong joist span before you pay.

You also do not need a contractor license or an account to buy from a yard. Most building supply houses in the St. Louis metro sell to the public.

The real gap is depth. A home center stocks a narrow band of fast-turning framing. A yard selling to builders carries more species, more grades, longer lengths, and treated lumber rated for the exposure you actually have. Ground contact is a different product from above ground, and grabbing the wrong one is the most common expensive mistake on a deck.

The second gap is who sorts. At a home center you cull the pile yourself, sighting down each edge for crown and twist. At a yard the will-call counter has your order banded and waiting when you pull up.

### What does the stamp on a piece of framing lumber tell you?

The stamp is the only objective quality information on a board, and it carries five things: the grading agency, the mill number, the grade, the species group, and the moisture content when the board was surfaced.

Grade — Select Structural, No. 1, No. 2, No. 3 and Stud, strongest to weakest. Most framing sold over the counter is No. 2 or better.

Species — SPF, southern yellow pine, Doug Fir-Larch and Hem-Fir span differently and are not interchangeable in a span table.

Moisture — S-GRN is surfaced green. S-DRY and KD-19 both mean 19 percent moisture or less. KD-15 or MC-15 means 15 percent or less.

Mill number and agency logo — what a building inspector looks for on a permitted job.

Drier lumber shrinks and twists less once nailed up, and grade drives span: a No. 1 joist reaches farther than a No. 2 of the same depth.

### What does a contractor account actually get you?

Trade credit and a person. A real account means net 30 terms instead of a credit card, purchases coded to a job address, quoted pricing held for a stated window, will-call staging, job-site delivery, a material takeoff run from your plans, and returns handled by someone who knows the account.

Net 30 matters most to anyone running crews — the yard is financing thirty days of material while you wait on a draw. Charges coded to an address also stop you guessing which project ate the margin. Homeowners can ask for a cash account and the same takeoff.

One thing to know in Missouri: a supplier who delivered material to your house can lien it even if you paid your contractor in full. Suppliers must give the owner ten days’ written notice before filing under RSMo 429.100, and liens run six months from the last material furnished. RSMo 429.012 makes the original contractor give owner-occupants a written disclosure saying exactly that. Ask for lien waivers from the supplier, not only the contractor.

Nothing to do with lumber — you will need a plumber eventually.

### What does building material delivery cost across the St. Louis metro?

Delivery is priced by the truck, not by the board. Expect a flat charge per drop inside a yard’s zone, a higher one when a boom truck or piggyback forklift has to place the load on a roof or behind a fence, and a hard edge where the zone stops. Ask the fee, the zone line, and what day they run your area.

Geography is the whole story. The St. Louis metropolitan area is 15 counties across roughly 8,458 square miles in two states. A yard in Maryland Heights and a yard in Belleville are both local to somebody and nowhere near each other, so most run set days per zone.

Know curbside from placed. Curbside means the load lands wherever the truck can reach, and a pallet of block at the end of the driveway is a long afternoon. Many yards also cut the fee above an order threshold, so folding three trips into one pays for itself.

### Where do you buy brick and mortar for an old St. Louis house?

A masonry supply yard, and the spec that matters most is the mortar, not the brick. National Park Service Preservation Brief 2 is explicit that masonry originally laid in lime mortar should not be repointed with Portland cement mortar. Hard mortar in a soft wall pushes stress into the brick face, and the faces spall off.

Clay from the Cheltenham deposit south of Forest Park fed dozens of brickyards from the 1840s on, and after the Great Fire of 1849 burned fifteen blocks of riverfront the city required new construction east of Jefferson Avenue to be brick. Fired cooler than modern brick, those units are soft and porous.

Under ASTM C270, mortar is graded by 28-day compressive strength: Type M at 2,500 psi, Type S at 1,800, Type N at 750, Type O at 350. On a soft historic wall you want the weakest mortar that will do the job, and a masonry supplier can mix a lime-rich Type O.

Used brick carries its own rule. The City of St. Louis licenses brick dealers under Ordinance 67392: a permitted dealer must photograph every seller, keep a register of purchases and sales, and see a demolition permit before taking used brick. Violations carry fines up to $500 plus at least fifty cents per brick.

### Is reclaimed and salvaged material worth the hassle?

For brick, solid doors, old-growth dimensional lumber, mantels, hardware and trim profiles nobody mills anymore, yes — salvage is often the only way to match what is already in the house. For anything with a code or safety function you cannot verify by looking at it, no.

What salvage costs you is certainty. No warranty, usually no return, and the quantity on the floor is the entire quantity that exists. If you find 900 bricks that match, buy 10 to 15 percent past your takeoff that day, because there is no reorder.

Dimensions surprise people: older framing runs closer to its nominal size, and old brick will not line up with new coursing. Assume painted material from a pre-1978 building may carry lead paint. The supply exists because crews here take buildings apart instead of knocking them flat, to save the brick and the lumber.

### How do you price a materials list without getting upgraded?

Write the spec, not the product, and hand every yard the identical list: species, grade, dimension, length, quantity, treatment rating. Ask each to quote line by line and flag substitutions in writing. Three comparable quotes is the whole defense against a cheerful upgrade.

Some upgrades are real. Ground-contact lumber where the code calls for ground contact is the job, not an upsell, and No. 1 across a long span may be structurally required. A “premium” stud on a garage partition usually is not.

Ask when the quote expires. The Random Lengths framing lumber composite that the National Association of Home Builders tracks sat at $558.19 per thousand board feet on August 7, 2026; it peaked near $1,515 in May 2021. Policy drives part of that swing: duties on most Canadian softwood ran 35.16 percent, and although Commerce preliminarily cut them to 24.83 percent in April 2026, a separate 10 percent Section 232 tariff from October 2025 sits on top.

Lumber is not automatically cheaper at a lumber yard. Compare delivered-and-taxed totals, not shelf prices. Missouri’s state sales tax is 4.225 percent and Illinois’s is 6.25 percent, before local add-ons. On a $9,000 order that is not rounding.

### What can you legally install yourself in Missouri and Illinois?

Missouri has no statewide general contractor, plumbing or HVAC license — those rules are set county by county and city by city. Illinois licenses plumbing and roofing at the state level. That difference decides who may install the material you just bought.

In St. Louis County, electrical and plumbing work must be done by a licensed contractor or by a pre-authorized homeowner who has passed an open-book test given by county inspections. The property has to be a single-family residence you occupy and hold the occupancy permit for, and the test may be taken only once every twelve months.

In the City of St. Louis, a permit is required for an entire new roof or any job replacing more than 25 percent of the roof sheathing, plus decks, porches, retaining walls, accessory buildings over 50 square feet and new fences. Tuckpointing, painting, and swapping windows and doors into existing openings do not.

The Illinois Plumbing License Law (225 ILCS 320) requires licensed plumbers, with a carve-out letting the owner-occupant of a single-family residence do their own — if the work meets the Illinois State Plumbing Code, stays open to inspection, and no unlicensed helper assists. The Illinois Roofing Industry Licensing Act (225 ILCS 335) requires a state license unless you are working on your own property. You can buy the shingles in Belleville; you cannot hand the install to an unlicensed handyman.

### What a supply yard sees from the other side of the counter

Ask an owner where the money is and it is not the lumber. Trade benchmarks put a typical dealer near a 23 percent gross margin and low single-digit pretax profit, with commodity dimensional lumber the thinnest line on the sheet — millwork, doors and windows run closer to 30 percent. That is what the pro desk is for: a package deal moves the mix, not just studs. Meanwhile the yard carries inventory whose replacement cost shifts weekly, extends net 30 to contractors, and runs a delivery fleet across 8,458 square miles. National building-material dealer sales came in at $33.7 billion in January 2026 against $42.3 billion the previous October. What owners tell each other is simpler: bring a list, not a sketch. Yards get found by neighborhood searches, which is why a complete listing is worth ten minutes — claim or add yours.

Not sure which yard stocks what your project needs? Browse building supplies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then send the same written material list to two of them and compare the quotes line by line.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Do I need a contractor license to buy from a lumberyard in St. Louis?

A.  No. Building supply yards across the metro sell to the public, and most will open a cash account for a homeowner and run a material takeoff from your drawings. What a contractor account adds is trade credit: net 30 terms, purchases coded to a job address, and quoted pricing held for a stated window.

### Q. Do lumber yards have better lumber than Home Depot?

A.  Better selection and better sorting, more than better boards. A yard carries more species, more grades, longer lengths and treated lumber rated for your actual exposure, and will-call has the order banded when you pull up. At a home center you cull the pile yourself.

### Q. Is lumber cheaper at a lumber yard?

A.  Not automatically. Dimensional lumber is the thinnest line on a dealer’s sheet, and the commodity moves weekly — the Random Lengths framing composite sat at $558.19 per thousand board feet on August 7, 2026 against a $1,515 peak in May 2021. Compare delivered-and-taxed totals on an identical list.

### Q. Where’s the cheapest place to get lumber?

A.  For old-growth dimensional lumber, salvage — no warranty, no return, no reorder. For new material, whichever of two or three yards comes back lowest on the identical written spec, delivered and taxed.

### Q. What does KD-19 mean on a 2x6?

A.  KD-19 means the board was kiln dried to 19 percent moisture content or less when it was surfaced. S-DRY signals that same ceiling reached by air or kiln drying, S-GRN means surfaced green, and KD-15 or MC-15 means 15 percent or less. Drier lumber shrinks and twists less after you nail it up.

### Q. How much does building material delivery cost in the St. Louis area?

A.  Delivery is priced per truckload rather than per item, so one flat charge usually covers a single drop inside a yard’s zone, with a higher rate when a boom truck places the load on a roof or behind a fence. Fee schedules and zone lines vary by yard, so get the charge printed on your quote.

### Q. What mortar should I use on a 100-year-old St. Louis brick house?

A.  Generally the weakest mortar that will do the job. National Park Service Preservation Brief 2 warns against repointing lime-mortar masonry with Portland cement mortar, because hard mortar drives stress into softer brick and pops the faces off. Under ASTM C270, Type O runs 350 psi and Type N 750, against 1,800 for Type S. Bring a piece of the original mortar to a masonry supplier.

### Q. Can I do my own plumbing or electrical work in St. Louis County?

A.  Within limits. St. Louis County lets a pre-authorized homeowner do their own electrical and plumbing work after passing an open-book test administered by county inspections. The property must be a single-family residence you occupy and hold the occupancy permit for, and the test may be taken only once every twelve months.

### Q. Where can I legally buy used brick in St. Louis?

A.  From a dealer holding a City of St. Louis brick dealer permit. Ordinance 67392 requires permitted dealers to photograph every person selling them bricks, keep a register of purchases and sales, and see a demolition permit and a valid city business license before accepting used brick. Permits expire October 15 each year, so ask to see the paperwork.

## How to Choose a Preschool in St. Louis: What to Check Before You Tour
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-preschool-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Tuesday night in Affton. The kid is finally asleep. You have a laptop open, eleven tabs of preschools, and a growing suspicion that every one of them uses the same three stock photos of wooden blocks.

Your sister in Florissant says her church program is wonderful and costs half what the place near your office charges. A coworker in St. Charles got on a list in February and still hasn’t heard anything. Somebody on a neighborhood page swears the Kirkwood program is worth the drive. Somebody else says the same about Belleville. None of them agree, and all of them sound certain.

Almost all of this is checkable, though. Licensing records, ratios, subsidy rules, real price ranges. Do the boring part in about an hour and you walk into every tour already knowing what to ask.

### How do you choose the best preschool in St. Louis?

Work in this order. Pull the state licensing record first, because it’s free and takes five minutes. Decide how you feel about license-exempt programs. Set your real monthly number and check whether you qualify for help. Get on two or three waitlists early. Tour last, mid-morning on a normal weekday.

Touring first is the mistake. You fall for a lobby, then find the open violation, the two-year wait, or the tuition that doesn’t work — and now you’re disappointed instead of informed.

### How do you check a preschool’s license and inspection history?

Both states publish it free. In Missouri, search the state Child Care Search tool at healthapps.dhss.mo.gov/childcaresearch by name, address, city, ZIP or county. In Illinois, use the DCFS Sunshine site at sunshine.dcfs.illinois.gov, which posts licensing compliance records gathered on or after January 1, 2010.

The two states hand you different amounts. Illinois’ Sunshine site is built around monitoring reports and violation records, so you can read what an inspector wrote and whether it got corrected. Missouri’s tool states plainly that the records shown may not reflect a facility’s complete history, and points you to the Office of Childhood inside the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education for the full public file. A thin Missouri record is a cue to request records, not proof there’s nothing there.

One note, because it changes who you call: as of July 1, 2026, Illinois child care licensing moved from the Department of Children and Family Services to the new Illinois Department of Early Childhood. The historical records still live on the DCFS Sunshine site, and Illinois staffs a daycare information line at 1-877-746-0829.

### Which type of preschool is best — licensed, church, Montessori or in-home?

A license means an inspector enforces written ratios. Missouri’s rule, 5 CSR 25-500.112, sets one adult per four children from birth to 36 months with a group cap of eight, one per eight for a room of two-year-olds, one per ten for three- and four-year-olds with a cap of twenty, and one per sixteen at age five and up. Illinois, under 89 Ill. Adm. Code 407.190, requires one per four for infants six weeks through fourteen months, one per five for toddlers through twenty-three months, one per eight for two-year-olds, and one per ten for threes and fours.

A license-exempt religious program is not the same as unregulated. In Missouri, a center under the exclusive control of a religious organization can operate without a license, but state law still requires it to hand parents a written notice of parental responsibility. That sheet names the agencies that inspect it for fire, health and safety, gives the date of the most recent inspection by each, lists the staff-to-child ratios it keeps by age band, confirms caregiver background checks were run, and describes its discipline and education philosophies. Ask for it. A good church program hands it over without blinking.

The word Montessori isn’t trademarked, so any program can use it. If the method matters, check the school locators run by the American Montessori Society and Association Montessori International/USA, and ask whether the lead teacher trained through a MACTE-accredited program. Reggio is looser still — the original Reggio Emilia schools are municipal programs in one Italian city, which is why honest American programs say “Reggio-inspired.” Judge that one by the walls: real documentation of children’s projects, not laminated alphabet charts.

In-home care sits on a threshold. Missouri doesn’t require a license to care for six or fewer children, including no more than three under age two, at one address. Above that, a family child care home gets licensed and inspected like anyone else. Illinois also runs ExceleRate Illinois, sorting programs into Licensed, Bronze, Silver and Gold Circles of Quality; Missouri uses a voluntary Quality Assurance Report instead.

### What does preschool cost per month in the St. Louis area?

Budget roughly $750 to $900 a month for full-time preschool-age care and $1,000 to $1,200 for an infant. Those are the Missouri statewide ranges Child Care Aware of Missouri published in April 2026, with toddler care landing between them at about $850 to $1,000. Metro programs generally sit at the top of a statewide range, not the bottom.

Illinois numbers need a caveat. Published state averages fold in Chicago and its collar counties, so a headline Illinois figure overstates what a program in Belleville or Edwardsville charges. Ask Metro East programs for the rate sheet instead.

Four things move your bill. Age is the biggest, because ratios are: an infant room legally costs more adults per child. Hours come second — five half-days is a different product from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Calendar is third, since a nine-month program and a twelve-month center aren’t comparable prices. Then the add-ons: registration fee, supply fee, deposit, sometimes a summer rate that jumps in June.

Free options get overlooked. St. Louis Public Schools runs no-cost pre-K at its elementary sites for children who turn three or four before August 1 of the enrollment year and are fully toilet trained. Missouri funds district pre-K through the school foundation formula, so many suburban districts run their own. In Illinois, Preschool for All provides at least 12.5 hours a week for eligible three- to five-year-olds. Call your district before you assume you’re paying retail.

Unrelated, and we know it — the first dentist visit sneaks up fast.

### Can you get help paying for preschool in Missouri or Illinois?

Both states subsidize child care, and the rules differ enough to matter. Missouri’s Child Care Subsidy Program, run by the DESE Office of Childhood, serves families at or below 150 percent of the federal poverty level — about $49,500 a year for a household of four in 2026. Illinois’ Child Care Assistance Program uses 225 percent at application, which its guidelines effective July 1, 2025 set at $6,028 a month for a family of four.

Missouri has a waitlist right now, and it is not moving quickly. The state opened it March 1, 2026 after demand outran the appropriation, and as of July 2026 there were 7,389 children on it. Applications are ranked by priority: documented special needs first, then children experiencing homelessness, then families below the poverty line. Above 150 percent of poverty, Transitional Child Care runs to 242 percent on a flat daily fee — $7.50 for a full day at the first level as of November 2025. Apply at childcare.mo.gov or call 573-415-8605.

Illinois families apply at getchildcareil.org and pay a sliding copay rather than a flat fee, with eligibility stretching to 275 percent of poverty at renewal. Whichever side of the river you’re on, ask a program whether it accepts subsidy before you tour it. Plenty don’t.

### When should you apply, and how long are the waitlists?

For a fall preschool spot, start the previous fall or early winter. Most programs open registration to current families and siblings first, often in January or February, and release whatever is left to the public after that. By spring the popular rooms are spoken for.

Infant rooms are the genuinely painful ones. St. Louis Magazine’s reporting on the region’s child care crunch described waitlists spanning a year or more, with two years quoted as typical at some centers, and summed up the advice parents keep getting: if you’re pregnant, you’re already behind. Preschool-age spots move faster, because a room of three- and four-year-olds legally holds far more children per teacher.

Get on three or four lists, not one. Ask where you sit, how many spots typically open in August, whether the deposit is refundable or applied to tuition, and whether they’ll call you or expect you to check in. Then check in anyway, every few weeks.

### What are the signs of a good preschool on a tour?

Go mid-morning on a normal weekday and watch the adults, not the toys. Count children and teachers in the room your child would join, and compare that with the state ratio. Then ask the question most parents skip: how long has the lead teacher in this room been here?

Ask how ratio holds up at the hard moments. Staff breaks, naptime, drop-off and pickup, and the day two teachers call in sick.

Watch a hard moment. A three-year-old will melt down while you’re standing there. How an adult handles that is the whole tour.

Look at the bathroom and the diapering area. Unglamorous, and the fastest read on how a place actually runs.

Ask about a violation you already found. You pulled the record, so name it. A director who explains what changed is a good sign; a defensive one is information too.

Ask the illness policy out loud. Fever threshold, how long a child stays home, and who covers you when they’re sent home at 10 a.m.

### What the director is doing while you tour

From the other side of the counter, ratios aren’t a safety rule, they’re the profit-and-loss statement. A Missouri infant room at one adult per four children carries a teacher’s whole salary on four tuitions. A preschool room at one per ten carries it on ten. That’s why infant care costs families the most and still tends to lose the center money — federal modeling of center finances found infant-and-toddler-only programs running a loss near 20 percent of revenue, with preschool tuition quietly holding the building up. Labor eats 60 to 80 percent of expenses, and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics put median childcare worker pay at $15.41 an hour in May 2024, which is why a two-dollar raise is a real decision. A preschool seat empty in September is empty all year, because families enroll on a school calendar. Directors trade the same story: the deposit in February, the no-show in August. Parents search for preschools by neighborhood, which is why a complete local listing earns its keep.
