Both are private. The realistic way onto either property is a spectator ticket or a volunteer shift — these tournaments run on hundreds of volunteers. What you cannot do is book a tee time.

The related question, what is the most prestigious golf course in St. Louis, gets settled by championship résumé, and Bellerive has the longest one: the 1965 U.S. Open, the 1992 and 2018 PGA Championships, the BMW Championship in 2008 and 2026, and the Presidents Cup scheduled for 2030. Prestige and playability are different measurements, though. The course that improves your golf this year is a public one twenty minutes from your house.

### Should you take lessons before you buy clubs?

For most new golfers, yes — one lesson before any equipment purchase, because a coach can tell you in ten minutes whether the hand-me-down set in your garage is close to the right length and lie angle. Bending a club is cheap. Replacing a bag you bought blind is not.

Instruction comes in three shapes: group clinics, the cheapest way in and full of other beginners; private lessons, usually sold in packages of three to six; and playing lessons, where a coach walks nine holes and fixes what a range never exposes. Look for a coach who belongs to the PGA of America — the association’s coach finder filters by area. The trial-lesson logic in our guide to choosing a martial arts school in St. Louis transfers straight across.

Once your swing repeats, fitting earns its keep. How can I determine which golf club is best for me? Not from a chart — from hitting into a launch monitor while a fitter changes one variable at a time: shaft flex and weight, club length, lie angle, grip size, head model. And what’s the 70/30 rule in golf? It’s the practice split coaches keep repeating: roughly 70% of practice time on the short game, 30% on full swings. Most amateurs do the reverse, which is why it keeps getting said.

### Where do you golf in St. Louis in the winter?

Indoors, and more people are doing it than ever. The National Golf Foundation’s 2026 Graffis Report, covering 2025 data, put total U.S. golf participation at an all-time high of 48.1 million once technology-enabled ranges, simulators and entertainment venues are counted alongside course play. Off-course formats alone accounted for 37.9 million participants, with 19 million people doing both.

In practice that means heated range stalls, indoor studios with launch monitors, simulator bays rented by the hour, and entertainment ranges built around groups. Winter simulator leagues run on weeknights. There’s a coaching argument for all of it too: a swing change holds better when you aren’t also managing wind, lie and score, so December through February is when a rebuilt grip actually sticks.

### What should a first-timer know before walking on?

Call the pro shop and say it plainly: first round, when’s a good time to come out. You’ll get a real answer, usually a weekday afternoon. Ask two more things while you have them — is there a dress code, and are metal spikes allowed. Plenty of courses want a collared shirt and soft spikes only, and learning that in the parking lot is the bad version.

On the course, pace is the entire etiquette conversation. Play the forward tees; they exist for exactly this. Play ready golf instead of strict honors — whoever is set hits. Pick up once you’ve reached double par and move on.

The rest is groundskeeping you do on the way past: rake the bunker behind you, fix your ball mark, fill divots from the sand bottle. Eighteen holes at a busy public course runs about four and a half hours. Fall more than a hole behind the group ahead and wave the group behind you through. People remember the golfer who does that, and nobody remembers the score.

### How do golf leagues and handicaps work around here?

Leagues are the cheapest standing tee time in golf, and they’re how most people find a regular group. A typical metro league is nine holes on a weeknight or weekday morning, priced for the season. The county course at Eagle Springs publishes a ladies league Tuesday and Thursday mornings, a Thursday night men’s league and a Friday couples league — a good template for what to ask other pro shops about.

A handicap is what lets a 24 and a 9 compete on the same card. You get one by joining a club or association that provides handicap service, then posting scores; the number recalculates as you play under the World Handicap System. You don’t need to be good to have one, just honest about posting.

### What a course operator sees from the other side of the counter

Green fees are the top line, but a lot of the margin lives in the cart, and food and beverage carries more of the year than golfers assume. The tee sheet is perishable inventory: an 8:10 Saturday foursome that never shows is revenue nobody can resell, which is why no-show policies keep tightening. Weekday mornings are the empty hours, and that is why operators chase leagues, corporate outings and shotgun-start charity scrambles. April through June and September through October pay for December through February, a rained-out Saturday in May is simply gone, and the maintenance budget runs whether anyone plays or not. Good operators manage pace with a real starter, price by demand, and build junior programs. People search for courses and coaches by neighborhood, so a complete, current listing is how a course turns up in a search that already happened.

Ready to book something instead of reading about it? Browse golf across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call one pro shop and ask the only question that matters for a first round — when is the tee sheet quiet enough for a new player.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is the best public golf course in St. Louis?

A.  Nobody agrees, and the honest answer depends on what you need from a round. Score candidates on drive time, walkability, pace, forgiveness for a new player, and tee times when you’re free. Then check reviews from the last three months, since conditions swing with weather, aeration and maintenance spending. A course that played rough two summers ago can be excellent now.

### Q. Which PGA event is taking place in St. Louis in 2026?

### Q. What’s the 70/30 rule in golf?

A.  A practice guideline, not a rule of the game: spend about 70% of practice time on the short game — putting, chipping, pitching — and 30% on full swings and driving. The reasoning is that a large share of the strokes in any round happen inside a hundred yards. Most amateurs invert it.

### Q. How can I determine which golf club is best for me?

A.  Get fitted rather than guessing. A fitter puts you on a launch monitor and changes one variable at a time — shaft flex and weight, length, lie angle, grip size, head design — watching what your swing does with each. If you’re brand new, start smaller: have a coach check the length and lie of clubs you already own. Bending is inexpensive; a wrong full bag is not.

### Q. What is the poor man’s pebble?

A.  It’s a California nickname, not a St. Louis one. Golfers use “poor man’s Pebble Beach” for affordable coastal courses near Monterey and Santa Barbara that give you ocean views at a fraction of Pebble Beach money — Pacific Grove Municipal gets the title most often. The local version of the idea is a modest public course with genuinely good design.

## How to Choose a Podiatrist in St. Louis (and What to Expect)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-podiatrist-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Thursday and you’ve been walking a little sideways for three weeks. It started on a parking-garage stairwell in Maryland Heights — a hot spot under the heel you decided to ignore. Now it meets you the second your foot hits the bedroom floor in Affton, quiets by mid-morning, then comes back loud after dinner.

Maybe it isn’t you. Maybe it’s your dad in Florissant, eleven years into type 2 diabetes, who used to grumble about his feet constantly and lately has said nothing at all. Maybe it’s a sixteen-year-old in Kirkwood hiding a sore toe since cross-country tryouts, or you at a desk in Belleville quietly ordering a half size up because something has started to rub.

Everybody ends up in the same spot: typing “foot doctor near me” at a kitchen table in St. Charles and getting a wall of names with the same three letters after each one. Here’s how to sort that list — what the credentials mean, how Missouri and Illinois license these doctors, what a first visit involves, and how the money works. What is wrong with your particular foot is a question only a clinician who examines it can answer.

What to look for when choosing a podiatrist? Three things you can verify before you call: an active license in the state where the office sits, training that fits your problem, and network status for your specific plan. A doctor of podiatric medicine completes four years of podiatric medical school plus a three-year hospital-based surgical residency. Then ask what the first visit includes and whether X-rays are taken on site.

### How do you pick a podiatrist in the St. Louis metro?

Match the doctor to the problem first, check the license second, check the network third. A practice that spends most of its week on diabetes-related foot care and nail surgery is not the same practice as one built around running injuries and custom orthotics, even though both put the same three letters on the door. Sorting by proximity alone is how people end up getting a second opinion two months later.

People search “Who is the best foot doctor in St. Louis?” constantly, and the honest answer is that there isn’t a single one. The right doctor for a long-time diabetic with a callus that won’t settle is not the right doctor for a teenager with forefoot pain after a cross-country season. Best means best-matched.

Five questions do most of the sorting on a phone call. Does this office see this problem weekly or a few times a year? Are X-rays taken here, or do I go elsewhere and come back? If orthotics come up, are they cast for my foot or pulled off a shelf? Where does the doctor operate? And — the one people skip — is the doctor personally in network, not just the group name on the building?

### What is a DPM, and how is that different from an orthopedic surgeon?

A podiatrist is a doctor of podiatric medicine, a DPM, and the American Podiatric Medical Association describes a DPM as “a physician and surgeon who treats the foot, ankle, and related structures of the leg.” The training runs four years of undergraduate education, four years of podiatric medical school, then a three-year hospital-based surgical residency. Board certification comes later, through added training, clinical experience and an exam — it is not automatic with the degree. (APMA, What is a Podiatrist?)

An orthopedic surgeon takes a different road to overlapping ground: medical school, then a residency in orthopaedic surgery covering the whole musculoskeletal system, with foot-and-ankle work typically added through a fellowship. Both routes are legitimate. The useful question isn’t which letters win — it’s how often the person in front of you handles your specific problem.

What is the most common problem treated by a podiatrist? Day to day, the case mix leans on heel and arch pain, nail and skin conditions, and foot care for people with diabetes. Medicare’s coverage page names hammer toe, bunion deformities and heel spurs as examples of foot conditions it will pay to treat. Whether your symptom belongs on that list is not something an article can tell you.

### How do you check that a podiatrist is licensed in Missouri or Illinois?

Both states publish a free license lookup, and checking takes about ninety seconds. Missouri licenses podiatrists through the State Board of Podiatric Medicine, part of the Division of Professional Registration in Jefferson City; verify a name through the state’s MOPRO licensee search. Illinois issues the credential as “Podiatric Physician” through the Department of Financial & Professional Regulation, verified at IDFPR’s license lookup. An office in Fairview Heights and an office in Chesterfield answer to different regulators.

Missouri draws its scope line in unusually plain language. Under RSMo 330.010, the term “human foot” includes the ankle and the tendons that insert into the foot. For ankle surgery specifically, the statute requires the DPM to be board certified in foot and ankle surgery by the American Board of Podiatric Surgery or to have completed a twenty-four-month postgraduate clinical residency in podiatric surgery — and any doctor newly licensed in Missouri after January 1, 2005 must have completed that residency.

The same statute adds a detail worth knowing as a patient: ankle surgery by a DPM may only be performed in a licensed acute care hospital or a licensed ambulatory surgical clinic, with approval from that facility’s physician credentialing committee. So if an ankle procedure comes up, asking where it would be done and where the surgeon holds privileges is the question the law already asks.

### What happens at a first podiatry visit?

Expect a history, a hands-on exam, and often imaging in the same hour. The APMA tells patients to arrive with a list of symptoms and questions, a list of all medications and previous surgeries, and relevant records from other doctors — X-rays, MRIs, lab results. It adds one instruction people ignore: “If your problem involves walking and/or exercise, bring your walking/exercise shoes with you to the appointment.”

Bring the shoes you actually wear, not the good pair. Wear patterns on a worn-out sole tell a doctor things you can’t put into words, and the shoe you stand in for ten hours matters more than the one you wore to the office. If your standing hours are about to change — a warehouse placement, a hospital shift — say so out loud; our guide to choosing a staffing agency in St. Louis is a useful companion while that is in progress.

Wildly off-topic — your flooring is what you stand on all day.

### What does insurance cover, and are orthotics durable medical equipment?

Medicare Part B covers podiatrist foot exams or treatment when the care is medically necessary for a foot injury or disease, and after the Part B deductible you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. What it usually will not cover is routine foot care: cutting or removing corns and calluses, trimming or clipping nails, and hygienic maintenance like cleaning and soaking. That one distinction explains most surprise podiatry bills. (Medicare foot care coverage)

Diabetes changes the math. Medicare covers a foot exam or treatment every six months for people with diabetic peripheral neuropathy and loss of protective sensation, as long as you haven’t seen a foot care professional for another reason between visits. A separate therapeutic shoe benefit covers people with diabetes and severe diabetes-related foot disease: per calendar year, either one pair of custom-molded shoes plus two more pairs of inserts, or one pair of extra-depth shoes plus three pairs of inserts.

That shoe benefit has a paperwork chain most people don’t expect. The doctor who treats your diabetes must certify the need, a podiatrist or other qualified doctor must write the order, and the shoes have to come from a podiatrist, orthotist, prosthetist, pedorthist or another qualified supplier — and the doctors and the supplier all have to be enrolled in Medicare, or the claim doesn’t get paid.

Orthotics are where the durable medical equipment question gets slippery. Medicare’s DME door for the lower limb is the brace benefit — leg, arm, back and neck braces, covered when medically necessary and ordered by a provider, at 20% after the deductible — and the other door is the diabetic shoe benefit above. A custom arch support prescribed for ordinary heel pain often walks through neither. Plans vary widely, so ask for the billing code before the device is made, then call your plan with it.

Paying cash gives you a federal right worth using. Under the No Surprises Act, in effect since January 1, 2022, providers must generally give people who don’t have or don’t use insurance a good faith estimate when care is scheduled at least three business days ahead or whenever you ask — and you may be able to dispute a bill that comes in at least $400 above that estimate. (CMS)

### What a foot-and-ankle practice looks like from the other side of the counter

Podiatry is a volume business with a thin per-visit margin, and owners know exactly which parts of the schedule pay. Routine nail and callus care fills chairs but is largely non-covered by Medicare, so it runs as cash or rides along with a visit that has a covered reason. The revenue that keeps the lights on sits in procedures, in-office imaging, and dispensed equipment — braces, inserts, therapeutic shoes — and each of those carries a documentation chain tracing back to another doctor’s chart. Ask a practice manager what eats the week and the answer is chasing the certifying physician’s records for a shoe order. Missouri adds a constraint: ankle surgery must happen in a licensed hospital or surgical clinic with credentialing approval, so surgical volume depends on privileges. Since patients start by searching a category and a suburb, being listed with complete, current details is part of how that schedule stays full.

Not sure which foot doctor fits the problem you actually have? Browse podiatrists across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two offices with the same three sentences about your symptom and see which one asks a follow-up question before quoting you a visit.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Can I go to a podiatrist without a referral?

A.  Usually yes. A DPM is a licensed physician and surgeon of the foot and ankle, and Original Medicare doesn’t require a referral to see one. The catch is your specific plan: many HMO products and some Medicare Advantage plans require a referral from a primary care doctor before a specialist claim gets paid. Call the number on your card and ask about referral and prior-authorization rules before booking.

### Q. How to know if a podiatrist is good?

A.  Look for signals you can check rather than adjectives. Verify the license in Missouri or Illinois, ask whether the doctor is board certified and in what, and ask how often the office treats your specific problem. A good sign in the room: the doctor examines both feet, looks at your shoes, explains what happens if you do nothing, and gives you a plan with a checkpoint date, not an open-ended one.

### Q. Will a podiatrist remove an ingrown toenail?

A.  Yes, that’s standard podiatric care. The APMA says a podiatrist will remove the ingrown portion of the nail and may prescribe topical or oral medication for infection, and that chronic cases can be corrected permanently by removing the offending corner along with its matrix. APMA is blunt about bathroom surgery: do-it-yourself removal should be avoided, and people with diabetes or circulatory problems should seek care rather than self-treat.

### Q. What doctor to see for peroneal tendonitis?

A.  A podiatrist or an orthopedic foot-and-ankle specialist can both evaluate tendon pain on the outside of the ankle, and in Missouri the podiatric scope explicitly includes the ankle and the tendons that insert into the foot under RSMo 330.010. Practically, start with whoever can examine you soonest and image it. Only the clinician who actually examines your ankle can say what is happening inside it.

### Q. Why don’t podiatrists like Skechers?

A.  That premise doesn’t survive contact with the evidence. Skechers is listed among the companies in the APMA Seal Program, which reviews footwear through a panel of APMA member physicians and requires objective clinical or laboratory data behind product claims. APMA is careful that the Seal is a recognition, not an endorsement. Individual doctors have opinions about specific shoes for specific feet, which isn’t a brand verdict.

### Q. How much should a podiatrist visit cost?

A.  There isn’t a metro price, and any single number quoted online is guesswork. Cost turns on whether the visit is covered, whether X-rays or a procedure happen the same day, whether the office is in network, and whether the doctor accepts assignment. Under Medicare Part B, medically necessary treatment runs 20% of the approved amount after the deductible. Paying cash, request a good faith estimate in writing before the appointment.

### Q. Are podiatrists worth it?

A.  For a foot or ankle problem that has outlasted new shoes and rest, a specialist visit is generally worth the copay, if only to replace guessing with imaging. APMA notes that conservative measures — shoe and exercise recommendations, taping or strapping, orthotic devices, anti-inflammatory medication — resolve most heel and arch pain without surgery. Whether yours is one of those is a judgment that belongs to a doctor who sees your foot.

One last practical note. Feet are what people negotiate with longest before mentioning them to anyone, and that negotiation is cheaper to end early — especially for anyone with diabetes, where APMA advises seeking care rather than waiting. Write down when the pain started and what changed. Then call two offices.

## Buying From an Independent Liquor Store in St. Louis: Missouri and Illinois Rules
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/independent-liquor-store-st-louis-missouri-illinois-rules

Imagine it’s a Saturday afternoon in Kirkwood and somebody has handed you a job you didn’t ask for. Bring the bottle. Not a bottle — the bottle, the one that makes the table look up when it lands. You have forty minutes and no real plan.

Maybe your version starts in Florissant, where the assignment is a case of something cold for a graduation party. Maybe you’re in Belleville on a Sunday morning, finding out that the shop you use in Illinois and the one you use in Missouri do not run on the same clock. Maybe a cousin in Affton keeps texting about a bourbon nobody seems to have, and you’d like to know whether that’s a real shortage or a good story.

Here’s the part worth knowing. The state line runs straight through this metro, and Missouri and Illinois write their alcohol rules differently enough that the side you shop on changes the hours, the paperwork behind the counter, and how much a clerk may pour you. Here’s the other part. A small shop can do three or four things a warehouse aisle structurally cannot, and almost nobody asks.

### What are the alcohol laws in St. Louis, Missouri?

Missouri is among the least restrictive alcohol states in the country. Under RSMo 311.290 a licensed retailer may sell from 6:00 a.m. to 1:30 a.m., and Missouri puts no wall between store types — RSMo 311.200 lets drug stores, grocery stores, general merchandise stores and delicatessens hold a package license covering spirits, wine and beer alike. That is why the whiskey sits four aisles from the milk here and does not in most states.

Sunday is the exception that catches people out. Selling intoxicating liquor between 6:00 a.m. Sunday and 1:30 a.m. Monday takes a separate Sunday license under RSMo 311.293, which runs an extra $200 a year to the state, and a city or county may charge up to $300 more on top. A retailer licensed only for malt liquor may sell beer in that same Sunday window without it. So on a Sunday morning in Missouri, beer and bourbon are genuinely two different questions, and the answer changes store by store.

Age is simple and not negotiable: 21. RSMo 311.310 makes it a misdemeanor for a licensee or an employee to supply intoxicating liquor to anyone under 21, and RSMo 311.328 spells out what a clerk may accept — a valid, unexpired driver’s or nondriver’s license from any state or territory, an unexpired identification card issued by a uniformed service of the United States, or an unexpired passport. A photo of your license on your phone is not on that list.

### How do Illinois rules differ once you cross the river?

Illinois pushes the decisions down to the town. Under 235 ILCS 5/4-1, local governing bodies determine the number, kind and classification of liquor licenses and set the local fees, and the Illinois Liquor Control Commission licenses on top of that local approval. Hours of sale come from the municipality, or from the county in unincorporated areas. Two Metro East shops fifteen minutes apart can lawfully keep different Sunday hours.

Illinois also trains the people at the register by statute. Under 235 ILCS 5/6-27.1, anyone who sells or serves open containers — and anyone whose job description includes checking identification — must hold a BASSET certificate, valid for three years. The requirement phased in by county size, starting July 1, 2015 in Cook County and finishing July 1, 2018 in the smallest counties. Missouri has no statewide equivalent, which is a real difference in who is standing across the counter.

### Is it cheaper to buy liquor at the liquor store or the grocery store?

Usually the grocery store on the dozen brands everybody already knows, and usually the bottle shop on everything else. In Missouri both may sell the same spirits, so a supermarket prices the famous bottles thin to pull carts through the door and makes the money back somewhere else in the building. A small shop cannot win that fight and mostly does not try. It earns on the middle and top of the shelf, where a good recommendation beats fifty cents.

The bigger lever is the river. Missouri’s state excise tax on spirits is $2.00 a gallon under RSMo 311.550. Illinois charges $8.55 a gallon on liquor above 20% alcohol by volume, $1.39 a gallon on wine at or below 20%, and $0.231 on beer and cider, under 235 ILCS 5/8-1 — all before a county or city adds anything. On a 750-milliliter bottle of whiskey, that state gap by itself is about $1.30.

Where can I find the cheapest alcohol in St. Louis? There is no permanent answer, and any price list you read today is stale by the next distributor cycle. Do it this way instead. Pick the exact bottle and size, price it at two stores on your own side of the line, then ask whether a case break or a mixed-six discount applies. That last one is rarely posted and is often the biggest number in the conversation.

### What can a bottle shop’s staff do that a big-box cannot?

Three things, mainly: match a bottle to a stated budget and a stated occasion, order something they don’t carry, and let you taste before you commit. The tasting part is licensed, and the two states license it differently.

In Missouri, a package store already licensed under RSMo 311.200 and 311.293 can apply for a special permit under RSMo 311.294 to hold wine, malt beverage and distilled spirit tastings on the premises — an extra $25 a year — and that permit still does not let the store sell drinks for consumption there. In Illinois, 235 ILCS 5/6-31 sets the pour itself: a quarter ounce of distilled spirits, one ounce of wine, or two ounces of beer, and no more than three samples to one person in a day. Those are tasting pours, not servings. Everything here assumes 21 and over, and that whoever is driving home isn’t the one sampling.

Wildly off-topic — some day you’ll need a mortgage lender too.

### How do special orders and allocated bottles actually work?

Almost nothing arrives by magic. RSMo 311.280 makes it unlawful for a Missouri retail liquor licensee to buy intoxicating liquor from anyone except a duly licensed wholesale dealer in this state, and Illinois runs the same three-tier structure. So a special order is really one question asked twice: is this bottle registered and carried by a distributor in this state, and will that distributor break a case?

That structure is also why hard-to-find whiskey behaves the way it does. An allocation arrives from the distributor in a quantity the shop did not choose, and a store that receives six bottles has to decide who gets them. Ask how a given shop releases allocated stock — a waiting list, a raffle, in-person only, or bundled with other purchases — and ask in September rather than the week before Christmas. A shop that knows your name and your ceiling is doing something a self-checkout lane is not built to do.

### Can you ship liquor as a gift from St. Louis?

Not personally, no. Shipping alcohol to a consumer is a licensed activity in both states, and carrying a bottle to a parcel counter yourself is not one of the legal routes. Missouri allows a wine manufacturer holding a Missouri wine direct shipper license to send up to two cases of wine a month to a resident 21 or older, for personal use and not for resale, with the carton labeled “CONTAINS ALCOHOL: SIGNATURE OF PERSON AGE 21 OR OLDER REQUIRED FOR DELIVERY” under RSMo 311.185.

Illinois is narrower. A wine shipper licensee may ship no more than 12 cases of wine a year to an Illinois resident who is 21 or older under 235 ILCS 5/6-29, and the state deliberately keeps direct shipment closed for spirits and beer under 235 ILCS 5/6-29.1. In plain terms: wine can reach your aunt in Edwardsville from a licensed winery, bourbon cannot, and the gift that actually works across town is a bottle handed over in person or a gift card from the shop itself.

### What are the rules on growlers and kegs?

Missouri wrote its growler rules into statute in 2016. Under RSMo 311.201, an original-package retailer may fill 32 to 128 fluid ounces of draft beer for consumption off the premises, the employee doing the filling must be at least 21, and containers may be filled only on demand — no prefilling and setting them in a cooler. The tag has to carry the brand, the brewer, the class of product, net contents, the filling business’s name and address, the date of fill, and the line “This product may be unfiltered and unpasteurized. Keep refrigerated at all times.”

Kegs come with their own paperwork. RSMo 311.082 requires the retailer to attach a numbered identification tag, check a valid ID, and take a deposit of at least $50, with the purchaser record kept for three months and no refund on a keg returned without an intact tag. That section also preempts local keg ordinances, so the rule reads the same in Affton as it does in St. Charles. On the Illinois side, ask the shop and the local liquor commissioner, because the local license decides more of this than the state does.

### What running a bottle shop actually looks like

Beer is the loss leader and most of the labor. It is heavy, it is cold, it carries code dates, and the walk-in is the most expensive room in the building. The margin lives in wine, in the middle and upper spirits shelf, and in the mixers, ice and glassware nobody price-compares. Sourcing is not where an owner gets clever — RSMo 311.280 means every retailer in Missouri buys from the same licensed wholesalers, so you win on what you choose to carry and on the rep who decides where six allocated bottles land. Seasonality is unforgiving and entirely predictable: Thanksgiving week through New Year’s Eve, the Fourth of July, and a home playoff run. Owners trade the same complaints — allocation lists, thinning beer margins, and the twenty-minute taster who buys the cheapest thing on the shelf. Because people search by neighborhood at five o’clock on a Friday, a complete listing is how a shop gets found at the only moment that counts.

Related reading: if the bottle is the whole point of the trip, here’s how to plan a winery day trip from St. Louis.

Not sure which shop is worth the extra four minutes? Browse liquor stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the closest one and ask two questions — do you do special orders, and do you hold a tasting permit. Those answers sort the list fast. Where you drink instead of buy is a different decision with its own rules — we walk through the kinds of bars this metro actually has separately.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Where can I find the cheapest alcohol in St. Louis?

A.  On the Missouri side, generally, and by comparing the exact bottle rather than the store. Missouri’s state excise on spirits is $2.00 a gallon; Illinois charges $8.55 a gallon above 20% alcohol by volume, so the same whiskey carries roughly $1.30 more in state tax alone before local add-ons. After that, price one specific bottle at two stores near you and ask about case and mixed-six discounts, which are usually unposted.

### Q. Who is the cheapest liquor store?

A.  It moves, so treat any name you read online as already out of date. Supermarkets and warehouse clubs usually win on the dozen national brands they use to pull traffic through the door. Independents win on the rest of the shelf and on knowing what is good at your number. Price the bottle you want at two nearby stores, ask about a case break, and buy where the gap is real.

### Q. Where is the nearest liquor store in St. Louis?

A.  Search by your neighborhood rather than the city, and check hours before distance. In Missouri a licensed retailer may sell from 6:00 a.m. to 1:30 a.m., and selling spirits on a Sunday requires a separate license, so the closest shop is not automatically the open one. In Illinois the municipality sets the hours. Call first on Sunday mornings and after midnight.

### Q. How profitable is owning a liquor store?

A.  It depends on the mix, and any single margin figure you find online will be wrong for your store. Beer moves in volume at a thin margin, while wine, the middle and upper spirits shelf and accessories like mixers and ice carry the profit. Every Missouri retailer buys from the same licensed wholesalers under RSMo 311.280, so the variables are what you stock, your rent and labor, and the fourth quarter.

### Q. How to price a liquor store?

A.  Start from the fact that the license does not come with the keys. RSMo 311.250 says a Missouri liquor license is not transferable or assignable, apart from narrow exceptions for a deceased licensee’s family or a remaining partner, so the buyer has to qualify on their own. You are pricing cash flow, the lease and location, and saleable inventory at cost — then confirming the buyer can be licensed at all. Use an accountant and an attorney who have closed one before.

### Q. Is liquor cheaper in Missouri or Kansas?

A.  That comparison rarely matters from here — the Kansas line sits roughly 250 miles west, while the border that changes your receipt is the Mississippi. Missouri taxes spirits at $2.00 a gallon under RSMo 311.550, and Illinois charges $8.55 a gallon above 20% alcohol by volume under 235 ILCS 5/8-1, plus whatever the county or city adds. Skip the state-versus-state headline and price the actual bottle on both sides of the river.

## Kitchen Remodel Cost in St. Louis: How to Budget and Hire
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/kitchen-remodel-cost-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Tuesday evening in Affton. The pot is boiling over, the range hood has never actually moved air, and the only outlet that still works is the one hiding behind the toaster. You yank the drawer that sticks. You stare at the soffit eating eight inches of wall above the cabinets. And you say it out loud for the first time: we should just do the whole kitchen.

By Thursday you have three numbers. A design-build company in Kirkwood sends eleven pages. A guy your cousin in Florissant swears by writes one sheet by hand. A company advertising all over Belleville quotes you over the phone without ever opening a cabinet door. The three prices sit wildly far apart, and none of them describe the same kitchen.

That is the real problem with a whole-kitchen remodel, and it has nothing to do with tile. The word remodel covers three different projects. The trades arrive in a fixed order. The permit rules change when you cross the Mississippi. And a bid can look cheap because it quietly left things out. Here is how to scope it, price it, and read what somebody hands you.

### What is a realistic budget for a kitchen remodel?

A realistic kitchen budget starts with scope, not with a dollar figure. Decide first which of three projects you are buying: a cosmetic refresh that keeps your cabinet boxes and your layout, a replace-in-place remodel with all-new cabinets in the same footprint, or a full remodel that moves walls, plumbing, gas or the vent run. Those three have very different ceilings.

For a dated national anchor, Zonda’s 38th annual Cost vs. Value Report, released September 18, 2025, put a midrange minor kitchen remodel at $28,458 nationally and $32,141 back at resale — 112.9% of cost recouped, and the only interior project in the national top five. Major kitchen remodels in the same report recoup far less, generally around half of what they cost. That gap between a focused refresh and a gut job is the most useful budgeting fact on this page.

Those are national averages, not a quote for your house in Maryland Heights or Edwardsville. Labor rates, cabinet lead times and appliance pricing all move, so any printed number goes stale — that one included. Treat published figures as a sanity check and nothing more. The number worth trusting is the middle of three itemized proposals written against the same one-page scope, from companies that each walked your kitchen.

Set your walk-away number before the first showroom visit, and say it on the first phone call. Is $10,000 enough for a kitchen remodel? Not for a full one. It is real money for a refresh, though, and a company worth hiring will tell you that instead of talking you up into a gut job.

### What actually drives the price of a kitchen remodel?

Four things move the number far more than anything you pick off a showroom shelf: whether the layout changes, the cabinets, the countertop, and what the demo crew finds behind the plaster. The rest is rounding.

Layout changes. The moment the sink, range or refrigerator moves, you add drain and vent work, new supply lines, new circuits, and possibly a header if the wall you want gone is carrying load. Keeping the sink and the range where they already sit is the cheapest big decision available to you.

Cabinets. Almost always the largest line on the bid. A budget breakdown widely cited from the National Kitchen & Bath Association puts cabinets near 29% of a kitchen budget, labor near 17% and appliances near 14% — useful as proportions even when your totals look nothing like the averages. Stock, semi-custom and full custom are three separate price worlds, and our guide to choosing a cabinet maker in St. Louis goes deeper on that one decision.

Countertops. The slab is only part of it. A fabricator cannot template until the cabinets are installed and leveled, so the counter gets ordered late and arrives later still. Build that dead window into the schedule instead of discovering it.

What is behind the wall. In older metro housing — the brick four-families in south city, the postwar ranches in Affton and Overland, the century-old frame houses on the Belleville side — demo turns up ungrounded circuits, undersized panels, galvanized supply lines and floors out of level by an inch across the room. That is not a contractor being difficult. Ask before you sign how the contract handles it: an allowance, a published unit price, or a change order at whatever it costs on the day.

Appliances. Choose them before the cabinets are ordered. A 36-inch range, a panel-ready refrigerator or a hood that needs a real exterior vent run changes framing, electrical and cabinet dimensions — and cabinets are the one thing you cannot un-order.

### What is the 30% rule in remodeling?

The 30% rule is an informal budgeting guideline — not a code, not a law, not a lender requirement. It says keep total renovation spending at or below roughly 30% of your home’s current market value, and within that, hold a kitchen to somewhere around 5% to 15%. Its entire purpose is to stop you overcapitalizing: putting more into a house than the street will ever hand back.

Use it as a guardrail, then override it deliberately. Staying twenty years and cooking every night? Daily use beats resale math. Selling inside three years? The rule and the resale ratio both matter, and the smaller focused project is the one that pays. What no rule replaces is a contingency — hold money back for the unknown before you spend the last of the budget on a backsplash.

If you want one genuinely old thing in the room — a hutch, a light fixture, a slab with some history — estate sales and St. Louis auction houses are where those turn up, often for less than the reproduction costs new.

Unrelated, and we know it — your stove is off, so order pizza.

### Do you need a permit and a licensed contractor in Missouri or Illinois?

For a whole-kitchen remodel, yes — a building permit is required almost everywhere in this metro, and the licensing rules genuinely differ across the river. Neither Missouri nor Illinois issues a statewide general contractor license, so licensed means something local on the Missouri side and something trade-specific on the Illinois side.

Missouri side. Licensing runs city by city and county by county. In unincorporated St. Louis County and in municipalities that contract with the county for residential code enforcement, a kitchen, bath and laundry remodel needs a permit, and the county issues trade permits only to licensed contractors — licensed master plumbers, licensed electrical contractors and licensed residential HVAC contractors. In the City of St. Louis, permits run through the Building Division. St. Charles County, Jefferson County and every incorporated municipality set their own rules, so ask which office is issuing your permit before you sign anything.

Missouri also gives you three business days to cancel a home solicitation sale — a contract signed at your house after someone solicited you there — under RSMo 407.705, which counts a business day as any day except Saturday, Sunday and legal holidays. It does not cover a contract you signed in a showroom you drove to. A knock on the door is a different animal from a company you went looking for.

Illinois side. Plumbing is licensed statewide. The Illinois Department of Public Health licenses plumbers and plumbing contractors under the Illinois Plumbing License Law, so the plumber touching your kitchen in Belleville, Edwardsville or O’Fallon holds a state license you can ask to see.

Illinois also writes consumer protection straight into your contract. Under the Home Repair and Remodeling Act (815 ILCS 513), work over $1,000 requires a written contract stating the total cost, including parts and materials, before work begins. The contractor must also hand you the Attorney General’s pamphlet titled “Home Repair: Know Your Consumer Rights” before you sign, and you sign an acknowledgment that you got it. Section 25 requires public liability and property damage insurance of at least $100,000 per person and $300,000 per occurrence for bodily injury, plus $50,000 per occurrence for property damage, unless the business has a net worth of at least $1,000,000. A contractor who has never heard of that pamphlet is telling on themselves; the Illinois Attorney General’s home repair page is worth ten minutes.

Pull the permit either way. An inspected kitchen leaves a paper trail, and unpermitted work has a habit of surfacing during a home inspection years later, when you are the one with a closing date.

### In what order do the trades work on a kitchen remodel?

A kitchen runs in a fixed sequence, and trying to jump it is what creates most delays. The order looks like this:

Design and final selections — cabinets, counters, tile, fixtures and appliance model numbers — locked before anyone swings a hammer.

Permit application and approval.

Demolition, disposal and the temporary kitchen setup.

Framing and structural work, including any header for a wall you removed.

Rough-in: plumbing, electrical, HVAC and the range vent.

Rough inspection. The job stops here until it passes.

Insulation, drywall, tape and first paint.

Flooring, when the floor runs under the cabinets.

Cabinet installation, shimmed and leveled.

Countertop template, fabrication and installation — usually the longest single wait in the job.

Backsplash, plumbing trim, electrical trim and appliance hookup.

Final inspection and punch list.

The consequence nobody warns you about: your sink is out of service from demo day until the counter is set and the plumber returns. Plan the temporary kitchen before demo — refrigerator relocated, microwave, coffee maker, folding table, dishwashing in the laundry sink. Households that skip that step eat out five nights a week and blow the budget sideways.

### How do you read a kitchen remodel bid?

Compare scope, not totals. A bid you can actually evaluate names the cabinet brand, door style and box construction, the countertop material and edge profile, the appliance model numbers, who pulls the permit, and what is excluded. When two bids land $20,000 apart, the difference is almost always in what one of them left out.

Allowances. Dollar placeholders for tile, fixtures or appliances you have not chosen. Ask what happens when you exceed one, and whether unused money comes back to you.

Exclusions. Painting the adjoining room, floor refinishing, panel upgrades and appliance haul-away are the common ones.

Permit responsibility. Name who applies and who pays the fee.

Payment schedule. Draws tied to completed milestones, not calendar dates.

Change order clause. In writing, priced, and signed before the extra work happens.

Lien waivers. From the contractor and the subcontractors with each draw, so a paid job cannot come back at you as a lien.

Warranty. How long on labor, and who chases a manufacturer defect on your behalf.

Substantial completion date and what happens if it slips.

Red flags: a single-page lump sum with no line items, a deposit large enough to fund somebody else’s job, verbal change orders, a price that expires if you do not sign tonight, and any company that will not put its license and insurance in writing.

### Where do kitchen remodels actually go wrong?

Most kitchen projects fail on decisions, not on craftsmanship. Unfinished selections are the number one schedule killer: a crew cannot set cabinets around a tile you have not chosen, and a crew standing still is a crew that has moved to another job and will come back when the calendar allows. Lock every selection before demo and put the list in the contract.

While we are at it is how a $45,000 kitchen becomes a $60,000 one without a single bad decision. Refinish the hall floor since the sander is here. Repaint the dining room since the trim is off. Each addition is reasonable alone; together they are the overage. If you want them, price them at bid time so they land in the plan instead of a change order.

The rest of the list is short and preventable: appliance specs chosen after the cabinets were ordered, no temporary kitchen, skipping the permit, and picking the low bid without first normalizing scope so you are comparing the same kitchen.

### What does a kitchen remodel look like from the remodeler’s side?

Margins are thinner than homeowners assume. In the National Association of Home Builders’ Remodelers’ Cost of Doing Business Study, published April 8, 2026 on 2024 results, remodelers averaged a 29.9% gross profit margin, spent 23.6% of revenue on operating expenses and finished with a 6.3% net profit margin. Trade contractor costs alone ate 30% of revenue in 2024, down from 36% in 2021. On a $60,000 kitchen that average net is under $4,000, and it evaporates when a crew sits idle two weeks waiting on a tile decision. The front end is the other invisible cost: measuring, drawing and pricing a kitchen takes unpaid hours, and most of those bids never become jobs, which is why more shops now charge a design retainer and why the complaint remodelers trade with each other is that a careful bid gets used as free estimating for somebody else’s contract. Being findable matters too — homeowners search this work by neighborhood, and local companies can get listed on St Louis Near Me Directory.

Ready for three real bids instead of three guesses? Browse kitchen remodelers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then write your scope on one page — layout change or not, cabinet grade, countertop material, appliance list — and hand that identical page to every company you call.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Can I redo my kitchen for $10,000?

A.  You can redo a kitchen for $10,000. You cannot rebuild one. At that level you keep the cabinet boxes and the layout and spend on paint or refacing, new hardware, a countertop on a modest footprint, a sink and faucet, lighting and flooring. Move the sink or order new cabinets and the number leaves that range immediately.

### Q. Is $30,000 enough for a kitchen remodel?

A.  Often yes, for a replace-in-place kitchen in a modest footprint: new stock or entry semi-custom cabinets in the same layout, a quartz or laminate counter, flooring, lighting and standard appliances. Zonda’s 2025 Cost vs. Value Report put the national midrange minor kitchen remodel at $28,458, so $30,000 is genuine money. It stops being enough the moment walls or plumbing move.

### Q. How much remodeling can be done with $100,000?

A.  In this metro, $100,000 generally reaches full-remodel territory for one kitchen: a layout change, custom or upper semi-custom cabinets, stone counters, upgraded appliances, new circuits and lighting, and finish work spilling into the adjoining room. It can also cover a mid-level kitchen plus a bathroom. What it should never do is get allocated down to the last dollar.

### Q. What is the new kitchen trend for 2026?

A.  The NKBA and KBIS 2026 Kitchen Trends Report, released September 18, 2025 from 634 industry professionals, points toward timeless over trendy. Seventy-two percent expect transitional or timeless kitchens to lead the next three years, and 96% name neutrals as the most popular colors, with greens at 86% and blues at 78%. White oak leads the woods at 51%, and quartz counters sit at 62%.

### Q. What are some reputable kitchen remodeling companies in Saint Louis, Missouri?

A.  No honest article hands you a ranked list, because reputable depends on your scope, your budget and your jurisdiction. Build the list yourself. Look for companies that pull permits where you live, carry current liability and workers’ compensation coverage, produce three references from kitchens finished within two years, and put an itemized scope in writing. Then call those references.

### Q. Who are some reputable kitchen remodelers in St. Louis?

A.  Whoever hands you a name — a neighbor, a search result, a directory listing — run the same four checks before you sign. Verify the trade licenses your jurisdiction requires, ask for a certificate of insurance sent directly from the agent, confirm in writing who pulls the permit, and read the change order clause twice. On the Illinois side, also ask for the Attorney General’s consumer rights pamphlet.

### Q. How long does a full kitchen remodel take?

A.  Plan in two stages. Design, selections, cabinet ordering and permits usually take longer than the construction itself, and cabinet lead time is the wild card — ask for the current lead time in writing before you sign. Once demo starts, the countertop template and fabrication window is the built-in pause. Ask for a written schedule showing the rough inspection and the template date.

### Q. Do I need to move out during a kitchen remodel?

A.  Most households stay put. Set up the temporary kitchen before demo: refrigerator relocated, microwave, coffee maker, a folding table, paper plates, and dishwashing in a laundry sink or a bathtub. Ask the contractor about dust containment, where the dumpster sits, working hours and which bathroom the crew uses. Families with a toddler often plan a week away during demo.

## How to Choose a Jeweler in St. Louis: Buying, Repair and Appraisals
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-jeweler-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Thursday night in Affton and you’re rinsing plates when something small pings off the edge of the sink. You look down. One prong on your ring is bare, bent back like a tiny open hand, and whatever it was holding is somewhere between the drain and the floor.

Maybe your version is quieter. A watch in a Florissant nightstand that stopped in 2019 and has been going to the shop ever since. Your grandmother’s pearls in a St. Charles closet, the silk gone gray and slack. A chain that let go at the clasp in Belleville. Or nothing broken at all — just a ring you plan to buy in the next four months, and a suspicion that the second you walk in, somebody starts selling.

Those are all the same errand. They end at a bench, with somebody holding a loupe, and the difference between a good outcome and an expensive one is mostly about which counter you walk up to.

### Who is the best jeweler in St. Louis?

There isn’t one, and a shop that claims the title is selling you something. “Best” splits by job. The store that sets a beautiful engagement ring is not automatically the shop you want retipping worn prongs, restringing pearls, or writing an appraisal your insurer will accept. Choose per task, using four tests.

First, is there a bench on site? Ask it plainly — “do you do the work here, or does it ship out?” Neither answer is disqualifying, but shipped-out work means longer turnaround and a middleman between you and the person holding the torch. Second, credentials: the recognized gemological credential is Graduate Gemologist (G.G.) from the Gemological Institute of America, and on the appraisal side an ASA Master Gemologist Appraiser or a National Association of Jewelry Appraisers certification. Third, a written estimate before any work starts, split into metal and labor.

The fourth test is the real one. Will they talk you out of something? A jeweler who says “that chain isn’t worth soldering, here’s why” is showing you how they think. Bring one small job first — a battery, a clasp, a cleaning — before you hand over the ring that matters.

### What can a local jeweler do that an online retailer can’t?

Everything that happens after the sale. Sizing, prong retipping, shank replacement, stone tightening, rhodium plating on white gold, pearl restringing, watch batteries and gaskets, band links, laser welding next to heat-sensitive stones, and an appraisal signed by someone you can go back and find. A website ships you a ring. It cannot put your ring under magnification and tell you a prong has gone thin.

Fit is the underrated one. Ring size shifts with heat, salt, pregnancy, weight and time of day — a hand sized in a July parking lot in Maryland Heights is not the same hand in January. A bench jeweler also knows when a ring cannot be sized: full eternity bands with stones all the way around, some tension settings, and pieces set with stones that will not tolerate a torch usually have to be remade rather than adjusted.

### Is it cheaper to go to a local jeweler?

On the sticker, sometimes not. On the total, often yes, because the sticker isn’t the whole price — add shipping, resizing an online ring somewhere else, a return that goes sideways, and repairs you now have no local relationship for. Metal cost is the same for everyone: gold traded around $4,395 per troy ounce on August 17, 2026, and every shop on both sides of the river buys at that market.

Sales tax is a genuine St. Louis variable. Missouri’s state rate is 4.225% plus local add-ons; Illinois taxes general merchandise at 6.25% plus local. On a $5,000 purchase that gap is not trivial, but local rates can close it or flip it, so ask for the out-the-door total in Kirkwood and in Edwardsville before deciding the river matters. One thing is settled: under Missouri statute 144.815, bullion and investment coins are exempt from sales tax. Jewelry is not, no matter how much gold is in it.

Wildly off-topic — the ring can wait, but a good coffee shop can’t.

### How do you buy an engagement ring without being sold to?

Decide the number before you walk in, say it out loud in the first two minutes, and ask to see the grading report on any center stone. That one sentence changes the conversation from “what can we get you into” to “what can we build at this number.” The old two-months-salary rule was marketing, not math.

Know the market so nobody can frame your budget as unusual. The Knot’s 2026 Real Weddings Study, covering weddings held in 2025, found 61% of engagement rings now have a lab-grown center stone, an average center of 1.9 carats, and average spend of $4,600. Lab-grown is real diamond, and the Federal Trade Commission’s Jewelry Guides at 16 CFR Part 23 require sellers to disclose clearly that a stone is laboratory-grown, and to disclose treatments that aren’t permanent or that need special care. If a stone’s origin or treatment history stays vague, the vagueness is your answer.

Then ask two questions. Which of the four Cs would you spend my money on, and which would you trade down? A jeweler who answers “cut, always, and I’d drop a color grade” is thinking about how the ring looks on a hand. And what does this ring cost to own — sizing, inspection schedule, and whether the warranty requires you to bring it back on a set interval to stay valid. Many service plans do.

### What month is jewelry cheapest?

No month carries a guaranteed discount, because jewelry pricing tracks metal markets and inventory rather than a sale calendar. What is real is how lopsided the year is. In 2019, the last clean year before the Census Bureau’s jewelry-store sales series was reclassified, December alone accounted for about $5.85 billion of roughly $30.9 billion in U.S. jewelry-store sales — close to a fifth of the year in one month.

The practical read: the quiet stretches are mid-January into early February and the back half of summer. That is when you get an unhurried hour with a jeweler, faster bench turnaround, and a real shot at negotiating on a case piece that has been sitting. Metal prices can still move against you, so a February break on labor doesn’t guarantee a lower total. Buy when you have time to ask questions.

### What jewelry repairs are worth doing, and what aren’t?

Worth doing, almost always: retipping or rebuilding prongs before a stone is lost, replacing a worn shank on a ring you wear daily, tightening stones, replacing a failed clasp, and restringing pearls. A prong retip is a fraction of the cost of replacing a lost center stone, and you rarely find the stone. Worth questioning: soldering a thin chain that has already broken twice, or plating a piece that will need replating every year. With gold near record levels, added metal is a real cost line, and an estimate split into metal and labor shows you which half you are paying for.

Maintenance, simple version. The Gemological Institute of America recommends professional cleaning and inspection roughly every six months to a year on pieces you wear often. Pearls strung on silk stretch — if they slide between the knots or the thread looks yellowed and frayed, it is past due, and regular-wear strands generally go back for restringing every one to two years, knotted between every pearl so a break costs you one pearl instead of the strand. Keep pearls, opals and oiled emeralds out of ultrasonic cleaners; the vibration and heat are exactly wrong for them.

### How do you get a watch battery and band done right?

Ask for the gasket and a pressure test, not just the cell. Opening a case back breaks the factory seal, and the rubber gasket that made the watch water resistant compresses and dries with age. A shop doing it properly inspects or replaces the seals, lubricates them, closes the case, and pressure-tests the watch to confirm it still meets its rating — ISO 22810 is the general water-resistance standard, ISO 6425 the stricter one for dive watches.

If the watch is dead, don’t assume the battery is the whole story. A quartz movement that sat with a leaking cell can be corroded past a simple swap, and a good counter tells you that before charging for a battery that fixes nothing. Band work is the easy win: sizing a bracelet, replacing spring bars before one shears in a parking lot, swapping a cracked strap. A shop with a watchmaker on staff often does those while you wait.

### What does an insurance appraisal actually do?

It sets the number your insurer will pay and gets your jewelry out from under the policy sublimit. Standard homeowners and renters policies cap jewelry theft losses low — commonly $1,000 to $2,500, with $1,500 the figure you see most — no matter what the ring is worth. Scheduling a piece with an appraisal replaces that cap with the appraised amount and usually broadens what is covered, including simply losing it.

Get the appraisal from someone whose interest is the document, not the merchandise; an appraiser who also wants to buy the piece has a reason to name a number in one direction or the other. Expect a full description — measurements, weights, grades, photographs — rather than a one-line value. Then revisit it. Most appraisers suggest updating every two to three years, and with gold up sharply over the past year, a 2021 appraisal is not describing 2026 replacement cost.

### What should you know before selling old gold or buying estate pieces?

Missouri regulates the transaction, and it is worth knowing before you hand anything across a counter. Under Missouri statute 407.292, a buyer of gold, silver or platinum must record a copy of your photo ID and your details on a form you sign, keep that record one year for law enforcement inspection, and hold each item unaltered for ten full days before it is altered or resold. Buying from a minor requires written authority from a parent or guardian. Pawnbrokers and scrap metal dealers sit outside that section. Illinois handles secondhand and resale dealers under its own statutes, so expect different paperwork at a Belleville or Edwardsville counter — ask what they are required to record before you choose where to sell.

Two checks on any older piece. Look for a maker’s mark beside the karat stamp: federal law at 15 U.S.C. § 297 requires a quality mark like 14K to carry the registered trademark or name of the firm standing behind it, so a stamp with nobody’s name attached deserves a test rather than trust. And get more than one offer, because scrap is quoted as a percentage of melt and that percentage is negotiable. Estate and vintage jewelry moves through the saleroom as well as the shop, so it is worth reading how St. Louis auction houses work before you assume a store is the only buyer or the only seller.

### What the counter looks like from the jeweler’s side

The display case is not where the money is. Loose diamonds often sit on memo — supplier goods a shop shows without owning — and bridal is the most price-shopped merchandise in the store. The steady margin is bench labor: sizings, retips, restrings, clasps, batteries. That is skill and time rather than inventory, which is why gold above $4,000 an ounce squeezes a display case far harder than it squeezes a repair ticket. The calendar is unforgiving too: December carries close to a fifth of the year, Valentine’s Day and Mother’s Day add two more spikes, and late summer is the quiet stretch when your repair actually turns around fast. The complaint jewelers trade with each other is the phone quote — a price demanded on a repair nobody has seen. People look for this work locally, block by block, which is why a complete, current listing is how a bench gets found; shops can add or claim a listing.

Got a ring sitting in a drawer waiting on a decision? Browse jewelry stores and jewelers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them with the same three questions — is the bench on site, what does a written estimate cost, and what is the turnaround this month. A good night of sleep outlasts most purchases — see how to buy a mattress without getting worked over.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much should jewelry cost?

A.  It depends on metal weight, stone quality and labor, so there is no single right number — but you can price it structurally. Ask for the quote split into metal, stones and bench time, ask what changes if you drop one grade of color or clarity, and compare two shops on the same specification rather than on a headline price. A piece you wear daily justifies more metal; a piece you wear twice a year does not.

### Q. Is $3,000 cheap for an engagement ring?

A.  No, it sits in normal territory. The Knot’s 2026 Real Weddings Study put average engagement ring spend at $4,600 for weddings held in 2025, with 61% of rings using a lab-grown center stone, and averages get pulled upward by a small number of very large purchases. What matters more than the number is where it goes: cut quality and a setting built to hold the stone outlive an extra tenth of a carat.

### Q. What are the 5 C’s of jewelry?

A.  Officially there are four. GIA founder Robert M. Shipley coined the four Cs — color, clarity, cut and carat weight — in the 1940s as a teaching device, and the earliest GIA course material naming them dates to 1949. The commonly cited fifth C is certification, meaning an independent grading report, but it was never part of GIA’s system. Treat it as good buying advice rather than a grading standard.

### Q. What is the 2:1:1 rule in jewelry?

A.  It is a styling ratio, not a valuation rule. The idea is to balance a look by mixing impact levels instead of piling everything in one place — commonly two quieter pieces, one medium and one statement, or two rings on one hand and one on the other. Interpretations vary by stylist, which tells you it is a guideline. It has nothing to do with quality, price, or how a jeweler quotes a repair.

### Q. What is the hottest jewelry right now?

A.  Lab-grown center stones are the clearest shift in the numbers: The Knot’s 2026 study found 61% of engagement rings now use one, a 239% jump since 2020, with average center size at 1.9 carats. Beyond bridal, gold’s run to record levels has pushed buyers toward lighter hollow chains, vintage and estate pieces, and remounting stones they already own instead of paying for new metal.

### Q. How often should I have my rings checked?

A.  Every six months to a year if you wear them daily, which matches GIA’s guidance on professional cleaning and inspection. The check takes minutes: a jeweler looks at prong tips, tests whether stones move under a probe, and inspects the shank for thinning. If your ring came with a service plan, read the interval — many require a documented inspection on a schedule to keep the coverage alive.

### Q. Can a local jeweler repair a ring I bought online?

A.  Usually yes, and this is where a bench relationship pays for itself. Sizing, prong work and stone tightening do not care where the ring came from. Two limits worth raising up front: full eternity bands and some tension settings cannot be sized conventionally, and repairs done elsewhere can void an online retailer’s own warranty, so check that policy before you hand the ring over.

## Hearing Aids in St. Louis: How to Get Tested, Fitted and Covered
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/hearing-aids-st-louis-what-to-expect

Imagine it’s a Sunday afternoon and you’re at the long table at a family birthday in Affton. Somebody down at the far end tells a story. Everybody laughs. You laugh a beat late, because you caught maybe half of it and filled in the rest. You blame the room. The room is loud.

Then it happens again over dinner in Kirkwood. Then in the car back to St. Charles, when your daughter has to say it twice. Your spouse has started mentioning the TV volume in a tone that isn’t really a question, and at some point you began aiming your good ear at the table without ever deciding to.

This is where most people stall — not because they don’t care, but because nobody tells them what the first step is. Who is qualified to test you. Whether the device advertised online for a couple hundred dollars is the same thing a clinic in Florissant or Belleville would fit. Below is the map. It is not medical advice, and nothing on this page can tell you whether your hearing loss is serious. Only a clinician who tests your ears can answer that.

### Who is the best hearing aid supplier?

There isn’t one, and any list that names a winner is ranking products, not your ears. What separates providers in the St. Louis metro is checkable in about ten minutes: whether the person holds a current state license, whether they verify the device’s output inside your ear canal instead of trusting the fitting software, what the written trial period and return terms say, and what the quoted price still includes after you walk out the door.

Two people with identical audiograms can end up with wildly different outcomes from the same model of hearing aid, because the fitting is the treatment. The device is just hardware. So the questions worth asking on the phone before you book are boring, specific, and revealing:

Are you a licensed audiologist or a licensed hearing instrument specialist — and can I have your license number?

Do you do real-ear (probe microphone) verification at the fitting?

How many follow-up visits are included in the price, and for how long?

What is the trial period, and what is nonrefundable if I return the aids?

If I buy through my insurance plan, what changes about the service I get?

Missouri and Illinois both publish licensee lookups, and both are free. The Missouri Board of Examiners for Hearing Instrument Specialists sits inside the state’s Division of Professional Registration and takes consumer complaints directly. In Illinois, hearing instrument dispensers are licensed through the Illinois Department of Public Health.

### What is the difference between an audiologist and a hearing instrument specialist?

Training and scope. An audiologist holds a graduate degree — typically an AuD or a PhD — and performs diagnostic hearing and balance evaluations. A hearing instrument specialist (you’ll also see hearing aid dispenser, fitter, or dealer) is a state-licensed professional who conducts basic hearing tests, then fits and dispenses hearing aids. Both can sell you a hearing aid. Only audiologists can bill insurance, including Medicare, for medically necessary hearing and balance evaluations, per the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association.

The two states license them through different doors, which trips people up crossing the river. In Missouri, hearing instrument specialists fall under Chapter 346 and their own Board of Examiners, while audiologists are licensed under Chapter 345 through the Board of Registration for the Healing Arts. In Illinois, dispensers answer to the Department of Public Health and audiologists to the Department of Financial and Professional Regulation.

Neither title is a verdict on quality. A meticulous specialist who runs real-ear measurements on every fitting will serve you better than an audiologist who skips them. The credential says what someone may do; the protocol says what they actually do.

### How are OTC hearing aids different from prescription ones?

Over-the-counter hearing aids are for adults 18 and older with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss, and you can buy them in a store or online with no exam, no prescription, and no professional fitting. That category took effect on October 17, 2022. A prescription hearing aid is, by the FDA’s definition, any hearing aid that is not an OTC hearing aid — available only through a licensed hearing health care professional who programs it to your specific loss, at any age and any severity.

The FDA is blunt about the ceiling: OTC devices are limited in maximum output and are not intended for severe or profound hearing loss. Anyone under 18 needs a prescription device. And the box has to earn its keep — FDA labeling rules require the outside packaging to show the words “OTC” and “hearing aid,” the warning conditions, battery information, whether a phone or remote is needed, whether the unit is used or rebuilt, and the manufacturer’s return policy. The FDA does not require a warranty at all, so read that panel before you pay.

One detail almost nobody knows: you can be tested by a professional and still buy elsewhere. The FDA says outright that you may request your hearing evaluation records and purchase your hearing aid somewhere else. A test and a purchase are two separate decisions.

### What happens at a hearing evaluation?

Expect roughly an hour, most of it sitting down. The clinician takes a history, looks in your ear canals, and then puts you in a sound-treated booth with headphones to find the softest tones you can detect across pitches, usually followed by word-repetition testing and a quick pressure test of the eardrum. Results land on an audiogram — a chart, not a diagnosis — and the clinician walks you through it.

Bring somebody whose voice you struggle with, because their presence changes what gets tested and what gets discussed. Bring a written list of the rooms that defeat you: the church basement in Maryland Heights, the shop floor, the restaurant with the tin ceiling, a tented graduation party in the yard. That last one is its own species of hard room — if you’re hosting it, our rundown of what to ask before booking party rentals in St. Louis covers the tent end of it.

If it goes as far as a fitting, ask about verification. Professional guidance from ASHA and the American Academy of Audiology says the prescribed output should be verified with a probe microphone placed in the ear canal — real-ear measurement — rather than assumed from the manufacturer’s software. Ear canals differ in length and shape, and a device set correctly on a screen can be badly off inside a particular ear.

### What are the red flags for audiology referrals?

The FDA prints a specific list on OTC hearing aid packaging under the heading “When to See a Doctor,” and it is the closest thing to an official answer. See a doctor, preferably an ear-nose-throat physician, if any of these apply to you:

Your ear has a birth defect or unusual shape, or was injured or deformed in an accident.

You saw blood, pus, or fluid coming out of your ear in the past six months.

Your ear feels painful or uncomfortable.

You have a lot of ear wax, or you think something could be in your ear.

You get really dizzy, or have a feeling of spinning or swaying.

Your hearing changed suddenly in the past six months.

Your hearing changes: it gets worse, then gets better again.

You have worse hearing in one ear.

You hear ringing or buzzing in only one ear.

That list is a routing instruction, not a diagnosis. It exists because hearing loss can come from something as ordinary as impacted wax or as consequential as a growth on the hearing nerve, and an amplifier fixes neither. Nobody reading a web page can tell you which you have.

### How much should a decent hearing aid cost?

It depends almost entirely on what is folded into the price, which is why quotes swing so hard. The National Council on Aging puts the typical cost of a pair of prescription hearing aids at roughly $2,500 to $3,690, citing published research, while OTC devices can start around $200. Neither number is a St. Louis price list. Both are a starting point for the only question that matters: what am I buying besides the plastic?

Traditional practices bundle. The FDA said as much in the 2022 rule, expecting OTC availability to lower costs by unbundling hearing aids from professional advice, fitting, adjustment, and maintenance. In a bundled quote, the device price is also paying for the fitting appointment, the tweaks at week six, cleanings, tubing changes, and often a loss-and-damage warranty for several years. In an unbundled quote, the device is cheaper and each visit has a fee. Neither is a scam. They are different structures, and comparing one to the other on the sticker alone will mislead you every time.

What genuinely moves the number: one device or two, the technology tier within a manufacturer’s lineup, rechargeable versus disposable batteries, years of follow-up included, warranty length, and whether an insurance contract sets the fee. What matters less than people assume: the physical style of the aid.

Nothing to do with ears — where to find St. Louis plumbers.

### How much does Medicare cover for a hearing aid?

Original Medicare covers nothing toward hearing aids, and nothing toward the exams used to fit them. Medicare.gov states it plainly: you pay all costs. What Part B does cover is diagnostic hearing and balance exams ordered by your doctor or other provider to determine whether you need medical treatment. After the Part B deductible you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, plus a copayment if the service happens in a hospital outpatient setting.

There is one useful wrinkle. Since January 1, 2023, you can see an audiologist once every 12 months without an order from a provider — but only for non-acute hearing conditions, such as hearing loss that developed over many years, and not for exams meant to prescribe or fit hearing aids. That distinction is the whole game with Medicare and hearing.

Medicare Advantage plans are a different animal and may add hearing benefits Original Medicare leaves out. Call your plan and ask three things: the hearing allowance, which providers are in network, and whether the benefit resets annually. Open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7, with new coverage starting January 1. Veterans have another road entirely — through VA audiology, hearing aids, repairs and batteries come at no charge to eligible enrolled veterans, and the VA St. Louis Health Care System keeps main campuses on North Grand Boulevard in the city and at Jefferson Barracks in south county.

### What does the trial period actually protect in Missouri and Illinois?

In Illinois, quite a lot. Under the Hearing Instrument Consumer Protection Act, every hearing instrument offered for sale must come with a 30-business-day return privilege, and the receipt or contract has to state your right to return it for a refund within 30 business days of delivery. If a nonrefundable dispensing fee or restocking fee will be withheld, those terms must be stated in writing too. Business day there excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays — so 30 business days is closer to six weeks on the calendar.

Missouri takes the disclosure route instead of setting a minimum. Section 346.020 requires the purchase agreement to carry the licensee’s signature, business address and license number, the make, model and serial number, the exact down payment, the length of any trial period, any fees tied to that trial, and any right you have to return the instrument.
