### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Is it cheaper to rent a tent or a venue?

A.  A tent is cheaper on the invoice and more expensive in everything else. A venue rolls tables, chairs, restrooms, power, parking and a rain plan into one number. A tent covers ground and nothing more, so the honest comparison adds everything you put under it plus the labor of running the day yourself.

### Q. How much does it cost to rent a 20x20 event tent?

A.  Ask for a written quote rather than trusting a number off the internet. The same 20x20 prices differently depending on how it is anchored, how tight the delivery window is, and whether the date falls in peak season. Staking into grass is cheapest; ballasting on pavement adds weights and labor. Sidewalls, lighting and the damage waiver move it further.

### Q. How much do chair rentals typically cost?

A.  Chairs price per chair, and that figure is only part of it. Style matters most — a white folding chair, a resin garden chair and a wooden crossback are three tiers. Then delivery, whether the crew sets them out or leaves them stacked, the waiver, and quantity. Ask for the all-in total, delivered.

### Q. Is it cheaper to buy or rent a bounce house?

A.  Renting wins unless you use one many times a year. A purchased inflatable brings storage, a blower, cleaning, patching and the setup you were paying someone else to do. It also brings the liability: a rental company carries insurance, checks anchoring, and in Illinois must hold a current state permit for public use.

### Q. Are bounce house rentals worth it?

A.  For a party with young kids it is usually the one item that earns its price, because it occupies the guests you were most worried about. The value drops fast if the yard is wrong — not enough flat space, no anchor points, a long carry from the truck. Confirm footprint, power and surface before booking.

### Q. What age is appropriate for a bounce house?

A.  Go by the unit, not a general rule. Every commercial inflatable carries a manufacturer placard listing age, height and weight limits and the maximum riders at once, and that placard governs. The practical rule operators use is to keep sizes separated, since little kids and big kids bouncing together is where injuries come from.

### Q. Where can I rent an event tent in St. Louis, MO?

A.  Search party equipment rentals by your municipality rather than the whole metro, since delivery zones and fees are drawn tightly around a company’s yard. A vendor twenty minutes closer often quotes better than a bigger name across the river. Ask each the same three things: tent size, anchoring, and their written weather policy.

## How to Book a Campsite Near St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-book-a-campsite-near-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Wednesday in March and somebody in the group chat types “let’s camp Memorial Day weekend.” Six people react with a thumbs up. Nobody books anything. Then it’s the second week of May, you finally open the reservation site, and every electric site within ninety minutes of Kirkwood is spoken for.

Maybe your version is different. You bought a used travel trailer off a driveway in Florissant over the winter and you still aren’t sure whether the cord coming out the back is 30 amp or 50. Or the kids are seven and four, nobody in the house has ever slept in a tent, and you want a first night out close enough to Affton that bailing at midnight is still an option.

Camping around here is genuinely easy. The booking is where people get burned, because the two states on either side of the river run separate systems, open their calendars at different times, cap your stay differently, and price a night outdoors far enough apart that the bridge is worth crossing.

### What is the best campground near St. Louis?

There isn’t a single best one, and any list that names one is guessing for you. The best campground near St. Louis is whichever one matches three things: what you sleep in, how far ahead you booked, and whether you need a shower. Sort by those and the field narrows fast.

On the Missouri side, the close ring of state park campgrounds includes Dr. Edmund A. Babler Memorial State Park at 800 Guy Park Drive in Wildwood, Robertsville State Park where the Meramec River and Calvey Creek meet in Franklin County, and Meramec State Park at 115 Meramec Park Drive in Sullivan, which puts Fisher Cave and river access in the same trip. Cuivre River State Park north of Troy and Washington State Park south of De Soto fill out the arc.

Cross the river and the math changes. Pere Marquette State Park in Grafton runs 80 reservable Class A sites with 20, 30 and 50 amp service and a shower building, plus non-reservable Class B tent sites. Eldon Hazlet State Recreation Area on Carlyle Lake is bigger than anything close on the Missouri side: 328 Class A sites with 30 and 50 amp hookups, 36 walk-in Class C tent sites and three shower buildings. Closest of all is Horseshoe Lake State Park in Madison, Illinois — 26 tent or trailer sites, a dump station, pit toilets and water hydrants, open May 1 through September 30, no reservations taken.

### How much does it cost to camp at a Missouri state park?

On the 2026 on-season chart, which covers April 1 through October 31, most Missouri state parks charge $15 a night for a basic or walk-in site, $27 for a 30-amp electric site and $29 for 50-amp. Electric and water together runs about $35. A full sewer, electric and water site lands between $42 and $57 depending on the park.

Backcountry sites are $10. A few parks sit below the common rate — Echo Bluff starts at $13 basic, St. Joe at $12 — and a few sit a dollar or two above. Off-season, November 1 through March 31, the same tiers drop to roughly $14 basic, $23 for 30 amp and $25 for 50 amp.

Add the booking cost on top. Missouri charges $6.50 per campsite reserved online, $8 through the call center at 877-422-6766, $5.25 to change a reservation and $10 to cancel one, with the original reservation fee forfeited either way. A $2 per night discount applies year-round for campers 65 and older, people with disabilities, and current, former and active-duty military families.

### How far ahead do campsite reservations open?

Missouri opens 12 months out. Illinois opens six. That one difference decides more summer weekends than anything else on this page. Missouri State Parks takes reservations starting at 7 a.m. Central Time exactly one year before your first night, so a Memorial Day site is claimable the previous May.

Illinois DNR releases sites 180 days ahead through ExploreMoreIL, also at 7 a.m. Central. Illinois also refuses last-minute bookings: a reservation has to be made at least three days before you need the site. Missouri goes the other direction and accepts same-day reservations up to 7 p.m. on your arrival date, with no reservation fee charged on those.

Length of stay is capped on both sides. Missouri limits you to any 15 days within a 30-consecutive-day period at one park under 10 CSR 90-2.030. Illinois caps reservations at 14 nights per 30-day period, and Horseshoe Lake tightens that to seven days in 30. The Illinois reservation fee is $5, non-refundable, and camping fees are refunded if you cancel three days out.

### What does a campsite fee actually include?

A basic Missouri state park site buys you a parking pad, a table, a grill and a lantern post. That is the whole list. Electric adds a 30- or 50-amp power supply, electric and water adds a private water hookup, and the top tier adds a sewer connection. Everything else — shelter, bedding, light, water containers, a way to cook — comes out of your car.

Illinois builds the fee the same way but shows the math on the receipt. Its published schedule splits each night into a camping fee plus a $10 utility fee, so a Class A site with showers, electricity and vehicle access is $10 plus $10, or $20 a night. Class B/E, electricity and vehicle access without showers, is $18. Class B/S, showers without electricity, is $10. Class C is $8 and Class D primitive tent sites are $6. Holiday weekends push Class A to $30.

Neither state charges you to drive through the gate. Illinois DNR says outright that it “does not charge an Entrance Fee to any state owned or operated land.” Missouri funds about three-fourths of its state park budget with the one-tenth of 1% Parks, Soils and Water Sales Tax, which voters renewed in 2026 with roughly 82% approval.

Nothing to do with tents — St. Louis gyms are here too.

### Do you need 30 amp or 50 amp, and does water come with it?

Check the cord before you book, not at the pedestal. A 50-amp rig plugged into a 30-amp site through an adapter is still limited to 30 amps, which in a St. Louis August usually means one air conditioner instead of two. Missouri lists more than 1,200 campsites with 50-amp service, and those pedestals carry 30 amp too, so the bigger site fits either rig.

Water is the part newcomers misread. On Missouri electric/water and sewer/electric/water sites, the private hookup runs only during the park’s on-season. Book one of those in February and you have paid for a spigot that isn’t running. Electric hookups, by contrast, stay live year-round at most Missouri parks.

Illinois handles the same problem with a price cut. Its published rule is that when cold weather forces buildings closed and water shut off in Class AA, A, A-P, B/S or B/S-P campgrounds, the fee drops to match what is actually available for use. Call the park office before any winter trip; that is the only reliable way to learn which shower house is open.

### What closes for the season, and what stays open?

Most campgrounds within reach of St. Louis stay open all winter at the lower off-season rate. What closes is the plumbing. Missouri’s 2026 off-season chart lists Babler, Robertsville, Meramec, Cuivre River, Hawn, Washington, St. Francois, Onondaga Cave and Graham Cave as available every day of the off-season. The system runs more than 3,500 campsites in all.

Illinois splits its year into a May 1 through September 30 spring and summer period and an October 1 through April 30 fall and winter period, and says camping is generally available year-round, weather permitting. Individual campgrounds are the exception that matters — Horseshoe Lake State Park’s campground runs May 1 to September 30 and nothing else.

Three Missouri parks start early rather than late. Roaring River, Bennett Spring and Montauk open their on-season February 25 because trout season does, and Table Rock runs March through November. None are day trips from the metro, but they answer the March weekend where you want the water actually on.

### What does a first-time camper actually need?

Sleep warm, then worry about the rest. Ground pulls heat out of a body far faster than air does, so an insulated sleeping pad does more for an April or October night around here than upgrading your sleeping bag. Add a tent with a full rainfly, two light sources per person, and more water than you think you need — the site’s hydrant may be a walk away, or shut off entirely.

Know the site’s limits before you pack. A typical Missouri state park campsite allows two sleeping units, only one of which can be wheeled, two non-sleeping vehicles and six people. Quiet hours run 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Check-in starts at 3 p.m., checkout is 2 p.m., and you have to arrive within the first 24 hours of the stay. Leashes are capped at 10 feet, with two dogs per site recommended.

Buy firewood, don’t forage it. Missouri State Parks asks campers not to gather or cut firewood in the parks, so plan on a bundle from the park store or a stand down the road. If you are planning a bigger trip around a camping leg, lock the campsite dates first — those are the ones with a release date you cannot negotiate.

### What campground owners around here wish campers knew

A campground makes its year in roughly fourteen weekends. Memorial Day through Labor Day carries the season, a few October leaf weekends help, and a rained-out Fourth of July cannot be made up in November. That is why monthly and seasonal sites exist: they fill Monday through Thursday when transient campers don’t come. A monthly site near $800 works out around $27 a night, well under a summer weekend rate. That trade buys stability, not profit.

The margin lives in the small stuff — firewood, ice, propane, laundry, the store — because the site itself has to cover a septic system, a well, gravel and mowing whether anyone is on it or not. What operators complain about to each other is holiday no-shows and August electric bills, when every rig on the property runs air conditioning at once. Being listed with accurate hookup amperage, pad length and season dates saves both sides that phone call, which is most of why owners keep a complete listing current.

Still deciding where to point the car? Browse campgrounds across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the one you like and ask two things: what amperage the site carries, and whether the water is on the weekend you want. Coming back into town thirsty? Our guide to visiting a St. Louis brewery taproom is the next stop.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is the 200 rule for camping?

A.  It’s the Leave No Trace guideline to camp at least 200 feet from lakes and streams — described as 70 to 80 adult steps — so riparian ground stays intact and wildlife keeps its access routes to water. The same buffer applies to washing dishes and burying waste. It governs backcountry and dispersed camping, not developed campgrounds, where you pitch on the pad the park assigns you.

### Q. What is the 3-3-3 rule for camping?

A.  It’s an RV travelers’ rule of thumb, not a regulation anybody enforces: drive no more than 300 miles in a day, be parked by 3 p.m., and stay at least three nights before moving again. The enforceable limits are different. Missouri caps camping at any 15 days within 30 consecutive days at one park, and Illinois caps reservations at 14 nights per 30-day period.

### Q. Are there any free campgrounds near St. Louis, Missouri?

A.  Not inside the metro. The closest genuinely free option is dispersed camping in Mark Twain National Forest, where you camp outside any developed campground with no fee and no permit required, typically for up to 14 days in a 30-day span. The nearest ground is the Potosi/Fredericktown Ranger District south of the metro. There is no pad, no toilet and no water, so check the district’s motor vehicle use map first.

### Q. What is the cheapest campground?

A.  Among developed sites near St. Louis, Illinois undercuts Missouri. A Class D primitive tent site on Illinois DNR land is $6 a night and a Class C site with vehicle access is $8, against $15 for a typical Missouri basic site and $10 for a Missouri backcountry site. Add $5 to reserve in Illinois or $6.50 online in Missouri. Free means dispersed national forest camping, with nothing provided.

### Q. How much do campsites cost per week?

A.  Public parks don’t discount by the week — it’s the nightly rate times seven, plus one reservation fee. Seven nights on a Missouri 30-amp electric site works out to about $189 plus $6.50 online. Seven nights on an Illinois Class A site is about $140 plus $5. Private RV parks around the metro do post weekly rates, commonly between $175 and $375 depending on hookups, as advertised in August 2026.

### Q. How much do most campgrounds cost per month?

A.  Around $800 a month for a full-hookup site at a private RV park in the St. Louis area, checked in August 2026, with electricity often metered separately on top. Public campgrounds are not an option for monthly stays at all: Missouri state parks cap you at 15 days in any 30, and Illinois caps reservations at 14 nights per 30-day period.

### Q. Can I just show up, or do I have to reserve?

A.  It depends on which side of the river. Missouri State Parks accepts same-day reservations up to 7 p.m. on your arrival date and waives the reservation fee on those. Illinois requires bookings at least three days ahead, so a spur-of-the-moment Illinois trip means a first-come campground — Horseshoe Lake State Park in Madison takes no camping reservations at all, May 1 through September 30.

## When a Travel Agent Is Worth It in St. Louis (and When to Book It Yourself)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/when-to-use-a-travel-agent-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Sunday night in Kirkwood and there are eleven browser tabs open. Two of them are the same hotel at two different prices. Your mother-in-law needs a ground-floor room, your brother is flying in from Denver, and the whole thing has to land in one week in June or it doesn’t happen at all.

Maybe your version starts in Belleville, where a cruise deposit is due Friday and nobody agrees on the cabin. Maybe it’s St. Charles, and you’re pricing nine days in Italy for four adults and a nine-year-old. Maybe you’re in Florissant holding a passport that expires in five months, with a wedding in Mexico already on the calendar.

Here’s the honest part. For a nonstop to Phoenix and three nights at a chain hotel, you do not need a travel agent, and anyone who says otherwise is selling. You’ll book it faster yourself. The trips above are a different animal — many moving parts, real money, and a decent chance of a 2 a.m. problem somewhere you don’t speak the language. Here’s how to tell which trip you have.

### How can I choose a reliable travel agency?

Ask three questions before you hand over a deposit: how do you get paid, what do you book most, and what happens if something goes wrong while I’m gone. A working advisor answers all three in about a minute. Vague answers on money are the loudest warning sign in this business.

Then check the mechanics. Pay by credit card — never by wire, Zelle, Venmo or personal check, which strip away your dispute rights. Ask for the supplier’s own confirmation number, not just the agency invoice, and log in to the cruise line or tour operator site yourself to confirm the booking exists. Get cancellation and change penalties in writing before you pay.

Finally, hire for the trip you’re taking. An advisor who books forty river cruises a year knows which cabins sit above the engine, and may be no better than you at a national-park road trip. Specialization is the real credential.

### How does a travel agent actually get paid?

Two ways, and most advisors use both. The first is commission paid by the supplier — the cruise line, tour operator, hotel or insurer — out of the price you were going to pay anyway. The second is a fee you pay directly, usually called a planning, consultation or service fee. Neither is a markup on the published fare.

The timing is the part almost nobody knows. Supplier commission is generally paid after you travel, not when you book, and if you cancel it is clawed back. It also applies only to the commissionable portion of a fare — port charges, taxes and prepaid gratuities usually pay nothing. Most independent advisors work under a host agency that holds the industry accreditation and keeps a slice of every commission.

Air is the exception that explains the planning fee. Delta ended base commissions on tickets sold in the United States and Canada in March 2002, and the rest of the industry followed within months. More than twenty years later, booking your domestic flights still pays an advisor essentially nothing — which is why fee-charging became normal rather than rude.

### Is it actually cheaper to use a travel agent?

Usually it’s the same price, sometimes it’s better value, and if you pay a planning fee the trip costs more by exactly that fee. Cruise lines, tour operators and most hotel brands hold advisors to the same published rates you see online, so the fantasy of a secret cheaper price is mostly a fantasy. What does move is what comes bundled with the price.

Where an advisor earns it back is in extras and errors. Onboard credit, a group amenity, a cabin upgrade at the same fare, a resort credit — those are real and supplier-funded. So is the mistake you didn’t make: the connection that was legal on paper and impossible in practice, the visa nobody mentioned, the shore excursion booked so tight a late tender leaves you on the dock. Say your budget plainly. An advisor who won’t work inside a number is telling you something useful.

### When is booking direct genuinely the better call?

Book it yourself when the trip is one flight and one hotel, when you’d happily rebook the whole thing in eight minutes, when you’re chasing status that only credits on a direct booking, or when a planning fee would be a meaningful slice of the trip. A weekend in Chicago or Branson does not need a professional.

Booking direct with the airline also gets you one rule an agency cannot. Under 14 CFR 259.5, a covered U.S. carrier must either hold a reservation at the quoted fare without payment, or allow cancellation without penalty, for at least 24 hours — but only if you booked seven or more days before departure. That obligation sits on the airline, not on ticket agents, so the same 24-hour grace is not guaranteed on a third-party booking.

### What do ASTA, IATA and CLIA after a name actually mean?

They are trade credentials, not government licenses, and knowing the difference protects you. ASTA is the American Society of Travel Advisors, the industry’s main trade association; members agree to its code of ethics, and membership is voluntary. An IATA or IATAN number is supplier accreditation, not a consumer safeguard — IATA’s own ID card eligibility rules ask only that a U.S. applicant work at least 20 hours a week in travel sales and have earned $5,000 in salary or commission over the past 12 months. CLIA is the cruise trade body and runs its own cruise-selling certifications.

Only four states register sellers of travel — California, Florida, Washington and Hawaii — and neither Missouri nor Illinois issues a travel agent license the way it licenses a real estate broker. Illinois does regulate the money, though. Under the Travel Promotion Consumer Protection Act, a travel promoter must deposit 90 percent of all sums received into a trust account at a federally insured bank, and may not draw on it except to pay the carriers and suppliers you contracted for or to issue refunds. Missouri has no travel-specific statute like it, which is a real difference between an agency in Edwardsville and one in Chesterfield.

Unrelated, and we know it — that airline-seat backache may want a chiropractor.

### What does travel insurance cover, and what does it not?

A comprehensive policy typically pays for trip cancellation and interruption for a list of named covered reasons, emergency medical treatment and medical evacuation abroad, and baggage problems. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners puts typical policy cost at 5 to 10 percent of the trip price. The medical piece is underrated: standard Medicare generally does not travel outside the United States, and an air ambulance home from a cruise port is a five-figure event.

The exclusions are broader than people expect. The NAIC lists pre-existing health conditions, pandemics, civil and political unrest, pregnancy and childbirth, and high-risk activities among the common ones. Changing your mind, or a storm already named when you bought, is usually out too. Some plans waive the pre-existing exclusion, but only if you buy soon after your first trip payment and insure the full nonrefundable cost — the insurer sets that window, so ask for it in writing.

Two traps worth naming. Cancel For Any Reason is an optional upgrade that reimburses a portion of your nonrefundable cost, not all of it — NAIC puts the usual range at 50 to 75 percent — and it carries its own purchase deadline. And the Illinois Department of Insurance warns that a cancellation waiver sold at checkout is not an insurance policy and is not regulated by the department. No policy and no advisor can guarantee a claim gets paid; the policy language decides that.

### What happens when something goes wrong mid-trip?

Federal rules cover the airline half, and they reach your travel agent too. Under the U.S. Department of Transportation’s 2024 refunds rule, now at 14 CFR Part 260, you are owed a refund when a flight is cancelled or significantly changed and you don’t accept what’s offered instead. Significant means departure or arrival moved three or more hours domestically, six or more internationally, plus different airports, added connections or a downgrade. Refunds are due within seven business days on a credit card and 20 calendar days on other payment methods — and when the ticket agent took your payment, the rule makes the airline push the money back to them.

Your credit card is the second layer. The Fair Credit Billing Act gives you the right to dispute a billing error in writing within 60 days of the statement on which it appeared, and the issuer must acknowledge and investigate. That is why a big tour deposit belongs on a card, and what a wire transfer throws away.

The third layer is a person. Rules do not rebook you; someone has to. When a sailing is cancelled or a hurricane closes an airport, an advisor works a trade line while you stand in a queue of four hundred people dialing the same number. That is what you’re buying on a multi-generation trip, a destination wedding, or a cruise where a missed connection means the ship leaves without you.

### What running a travel agency actually looks like

The money arrives long after the work does. An advisor sells a November cruise in January, does every hour of the labor in January, and collects commission after the ship sails — and if the client cancels, that commission is recalled. That single fact shapes the trade. It is why wave season, roughly January through March, is the stretch that makes or breaks the year, and why air-only requests are the quiet complaint in every agent group chat: since base commissions ended in 2002, four hours rebuilding your flights pays nothing. Most independents run under a host agency that holds the accreditation and keeps a share of each commission, so take-home is smaller than the headline percentage. The client good operators dread is the one who asks for a full itinerary and then books it online. Because people search for this help locally, keeping a complete listing is how a small agency gets found at all.

Related reading: a destination wedding still starts with the dress — here’s the St. Louis wedding dress shopping timeline

Got a trip with more than three moving parts? Browse travel agencies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them with the same two questions — what do you book most, and do you charge a planning fee. That sorts the list in one afternoon.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Is it actually cheaper to use a travel agent?

A.  Rarely cheaper on the sticker price, often better value, and more expensive by exactly the fee if you pay one. Cruise lines, tour operators and hotel brands hold advisors to the same published rates you can see yourself. The gap shows up as supplier-funded extras — onboard credit, a better cabin at the same fare — and as the expensive mistake you avoided.

### Q. What is a normal fee for a travel agent?

A.  There isn’t one national number, and treat any figure you read as a guess about somebody else’s business. Fees are set per advisor and scale with complexity: a flat charge for one hotel booking, more for a multi-country itinerary or a group. Ask how much, what it covers, and whether it is credited back if you book — before any research starts.

### Q. What is the average cost of using a travel agent?

A.  For most leisure bookings the direct cost is zero, because the advisor is paid a commission by the cruise line, tour operator or hotel out of the fare you were already paying. Where a planning fee applies, it is disclosed up front, before work begins. The real question is not the average — it is what this advisor charges you, in writing.

### Q. How much does a travel agent make on a $10,000 trip?

A.  It depends entirely on what the $10,000 is made of. Only the commissionable portion pays — port charges, taxes and prepaid gratuities usually don’t, and domestic airfare pays essentially nothing since base commissions ended in 2002. Whatever the supplier does pay is split with the host agency and lands after travel, not at booking. Cancel and it is taken back.

### Q. Who are the best travel agents in St. Louis?

A.  There is no single best one, because the right advisor depends on the product. Pick for specialization: someone who sells river cruises weekly, or Disney weekly, or Italy weekly, beats a generalist on your specific trip. Ask how many of your exact product they sold this year, how they are paid, and who answers at 2 a.m. overseas.

### Q. Who are some good travel agents in St. Charles, MO?

A.  Search by your side of the metro, then screen on the same three questions rather than on the storefront. Plenty of advisors in St. Charles County work from home under a host agency and never open a storefront — normal in 2026, not a red flag. What matters is who they book, how they charge, and whether they hand you the supplier’s own confirmation number.

### Q. Do I need travel insurance if my credit card already has it?

A.  Sometimes, but read the card benefit guide first. Card coverage is usually secondary, capped well below a big trip’s cost, and often triggered only if you charged the full fare to that card. It also rarely includes medical evacuation, the expensive part of an overseas emergency. Compare the card’s covered reasons and limits against a standalone policy.

## St. Louis Auction Houses: What to Know Before You Bid or Consign
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-auction-houses-work-st-louis

Picture a Thursday night in Affton. Laptop open on the kitchen table, a timed online auction closing in eleven minutes, and a walnut dresser sitting at $85 with two other bidders circling it. Your pulse is doing something ridiculous over a piece of furniture you have never touched.

Now picture the other end of the same business. A family in Florissant has to have a parent’s house empty by the thirtieth. Forty years of belongings, three siblings with three opinions, nobody sleeping well. Somebody says the word “auction” and everyone nods, because it sounds like a plan and nobody has a better one.

Both of those people are about to agree to the same document without reading it: the terms of sale. That one page decides what the dresser actually costs, what the family actually nets, and when the money lands. Here is how auction houses work across the St. Louis metro from both sides of the paddle — buying and selling — and what to check before you commit to either.

### How do I find a reputable auction house?

Start with the license, because that is the piece you can verify in about five minutes. In Illinois, auctioneers and auction firms are licensed by the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation under the Auction License Act, 225 ILCS 407, and IDFPR runs a public license lookup. In Missouri, auctioneers are licensed county by county under RSMo Chapter 343 rather than by a state board, so you ask the county, not Jefferson City.

Missouri’s rule is not decorative. RSMo 343.010 says no person shall exercise the trade or business of a public auctioneer by selling any goods, property or real estate without a license, and RSMo 343.250 makes a violation a class C misdemeanor carrying a $20 to $500 fine plus a one-year bar from practicing. The rate is modest — RSMo 343.080 sets $10 for one month and $50 for twelve, plus a $2 clerk issuance fee under RSMo 343.090. Which tells you something: the license is a low bar, and anyone who has not cleared it has a reason.

After the license, ask five questions and listen to how fast the answers come:

Where are your terms of sale published, and may I read them before I consign or register?

How many business days after the sale do you settle, and is that number in the contract?

Will I get an itemized settlement statement showing what each lot brought?

Which fees come out of my proceeds — hauling, photography, cataloging, unsold lots?

What happens when a winning bidder never pays or never picks up?

An operator who has run sales in this metro for years answers all five without checking a note. Estate attorneys and bank trust officers in Clayton and St. Charles refer the same handful of houses repeatedly, so ask them.

### What does a buyer’s premium do to the price you actually pay?

A buyer’s premium is a fee added on top of the hammer price, so the number the auctioneer shouts is never the number on your invoice. Illinois defines it plainly in 225 ILCS 407/5-10 as any fee or compensation paid by the successful purchaser other than the purchase price. Rates differ by house, by sale and sometimes by lot value, and every one of them is printed in the terms of sale.

The structure is what matters, not any one rate. An auction house is paid from both sides of a single transaction: the seller pays a commission taken out of the proceeds, and the buyer pays a premium stacked on top of the hammer. Some houses run a sliding scale where the percentage drops as the lot price climbs. Then sales tax generally applies unless you have a valid exemption on file, a card surcharge may apply, and an online platform can add its own fee. Four small numbers stacked on one small number stop being small.

So bid backwards. Decide the amount you are willing to watch leave your bank account, subtract the premium, tax and card fee listed in the terms, and let what is left be your maximum bid. Doing that arithmetic in the last forty seconds of a live lot is how people overpay for a dresser.

### What should you check before you bid on anything?

Go to the preview, or make the catalog work like one. Almost every auction sells as-is, where-is, with no returns and no warranty, and Missouri’s commercial code backs the finality: under RSMo 400.2-328 a sale by auction is complete when the auctioneer so announces by the fall of the hammer or in another customary manner, and a bidder may retract a bid only up until that announcement. After the hammer, the conversation is over.

Preview day is the whole game. Open every drawer and run it. Look for lifted veneer, fresh glue, replaced hardware and repairs done in a hurry. If there is power, plug it in. On an online-only sale, request a condition report in writing and ask directly whether the photos show all of the damage — a straight answer to that tells you more about the house than any review. And ask whether a lot is a box lot, because what is under the top layer is rarely what sold you on it.

### How does absentee and online bidding actually work?

You leave a maximum, and the system bids for you. In absentee or proxy bidding you enter the most you will pay, and the platform raises your bid one increment at a time only as it needs to, so you often win below your maximum. Timed online auctions almost always use extended bidding, or a soft close: a bid in the final moments pushes the clock out, which is why a lot closing at 7:02 is somehow still open at 7:19.

A live sale with simulcast is different again. You bid against the room, the phones and the internet at once, and the room usually has the timing advantage. Whichever format, read three lines in the terms before registering: the pickup window, the storage or abandonment fee if you miss it, and the authorization hold placed on your card. People who win from a couch in Maryland Heights and forget they now have to move a china cabinet out of Belleville by Saturday are a genuine category.

Unrelated, and we know it — your car is filthy. Find a car wash.

### Should you sell by consignment, estate sale, or an outright offer?

Three routes, three different trades between price and certainty. Consignment auction keeps you as the owner until the hammer falls; the house takes its commission out of what the lots bring, so a strong night pays you well and a soft night does not. An on-site estate sale prices everything with tags and brings the crowd to the house, which handles volume better than it handles one exceptional object. An outright offer or buy-out is the fastest and usually the lowest ceiling, and for some families that certainty is worth more than the difference.

If the house is on the Illinois side, one rule changed recently and it catches people. As of January 1, 2026, under Public Act 104-0145, an estate sale in Illinois must be conducted by a licensed auctioneer when all four of these are true: it is for another person and for compensation; it is advertised and scheduled for a certain date and time; it is open to the public; and personal property is being bid on or negotiated for purchase. IDFPR’s estate sale guidance lists the exceptions — a sale run by an owner of the property, a beneficiary of a trust or will, an executor or administrator, or a guardian or receiver under court order needs no auctioneer, and neither does transferring or donating the goods to a third-party reseller or consignment shop. For families in Belleville, Edwardsville and O’Fallon hiring somebody to run the sale, ask that directly.

What sells well surprises almost everyone. Tools, shop equipment, sporting goods, quality mid-century pieces and anything genuinely scarce tend to find bidders. Large formal furniture and mass-produced collectibles often bring less than a family expects. Small dense things — coins, watches, estate jewelry, firearms and good silver — often outperform a whole room of casegoods, which is why they get pulled into specialty sales. Ask the auctioneer what has been bringing money in their room lately.

### What does a reserve do, and what does “absolute” mean?

A reserve is a floor: below it, the lot does not sell. Under RSMo 400.2-328 an auction is with reserve unless it is announced otherwise, which means the default protects the seller and the auctioneer may withdraw a lot any time before completion. In an auction announced without reserve — the absolute auction — once the auctioneer calls for bids the lot cannot be withdrawn unless no bid arrives within a reasonable time. That is why absolute sales draw a bigger crowd. Bidders know the item is genuinely selling.

Two more lines from that statute are worth carrying. Retracting a bid does not revive the previous one. And if an auctioneer knowingly takes a bid on the seller’s behalf without notice that the privilege exists, the buyer may walk away from the sale or take the goods at the last good-faith bid. Sellers should also ask what a no-sale costs: many houses charge a buy-back fee when a reserve sits above the market and nothing clears it.

### When do you actually get paid after the sale?

Not the next morning. Settlement follows a set number of business days after the sale closes, and that number belongs in your written contract before you hand over a single box. The delay is not stalling — buyers have to pay, cards have to clear, the pickup window has to close, and non-paying bidders get chased or their lots re-offered. A house that will not put the settlement window in writing is telling you something.

Ask for the settlement statement itemized lot by lot, not one net figure. You want the hammer price, the commission, and each pass-through for hauling, photography, cataloging or unsold lots on its own line. Ask who absorbs a non-paying bidder, too — in some contracts the lot comes back to you and gets re-run later, which moves your timeline by weeks.

### What if you are only doing this because someone died?

Then slow down by one day, because the mistakes here are permanent. Before anyone loads a truck, walk the house for paper and personal items: titles, deeds, insurance policies, savings bonds, military discharge papers, tax records, photographs and address books. Check coat pockets, the backs of drawers, inside book pages, and the freezer. Firearms, ammunition, prescription medication and anything with a title need separate handling, and you should say so to the auctioneer up front rather than letting them discover it.

Two more things. Do not pre-clean, polish or refinish anything to make it presentable — on the wrong piece that removes value instead of adding it. And do not throw out the junk drawer or the garage shelf before someone who does this for a living has looked, because that is exactly where the surprises live. If three siblings are deciding by group text at midnight, ask for a second walkthrough. A good house will do one.

### What auction owners wish more families understood

The fee structure is the visible part of the business. The invisible part is labor. Pack-out is people, a truck and days — sorting, hauling, photographing and cataloging hundreds of lots before a single bid exists — and that cost is spent whether the sale is strong or soft. For an estate, the product an auction house is really selling is an empty house by the deadline, not a headline price on one object. Seasonality is real too: estate work clusters when houses turn over in spring and fall, and online-only timed sales carry the calendar through the dead stretch of winter. What operators talk about among themselves is the winner who never pays and the winner who never comes to pick up, both of which cost real money after the gavel. And people find the sale before they find the lot — someone searching auction houses near them in this metro is the top of that funnel, which is why a complete, current listing on St Louis Near Me Directory earns its keep.

Ready to bid, or ready to let it go? Browse auction houses across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them, describe what you have or what you are hunting, and ask each one when they settle.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What percentage do auction houses take?

A.  There is no single figure, because a house is paid from both sides. The seller pays a commission deducted from the hammer price, and the buyer pays a premium added on top of it — Illinois defines that premium in 225 ILCS 407/5-10 as compensation from the successful purchaser beyond the purchase price. Rates vary by house, sale format and lot value, and many use a sliding scale. The published terms of sale for that specific auction are the only reliable source.

### Q. What are typical auction fees?

A.  Beyond commission and buyer’s premium, expect some combination of hauling or pack-out, photography and cataloging, credit card surcharge, an online platform fee, storage if you miss the pickup window, and an unsold-lot or buy-back fee when a reserve is not met. Sales tax generally applies to buyers without an exemption on file. Ask which of these are pass-throughs deducted from your settlement and which are billed separately.

### Q. What do most auction houses charge?

A.  The honest answer is that the total take is split across a seller commission and a buyer premium, and quoting one house’s rate tells you nothing about the next one. Rates also move with the format and the category of goods. Get your number in writing before you register or consign, for your sale specifically.

### Q. What are common auction mistakes?

A.  Bidding the hammer price instead of the all-in price. Skipping the preview and trusting eight photographs. Setting a reserve above what the room will pay, then owing a buy-back fee on a lot that did not sell. Winning something in Kirkwood you have no way to move by Saturday. And on the selling side, cleaning or refinishing an item before anyone who knows the category has seen it.

### Q. How do I find a reputable auction house?

A.  Verify the license first: IDFPR licenses auctioneers and auction firms in Illinois under 225 ILCS 407 and publishes a lookup, while Missouri licenses auctioneers at the county level under RSMo Chapter 343. Then read the published terms of sale, ask how many business days until settlement and whether that appears in the contract, and ask an estate attorney or a bank trust officer who they send families to.

### Q. What are the upcoming auctions happening in St. Louis?

A.  Sale calendars move week to week, so the current list lives with the houses themselves rather than in any article. Check each auctioneer’s own calendar page and email list, and check the online bidding platforms they use, since many metro sales now run timed-online or live-with-simulcast. Preview times are usually posted with the catalog, and the preview is the part worth putting on your calendar.

### Q. How much money do you need for an auction house?

A.  As a buyer, less than people assume — box lots and utility furniture often open low, though you should register with a card that can carry the authorization hold and budget for the premium and tax. As someone considering starting a house, the license is the cheap part: Missouri’s statutory rate under RSMo 343.080 tops out at $50 for a twelve-month license. Trucks, storage, staff and insurance are the real capital.

### Q. Can you provide me with a list of foreclosures in Saint Louis City?

A.  Those are a different process from the auction houses in this category. RSMo 343.010 specifically excludes court-ordered sales and judicial foreclosures from the definition of a public auctioneer, so foreclosure and delinquent-tax sales run through the courts and county offices rather than through a consignment auction house. Contact the relevant sheriff’s office or collector of revenue for their published sale lists and schedules.

## How to Walk Into a St. Louis Art Gallery (and Actually Buy)
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/visiting-buying-st-louis-art-galleries

Imagine it’s a Saturday afternoon and you have two free hours before you are due at a friend’s place in Kirkwood. You pass a lit storefront on Washington Boulevard with three enormous paintings in the window and nobody inside except one person at a desk, and you keep going. Not because you didn’t want to see it. Because you assumed the door was for somebody else.

It isn’t. Commercial art galleries are free to walk into, the same way a shoe store is free to walk into, and nobody asks what you do for a living. That is the most useful thing anyone can tell you about art in St. Louis, and almost nobody says it out loud.

The barrier here is social, not financial. You are not underdressed. You do not need the vocabulary. Florissant, Belleville, St. Charles, Maplewood — doesn’t matter. Here is how the thing actually works: visiting, districts, openings, pricing, splits, payment plans, commissions and framing.

### What’s the difference between art museums and galleries?

A museum owns a collection and exists to conserve and show it. A commercial gallery owns almost nothing on its walls — it takes work on consignment from living artists and sells it. Both are free to walk into. Only the gallery is in the business of selling you the thing you are looking at, and it will not push.

There is a third model people mix up with both: the artist co-op, or artist-run space. Members pay dues, hang their own shows and take turns sitting the desk, so the person who greets you is frequently the person who made the work. Ask them anything. That is the point of the format.

On the museum side the free-admission tradition here runs deep. The Saint Louis Art Museum in Forest Park is free to everyone every day it is open, Tuesday through Sunday 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and until 9 p.m. Fridays. The Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis at 3750 Washington Boulevard is free, no ticket required, and the Pulitzer Arts Foundation at 3716 Washington is free with free parking.

### Do you have to buy anything to walk into a gallery?

No. Not a dollar, not a donation, not an email address. Commercial galleries are retail spaces with no admission charge, and most people who come through will never buy anything. Owners budget for that on purpose. Foot traffic today is how a collector gets made five years from now.

Once inside, walk the room without reading a single label, then go back to whatever stopped you. Ask for the price list — that exact phrase, and it is a normal question, not a commitment. Prices are often off the wall because a printed sheet keeps the numbers consistent.

Don’t touch the work, sculpture and frames included. Ask before photographing; most will say yes, without flash. A red dot beside a piece means sold. And when the person at the desk asks whether you have questions, they are not sizing you up as a buyer. They are bored.

### Is there an art district in St. Louis?

Yes. The Grand Center Arts District, clustered around North Grand Boulevard and Washington Boulevard just north of Saint Louis University, is the closest thing the metro has to a formal arts district — Forbes called it the most exciting emerging arts district in America in 2023. Inside a few blocks sit the Contemporary Art Museum, the Pulitzer Arts Foundation, the Sheldon Art Galleries at 3648 Washington and the Saint Louis University Museum of Art.

It is not the only one. Cherokee Street on the south side runs on artist-run spaces, storefront galleries and murals, scrappier and considerably cheaper than Grand Center. Laumeier Sculpture Park in Sunset Hills is a 105-acre outdoor museum holding more than 60 large-scale sculptures, free daily, run in partnership with St. Louis County Parks — and it exists because St. Louis-born sculptor Ernest Trova handed the county 40 of his works.

The Illinois side has its own anchor. Art on the Square takes over the historic Public Square in downtown Belleville each May, a juried fine art show running since 2002 that drew more than 100 artists from over 27 states this year.

### What actually happens at a First Friday opening?

In Grand Center, First Fridays means the district’s museums and galleries are free and open until 9 p.m. on the first Friday of every month. Elsewhere, an opening reception is a two- or three-hour window on a Friday or Saturday evening marking a new show, free and unticketed.

The behavior is simpler than it looks. Arrive any time inside the window; nobody shows up at the start. Dress the way you would for dinner out. There is often free wine or beer, and one glass is the correct number if you intend to talk to the artist. Do talk to the artist — they are standing there to be talked to, and “what were you working from?” beats any attempt at art vocabulary.

An opening is the worst time to look at art and the best time to meet people, so come back on a quiet Wednesday if a piece is seriously in play. If you do want to buy that night, say so early. Good work at a well-attended opening can be gone inside the first hour.

Nothing to do with art — somebody in your life needs flowers.

### How does gallery pricing work, and why does the gallery take half?

The standard consignment split in the commercial gallery trade is 50/50: half the retail price to the artist, half to the gallery. That is the default, and most established galleries will not go under it. Spaces built around emerging artists sometimes take 40%. Online marketplaces typically run 20% to 40%, because they are not paying for a room.

The artist ships work and gets a wall. The gallery carries rent, insurance, install labor and the reception whether or not a single piece moves, which is what the other half pays for.

Two things worth knowing as a buyer. Price parity is the norm — a serious artist quotes the same number in the studio that the gallery quotes on the wall, so angling for a side deal mostly burns a relationship you might want later. And a courtesy discount around 10% exists in much of the trade, but it is a courtesy, not a right. Ask once, politely, and take the answer.

Sales tax lands on art like anything else, and it is one place the state line shows. Missouri’s state rate is 4.225% before local add-ons, which push the City of St. Louis combined rate to roughly 9.68%. Illinois starts at 6.25% at the state level before its own local layers. On a $3,000 painting that gap is real money, so ask for the out-the-door number.

### Can you buy art on a payment plan?

Often, yes, and it is one of the least advertised facts in the trade. Plenty of commercial galleries will split a purchase into interest-free installments — three months, six, sometimes twelve — and hold the piece until the last payment clears. No national program sits behind this in the United States. It is a per-gallery arrangement, decided case by case.

Which means you have to ask out loud. The sentence is short: is there any flexibility on payment? Then get the terms in writing — total, number of payments, dates, and what happens if you stop. A deposit of 25% to 50% is a common starting point. Galleries say yes more often than people expect, because a sold piece on a slow schedule still beats an unsold one.

### How do you commission a piece from a local artist?

Start with an artist whose finished work you already love, then ask the gallery to introduce you. A commission is not a cheaper route to something similar — it usually costs more than a comparable finished piece, because the artist carries your risk on top of their own.

A workable commission settles five things before anyone touches a canvas: size, medium, delivery window, total price and deposit. Half up front is common, the balance on approval. Bring photos of the actual wall with a chair or lamp in frame for scale, and be blunt about colors you cannot live with. Agree in advance how many rounds of revision exist, because open-ended is how commissions turn ugly.

One legal point people get wrong constantly: buying the artwork does not buy the copyright. Under U.S. copyright law, owning the object is separate from owning the rights in it, and any transfer has to be in a signed writing. You own the painting. The artist still controls reproduction unless you paid for that and put it on paper.

### What does it cost to frame what you buy?

Custom framing generally lands between $50 and $500 a piece according to national cost guides, and size plus glazing drives nearly all of it. A small print in plain moulding sits at the bottom; a large work on paper with a hand-cut mat and UV-filtering conservation glass sits at the top. Take the conservation glazing on anything you care about. It is what keeps paper from going yellow in a sunny room.

Ready-made frames start well under $50 and are fine for anything reproduced or unsigned. Stretched canvases often need nothing, or a simple floater frame. Ask the gallery what the artist prefers; most have a framer they trust, and some will fold framing into the deal if you raise it before the sale closes.

### What does a gallery look like from the owner’s side of the counter?

The economics are stranger than they look. A gallery keeps roughly half of every sale but buys no inventory — the work is consigned, so the whole risk sits in fixed costs: street-level rent, insurance on other people’s property, track lighting, install labor, the reception, and art fair booths paid for months before anything sells. A dead quarter carries the same overhead as a great one.

The calendar is predictable and unforgiving. September through early December and February through May carry the year; July and August are dead; January is quiet enough that many spaces spend it on inventory and framing. Owners trade the same two complaints: the visitor who photographs a piece to have it copied cheaper, and the buyer who commits at an opening and evaporates at pickup.

Good operators answer with a real mailing list, identical pricing across every channel, and delivery that includes hanging it — plus being findable when somebody two suburbs over decides today is the day, which is why a complete listing on St Louis Near Me Directory earns its twenty minutes.

And if the buying is what interests you, a gallery is only one door. The saleroom prices art on completely different logic — worth reading how St. Louis auction houses work before you bid on anything with a frame around it.

Ready to just open the door? Browse art galleries across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then pick one within fifteen minutes of home and go look at three things you cannot afford.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much do art galleries charge?

A.  Visitors are charged nothing — no admission, no fee, no obligation. Artists are the ones who pay, through a commission taken from each sale, most often 50% of retail and sometimes 40% at spaces built for emerging work. Be wary of a gallery that charges an artist a wall fee up front. That is a rental model, not representation.

### Q. Why do galleries take 50%?

A.  Because the gallery carries every cost of selling and the artist carries none. Street-level rent, insurance on work the gallery does not own, lighting, installation, printing, the opening reception, art fair fees and collector relationships built over years all come out of that half. It is the trade default, and a below-50% deal usually means the gallery is doing less.

### Q. What are some artsy things to do in St. Louis?

A.  Free and open to anyone: the Saint Louis Art Museum in Forest Park, the Contemporary Art Museum and the Pulitzer Arts Foundation on Washington Boulevard, the Sheldon Art Galleries, and Laumeier Sculpture Park in Sunset Hills with 60-plus outdoor sculptures across 105 acres. Add Grand Center’s First Fridays, when district venues stay open free until 9 p.m., and Cherokee Street’s murals.

### Q. What famous artists are from St. Louis?

A.  Ernest Trova, born in St. Louis in 1927, was a self-taught painter and sculptor best known for his Falling Man series; his gift of 40 works to St. Louis County created Laumeier Sculpture Park. Mary Engelbreit, born here on June 5, 1952, built one of the country’s most widely licensed illustration studios, still based in St. Louis.

### Q. What is the 2/3 rule for art?

A.  It is a hanging guideline, not an art-history term. A piece hung over furniture should be roughly two-thirds the width of whatever sits below it, with 6 to 8 inches of gap between the top of the sofa and the bottom of the frame. Pair it with the gallery standard of centering the work near 57 inches off the floor, which is average eye level.

### Q. What is the 70/30 rule in art?

A.  It is a composition rule of thumb: let one element dominate roughly 70% of the picture and give the second the other 30%, so the eye has somewhere to land instead of splitting the difference. Artists apply the same ratio to color, giving a canvas one majority temperature and a smaller counterweight. It is a starting habit, not a law.

### Q. How much does it cost to rent the St. Louis art museum for a wedding?

A.  The Saint Louis Art Museum does host weddings and private events through its events office, but it does not publish rates — you request a quote for the date and space. Wedding marketplaces list a reception rental fee in the $3,000 to $5,000 range plus a food-and-beverage minimum, which is a ballpark and nothing more. Confirm directly before budgeting.

## Wedding Dress Shopping in St. Louis: The Timeline Nobody Explains
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/wedding-dress-shopping-timeline-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Sunday in February, the ring is nine days old, and three people have already asked you for a date. You don’t have a date. You have a group text lighting up from Florissant, an aunt in Belleville with opinions about sleeves, and a vague sense that a wedding dress takes a while to get.

Maybe the wedding is next October in Kirkwood and you figure there’s time. Maybe it’s five months out at a hall in Affton and someone has already told you, twice, that you’re late. Maybe you’re the groom in Maryland Heights who assumed a suit was a Saturday errand, or the mother of the groom in St. Charles waiting for permission to buy anything at all.

Almost nobody walks into a bridal shop knowing the one fact that governs the whole calendar: most wedding gowns aren’t sitting in a stockroom. They’re ordered, then made, then shipped, then altered. That’s four separate clocks, and only one of them is yours to speed up. Here’s how it actually runs across the St. Louis metro.

### How far ahead should you order a wedding dress?

Order eight to ten months before the wedding, and start trying gowns on a month or two before that. Most made-to-order bridal gowns take roughly four to six months to produce and ship; heavily customized or couture styles can run six to nine. Alterations then need their own six to eight weeks after the dress lands.

That sequence surprises people. When you say yes in the shop, nothing gets pulled off a shelf. The store places a special order, the designer cuts and sews your gown in a production run with other orders, and it ships to the store — not to your house. Only then does anyone touch a needle to fit it to you.

Rush production exists, compressing the making of a gown into roughly eight to twelve weeks for an added fee. The quieter cost is that a rush order eats the buffer you meant to spend on alterations. Whatever your timeline, ask for the designer’s current quoted ship window in writing, and ask what the shop does if it slips. Ship windows are factory estimates, not store promises, and good shops say so before you sign.

### What are the most common mistakes brides make at a bridal appointment?

The most common mistakes are stacking too many appointments into one day, bringing too large an audience, arriving without a real budget number, and trying on gowns priced well above it. Add showing up with no supportive undergarments and no shoes near your ceremony heel height. Two or three shops in a weekend is plenty.

Both of those middle ones are fixable in a sentence. Six opinions in a small fitting room produces a stalemate, and the person outvoted is usually the one wearing the dress — so bring the two or three people whose reaction you actually want. Then say your ceiling out loud at the start, including whether it covers alterations and a veil. Nobody in the trade is offended by a budget. They’re offended by hearing it at checkout.

### What actually happens at a trying-on appointment?

You get an hour or so with a consultant, a fitting room, and roughly five to eight gowns. Shops stock only one to three sample sizes per style, so most dresses on the floor get clipped, pinned or laced onto you to show the silhouette. Nothing on that rack is expected to fit as-is, for anyone who walks in.

Two things about bridal sizing are worth knowing before the first appointment. Bridal size charts run roughly one to two sizes smaller than street sizing — they’re a manufacturer’s measurement chart, not a comment on you. And sample ranges vary widely by shop: many boutiques carry a core run through the middle of the chart plus a separate set of larger samples, while some keep a much broader floor.

So call ahead and ask one plain question: what size range is on your floor right now? A shop that answers straight is telling you something about how it treats people. Your gown gets ordered to your current measurements — bust, waist, hip, hollow-to-hem — then taken in or let out later. There is no version of this where you order to a body you don’t have yet. Bring the undergarments you plan to wear and shoes at your ceremony heel height, and say what you actually think about each gown.

### Why are alterations a separate cost and a separate calendar?

Alterations are billed separately from the gown at nearly every bridal shop in the metro, because they’re skilled hand labor priced by the job. Plan on two to three fittings across six to eight weeks, with the first fitting booked eight to ten weeks before the wedding. It is a real line in the budget, not a rounding error, and a shop that quotes it up front is being straight with you.

What drives that bill is how much construction has to be rebuilt. Taking in a side seam on a plain crepe sheath is one kind of work. Reshaping a beaded bodice means lifting the beadwork, moving the boning underneath, then putting the beads back so the pattern still reads. Add a bustle — every gown with a train needs one — plus cups or straps.

Bring the same shoes and the same undergarments to every fitting; change either and the hem is wrong. At the last fitting, bring whoever is bustling the dress at the reception and make the seamstress teach them on the dress, with their hands. A bustle explained in words at 10 p.m. in a St. Charles reception hall has never once worked.

Unrelated, and we know it — the metro’s gas stations.

### What are off-the-rack gowns, sample sales and trunk shows?

Three different things that all sound like a discount. Off-the-rack means you buy the actual gown in the shop and carry it out that day. A sample sale is a store clearing floor samples it’s retiring, sold as-is. A trunk show is a designer sending a full collection to one store for a weekend, usually with an ordering incentive attached.

Off-the-rack is the answer when the wedding is close. You skip the production clock entirely and go straight to alterations, which keeps a gown achievable at three or four months out. The trade-off is real: the dress has been tried on, it may carry a floor mark or a loose bead, and you buy the size that exists. Check the hem, underarms and zipper in good light, and price the alterations before calling it a bargain.

Trunk shows work differently. The designer ships far more of the line than the store normally stocks, sometimes including unreleased styles, and orders placed during the event commonly carry an incentive around ten percent. Useful once you’ve narrowed to one designer — much less useful as a first appointment, since you’ll spend the hour inside a single aesthetic.

### What do suits, tuxedos, bridesmaids and mothers need?

Everyone else in the photos has a timeline too, and all of them are shorter than the bride’s. Formalwear rental wants measurements two to three months out, garments in hand about two weeks before the date, and charges rush fees inside roughly two weeks. Bridesmaid dresses are usually made to order as well, on a four-to-six-month clock.

For the men it’s a math question about how many weddings are coming. Rental gets a coordinated look across groomsmen scattered between Wentzville, Belleville and out of state. Buying makes sense if the same suit is going to three more weddings and a funeral. Either way, get every groomsman measured by a real tailor rather than guessing off an old shirt, and set the deadline two months out.

For the mothers, the etiquette is simpler than the internet makes it. Neither mother wears white, ivory, or a champagne pale enough to read white in a flash. Past that the goal is coordination, not matching — same formality, colors that sit comfortably beside each other and the wedding palette. Tradition gives the mother of the bride first pick, and a short text between the two of them settles it faster than any rule. If you’re also sorting rings and gifts, our guide to choosing a jeweler in St. Louis covers the other half of that list.

### What does a bridal deposit actually commit you to?

A bridal deposit commits you to a custom order, which is a different animal from a retail purchase. Once the shop transmits the order and the designer cuts fabric to your measurements, there’s nothing to restock. No Missouri or Illinois law gives you a cooling-off right on an in-store special order, so the contract you sign is the deal.

Read four things first. The cancellation window, often measured in hours or a few days rather than weeks. The ship-window language, and whether a slipped estimate counts as a breach. Whether alterations are included, referred out, or required in-house. And what happens to your money if the shop closes — a fair question for anyone holding a four-figure deposit for eight months.

Pay the deposit with a credit card rather than cash, a check or a debit card, because card networks give you a dispute path that cash does not. If something goes genuinely wrong, Missouri shoppers can file with the Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Unit through ago.mo.gov or its hotline at 1-800-392-8222; Illinois shoppers file with the Attorney General’s Consumer Fraud Bureau, whose published helplines include 1-800-243-0618.

One cross-river detail matters on a purchase this size. Missouri’s state sales tax rate is 4.225% plus local rates; Illinois taxes general merchandise at 6.25% plus local. On a four-figure gown that spread is real money, and it lands on whichever side of the river the shop sits. For scale, The Knot’s 2026 Real Weddings Study, based on 10,474 U.S. couples married in 2025, put average gown spending near $2,100 nationally and about $2,500 in the Midwest.

### How soon should you clean and preserve the dress afterward?

Get the gown to a cleaner within about a week of the wedding, before invisible stains set. Sugar from champagne, cake and soda dries clear, then oxidizes brown over months; sweat and deodorant do the same at the underarms. Preservation itself typically takes six to ten weeks, so only the drop-off is urgent.

Preservation means the gown is cleaned, then packed with acid-free tissue in an acid-free, breathable box that keeps light, dust and humidity off it. Ask whether the cleaner works in-house or ships the gown out, whether the box can be opened and reclosed without voiding anything, and what happens if it yellows anyway. Store it flat and indoors — not a St. Louis attic in August, not a basement in a wet spring. Selling, donating or cutting the dress down are fine endings too, and all three go better after a prompt cleaning.

### What the shop owner is doing while you try on gowns

From behind the counter the math isn’t what shoppers assume. Those samples were bought at wholesale and are inventory that never sells at full price — tried on for a season or two, then moved at a sample sale. Your gown is a special order the shop owes the designer for long before your balance clears, so a February appointment is spring money and late-summer labor. Peak is engagement season, roughly Thanksgiving through Valentine’s Day, which packs January through spring with Saturday appointments — and a Saturday no-show is an hour nobody can resell. Accessories and alterations, not gowns, are where a small shop holds its margin. Every owner has also watched somebody photograph a sample, then order a look-alike overseas.

Which is why a complete listing earns its keep: shoppers search this category by neighborhood, and hours, appointment policy, the size range on the floor and the designers carried are exactly what they’re trying to learn before they call. Shops can add themselves on St Louis Near Me Directory.
