The answer tells you what kind of gym it is.

The hours question is the one that reshapes a household. Rec is one hour. Pre-team is commonly two short practices. A Development Program team schedule climbs steadily from there and, at the upper optional levels, becomes the dominant fixed object in a family’s week — several evenings plus meet Saturdays through the winter and spring. Ask for the actual practice schedule for each level in writing before you say yes to team. Not the range. The schedule.

Unrelated, and we know it — that ceiling stain means you need a roofer.

### What does gymnastics cost in St. Louis?

Tuition is the smallest line on a competitive season sheet, and no honest article can quote you a metro-wide rec class price, because gyms bill by the session, by the month and by the punch card and none of it is standardized. What can be quoted are the fixed national fees, and those are the ones parents never see coming.

USA Gymnastics athlete membership for the 2026-2027 season is $75, or $27 for a first-time athlete, covering August 1, 2026 through July 31, 2027. That fee is per athlete, per year, and it is entirely separate from whatever your gym charges. On the Illinois side there is one more small one: Region 5 collects $2.00 per athlete at any USA Gymnastics sanctioned event held in Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan or Ohio.

The honest cost ladder runs bottom to top like this. A weekly rec class is monthly tuition and nothing else. Pre-team adds a second practice, so roughly a second tuition. Entry-level team adds the $75 USA Gymnastics athlete membership, a competition leotard, warm-ups, a team fee, and a per-meet entry fee for every meet on the schedule. Upper-level team adds travel — hotel nights, gas, meals, and a coach travel share that gyms commonly split across the athletes attending each meet. Nobody hands you that whole stack at once. Ask for it at once.

Three questions get you most of the way to a real number before you sign anything. What is the total of the season fees, listed line by line, for the level we’re joining? How many meets are on the schedule and what is the entry fee for each one? And what happens if we withdraw mid-season — is the season fee refundable, prorated, or gone? Get all three answers in writing, from the gym, before the season opens.

### What safety and coach credentials should you ask about?

Ask whether every coach on the floor holds a current USA Gymnastics professional membership, and ask to see it. For the 2026-2027 season a USA Gymnastics Competitive Coach membership costs $99 and requires a background check renewed every two years, the U110 U.S. Center for SafeSport core course, USA Gymnastics Safety Certification renewed every four years, the U100 fundamental instruction course, the U112 course on tough coaching and emotional abuse, and a concussion education acknowledgment.

Those are requirements, not suggestions, and a gym that has done the work will answer in one sentence without getting defensive. Worth knowing too: under the Protecting Young Victims from Sexual Abuse and Safe Sport Authorization Act of 2017, signed into law in February 2018, an adult authorized to interact with a minor amateur athlete must report a reasonable suspicion of child abuse within 24 hours. That is federal law and it applies to your kid’s gym.

You can also check names yourself, for free, before the first class. The U.S. Center for SafeSport maintains a public Centralized Disciplinary Database at cdd.uscenterforsafesport.org, searchable by name, city, state and sport affiliation. USA Gymnastics separately publishes a list of suspended, restricted and permanently ineligible participants. Five minutes with both is an ordinary thing for a parent to do and nothing to feel awkward about.

Then look at the floor itself. Where is the AED and who on shift is trained to use it? Is there a written concussion protocol, and who has authority to sit a kid down? How often is equipment inspected and pit foam replaced? Is anyone spotting new skills, or are kids attempting them alone at the end of a rotation? A gym that has thought about injuries answers fast. And if an injury does show up and keeps showing up, that is a physician’s call, not a coach’s — our guide on when to see an orthopedist in St. Louis covers what actually warrants the appointment.

### Does it matter which side of the river your gym is on?

Yes, in two concrete ways. Competitively, Missouri and Illinois sit in different USA Gymnastics regions, so two St. Louis gyms twenty minutes apart send their teams to different state and regional championships. Legally, Illinois carries an AED requirement for fitness facilities that Missouri does not.

Take the competitive side first. In women’s gymnastics, Missouri sits in Region 4 alongside Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota. Illinois sits in Region 5 with Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan and Ohio. A team out of Chesterfield or Florissant qualifies through Missouri state and then heads north and west for regionals. A team out of Belleville or Edwardsville qualifies through Illinois state and travels east. If your family already crosses the river for work, ask a prospective gym where its meets physically are before assuming the travel is equivalent.

On safety law, Illinois requires a physical fitness facility to keep at least one AED on the premises and to have a trained AED user on staff during staffed business hours, under the Physical Fitness Facility Medical Emergency Preparedness Act (210 ILCS 74). The Act carves out hospital and hotel facilities, outdoor park district facilities, and any place that employs nobody to provide instruction — a staffed Illinois gymnastics club with paid coaches is not an obvious fit for those carve-outs, though the club can tell you where it lands. Missouri has no equivalent statewide mandate for fitness facilities. RSMo 190.092 governs how an AED must be maintained and who must be trained once a Missouri business chooses to own one, but nothing forces it to own one. On the Missouri side, that question is yours to ask.

One more Missouri note if someone hands you a long contract. The Missouri Attorney General’s office regulates health and fitness club contracts: they must be in writing, cannot exceed 36 months, must disclose cancellation rights, and a consumer who cancels within three days is owed a refund within 30 days. Covered clubs register with that office and pay a $100 annual filing fee. Whether a particular gymnastics club falls under that law depends on how its contract is written, so if you’re being asked to prepay a full year, call the Attorney General’s consumer line before you sign rather than after.

### What gym owners wish parents understood

Ceiling height and clear-span floor space are the two things a gymnastics club cannot fake, and that fixed footprint is the whole business model. The lease does not shrink when enrollment does. Rec classes are the volume that pays for the building; the competitive team is the identity and the retention engine, but it is coach-hour expensive — low athlete-to-coach ratios, long evenings, and weekend meets where a coach stands on a floor all day. Birthday parties and open gym exist because a Saturday afternoon with a dark floor is pure loss.

The year is largely made in late August and September. Registration season is the year, summer camps bridge the dead stretch, and a family that quietly disappears in October leaves a slot that cannot be refilled mid-session. Owners also carry costs parents never see: annual club membership with USA Gymnastics, coach certifications, background screening, liability insurance and equipment replacement. What they say to each other is that a $99 coach certification and a multi-night team program get compared to a drop-in class as though they were the same product. Parents in Ballwin and Granite City search for this by town, so being listed and complete is how a good club gets found — owners can add their gym to St Louis Near Me Directory.

### How do you know when to stop or switch tracks?

When the hours stop matching what your kid actually wants from the sport. The clearest signals are dread before practice that lasts more than a few weeks, a kid who used to talk about gymnastics at dinner and now doesn’t, and pain that keeps returning to the same joint. None of those automatically mean quit. Most of them mean move tracks.

Two structural moments squeeze families hardest. The first is the invitation to team, usually somewhere between six and eight, when a one-hour habit becomes a schedule. The second is the jump into the upper optional levels, where hours and travel step up together. Both are legitimate places to move from the Development Program to Xcel rather than leave the sport. USA Gymnastics publishes rules for changing tracks, including petition procedures, and a coach who frames a move to Xcel as a demotion is telling you something about the gym rather than about your kid.

There is also a version of this sport with no ladder at all. Open gym, tumbling classes, a recreational hour that a kid keeps for eight years for no reason except that Wednesday is better with it. That is a completely legitimate outcome, and it is what most kids who start in a preschool class in Maryland Heights are ultimately going to want.

Ready to book that first class instead of reading about it? Browse gymnastics across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two gyms, ask each one for a trial class, and ask both for a written season fee schedule before you pick.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What age is too late to start gymnastics?

A.  There isn’t one for recreational gymnastics, and it is later than most parents assume for competition. USA Gymnastics lets a gymnast with no previous competitive experience enter the Xcel program at Bronze, Silver or Gold at her coach’s discretion, and Gold’s only stated requirement is having reached the 7th birthday. Elite is a different conversation. A competitive season is not.

### Q. Is 7 too late to start gymnastics?

A.  No. Seven is the published minimum age for Development Program Levels 4 through 7 and for Xcel Gold, so a seven-year-old is arriving at the age floor for several entry points rather than behind them. A brand-new seven-year-old will start in a rec or pre-team class and get evaluated from there like everyone else does.

### Q. Is 4 too old to start gymnastics?

A.  Not remotely. Four is the youngest competitive age anywhere in the USA Gymnastics Development Program — Level 1 requires an athlete to have reached her 4th birthday, and Xcel Bronze requires the 5th. A four-year-old walking into a preschool class is at the front of the pack, not the back of it, by the sport’s own rules.

### Q. Should I put my 3 year old in gymnastics?

A.  Only if you want the motor skills and the fun, because nothing competitive is available yet. USA Gymnastics competition begins at the 4th birthday. A three-year-old class is balance, hanging, rolling, listening and taking turns, which is genuinely valuable, but no three-year-old is getting a head start on a level ladder that has not opened.

### Q. Why is gymnastics so expensive?

A.  Because the building, the coach ratios and the certifications are all expensive and none of them scale down. A club needs clear-span floor space, pits, springs and beams. Team coaching runs at low athlete-to-coach ratios across long evenings plus weekend meets. On top of that sit annual USA Gymnastics memberships, background screening, safety certification, insurance and a per-meet entry fee.

### Q. How much does it cost to compete in gymnastics?

A.  More than tuition, and the fixed piece is published. USA Gymnastics athlete membership for the 2026-2027 season is $75, or $27 for a first-time athlete, covering August 1, 2026 through July 31, 2027. Team fees, a competition leotard and warm-ups, a per-meet entry fee for every meet, and travel at the upper levels all stack on top.

### Q. How to choose a gymnastics gym?

A.  Watch a class before you pay, then ask four questions. Do all coaches on the floor hold current USA Gymnastics professional membership? Does the gym field an Xcel team as well as a Development Program team? What is the written practice schedule and season fee list for the level you would be joining? And what happens financially if you withdraw mid-season?

### Q. What age do most kids quit gymnastics?

A.  There is no reliable gymnastics-specific national figure, so treat any number you are quoted with suspicion. What is predictable is where the pressure points sit: the move from a one-hour rec class to a multi-night team schedule, usually between six and eight, and the hours-and-travel jump into the upper optional levels a few years after that.

### Q. What are 6 types of gymnastics?

A.  The six most people mean are women’s artistic, men’s artistic, rhythmic, trampoline and tumbling, acrobatic, and gymnastics for all. USA Gymnastics currently lists a seventh discipline as well, parkour, alongside its college program. Most clubs around the St. Louis metro offer artistic gymnastics, and trampoline and tumbling turns up at some of them.

### Q. Where can I find adult gymnastics classes in St. Louis?

A.  Look for adult tumbling classes, adult open gym and drop-in sessions at USA Gymnastics member clubs around the metro rather than at fitness gyms, since the equipment is the entire point. Availability shifts by season, so call ahead and ask specifically about adult open gym hours, drop-in pricing, and whether true beginners are welcome on the apparatus.

## How Much Does an Inground Pool Cost in St. Louis?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-an-inground-pool-costs-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s the first genuinely hot Saturday in May. You’re standing in the back yard in Kirkwood with a coffee going cold, staring at a rectangle of grass and doing arithmetic in your head. The kids are eight and eleven. You figure you have maybe six good summers left before one of them would rather be anywhere else. Somebody at work in Maryland Heights mentioned their pool came in around thirty grand, and that number has been rattling around your skull for a week.

Or maybe you’re in Belleville, and the neighbor two doors down had a dig truck parked in the side yard for nine days before you finally worked up the nerve to ask what it cost. Or you’re in Florissant at eleven at night, scrolling three proposals from three builders, and the totals are so far apart you assume somebody made a mistake.

Nobody made a mistake. Here is the part that rarely gets said out loud: the number on the proposal is not the number you will spend, and that is usually not because anyone is being slippery. A pool price and a back yard price are two different products, and half of this fight is knowing which one you’re holding. So let’s put real, current, sourced figures against it — on both sides of the river, where the rules genuinely differ.

### What is the average cost of an inground pool in St. Louis?

A St. Louis-area inground pool runs roughly $35,000 to $110,000-plus for the pool and its installation. Aloha Pools, a St. Louis-area builder, published this breakdown on August 11, 2026: vinyl $35,000 to $68,000, fiberglass $42,000 to $78,000, gunite $55,000 to $110,000 and up. That range covers the pool. It does not cover the yard around it.

Now the honest complication. Blue Haven’s St. Louis blog puts a basic 32-foot-by-16-foot vinyl-lined pool at around $75,000, gunite at $85,000 to $120,000 installed, and fiberglass at $65,000 to $95,000. Two St. Louis builders, two very different pictures of the same city. Neither is lying. One is describing a shell-and-install price and one is describing a finished project with more spec in it.

National guides land higher still. Thursday Pools, updated July 30, 2026, lists vinyl at $35,000 to $80,000 and concrete at $50,000 to $120,000 or more, with fiberglass priced by size: about $74,000 for a small pool under 26 feet, $109,000 for a medium one, $113,000 for a large one. River Pools, updated December 8, 2025, quotes turnkey packages of $45,000 to $100,000 for vinyl, $85,000 to $200,000 for fiberglass and $95,000 to $225,000 for concrete — and adds that most homeowners spend another $25,000 to $50,000 on electrical, patio work, fencing and accessories.

The practical takeaway is not a single average. It’s that a St. Louis quote means nothing until you know what it includes. Three bids on identical written scope is the only comparison worth making.

### Can I get an inground pool for $30,000?

Not for a finished, permitted, contractor-built inground pool in the St. Louis metro in 2026. Thirty thousand dollars sits below every published local starting price. The lowest current one is Aloha Pools’ $35,000 vinyl figure from August 11, 2026 — and that number is the pool alone, with no decking, no fence, no electrical and no permits attached to it.

So what does $30,000 actually do? Three useful things. It makes a substantial down payment on a financed build. It covers the entire surround — patio, fence, electrical, cover — on a pool you finance separately. Or it buys a very good above-ground pool with a real deck, which in a town where you swim from late May to early September is a less ridiculous idea than pool people like to admit.

What about $20,000? That is roughly $15,000 short of the lowest local inground entry price, before any of the excluded items. At that level you are shopping above-ground, semi-inground, or a kit where you personally arrange excavation, concrete and licensed electrical work. If an inground bid lands at $20,000, the correct response is not excitement. It is a line-by-line read of what the bid leaves out.

### How much do vinyl, fiberglass and gunite pools cost, and which one lasts?

Vinyl is the cheapest way in — $35,000 to $68,000 locally per Aloha Pools, August 11, 2026 — and the liner is a wear part, not a permanent surface. Thursday Pools puts liner replacement at $3,000 to $7,500 every 5 to 15 years as of July 30, 2026; Blue Haven’s St. Louis figures say every 7 to 10 years. Budget for at least one replacement inside your first decade.

Fiberglass runs $42,000 to $78,000 locally. The shell shows up molded on a truck, which makes the install fast — days rather than weeks — but locks you into the manufacturer’s sizes and shapes. Delivery is its own line item: River Pools lists $1,500 to $4,500 and up, updated December 8, 2025. If your yard has a tight gate, a power line over the drive, or a Webster Groves lot with six feet of side yard, ask about crane access before you fall in love with a model.

Gunite is $55,000 to $110,000 and up locally, and it is the only one that will be whatever shape you draw. It also has the longest build and the biggest long-run maintenance line: Blue Haven’s St. Louis figures put resurfacing at $8,000 to $10,000 every 15 to 25 years. Gunite is weather-dependent work, which matters here — a hard freeze stops a pour, and that is exactly why good builders sell in the fall for a spring dig.

### What does a pool quote leave out?

Almost everything that turns a hole full of water into a back yard. Using Thursday Pools’ July 30, 2026 figures: permits $100 to $1,000 or more, excavation $1,000 to $5,000, fencing $10 to $45 per linear foot (about $2,000 to $13,500 for a typical 200 to 300 feet), electrical $2,000 to $10,000 with a realistic minimum of $3,000 to $5,000, and patio or decking $2,000 to $14,000 for a 20-by-20 area.

Then the optional-but-not-really items. A heater is $1,200 to $6,000. A winter cover is $75 to $250, a manual retractable cover $1,500 to $6,000, and an automatic cover $8,000 to $20,000 — that last one alone can be a fifth of a vinyl pool’s entire price. Add water to fill it, landscaping repair after the machines leave, and a gate that meets code.

The permit line deserves special attention around here, because it is rarely one permit. Hazelwood, Missouri requires a separate fence permit for the enclosure, plus separate St. Louis County plumbing and electrical permits, and it requires inground pool construction drawings carrying a registered Missouri engineer’s seal, signed and dated. Three permits and a sealed drawing is a different afternoon than one form.

The excavation surprise is the real one, though. St. Louis-area yards sit on clay and limestone. Rock, a high water table, a buried lateral or a utility easement running through the only flat part of the yard can all change the dig, and the contract language about who pays for that is the single most important paragraph you will sign.

### What do the fence and permit rules cost you in Missouri and Illinois?

Both states leave residential pool barriers to local government, so the number you have to hit is set at city hall, not in Jefferson City or Springfield. In practice the Missouri suburbs converge on a 48-inch barrier; in metro-east Illinois each city writes its own, and Belleville’s is 4 feet. The difference is that Missouri’s figure comes from cities adopting the International Residential Code, while Illinois has no statewide residential rule at all.

On the Missouri side, Town and Country’s swimming pool guide is a good template for what your city will want: a barrier at least 48 inches high measured from finished grade, openings no more than 4 inches, no more than a 2-inch gap between grade and the bottom of the barrier, gates that swing away from the pool and are self-closing and self-latching, and a latch release on the pool side at least 3 inches below the top of the gate when it sits under 54 inches. Construction must meet the 2018 International Residential Code, and every metallic part within 5 feet of the water — rails, ladders, lights, the pool frame — must be bonded with solid copper no smaller than #8.

Town and Country adds a zoning trap worth knowing before you draw anything: a pool larger than 1,000 square feet of water surface, or sitting more than 30 feet from the primary structure, needs a conditional use permit — three public meetings, typically a 60 to 90 day process. That can move your swim date by a season.

O’Fallon, Missouri goes further than most. Its pool guide requires a 48-inch enclosure, puts pools in the rear yard only and 10 feet off the rear property line, and requires every doorway and grade-level or deck-access window from the house to the pool area to be alarmed — on an alarm separate from your home security system — or self-closing and self-latching. Heaters and pumps must have automatic timers, heated pools need a vapor-retardant cover, and no pool may be used at all until the permanent enclosure is installed and final approval is granted. Violations there carry fines up to $500 per day.

On the Illinois side, do not assume looser. Assume less uniform. Illinois has no statewide barrier statute for private residential pools. A bill that would have created one — HB2495, the Private Swimming Pool Enclosure Act, known as Zoe’s Law, which proposed a 42-inch statewide minimum and would have required every municipality to run a pool permitting process — was re-referred to the House Rules Committee on April 11, 2025 and has not become law. So metro-east rules are purely municipal. Belleville’s code, section 162.398, requires any pool more than two feet deep to be enclosed by a wall or fence at least four feet high with a gate, and keeps pools out of front yards. Call your own city before you sign anything.

Licensing splits the same way. Missouri issues no statewide general contractor license — but St. Charles County licenses pool installers specifically and requires them to be bonded and insured. That is a real, checkable credential you can ask for by name if your project is in St. Peters, O’Fallon or Wentzville.

Wildly off-topic — if the dog swims too, meet the vets.

### How much does a pool cost to run every year in St. Louis?

Plan on $1,500 to $5,000 a year. Aloha Pools’ August 11, 2026 figures break that into electricity of $70 to $350 a month during swim season and chemicals of $50 to $150 a month, plus opening, closing and the parts that wear out. In a metro that freezes hard, winterizing is not optional maintenance — it is the thing that stops a cracked line in February.

Your pump is the biggest single lever on that electric bill, and federal rules already moved it. Under the U.S. Department of Energy’s dedicated purpose pool pump standards, effective July 19, 2021, residential pool pump motors of 0.5 total horsepower and above manufactured on or after that date must be variable-speed. Variable-speed equipment costs more on the quote and much less every month it runs, so a bid that saves you money on the pump is often selling you a higher summer utility bill.

Then the periodic hits. Vinyl liners: $3,000 to $7,500 every 5 to 15 years, per Thursday Pools, July 30, 2026. Gunite resurfacing: $8,000 to $10,000 every 15 to 25 years, per Blue Haven’s St. Louis figures. Two more calls are worth making before you sign — your insurance carrier, because a pool changes your liability exposure, and your county assessor, because a permitted pool is a permanent improvement and the assessor sees the permit. Neither conversation is fun. Both are cheaper than the surprise. If the tax side gets complicated, our guide to what a tax preparer costs in St. Louis is a reasonable next stop.

### Why does a pool not add value to a house?

Because buyers price a pool as a liability at least as often as an amenity. In the 2023 Remodeling Impact Report: Outdoor Features, published by the National Association of REALTORS and the National Association of Landscape Professionals in March 2023, landscape professionals priced an 18-by-36-foot gunite pool with standard filtration at $90,000, and REALTORS estimated $50,000 recovered at resale. That is 56 percent — the lowest cost recovery of the eleven outdoor projects in the report.

The sharper number in that same report: just 1 percent of REALTORS said they would recommend an inground pool addition before selling. Standard lawn care service recovered 217 percent. A new patio recovered 95 percent. The pool sat alone at the bottom of the list.

And yet the same report gave the inground pool a Joy Score of 10 out of 10 — the highest in the study, tied with landscape lighting — with 90 percent of owners reporting a greater sense of enjoyment at home afterward. That is the honest frame for this purchase. You are buying summers with your kids, not equity. Price it like a boat, not like a kitchen.

### What pads a pool quote, and what should you push back on?

Start with allowances. A line that reads decking allowance of $8,000 is a placeholder, not a price, and the true number arrives after you have already committed. Ask for actual square footage, an actual material and an actual unit price. Do the same for coping, tile and any “to be determined” landscaping line.

Next, the unsuitable-soil and rock clause. Read who pays, and at what rate. Then the bundles: an automatic cover at $8,000 to $20,000, a heater at $1,200 to $6,000 and a water feature can each get folded into a package that looks like one discount and is really three decisions you never made separately. And be careful with any builder who quotes a monthly payment instead of a total — a payment can be made to look like almost anything by stretching the term.

The fix is unglamorous and it works. Write the scope yourself — size, shell type, decking square footage, fence linear footage, equipment, cover — and hand the identical page to three builders. Ask each one for an itemized total with a written exclusions list. It is the same discipline that protects you on any big-ticket back yard project, including solar panels in St. Louis, where the quote spread is just as wide.

### What does this look like from the pool builder’s side?

The build is the risky part of this trade, not the profitable-forever part. A pool contract is a fixed price against a hole nobody has seen the bottom of yet, and on clay and limestone a dig that finds rock or a high water table can eat a job’s margin in two days. That is why the excavation language is written so carefully. It is the clause the whole trade argues about.

The calendar is the other squeeze. A hard freeze stops a pour, so the builders who stay sane are selling in October for a spring dig, while the phone rings hardest in June from people who wanted to swim last weekend. Meanwhile the money that actually recurs is service — openings, closings, liners, pumps — not the build. What operators here complain about to each other is being priced against a bid that quietly excluded the deck. Homeowners search for a pool builder locally and in season, which is why a complete, findable directory listing is worth keeping current.

Ready to put real numbers against your own back yard? Browse swimming pool contractors across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then ask three of them to bid one identical written scope — same size, same decking, same fence — so you are comparing pools instead of paragraphs.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much does it cost to have an inground pool installed in Missouri?

A.  In the St. Louis metro, budget $35,000 to $110,000 and up for the pool and installation. St. Louis-area builder Aloha Pools listed vinyl at $35,000 to $68,000, fiberglass at $42,000 to $78,000 and gunite at $55,000 to $110,000-plus on August 11, 2026. Missouri sets no statewide pool price and no statewide contractor license, so both your quote and the code you must meet are decided locally.

### Q. Can I get an inground pool for $20,000?

A.  Not a contractor-built one in this market. Twenty thousand dollars falls roughly $15,000 short of the lowest current St. Louis-area starting price for a vinyl inground pool, and that starting price already excludes decking, fencing, electrical and permits. Realistically $20,000 buys an above-ground pool with a proper deck, or covers the fence-and-electrical half of an inground project you finance.

### Q. What size pool can I get for $30,000?

A.  In the St. Louis area, $30,000 does not reliably buy a finished inground pool of any size. It sits under the $35,000 local floor for a basic vinyl build, and that floor comes before decking, fence, electrical and permits. The money goes further as a down payment on a financed pool, or as the full budget for the surround on a pool financed separately.

### Q. What does a $10,000 pool look like?

A.  An above-ground pool, professionally installed, with a basic pump and filter, a ladder and a simple surround. It is not an inground shell. No current source puts a professionally built inground pool anywhere near $10,000 in the St. Louis metro, so if an inground bid arrives at that figure, read the exclusions list line by line before you get excited.

### Q. Can I write off a swimming pool on taxes?

A.  Usually no. IRS Publication 502 treats a pool as a deductible medical capital expense only when it is installed primarily for medical care a doctor has prescribed, and then only for the amount by which the cost exceeds the resulting increase in your home’s value. Medical expenses are also deductible only above 7.5 percent of adjusted gross income. Talk to a tax preparer before you count on it.

### Q. How to choose the right pool contractor?

A.  Hand three builders one identical written scope, then compare their exclusion lists rather than their totals. Confirm the credential your jurisdiction actually requires — St. Charles County, for example, licenses pool installers and requires them to be bonded and insured. Ask who pulls each permit, who supplies the code-compliant fence, and exactly what happens to the price if the excavation hits rock.

### Q. What are common red flags when hiring a swimming pool contractor?

A.  A verbal-only price, a large deposit collected before permits are pulled, no written exclusions list, and a bid conspicuously below two others on identical scope. Treat vagueness about the permit path or the fence spec as a risk too: in O’Fallon, Missouri, a pool may not be used at all until the permanent enclosure is installed and the city grants final approval.

### Q. What not to tell a contractor?

A.  Do not lead with your maximum budget, and do not lead with the monthly payment you could handle. Both invite a quote to grow until it fits. Lead with scope instead: pool size, shell type, decking square footage, fence linear footage, equipment and your two non-negotiables. Then ask for one itemized total with the exclusions written down.

### Q. What do pool contractors do?

A.  They design the pool, pull the permits, excavate, set the shell or shoot the gunite, plumb and wire the equipment, bond the metal parts, install coping and decking, fill the pool and balance the startup chemistry, and schedule the required inspections. Many also carry the work forward with seasonal openings and closings, liner replacements and equipment swaps.

### Q. How much profit do pool contractors make?

A.  There is no reliable published margin figure for St. Louis pool builders, and anyone quoting you a confident one is guessing. Structurally, the build is a fixed-price contract exposed to excavation surprises and material price swings, while the steadier income sits in service work — openings, closings, liner replacements and equipment. That is why so many builders push the maintenance side of the business.

## Where to Buy Sporting Goods in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/where-to-buy-sporting-goods-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Tuesday evening in Florissant and the league email finally lands. Your daughter made the 12U team, and attached is a one-page equipment list: a bat, a batting helmet with a faceguard, sliding shorts, molded cleats, and a glove sized for a hand two inches bigger than the one that fit last spring. First practice is Saturday.

Or maybe you’re across the river in Belleville holding a shorter but stranger list — shin guards, a mouthguard, and a ball in a size you have never heard of. Or you’re standing in an Affton garage looking at a crate of gear your kid outgrew in one season, wondering whether any of it is worth anything to anybody.

Here’s the part nobody explains. The St. Louis metro does not have one kind of sporting goods store. It has five. They stock different things, they price differently, and buying the wrong item at the wrong one is how a $180 list quietly becomes $340. This is the map.

### What are some good sporting goods stores in Saint Louis, MO?

The honest answer is that the right store depends on the item, because metro sporting goods retail splits into five channels: national big boxes, outdoor and hunting superstores, single-sport specialty shops, used and consignment gear traders, and team dealers who sell to schools and leagues instead of walk-in shoppers. Match the channel to the item and you rarely overpay.

Big boxes carry breadth. Dick’s Sporting Goods has metro stores that include 1507 S. Brentwood Blvd. in Brentwood and 64 THF Blvd. at Chesterfield Commons, and Academy Sports + Outdoors sits at 14260 Manchester Rd. in Manchester. This is the easiest single trip for a cleat, a youth glove, a soccer ball, a basketball or a starter bat. Breadth is the product. Depth inside any one sport is not.

Outdoor and hunting superstores are a different animal. The Cabela’s at 5555 St. Louis Mills Blvd. in Hazelwood runs a 130,000-square-foot showroom just off I-270, and Bass Pro Shops and Cabela’s stores sell state hunting and fishing licenses at the counter. That detail matters here: the Missouri Department of Conservation sells permits online, by phone, at its own offices and, in its words, “from more than a thousand vendors around the state,” which is why buying a rod and a permit in one stop is normal in Missouri.

Single-sport specialty shops trade breadth for fit. Run shops put you on a treadmill instead of guessing at a size. Big River Running keeps three metro stores — West County in Manchester, South City in St. Louis, and University City — and its fitting process measures foot length, width and arch, watches your gait on a treadmill, and generates a digital foot scan that shows pressure points and pronation. Alpine Shop, the locally owned outdoor retailer at 440 N. Kirkwood Rd. in Kirkwood, has been in business since 1973 and runs a ski shop. REI keeps a store at 1703 S. Brentwood Blvd. Bike shops, hockey shops and golf pro shops belong in this tier too, and they survive the same way the good neighborhood hardware stores do — on the person behind the counter, not the shelf.

Used and consignment is the channel families underuse. Play It Again Sports buys, sells and trades used sports and fitness equipment at its Kirkwood and Arnold stores, pays cash on the spot for gear it accepts, and takes walk-ins with no appointment. Inventory turns constantly, which is both the appeal and the catch. What is on the rack today was not there last week.

Team dealers are the channel shoppers never see. They sell uniforms, decorated apparel and bulk equipment to schools, parishes and leagues on purchase orders, usually with no browsable storefront. When a coach hands you a list and says the jerseys are already handled, a team dealer is why.

### What is considered a sporting goods store?

A sporting goods store is a retailer whose main business is equipment, apparel and footwear for sport, fitness and outdoor recreation — balls, bats, sticks, racquets, protective gear, athletic shoes, and camping, hunting and fishing equipment. The definition is wider than most people picture, and it pulls in several storefronts that never put the phrase on the sign.

Inside the category: bike shops, run specialty stores, golf pro shops, hockey shops, dive shops, archery shops, hunting and fishing outfitters, fitness equipment dealers, and the used gear traders. Next door but genuinely something else: licensed team apparel stores, which sell fan merchandise rather than playing equipment; general discount retail, which carries a seasonal end-cap of balls and bikes without staff who fit anything; and screen printers and embroiderers, who decorate garments they did not manufacture.

The distinction is worth holding onto because it predicts service. A store that sells equipment has to know sizing, certification marks and league rules, and it usually staffs for that. A store that sells sports-themed goods does not, and it does not pretend to.

### When is used sports gear the smart buy?

Used is the right call when the item wears slowly, carries no certification clock, and will be outgrown long before it wears out. That describes most of a youth athlete’s kit and a good share of an adult’s, which is why the used channel is where the real savings sit.

Gloves and mitts. Leather gets better with use. A broken-in glove at half price is an upgrade, not a compromise.

Cleats, skates and court shoes for growing kids. A pair worn for one season by a child who grew two sizes is barely used.

Bats, if the certification stamp still matches the league. The stamp is the whole question, and it is covered in the next section.

Golf clubs, dumbbells, kettlebells and benches. Essentially inert. Steel does not age out.

Kayaks, canoes, paddles and racks. Big-ticket, slow-wearing, and painful to store, which is exactly why they turn up used.

Bikes. Buy the bike used, then pay a shop for a safety check and tune. That is still far cheaper than new.

Non-certified padding. Hockey pants, shin guards, sliding shorts and bags have no expiration and no rating to void.

Timing helps. The used channel refills right after a season ends, because that is when garages get cleared and trade-in counters fill up. If you can buy a season behind, do it.

### What sports gear should you never buy used?

Anything carrying a safety certification with a clock attached. Helmets lead that list in every sport, because a helmet’s certification is tied to its manufacture date and its impact history, and a helmet bought from a stranger comes with neither documented. Here is what the standards bodies actually say.

Football, lacrosse, ice hockey, baseball and softball helmets. The National Operating Committee on Standards for Athletic Equipment publishes recertification standards for football helmets (ND004), football faceguards (ND087), lacrosse helmets (ND043), ice hockey helmets (ND032), and baseball and softball batter’s and catcher’s helmets (ND026). NOCSAE states that recertification is not mandatory under its standards but is strongly recommended, and that the interval is set by years elapsed rather than by use. It recommends annual recertification for helmets made before January 2017. Reconditioners will not recertify a helmet 10 or more years old — a useful-life rule set by NAERA, the reconditioners’ trade association, not by NOCSAE.

Ice hockey helmets specifically. The Hockey Equipment Certification Council prints an expiration date on its label 6.5 years after the helmet’s date of manufacture. HECC also states that if the label is removed, totally illegible or missing, the helmet is no longer HECC certified — and that HECC cannot replace those labels. A used helmet with a peeled sticker is not a bargain; it is a helmet a league can refuse.

Bicycle helmets. Federal standard 16 CFR Part 1203 has applied to bicycle helmets manufactured after March 10, 1999, and it requires a warning telling the wearer that after an impact a helmet may be damaged badly enough that it no longer protects the head. A crash that leaves no visible mark can still crush foam. You cannot audit a stranger’s crash history.

Life jackets. Federal boating rules turn on Coast Guard approval, and approval is shown on the label. A jacket with a faded, torn or missing label is not a jacket you want on a kid on the Meramec.

Running shoes. Midsole foam compresses with miles you cannot see from the outside. A used pair carries an unknown mileage count and an unknown wear pattern from somebody else’s stride.

The workable middle ground is buying used from a shop rather than an individual. A trade-in counter inspects what it accepts and can tell you the manufacture date on a helmet, which a garage sale cannot.

Nothing to do with cleats — who to call about storm-damaged trees.

### How do team and league equipment lists actually get filled around here?

Two ways, and knowing which is which saves money. The league or school supplies the shared, expensive items — catcher’s gear, team balls, goals, blocking pads, scorebooks — usually through a team dealer on a purchase order. Families buy the personal-fit items: shoes, gloves, mouthguards, bats and, in most youth programs, the helmet.

The certification wording on that list is the part parents skim and the part that decides whether the gear is legal. Youth baseball’s national member organizations — Little League, Babe Ruth and Cal Ripken, PONY, AABC and NABF among them — adopted the USABat standard effective January 1, 2018, so a youth bat needs the USA Baseball mark. High school and college play runs on the BBCOR .50 standard, in place since 2011. And a change is already scheduled: effective January 1, 2028, the National Federation of State High School Associations will require a non-wood bat to be a USA BBCOR bat, a BBCOR .50 bat, or a USABat -4, -5 or -6. Missouri and Illinois high schools both play under NFHS playing rules, so that date lands on both sides of the river at once.

A sequence that works: get the league’s exact certification wording in writing before you shop, buy the helmet last and in person after somebody measures the head, and hold the receipt for anything with a warranty. Sign-up season is where the real costs hide in every youth sport, which is just as true when you are signing a kid up for gymnastics as it is at a baseball registration table.

### When is the best time to buy sporting goods in St. Louis?

Two calendars matter, and they do not line up the way shoppers hope: the sales tax calendar and the clearance calendar. The tax holidays are the ones people plan around, and for sports gear they mostly disappoint.

Missouri ran its 2026 back-to-school sales tax holiday from 12:01 a.m. Friday, August 7 through midnight Sunday, August 9. Clothing valued at $100 or less is exempt during it, and the statute defines clothing as any article of wearing apparel intended to be worn on or about the human body. Sporting equipment, though, is written out by name: the school-supplies definition explicitly excludes sporting equipment. Practice shorts and plain athletic shoes can qualify. The bat and the helmet never do.

Illinois works differently and, in 2026, ran longer. The Illinois Department of Revenue set a back-to-school holiday from August 7 through August 16, 2026, cutting the state sales tax rate on qualifying items from 6.25% to 1.25% while local taxes still applied. Qualifying clothing and footwear had to be priced under $125 per item, and the exclusion list is unusually specific about sport: gloves including baseball, bowling, boxing, hockey and golf gloves; goggles; hand and elbow guards; hard hats and helmets; shoulder pads; and cleated or spiked athletic shoes, roller and ice skates and ski boots. Illinois had not run a back-to-school holiday since 2022, so 2026 was the first in four years.

The clearance calendar is a trade rhythm rather than a published schedule, and it is worth more money than either tax holiday. Winter hardgoods get marked down as the season ends and spring inventory needs the floor. Baseball and softball stock thins and discounts after the summer season rather than before it. Fall sports gear is deepest and priciest in August. Buying one season behind the sport you play is the single biggest lever a family has, and it beats both states’ tax holidays by a wide margin on any item over about $60.

### What should you check about fitting and returns before you buy?

Check three things before you pay: whether the store fits the item, whether you can return it after actually using it, and how long the window runs. Those answers vary far more between store types than prices do, and they are the reason a specialty shop can be worth a longer drive.

On fitting, run specialty is the clearest example. Big River Running lists a fit process that measures foot length, width and arch, analyzes gait on a treadmill and produces a digital foot scan for pressure points and pronation. Ski and snowboard boots are the other item that genuinely requires a bootfitter rather than a size chart. Helmets are the third: a helmet should sit level, roughly one to two finger widths above the eyebrows, with the straps forming a V under each ear and enough tension that it does not shift when you shake your head. Head shape does not come through a size chart, so buy the helmet in a store.

On returns, policies differ by channel and change over time, so confirm the current window at the register rather than trusting what was true last year. Big boxes generally want unworn goods with tags and the receipt. Specialty shops are often the most flexible on shoes that have actually been run in, which is the point of buying there. Big River Running publishes a 30-day return or exchange window on online orders. Used and consignment sales are frequently final or store credit only, which is a fair trade for the price and a nasty surprise if you assumed otherwise. Keep receipts for bats and anything else with a warranty clock, since those are typically dated from purchase. And if a fit problem has already turned into a nagging injury, the shopping question becomes a medical one — that is when to see an orthopedist in St. Louis.

### What running a sporting goods shop here actually looks like

From behind the counter the economics are not what shoppers assume. Hardgoods — bats, sticks, skis, bikes — are the thin-margin half of the store, and most are sold under manufacturer minimum-advertised-price rules, so nobody in the metro is quietly undercutting anybody on the sticker. The margin lives in footwear, apparel, accessories and service labor. A run shop makes its month on socks, insoles and the second pair; a bike shop makes it on wrench hours, not on the bike. The year is narrow too: August fall sports, Thanksgiving through Christmas, then the February-to-April baseball and softball rush, with January and late spring paying almost nothing. The thing owners vent about to each other is certification churn — every time a governing body moves a standard, like the NFHS non-wood bat rule landing January 1, 2028, a wall of stock gets harder to move and the phone fills with parents asking whether last year’s bat is still legal. Shops that answer that question for free are the ones people drive past two big boxes to reach, which only works if those people can find the shop, so a complete local listing — including on St Louis Near Me Directory — is part of the job.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is considered sporting goods?

A.  Sporting goods are the equipment, apparel and footwear used to play sports, train, or recreate outdoors: balls, bats, sticks, racquets, gloves, protective pads and helmets, athletic shoes and uniforms, plus camping, hunting, fishing and water gear. Fan merchandise is not sporting goods. A jersey you wear to a game is apparel; the jersey a team plays in is equipment, usually ordered through a team dealer.

### Q. What are examples of sporting goods?

A.  Concrete examples: a BBCOR baseball bat, a catcher’s mask, soccer shin guards, molded cleats, a basketball, a tennis racquet, running shoes, swim goggles, a bike helmet, hockey skates, a golf bag, a life jacket, a compound bow, a rod and reel, dumbbells, a yoga mat, a kayak and a two-person tent. If you carry it, wear it or use it to play or train, it counts.

### Q. What are sport accessories?

A.  Accessories are the small, fast-moving items around the main equipment: socks, insoles, laces, grip tape, mouthguards, wristbands, bat grips, glove conditioner, water bottles, hydration packs, gear bags, chalk, resistance bands and pumps. Individually they are cheap; together they routinely add a third to an equipment list. They are also the items a coach quietly assumes you already own.

### Q. What happened to sporting goods stores?

A.  The big-box middle collapsed. Sports Authority, then the largest US sporting goods chain, filed Chapter 11 on March 2, 2016, converted to liquidation and closed all 463 stores that year, and Dick’s Sporting Goods bought its brand and intellectual property out of the bankruptcy. Gander Mountain filed Chapter 11 in March 2017 and liquidated dozens of stores. Online sellers and single-sport specialists absorbed the business the middle used to hold.

### Q. Is there a Dick’s sporting goods store in St. Louis?

A.  Yes, and more than one. Two you can check quickly are 1507 S. Brentwood Blvd. in Brentwood and 64 THF Blvd. at Chesterfield Commons in Chesterfield, and the chain lists additional stores around the metro. Hours shift seasonally, so look at the specific store page before you drive out. If you need a particular size held, calling the store beats trusting an online stock count.

### Q. Can I trade in old sports equipment at Dick’s?

A.  Bats, yes. On March 3, 2026, Dick’s Sporting Goods launched a baseball and softball bat trade-in program powered by SidelineSwap, running in stores and through its trade-in site. You get an instant quote, drop the bat at a store or ship it with a prepaid label, and you are paid in a Dick’s gift card; the company put the average payout around $70. It covers bats, not general used equipment.

### Q. What are the big 5 sporting goods?

A.  Big 5 Sporting Goods is a retail chain, not a category of gear. Its own filings describe it as a leading sporting goods retailer in the western United States, and it operated roughly 410 stores when it agreed on June 30, 2025 to be acquired by a partnership of Worldwide Golf and Capitol Hill Group. Stockholders approved that deal on September 26, 2025 and the company went private. Its footprint does not reach Missouri or Illinois.

### Q. Where is the largest sporting goods store in the US?

A.  By floor area it is the Scheels in The Colony, Texas, at roughly 331,000 square feet, opened in 2020, complete with a 65-foot indoor Ferris wheel and a walk-through saltwater aquarium. Nothing in the St. Louis metro approaches that scale. The largest single showroom in this region is the Cabela’s in Hazelwood at about 130,000 square feet.

### Q. Where can I get cheap sports gear?

A.  Three channels beat full retail. Used and trade shops such as Play It Again Sports in Kirkwood and Arnold price well under new and pay cash for gear you bring in. Online resale marketplaces built for sports move the same inventory nationally. And end-of-season clearance at big boxes and specialty shops is where new gear finally gets cheap. Buy a season behind and you rarely pay list.

### Q. What do all athletes need?

A.  Whatever the sport: footwear matched to the surface, socks that do not blister, a properly fitted helmet where the sport requires one, a mouthguard wherever contact is likely, a water bottle, and a bag that keeps wet gear away from clean gear. Everything after that is sport-specific. Fit beats brand every time, because an expensive item in the wrong size performs worse than a mid-priced one that fits.

Not sure which kind of shop your equipment list actually calls for? Browse sporting goods stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call ahead with the exact certification wording from the league email — that one phone call is what saves the second trip.

## What to Know About Mobile Home Parks in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-about-mobile-home-parks-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Saturday in late September and you’re helping your sister look at housing she can actually afford. The apartment listings around Maryland Heights all want three times the rent in monthly income. The two decent duplexes in Florissant went the same week they posted. Then a friend in Belleville mentions her uncle, who bought a three-bedroom outright in a park off the state highway — deck, shed, a real yard — and pays a few hundred a month for the ground it sits on.

That last part is the part almost nobody explains. In a mobile home park you generally own the house and rent the dirt. Two separate deals, two separate sets of rules, and the second one is where people get caught off guard.

This is real housing for real families across the metro, from Jefferson County down south to the flat stretches out past Granite City. Here is how the arrangement works, what the law says on each side of the river, and where the money goes.

### What are you actually buying in a mobile home park?

Two separate things. You buy the home — outright or financed — and you rent a lot from the park by the month. The home belongs to you and carries its own title. The land does not, and will not, no matter how long you stay or how much you improve the yard.

Nearly every home sold today is a manufactured home, built in a factory to HUD’s Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards at 24 CFR Part 3280 — the federal code that has governed these homes since June 15, 1976. Missouri draws the same line in statute: RSMo 700.600 defines a “mobile home” as a factory-built residence that is not certified under the HUD Code and instead meets the older ANSI standards. A 1974 unit and a 2024 unit are not the same product, and nobody should tell you otherwise.

The word “mobile” is misleading too. In its May 2021 report on manufactured housing finance, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau put it plainly: once placed, manufactured homes are typically not moved from their original site. A move costs real money, and plenty of older homes will not survive one. Plan as though the home stays where it lands, because it usually does.

### What does lot rent cover, and what does it not?

Lot rent buys the pad, the roads, and whatever utilities and services the park has agreed in writing to provide — commonly water and sewer lines, trash pickup, snow removal, and the common areas. It does not cover your roof, your furnace, your water heater, your skirting, your steps, or insurance on the home. Those are yours.

Illinois puts that in statute. Under 765 ILCS 745/9, every charge — ground or lot rent, unit rent, services, anything else — has to be itemized in the lease and in every bill you receive. Section 11 of the same Act binds an Illinois park owner, for the whole lease term, to keep the electrical, plumbing and gas utilities it provides in working order, to maintain subsurface water and sewage lines, to keep the roads in good condition, and to state which services it provides, from lawn care and snow removal to the laundry room.

Missouri has no matching park statute, so in Missouri the lease is the entire deal. Get the list in writing before you sign: who fixes a water line break under the pad, who pays for the road, how water and sewer are billed, and whether that billing is a flat rate or an actual meter reading.

Skirting, steps, tie-downs and the shed are on you in either state. Illinois protects your right to shop for them — under 765 ILCS 745/19 a park owner cannot restrict your choice of seller for goods or services connected to the home unless health or safety requires it, though the park may set rules on the style or quality of exterior equipment. When you are pricing that kind of work, a hardware store counter usually beats a big-box aisle for anchors, skirting clips and advice.

Setup itself is regulated in Missouri, which surprises people. The Manufactured Home Installation Act (RSMo 700.650 to 700.692) requires anyone installing a manufactured home in the state to hold a Missouri installer license, and the Missouri Public Service Commission registers manufacturers and dealers, licenses installers, handles inspection requests and consumer complaints, and administers a Manufactured Housing Consumer Recovery Fund. Its manufactured housing hotline is 1-800-819-3180.

### How much notice do you get before lot rent goes up?

In Illinois, 90 days, in writing, every time. Section 6 of the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Rights Act (765 ILCS 745/6) requires the park owner to give 90 days’ notice of any rent increase, and no increase takes effect until 90 days after that notice. Missouri has no mobile-home-specific rule at all — there, the lease sets the terms.

The Illinois rule has more to it than the calendar. Once the notice arrives you have 30 days to accept or reject it, and if you reject it you tell the park the date you will move out, which has to fall before the increase starts. A month-to-month agreement in an Illinois park must also carry 90 days’ notice before any increase. At renewal, notice of the increase has to be delivered 90 days before the lease expires (765 ILCS 745/9). Illinois even runs a rent deferral program: a tenant who swears an affidavit that the new rent would exceed 45% of household income, lists the home for sale and documents that income can defer the increase for up to a year (765 ILCS 745/6.4).

Illinois also makes the park show its history. Under the disclosure section amended by Public Act 98-1062, effective January 1, 2015, an Illinois park owner must give you in writing, with every lease, sale and renewal, the rent charged on that lot for the past five years, every fee above base rent, the privilege tax that applies, the security deposit rules, and a three-year rent increase projection covering the two lease years plus the year after (765 ILCS 745/6.5). Ask for it. It is the single most useful document in the transaction.

Missouri answers with two narrower protections. RSMo 441.060 provides that when you own the home and lease the lot, a landlord ending a tenancy of less than one year must give written notice that the tenancy ends no sooner than 60 days from the date the next rent payment comes due, regardless of what the lease says about earlier termination. And RSMo 700.600 bars a Missouri land-lease community from raising rent — except for an increase based solely on higher property taxes — during the 60 days before it issues a change-of-use notice, or at any time after.

### Who approves you, and what can park rules require?

Parks screen applicants and enforce written rules, and both states allow it. Illinois limits how far those rules reach: under 765 ILCS 745/14 a rule binds you only if you received a copy before signing the lease, it serves convenience, safety, welfare or park upkeep, it applies to all tenants fairly, and it is specific enough to tell you what you must or must not do. A rule adopted during your lease is enforceable only with 30 days’ written notice.

Illinois stacks several more protections into the lease itself. The park must offer a written lease of at least 24 months unless you waive that right and agree to a different term (765 ILCS 745/6). You get three business days to cancel after signing. A security deposit cannot exceed one month’s rent, a late fee cannot land until at least five days after rent is due, the park cannot move your home to a different lot during the lease, and it cannot require you to buy your home from the park (765 ILCS 745/12 and 12a). Every Illinois lease must print a plain-language notice stating that the rules have to be fair and reasonable and that you may stay as long as you pay rent and follow them (765 ILCS 745/17). Eviction grounds are limited to nonpayment, rule violations and violations of law, and retaliation against a tenant for complaining to a government agency or for organizing a homeowners association is barred (765 ILCS 745/15 and 16).

In Missouri none of that is automatic. The rules are whatever the lease and the park regulations say, enforced under the general landlord-tenant chapter. That makes reading the rules before you sign a bigger deal in Missouri, not a smaller one. Ask for them in writing, ask what changed in the past two years, and ask specifically how guests, pets, vehicles, and exterior work are handled.

Unrelated, and we know it — the metro’s coffee shops deserve a slow morning.

### What happens if the park is sold or closes?

You get advance notice, and how much depends on the state. Missouri requires a manufactured or mobile home land-lease community to give written notice to every tenant who owns their home at least 120 days before requiring them to vacate because of a change in use of the property (RSMo 700.600). Illinois requires at least 12 months’ notice when a park owner stops operating all or part of the park (765 ILCS 745/8.5).

Illinois fills in more of the details. If 12 months or more remain on your lease when the notice arrives, you keep the balance of the term up to the closing date; if less remains, you get the balance plus a written month-to-month tenancy at the expiring lease rate, so the notice adds up to a full 12 months. Within 20 days after a park sale closes, the buyer must notify each homeowner in writing of the new owner and the property manager or agent (765 ILCS 745/6.5). If a bankruptcy case or foreclosure proceeding involving the park owner is filed, tenants must be told within 30 days (765 ILCS 745/6.6).

Now the hard part, said out loud: notice is not the same as somewhere to go. Because homes usually cannot be moved economically, a closure notice often means selling the home for far less than it is worth to you, or walking away from it entirely. If you are shopping parks, ask who owns the land, whether it has changed hands recently, and how the surrounding parcels are zoned. Those three answers say more about your next ten years than the model of the home does.

### How is a manufactured home titled in Missouri versus Illinois?

Missouri issues a certificate of title through the Department of Revenue, much like a vehicle title (RSMo 700.320). Illinois titles mobile homes under the Illinois Vehicle Code through the Secretary of State. In both states a home on a rented lot stays personal property — it becomes real estate only when it is permanently affixed to land the owner holds.

In Missouri that conversion runs through RSMo 442.015 and 700.111. You record an affidavit of affixation with the recorder of deeds in the county where the land sits, then surrender the certificate of title to the Director of Revenue. A home counts as permanently affixed when it is anchored to a permanent foundation built to state and local codes and to the federal installation standards at 24 CFR Part 3285, and connected to residential utilities. The Department of Revenue is equally clear about the other direction: once a home is recorded as affixed, no title is issued again until the home is severed from the real property.

Illinois handles conversion under the Conveyance and Encumbrance of Manufactured Homes as Real Property and Severance Act, 765 ILCS 170, created by Public Act 98-749 effective July 16, 2014 — and written for homes located outside mobile home parks. Severance there requires an affidavit recorded with the county recorder and a certified copy filed with the Secretary of State.

The tax bill follows the title, and this is where the two states look least alike. In Illinois a home in a park is taxed as chattel under the Mobile Home Local Services Tax Act (35 ILCS 515), a privilege tax on square footage that steps down as the home ages — 15 cents per square foot in the first two years, falling to 7.5 cents once the home is 15 years or older — with a 20% reduction for owners who live in the home and are 65 or older or have a disability, applied for through the county clerk (35 ILCS 515/7). Illinois homes outside parks are taxed as real property. In Missouri, a manufactured home actually used as a dwelling unit is assessed at the same percentage of true value as residential real property, which is 19% (RSMo 137.115), and on a rented lot it lands on your personal property tax bill.

### Why is the loan called a chattel loan instead of a mortgage?

Because it is secured by the home only, not by land. In a May 2021 report built on 2019 federal mortgage disclosure data, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau found that roughly 42% of manufactured housing loans are chattel loans, and that the median interest rate on them was 8.6% — against 4.9% for manufactured home mortgages and 4.1% for site-built mortgages.

The same report found that 93.8% of chattel originations were higher-priced mortgage loans, compared with 11.1% of site-built loans, and that 42% of manufactured home purchase applications were denied, including 50% of chattel applications, against 7% of site-built applications. Chattel loans are not covered by the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, so the closing protections you would expect on a house do not come along automatically. Fewer than 4% of chattel originations in 2019 were refinances, which means a high rate tends to stay a high rate.

None of that makes the loan a trap. It is a different product with different math, and it argues for two habits. Shorten the term if you can carry the payment, and collect more than one quote — the CFPB found the chattel market heavily concentrated, with the top five lenders writing nearly 75% of chattel loans. If you own the land and the home is affixed to it, ask whether you qualify for a mortgage instead. FHA also insures manufactured home loans under its Title I program, which is built around the home rather than the land.

### Is it worth buying a mobile home in a park?

It can be, and for plenty of families across the metro it is. The math turns on a single fact: you own a structure that usually loses value, on ground you rent at a price you do not control. When the home is bought outright or paid off quickly, and the park itemizes its charges and raises them predictably, the monthly cost can beat anything comparable on the rental market — and unlike rent, the housing payment eventually ends.

It works badly in the mirror-image case: a long, high-rate loan on an older home, on a lot whose rent climbs faster than your income, in a park you never researched. That combination has no exit, because the home is hard to move and hard to sell. The deciding variables are the loan term, the rent history, and who owns the land — not the countertops.

Ask about resident-owned communities as well. The CFPB notes that in a small number of communities the land is owned by a cooperative of the homeowners themselves. Where that structure exists, the lot rent question changes completely, because the people paying it are the people setting it.

### Can you sell the home and leave it in the park?

In Illinois, yes, and the law defends it. Under 765 ILCS 745/24 a park owner cannot prohibit, limit, restrict or obstruct your freedom to sell your home to a buyer of your choice, though the park may apply its general qualifications to that buyer, who must have a signed lease before closing. The park cannot charge a transfer or selling fee on a sale that keeps the home in the park unless it renders a service (765 ILCS 745/9), and it cannot require removal of the home on sale unless the home is under 12 feet wide or significantly deteriorated — with the burden of proof on the park owner.

Missouri leaves resale to the lease, so read that section closely before you buy, not after. Ask whether the park charges a transfer fee, whether it screens buyers, and whether it can require the home to be moved. If a home is abandoned on rented ground in Missouri, RSMo 700.525 to 700.541 lays out the process the landowner and any lienholder follow to take possession and title — worth reading once, precisely so it never happens to you quietly.

### What a park looks like from the office side

Operators will tell you the revenue is simple and the costs are not. Money comes in as lot rent plus whatever utilities get passed through. The expense that decides everything is underground: water lines, sewer lines and roads that earn nothing and, at properties built decades ago, tend to fail together. A vacant lot is worse than a vacant apartment, because filling it means moving a home in, and homes mostly do not move once they are set. In Illinois the park itself is licensed by the Illinois Department of Public Health at $100 a year plus $4 per space, renewed by April 30 (210 ILCS 115/6). When a resident walks away, the operator inherits a unit it may not be able to sell and a statutory lien process to work through. The ones who do this well post the rules, itemize the bill, and answer the water question before it gets asked — and they make the community easy to find, which is what a complete listing on St Louis Near Me Directory is for.

Trying to work out which community actually fits? Browse mobile home parks across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them and ask the same three questions: what lot rent covers, when it last went up, and who owns the land.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much is rent in a mobile home park per month?

A.  It varies by park, by lot, and by what is included, and no reliable published figure covers the St. Louis metro specifically. Ask each park for the current lot rent, what it covers, and the last three increases. In Illinois the park owner must disclose the rent charged on that lot for the past five years (765 ILCS 745/6.5).

### Q. Is buying a mobile home in a park a good idea?

A.  It is a good idea when the home is cheap enough to buy outright or pay off fast, the park itemizes its charges, and the lot rent has a documented history. It is a poor idea when a long, high-rate loan on an older home sits on a lot rent nobody will explain. The exit matters more than the entry.

### Q. Why does Dave Ramsey say not to buy a mobile home?

A.  His published argument is depreciation. A manufactured home is usually titled as personal property and loses value the way a vehicle does, while the land — the part that appreciates — belongs to the park. Financing compounds it: the CFPB found a median chattel rate of 8.6% in 2019 against 4.1% for site-built mortgages.

### Q. What is the downside to living in a mobile home?

A.  It is structural rather than personal. You own a depreciating home on land you rent, so a rent increase or a park sale can change your housing costs without you doing anything wrong. Financing costs more, insurance can be harder to place, and moving the home is expensive. Missouri at least requires a licensed installer (RSMo 700.650 to 700.692).

### Q. Is it cheaper to live in a trailer park or an apartment?

A.  Often yes month to month, because lot rent on a paid-off home usually runs below market rent for comparable space. The honest comparison adds what an apartment includes and you now cover: repairs, the roof, the furnace, insurance, and property or privilege tax. Run both totals across a full year, loan payment included.

### Q. What are common issues with mobile home park living conditions?

A.  The recurring ones are aging underground infrastructure — water lines, sewer lines and roads — plus drainage and disputes over how water is billed. Illinois addresses that directly: 765 ILCS 745/11 requires park owners to maintain subsurface water and sewage lines, the utilities they supply, and the roads. Illinois parks are also licensed and inspected by the state health department.

### Q. How many acres are needed for a mobile home park?

A.  There is no statewide acreage minimum in either state. Density comes from local zoning and site standards for lot size, setbacks, roads and utilities. Illinois defines a mobile home park as a tract with utilities for five or more independent homes and requires a license from the Illinois Department of Public Health (210 ILCS 115), except inside home rule municipalities.

### Q. What are the pros and cons of owning a mobile home park?

A.  The upside is stability: residents own their homes and rarely move them, so occupancy is sticky. The downside is capital. Water lines, sewer lines and roads generate no revenue and fail in clusters at older properties, a vacant lot is slow and costly to fill, and an abandoned home leaves a unit to dispose of through a lien process.

### Q. What is the cheapest price for a mobile home?

A.  A used home already sited in a park is the least expensive way in, and it sells well below new pricing — but a low sticker hides the rest of the bill. Add delivery and licensed setup if the home has to move, skirting, steps, anchoring, any lender-required repairs, and the lot rent you pay for as long as you own it.

### Q. What are some good mobile home parks in Saint Louis, Missouri?

A.  We do not rank parks, and a list that does is usually selling something. Judge them on four checkable things: who owns the land and how recently it changed hands, how lot rent has moved over five years, how water and sewer are billed, and what the rules say about resale and guests.

## What to Know About Buying Lighting Fixtures in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-about-buying-lighting-fixtures-in-st-louis

Picture a Saturday in October. You finally pried the ugly dome light off the dining room ceiling in Affton and came home with the one fixture you kept going back to. You hang it, flip the switch, and the room looks wrong. Not dim. Wrong. The oak table reads gray, and the whole place feels like a break room at 6 a.m.

Or it’s a bungalow in Florissant, and the new can lights hum on the dimmer like a refrigerator. Or a porch fixture in Belleville that filled with water after one August storm. Or a Kirkwood entry where the chandelier is genuinely beautiful and the ceiling box behind it was never built to hold that kind of weight.

None of those are taste problems. They’re the same mistake in different rooms: buying the picture instead of reading the spec. A light fixture is one of the few things you buy for a house that prints almost everything you need to know right on the carton, and almost nobody turns the carton over. Here’s what those numbers mean, and what a century of St. Louis housing stock does to the math.

### How do I know what kind of light fixture I need?

Four numbers and one ceiling. Lumens tell you how bright it is. Kelvin tells you what color the light will look. CRI tells you how honestly it renders the colors already in the room. The location listing — dry, damp, or wet — tells you where it is allowed to hang. Then you check what the box in your ceiling can actually carry.

Everything else on the shelf is styling. Two fixtures with identical spec sheets and different silhouettes light a room the same way. Two that look like twins with different Kelvin values do not. Checking takes ninety seconds.

Bulb packaging makes it easy. The Federal Trade Commission requires a Lighting Facts label on packaging for most general service lamps with medium screw bases — incandescent, CFL and LED alike — and it puts brightness in lumens on the front of the package instead of leading with watts. Integrated LED fixtures, where the light source is built in and can’t be replaced, print lumens, Kelvin and CRI on the carton or the spec sheet instead. If a fixture won’t tell you those three numbers anywhere, that itself is information.

### Lumens or watts — which number tells you how bright it is?

Lumens. Watts measure how much power a lamp draws, not how much light comes out, and the two came apart permanently once LEDs took over. The FTC label leads with lumens for exactly that reason, and pairs it with an estimated yearly energy cost — which turns wattage into a bill question rather than a brightness question.

The Department of Energy general service lamp standard finished that shift. The rule requires covered lamps to produce at least 45 lumens per watt, and full enforcement across manufacture, import and retail sale landed by August 1, 2023. Almost no standard incandescent or halogen bulb can hit 45 lumens per watt, which is why the shelf looks the way it does now. A watt number on a modern bulb tells you far less about brightness than it did in 1998.

Packaging still prints old-wattage equivalents, and the long-standing industry shorthand runs roughly 450 lumens for an old 40-watt bulb, 800 for a 60, 1,100 for a 75 and 1,600 for a 100. Treat that as a translation aid, not a promise. Better habit: buy dimmable and aim a little brighter than you think you need. You can always take light away. You can’t add it once the fixture is on the ceiling.

### What does 2700K look like next to 4000K?

2700K is the warm, slightly yellow light people mean when they say a room feels cozy — the closest match to the old incandescent look. 4000K is neutral white, noticeably cooler and cleaner. Put them side by side and 2700K reads amber while 4000K reads faintly blue, even though each looks normal on its own.
