How much does a studio photoshoot cost? Renting the room in St. Louis averages $103 per hour, according to Peerspace’s St. Louis photo studio listings checked in August 2026, with its published rate graphic running up to about $183 per hour. Most bookings on that platform are scheduled for two hours with five people on site, which puts a short session right around $206 for the space alone.

That is only half the bill for most people. The room is one line; the person behind the camera is a separate line and usually the larger one. If you are hiring rather than shooting, the pricing on that side works differently and we cover it in what hiring a photographer costs. If you shoot your own product or your own clients, you skip that line entirely and the studio rental is the whole bill. Booking coverage at a venue instead of a room is a third structure again, and we lay that one out in what an event photographer actually covers.

Rate cards from actual metro rooms land in the same band. One 1,500-square-foot St. Louis soundstage publishes $100 an hour, $300 for a four-hour weekday half day, and $600 to $700 for a full eight-hour day, with a ten-hour day at $900 and evening or weekend bookings starting at $150 an hour on a $600 minimum. That shape — flat hourly, discounted weekday block, premium after five o’clock — is the structure to expect anywhere in the metro. A room quoting far under it is usually a converted retail bay with no grid and no cyc. A room quoting far over it is usually selling you crew and gear you have not agreed to yet.

### How much cheaper is a half day than paying by the hour?

About 25 percent, if the published St. Louis rate card above is typical: $300 for four hours is $75 an hour against a $100 hourly rate. Eight hours at $600 holds that same $75. Ten hours at $900 works out to $90 because the evening premium is baked in. Blocks are the cheapest hours you can buy in a studio.

The catch is the minimum, and minimums in this market are all over the place. Listings run from a one-hour minimum at the small end up to two- and four-hour minimums at rooms with real grids and cyc walls. A one-hour minimum sounds friendly until you realize what has to happen inside that hour.

Ask one question before you book anything: does the clock include setup and strike? Almost always, yes. Your hour starts when your access starts, not when the first frame fires. Rolling in a cart, building two lights, taping down cables, shooting, then breaking it all down and sweeping — that is not a one-hour day for anybody. For eleven matching headshots you want three hours minimum: one to build and test, one to shoot, one to tear down without paying overtime. Booking exactly the hours you plan to shoot is the single most expensive mistake renters make, because the overtime rate is never the discounted rate.

### What does “gear included” actually get you?

Usually grip, not light. The St. Louis soundstage cited above includes C-stands, light stands, apple boxes, sandbags, clamps, gels, gaff tape, cables and extension cords at no additional charge — and rents lighting, cameras and lenses separately. That split is the industry norm. Grip is the stuff that holds things up; it comes with the room. The things that make light are a separate line.

When a listing does say lights are included, get three specifics in writing. How many heads. Strobe or continuous. Which modifiers.

Strobes fire a burst. They freeze motion, they overpower ambient light coming through a window, and they let you shoot at low ISO with a clean file. They also need a trigger on your camera’s hot shoe, and this is where renters get stranded: a trigger for one manufacturer’s heads will not fire another manufacturer’s heads. Ask what brand the strobes are and whether the studio supplies a matching trigger, or bring your own and confirm compatibility before you drive out to Maryland Heights.

Continuous lights — LED panels, COB fixtures with a bowl reflector — are what you see is what you get. Easier if you are new, and mandatory if you are shooting video in the same session. The trade is output. At the same apparent brightness on your subject, continuous fixtures push you to a higher ISO or a slower shutter than a strobe would, which shows up in a hero product shot at 100 percent zoom.

Modifiers matter more than head count. One head in a big softbox beats three heads in bare reflectors for a headshot every time. Ask what softboxes, umbrellas, grids and scrims are in the room, and ask about the power supply while you are at it — how many separate circuits serve the shooting floor, and whether the space heater in a January booking is on the same one as your pack.

### How much does seamless paper add to your studio bill?

Seamless paper is the most common surprise line on a studio invoice, because it is a consumable and the studio does not get it back. Savage sells its standard seamless rolls at 53 inches wide by 12 yards — 36 feet of paper — with wider 86-inch and 107-inch rolls also made, the widest of which ships by special trucking. Studios that charge for paper charge by the foot you pull.

That is fair, and it is worth understanding rather than resenting. Once paper has been walked on in street shoes it is finished; it gets cut off and thrown away. A seated headshot on a 53-inch roll may cost the studio a couple of feet. A full-length standing shot with a subject three feet off the background, on a 107-inch roll, eats a long sweep and a good chunk of an expensive roll. Ask the per-foot rate before you book. It is almost never printed on the listing page, and it is the difference between the quote and the invoice.

A cyclorama is the other option, and it works on completely different economics. A cyc is a permanent hard-coved corner — wall curving into floor with no visible seam — built into the building. The St. Louis soundstage above lists a 17-foot cyc under 16-foot ceilings. Nobody charges you by the foot for a cyc, because nothing is consumed. What a cyc costs the owner is paint and labor, so expect a scuff clause: shoot in socks or clean-soled shoes, keep carts off it, and read whether the agreement passes a repaint fee along if you damage the cove.

Pick by the job. Cyc for full-length figures, motion, video, and wide product sets where you need floor and wall to read as one surface. Seamless for headshots, for colored backgrounds, and for small product work where a 53-inch roll on a stand is all the background that will ever be in frame.

### What do deposits, overtime and cleanup rules really cost you?

A refundable security deposit in the $500 range is standard for larger bookings. The St. Louis soundstage in this article requires a refundable $500 deposit for groups of eight or more — or a certificate of insurance instead. Read that as a menu: paperwork or cash, pick one. Smaller rooms often hold a card on file rather than taking a deposit.

Overtime is where budgets break. Ask whether overtime bills in 30-minute increments or rounds up to a full hour, and whether it bills at the hourly rate or above it. A studio with a booking behind yours has every reason to price the overage painfully, because your extra 20 minutes costs the next renter their setup time.

Cleanup is usually broom-clean: paper cut and bagged, furniture back where it started, trash out, gaff tape pulled off the floor. Cleaning fees come out of the deposit and they are not small. Also check the cancellation window in writing — many rooms keep the full first hour inside 48 hours, and a weather cancellation in a February ice storm is still a cancellation under most agreements.

Wildly off-topic — your yard also needs a lawn crew.

### What insurance does a St. Louis studio expect you to carry?

A certificate of insurance showing $1,000,000 in general liability per occurrence, on a standard ACORD form, with the studio named as an additional insured. That is the figure Peerspace states for bookings where a certificate is required, and individual hosts can set their own terms on top of it. Independent studios in the metro ask for the same thing in almost the same words.

Two policies people assume will cover this, and will not. A homeowner or renter policy does not extend to a commercial shoot in a rented commercial space. And your camera insurance is inland marine coverage — it protects your equipment, not somebody else’s floor and not the ankle of a model who trips on your cable. General liability is a separate purchase, available as an annual policy through a trade body or as a short-term event policy bought for one day.

Lead time is the real trap. The certificate has to be issued naming the correct entity, which takes your agent a day or two. The Missouri Botanical Garden, for a comparable standard on the location side, requires a certificate showing $1,000,000 in liability with the Garden as additional insured, submitted no later than two business days before a commercial shoot. Build the same two-day cushion into a studio booking and you will never be the person emailing an agent at 9 p.m. the night before.

### How much do load-in, parking and ceiling height change the day?

They do not change the rate. They change how many of your paid hours you actually spend shooting, which is the same thing as money. Ask these before you sign: is there a loading door at grade or a flight of stairs, what are the freight elevator dimensions, and where does the crew park.

Parking is a genuine metro variable. A converted warehouse in the city may put you on metered street spots and a permit zone; a flex bay off Page in St. Louis County or a room across the river in Belleville usually hands you a lot. Two trips with a cart from a metered space three blocks away is an hour of your block gone.

Ceiling height decides what your pictures can look like. Sixteen feet with a wired grid means a light can be boomed above and behind a standing adult, a background can be lit separately from the subject, and a full-length shot has room to breathe. A nine-foot ceiling forces the key light low and close, which reads flat and puts a hard shadow on the wall behind your subject. If you are shooting standing figures, ceiling height is not a nice-to-have; it is the reason to rent instead of clearing out the living room.

### Does Missouri or Illinois sales tax show up on a studio invoice?

In Missouri, often yes, and it catches renters off guard. In Letter Ruling LR 8013, issued January 24, 2019, the Missouri Department of Revenue concluded that charges for daily and hourly rentals of studio rooms for photographic sessions are subject to sales tax under Section 144.020.1(6), RSMo — the four percent provision covering rooms regularly served to the public — with local rates layered on top. A letter ruling binds the Department only as to the taxpayer who asked for it, but it tells you exactly how Missouri reads the transaction.

Illinois arrives at the tax from a different direction. A room is real property, so a straight space rental does not fall under that kind of room provision. Equipment is another story: since January 1, 2025, under Public Act 103-0592, leases and rentals of tangible personal property in Illinois are subject to Illinois sales and use tax, and lessors must register with the Illinois Department of Revenue and tax their rental receipts. So a light kit, a lens or a backdrop system rented on the Belleville or Edwardsville side now carries tax on each rental payment.

The practical move is the same on both sides of the river. Ask whether the quote is tax-inclusive, and ask whether the gear is billed on the same line as the room or separately. A $600 day that arrives as $600 plus room tax plus a separately taxed equipment line is a materially different number than the one you budgeted.

### Is a home or garage studio a real alternative?

For a narrow slice of work, yes, and the break-even is closer than people expect. Ten two-hour sessions a year at the $103 St. Louis average is about $2,060 — not enough to convert a garage, but real money against a light kit and a couple of stands if all you shoot is small product on a table.

What a home space genuinely buys you is control and no clock. Nobody is knocking at the four-hour mark. You can leave a set built overnight and finish in the morning. For a candle maker in Affton photographing thirty SKUs across three weeks, that alone can beat any rental math.

What it does not buy you is height, climate or power. A residential ceiling will not let you boom a light above a standing adult, which is precisely the thing a rented soundstage exists to provide. An uninsulated St. Louis garage is unusable in July and unpleasant in January, and clients notice. And a garage typically runs off one or two circuits shared with a freezer and a garage door opener, so two strobe packs and a heater will find the breaker.

One more thing to check before you advertise a home address: home occupation rules. Clients arriving at a residence for a paid session is a different land-use question than editing at your desk, and this metro is a patchwork — St. Louis City, dozens of separate St. Louis County municipalities, St. Charles County, and the Illinois side each write their own code. Call your own city hall and ask specifically about clients on site and signage. It is a ten-minute call that beats a complaint from a neighbor across the street in St. Charles.

### What does the studio owner see that renters don’t?

A room like that is a utilization business, not a rate business. The lease is on flex or light-industrial square footage — that is what a 16-foot ceiling and a hard cyc require — and it costs the same on a dark Tuesday as on a booked Saturday. The cyc is a capital item that gets repainted, not a backdrop that gets replaced. Fall is the year: senior portraits, family sessions before the holidays, corporate headshot refreshes before the fiscal close, all stacked into about ten weeks that have to carry a dead January. Owners also police an odd Missouri line item — the Department of Revenue photographers tax matrix, revised March 28, 2025, makes a shoot delivered as a download exempt while the same shoot handed over on a USB drive is taxable, and equipment the studio buys, from light kits to backdrops, is taxable to the studio. Renters see an hourly rate; owners see occupancy, paint and sales tax. People search this category locally by the hour, which is why a complete, current listing is worth the twenty minutes it takes to write.

Need a room with a cyc wall and a door you can back a cart through? Browse photography studios across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them and ask the same three questions: what is the minimum, what does paper cost by the foot, and what does the certificate of insurance need to say.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is a reasonable price for a photoshoot?

A.  Split it into room and talent. The room in St. Louis averages $103 an hour on Peerspace as of August 2026, and metro rate cards commonly show $100 hourly, $300 for a weekday half day and $600 or more for a full day. Talent is priced separately and varies far more. A reasonable total is one where you can see both numbers before you book.

### Q. Is $100 an hour good for a photographer?

A.  Careful — $100 an hour is also roughly what the room costs. Published St. Louis studio rate cards sit at $100 hourly, and Peerspace puts the local studio average at $103. If a quote of $100 an hour is meant to cover the photographer, the space, the lighting and the edited files, ask which of those four it actually includes before you compare it to anything.

### Q. How much should a 20 minute photoshoot cost?

A.  You will rarely pay for 20 minutes of studio time, because minimums start at one hour and commonly run two to four. A 20-minute mini session is a scheduling unit, not a rental unit — the studio bills the block and the photographer fits several sittings inside it. Budget at least one hour of room time, around $100 in this metro, even for a very short sitting.

### Q. How do I choose the right photography studio?

A.  Choose on fit, then price. Confirm ceiling height and cyc or seamless before anything else, because those decide what your pictures can look like. Then check the minimum, whether setup and strike sit inside your clock, what lighting is included versus rented, the per-foot paper charge, the deposit, and the insurance certificate requirement. Visit once before a paid booking if the room is new to you.

### Q. Where can I find a good photo studio in Saint Louis?

A.  Three places to look. Marketplace platforms such as Peerspace and Giggster list metro rooms with hourly rates and minimums attached. Independent rooms often skip the marketplaces entirely, so search a local directory as well — the photography studio category on St Louis Near Me Directory is one place to start. And working photographers will tell you which rooms have real grids and honest cleanup rules, which no listing page ever says.

### Q. What are some good photography locations in Saint Louis?

A.  Rules differ by property, so check before you shoot. Tower Grove Park states plainly that photography permits are not needed in the park. The Missouri Botanical Garden welcomes personal-use portraits with regular admission but requires a permit for formal and group sessions, and charges commercial shoots a base location fee of $300 to $500 an hour plus a $1,000,000 insurance certificate.

### Q. How much does a photography studio cost to own?

A.  Nobody publishes a reliable St. Louis figure, so treat the cost drivers as the answer: a lease on flex space tall enough for a 16-foot ceiling, building and repainting a cyc wall, a wired lighting grid, general liability coverage, and equipment. Missouri adds a wrinkle — the state Department of Revenue photographers matrix, revised March 28, 2025, makes light kits, backdrops and props taxable purchases for the studio.

### Q. Is owning a photography studio profitable?

A.  It depends almost entirely on utilization. Run the arithmetic on a published metro rate: a room at $100 an hour booked ten hours a week grosses about $52,000 a year before rent, utilities, insurance, paint and sales tax. Booked thirty hours a week it is a different business. The rate is not the lever — the calendar is, and January is the month that decides it.

### Q. Do photography studios make money?

A.  Most that survive do not live on room rental alone. They add equipment rental, crew, editing suites, classes and event use of the same square footage, which spreads a fixed lease across more hours. Missouri also treats those revenue lines differently for sales tax — a room rental was ruled taxable in Letter Ruling LR 8013 in January 2019, while a purely digital delivery is exempt.

## How Much Does Medical Weight Loss Cost in St. Louis?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-medical-weight-loss-costs-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Tuesday night in Florissant and you’re four browser tabs deep. One clinic advertises ninety-nine dollars a month. Another wants a membership plus labs and won’t say what the labs run. A telehealth ad promises a shot for a low starter price and goes quiet about month four. Not one of them will give you a total before you book.

Maybe you already sat with a doctor in Kirkwood who said the word “medication” and then said the words “prior authorization,” and you walked out without a number. Maybe a coworker in Belleville pays almost nothing because her employer bought the drug rider, and your plan on the Missouri side does not include it at all.

This is a money question, and money questions deserve real figures. Below is what each tier of medically supervised weight loss actually costs around St. Louis in 2026, what a monthly clinic fee covers versus what gets billed on top, where Missouri and Illinois split hard on paying for the medication, and what the bill does when you stop.

### How much do weight loss clinics usually cost?

Budget in two parts, because every program bills in two parts: a service fee and the drug. Commercial coaching subscriptions are the cheapest tier — Sesame’s Success by Sesame starts at $59 a month on an annual plan, per Sesame’s own page updated January 6, 2026. Physician-supervised clinics add a monthly membership on top of labs. The medication is the biggest line at $299 to $449 a month in manufacturer self-pay pricing as of December 2025. Surgery is a five-figure package.

Clinic membership fees are the one figure nobody in this field publishes consistently, which is exactly why you have to ask for yours in writing rather than trust a range from the internet. What you can pin down in advance is everything around it: the drug price, the lab panel, and what your plan will and will not pay. A program that quotes a monthly fee and stops talking has told you maybe a third of what you will spend.

### What are the four tiers, and what does each one actually run?

Four distinct products get sold under the same phrase, and they are not close in price. Sorting yours before you call anyone saves a month of confusion.

### 1. Commercial coaching programs

Structured food, activity and behavior coaching, delivered by an app, a coach, or a group. No physician, or a physician only at the prescribing step. Sesame’s Success by Sesame starts at $59 a month on an annual subscription. The older Costco-member version, $179 for three months, closed to new enrollment; existing members kept their rate. Medication and labs were never included in either fee.

### 2. Physician-supervised clinics

A clinician examines you, orders labs, prescribes, adjusts doses, and watches side effects. This is where the monthly membership model lives. The fee buys clinical time and coordination. It does not buy the drug, and in most cases it does not buy the lab panel either.

### 3. GLP-1 prescription management

Usually telehealth. A short visit fee or subscription covers the prescription and dose titration; the pharmacy bills you separately. Cheapest on paper, and the tier where people most often get surprised, because the advertised price is the service and the medication arrives as its own charge.

### 4. Bariatric surgery

A hospital or surgical center procedure, quoted as a bundled self-pay package or run through insurance with a required supervised program first. Largest single bill, and the only tier where the big number is mostly one-time rather than monthly.

### What does a monthly clinic fee include, and what gets billed on top?

A typical monthly membership covers the visits, dose adjustments, weigh-ins, and messaging between appointments. It usually does not cover the medication, the initial lab panel, repeat labs, or anything sent out to a reference lab. Those three exclusions are where the quoted price and the real price separate.

Labs deserve their own line in your budget. A baseline panel before starting a GLP-1 commonly includes metabolic and thyroid work, and it gets repeated. If the clinic draws blood on site but sends the specimen out, the lab bills you directly and the clinic never sees that invoice. Our guide to getting lab work done in St. Louis covers how to find out what a panel will cost before the needle goes in.

Get five answers in writing before you sign anything: the monthly fee, whether medication is included, who pays for labs, what happens if the pharmacy price changes mid-month, and what it costs to cancel. A program that will put those in an email is telling you something good about how it operates.

### How much does the medication itself cost without insurance?

Manufacturer direct-to-consumer channels now carry the lowest published self-pay prices. Effective December 1, 2025, Eli Lilly lists Zepbound single-dose vials through LillyDirect at $299 for the 2.5 mg starter dose, $399 for 5 mg, and $449 for 7.5 mg through 15 mg, with higher doses requiring a refill within 45 days to hold that price.

Novo Nordisk moved first. Since mid-November 2025 Wegovy has been listed at $349 a month for all doses through NovoCare Pharmacy and participating retail and telehealth partners, with the oral version starting near $149 a month depending on dose. Both companies cut prices twice during 2025, so check the number on the day you buy rather than trusting a figure from a blog — including this one.

Retail pharmacy list prices without any of these programs run considerably higher. That gap is the whole reason the direct channels exist, and it is why a clinic that quietly marks up a drug you could buy direct is worth a question.

### Will insurance pay for any of this in Missouri or Illinois?

Coverage usually splits three ways: the visit, the counseling, and the drug. The visit and labs are typically handled like any other medical care. Counseling is often free. The medication is the fight.

Behavioral counseling has a legal floor. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force gave intensive, multicomponent behavioral intervention for adults with a BMI of 30 or higher a Grade B recommendation on September 18, 2018. A Grade B rating means most non-grandfathered private plans must cover it without cost sharing under the Affordable Care Act’s preventive services rule.

On Medicare, Part B covers obesity screening and behavioral counseling at no cost to you if your primary care provider accepts assignment, for people with a BMI of 30 or more, delivered in a primary care setting. Medication is newer: the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge demonstration started July 1, 2026 and runs through December 31, 2027, offering eligible Part D enrollees Wegovy, Foundayo, or the Zepbound KwikPen for a $50 monthly copay. Per KFF’s analysis updated May 11, 2026, that $50 does not count toward the Part D deductible or the $2,100 out-of-pocket cap.

For employer coverage on either side of the river, the deciding factor is whether your employer purchased weight-management drug coverage as part of the plan. Two people at the same clinic in Maryland Heights, both with the same insurer’s card in their wallet, can get opposite answers. Ask your plan for its weight-management drug policy in writing before you commit to a membership.

### Does Medicaid cover GLP-1 medication for weight loss on either side of the river?

This is the sharpest Missouri-Illinois difference in the whole subject, and as of August 2026 the two states’ own drug lists do not read the same way at all.

Missouri’s MO HealthNet Preferred Drug List, in the version effective August 1, 2026, carries a drug class named outright “GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Indicated for Obesity,” and Wegovy, Zepbound, and the Zepbound KwikPen appear in it. Missouri has put a weight-management GLP-1 class on the list as a category of its own, separate from the diabetes class.

Illinois has not. The Illinois Medicaid Preferred Drug List effective July 27, 2026 runs 150 pages and contains no obesity or weight-management class at all. GLP-1 medications appear only under the antidiabetics heading — Victoza, Ozempic, Rybelsus, Mounjaro and their generics — and Wegovy, Zepbound, and Saxenda do not appear anywhere in the document.

Two honest caveats. Appearing on a preferred drug list is not the same as being handed the medication: prior authorization and clinical criteria still apply in Missouri, and a managed care plan can differ from fee-for-service. And these lists get revised on a rolling basis, so a reader in 2027 should pull the current version rather than trust this paragraph. The national picture is also unsettled — KFF reported on January 16, 2026 that 13 state Medicaid programs covered GLP-1s for obesity under fee-for-service, and that four states dropped coverage between October 2025 and January 2026. Federal Medicaid law has long permitted states to exclude drugs used for weight loss, which is why the map looks like a patchwork.

Wildly off-topic — somebody in your life deserves flowers this week.

### Is compounded semaglutide cheaper, and is it still legal?

The price gap has mostly closed, and the legal ground has moved. Compounded copies were the cheap tier in 2023 and 2024 because the brand drugs were in shortage, which opened a temporary compounding pathway. That pathway shut. The FDA removed tirzepatide from its drug shortage list in October 2024 and semaglutide in February 2025, and the grace periods for compounders ended in 2025 — February and March for tirzepatide, April and May for semaglutide.

Then the FDA went further. On April 30, 2026 the agency proposed excluding semaglutide, tirzepatide, and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list, concluding there is no clinical need for outsourcing facilities to compound them from bulk substances while approved versions are available. The comment docket closed at the end of June 2026. As of this writing in August 2026 the exclusion is a proposal, not a final rule, so treat the current status as genuinely in flux and ask any clinic to explain its sourcing in plain terms.

The risk side is not a rumor. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and are not reviewed by the agency for safety, effectiveness, or quality. Figures cited in reporting on the 2026 proposal put FDA adverse event reports above 450 for compounded semaglutide and above 320 for compounded tirzepatide as of early 2025, with a recurring theme of dosing errors — people drawing the wrong volume out of a multi-dose vial. The FDA has also warned about products made with semaglutide salt forms, which are not the same active ingredient as the approved drugs.

On price, saving forty dollars a month against a $299 vial is a much weaker trade than saving four hundred was in 2023. If a clinic still offers a compounded version, ask which pharmacy fills it, whether that pharmacy is a 503A or 503B facility, and what the concentration and syringe markings are. Those are fair questions and a good operator will answer them without flinching.

### How much does bariatric surgery cost, and how do you get your own number?

Self-pay bariatric packages are quoted in five figures, and any single national average you find online is close to useless for planning — the spread between facilities is wider than the average is meaningful. Skip the average and get your own quote instead.

Medicare covers some bariatric procedures under Part B for people who meet its conditions, and Medicare’s own guidance says costs are hard to predict in advance and tells you to ask the doctor, hospital, or facility directly. That is unglamorous advice and it is correct. Federal hospital price transparency rules, in effect since January 1, 2021, also require hospitals to publish their standard charges, so a determined reader can look up the specific hospital rather than settle for a national figure.

Ask the surgical program for a written self-pay package price and, more importantly, for the exclusion list. Pre-operative psychological evaluation, nutrition visits, endoscopy, revisions, and any complication care frequently sit outside the package. If you are going through insurance, budget for the supervised program many plans require first — several months of visit copays before approval is even considered.

### What happens to the cost when you stop?

The monthly charge goes to zero and the underlying condition does not. The clearest published evidence comes from the STEP 1 trial extension, reported in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism in 2022: among 327 participants who averaged 17.3 percent weight loss over 68 weeks on semaglutide, one year after stopping the medication and the lifestyle program, they had regained about two-thirds of that loss, ending roughly 5.6 percent below where they started.

The study authors’ conclusion is the practical point. Obesity behaves like a chronic condition, and ongoing treatment is what maintains the result — the same way blood pressure medication works. That reframes the money question entirely. You are not pricing a course of treatment with an end date; you are pricing a recurring line in your budget, the way you would a phone bill or a prescription you expect to keep filling.

So ask any program the maintenance question up front. What does the fee look like once dosing is stable? Are visits less frequent and cheaper after month six, or does the membership stay flat forever? A clinic that has thought about the second year will have an answer ready.

### What does low-cost or no-cost care actually look like here?

Four real doors exist, and none of them involves a discount code. First, preventive counseling: no cost sharing under Medicare Part B with an assignment-accepting primary care provider, and no cost sharing in most non-grandfathered private plans thanks to that Grade B rating.

Second, community health centers. Federally supported health centers on both sides of the metro — Missouri and Illinois alike — charge on a sliding fee scale tied to household income, and they handle primary care, labs, and prescriptions. HRSA runs a public find-a-health-center tool for locating the nearest one.

Third, hospital financial assistance. Nonprofit hospitals are required by federal tax rules to maintain and publish a written financial assistance policy, and those policies routinely cover people well above the poverty line. Ask for the policy by name at registration rather than waiting for a bill.

Fourth, manufacturer savings programs, which mostly help people who already have commercial insurance. One caution worth stating plainly: in weight loss advertising, “free” nearly always means a free consultation. A free consult is not free treatment, and the difference shows up on the second invoice.

### What this looks like from behind the front desk

A weight loss clinic does not earn its living on the first visit. It earns it on month seven. Consults get priced low or given away because the business is a subscription, and the number that keeps the lights on is how many members are still on the books half a year in.

That model took a genuine hit. Clinics that built their pricing around compounded semaglutide margin lost it when the compounding pathway closed during 2025, and rebuilding around brand medication they cannot mark up meant learning to charge for the service instead of the vial. Deductibles resetting every January 1 reshape the whole calendar — labs that ran cheap in December are suddenly out of pocket, and cancellations cluster right there.

The thing owners in this field say to each other is about prior authorization: unpaid hours of paperwork per patient, then a denial with no usable explanation. People search for this kind of care locally and quietly, so being listed and accurate on St Louis Near Me Directory is part of simply being findable.

Want the real number before you commit? Browse weight loss centers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call two of them and ask the identical four questions: monthly fee, is medication included, who pays for labs, and what cancellation costs.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Where can I get weight loss shots in St. Louis, Mo?

A.  Three routes exist across the metro. A primary care doctor can prescribe and send it to your regular pharmacy. A physician-supervised clinic handles prescribing plus monitoring for a membership fee. A telehealth service ships to your door. All three prescribe the same FDA-approved medications; what differs is the service fee, who orders labs, and how fast someone answers when a dose goes badly.

### Q. What is the Costco $179 3 month subscription weight loss program?

A.  It was a Costco member benefit run by Sesame — $179 for three months of telehealth weight management, with medication and lab costs billed separately. Sesame’s own page, updated January 6, 2026, says the original program closed to new enrollment while existing members keep their rate. The replacement, Success by Sesame, starts at $59 a month on an annual plan.

### Q. How much do weight loss centers cost?

A.  Budget by the year, not by the visit. A physician-supervised program is normally a monthly membership plus lab work, with medication as a separate line. Ask what twelve months totals, including the baseline panel, repeat labs, and dose increases. Centers advertise the entry price; the annual figure is the one that decides whether you can actually sustain it.

### Q. What is the cheapest GLP 1 without insurance?

A.  As of December 1, 2025, the lowest published self-pay prices come straight from the manufacturers. Eli Lilly lists Zepbound single-dose vials on LillyDirect at $299 for 2.5 mg, $399 for 5 mg, and $449 above that. Novo Nordisk lists Wegovy at $349 a month through NovoCare, with the oral version starting near $149. Confirm on the day you buy.

### Q. Is it worth going to a weight loss clinic?

A.  It depends on what a clinic gives you that a primary care visit does not. You are buying faster dose titration, someone tracking side effects between appointments, and staff who fight prior authorizations for you. If your own doctor will prescribe and your plan already covers the drug, a membership may be paying for coordination you could get for a copay.

### Q. Does insurance cover weight loss centers?

A.  Often partly. Most plans handle the medical visit and labs like any other office visit, then treat the medication and any membership fee as separate questions. Whether the drug is covered depends on your specific formulary and what your employer bought, not on the clinic. Ask your plan for its weight-management drug policy in writing before signing a membership agreement.

### Q. What is the least expensive weight loss program?

A.  Usually the one already built into coverage you hold. Medicare Part B pays for obesity screening and behavioral counseling at no cost to you when your primary care provider accepts assignment, and most non-grandfathered private plans must cover intensive behavioral counseling without cost sharing. Community health centers in Missouri and Illinois price visits on a sliding scale by income.

### Q. Can I get free weight loss treatment?

A.  Parts of it, yes. Behavioral counseling is a covered preventive service at no cost under Medicare Part B and most private plans. Nonprofit hospitals must publish a financial assistance policy, and federally supported health centers on both sides of the river use sliding fee scales. Free medication is far rarer, and a free consultation is not free treatment.

### Q. What is the cheapest weight loss treatment?

A.  By raw price, behavioral and nutrition counseling delivered through coverage you already have, which can cost nothing out of pocket. Medication is the expensive tier at $299 to $449 a month in manufacturer self-pay pricing as of December 2025. Surgery is the biggest single bill but is largely one-time, aside from follow-up visits and lifelong supplements.

## What to Know About Solar Panels in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-about-solar-panels-in-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Saturday morning in Affton and there’s a guy on your porch with a tablet, telling you your roof faces the right way and you’ve already been pre-approved. Two weeks ago your cousin in Florissant got the same knock. A neighbor in Kirkwood put panels up three years back and won’t stop talking about how good it was. Somebody in Belleville took theirs down last spring and gets quiet when you ask why.

All four of those can be true at once, which is why this is so hard to research. Solar here isn’t one product with one answer. It’s a roof question, an insurance question, a utility-tariff question and a resale question stacked on each other — and the tax rules underneath all of it changed less than a year ago.

So here’s the honest version, sources named and dated, no pitch. If you read one section, read the next one. It holds the fact most likely to be wrong in whatever quote is sitting on your kitchen table.

### Is the 30% solar tax credit going away in 2026?

It already went away. The 30% federal Residential Clean Energy Credit — Section 25D, the one homeowners claimed on their own tax return — does not apply to a system finished after December 31, 2025. The IRS page for the credit, last reviewed or updated July 4, 2026, states flatly that the credit “is not available for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025.”

The change came from Public Law 119-21, signed July 4, 2025. The IRS then issued fact sheet FS-2025-05 on August 21, 2025, spelling out the timing trap: an expenditure “is treated as made when the original installation of the item is completed.” Not when you signed. Not when you paid the deposit. If installation wrapped up in 2026, the IRS treats the expenditure as made in 2026, and there is no 25D credit to claim. The companion Section 25C credit for insulation, windows and efficient HVAC ended on the same date. So if anyone quoting you in 2026 subtracts a 30% federal credit from your purchase price, that quote is wrong. Verify it yourself at irs.gov before you sign — this is a five-figure decision that deserves ninety seconds of checking.

Two things did survive, and pitches blur them together on purpose. First, the business-side clean electricity investment credit, Section 48E, was not repealed on the 25D schedule. That is the credit a leasing company or PPA fund claims on equipment it owns and puts on your roof. You never claim it and it never appears on your return. Second, Illinois still runs state-level solar programs, which is a genuinely different situation from Missouri. If you did finish an installation in 2025, ask a CPA about carrying an unused amount forward; the IRS describes 25D as nonrefundable with carryforward of unused amounts, but how that lands on your return is a question for your own preparer.

### Is solar worth it in Missouri?

In Missouri it now hinges almost entirely on how much of your own power you use the moment you make it, because Ameren Missouri does not buy your surplus at retail. Its customer-owned solar page, checked August 2026, credits excess generation at 3.84 cents per kWh in summer (June through September) and 3.39 cents per kWh in winter (October through May). Every kWh your house consumes while the panels are making it is worth full retail to you. Every kWh you export comes back at roughly four cents. That spread is the whole Missouri argument, and it is why storage, load shifting and running the dryer at 1 p.m. matter more here than in retail-buyback states.

The rules sit in the Missouri Net Metering and Easy Connection Act, RSMo 386.890, with the Public Service Commission rule at 20 CSR 4240-20.065. As the Missouri Department of Natural Resources explains, the program covers systems up to 100 kW, credits excess at the utility’s avoided fuel cost, and bars a utility from charging “any additional standby, capacity, interconnection or other fee or charge that would be unique to a customer generator.” For systems of 10 kW or less, no extra liability insurance or additional distribution equipment can be required. Utilities must answer an application within 30 days for systems 10 kW and under, or 90 days up to 100 kW.

Nothing is left on the incentive side either. Ameren Missouri’s solar rebate ran under RSMo 393.1670 at 50 cents per watt for systems operational between January 1 and June 30, 2019, then 25 cents per watt through December 31, 2023 — and it ended there. Add the repealed federal credit and a Missouri homeowner buying outright in 2026 has no federal credit, no state credit and no utility rebate. The sunshine is unchanged; the subsidy stack is not.

One more wrinkle worth a call to your county assessor. RSMo 137.100 lists “solar energy systems not held for resale” among exempt property, but the Missouri Supreme Court held that exemption unconstitutional in Johnson v. Springfield Solar 1, LLC, docket SC99441, decided August 9, 2022. That case involved a commercial facility in Greene County, and how assessors treat a residential rooftop array varies — ask St. Louis County, St. Charles County or Jefferson County directly. To run your own numbers, pull twelve months of Ameren statements, total the dollars, total the kWh, and divide.

### How is solar different on the Illinois side of the river?

Illinois is a meaningfully better policy environment than Missouri right now, and the difference is state law, not sunshine. Homeowners in Belleville, Edwardsville, Granite City and O’Fallon sit under Illinois Shines, a state program in which Illinois utilities purchase renewable energy credits from qualified solar projects. The incentive is paid to a state-Approved Vendor and, as the program puts it, “may be passed on to customers as savings.” Missouri has no statewide equivalent.

Net metering there changed recently too. Under the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, Ameren Illinois applies a new crediting structure for applications after January 1, 2025: excess generation earns credit against the supply and transmission portions of the bill and no longer offsets delivery service charges. Customers who applied before that date keep the older arrangement, and net metering covers systems 100 kW and smaller. In exchange, Ameren Illinois posts a smart inverter, or distributed generation, rebate — for residential DS-1 customers, $300 per kW-DC for the inverter connecting a solar generator and $300 per kWh for an energy storage system inverter. The rebate and the supply-only crediting travel together, so a good Illinois quote shows both sides of that trade in dollars, not adjectives.

Then there is Illinois Solar for All, the income-qualified program for households at or below 80% of area median income. It is the closest thing to genuine no-up-front-cost residential solar in this metro, and its structure requires that a participant’s savings exceed any subscription or loan payment. It is also popular: the program announced that its single-family and two-to-four-unit categories reached capacity in 2025, with residents likely waiting on more funding in 2026. Two houses ten miles apart, one in Webster Groves and one in Granite City, get different answers to the same question.

### What is the 20% rule for solar, and is there a 33% rule?

Neither is a law, a tax rule or a utility requirement. Both are internet rules of thumb, and they don’t even carry the same meaning from one website to the next. The 20% rule is usually a sizing buffer — some writers use it to mean building headroom above average usage for cloudy stretches and system losses, others to mean deliberately undersizing. The 33% rule most often refers to fire-code limits on how much of a roof’s plan area an array may cover before extra access pathways and setbacks kick in, and sometimes to oversizing a DC array relative to its inverter. Conversation starters, not standards.

Here is the sizing rule that actually binds you in Ameren Missouri territory, from Ameren’s own customer-owned solar page: most recent 12 billing months in kWh, divided by 8,760 hours times a 15.6% capacity factor, equals your maximum allowable nameplate capacity in kW DC. Ameren’s worked example uses a home at 13,512 kWh a year: 13,512 ÷ (8,760 × 0.156) = 9.887 kW.

Two useful things fall out of that. Your size is anchored to what you have already used, not what you plan to use — so if an EV or a heat pump is coming next year, raise it early, because last year’s bills are the input. And Ameren’s 15.6% capacity factor works out to roughly 1,370 kWh a year for every kW DC installed in its Missouri territory, a utility-published local planning number that beats any national average in an ad. For your address specifically, run the free PVWatts calculator the National Renewable Energy Laboratory publishes at nrel.gov. On roof coverage, what governs your house is whichever fire code edition your city adopted. St. Louis County alone contains more than 80 municipalities, so setbacks and permit fees can differ from one side of a street to the other.

Wildly off-topic — the roof crew will want sandwich shops at noon.

### What do St. Louis hail, roofs and tree cover do to a solar system?

Hail is the most underrated line item in a St. Louis solar decision. Using National Weather Service Storm Prediction Center counts of hailstones one inch or larger, the Insurance Information Institute reports Missouri had 253 hail events in 2025 — fifth-most of any state — and Illinois had 167, ninth-most. Texas led with 902, Kansas followed with 375. This is not a distant risk. It is our normal spring.

So call your homeowners carrier before you sign, not after the first storm. Ask three questions and get the answers in writing: is a permanently mounted rooftop array covered as part of the dwelling or does it need its own endorsement; what is my wind and hail deductible, and is it a flat dollar amount or a percentage of dwelling coverage; and does adding an array change my premium, deductible or eligibility at renewal. Percentage wind-and-hail deductibles are common here, and the gap between a $1,000 deductible and 2% of a $400,000 dwelling is not a rounding error.

Roof age is next. A quality array is built to sit up there for decades; shingles in this climate are not. If your roof has fewer than about ten years left, replace it first, or you are buying a future removal-and-reinstall job nobody budgets for at signing. A good local company will tell you to do the roof first and lose the sale — take that as a signal. If you’re pricing materials for that roof job, the counters at St. Louis hardware stores are still good for exactly that kind of question.

Then trees. Older neighborhoods — Webster Groves, Maplewood, Ferguson, big stretches of south city — carry serious canopy, and shading does not cut output in a neat straight line. A branch across one corner of an array in late afternoon can cost far more than its shadow suggests, depending on whether the system uses a string inverter, optimizers or microinverters. Ask for a shade analysis taken on site, tied to your actual roof planes. A satellite screenshot with a sunny-day overlay is a sales graphic, not an engineering study.

### Buying, leasing or a PPA — which is which?

Three ways end up with panels on your roof, and they are wildly different assets. You buy with cash or a loan and own it outright. You lease, paying a fixed monthly amount for equipment you do not own. Or you sign a power purchase agreement and buy the electricity the system makes, at a per-kWh rate, from the company that owns it.

Since the homeowner credit ended, far more 2026 offers steer toward leases and PPAs, and there is a real reason for it: Public Law 119-21 repealed residential 25D but left the business-side Section 48E credit standing on a different timetable, so the fund that owns the equipment can still claim a federal credit you cannot. That is legal and normal. The fair question is how much of it is reflected in your monthly payment — ask for the answer as a number. Then get five items in writing: term length, the annual escalator percentage, the buyout schedule year by year, who pays to remove and reinstall the array when your roof is replaced, and what happens at the end of the term. A 2.9% escalator sounds harmless in year one and is a very different number in year eighteen.

### Why is it so hard to sell a house with solar panels?

Usually it isn’t the panels — it’s the paperwork bolted to them. A leased or PPA system is a long-term contract sitting on your roof, and it commonly carries a UCC-1 fixture filing recorded against the property. At closing that gets resolved one of three ways: the buyer qualifies with the solar company and formally assumes the agreement, the seller buys the contract out, or the filing is released so title passes clean. Each takes time, in the middle of a purchase contract with a clock running.

An owned, paid-off system is a different story — simply an improvement to the house, like a finished basement. An owned system with a loan against it typically gets paid off at closing like any other lien. The friction concentrates almost entirely in third-party ownership, worth knowing now if there is any chance you move within the decade. Whatever you own, keep a folder from day one: the signed interconnection agreement with Ameren, the permit and final inspection, warranties with registration confirmations, the monitoring login, and the production history. And be skeptical of any resale-premium percentage a salesperson quotes for this metro — there is no current, credible St. Louis-specific figure behind one.

### Why are people getting rid of their solar panels?

About seven honest reasons, most of which have nothing to do with solar being a bad idea in principle. A roof needs replacing and the array has to come off. The installer went out of business, so the workmanship warranty is worthless and nobody else wants to touch the system. A lease payment escalated past the value it delivers. An inverter failed after its warranty ended. Storm damage where the deductible ate most of the claim. Production that never came close to the projection, usually from shading or an oversold estimate. And squirrels or birds nesting under the panels and chewing wiring, a common and expensive nuisance in wooded neighborhoods. Worth noting that much of what looks like removal is really removal and reinstall around a roofing job, and the panels go right back up.

### Why is my electric bill high if I have solar?

Because solar reduces the energy portion of your bill, not the whole bill. The fixed monthly customer charge stays. Delivery charges largely stay. In Ameren Illinois, for applications after January 1, 2025, excess generation credits do not offset delivery service charges at all. In Ameren Missouri, exported kilowatt-hours come back at 3.84 cents in summer and 3.39 cents in winter, not at what you pay to buy power in the evening.

The other usual suspects: new load that arrived after the system was sized, such as an EV charger, a heat pump or a hot tub; an annual true-up landing in one lump; snow or leaves sitting on the array; and an inverter that faulted out and went unnoticed for weeks because nobody opened the monitoring app. Set a monthly reminder to check production. Then handle the boring load-side work — a house full of old fixtures and bulbs quietly raises the size of system you need, and swapping lighting fixtures costs far less per kilowatt-hour saved than adding panels.

### Can you really get free solar panels in Illinois or Missouri?

On the Illinois side something close to it exists and it is real: Illinois Solar for All serves households at or below 80% of area median income, with no up-front cost and a program requirement that savings exceed any subscription or loan payment. It is state-run, works through Approved Vendors, and has run out of room before — both its single-family and two-to-four-unit categories hit capacity in 2025. In Missouri there is no statewide equivalent and no state program giving away residential panels. Nearly every free-solar ad aimed at a Missouri address is a lease or PPA with no money down. That can still work for the right household, but it is financing, not a giveaway, and the word free is your cue to read the contract twice.

### What solar installers wish St. Louis homeowners knew

From the other side of the counter, a residential solar company is a sales operation with a construction crew attached, and customer acquisition — not hardware — is the line item that decides whether the shop survives the year. That is why you get knocked on. Because 25D turned on completed installation rather than payment, late 2025 was a scramble to finish jobs by December 31 and early 2026 was the quiet side of that cliff, which is much of why so many companies now lead with lease and PPA offers instead of cash quotes. The other quiet tax is paperwork: with more than 80 municipalities in St. Louis County, the same 8 kW job runs through a different building department, fire official and fee schedule depending on the address. The good operators pull your last twelve months of usage before quoting, and walk away from a roof with five years left in it. That work still has to be findable locally, which is what a complete listing on St Louis Near Me Directory is for.

Ready for three real quotes instead of one porch pitch? Browse solar installation companies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then hand each one the same twelve months of Ameren bills and ask all three for a written shade analysis tied to your address.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is the biggest downside to solar electricity?

A.  It only makes power while the sun is up, so its value depends on what your utility pays for surplus. In Ameren Missouri territory, excess generation is credited at 3.84 cents per kWh in summer and 3.39 cents in winter — far below what you pay after dark. That timing mismatch, not panel quality, is what most often disappoints homeowners here.

### Q. How much does a solar system cost for a 2000 sq ft house?

A.  Square footage does not set the price — your electricity usage does. Ameren Missouri sizes systems from your most recent twelve billing months, divided by 8,760 hours times a 15.6% capacity factor, so two 2,000-square-foot houses can need very different arrays. Get three itemized quotes priced per watt installed off the same usage data. Anyone quoting from square footage alone has not read your bills.

### Q. What is the 33% rule for solar panels?

A.  A rule of thumb, not a legal standard. Most often it refers to fire-code limits on how much of a roof’s plan area an array can cover before extra access pathways and setbacks are required; sometimes it describes oversizing a DC array relative to its inverter. What governs your roof is the fire code edition your municipality adopted, so ask your installer to name it.

### Q. What I wish I knew before getting solar panels?

A.  The four regrets that come up most: not replacing an aging roof first, not calling the insurance carrier about wind and hail deductibles, not grasping that surplus power sells back for pennies rather than retail, and signing a lease without reading the escalator and buyout schedule. All four are avoidable in one afternoon of phone calls before anybody gets a signature.

### Q. Can you get free solar panels in Missouri?

A.  No. Missouri has no statewide program that installs residential panels for free, and Ameren Missouri’s solar rebate ended December 31, 2023 under RSMo 393.1670. The federal 25D credit ended for systems completed after December 31, 2025. A free-solar ad aimed at a Missouri address is almost always a lease or power purchase agreement with no money down.

### Q. Can you really get solar panels for free in Illinois?

A.  Something close, if you qualify. Illinois Solar for All serves households at or below 80% of area median income, with no up-front cost and a requirement that savings exceed any subscription or loan payment. It runs through state-Approved Vendors and has limited room — the program reported its single-family and two-to-four-unit categories reached capacity in 2025, with more funding expected in 2026.

### Q. Will the government pay you to install solar panels?

A.  Not a Missouri homeowner in 2026. The federal residential credit ended for systems placed in service after December 31, 2025, and Missouri has no state credit or utility rebate left. In Illinois, yes indirectly: Illinois Shines has utilities buy renewable energy credits through Approved Vendors, and Ameren Illinois posts a $300 per kW-DC smart inverter rebate for residential customers.

### Q. How to apply for free solar scheme in 2026?

A.  If you are in Illinois and income-qualified, apply through an Approved Vendor listed by Illinois Solar for All at illinoissfa.com, and check current capacity first, since categories have filled up before. If you are in Missouri, there is no such program to apply for. Ignore any text message or door pitch claiming a government solar scheme is enrolling your address.

### Q. Is solar worth it financially?

A.  That depends on your blended rate, your roof and which state you are in — and the honest answer changed in 2026, when the 30% federal credit ended. Do the math yourself: total the dollars and the kWh across twelve months of bills, divide for your real rate, then estimate how much production you would use on-site rather than export at pennies.

### Q. What are 5 disadvantages of solar power?

A.  One, output stops when the sun does. Two, exported surplus is credited well below retail in Ameren Missouri territory. Three, an aging roof has to come off and go back on around the array. Four, hail exposure is real here, with Missouri fifth nationally in 2025 hail events. Five, leased and PPA systems complicate a home sale through recorded fixture filings.

## What St. Louis Hardware Stores Still Do for You
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-st-louis-hardware-stores-still-do-for-you

Imagine it’s a Tuesday evening in Affton and the screen on your back door finally lets go where the cat has been leaning on it for three years. It’s a four-inch tear. The frame is straight. The door still closes right. The only thing standing between you and a bug-free kitchen is somebody with a spline roller and eight feet of mesh.

Maybe you’ve come home to a different version of the same evening. A house key that needs a twin before your kid starts feeding the neighbor’s cat in Kirkwood. A closet jamb with one paint chip pried loose because the color went out of production years ago. A run of chain that has to be seven feet, not ten. A propane tank in Florissant with a date on the collar you have never looked at.

None of those are shopping trips. They’re counter work — jobs a person performs for you, on a machine bolted to a bench, while you stand there. That is the part of a hardware store a warehouse aisle cannot copy, and it is the part most people around the St. Louis metro forget exists until they need it at 6:40 on a weeknight.

### What does a hardware store do?

A hardware store sells small quantities of repair and building goods — fasteners, plumbing and electrical parts, paint, hand tools, lawn and garden supplies — and it performs services at the counter while you wait. The usual list: cutting keys, matching and mixing paint, re-screening windows and doors, cutting glass and acrylic, cutting and threading pipe, cutting chain and rope to length, handling propane, and sharpening blades.

That second half is the real definition. Federal industry statistics file hardware stores and home centers as two separate retail categories, and the difference you can see from the parking lot is the bench: a home center is built around self-service aisles and volume, a hardware store around a counter with equipment behind it and somebody who knows how to run it.

Nothing about that service list is standardized. One store on Manchester Road might re-screen, thread pipe and sharpen chainsaw chains. Another the same size out in St. Charles does keys and paint and nothing else, because a previous owner sold the threading machine. So the most useful habit in this whole article is the phone call: ask before you load the frame into the car.

### Which keys can a hardware store copy, and which ones can’t it?

Most house, padlock, cabinet and desk keys copy in about ninety seconds, as long as the store stocks the matching blank. What actually blocks a copy is almost never the words stamped on the key. It’s the blank. Patented, restricted keyways are sold only to authorized dealers, so if the store cannot buy the blank, no machine in the building will help you.

That surprises people who bring in a key stamped “DO NOT DUPLICATE.” The Associated Locksmiths of America has long treated that stamp as advisory rather than legal in most of the country, and warns that stamping ordinary commercial blanks gives building owners a false sense of security. In most states it is a request, and honoring it is store policy. Real restriction comes from patent protection on the blank itself — the high-security lines used on schools and office buildings.

One category is genuinely off-limits, and it’s federal. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1704, knowingly and unlawfully making, forging or counterfeiting a key to a Postal Service lock, or to any authorized mail receptacle, carries a fine or up to ten years in prison. If your mail arrives at a cluster box the Postal Service maintains — the norm in newer subdivisions toward Wentzville and O’Fallon — that lock is theirs. The counter sends you to the post office, and that is the statute talking, not the clerk.

Who may go further than copying differs across the river. Illinois licenses locksmiths under the Private Detective, Private Alarm, Private Security, Fingerprint Vendor, and Locksmith Act of 2004 (225 ILCS 447), and Article 30 exempts a retail merchant “selling locks or similar security accessories, duplicating keys” plus employees “working in the capacity of key cutters,” so long as nobody holds themselves out as a locksmith. Missouri’s Division of Professional Registration oversees roughly forty licensed professions, and locksmith is not among them. A counter in Belleville and one in Maplewood can both cut your key; rekeying a cylinder is not on that exemption list.

A car key is a different job, and this is where the driveway frustration happens. A key cut on a duplicator is a mechanical copy: it turns the lock and does not start the engine, because most vehicles built since the late 1990s carry a transponder chip the immobilizer must recognize before it releases fuel or spark. A fob adds a rolling-code remote, and programming takes a diagnostic tool plus, on many models, a security code from the manufacturer. Some stores host a kiosk that clones certain chipped keys; plenty cannot touch a proximity fob. Call first, and bring a key that already works.

### How does paint color matching actually work?

The counter puts your sample under a spectrophotometer, which reads the color under controlled light and returns the closest formula the store’s tinting system can mix into a base. A dispenser then squirts colorant into the can and a shaker does the rest. The whole thing takes about ten minutes, and it lives or dies on the sample you bring.

Bring something physical. A chip of the old paint pried off a jamb, a switch plate, a drawer front, a scrap of trim. A photograph on your phone cannot be matched, because your camera made its own decisions about white balance and your screen is making more of them. Aim for a flat, clean piece at least the size of a quarter, taken from a spot that has not been sun-bleached. Paint off a south-facing wall reads differently than the same paint pulled from a closet.

Two more things bend the result. Sheen changes how a color reads, so one formula in flat and in semi-gloss will not look like the same color on a wall. And a formula matched into a different product line gets you the color, not the finish — an old oil enamel matched into a modern water-based base reflects differently even when the pigment is right. If the match matters, buy a sample size, paint a patch, let it cure, and look at it day and night.

One money note: once a base is tinted, it is yours. Tinted paint is generally not returnable anywhere, which is why testing beats guessing on a four-gallon order. And for touch-up on an aged wall, cut to the nearest corner rather than feathering a patch in the middle. Even a perfect match shows against ten years of dust.

### Can a hardware store fix a window or door screen?

Yes, and re-screening is one of the most common counter jobs in the metro. Bring the whole frame, not the torn mesh. The tech pulls the old spline out of the channel, lays new mesh over the frame, rolls the spline back in with a wheel, and trims the excess. Some stores turn it around the same day; in April and May, expect a few days.

The choice you get to make is mesh. Standard fiberglass is cheap and forgiving. Aluminum holds its shape and shows every dent. Pet-resistant mesh is a heavier vinyl-coated polyester meant to survive a dog that thinks the door is optional. Solar mesh cuts real heat gain, worth asking about for a west-facing porch in July. Spline diameter matters too, which is another reason the frame rides along.

The skill is tension. Too tight and the frame bows into a shallow diamond; too loose and the mesh ripples in the first breeze. If the frame is bent, corroded or split at a corner, most shops that re-screen can build a new one from stock in standard colors. Full screen-porch panels on an older bungalow are a bigger job and usually a separate quote — ask before you assume it is the same service.

### What can a hardware counter cut to size for you?

Pipe, glass, acrylic, chain, wire rope, rope and cord, threaded rod, and sometimes keystock. Cutting to length is the oldest service in the trade and still the reason plenty of people walk in: you need seven feet of something that comes in a ten-foot package, and buying the package means paying for three feet of scrap you then have to store.

Pipe is the one that intimidates people, and it should not. A store with a threading machine cuts black iron or galvanized pipe to your measurement, reams the burr out of the inside, and cuts tapered threads on the ends. Give the counter the finished end-to-end length and say whether that includes the threads, because half an inch of confusion is a return trip. Two cautions: cutting pipe is not approving your installation, and gas piping is permit-and-inspection work in most municipalities on both sides of the river.

Glass is the service with a code rule attached. A counter can cut single-strength window glass for a broken sash, and acrylic sheet, which scores and snaps or goes on a saw. But safety glazing — tempered glass — is required by residential code in and around doors, next to stairs, and around tubs and showers, and tempered glass cannot be cut: any cut shatters it into gravel. If the broken pane is in a storm door or beside a bathtub, the answer is a new tempered piece ordered to size.

Chain, cable and rope come off a reel by the foot, and the number you want off the tag is the working load limit, not the breaking strength. Those are not the same figure and not close. Chain comes in grades, and proof-coil chain off a hardware reel is not overhead lifting chain no matter how stout it looks. Tell the counter what it has to hold. Same with rope: nylon stretches and absorbs shock, polypropylene floats and hates sunlight.

Wildly off-topic — but somebody owes you dinner. Find a St. Louis steakhouse.

### Should you exchange a propane tank or have it refilled?

Refill if you want all the gas you paid for. Exchange if you want speed, or if your tank is out of date. A 20-pound cylinder holds 20 pounds of propane; exchange cylinders are commonly filled to 15. The Federal Trade Commission’s October 2014 case against Blue Rhino and AmeriGas — which together held roughly 80 percent of the wholesale exchange market — described both companies cutting fills from 17 pounds to 15 back in 2008 without a matching cut in price.

A refill station fills your own cylinder by weight and hands it back. You keep the tank you own, you pay for what goes in, and you can top off a half-full tank in May instead of surrendering the gas still in it. The catch is that refills exist only where somebody has built and staffed one, and the hours on it are often shorter than the store’s.

Exchange has one situation where it clearly wins: an expired cylinder. Under federal rules at 49 CFR 180.209, cylinders in liquefied petroleum service must be requalified on a cycle, and the common barbecue-tank path is twelve years from the manufacture date stamped on the collar, then external visual re-inspection every five years. A tank past date is one nobody may legally fill, and swapping it into a cage makes that someone else’s problem. Check the valve while you are there: NFPA 58 has required an overfill prevention device on cylinders of 40 pounds and under in order to refill them since April 1, 2002. The tell is a triangular handwheel.

Regulation differs by state, which is why refill stations are scattered rather than everywhere. In Missouri, the Missouri Propane Safety Commission registers propane businesses by class: Class VI is LP Gas Dispenser Operator for non-metered sales, requiring an owner or full-time manager holding a current Dispensing Certified Employee Training Program credential or approved equivalent, while Class VII is Cylinder Exchange Dealer. Filling your tank and swapping a cage are two different registrations here. In Illinois, LP gas falls under the Office of the State Fire Marshal’s Division of Petroleum and Chemical Safety, and installing a tank used to dispense it requires an application to the OSFM. A refill station is a licensed installation, not a shelf.

### Is it worth having a mower blade sharpened instead of replaced?

Usually yes, right up until the steel is thin, the nicks are deep, or the sail at the back of the blade is worn round. Sharpening costs a fraction of a new blade and takes minutes. What matters more than the edge is what happens after: a sharpened blade has to be balanced, and balance is what people skip in the garage with an angle grinder. An out-of-balance blade shakes the spindle, and on a walk-behind, the crankshaft it is bolted to.

Counters that sharpen usually take more than mower blades — chainsaw chains tooth by tooth on a grinder, hedge trimmer blades, pruners and loppers, shears, garden tools, kitchen knives, scissors, and at some shops planer and jointer knives. It is frequently handled by one specialist who comes through on a schedule, so ask what day things go out and what day they come back.

Small engine repair is the deeper version of the same counter: mowers, trimmers, blowers, tillers, snowblowers, generators. The most common ticket is a fuel-system cleanup, because gasoline blended with ethanol draws in moisture and leaves varnish in a carburetor bowl over a winter of sitting. Which leads to a rule people get wrong at the pump: the EPA does not permit E15 in nonroad engines — mowers, chainsaws, generators, boats — and pumps dispensing it carry a federally required E15 label.

It matters more here than in much of the country. Illinois has pushed higher blends: Senate Bill 1963, signed in 2023, granted a 10 percent state sales tax exemption on E15, 20 percent on mid-range blends and 100 percent on E85, all sunsetting December 31, 2028. Cheaper E15 at an Illinois pump is fine for a 2001-or-newer car and wrong for the can in your trunk. Ask the counter about ethanol-free fuel or a stabilizer. And the dead months are when turnaround is fast: snowblower in September, mower in November.

### When does the counter beat a big box, and when does it not?

The counter wins when the job is small, odd, or needs a human being: one machine screw, seven feet of chain, a screen re-mesh, a color matched off a chip, a propane refill, a blade sharpened, a repair part for a fixture that stopped being made decades ago. The big box wins on volume and on price for commodity goods — sheet goods, appliances, bulk lumber, contractor packs, and anything you would buy fifty of.

Be honest about the rest of the trade-off. A large home center usually has longer hours, deeper stock in a given brand, and an easier return desk. Independents around here often close at six or seven and go home early on Sunday. The small counter gives back parking, a person who answers, fasteners sold loose instead of a blister pack of twelve, and someone willing to look at the broken part in your hand. The cheapest fix of your month is usually a four-dollar repair kit, and no self-checkout lane will tell you it exists.

Two adjacent jobs are worth naming so you do not drive to the wrong counter. Many hardware stores keep a carpet-cleaning machine on a day rate; the wider equipment question is covered in renting tools and equipment in St. Louis. If your question is which tools belong in your own garage rather than which jobs to hand across a counter, start with must-have handyman tools for St. Louis homeowners. Bulbs and fixtures are their own decision, covered in what to know about buying lighting fixtures in St. Louis.

### What the counter looks like from the other side

The North American Hardware and Paint Association’s 2025 Cost of Doing Business Study, covering fiscal 2024 across 1,082 independent stores, put the typical hardware store’s gross margin after rebate at 42.6 percent and profit before taxes at 4.7 percent, on an average sale of $39. The margin lives in small, loose, unglamorous goods — a hex bolt carries a markup a sheet of plywood never will. Services are mostly traffic: keys, screens, propane and sharpening are priced to get somebody through the door, not to carry payroll. The word “rebate” is the co-op model showing up; Ace Hardware, which reported record second-quarter revenue of $3.0 billion on August 12, 2026, is the largest, with over 5,000 mostly independent stores. Seasonality is unforgiving: spring green goods and the first hard freeze make the year. The complaint operators trade is the twenty-minute counter diagnosis that ends in an online order. The ones who do well are findable, which is why a complete listing on St Louis Near Me Directory is worth ten minutes to claim and fill out.

Need a counter that actually cuts, mixes and fixes? Browse hardware stores across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the closest one and ask two questions before you drive over: do you re-screen, and do you refill propane.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What makes a good hardware store?

A.  Depth of service and depth of small parts. A good one cuts keys and matches paint, and it also re-screens, cuts glass, threads pipe, cuts chain by the foot and sharpens blades. It sells fasteners loose by the piece, and somebody there will look at your broken part and name it. Hours and parking beat square footage.

### Q. What are the most common things people buy at a hardware store?

A.  Fasteners, batteries, light bulbs, tape, adhesives, cleaning supplies, plumbing repair parts like washers and supply lines, electrical odds and ends, paint and painting sundries, hand tools, lawn and garden goods, and propane. Most trips are one broken thing plus two more items remembered in the aisle.

### Q. Is Home Depot considered a hardware store?

A.  In everyday speech, yes. In the trade and in federal industry statistics, no — it is a home center, a different retail category from hardware stores. The practical difference is the counter. Home centers are built around self-service aisles and volume; hardware stores around a service bench with equipment behind it and staff who run it.

### Q. What store is cheaper, Home Depot or Ace Hardware?

A.  It depends on the item, and no reliable public price index compares them across the St. Louis metro. Warehouse home centers generally win on lumber, sheet goods, appliances and bulk quantities.
