### Do cellular shades actually lower your energy bills?

They measurably help, and the U.S. Department of Energy has the numbers. In an Oak Ridge National Laboratory study, cellular shades saved up to 20 percent on heating energy and up to 15 percent on total heating and cooling energy compared with no shades at all, per the DOE factsheet Interior Cellular Shades Boost Home Energy Performance (DOE/EE-2519, October 2021).

Two caveats, stated plainly. That testing ran in a research house in Knoxville, Tennessee from December 2019 to May 2020 and was then modeled across 15 climate zones for a 2,380-square-foot home. It is not a measurement of your house on a January night in Ferguson. The same factsheet also notes the experiments focused on the heating season, with more research needed on cooling-season control strategies.

The mechanism still travels well to a Missouri winter. Cellular shades trap air inside the honeycomb cells and in the pocket between shade and glass, which cuts nighttime heat loss and the cold draft that pools at the floor under an old window. That same DOE factsheet reports window attachments can save about 15 percent of a household’s annual heating and cooling energy compared with vinyl blinds — and vinyl or metal blinds are roughly 60 percent of what is hanging in American homes.

Fit is the whole game. A cellular shade with a two-inch gap down each side is a decorative object. If you want the insulating effect you want a tight inside mount, and on the coldest windows you want side channels or a valance that closes off the top, both of which cost extra. To compare products on measured performance instead of showroom claims, look for a rating label from the Attachments Energy Rating Council, the nonprofit DOE points consumers toward for exactly this.

If your problem is summer solar heat rather than winter draft, coverings are not the only lever — the companion piece on home window tinting in St. Louis handles the film side of that question.

### Is there a tax credit for energy efficient blinds or shades?

No, on two separate counts. Window coverings were never listed as qualifying property under the federal 25C Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit. The IRS building envelope list covers exterior doors, windows, skylights, insulation and air sealing — not shades, blinds or other window attachments.

And 25C is gone regardless. Under Public Law 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025, the IRS states in its official FAQ that the credit will not be allowed for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025. If a salesperson tells you your shades qualify for a federal credit, that is wrong twice over.

Utility rebate programs are a separate question and they change from year to year, so check your own provider’s current residential rebate list rather than taking a showroom’s word for it. Buy cellular shades because they cut drafts and shave the heating bill, not because you are counting on a refund in April.

### Are corded blinds still sold, and does cordless cost more?

Ready-made blinds sold off the shelf have had to be cordless, have inaccessible cords, or have cords no longer than 8 inches since the ANSI/WCMA A100.1-2018 standard took effect December 15, 2018, as documented in the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s Federal Register rulemaking of November 28, 2022. Made-to-order custom products were the gap.

The reason is not academic. In that same rulemaking, CPSC said it was aware of 209 fatal and near-miss strangulations on window covering cords among children eight years old and younger between January 2009 and December 2021. If there is a crawler or a toddler in the house, cordless in every room they can reach is not an upgrade tier. It is the floor.

The regulatory picture is genuinely messy, and it is worth saying so. CPSC issued a federal rule extending the cordless requirements to custom window coverings, but a federal appeals court vacated that rule in September 2023 after a challenge from the Window Covering Manufacturers Association. The industry then moved to the voluntary ANSI/WCMA A100.1-2022 standard, which WCMA says took effect June 1, 2024 and eliminates free-hanging operating cords on made-to-order products. So the requirement on custom today comes from the industry standard rather than a federal regulation, and it is fair to ask a dealer to confirm in writing that what you are ordering meets it.

On price: CPSC noted that after the stock market shifted to cordless in 2018, sales of stock products actually rose even though prices in some cases doubled. Expect cordless lift to be baked into anything current rather than sold as a cheap add-on, and treat a bargain corded unit from old inventory as the tradeoff it plainly is.

### Where is the most affordable place to get blinds?

Cheapest to most expensive, there are four channels: ready-made stock off a big-box shelf, cut-to-size stock trimmed in store, cut-to-size ordered online from your own measurements, and a local dealer who measures and installs. Each step up buys fit and accountability, and Angi’s 2026 spread of roughly $30 to $600 per window is essentially that ladder.

Ready-made works when your openings are standard and you can live with a gap. In-store cutting is the sweet spot for a lot of St. Louis County ranches and newer builds in O’Fallon on either side of the river, where the windows really are uniform. Ordering cut-to-size online is the cheapest route to an exact width, and the highest-risk one, because the moment you supply the measurement you own every error in it.

A local dealer costs the most per window and is the only channel that solves bays, arches, transoms, oversized sliders and out-of-square plaster openings. On those windows a dealer is often cheaper in real terms, because the alternative is buying the wrong thing twice. Mixing channels inside one house is completely normal — stock in the bedrooms, dealer on the front bay.

### What this looks like from the blind shop’s side of the counter

The product is not where the money is. Fabric and hardware come from a handful of manufacturers on set dealer pricing, so a small shop in Maryland Heights and one in Belleville are quoting off very similar cost sheets. What separates them is measure-and-install — labor they control, and the one part of the sale a customer cannot do at 11 p.m. on a phone. That is why the free in-home measure exists: it is the point where a local operator can out-serve a website.

It is also where the losses live. A custom unit is cut to a number and cannot be resold, so remakes come straight out of margin. The quiet complaint in this trade is the customer who measures their own openings, orders wrong, and expects the dealer to eat it. Seasonality is lumpy too: spring and early summer move with home sales and move-ins, there is a real push before the holidays when company is coming, and January and February run thin enough that many shops lean on property managers, apartment turns and small commercial work to bridge the gap.

Homeowners here search by neighborhood and by problem, not by brand, so a complete listing with a real service area and current photos is how a shop turns up in that search at all. If you run one, you can get listed on St Louis Near Me Directory.

Tired of guessing at your own window measurements? Browse shades and blinds companies across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then book two free in-home measures in the same week so you are comparing quotes on identical openings.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How much do shades typically cost?

A.  Cellular shades run about $70 to $350 per window installed, and custom shades $250 to $2,600 per window installed, according to HomeGuide’s 2026 window shades cost data. Ready-made shades cost a fraction of that. The spread comes down to whether the shade is built to your exact opening, the fabric opacity you choose, and whether the lift is manual or motorized.

### Q. Are shades cheaper than blinds?

A.  Usually not at the entry level. The least expensive thing on the wall is a basic aluminum or vinyl slat blind, and shades start higher than that. From mid-range up, the two overlap almost completely, and the bigger price driver becomes stock versus custom sizing rather than the shade-or-blind decision itself.

### Q. Is it better to have blinds or shades?

A.  Blinds win where you want to tilt slats for light and view without opening fully — kitchens, home offices, street-facing rooms. Shades win on insulation, on softness, and on wide openings where slat blinds get heavy to lift. For a cold St. Louis bedroom window in February, a tightly fitted cellular shade does more than any slat blind will.

### Q. What are the drawbacks of cellular shades?

A.  The honeycomb cells collect dust and cannot be wiped down like a hard slat, so cleaning means a vacuum brush attachment. There is no tilt option, so it is open or closed with nothing in between. Cordless lift mechanisms wear out over years of daily use, and top-down bottom-up hardware roughly doubles the cost per window.

### Q. What are the disadvantages of blackout shades?

A.  Light still leaks around the edges unless you add side channels, which cost extra, so an inside-mounted blackout shade is rarely truly black. Heat builds up in the pocket between the shade and the glass on a south or west exposure. And with no partial setting that keeps a view, a blackout shade makes daylight in that room an all-or-nothing choice.

### Q. How much do blinds cost generally?

A.  As a whole project rather than a single window, Angi’s 2026 data puts a typical eight-window blinds job at $211 to $1,343, averaging $760 in stock-grade product. Custom sizing and better materials at $200 to $600 per window push those same eight openings to roughly $1,600 to $4,800 before any motorization is added.

### Q. Does Lowes cut blinds for free?

A.  Lowe’s advertises free in-store cutting on eligible cut-to-size blinds bought there, notably its Levolor Trim+Go line, trimmed to the measurement you bring in. It will not cut blinds purchased elsewhere and does not cut at your home. Program details and eligible product lines change, so call the store before you drive out with numbers.

### Q. Does Costco sell blinds or shades?

A.  Yes. Costco sells custom blinds, shades and shutters to members through partner programs listed under its Home & Installation Services, including an in-home measure and installation rather than an over-the-counter purchase. Because it is a custom order, treat the pricing the way you would any dealer quote and confirm the remake policy before you sign.

### Q. Should blinds be lighter or darker than the walls?

A.  A covering slightly lighter than the wall makes a window read larger and keeps a small room from closing in. Darker reads as a deliberate frame and hides dust better. There is a cost angle too: standard white and alabaster are almost always the cheapest colorways, and specialty colors, stains and fabric upgrades carry an upcharge per window.

## What to Know Before Buying a Commercial Truck in St. Louis
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-to-know-before-buying-a-commercial-truck-in-st-louis

Picture a Thursday morning in Fenton. The service van has 214,000 miles on it, third gear is slipping, and you have two calls booked in Pagedale before noon and a bid to walk across the river in Pontoon Beach at three. You have been putting the truck decision off for about two years. This is the morning it stops being optional.

So you start looking, and inside twenty minutes you hit the thing nobody warns you about. Buying a truck for work is not the same transaction as buying a truck. The lot that will sell you a crew cab on a Saturday afternoon is not the desk that orders a chassis with the right cab-to-axle dimension for a service body. The financing is different. The plates are different. The federal rules that attach to the vehicle are different — and Missouri and Illinois differ from each other, which matters if your work crosses the river.

This one is written for the plumber in Pagedale, the landscaper in Pontoon Beach, the electrician in Fenton, and the two-truck outfit trying to become a four-truck outfit. If you are shopping for a personal pickup instead, the negotiation and finance-office side of that purchase is covered in buying a car from a St. Louis dealership. Everything below is about a truck that has to earn money.

### What’s the best place to buy a truck?

For a work truck, the seller is decided by weight rating, not by badge. Up to about 14,000 pounds GVWR you belong at a franchise dealer’s commercial or fleet desk. Above that you belong at a medium- and heavy-duty truck dealer — different building, different parts counter, different process. Walking into the wrong one costs weeks.

The retail showroom sells finished vehicles sitting on a lot. The commercial desk inside that same franchise sells incomplete chassis, books factory build slots, and talks to body companies for a living. The medium- and heavy-duty store covers Class 4 through Class 8 and runs on parts and service. NADA’s American Truck Dealers division counted 3,798 franchised new-truck dealerships nationwide in 2025, including 98 in Missouri and 141 in Illinois (ATD Data 2025). They are not spread evenly across the metro, and the store that stocks your engine family is probably the one you stay with for a decade.

A third door exists and plenty of small shops use it: wholesale and public auctions, fleet remarketing, municipal surplus. That route buys price and gives up warranty, build spec and service history. The fourth door is the one first-time buyers forget — the body company that finishes the truck. On many work-truck purchases the chassis and the body are two orders, two invoices and two delivery dates.

### What does the 10,001-pound line actually change?

It moves you out of vehicle rules and into carrier rules. A vehicle used on a highway in interstate commerce with a gross vehicle weight rating or gross combination weight rating of 10,001 pounds or more meets the federal definition of a commercial motor vehicle in 49 CFR 390.5. That single number pulls the truck, the driver and the company itself under the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations.

The eight-class weight system underneath all of this is straightforward. Using the U.S. Department of Energy Alternative Fuels Data Center table: Class 1 is under 6,000 pounds GVWR, Class 2 is 6,001 to 10,000, Class 3 is 10,001 to 14,000, Class 4 is 14,001 to 16,000, Class 5 is 16,001 to 19,500, Class 6 is 19,501 to 26,000, Class 7 is 26,001 to 33,000, and Class 8 is 33,001 and up. Classes 1 and 2 are light duty, 3 through 6 are medium duty, 7 and 8 are heavy duty.

Here is what surprises people. A one-ton dually or a 4500-series chassis cab is usually Class 3, already past 10,001 pounds GVWR. It looks like a pickup, parks like a pickup, and is legally a commercial motor vehicle the moment it crosses a state line for business. Four thresholds are worth memorizing: 6,000 pounds changes the tax treatment, 10,001 triggers the federal carrier rules, 26,001 brings in the CDL and apportioned registration, and 33,001 adds a 12% federal excise tax at purchase.

### Do you need a CDL to drive a work truck?

Usually not, and that is the most common wrong assumption in this whole purchase. The federal floor is 26,001 pounds. FMCSA requires a Class B for a single vehicle rated 26,001 pounds or more, and a Class A for a combination rated 26,001 pounds or more that tows a unit rated over 10,000 pounds. Almost every Class 3 through Class 6 work truck sits underneath that.

The trap is the trailer, not the truck. A Class 5 truck rated at 19,500 pounds is comfortably non-CDL on its own. Hook a 12,000-pound equipment trailer behind it and the combination rating is 31,500 pounds with a towed unit over 10,000 — that is a Class A, and the officer at the scale reads the door-jamb rating, not what you happen to be hauling that day. A skid steer on a big deck trailer is how a lot of landscaping outfits find this out.

Two pieces sit on top of the federal floor. Since February 7, 2022, anyone getting a first Class A or Class B CDL, upgrading a class, or adding a hazmat, passenger or school bus endorsement must complete Entry-Level Driver Training through a provider on FMCSA’s Training Provider Registry before the state will test them. And drivers aged 18 to 20 can hold a CDL for intrastate work but generally cannot operate in interstate commerce, so a young driver on a Missouri CDL cannot legally run the truck across the river to an Illinois job. Missouri issues CDLs through the Department of Revenue; Illinois through the Secretary of State.

### When does a small business actually need a USDOT number?

If you operate in interstate commerce with a vehicle rated 10,001 pounds GVWR or more, you need one, and it is free. FMCSA requires companies operating commercial vehicles in interstate commerce to register and carry a USDOT number. For a St. Louis contractor that is not a trucking question — a single job in Granite City or Fairview Heights can be the thing that triggers it.

Intrastate is where the two states split, and the split is genuinely large. Missouri law at RSMo 307.400 adopts 49 CFR Parts 390 through 397 for intrastate operation, then carves out a big exemption: those parts “shall not apply to commercial motor vehicles operated in intrastate commerce to transport property, which have a gross vehicle weight rating or gross combination weight rating of twenty-six thousand pounds or less.” Hazmat vehicles and vehicles designed for 16 or more passengers stay in regardless.

Illinois draws the line at 10,001 pounds instead. The Illinois Motor Carrier Safety Regulations, enforced by the Illinois State Police under the Illinois Motor Carrier Safety Law at 625 ILCS 5, Chapter 18b, apply to carriers, drivers and commercial motor vehicles transporting property or passengers in interstate or intrastate commerce, with a commercial motor vehicle defined at 10,001 pounds GVWR or GCWR and up. Read that against the Missouri carve-out and the practical result is stark: a 14,000-pound dump-body truck working only in St. Louis County sits outside those federal safety parts, while the identical truck working only in St. Clair County sits inside them.

Above Missouri’s line, the Missouri State Highway Patrol’s Commercial Vehicle Enforcement division is direct about the number itself: a private carrier operating solely in intrastate commerce must have a USDOT number assigned to the company and marked on its vehicles, and because no state agency issues those to private intrastate carriers, you register with FMCSA. Missouri for-hire carriers hauling intrastate also need operating authority through MoDOT Motor Carrier Services. Confirm your own situation with MSHP or the Illinois State Police before assuming you are exempt — the exemptions turn on cargo, weight and whether you are for-hire, and one job across the river can move you.

Unrelated, and we know it — that dead box truck needs junk removal.

### How do Missouri and Illinois plate a commercial truck?

Structurally differently, and it shows up on the bill every year. Missouri registers trucks on a gross weight you declare, at two rate tiers: local, meaning within 50 miles of home, and beyond-local for anything wider. Illinois charges a flat weight tax set in statute, assigned to lettered classes by gross weight. Same truck, very different numbers.

Missouri’s fee chart, Form 1659 revised August 2025, shows a local 6,000-pound truck registration at $15.75 a year and a local 12,000-pound truck at $18.25, with the beyond-local versions at $25.75 and $38.25, plus a $9.00 processing fee per one-year registration. Declare 18,000 pounds or more and Missouri prorates quarterly and issues a single front plate; a rear plate costs extra. Your declared weight must include any trailer and property you plan to haul that period, so under-declaring is how people end up cited at a scale.

Illinois runs the flat weight tax at 625 ILCS 5/3-815. As the statute reads, Class B covers 8,000 pounds and less at $148, Class C runs 8,001 to 10,000 at $218, Class D runs 10,001 to 12,000 at $238, Class F runs 12,001 to 16,000 at $342, and Class H covers 16,001 to 26,000 at $590. What you hand over at the counter can run a few dollars above the statutory figure, and the schedule gets amended, so price your class before you budget it.

Before you conclude Missouri is simply cheaper, there is a counterweight, and it is the reason the comparison is not really a comparison. Missouri counties bill business personal property tax on vehicles every December, assessed at 33 1/3% of true value under RSMo 137.115. Illinois abolished ad valorem personal property taxes as of January 1, 1979 under Article IX, Section 5 of its 1970 constitution and replaced the revenue with the Personal Property Replacement Tax on business income. So Missouri gives you a cheap plate and an annual tax bill on the truck itself; Illinois gives you an expensive plate and no property tax on the asset.

One more registration item catches growing shops. If a power unit is licensed at 26,001 pounds or heavier, has more than two axles regardless of weight, or runs in a combination at 26,001 pounds or heavier, and it operates in two or more jurisdictions, MoDOT requires apportioned plates under the International Registration Plan instead of a standard Missouri plate. Crossing the Poplar Street Bridge with a loaded combination is exactly what puts a small St. Louis fleet into IRP.

### What can a business actually deduct on a work truck?

More than most owners expect, and the deciding factor is often a tape measure. For tax years beginning in 2026 the Section 179 expensing cap is $2,560,000, reduced dollar for dollar once Section 179 property placed in service exceeds $4,090,000, per IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32. Separately, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act restored 100% bonus depreciation for qualifying property acquired and placed in service after January 19, 2025.

The 6,000-pound rating is the first gate. Internal Revenue Code Section 280F(d)(5) defines a passenger automobile as, for a truck or van, one rated at 6,000 pounds gross vehicle weight or less — so a truck above that rating is not a passenger automobile and escapes the luxury-auto depreciation caps that throttle a car purchase. Nearly every real work truck clears it.

The second gate is the one that costs people money. Section 179(b)(5) caps the deduction on a sport utility vehicle rated between 6,000 and 14,000 pounds GVWR at $32,000 for 2026 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32). But Section 179(b)(5)(B) excludes from that definition any vehicle with a cargo area of at least six feet in interior length that is an open area, or is enclosed by a cap and not readily accessible directly from the passenger compartment. In plain terms: a short-bed crew cab can land under the $32,000 cap while the same truck with a long bed does not. If the bed is anywhere near six feet, get the exact interior dimension from the manufacturer in writing before you sign.

Two conditions sit under all of it. Section 179 requires the vehicle be used more than 50% in the active conduct of your trade or business in the year it is placed in service, and if business use later drops to 50% or below, part of the deduction gets recaptured as income (IRS Publication 946). Take every number here to your own CPA before you buy.

### Why the sticker price is not the truck price

Because a work truck usually leaves the factory unfinished. A chassis cab is an incomplete vehicle — frame, cab, drivetrain, no body. Whatever goes on the back, whether that is a service body, flatbed, dump, van box or stake bed, is installed afterward by a body company. That is a separate invoice and a separate calendar, and it is where work-truck budgets break.

The mechanics matter before you order, because they are not reversible. Cab-to-axle dimension has to match the body you intend to mount, so the body decision comes before the chassis order. Frame rail height, wheelbase and rear axle ratio all get spec’d against the body and the load. If anything runs on hydraulics — a dump, a crane, a liftgate — order power-take-off provision from the factory rather than adding it later. Upfitter switches and an auxiliary power feed cost almost nothing at build time and real money retrofitted.

Then watch the payload sticker, not the tow rating. A steel service body can run well over a thousand pounds empty, a liftgate adds several hundred more, and a ladder rack, a compressor and a water tank eat the rest. You can absolutely buy a truck with an impressive towing number and almost no legal payload left once it is built the way you need it. The completed vehicle also gets a new certification label from the final-stage manufacturer, and that label is what registration and enforcement read.

At the top of the range the tax code joins in. Internal Revenue Code Section 4051 imposes a 12% federal excise tax on the first retail sale of truck chassis and bodies suitable for use with a vehicle over 33,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, and on trailer chassis and bodies over 26,000 pounds. That tax lands on the completed unit, body included, which is why a Class 8 quote and a Class 7 quote are further apart than the spec sheets suggest. Once the truck is working, what it costs to keep working is a separate budget line entirely — that is covered in what truck repair really costs in St. Louis.

### New, used or leased — which one protects cash flow?

Judge this on downtime and cash, not on preference. A used truck preserves capital and spends availability. A new truck spends capital and buys warranty plus a build spec that actually fits the work. A lease keeps cash in the business and moves residual risk off your balance sheet. For a shop with one or two trucks, the real question is what happens on the day the truck does not start.

The used market is not a small discount. ATD Data 2025 put the average retail selling price of a used Class 8 truck at $64,163 in 2025 against $178,775 for a new one. That gap is real, and so is what comes with it: somebody else’s maintenance decisions, no build spec of your own, and an upfit designed for a different trade. Ask for the maintenance file and the most recent inspection report. If the seller cannot produce either, you are buying the paint.

Leasing works differently on the commercial side than it does on the consumer side, and advice from car forums does not transfer. Commercial vehicle leases commonly use a terminal rental adjustment clause, and under Internal Revenue Code Section 7701(h) a qualified motor vehicle operating agreement containing a TRAC is still treated as a lease for tax purposes, with the lessor as owner, provided the lessee certifies the vehicles will be used more than 50% in its trade or business. That structure is why fleets lease and consumers usually should not. It also means your deduction is rent rather than depreciation, which is a different conversation with your accountant than the Section 179 one above.

Whichever way you go, price the backup before you need it. A one-truck business stops when a turbo does, and the cost of that week rarely shows up in anyone’s purchase spreadsheet.

### What a truck dealership looks like from behind the counter

The truck itself is close to a loss leader. In 2025 the average franchised new-truck dealership booked 58.6% of total sales in the new-truck department but took only 19.7% of its gross profit there, and gross on a new Class 8 averaged 6.0% of a $178,775 selling price — $10,803 a unit. The used department averaged a retail net loss of $2,690 per used Class 8 retailed. Service, parts and body shop produced 77.5% of total gross profit on 36.5% of sales (ATD Data 2025). Total commercial truck sales fell 13.6% that year while average dealership revenue still rose 5.8%, because the money is behind the building, not on the front lot. That is why a good commercial salesperson asks about your routes and your body before your budget: the unit is thin, the relationship is not. Shops that get found locally get the second truck and the parts business that follows it, which is the whole argument for a complete, current listing on St Louis Near Me Directory.

Ready to spec the truck instead of guessing at it? Browse truck dealers across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then call the commercial or fleet desk directly and open with your GVWR target, your body, and whether you cross the river.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is the cheapest month to buy a truck?

A.  For a work truck the calendar matters less than the build slot. A chassis ordered to spec is priced when the order is placed and delivered months later, so year-end shopping advice barely applies. NADA’s ATD Data 2025 expects 2026 commercial sales up slightly on 2025, with pre-buy activity ahead of pending EPA 2027 rules pulling demand forward.

### Q. Which truck brand is most reliable?

A.  No federal agency publishes a neutral reliability ranking for work trucks, so treat any single answer as marketing. What is checkable is service coverage on the routes you actually run: how far the nearest authorized service point is, whether it stocks your engine family, and how fast warranty work moves. Uptime, not badge, is the reliability question that pays you.

### Q. Where can I find truck sales in Missouri?

A.  Missouri had 98 franchised new-truck dealerships in 2025 — 48 medium- and heavy-duty stores plus 50 Chevrolet and Ram medium-duty points (ATD Data 2025). Anyone in the business of selling vehicles in Missouri must hold a state license under RSMo 301.559, and operating without one is a class A misdemeanor. Commercial units also move through licensed wholesale and public auctions.

### Q. How much is a $70,000 truck payment?

A.  About $1,391 a month if you finance the full $70,000 over 60 months at 7.14%, the rate the Federal Reserve reported for 60-month new car loans at commercial banks in June 2026 (G.19 release). That works out to roughly $13,400 in total interest. Commercial equipment financing is quoted separately and can land above or below that.

### Q. How many miles is too much for a used truck?

A.  Mileage is the wrong gauge on a work truck. A gas half-ton and a Class 6 diesel age on completely different curves, and on a service truck idle hours often do more damage than road miles. Ask for engine hours, the maintenance file and the most recent inspection report, then weigh the odometer last rather than first.

### Q. Which state is cheaper to buy a truck?

A.  For a St. Louis business it is not really a choice, because you register where the business is domiciled rather than where you shopped. Missouri plates are cheap, but Missouri counties tax business vehicles as personal property at 33 1/3% of value (RSMo 137.115). Illinois charges far more at the plate and abolished personal property tax back in 1979.

### Q. What kind of truck can I get for $400 a month?

A.  Roughly $20,100 financed over 60 months at 7.14%, the Federal Reserve’s June 2026 average for 60-month new car loans (G.19 release). In work-truck terms that buys a used half-ton or a high-mileage cargo van, before any upfit. Stretching to 72 months lifts the amount to about $23,400 and adds interest rather than value.

### Q. Do car dealerships actually make money?

A.  Truck dealerships do, but not where buyers assume. In 2025 the average franchised new-truck dealership took 58.6% of its sales but only 19.7% of its gross profit from the new-truck department, while service, parts and body shop delivered 77.5% of gross profit on 36.5% of sales (ATD Data 2025). The used department averaged a net loss per unit retailed.

### Q. Why are dealerships necessary?

A.  Legally, because both states license them: Missouri makes it unlawful to act as a motor vehicle dealer without a license under RSMo 301.559, and Illinois licenses dealers through the Secretary of State. Practically, because a franchised store handles titling, warranty claims, recall work, and the chassis order that a body company has to build against.

### Q. Will truck prices go down in 2026?

A.  Nobody can promise that, and the industry forecast points the other way. NADA’s ATD Data 2025 expects commercial truck sales in 2026 to be up slightly on 2025, flags new equipment prices continuing to rise while interest rates stay high, and anticipates pre-buy activity ahead of pending EPA 2027 regulations. Plan on flat to higher.

## Your Staff Is Already Using AI. You Just Don’t Know Which Parts.
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/your-staff-is-already-using-ai-shadow-ai-st-louis

Imagine it’s a Thursday morning and the estimate your office manager sent out on Tuesday has come back with a question you cannot answer. The document reads well. Cleaner than anything that has left your Rock Hill shop in years. The tone is right, the scope is right, and buried in the middle is one tidy paragraph describing a warranty you have never offered in your life.

So you ask her where that came from. She says the customer was waiting, she was slammed, and she got most of it out of the chat app on her phone. She isn’t hiding anything. She’s a little proud of it, honestly. A two-hour job took twenty minutes and the customer replied the same afternoon.

That moment is the entire subject of this article, and some version of it is playing out in small offices from Wentzville to Waterloo this week. Nobody made a technology decision. A person under time pressure found something that worked, used it, and never thought to mention it — because nobody ever told her there was a line, much less where it sits.

### Why do the numbers on AI adoption contradict each other?

Because they count two different things. Firm-level surveys ask the business. Worker-level surveys ask the person doing the typing. The U.S. Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey, published May 26, 2026 and covering December 14, 2025 through May 3, 2026, found fewer than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees using AI. Ask workers directly and the share is roughly double that.

Here are the firm-level figures side by side. Census BTOS, same May 2026 release: under 20% for firms with four or fewer employees, 32% for firms with 100 to 249 employees, and 37% for firms with 250 or more. A Federal Reserve FEDS Note published April 3, 2026 put overall firm adoption at roughly 18% as of year-end 2025, using that same BTOS data. Those are government numbers, collected from businesses, and they say the same thing: the smaller the company, the less likely it is to describe itself as an AI user.

Now the worker side. That same Federal Reserve note points to the Real-Time Population Survey run by economists Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin and David Deming, which asks individuals a plain question: do you use generative AI for your job? As of November 2025, about 41% of workers said yes. Non-work use ran closer to 50%. That is not a vendor number and not a press release. It is a research survey asking people about their own hands on their own keyboards.

The Federal Reserve note explains part of the gap in the driest possible language, and it is worth understanding: a random sample of workers pulls disproportionately from large employers, because large employers employ most people. So a worker survey naturally leans toward the kinds of companies where AI is already normal. That is real, and it explains some of the distance between 18% and 41%.

But it does not explain all of it, and the remainder is the part that matters to you. A firm survey asks an owner or a manager to characterize the company. A worker survey asks a person to characterize themselves. When those two disagree, the most likely explanation is not that anyone lied. It is that the company has not adopted AI and its people have. If you want the adoption statistics pulled apart in more detail, including why a question-wording change in November 2025 broke the trend line, that is covered in what percent of small businesses actually use AI.

### What shadow AI looks like inside a six-person business

Shadow AI is any use of an AI tool at work that the business never chose, never paid for, and does not know about. In a small company it almost never looks like software. It looks like a phone, a browser tab, and somebody trying to get out the door by five.

Concretely, in a metro-area shop with a handful of employees, it looks like this:

A quote or proposal drafted in a free chatbot and lightly edited before it goes to the customer.

A difficult email to an unhappy client rewritten to sound calmer, with the original complaint pasted in to give the tool context.

A spreadsheet of names, addresses and job totals dropped into a chat window so it can be summarized or sorted.

Social posts, service-page copy and review replies generated in bulk from a rough prompt.

A contract, lease or insurance certificate uploaded so somebody can ask, in plain English, what it actually says.

A transcript or recording of a meeting run through a free summarizer that nobody in the room agreed to.

None of that requires an IT department to permit or a credit card to start. That is the point. The barrier to a staff member adopting AI is a login, and the barrier to a company adopting AI is a decision, a budget and a conversation. The first one is lower by an enormous margin, which is exactly why the two sets of numbers came apart.

### Where does the 49% to 78% range come from, and how solid is it?

Those shadow-AI percentages come from vendor surveys, not from government statistics, and you should treat them accordingly. Two are quoted constantly. BlackFog, a cybersecurity company, reported 49%. WalkMe, a software adoption company, reported 78%. Both companies sell products that address the problem their research describes. That does not make the numbers false. It does mean you read the methodology before you repeat the headline.

The BlackFog figure, published January 27, 2026, comes from research conducted by Sapio Research in November 2025 among 2,000 respondents, 1,000 in the United States and 1,000 in the United Kingdom, all at organizations with more than 500 employees. Of that whole sample, 49% said they use AI tools their employer has not sanctioned. Among those people, 58% were using free versions of those tools.

The WalkMe figure, published August 27, 2025, comes from a Propeller Insights survey fielded July 16 to 23, 2025, with a margin of error of about three percentage points. The sample was 1,000 working U.S. adults — and here is the part that gets dropped when the number travels — screened so that every respondent already uses AI in their job. WalkMe says so plainly in its own release: the 100% adoption rate in that sample is by design, not a picture of the American workforce. The exact claim is that 78% say they use AI tools not provided by their employer, which is a softer statement than tools their employer forbade.

So the 29-point spread is not two studies disagreeing about reality. It is two studies asking different questions of different people. One is 49% of everybody at a big company. The other is 78% of people who already use AI at work. Stack them in a slide deck and you get a scary range; take them apart and you get two narrow findings that never had the same denominator.

Compare that with how the Census Bureau builds its number. BTOS is a recurring survey of a large probability sample of U.S. employer businesses, reported by firm size and industry, with the question wording published and the reference period stated on the page. When the Bureau changed that wording in November 2025 from AI used to produce goods or services to AI used in any business function, reported rates jumped by 47% to 159% depending on industry — and the Bureau said so, which is why anyone can adjust for it. A vendor survey rarely gives you enough to do that.

One more honest caveat, and it is a big one: neither shadow-AI survey looked at a business like yours. BlackFog sampled companies with 500-plus employees. WalkMe sampled people who already use AI. Nobody has published a solid measurement of unapproved AI use inside a nine-person landscaping company in St. Charles County. The direction of these findings is believable. The precise percentage, applied to your payroll, is not something anyone has actually measured.

### Why is shadow AI a problem?

Shadow AI is a problem because three things happen without anyone deciding they should: confidential information leaves the business through a free consumer account, output nobody checked reaches a paying customer, and the company keeps no record of which work was AI-assisted. Each is survivable on its own. Together they mean you cannot answer basic questions about your own files.

Take them one at a time, because the fixes are different.

Client information in a free consumer tool. The BlackFog research from November 2025 asked what people actually put in. Among respondents, 33% had shared company research or datasets, 27% had shared employee data including names, payroll and performance information, and 23% had shared financial statements or sales figures. Free consumer tiers generally have looser data handling than paid business tiers, and 58% of the people using unsanctioned tools in that study were on free versions. If you carry client confidentiality obligations — medical, legal, financial, anything involving a signed agreement — that paste is the exposure, not the AI. The practical boundaries are worked through in what is safe to paste into ChatGPT for your business.

Unreviewed output reaching a customer. This is the failure that costs money soonest, and it is the one in the estimate at the top of this article. A generated draft is confident and fluent whether or not it is correct. It will invent a warranty term, quote a lead time you cannot hit, cite a code section that does not apply in your county, or promise a same-day response your crew has never once delivered. A customer holding a written promise does not care which software produced it.

No record of what was AI-assisted. Six months later a dispute comes up and you want to know how a sentence got into a document. Nobody remembers. There is no draft history, no note, no version marked. The work looks the same as everything else in the folder. That is not a technology gap; it is a bookkeeping gap, and it is the one owners underestimate.

Wildly off-topic — if the office is relocating this fall, start with St. Louis movers.

### Can you actually tell which work was AI-assisted?

Not reliably, and you should stop planning around the idea that you can. OpenAI launched its own AI Text Classifier on January 31, 2023 and pulled it on July 20, 2023, citing a low rate of accuracy; in its own evaluation the tool flagged only 26% of AI-written text correctly. If the company that built the model could not detect the model, a third-party detector on a marketing site is not going to settle an argument in your office.

Detectors also fail in the direction that hurts most. They flag plain, competent, unadorned writing as machine-made, which is exactly what a careful employee produces. Accusing your best writer of using a chatbot because a website scored her paragraph at 94% is a fast way to lose her.

So the answer is not detection. It is disclosure, and it is cheap. A one-line note in the job file — drafted with AI, reviewed by me, sent 8/14 — costs four seconds and answers the question permanently. The businesses that get this right are not the ones with better software. They are the ones where saying so is normal and nobody gets in trouble for it.

That last part is the whole game. WalkMe’s July 2025 survey found 49% of respondents had hidden their use of AI to avoid judgment, rising to 62% among the youngest workers, and that only 7.5% had received extensive training while 23% had received none at all. Again, a vendor survey of self-selected AI users — but the shape of it matches what owners describe. People conceal the tool because they think using it looks like cheating, and no one has told them otherwise. If the answer to that is training, it is worth knowing how to judge an AI course before you pay for one — most of what is sold to small businesses does not survive a serious look.

### Missouri and Illinois are not in the same place on this

If you employ anyone in Illinois, the rules changed on January 1, 2026. House Bill 3773 amended the Illinois Human Rights Act to prohibit employers from using AI in a way that has the effect of discriminating on the basis of a protected class in recruitment, hiring, promotion, training selection, discharge, discipline, tenure, or the terms and conditions of employment. It also bars using ZIP codes as a proxy for a protected class, and it requires notifying applicants and employees when AI is used in those decisions.

Two details make that matter for a small shop rather than only for a corporation. First, the Illinois Human Rights Act has covered employers with one or more employees since July 1, 2020, under Public Act 101-0430, so there is no small-business exemption to hide behind in Metro East. Second, the statute reaches the effect of the AI, not the intent behind it. An office manager in Fairview Heights who pastes a stack of resumes into a chatbot and asks it to rank them has just used AI in a hiring decision, whether or not you knew, approved, or ever heard about it. The Illinois Department of Human Rights has been working through implementing rules on notice and disclosure during 2026; the statute itself is already in force.

Missouri has no equivalent AI-in-employment statute as of August 2026. That is not the same as no rules. Federal and Missouri anti-discrimination law still applies to the outcome of any screening or evaluation process, and outsourcing the judgment to software does not move the responsibility off the employer. The practical difference is disclosure: Illinois has written the notice obligation into statute, and Missouri has not.

If your service area crosses the river — and for most St. Louis metro businesses it does — write your policy to the Illinois standard. Running one rule is simpler than running two, and the stricter of the two is the one you would rather be caught complying with.

### The one-page AI policy you can write this week

A workable small-business AI policy answers three questions and nothing else: what may be pasted in, what may never be pasted in, and who reads the output before it leaves the building. You do not need a law firm or a template pack. You need one page, five decisions, and a staff meeting to say it out loud.

1. AI is allowed here, and you will not get in trouble for saying you used it. Put that first, in that order. Every rule below it depends on people telling you the truth, and they will not if the opening line reads like a threat. A ban does not stop the behavior; the surveys above are what a ban looks like in practice.

2. What may be pasted. Your own marketing copy. Public pricing. Published spec sheets and manufacturer instructions. Job descriptions. Anything already on your website. A customer question with names, addresses and account numbers stripped out. If it could be printed in the newspaper without a phone call from anyone, it can go in a chat window.

3. What may not be pasted, ever. Customer names, addresses, phone numbers or emails. Payment or bank details. Anything from a signed confidentiality or vendor agreement. Employee records, payroll, medical notes, disciplinary write-ups. Insurance claim files. Photographs of a customer’s home interior. Resumes, applications, or anything used to sort, rank or screen a candidate — that one is a legal line in Illinois, not a preference. Name the categories in your own words, on paper, so nobody has to guess.

4. Nothing goes to a customer unread. Pick the reviewer by name, not by title. In a six-person company that is usually you, or the one person who has been quoting jobs for a decade. The reviewer checks three things: are the numbers ours, are the promises ones we keep, and does it sound like a person here wrote it. Estimates, contracts, warranty language, anything with a date or a dollar figure gets read twice.

5. Say so in the file. One line where the work lives: drafted with AI, reviewed by whom, sent when. That is the whole record-keeping requirement. It takes seconds and it is the only thing that will answer a question in March about a document from August.

Then do the part most owners skip: ask what people are already using, and do not react badly to the answer. You will usually learn that two or three staff members have been doing this for months, that one of them is genuinely good at it, and that nobody was hiding anything on purpose. If you would rather work through the setup with other local owners than write it cold, that is a large part of what the AI workshops are for.

### What this looks like from the owner’s side

In a small local service business, the crew is not usually the constraint. The office is. One person answers the phone, schedules, orders parts, chases the insurance adjuster, writes the estimates and follows up on the ones that went quiet — and almost none of that time is billable. The free estimate is the loss leader of the whole trade, and every owner has done the math on what an hour of quoting costs against a close rate that never gets above a certain number. Add the seasonality — the stretch from late spring through the first cold snap carries the year, and February is where nobody wants to look at the books — and the pattern is obvious: the busier you are, the more the unbilled work gets rushed. That is precisely where the chatbot shows up. Not because anyone chose AI, but because the quoting and the follow-up are the parts nobody is paid for. If you run one of these shops and want people to find you when they search locally, a complete listing on St Louis Near Me Directory is the low-effort half of that.

Would rather talk it through than read about it?
