### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What are examples of shadow AI?

A.  A quote drafted in a free chatbot on someone’s phone. A client spreadsheet uploaded to be summarized. A meeting recording run through a transcription tool nobody in the room approved. Review replies and social posts generated in bulk. A contract uploaded so somebody can ask what it means. The common thread is a personal login, no invoice, and no record at the company.

### Q. Can employers tell if you have used AI?

A.  Generally no. OpenAI discontinued its own AI Text Classifier on July 20, 2023, citing low accuracy after it correctly flagged only 26% of AI-written text. Commercial detectors also produce false accusations against plain, careful human writing. An employer can see browser history or account activity on company equipment, but proving a specific paragraph was generated is not realistic.

### Q. Can an employee refuse to use AI?

A.  In at-will states like Missouri and Illinois, an employer can generally require the use of a lawful tool as part of the job, and refusing can carry consequences. The usual exceptions still apply: a disability accommodation, a sincerely held religious objection, a union contract, or a licensed professional duty that requires personal judgment. Most refusals in practice are about accuracy or credit, and are worth hearing out before they become a discipline question.

### Q. Is IT acceptable to use AI in the workplace?

A.  Yes, within limits your business sets in writing. What makes it acceptable is not the tool but the boundary around it: no confidential customer, employee or financial data pasted into a consumer account, a named human reading anything before it reaches a customer, and a note in the file saying it was used. Without those three, it is not the AI that creates the risk.

### Q. What is a good AI policy for a company?

A.  A good one is one page, written in your own words, and specific enough to act on at four o’clock on a Friday. It names the data categories that may never be pasted, names the person who reviews customer-facing output, and states plainly that disclosing AI use carries no penalty. Long policies nobody reads score worse than a short one taped inside a cabinet door.

### Q. How do I create an AI policy for my company?

A.  Start by asking staff what they already use, with amnesty attached, because you are documenting existing behavior rather than inventing rules. Write the never-paste list first, since it is the shortest and the most consequential. Name a reviewer by name. Add the one-line disclosure habit. Read it aloud at a meeting, take the objections, revise once. Two hours total is realistic for a small shop.

### Q. What is the 30% rule in AI?

A.  It is a rule of thumb that circulates online rather than a research finding, and the versions people quote do not agree with each other. Treat any tidy AI percentage rule as a consulting framework until someone shows you the study behind it. The batch companion post on the AI rules people quote traces each one to its actual origin.

### Q. What can AI do for small business owners?

A.  Realistically, it drafts and it summarizes. First-pass estimates, follow-up emails, review replies, listing descriptions, turning a long document into plain English. It does not know your pricing, your suppliers, your code requirements or your crew’s schedule, and it will guess confidently about all four. For a broader look at where it fits locally, see AI for St. Louis and how local businesses can actually use it.

### Q. Are people losing jobs due to AI?

A.  No public dataset cleanly isolates AI as the cause of a layoff, and any figure claiming to is an estimate built on assumptions. What is visible in small local businesses is narrower: tasks moving, not roles disappearing — first drafts, summaries and routine replies. Physical, licensed and on-site work is a different question, handled in what AI will not replace in a local service business.

## What Percent of Small Businesses Actually Use AI?
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-percent-of-small-businesses-use-ai

Imagine it’s a Wednesday morning in Ballwin and you’re standing at the back counter with coffee going cold, reading an email that says 77 percent of small businesses now use AI. You put the phone down. An hour later a trade newsletter lands in the same inbox and says the real figure is about 18 percent. Same country, same year, same question, and a gap of nearly sixty points.

Maybe you’ve had the same whiplash. A contractor in Herculaneum gets a sales call that opens with “most of your competitors are already using this.” A shop owner in Waterloo reads a state-level roundup that says adoption is still in the single digits for firms her size. Both people were told a number. Neither was told what the number counted.

So here’s the honest version, with the sources and the dates attached, and then the part that actually matters: how to tell within about thirty seconds whether an AI adoption figure means anything at all.

### What percentage of businesses have adopted AI?

About 17 to 20 percent of U.S. businesses report using AI, according to the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey covering December 14, 2025 through May 3, 2026, published May 26, 2026. A Federal Reserve FEDS Note dated April 3, 2026 put it at roughly 18 percent of firms at the end of 2025. Those are the two federal readings, and they agree.

Both are firm-weighted. That word does a lot of work. Firm-weighted means every business counts once — the sole-proprietor lawn service in Jefferson County counts exactly as much as a company with 4,000 employees. Since the overwhelming majority of American businesses are tiny, a firm-weighted number is mostly a measurement of what tiny businesses are doing.

The Census survey is not a small poll. It goes to a rotating panel drawn from about 1.2 million U.S. businesses, with cohorts of roughly 200,000 firms surveyed every 12 weeks. That is the largest recurring read on this question anyone has. When a vendor tells you a number based on 500 respondents, this is the thing it should be measured against.

### Why does every source give a different number?

Because they are counting different things. The Federal Reserve note from April 3, 2026 lined up three federal or academic surveys side by side and got 18 percent, 41 percent, and 78 percent — all defensible, all measuring something else. That spread is not a scandal. It is the answer.

The Business Trends and Outlook Survey asked firms whether the business used AI, and returned about 18 percent as of December 2025. The Real-Time Population Survey asked individual workers whether they use generative AI for their job, and returned 41 percent as of November 2025. The Survey of Business Uncertainty asked around 1,032 business executives and returned 78 percent — but that figure is employment-weighted, meaning it approximates the share of the workforce employed at firms that have adopted AI, not the share of firms.

Read those three again and notice that none of them contradicts the others. Most firms have not adopted AI. A large minority of workers use it anyway. And most employed people work somewhere that has adopted it, because big employers adopt first and big employers hold most of the jobs. The Fed’s own explanation names the cause plainly: the biggest driver of variation relates to differences in sampling distributions and units of analysis, with question framing, information gaps between respondents, and social desirability bias also in play.

That last one matters more than people admit. The Fed note observed that 10 to 11 percent of Census respondents answered that they did not know whether their firm used AI. If a tenth of respondents cannot answer the question, the confident single number you saw in a headline is doing a lot of pretending. There is a related and uncomfortable version of this problem covered in what happens when your staff adopts AI before the company does.

### Does AI use rise with the size of the company?

Yes, steadily and without exception in the federal data. In the Census reading published May 26, 2026, less than 20 percent of firms with four or fewer employees reported using AI, 32 percent of firms with 100 to 249 employees did, and 37 percent of firms with 250 or more did. The article’s own headline says it: large firms with at least 20 employees are the biggest AI users.

The gradient is the most reliable finding in this whole subject. Every credible survey that breaks results out by headcount finds the same slope, and the slope is steep at the bottom. A 250-person company is roughly twice as likely to report AI use as a four-person one.

There is a second detail in that Census release worth more than the headline percentages. Between December 2025 and May 2026, AI use increased among firms with at least 20 employees but did not change significantly among firms with fewer than 20. The growth everyone is describing as explosive is happening above a headcount line that most St. Louis businesses sit well below.

By industry the same survey put Information at 39.7 percent, Finance and Insurance at 33.9 percent, and Retail Trade at roughly 14 percent as of May 3, 2026. If someone quotes you a national average and your work is retail or trades, the national average is not describing your industry.

### Why did the AI numbers jump in November 2025?

Because the Census Bureau changed the question, not because businesses changed their behavior. Before November 2025 the survey asked whether the business used AI in producing goods or services. After November 2025 it asked whether the business used AI in any of its business functions. That single edit raised reported adoption by 47 percent to 159 percent depending on industry, per the Federal Reserve note of April 3, 2026.

The two ends of that range are worth sitting with. Professional services rose about 47 percent, an increase of 10.6 percentage points. Manufacturing rose about 159 percent, an increase of 7.5 percentage points. Nothing was installed. Nobody bought anything. The wording moved, and drafting an email with a chatbot went from not counting to counting.

This is why any AI trend line that crosses November 2025 is broken, and why a chart showing adoption “doubling” over the last two years should be treated as a chart of two different questions stapled together. Under the older, stricter wording, the U.S. Small Business Administration’s Office of Advocacy reported on September 24, 2025 that firms under 250 employees were at 8.8 percent as of August 2025, up from 6.3 percent six months earlier. Real growth, in a real series, at a scale nobody puts in a headline.

Hold those two facts next to each other. Genuine adoption among small firms moved about two and a half points in half a year. A question rewrite moved the reported rate by seven to eleven points overnight. The wording change did more to the number than the businesses did.

Wildly off-topic — your roots need doing too. Find a salon nearby.

### Why do vendor surveys say 58 percent or 77 percent?

Because they ask a much easier question, of a self-selected group, and they count everything. The Intuit QuickBooks 2026 AI Impact Report, published May 12, 2026, found that 77 percent of U.S. businesses use AI regularly, up from 48 percent in July 2024. Read its own definition and the gap resolves: the report states that this includes any kind of AI use, from free tools and built-in features to dedicated paid subscriptions.

Built-in features. If your accounting software added an AI categorization button and you clicked it once, you are inside that 77 percent. That is a defensible thing to measure and it is not the same thing the Census measures. Intuit is also a company that sells AI features, which does not make the survey false but does belong in the sentence whenever the figure is quoted.

For scale, that report draws on responses from more than 34,000 business owners across the U.S., Canada, the U.K., and Australia, plus anonymized data from more than 5.3 million QuickBooks businesses, developed with economists at the University of Chicago. It is a serious piece of work. It simply answers a different question than “what share of American firms have adopted AI.”

The trade-association version lands in the same territory. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce Technology Engagement Center, working with Teneo Research, reported on August 18, 2025 that 58 percent of small businesses self-identified as using generative AI. Now put that beside the federal figure from the same month: 8.8 percent under the production-based wording. One month, one country, 58 percent versus 8.8 percent. Neither side lied. They asked different questions of different samples and let the press round the difference into a trend.

### How do you read an AI statistic before you repeat it?

Ask five questions, in this order, and most AI statistics fall apart or become useful within about thirty seconds. Who ran the survey and do they sell AI. What exactly was asked. Who counts as one unit — a firm, a worker, or a job. What date does the figure describe. And does the series cross November 2025.

The unit question is the one people skip and it is the one that swings results hardest. Firm-weighted numbers are dominated by tiny businesses, so they read low. Employment-weighted numbers are dominated by large employers, so they read high. Worker-level numbers describe people, not companies, and a company can show up as a non-adopter while half its staff quietly uses a chatbot at home.

Apply the same test to the pessimistic statistics, not only the flattering ones. The widely repeated claim that 95 percent of generative AI pilots fail comes from a July 2025 MIT Media Lab Project NANDA report titled The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025, built on roughly 150 leader interviews, 350 employee surveys, and 300 public deployments. That is a preprint from a research lab, not a peer-reviewed census, and what it actually measured was pilots with no documented profit-and-loss impact — which frequently means no baseline was recorded before the pilot started. It is a real finding and a poor headline.

The same discipline works on the rules of thumb people quote at each other, which is its own small industry — there is a longer look at which AI rules of thumb survive contact with evidence. And if the number you actually need is a dollar figure rather than a percentage, the honest ranges live in what AI actually costs a small business.

### What should a metro of mostly small firms conclude?

That the national headline number is not about you, and the low number is not permission to ignore the subject. Nearly every business in the St. Louis metro sits in the exact size bucket the Census reports at under 20 percent — and most sit below even that, in the no-employee tier.

The SBA Office of Advocacy 2025 Small Business Profiles, drawing on Census Nonemployer Statistics and Statistics of U.S. Businesses, count 590,131 small businesses in Missouri, which is 99.4 percent of Missouri businesses. Of those, 475,437 have no employees at all, 100,524 have 1 to 19 employees, and 14,170 have 20 to 499. Run the arithmetic and 97.6 percent of Missouri small businesses have fewer than 20 people.

Across the river the shape is identical. Illinois has 1,353,957 small businesses, 99.6 percent of Illinois businesses, of which 1,100,655 have no employees, 224,490 have 1 to 19, and 28,812 have 20 to 499. That is 97.9 percent under 20 employees. Small businesses employ 44.4 percent of Missouri workers and 43.7 percent of Illinois workers, so this is not a rounding error in the regional economy. It is the regional economy.

Two practical consequences. First, when a salesperson tells you that most businesses like yours already use AI, the federal data says otherwise for firms your size, and you can say so out loud. Second, the segment where adoption stalled between December 2025 and May 2026 is firms under 20 employees — so the competitive pressure on a four-person operation in Herculaneum or Waterloo is genuinely lighter than the trade press implies. That buys time to learn properly rather than to buy quickly. The workshop material behind the AI workshops for St. Louis business owners exists for that reason, and the broader overview in AI for St. Louis covers where a first hour is usually best spent.

### From the owner’s side of the counter

If you run a small local operation, you already know why the adoption numbers look the way they do. Your constraint is not curiosity. It is that the person who would have to learn the tool is also the person answering the phone, running the truck, closing out the drawer, and doing payroll on a Sunday. Evaluation time is the scarcest input in the building, and it does not appear on any survey.

The seasonality makes it worse. Most local trades have two or three weeks that carry the year and one dead stretch where the thinking could actually happen — and the dead stretch is usually when cash is tightest, which is exactly when nobody signs up for anything. That is why owners in this position tend to complain to each other about the same thing: not that AI is useless, but that every pitch assumes a spare afternoon and a spare budget in the same month. The operators who get somewhere start with one repeating task, usually written follow-up or quoting, and give it four weeks before deciding.

One connected point, and it costs nothing. People search this metro by category and neighborhood constantly, and assistants now summarize whatever they can read about you. A complete, accurate listing is the cheapest version of being findable there, which is what a directory listing is for.

Tired of being sold a statistic instead of a skill? Browse AI workshops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then bring the one repeating task in your week that eats the most hours — that is the task worth testing first.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. What is the 30% rule in AI?

A.  There isn’t a standard one. No government agency or peer-reviewed body defines a 30 percent rule in AI, and the phrase is used for at least three unrelated ideas online: a limit on how much of a task to hand over, a training-data split, and a productivity claim. Treat any number-plus-rule phrasing as a slogan until someone shows you the study behind it.

### Q. Which 5 jobs will survive AI?

A.  No credible source publishes a list of five. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects occupational growth but does not rank jobs by AI survival, and anyone offering exactly five is writing a listicle, not research. What the data does support is that hands-on, licensed, on-site work in a specific location is the hardest category to automate, which describes most local trades.

### Q. What is the biggest user of AI?

A.  By industry, Information leads at 39.7 percent, followed by Finance and Insurance at 33.9 percent, per the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey as of May 3, 2026. Retail Trade sits near 14 percent. By company size, firms with 250 or more employees lead at 37 percent, roughly double the rate of firms with four or fewer.

### Q. What percentage of businesses have adopted AI?

A.  Roughly 17 to 20 percent of U.S. firms, per Census data covering December 14, 2025 to May 3, 2026 and published May 26, 2026, with the Federal Reserve reporting about 18 percent at year-end 2025 in an April 3, 2026 note. Surveys reporting 58 to 77 percent are measuring workers, executives, or any use of any built-in feature.

### Q. Is AI being adopted by small businesses?

A.  Yes, but slowly and from a low base. The SBA Office of Advocacy reported on September 24, 2025 that firms under 250 employees reached 8.8 percent as of August 2025, up from 6.3 percent six months earlier under the older survey wording. Census data shows firms with fewer than 20 employees saw no significant change between December 2025 and May 2026.

### Q. What is the failure rate of AI adoption projects?

A.  The widely quoted 95 percent comes from a July 2025 MIT Media Lab Project NANDA report built on about 150 leader interviews, 350 employee surveys, and 300 public deployments. It counted pilots showing no measurable profit-and-loss impact, which often reflects missing baseline measurement rather than technical failure. It is a preprint from one lab, not a federal statistic.

### Q. How many companies are actually using AI?

A.  In firm-weighted federal terms, about one in five or fewer. The Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey samples from roughly 1.2 million U.S. businesses in rotating cohorts of about 200,000 every 12 weeks, and returned 17 to 20 percent through May 3, 2026. Note that 10 to 11 percent of respondents answered that they did not know.

### Q. Who are the big 4 of AI?

A.  There is no official designation, and the list changes depending on who is writing it — some group by consumer chatbots, some by cloud platforms, some by chip suppliers. For a small business the question rarely matters, because the practical choice is which tool fits one repeating task, at what monthly cost, with what happens to your customer data.

### Q. How many Fortune 500 companies use AI?

A.  Nobody publishes an authoritative count of use, only counts of disclosure. The Conference Board and ESGAUGE reported on October 6, 2025 that 72 percent of S&P 500 companies flagged AI as a material risk in 10-K filings available through August 15, 2025, up from 12 percent in 2023. That measures what lawyers wrote, not what the company deployed.

## Google AI Mode, Explained for a Local Business Owner
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/google-ai-mode-explained-for-local-business

Imagine it’s a Tuesday morning in Maplewood and the second voicemail of the day is another pitch. This one says your business is “missing from Google’s AI,” and that for a monthly fee they can fix it. The caller sounds like he knows something you don’t. That is the entire trick.

Maybe you’ve had a version of that call. Or a customer from Edwardsville mentioned she found your competitor “in the AI thing” and you nodded like you knew what she meant. Or your nephew in St. Peters typed a whole paragraph into Google in front of you and got back something that read like a written answer instead of a page of links, and you thought: when did that happen, and how long has it been happening to my customers.

Here is the plain version, with no jargon and nothing to buy. What Google AI Mode actually is, what it costs, what makes it show up instead of ordinary results, whether anybody on earth can sell you a place inside it, and how to get your old blue links back in about four seconds if you hate the whole thing.

### What is Google AI Mode, in plain English?

Google AI Mode is a mode inside Google Search that returns a written answer assembled from several web sources at once, with links to those sources shown alongside it, instead of the familiar list of ten blue links. You reach it from the AI Mode button next to the Google search box, or directly at google.com/ai. There is nothing to install and nothing to sign up for.

It is not the same thing as an AI Overview, and the difference is worth thirty seconds of your time. An AI Overview is the summary paragraph that shows up on top of ordinary search results whether you asked for it or not. AI Mode is a place you go on purpose. You land on a page that is mostly answer, and you can keep asking follow-up questions without repeating what you already said, the way you would with a person who was still listening.

Under the hood, Google splits your question into smaller questions and runs them all at the same time. Google’s own developer documentation calls this a “query fan-out” and says it lets the system display a wider and more diverse set of helpful links than a single search would (Google Search Central, AI Features and Your Website, last updated December 10, 2025). That is why a long, specific question often produces a better answer in AI Mode than a short one does.

The engine behind it changes constantly, which is the first thing to know before anybody tells you they have this figured out. Google made Gemini 3.5 Flash the default model in AI Mode globally on May 19, 2026, according to its own announcement. By August 21, 2026, Search Engine Roundtable reported Google was already running Gemini 3.7 Flash on some AI Mode queries. Two model swaps in three months. Any advice you get about AI Mode that does not carry a date on it is worth about what you paid for it.

And it is not a niche experiment anymore. On the Alphabet earnings call of July 22, 2026, Sundar Pichai told investors: “Since expanding AI Mode globally last October, we’ve surpassed 1 billion monthly active users.” That is a company figure reported to shareholders rather than an independent count, so weigh it accordingly — but a company does not hand investors a number it expects to be laughed at.

### Is Google AI mode free?

Yes. Google AI Mode costs nothing to use. There is no subscription, no trial that quietly converts, and no paid tier that makes your business appear inside it. When Google expanded the Personal Intelligence features in AI Mode to nearly 200 countries and territories across 98 languages on May 19, 2026, its own announcement attached the phrase “no subscription required.”

Signing in is the murky part, and it has moved more than once. AI Mode launched in 2025 inside Search Labs and needed a signed-in Google account to use at all. Search trade press through 2026 has reported Google testing an AI-first homepage on which people who are not signed in can use AI Mode too. That is a test, not a settled rule, and it is the one detail here most likely to have changed by the time you read this. The practical answer: open it. If Google asks you to sign in, sign in with any free Google account. Either way, nobody charges you a dime.

Hold onto that, because it is the load-bearing fact in every conversation that follows. The surface is free to the person searching, and free to the business being searched for.

### What makes an AI answer appear instead of a list of links?

Google does not publish a list of triggers, and anyone who hands you one is guessing. Broadly: questions and full-sentence, conversational phrasing tend to produce an assembled answer, while a bare one- or two-word search usually still returns links. That is the honest shape of it. Nobody outside Google has the actual rule, and Google has been deliberate about not writing it down.

Two statements from Google are worth keeping in your head. Its developer documentation says AI Overviews “are only shown when our systems determine that it is additive to classic Search, and as such, often don’t trigger” (Google Search Central, last updated December 10, 2025). And Liz Reid, who runs Google Search, put it more bluntly in an interview published by Search Engine Land on April 23, 2026: “we shouldn’t give you AI for the sake of giving AI, right? The point is for it when we think it adds value.”

In that same April 23, 2026 interview, Reid described what lands in AI Mode as “more longer complex, more conversational queries,” and made a point that explains more than any keyword list would. For twenty-odd years people compressed a real need into two or three words because the search box could not handle the real version. The box handles it now, so people are typing the real version. That change happened on the customer’s side, not yours.

One more distinction that keeps people confused. AI Mode is opt-in per search — you click into it, or you don’t. AI Overviews get shown to you without asking. So when somebody says “Google is all AI now,” they are usually describing an AI Overview sitting on a normal results page, not AI Mode. The two get mixed up constantly, including by people selling services.

### Can anyone sell you a spot inside a Google AI answer?

No. There is no product, from Google or from anybody else, that buys your business a mention inside the unpaid part of an AI answer. Google’s own documentation for site owners says it plainly: “there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary” (Google Search Central, last updated December 10, 2025). No fee, no application, no partner program, no back door.

Now the part a straight answer has to include, because leaving it out would make the paragraph above look like a lie the first time you see an ad. Ads do run inside AI Mode. At Google Marketing Live on May 20, 2026, Google described new formats — Conversational Discovery ads and Highlighted Answers among them — being tested inside AI Mode in the US on mobile and desktop, and said those formats will continue to be clearly labeled as “Sponsored.”

So both things are true at once, and the distinction is the whole ballgame. You can buy an ad that appears in AI Mode, through Google Ads, the same way you have always been able to buy a search ad, and it carries a label. You cannot buy your way into the written answer itself, or into the sources it cites. When a caller offers to “get you into Google’s AI,” they are selling one of three things: a Google Ads account with a markup on top, ordinary marketing work described in mysterious language, or nothing at all.

Three questions end that call in under a minute:

What is the Google product called? If the answer is not “Google Ads” or “Google Business Profile” — both of which you can set up yourself, and the profile is free — ask them to spell it. There is no third product.

Am I paying you, or paying Google? If the money goes to them and they place the ads, ask what share is markup and what share is media spend. A real agency will tell you without flinching.

What happens the month I stop paying? If the answer is that you vanish from the AI, they are describing advertising, not visibility. Say that out loud and listen to how they respond.

None of that makes marketing help a scam. Plenty of it is worth the money, and a good operator will save you more than the fee. It means the specific claim — paid placement inside an AI answer — is not a thing that exists, and the person selling it either knows that or never bothered to check.

Nothing to do with search — somebody to detail the truck.

### Why does this land harder on a local service business?

Because the way people ask for a service was already a sentence, not a keyword. “Who can look at a water heater tonight in south county.” “Which shop works on diesel trucks and is open Saturday morning.” “Who takes walk-ins near Edwardsville and does not charge just to look.” Those are exactly the long, conversational questions that produce an assembled answer rather than a list, which is why local service categories met this surface before most industries knew it existed.

Think about what a customer actually wants to know before they call you. Not your category. They want to know whether you handle their specific problem, whether you can get there inside the window they have, and whether the last forty people who hired you were glad about it. With a page of blue links, they had to open six tabs to find that out. With an assembled answer, something else opens the tabs and hands them a paragraph.

The state line does not split any of this. A shop in St. Peters and a shop in Edwardsville are being read by the same system, and a customer in Maplewood asking a question at 9pm gets one answer, not a Missouri one and an Illinois one. What differs across the river is your licensing, your taxes and your paperwork — not which Google your customers are using.

Which businesses actually get named inside one of those answers is a separate subject with its own moving parts, and a companion piece takes it apart properly: how AI decides which local businesses to name. The short version is that an assembled answer gets built out of things that already exist about you in public. If your Google Business Profile is thin or half-finished, start with the profile mechanics before anything else. And for the wider view of where AI fits into a small business at all — the drafting, the scheduling, the review replies — that ground is already covered here.

### How do you get plain blue links back?

Use the Web filter. Run your search the normal way, then click “Web” in the row of filters under the search box, and the page redraws as nothing but text links. On a narrow screen it hides under “More.” Faster still, and this is the one people pass around to each other: add &udm=14 to the end of the search URL and press enter.

The filter is a real Google feature, not a workaround somebody discovered. Danny Sullivan, then Google’s Search Liaison, announced it on May 15, 2024, describing it as a view for people who want only links to web pages (reported by Search Engine Land the same day). It has survived every change since, and &udm=14 is simply the URL version of clicking that button.

The catch is that it lasts exactly one search. Your next query goes back to the normal page. To make it stick, add a custom search engine in your browser settings pointing at https://www.google.com/search?q=%s&udm=14 and set it as your default. From then on, every search typed into the address bar comes back as plain links. Browser extensions do the same job if you would rather not edit settings yourself.

What does not exist, as of August 22, 2026, is a switch inside your Google account that turns AI answers off everywhere. There is no setting that removes the AI Mode button, and no opt-out for AI Overviews on ordinary results. Google has treated these as parts of Search rather than as add-ons. Anything you personally opted into through Search Labs can be turned off in Labs, but that is a different and much smaller thing. This is also the piece most likely to change, so look at the filter row yourself before taking anyone’s word for it, including this article’s.

### What should an owner actually do about any of this?

Go look. That is the whole assignment, and it takes about fifteen minutes. Open AI Mode and type the three questions a customer would really type about your trade in your town — not your business name, the problem. Then write down, on paper, which businesses got named and what the answer said about them.

Do it a second time with the Web filter on, so you see the same search both ways. That side-by-side is the most useful fifteen minutes in this article, because it turns an abstract worry into a page you are looking at. Most owners find one of two things: they are not mentioned at all, or they are mentioned with something wrong — old hours, a service they dropped two years ago, an address they moved out of.

A companion piece walks through what to do with that list once you have it: what AI says about your business, and how to fix it. And if doing this in a room with other local owners sounds better than doing it alone at the kitchen table at 11pm, that is what the AI workshops are for.

### What this looks like from behind the counter

Most local service operators do not have a marketing problem so much as a phone problem. The phone is the profit and loss statement. A missed call at 4:40 on a Friday is not a lost call, it is a lost job, and in the trades one job can be a real slice of a slow week. The busy stretch pays for the dead one — the first hard freeze, the first warm Saturday, the week everybody discovers their air conditioner at the same hour — and the months in between are spent trying not to give that margin back. Meanwhile the pitches keep coming: the lead service that sells the same homeowner’s phone number to four companies at once, the retainer with a monthly report nobody reads, and now the AI call. What the good operators do differently is unglamorous. They answer the phone, they keep their hours accurate in every place they are listed, and they ask every caller how they found them and actually write it down. That last habit is the only thing that ever tells you whether any of this is working. Being listed and complete where people are already looking is part of the same discipline — a complete listing is one more place where the right answer about you exists in public.

Would you rather learn this with other owners than from a cold call? See the AI workshops for local business owners on St Louis Near Me Directory, then run those three customer questions in AI Mode tonight and bring the answers with you.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Is Google AI to be trusted?

A.  Treat it as a fast, well-read assistant that can be confidently wrong. Google’s own AI Mode page carries the line that it is experimental and may make mistakes. The practical rule for a business owner: anything checkable — hours, prices, license status, whether a company still exists — gets verified before you repeat it or act on it. Use it to get oriented quickly, not as the last word on anything that costs money.

### Q. How do I use Google AI Mode?

A.  Type a full question instead of keywords, then keep going. Ask a follow-up without restating what you already said, because the conversation carries your context forward. Click the source links beside the answer to see where a claim actually came from. Google’s AI Mode page says you can type, talk, snap a photo or upload an image, so a picture of a part or a form works as an input too.

### Q. How do I turn on Google AI mode?

A.  There is nothing to turn on. Look for the AI Mode button beside or inside the Google search box, or go straight to google.com/ai. On a phone it also appears in the Google app. If you cannot find it at all, the usual reasons are that you are signed out, or you are in a country or language where it has not rolled out. It is not a paid feature and there is no waiting list.

### Q. How much does Google AI mode cost?

A.  Nothing. There is no subscription and no per-search charge. Google’s May 19, 2026 announcement expanding Personal Intelligence in AI Mode to nearly 200 countries and 98 languages used the phrase “no subscription required.” What can cost money is advertising inside the surface: Google described ad formats being tested in AI Mode at Google Marketing Live on May 20, 2026. Those carry a Sponsored label and sit apart from the answer itself.

### Q. How do I activate AI Mode in Google Search?

A.  The most direct route is google.com/ai, which drops you straight in. Otherwise use the AI Mode button on the search results page or in the Google app. Google’s own AI Mode landing page offers a “Try it now” link that simply carries a URL parameter opening the same thing. If the button never appears, sign in to a Google account and confirm your region and language are supported.

### Q. How do I force Google to use AI Mode?

A.  Go into AI Mode deliberately rather than hoping an ordinary search produces an AI answer. Google does not publish a list of triggering keywords, so no phrasing guarantees one on a normal results page — its documentation says AI answers appear only when its systems judge them additive to classic Search, and often do not trigger at all. Starting from the AI Mode entry point is the only reliable method.

### Q. Can I get rid of the AI feature on Google?

A.  Not permanently, and not from a setting. You can avoid it search by search with the Web filter, or by adding &udm=14 to the search URL, and you can make that automatic by adding a custom search engine in your browser. As of August 22, 2026 there is no toggle inside a Google account that removes AI answers or hides the AI Mode button. Filters and browser tools are the available options.

### Q. How do I change my Google Search back to normal?

A.  Click “Web” in the filter row under the search box and the page redraws as plain text links with no AI summary. That lasts one search. To keep it, set a custom search engine in your browser pointing at https://www.google.com/search?q=%s&udm=14 and make it the default. The Web filter is an official Google feature, announced by Search Liaison Danny Sullivan on May 15, 2024.

### Q. How can I disable unwanted Google AI features?

A.  Your options are filters and browser tools rather than switches. The Web filter, or the equivalent &udm=14 parameter, strips AI answers from a results page, and browser extensions can apply it to every search automatically. Anything you personally opted into through Search Labs can be switched back off in Labs. What is not available is an account-level setting that removes AI answers from Google Search everywhere.

### Q. Why is Google pushing AI?

A.  Usage and revenue both point that direction. Sundar Pichai told investors on July 22, 2026 that AI Mode had passed 1 billion monthly active users since expanding globally the previous October, and Google began testing ad formats inside AI Mode in 2026. Google’s stated position is that AI answers appear only where they add something over classic results. Read the push as a product bet with an advertising business attached to it.

## What AI Says About Your Business, and How to Fix It When It’s Wrong
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/what-ai-says-about-your-business-and-how-to-fix-it

Imagine it’s a Tuesday night in Des Peres and you’re half watching a ballgame. On a whim you open an AI assistant on your phone and type your own business name. You’re curious, not worried. Thirty seconds later you’re worried.

It has your Saturday hours off by an hour. It says you cover a chunk of the county you stopped serving two years ago, and it has never heard of the service that now pays your rent. A friend in Overland runs the same test and gets a phone number that rang at her old suite. An owner in Granite City gets something stranger: a clean, confident, beautifully formatted answer about her competitor, and no mention of her at all.

None of that is a bug you can call someone about. It’s an answer assembled from sources, and the sources are fixable. Here’s the check, where the bad data actually lives, and the repair order that keeps you from wasting three weeks.

### How to correct incorrect AI information?

You can’t edit an AI answer. You correct the sources it was assembled from — your Google Business Profile, your Apple and Bing listings, your own website, and the directory records that repeat your details — and then wait for the assistants to read them again. There is no support line for “the AI said something wrong about my business.”

Google does have a feedback path, and it’s worth using, but be clear about what it is. Google’s Search help says that at the bottom of each AI Overview there’s a thumbs up and thumbs down; clicking thumbs down leads to Report a problem, where you pick a category and add detail. That’s feedback for improving the feature, not a ticket that gets your hours changed. Google states plainly on the same page that AI Overviews “can and will make mistakes.”

ChatGPT has no business-facts correction channel at all. OpenAI’s privacy portal accepts a “Remove my personal data from ChatGPT responses” request, and its help documentation is explicit that this covers personal information about an individual that is inaccurate, excessive, irrelevant, or no longer appropriate. It requires government-issued ID and is assessed case by case. It is not a form for “my shop closes at 6, not 5.”

So the work is upstream. Everything below is about finding which upstream source is lying and fixing that one.

### How do you check what AI says about your business?

You ask the assistants directly, in writing, and you log what comes back. Budget 15 minutes: eight fixed prompts, run in three places, recorded on one page. The point is not to feel bad about the answers. It is to produce a list of specific wrong facts, each traced to the source that most likely fed it.

Open a blank page, split it into three columns — what it said, what’s true, where that probably came from — and run these eight prompts in at least three places: ChatGPT, Google (both the AI Overview and AI Mode), and Microsoft Copilot. Same prompts every time, so next quarter’s run is comparable.

Substitute your own details for the brackets:

What is [business name] in [your town], Missouri? — you’re checking whether it knows you exist and what it thinks you do.

What are [business name]’s hours? — the most damaging thing on this list to get wrong, because it costs you customers who never call.

What’s the phone number and address for [business name]? — watch for an old suite number, an old area code, or a tracking number you retired.

Does [business name] do [your highest-margin service]? — assistants routinely describe you by the service you led with five years ago.

What areas does [business name] serve? — especially important across the river, where an assistant will happily put a Missouri-only operator in Illinois or the reverse.

Who are the best [your trade] near [your town]? — the hard one. You’re not checking your facts here. You’re checking whether you are named at all.

Is [business name] still open? — this catches ghost records, old locations, and a stray “permanently closed” flag.

What do people say about [business name]? — this shows which reviews the model is weighting, which is usually not the ones you would pick.

Two rules make the exercise worth the quarter hour. First, screenshot everything, with the date and the exact prompt visible. You’ll want the before-and-after in 90 days, and you’ll want proof if a wrong answer ever costs you something. Second, write down every source the assistant cites. Those citations are the map. When an assistant links a 2019 chamber page carrying your old phone number, you’ve just found the thing to fix, and you found it in about forty seconds.

Before you compare anything, spend ten minutes writing your one-page source of truth: legal name, the public-facing name exactly as it appears on your sign, street address formatted the way it appears on your Business Profile, one phone number, hours including holidays, the actual list of services you sell today, and the towns you actually drive to. Everything downstream gets copied from that page. Skip it and you’ll publish three slightly different versions of yourself, which is the exact problem you’re trying to solve.

### Why does AI give incorrect information?

Because the answer is assembled, not looked up. An assistant pulls fragments from a search index, from structured listings, and from patterns it absorbed in training, then writes smooth prose over the top. If your hours are stale in one place and correct in another, nothing in that process knows which is current. It picks. The fluency of the sentence tells you nothing about the accuracy of the fact.

The failure rate is measurable. The European Broadcasting Union and the BBC published the largest study of its kind on 22 October 2025: 22 public service media organizations across 18 countries, working in 14 languages, assessed more than 3,000 answers from ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and Perplexity. 45% of answers had at least one significant issue. Sourcing was the worst category at 31%, and accuracy problems affected 20%. Gemini fared worst on sourcing, with significant issues in 76% of its responses.

That study looked at news, not at whether a heating company in Festus is open on Sunday. Nobody has published equivalent research on local business facts, so don’t treat 45% as your number. Treat it as evidence that the failure mode is real and systemic rather than a fluke you happened to hit.

### Where do the wrong answers actually come from?

Six sources cause most of it, and they fail in different ways.

A stale Google Business Profile. This is the loudest source, and the one most owners have not touched since the year they claimed it. If your services list, hours, or categories are two years old, an assistant reading Google’s data is reading a two-year-old business. The mechanics of getting that profile complete are covered properly in our guide to optimizing your Google Business Profile — there’s no reason to repeat it here. What matters for this audit is one specific screen.

Edits Google made for you. Google’s own documentation says it gathers business information from sources including user reports and licensed content, and that if sources report your info is incorrect or outdated, it may update your profile. In the profile editor, blue text means Google changed that field, not you. Most owners have never looked. Go look. A Google update you never noticed is a wrong answer with a very respectable source behind it.

Inconsistent listings across directories. You moved, or added a suite number, or switched to a cell phone, and you updated four places out of eleven. Every stale record is a vote for the old version. Assistants don’t audit, they aggregate, and the version that appears most often tends to win.

Old citations nobody maintains. A 2018 press release. A chamber directory PDF. An event sponsor page from a 5K. A supplier’s dealer locator built from a spreadsheet in 2016. These sit quietly for years, get crawled, and hand a model an address you left a decade ago.

Closed-location records nobody removed. The nastiest one. You moved from one strip center to another and the old record stayed live. Now there are two of you, one stranded at an address where a nail salon operates, and assistants will merge, average, or simply pick between them. Same problem when a business changed hands and the previous owner’s profile was never closed out.

Review content. Assistants summarize what reviewers wrote, and reviewers write about the visit they had, not the business you run now. A cluster of 2022 reviews complaining about a policy you scrapped in 2023 will still shape the paragraph an assistant writes about you.

Wildly off-topic — something is in your basement. Pest control near you.

### What can you get corrected, and how long does each fix take?

Be honest with yourself about which of these are levers and which are walls. Roughly, in order of how much control you actually have:

Your own website — total control, minutes. The one source you fully own. Put your name, address, phone, hours, service list, and service-area towns in plain readable text on a page, not baked into an image and not trapped behind a script. This is the cheapest fix on the list and the one people skip.

Your Google Business Profile — strong control, 10 minutes to 30 days. Sign in to the Google Account linked to the profile, open Edit profile, change the field, save. Google’s documentation is specific: edits usually take up to 10 minutes to review, but sometimes up to 30 days, and each edit shows as accepted, pending, or not approved. If Google can’t confirm accuracy it may decline the change, and rejected business information edits can be appealed. Changing your business name after verification may force you to verify again — plan around that, don’t discover it on a Friday.

A profile you don’t own — partial control, unpredictable. For the ghost record at your old address, or a duplicate, Google Maps offers Suggest an edit. Under Place closed or not here you can mark a place temporarily closed, permanently closed, doesn’t exist here, duplicate of another place, or moved to a new location. Google reviews these; it does not promise to act on them, and its documentation warns that edits which would significantly change a business may be rejected.

Apple — free, and it changed names this year. Apple announced Apple Business on 24 March 2026 and launched it on 14 April 2026 as a free service in the US and 200-plus countries and regions. It replaced Apple Business Connect, Apple Business Essentials, and Apple Business Manager, and Apple says existing Business Connect data — claimed locations, place card information, photos, account details — migrated automatically. If you claimed your place card under the old name, your account moved with it. This is the record behind Apple Maps, Siri, Spotlight, and Safari, which is a large share of the phones in this metro.

Bing — free, and it feeds Copilot. Microsoft’s support documentation points business owners to Bing Places for Business to claim or update the listing that appears in Bing Maps results. Since Copilot is grounded in Microsoft’s index, this is not an optional afterthought for anyone who cares what Copilot says about them.

Directory and industry listings — varies wildly. Some let you edit in five minutes. Some make you prove ownership. Some belong to a trade association that updates once a year. Handle the ones where you already appear first; chasing new ones is a different project.

Old news articles, PDFs, and defunct pages — effectively unfixable. You can email a webmaster and sometimes it works. Often the site is abandoned and nobody is home. Accept that, and spend the energy making the correct sources louder and more numerous instead.

Reviews — you can respond, not rewrite. You cannot delete a review for being outdated or unfair. You can reply, and a reply saying the policy changed in 2023 is itself text that gets read.

The AI answer itself — no correction channel, and no published timeline. This is the honest gap. Nobody publishes how quickly a corrected Business Profile shows up in a given assistant’s answer, and the mechanism differs by product: some answers are retrieved live at query time, some lean on cached data, some on training. Anyone who tells you it takes exactly two weeks is guessing. Re-run your check at 30 days and again at 90, log what changed, and build your own evidence.

### Fix things in this order, because the wrong order wastes weeks

Sequence matters more than speed here. Work down this list:

Write the source-of-truth page first. Ten minutes. Everything else copies from it. Fix listings before this exists and you will hand three platforms three slightly different versions of your address.

Fix your own website. You control it, it’s instant, and it’s the page other platforms and crawlers check you against.

Kill the ghosts before you polish the good record. Old locations, duplicates, a previous owner’s profile. Doing this after you optimize the real profile is how people spend a month improving a listing that keeps getting confused with a dead one.

Then your Google Business Profile. Hours, categories, services, service area, and the description — and clear any Google-made updates showing in blue.

Then Apple and Bing. Two accounts, both free, and between them they cover iPhone answers and Copilot answers. Most owners have done neither.

Then the directories where you already exist. Work from the citation list your 15-minute check produced. You already know which ones an assistant is actually reading.

Then the stragglers. Old chamber pages, supplier locators, sponsor listings. Email them. Expect a mixed response and don’t let it stall the rest.

Then reviews. Reply to the ones describing something you have since changed, and say what changed and when.

Re-run the identical check at 30 days and 90 days. Same eight prompts, same three assistants. Keep the screenshots together.

The wasted-weeks failure is almost always the same one: fixing the visible thing first. The Business Profile is visible and satisfying to polish, so people start there, while an eight-year-old duplicate at a dead address quietly keeps voting against them. Ghosts first. Then polish.

If this feels like it needs a working session rather than an article, that’s fair — it’s the sort of thing the AI workshops are built around, with your own business on the screen. And if the question you keep circling is not what the assistants say about you but how they choose whom to name at all, that mechanism is its own subject, covered in how AI decides which local businesses to name. For the wider picture of what AI is and isn’t good for in a small local operation, start with AI for St. Louis.

### What this looks like from the owner’s side of the counter

For most local service operators the fixed cost is the truck and the tech, and the unit that decides your month is a booked day. That’s why a wrong hours field is a different animal from a wrong description. A wrong description costs you part of one conversation. A Saturday marked closed when you’re open costs the whole day’s inbound calls, and here’s the part that stings: there is no missed-call log for the customer who never dialed. The phone simply doesn’t ring, the day looks slow, and you blame the weather.

The thing operators actually complain about to each other is paying for the same job twice — once to a lead platform, and again in the drive time when the address turned out to be wrong. The ones who run this tight keep a single written source of truth and update every platform from it on one afternoon, usually in January when the phone is quiet. Being listed accurately in more than one place is the unglamorous version of that habit. If you want your record on St Louis Near Me Directory to match the rest, you can add or update your listing.

Ran the check and didn’t like what you saw? Bring the screenshots to the AI workshops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then block out one afternoon to fix the sources in the order above — ghosts first.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Can I trust Google AI mode?

A.  Treat it as a fast draft, not a record. Google’s own Search help says AI responses may include mistakes, and states that AI Overviews can and will make mistakes. For anything checkable about your own business, verify against your Business Profile and your website before acting on it. The practical risk isn’t that it insults you. It’s that it is confidently wrong about your hours.

### Q. Can AI Search be trusted?

A.  For summarizing low-stakes material, mostly. For checkable facts, verify. The European Broadcasting Union and the BBC published a study on 22 October 2025 covering more than 3,000 answers from ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and Perplexity: 45% had at least one significant issue and 31% had serious sourcing problems. That research examined news coverage, not local business listings, but the underlying failure is the same.

### Q. Is Google AI as good as ChatGPT?

A.  There is no reliable head-to-head test on local business facts, so treat any ranking you read as marketing until proven otherwise. In the European Broadcasting Union and BBC study published 22 October 2025, all four assistants tested showed significant issues, with Gemini worst on sourcing at 76%. The useful answer for an owner is to check all of them about yourself, because they draw on different sources.

### Q. Why does AI give incorrect information?

A.  Because the answer is assembled rather than looked up. The assistant pulls fragments from an index, from structured listings, and from training data, then writes fluent prose over the top. When your hours are stale in one place and correct in another, nothing in that process knows which is current, so it picks. Smooth wording is not evidence of an accurate fact.

### Q. What should I do if an AI gives me a wrong answer?

A.  Screenshot it with the date and the exact prompt visible, and note every source it cited. Then go fix those sources instead of arguing with the assistant. In Google, thumbs down on an AI Overview opens Report a problem, which is product feedback rather than a correction ticket. Re-run the identical prompt at 30 and 90 days and keep the before and after together.

### Q. Who is responsible if AI makes a mistake?

A.  For a third-party assistant there is no settled general answer, and no company owes you a correction. For a chatbot on your own website the picture is clearer: in Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149, decided 14 February 2024, a British Columbia tribunal held the airline liable for wrong information its own chatbot gave a customer. That is a Canadian tribunal rather than US law, but it is worth knowing before you add a bot to your site.

### Q. How to correct incorrect information on Google?

A.  It depends who owns it. Your own Business Profile: sign in and edit it directly. A record you don’t own, such as an old location or a duplicate: use Suggest an edit in Google Maps, including Place closed or not here for a permanently closed record. Something on a third-party website that Google merely indexes: contact that website, because Google will not rewrite someone else’s page for you.

### Q. How to correct business information on Google?

A.  Sign in to the Google Account linked to your profile, go to your Business Profile, select Edit profile, change the field, and save. Google says edits usually take up to 10 minutes to review but sometimes up to 30 days, and each shows as accepted, pending, or not approved. Rejected business information edits can be appealed. Changing a verified business name may require verifying again.

### Q. Can I turn off AI on Google?

A.  Not really. Google’s Search help states that AI Overviews are a core Search feature, like knowledge panels, and that features cannot be turned off. You can select the Web filter after running a search, which displays only text-based links without AI Overviews. There is a separate Labs toggle for experimental AI in Search features, which is a different setting and does not remove AI Overviews. For what the newer conversational surface is and how it behaves, see Google AI Mode explained for local business.

### Q. How much does it cost to amend your business name?

A.  Two separate bills. Updating the name on Google, Apple, Bing, and directory listings costs nothing. Changing the registered name does: Missouri charges $25 to file an Amendment of Articles of Organization for an LLC and $7 to register a fictitious name, while Illinois charges $50 for LLC Articles of Amendment, form LLC 5.25, with expedited service extra. Confirm the current fee schedule before filing.

## Can I Use ChatGPT for My Business? What’s Safe to Paste and What Isn’t
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/can-i-use-chatgpt-for-my-business

Imagine it’s a Wednesday afternoon and you’re parked outside a job in Brentwood with forty minutes before your next call. A proposal is due by five. You open the chat app on your phone and paste in the customer’s name, their address, the scope you sketched on the back of an invoice, and the price you landed on. Twenty seconds later you have a clean, professional document. It reads better than anything you have sent this year.

Maybe you’ve done a version of that. Maybe your office manager in Hazelwood has, or your bookkeeper who works from home in Collinsville and has been quietly running your collections letters through the same free tool since spring. Nobody did anything reckless. Everybody was busy.

And somewhere around the third or fourth time, the question shows up: was that okay? That is the question most owners ask third, after “does it work” and “what does it cost.” It should be first, and the good news is that it has an answer. Not a lawyer’s answer. A practical one, made of published policies you can read yourself and four settings screens you can fix in ten minutes.

### What happens if I put confidential information into ChatGPT?

Nothing visible happens, and that is exactly the problem. On a free or personal paid account, the text is stored in your chat history, and unless you have turned training off, OpenAI states it may use that content to improve its models. It is not published, and no stranger can search it. But you have handed a third party information you may have promised someone else you would keep.

So the real damage is almost never the dramatic version people picture. Your customer list does not pop out of the machine in front of a competitor. The damage is quieter and more ordinary: you broke a term in a contract you signed, or you moved regulated records to a vendor you have no agreement with, or you now cannot tell a client what happened to their file because you have no record of what went where.

It also is not fully undoable. OpenAI’s own help documentation, updated on August 18, 2026, says a deleted chat is scheduled for permanent deletion from its systems within 30 days, unless it has already been de-identified and disassociated from your account, or unless the company must retain it for security or legal obligations. Read that carefully. Deleting the conversation cleans up your account. It does not reach back into anything already used for training.

None of which means put the phone down. Millions of businesses use these tools daily without incident, and our broader piece on how local businesses can actually use AI covers what they are good for. This one covers where the line sits.

### Which tier decides who is allowed to train on what you type?

Consumer tiers and business tiers are two different contracts, not two price points. On consumer tiers, your content may be used to train models unless you opt out. On business tiers, the vendor agrees up front not to train on it at all. Every major provider draws the line in the same place, and each publishes it. Here is what all four say right now.

### OpenAI (ChatGPT, Codex)

OpenAI’s help center article on how your data is used to improve model performance, updated August 18, 2026, splits its products in two. For services for individuals such as ChatGPT and Codex: we may use your content to train our models, with an opt-out. For services for businesses: by default, we do not train on any inputs or outputs from our products for business users, including ChatGPT Business, ChatGPT Enterprise, and the API. That is the whole distinction, stated by the vendor, in one page.

### Anthropic (Claude)

Anthropic’s consumer article, dated March 16, 2026, says it will use your chats to improve its models if you choose to allow it in Privacy Settings, if a conversation is flagged for safety review, or if you opt in to a program such as its Trusted Tester Program. Incognito chats are excluded even when Model Improvement is switched on. For commercial products the company’s published position is the opposite default: by design it will not use inputs or outputs from Claude for Work or the Anthropic API to train its models.

One detail owners miss: Anthropic states that pressing the thumbs up or thumbs down button stores the entire related conversation in its back end for up to five years. That click is not a small gesture.

### Google (Gemini)

Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub is the bluntest of the four. Keep Activity is on by default for users 18 and over, human reviewers read some conversations, and Google tells you in plain words not to enter data that is confidential or that you would not want a reviewer to see. With Keep Activity on, activity older than 18 months is auto-deleted by default and you can change that to 3 months, 36 months, or never. With Keep Activity off, conversations are still held for up to 72 hours so Google can serve the request and process feedback.

### Microsoft (Copilot)

Microsoft splits on account type rather than plan name. Signed in with a personal Microsoft account, conversation history is retained 18 months by default and your conversations may be used for model training unless you opt out. Signed in with a work or school account, Microsoft Learn’s enterprise data protection page, last updated August 18, 2026, states that the prompts, responses, and data accessed through Microsoft Graph are not used to train foundation models. Same product name on the icon. Different contract underneath.

Notice what is missing from all four: the personal paid upgrade. Paying for the consumer plan buys you a better model and more capacity. It does not change the data terms by one line. What changes the terms is a workspace or business account with business terms attached to it. If the reason you never moved is that nobody explained that difference, you are the reason this article exists.

### What is actually safe to paste, which is more than most owners assume

Almost everything you do in a week is safe to paste. Your own marketing copy, your public pricing, your website text, a job posting with no names in it, a generic warranty letter, your notes turned into a checklist, a rewrite of something you already published, an error message off a piece of software. If you would be comfortable seeing it in your own newsletter, it is fine.

The trick that frees up most of the rest is redaction, and it takes fifteen seconds. The model does not need the customer’s name to write the collections letter, or the address to describe the scope. Swap in Customer A, 1980s ranch, unit is 14 years old, and you get the same output with none of the exposure. Paste the shape of the problem, not the identity attached to it.

### What should never go into a consumer chatbot?

Six categories stay off the table on a consumer tier, whether or not you turned training off. Each one carries an obligation that lives with you rather than with the vendor.

Customer personal data. Names paired with addresses, phone numbers, account numbers, or anything else identifying. A CRM export, a route list, a spreadsheet of past jobs.

Employee records. Social Security numbers, I-9s, W-4s, background check results, medical leave notes, disciplinary write-ups, and performance reviews with a real name on them.

Anything under a confidentiality obligation. If you signed an NDA, if a client contract says you will keep their material confidential, or if you are a subcontractor bound by the general contractor’s terms, the obligation follows the document into the chat box.

Health information. Patient details, treatment notes, injury reports, insurance claim files. This is the category with the sharpest legal edge and the one people paste most casually.

Payment details. Card numbers, bank account and routing numbers, full merchant statements, a screenshot of a processor dashboard with account data visible.

Unreleased contracts and bids. The bid you have not submitted, the letter of intent, the lease under negotiation, the pricing you are about to hand a general contractor. Confidential today, public next month, and the gap is exactly when it matters.

If you want the short version to tape to a wall: no names, no numbers that identify a person, no health, no money credentials, nothing somebody else made you promise to protect.

Unrelated, and we know it — if that panel is humming, call an electrician.

### If you handle health records, financial files, or client matters, convenience does not move the obligation

The obligation belongs to you, not to the software. A dental office, a home health agency, a chiropractor, a tax preparer, a title company, a lawyer — each of those is already under rules that say what a third party has to sign before it touches the file. A chat box being fast has no effect on any of that. This is not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for asking your own counsel or compliance person. It is a flag that the question exists and that it is yours.

The concrete version, on health information, is a Business Associate Agreement. OpenAI publishes a list of which of its products are HIPAA eligible with a BAA, updated August 18, 2026: ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Enterprise with Regulated Workspace, ChatGPT FedRAMP, ChatGPT for Clinicians, API with Modified Retention, and API FedRAMP with Modified Retention. Look at what is not on that list. ChatGPT Free, Plus, and Pro are not on it. Neither is ChatGPT Business, the self-serve team plan. If you handle protected health information, the plan you almost certainly signed up for is not one of the eligible ones.

Microsoft states its own position in a footnote on the enterprise data protection page updated August 18, 2026: Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Chat support HIPAA compliance for properly configured implementations, and HIPAA compliance does not apply to web search queries, because those queries are not covered by the Data Protection Addendum and BAA. So even inside a compliant deployment, one part of the product sits outside the agreement.

For lawyers on either side of the river, the confidentiality duty is written into the professional conduct rules directly. Missouri Rule 4-1.6 requires a lawyer to make reasonable efforts to prevent inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of, or unauthorized access to, information relating to the representation of a client. Illinois Rule 1.6 covers the same ground for Illinois lawyers. Neither rule mentions AI, and neither has to. Reasonable efforts is a standard that adapts to whatever tool you just adopted.

The practical takeaway is short. Before the tool touches a regulated record, somebody checks whether a signed agreement covers it. If the answer is no, the record does not go in. That is an afternoon of work once, not every week.

### Somebody already pasted something they shouldn’t have. What now?

Start by not panicking and not deleting. The first move is a written record of what actually happened, because every decision after this depends on it. Then work through six steps in order.

Write down what went in. What text or file, roughly when, from which account, and whose account it was. Personal login or company workspace matters enormously for what comes next.

Turn training off on that account now. It is forward-looking only — OpenAI states that once you opt out, new conversations will not be used to train its models — but it stops the bleeding while you sort out the rest.

Delete the conversation, knowing what deletion does. It removes the chat from the account and schedules it for permanent deletion within 30 days, subject to the de-identification and legal-retention exceptions the vendor publishes. It does not unwind training that already happened.

Decide whether it is reportable, and get help deciding. This is the step with an actual legal answer, and it is not one to settle from a search result. Call your attorney or your cyber liability carrier. Most policies want notice early, and calling does not commit you to filing anything.

Check your client contracts before you check the statute. If a customer agreement requires notice of a disclosure, that clock is usually shorter than anything the state imposes, and it is the one people forget.

Tell the person what the line is. They were trying to get work out the door. If nobody had told them where the boundary was, that is a management gap, not a discipline problem.

On that last point: this happens more than owners think, and it usually happens without anybody meaning to hide it. Our companion piece on staff already using AI without the owner knowing covers why, and how to write the one-page policy that prevents the repeat.

### Missouri and Illinois do not handle the aftermath the same way

If a disclosure does turn out to be a reportable breach, which state your affected people live in changes the deadline and the threshold. Most St. Louis metro businesses serve both, so both apply.

Missouri, under RSMo 407.1500, requires notice to affected consumers without unreasonable delay. Notify more than one thousand consumers at once and you must also notify the Attorney General’s office and all consumer reporting agencies. Missouri also lets a business conclude notice is not required if, after an appropriate investigation, identity theft or other fraud is not reasonably likely — but that determination must be documented in writing and kept five years.

Illinois, under the Personal Information Protection Act at 815 ILCS 530, requires notice in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay. Notice to the Illinois Attorney General is triggered at more than five hundred Illinois residents, and it must be given within 45 days of discovery or when consumers are notified, whichever comes first.

Illinois sets a shorter fuse and a lower threshold; Missouri sets a documentation duty that runs five years. Whether pasting into an AI tool is a breach under either statute turns on the specific facts, and this article cannot answer that for you. Both states make the same thing obvious: start the paperwork trail on day one rather than reconstruct it in month three.

### The settings that actually matter, named, on each major tool

Four screens, ten minutes, no purchase required. These are the current control names as published by each vendor this month.

ChatGPT. Settings, then Data Controls, then switch off Improve the model for everyone. It syncs across web and mobile on the same account. Separately, Temporary Chat, reachable from the icon at the top right of the chat screen, is not used for training, does not appear in history, does not create memories, and is deleted from OpenAI’s systems after 30 days, though it may be reviewed to monitor for abuse.

Claude. Privacy Settings, then Model Improvement. Incognito chats are excluded from model improvement even if that setting is on.

Gemini. Keep Activity. Off means chats are still held about 72 hours. On means an 18-month auto-delete by default, which you can change to 3 months, 36 months, or off entirely.

Copilot. On copilot.com, the profile icon, then your profile name, then Privacy, then Training on conversation activity and Training on voice conversations. Microsoft shipped an updated Copilot app on August 18, 2026 and moved some of this documentation, so if your app does not look like the screenshots you find, go to Privacy under your profile menu and read what is there.

Two honest caveats. First, opting out is forward-looking on every one of these platforms; it governs what happens next, not what already happened. Second, none of these settings changes what tier you are on. Turning training off on a free account does not give you a business agreement, and it does not give you a BAA.

The related question owners ask is whether moving staff into a workspace lets them read everyone’s chats. Mostly no. OpenAI’s ChatGPT Business documentation, updated August 20, 2026, states that each member has their own chat history and chooses what to share, and that by default admins and owners cannot see all private member chats. Enterprise and Edu workspaces add a Compliance API for retrieval. Worth knowing before you announce the change, because it is the first thing your team will ask.

If reading four vendor policy pages is not how you want to spend a Thursday, that is fair, and it is roughly what the AI workshops for metro business owners exist to shortcut — sitting down with the actual screens instead of a slide about them.
