Here is why this landed in your office before it landed in your field crew. In a small service business the truck hours are billable and the office hours are not. Estimating, permit paperwork, warranty letters, review replies, the third follow-up on an unpaid invoice — that is real work nobody pays for, and on a two-truck operation it gets absorbed at night by whoever is left. AI ate the unbilled hour first because the unbilled hour is where the pain was.

Seasonality sharpens it. The first genuinely hot week and the first hard freeze are when the phone does not stop, and that is exactly when whoever answers it takes the shortcut. What owners in the trades complain to each other about is not the technology. It is learning something went out wrong only after the customer replied. Operators who avoid that do one unglamorous thing: a human reads anything with a customer name on it before it leaves the building.

The other half of getting found is even less glamorous. People search these trades locally, by name and by neighborhood, and a listing that is complete and current is how they land on you instead of the next result. Getting listed on St Louis Near Me Directory is the low-effort half of that.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Is it worth getting ChatGPT for business?

A.  It depends less on features than on whether your people already use it. If staff are pasting work into personal accounts, a business workspace mostly buys you a contract: OpenAI states it does not train on business workspace data by default. If you use it alone, for marketing copy and nothing sensitive, the free tier with training switched off may be enough.

### Q. Can businesses use ChatGPT for free?

A.  Yes. There is no rule against a business using the free tier, and plenty do. What you should know is that free, Plus and Pro are all services for individuals under OpenAI’s own classification, which means your content may be used to train models unless you opt out, and no Business Associate Agreement is available on them. Free is fine for work that carries no confidentiality obligation.

### Q. Is it okay to use ChatGPT for a business plan?

A.  For structure, drafting and pressure-testing assumptions, yes, and it is one of the better uses. Two cautions. Keep unreleased financials, a signed letter of intent, and any lender’s confidential terms out of it on a consumer account. And verify every number — it does not know your market, your rents, or local wage rates, and will produce a confident figure anyway.

### Q. Which AI is best for small business owners?

A.  There is no credible head-to-head answer, and anyone offering one is usually selling something. Pick on two practical grounds: the data terms you can live with, and what you already pay for. If your business runs on Microsoft 365 work accounts, Copilot already sits inside enterprise data protection. Capability gaps between the leaders shift monthly. Contracts do not.

### Q. Does ChatGPT business protect my data?

A.  OpenAI’s documentation, updated August 20, 2026, says ChatGPT Business is governed by OpenAI Business Terms and the Enterprise Privacy commitments, and that it does not train on your workspace data by default. Two limits worth knowing before you rely on it: OpenAI does not offer a Business Associate Agreement for ChatGPT Business, and data export is not available from a Business workspace.

### Q. Can companies see what you put into ChatGPT?

A.  The vendor can access content in limited circumstances such as investigating abuse, providing support, or meeting legal obligations, and reviewers may see content flagged for safety. Google puts it more bluntly for Gemini, warning users not to enter data they would not want a reviewer to see. Assume a person could read it, and paste accordingly.

### Q. What are five things I should never tell ChatGPT?

A.  Customer personal data, meaning names paired with addresses or account numbers. Employee records, including Social Security numbers and medical leave notes. Anything covered by an NDA or a client confidentiality obligation. Health information about a patient or claimant. Payment credentials such as card and bank routing numbers. A sixth belongs there too: unreleased contracts, bids and pricing.

### Q. Can my company see my ChatGPT conversations?

A.  If you are signed in to a personal account you pay for yourself, your employer has no window into it. If you are in a company workspace, OpenAI states that each member has their own chat history and that by default admins and owners cannot see all private member chats. Enterprise and Edu workspaces add a Compliance API that can retrieve conversations for compliance purposes, so treat those as reviewable.

### Q. Is ChatGPT secure for business?

A.  Security and confidentiality are different questions and get conflated constantly. Encryption is not where small businesses get hurt. The exposures that matter are contractual: whether your tier permits training on your inputs, how long conversations are retained, and whether an agreement covers regulated records. Answer those three for your tier and you have answered the real question.

### Q. Can admins see chats in ChatGPT business?

A.  Not by default. OpenAI’s ChatGPT Business documentation states that each member has their own chat history and can choose what to share, and that by default admins and owners cannot see all private member chats. That is a deliberate design choice, and it is worth telling your team when you move them onto a workspace, because assuming otherwise is the most common reason staff quietly keep using a personal account instead.

## How AI Decides Which Local Businesses to Name
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-ai-decides-which-local-businesses-to-name

Imagine it’s a Thursday night in Shrewsbury and the water heater has started making a noise you have never heard before. You don’t open a search tab and scroll. You type the whole problem into an assistant, in a full sentence, the way you’d text a friend. Twelve seconds later you have three business names, a line about each, and no list of ten.

Maybe you have been on the other side of that moment. A remodeler in Bridgeton hears from a customer who says an assistant recommended somebody else. A shop owner in Fairview Heights takes a cold call the same week promising to get her business “into ChatGPT” for a monthly fee. Nobody in either conversation can say where those three names actually came from.

That is the question worth answering. Not a checklist — the mechanism. Where an assembled answer finds business names, what makes one name survive while another gets dropped, and which parts of this are documented by the companies building these systems versus inferred from outside. Both are here, and each is labeled as what it is.

### How do you get AI to recommend your business?

You can’t buy it, and there is no submission form. An assistant names businesses it can retrieve, read and corroborate, so the practical answer is to make your business easy to find, easy to verify, and consistent everywhere it already appears. That is the entire mechanism. The rest of this explains why it works that way, which is the part that tells you what to ignore.

Google says a version of this about its own products. Its Search Central guide to optimizing for generative AI features, last updated July 10, 2026, states that its generative AI features on Google Search are rooted in its core Search ranking and quality systems, and that structured data is not required for generative AI search and there is no special schema.org markup you need to add. The companion page, AI features and your website, updated December 10, 2025, is blunter: there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and no other special optimizations necessary. To be eligible as a supporting link, a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet.

So the plumbing is documented. The selection rule is not. No provider publishes the criteria that decide your name goes into an answer and the shop two miles away does not. Any tidy ranked list of “AI ranking factors” is inference wearing a lab coat. What follows separates the two: documented gets a source and a date, inferred gets said out loud. For the wide-angle version first, the overview of what AI actually does for a St. Louis business covers the ground floor. This is the floor underneath it.

### Where does an assembled answer get its business names?

From a live search index, not from the model’s memory. When you ask for a local recommendation, the system runs searches, pulls back pages, and writes an answer out of what it just read. The business names come from those retrieved pages — profiles, directories, review sites, news coverage, and the businesses’ own websites. Nothing is recalled. It is fetched.

Google described the retrieval side publicly when it announced AI Mode on May 20, 2025: under the hood, AI Mode uses its query fan-out technique, breaking a question into subtopics and issuing a multitude of queries simultaneously on the user’s behalf. Its July 10, 2026 guide names the other half, retrieval-augmented generation, and says the grounding relies on core Search ranking systems to retrieve relevant, up-to-date web pages. Translated: one question you typed becomes a fan of searches you never saw, and your business either surfaces in some of them or it does not exist for that answer.

The other big surfaces run the same shape through different pipes. OpenAI documents three separate agents: OAI-SearchBot, used to surface websites in ChatGPT’s search features; GPTBot, used to crawl content that may be used in training its foundation models; and ChatGPT-User, used when someone asks a question and the system needs to visit a page. Those are different jobs, and blocking one is not blocking the others. A site that disallows OAI-SearchBot in robots.txt has quietly opted out of being named on that surface. That is a checkable fact about your own site, and it takes ninety seconds to look.

Microsoft’s Copilot answers are grounded in the Bing index, and Microsoft now reports on it. Bing Webmaster Tools added an AI Performance report in public preview, covered by Search Engine Land on February 10, 2026, showing how often a site is cited across Microsoft Copilot, Bing’s AI summaries and select partner integrations.

Sort the sources into buckets and it gets practical. An assembled local answer is usually built from your own website; your verified profiles, which Google’s July 10, 2026 guide says can help your products and services be visible in both AI responses and other Google Search results; directory and listing pages; review platforms; and third-party mentions such as trade association rosters, chamber pages, supplier locators and local press. None of those is the answer. The answer is stitched across them, which is the most important thing to understand here.

One boundary worth drawing: this is not the same subject as ranking in ordinary search. Getting found in blue links and the map pack is its own craft, and it lives in the near-me search guide for St. Louis. What happens here sits downstream of that, after pages are retrieved, while an answer is being written.

### Why does consistency across sources beat one perfect page?

Because the system is not reading one page. It is reading several at once and has to decide they describe the same business. Matching name, address, phone, hours and services make that decision cheap. Contradictions make it expensive, and an expensive name is an easy name to leave out of a three-name answer.

This part is informed inference, and it deserves to be said in those words: no provider has published a document saying it drops businesses whose listings disagree. What is documented is that the answer is grounded in multiple retrieved sources at once. The inference follows mechanically from that. If four sources say you close at 5 and one says 7, an assembled answer has three options — pick one and risk being wrong, hedge and go vague, or drop the detail. A recommendation without hours is a weaker recommendation, and the weaker one is what gets cut when an answer is trimmed to three names.

The failure is almost never dramatic. It is a phone number from two vans ago, still live on a listing nobody remembers creating. A suite number that changed in 2021. A business name written four ways: with LLC, without LLC, with the founder’s name in front, and with an ampersand where the profile spells out the word and. Each one alone is trivial. Together they make you a harder entity to assert, and asserting things is the entire job an assembled answer is doing.

There is a second-order version that catches good operators off guard. If a staff member drafts a services page with an assistant and nobody checks the service area against what the crew actually covers, you have published a fresh contradiction into your own source set. Worth reading separately, because most owners have no idea which parts of their own copy are AI-assisted.

### Why can nobody sell you a slot inside an AI answer?

Because the names inside an answer are not inventory. There is no product to buy, no partner program, no submission fee. Google’s Search Central documentation, last updated June 5, 2026, states it never accepts money to include or rank sites in its search results, that it costs nothing to appear in organic results, and that advertising with Google will not have any effect on a site’s presence in those results. It also says plainly that no one can guarantee a number one ranking.

Now the nuance, because getting it exactly right is what protects you from the pitch. Advertising does exist next to AI answers. Google sells placements that render alongside AI Overviews and AI Mode, labeled Sponsored. OpenAI began testing ads in ChatGPT for U.S. users on February 9, 2026, and said at the time that ads will always be clearly labeled as sponsored and separated from the organic content, and that ads do not influence the answers ChatGPT gives you.

So the honest line is narrow. You can buy an advertisement that appears near an AI answer, clearly marked as an advertisement. You cannot buy the sentence in the answer that names your business. Two different products, and the phone pitch blurs them on purpose.

Owners across the metro are being sold that blur right now. The tells repeat: a monthly fee to be added to the “AI index,” a claimed partnership with a named assistant, a guaranteed placement, a private submission portal, an offer to register your business with ChatGPT. None of those exist as described. There is no registry. Ask the caller for the provider documentation describing what they are selling, and the call usually ends there.

Nothing to do with AI — the garage pile. Get it hauled off.

### Why do plain answers get quoted and buried ones do not?

Because a passage has to still make sense once it is separated from your page. A sentence that says what you do, where you do it and roughly what it runs stands on its own. A sentence that says your experienced team handles all of that carries no facts out the door with it, so there is nothing to lift.

Part of this is documented. Google’s July 10, 2026 guide warns against commodity content, using the example of something like “7 Tips for First-Time Homebuyers,” which it describes as based on common knowledge that could originate from anyone and typically adds little unique insight for readers. It tells site owners not to recycle what others on the internet have already said, and to write from experience they actually have. That is a published position, not a theory.

The extraction part — that self-contained phrasing gets quoted more often than buried phrasing — is informed inference. It follows from the mechanism rather than any published rule. A system assembling an answer out of retrieved passages has to be able to use a passage without the page around it. Anything written as a continuation of the paragraph above it arrives incomplete.

What that looks like for a local trade, vague version against liftable version:

Vague: we proudly serve the greater St. Louis area. Liftable: we cover south St. Louis County and the city south of Interstate 44, plus St. Clair County on the Illinois side.

Vague: we are here when you need us. Liftable: we answer emergency calls until 10 p.m. seven days a week, and same-day slots are usually gone by 9 a.m.

Vague: full-service solutions. Liftable: we do camera inspection, cleaning and spot repair; we do not do full sewer lateral replacement, and we will tell you who does.

Vague: competitive pricing. Liftable: a standard service call runs a stated range, and here is what pushes a job to the top of it.

The strongest signal there is the stated no. Naming the work you refuse is unusual, specific and impossible to confuse with a competitor, which makes it the kind of sentence that survives being pulled out of context. It also does something better than visibility: it kills the calls you were going to turn down anyway.

### Which local details decide whether you get named?

Four, mostly: the area you actually serve, the hours you actually keep, the specific work you actually take, and whether an answer can tell you apart from the similarly named business across the river. Local questions turn on those four, and those four are the details most likely to be stale in the places an assistant reads.

Service area breaks hardest here, because the metro crosses a state line. A question asked in Fairview Heights and one asked in Shrewsbury are different markets even though both were phrased as “near me.” A service-area business with a Missouri address that happily takes calls in St. Clair and Madison counties has to say so in words, because nothing else will say it on your behalf. Licensing and registration requirements differ between Missouri and Illinois across a long list of trades, and if you hold both, say so plainly rather than implying it with a map graphic no crawler can read.

Hours are the cheapest fix and the most commonly wrong. Holiday hours nobody updated. A Monday closure that ended two years ago. Seasonal hours from a season that has passed. Google’s July 10, 2026 guide points local businesses specifically at Google Business Profiles as a way to be visible in AI responses as well as ordinary results, which makes stale profile hours an unusually expensive small mistake.

Scope is the third. Landscaping covers mowing, design, drainage, hardscape and tree work, and almost nobody does all five. An answer built for somebody with a standing-water problem is looking for a business that says the word drainage. If your site says landscaping, your profile category says landscaping, and neither says drainage, you are not in that answer, and no amount of general prominence fixes it.

### How does an assistant tell you apart from a business with the same name?

It looks for something only one of you has: a verified profile, a distinct address, a matching phone number, an owned domain, and a business name written the same way everywhere. When two businesses share a name and nothing separates them, an assembled answer sometimes merges them, and the merged version is usually wrong in a way that costs the better operator.

This metro produces the problem constantly. Trade names built out of the region are close to unavoidable, so unrelated businesses end up with near-identical names across two states, plus a franchise or two carrying the same brand with different owners and different service areas. Add one business that rebranded and left the old name live on eight listings, and you have a hard disambiguation problem nobody created on purpose.

Untangling it is unglamorous. Pick one exact legal or trade name and use that string everywhere, character for character. Keep one primary phone number on every source. Make sure the domain in each profile matches the domain you actually operate. If you moved, close the old listing rather than leaving it to rot, because a live stale listing is a competing claim about who you are. That is inference about how entity matching behaves, not published policy, but it costs nothing and removes ambiguity a machine cannot resolve on its own.

### What can you actually measure, and what can nobody measure?

One surface publishes numbers. Bing Webmaster Tools added an AI Performance report in public preview, reported by Search Engine Land on February 10, 2026, showing total citations, page-level citation activity, grounding queries and visibility trends across Microsoft Copilot, Bing’s AI summaries and select partner integrations. Google and OpenAI publish no equivalent for a small business owner.

Read the limits alongside the numbers. Search Engine Land noted in that same February 10, 2026 report that the metrics do not indicate ranking or prominence, do not show how a page contributed to any specific AI answer, and carry no click or traffic data. It tells you that you were cited. It does not tell you that anybody came.

Everything else on the market is sampling, and sampling is not ranking. Assistants are not deterministic: the same question asked twice can return different names, and location, phrasing, account history and time of day all move the result. A vendor showing you an “AI rank” is showing you a sample of a conversation. Sampling is a reasonable thing to do and an unreasonable thing to sell as a position. The same skepticism belongs on any AI adoption figure quoted at you on a sales call, which is why the real numbers on small business AI use are worth knowing before the phone rings.

The version that costs nothing: pick the five questions a customer would ask before calling you, put each one to three different assistants from a phone physically inside your service area, and write down every business named and every fact they got wrong about you. Repeat in thirty days. One check proves nothing; six show a pattern, and the pattern points at which source needs fixing. If you would rather work through that with other owners than alone at a kitchen table, that is what the AI workshops are for.

### What this looks like from the owner’s side of the counter

From behind the counter this is a margin question, not a technology question. A local service business lives on a handful of jobs a week, and the cost of the next lead decides whether the month works. Paid channels price that lead at whatever the auction says, and the auction only goes up. A name spoken inside an answer costs nothing per click and arrives half-sold, because the caller already heard a reason and not just a phone number. That is why owners fixate on this, and why the cold calls selling it work so well.

What separates the operators who do fine here is unglamorous. One person owns the listings. Hours change the same day they change. Nobody writes a service-area sentence the crew cannot deliver on. The complaint owners trade is drift — the number from two vans ago, the address from the old shop, the category that was right in 2019. If you want your details in one more place that gets read, add your business and keep it current yourself.

Would you rather understand this than be sold it? Browse AI workshops across the St. Louis metro on St Louis Near Me Directory, then bring the three questions customers ask you before they book — those are the sentences worth rewriting on your own site in plain, liftable language.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. How do I get my business to show up when Googled?

A.  Two different systems are in play. Ordinary results and the map pack are ranked; an AI answer is assembled from pages retrieved the moment you ask. Being indexed and complete feeds both, but the ranked side is its own craft, covered in the near-me search guide on this site. For the assembled side the requirement is simpler: be retrievable, and say the same thing about yourself everywhere.

### Q. How to get AI to mention your business?

A.  Be reachable by the agents that feed the answer. OpenAI documents OAI-SearchBot as the crawler used to surface websites in ChatGPT’s search features, so a robots.txt file blocking it removes you from that surface. Google’s documentation, updated December 10, 2025, says a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown with a snippet. Nothing gets mentioned that cannot first be fetched.

### Q. How do I get AI to suggest my business?

A.  Corroboration. A suggestion is a claim the system has to be willing to make, and it is easier to make when several independent sources agree on your name, address, phone, hours and services. One immaculate website contradicting four listings is weaker than five plain sources that match. That is informed inference, not published policy, but it follows from answers being grounded in several sources at once.

### Q. How do I track my company’s visibility across AI search platforms?

A.  Only one platform publishes it. Bing Webmaster Tools added an AI Performance report in public preview, reported by Search Engine Land on February 10, 2026, showing citations across Microsoft Copilot, Bing’s AI summaries and select partner integrations. Google and OpenAI publish no equivalent for a small business. Everything past that report is sampling: useful for catching errors, useless as a measure of position.

### Q. How do I get my company to show up on AI searches?

A.  Answer the local question before it is asked. Name the municipalities and counties you actually cover, the hours you actually keep, and the specific jobs you take and refuse. Local answers turn on those specifics. A vague coverage claim gives an assembled answer nothing to attach to your name, so the name that gets used is the one with real detail beside it.

### Q. How to win brand visibility in AI search?

A.  There is nothing to win, and that is the useful part. No auction, no slot, no scoreboard. Google’s documentation, updated June 5, 2026, states it never accepts money to include or rank sites in its search results and that no one can guarantee a number one ranking. The same logic covers an assembled answer: earned by being verifiable and consistent, and not for sale.

### Q. How can I track my brand’s visibility in AI search results?

A.  Sample it yourself, on a schedule. Ask three assistants the questions a customer would ask, from a device physically inside your service area, and log every name returned and every error about you. Repeat monthly. Answers vary between runs, so one check proves nothing and six show a pattern. Search Engine Land noted on February 10, 2026 that even Bing’s citation data does not indicate ranking or prominence.

### Q. What businesses will benefit the most from AI?

A.  Benefit and adoption are different questions, and only adoption gets measured. Census Bureau data published May 26, 2026 shows under 20% of firms with four or fewer employees reporting AI use, against 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees and 37% of firms with 250 or more. Whether the smallest firms benefit least, or are simply slower to report, that data cannot settle.

### Q. Who are the top 5 companies in AI?

A.  There is no official list, and any ranking depends on whether you count revenue, model quality, users or research output. For a local business the narrower question matters more: which assistants do your customers actually use. The systems whose behavior is documented above are built by Google, Microsoft and OpenAI, and those three are where most local answers get assembled today.

## How to Judge an AI Course Before You Pay for One
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/how-to-judge-an-ai-course-for-business-owners

Imagine it’s a Thursday night in University City and you are nine tabs deep. Somebody in a Facebook group swore by a course. The sales page has a countdown clock, a wall of logos, and a price that just fell from $1,997 to $497 for the next eleven minutes. You have a business to open in the morning. You mostly want to know one thing: is this real, or is it a webinar with a shopping cart attached?

Maybe you have already bought one. A shop owner in Arnold pays for a weekend intensive, watches four hours of it on a Sunday, and never opens the workbook. A contractor in Swansea signs up for a free ninety-minute session and gets eighty minutes of hype and ten minutes of a pitch for the thing that actually teaches you something. Neither one learned a skill. Both of them came away a little more convinced that AI is for other people.

This is a buyer’s guide with no course names in it. Not one, on purpose. What you get instead is a test — three questions that separate training which changes how you work on Monday from an expensive video, the free options that genuinely exist on both sides of the river, the red flags that should end a sales call, and a straight answer about certificates. One thing up front: the site you are reading this on runs its own AI workshops. The same test gets pointed at them, in public, further down the page.

### Is there an AI course that will help my business?

Yes, if it passes three tests. Does the training use your business as the working example instead of a generic one? Do you leave with something running rather than a page of notes? Does the person teaching it use these tools on their own work every week? Training that fails any one of those three is entertainment you paid for.

That framing matters because this market is young and almost entirely unregulated. There is no licensing board for AI instructors and no accreditation body. Nobody checks whether the person on the sales page has ever run a business with employees in it. Somebody who watched forty hours of YouTube in June can sell a course in July, and some do. The burden of judging sits with you.

One piece of context worth holding while you shop. The U.S. Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey, published May 26, 2026 and covering December 14, 2025 through May 3, 2026, found that fewer than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees reported using AI, against 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees and 37% of firms with 250 or more. You are not behind. You are normal, and anyone telling you the whole world already figured this out is selling you urgency. Our companion piece on what percent of small businesses actually use AI takes those numbers apart properly.

### Can I learn AI for free?

Yes, and you should spend a few hours doing exactly that before you pay anyone. The companies that build these tools publish their own free training, and several St. Louis-area institutions run no-cost help for business owners. Between them you can cover the basics without a credit card. Here is what is actually live as of August 2026, with the catch on each one named.

The AI companies teach their own tools, free. OpenAI runs a free self-paced site at academy.openai.com with an AI for Small Business collection, including sessions called ChatGPT 101 and ChatGPT 102. Anthropic runs a free course site at academy.claude.com whose catalog includes AI Fluency for Small Businesses, which teaches a four-part framework for handing work to a model and ends with a certificate. Microsoft publishes free learning paths on Microsoft Learn, including one titled Transform business workflows with generative AI. The catch is worth saying out loud: each company teaches its own product, and none will tell you the job you have in mind might not need AI at all. Useful, free, and self-interested. Take all three.

The Small Business Development Centers are free and local. On the Missouri side, the Missouri SBDC for the St. Louis region operates through the St. Louis Economic Development Partnership and describes its service as confidential, no-cost one-on-one business consulting plus no-cost and low-cost training events. On the Illinois side, the Illinois SBDC for the Metro East at SIUE offers confidential, no-cost advising across nine Metro East counties — Madison, St. Clair, Clinton, Calhoun, Jersey, Bond, Monroe, Washington and Randolph — and takes calls at (618) 650-2929. SCORE’s St. Louis Bi-State chapter describes its mentoring as free and its workshops as free or inexpensive. None of the three is an AI school. Each is an experienced person who will sit with you for an hour, for nothing, and tell you whether the problem you want AI to solve is really a pricing problem. That hour often beats the course.

A note on the federal bill, because the internet is getting this wrong. H.R. 5764, the AI for Main Street Act, would direct Small Business Development Centers to help small businesses evaluate AI. It passed the House on January 20, 2026 by a vote of 395 to 14, and a Senate companion, S. 3586, was introduced. It had not become law as of this writing, and the bill authorizes no additional funding to pay for the work. Several marketing blogs currently describe it as signed and funded. It is neither. If a provider tells you their program is part of a federal AI mandate, that is your first red flag and you got it for free.

The library is the quietest option and the most overlooked. St. Louis County Library states that all of its technology classes are free, that registration is required, and that it opens the first day of the month before the class date; sign up online or call 314-994-3300. The standing class list is computer basics, Word and Excel rather than AI, so AI shows up through the library’s Tech Talks program and events calendar instead. Library staff also maintain a research guide titled Artificial Intelligence (AI) 2026 Guide — Chatbots, Agents, and More, last updated August 3, 2026, which lists upcoming AI programs and points cardholders at LinkedIn Learning and Udemy. A card costs nothing.

### Does the training use your business as the example?

This is the first question because it is the one most training fails. A course built around a fictional online store teaches you a fictional online store. You run a flooring crew, or a dental practice, or a two-chair salon on Manchester, and the gap between the demo and your Tuesday is the whole problem. Ask a provider to walk one of your real tasks through the tool before you pay.

There is a practical way to run this test. Write down the single task that eats the most of your week and bores you most. Quoting. Callbacks. The same six-paragraph email you retype for every new customer. Then hand that task to the provider and watch. A good one asks three follow-up questions about how your business actually works before touching a keyboard. A weak one changes the subject to a feature list.

### Do you leave with something working, or with notes?

The clearest test of AI training is what exists at the end that did not exist at the start. A saved prompt that writes your quote follow-ups in your voice. A spreadsheet that reads your invoices. A draft of the policy page your insurer keeps asking about. If the only artifact is a slide deck and a list of tool names, you attended a presentation.

Ask the question in exactly this shape when you call: what will I have built by the time this ends? The answer tells you the format instantly. Someone running real training says something small and concrete — one automation, one working prompt, one cleaned-up listing. Someone running a lead magnet says you will have clarity, or a roadmap, or a framework. Clarity is not a deliverable. You cannot bill it, save it, or hand it to your front desk person.

Be reasonable about scale. Ninety minutes does not transform a business, and a provider who promises that is telling you about their honesty rather than their curriculum. Ninety honest minutes gets you one thing built and one habit started.

### Does the person teaching actually use the tools on their own work?

Ask directly: what did you use this for last week, in your own business, and what went wrong with it? The answer separates practitioners from resellers in about fifteen seconds. Someone who uses these tools daily has a story about a model inventing a fact, a workflow that broke, a thing they stopped doing. Someone who does not will answer in benefits and adjectives.

The failure stories are the tell. Everyone who works with these tools for real has been burned — a made-up citation, a confident wrong number, a summary that quietly dropped the one line that mattered. An instructor who has never hit that has not done enough of the work to teach it, because half of using AI well is knowing where it lies to you.

Wildly off-topic — a florist who arranges the flowers herself.

### What are the red flags in an AI course for business owners?

Five things should end the conversation: a guaranteed result, a promised revenue number, secret or proprietary prompts, a free session whose only real content is a pitch for the paid one, and any claim of official certification or government backing. Each is a signal about the seller rather than about AI, which is why they work as filters even if you know nothing about the subject.

Guaranteed results and revenue numbers. Nobody can guarantee what a tool does inside your business, because the outcome depends on your margins, your staff, your customers and your follow-through. A provider who says you will add a specific dollar figure, or double anything, has made a promise with no mechanism behind it. Note that this is separate from a refund policy. A clear refund policy is a good sign. A guaranteed outcome is a bad one.

Secret prompts. The proprietary prompt vault is the most durable piece of nonsense in this market. Prompts are plain English sentences. They copy in one keystroke, they drift out of date when the model changes, and good ones get posted publicly within days. A prompt written for a generic business is also worth less to you than four clumsy sentences you wrote about your own job, because yours carries the context. Anyone selling secrecy is selling a scarcity that does not exist.

The upsell-only format. You can spot this before you register. Look at the run time and the agenda. If a free session runs ninety minutes with no published agenda and the registration page mentions a limited-time offer at the end, the session is the sales call. That is not disqualifying by itself — every business sells something — but know which meeting you are in before you give up an evening.

Certification and mandate language. There is no government-recognized certification for AI use in a small business, and no federal program that has appointed anyone to train you. Watch for phrasing that hints otherwise: officially certified, approved provider, required under the new AI rules. The closest real thing is H.R. 5764, a bill that has passed one chamber of Congress, carries no funding, and is not law.

One more, quieter than the rest. If the class exists so that you end up on a monthly plan for the provider’s own software, ask what you are expected to be paying six months later, and to whom.

### Are AI certificates worth anything if you are not job hunting?

To a business owner, an AI certificate is a receipt for finishing a course. It is not a license, and it is not a credential anyone will check. No board issues it, no state recognizes it, and your customers will never ask. It has real value in exactly two places: as proof to yourself that you finished, and as a line on a staff member’s record if they want it for their own career.

That second use is worth more than it sounds. A certificate an employee can post on LinkedIn is a small piece of compensation that costs you nothing, and it makes training read as an investment in them rather than an assignment. Several of the free first-party courses issue one, which is a fine reason to prefer a course that offers it and a poor reason to pay hundreds of dollars for one.

The job-market questions people search alongside this one — which certificate is most valuable, which credentials lead to a six-figure salary — belong to a different reader with a different problem. If you own the business, nobody is hiring you. You are trying to get four hours a week back. Judge the training on whether it does that, and treat the certificate as packaging.

So a buyer’s guide published here has a thumb on the scale, and pretending otherwise would be worse than the conflict itself. Read the rest of this section as the receipt.

Start with the part people mistake for a defense. Our sessions are free, and free is not the same as disinterested. This site sells directory listings, and a workshop about how AI answers decide which local businesses to name sits next door to a product we sell. Do that to us too.

### What this looks like from behind the counter

An hour is not free for an owner-operator, and course marketing never prices that in. A florist’s year is largely decided by two weeks — Valentine’s Day and Mother’s Day — and nobody in that shop is learning anything new in the first half of February. An HVAC company earns its margin in July. A tax preparer lives from January to April and then vanishes. Training inside the season does not happen, and training in the dead month competes with the only stretch of year you get for billing, the truck, and your family. The hour has a price you could write down, which is why walking out with something working is the only way it pays for itself. It is also why the dull version of this work still matters: people search by trade and by town, and being listed and complete is how that search reaches you.

### What should I do in the next 30 days?

Spend nothing for three weeks, then decide. The sequence below takes a few hours total and lets you judge any paid course on evidence rather than on a sales page. Most owners who work through it find they need one narrow piece of help rather than a general AI education.

Week one: name the task. One task, written on paper. The thing that eats your week and bores you. This sentence is the single most valuable asset you bring to any provider, free or paid, because it converts an open-ended subject into a job with an edge around it.

Week one: run one free first-party course. Ninety minutes at academy.openai.com, academy.claude.com or Microsoft Learn, with your named task open in another window. Do not take notes. Try to do the task. You will learn more from failing at it once than from finishing three courses.

Week two: ask your staff what they already use. This is uncomfortable and it is the highest-value hour in the list. People are already pasting work into these tools without telling anyone, which brings real exposure with it; our piece on the AI your staff is already using covers what that actually risks. You cannot train a team whose current habits you have never asked about.

Week two: book the no-cost SBDC hour. Missouri side or Illinois side, whichever your address puts you in. Bring the task sentence. Ask them straight whether AI is the right lever for it, and be prepared to hear no.

Week three: only now consider paying. Put the three questions to the provider in writing, by email, so you have the answers in a form you can reread. Anyone who will not answer in writing has answered.

Week four: measure one thing, and make it hours. Not revenue — revenue moves for a dozen reasons and you will never untangle which one was the course. Hours saved on the task you named is checkable, and if it is zero after a month the training failed however good the class felt. For the wider view, the broad overview of AI for St. Louis businesses is the place to start.

Would you rather test this in a room than on a sales page? See the AI workshops for local business owners on St Louis Near Me Directory, and put your one named task in the box that asks what you want to learn — that is the field that decides whether the hour is about your business or about nobody’s.

### Frequently asked questions

### Q. Can I learn AI for free?

A.  Yes. OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft all publish free self-paced training on their own sites, and each one teaches its own product. Locally, the Missouri SBDC through the St. Louis Economic Development Partnership and the Illinois SBDC for the Metro East at SIUE both provide no-cost business advising, and St. Louis County Library technology classes are free with registration.

### Q. What is the best AI training for beginners?

A.  The best beginner training is whichever one makes you do a real task from your own week inside the first thirty minutes. Watching is not learning here. A free ninety-minute course you apply to your quoting or your callbacks beats a paid ten-hour course you finish and never reopen.

### Q. How can I learn AI on my own?

A.  Pick one repetitive task, open a mainstream assistant, and spend two weeks doing that task with it every day. Keep what works in a plain text file. This teaches more than any curriculum, because you learn where the tool fails on your specific work, which no course can predict for you.

### Q. What is the best way to learn AI for business?

A.  Start from a job, not from the technology. Name the task that eats your week, then find the shortest path to doing that one task with a tool. Owners who start from a task get something useful in a few hours. Owners who start from a course usually collect vocabulary and stop.

### Q. Which AI is best for small business owners?

A.  There is no single best one, and the mainstream general-purpose assistants are close enough in ability that the choice matters far less than what you feed them. The practical answer is to use whichever one is already built into software you pay for, so you are not adding a subscription to learn a habit.

### Q. Which AI certificate is most valuable?

A.  For a business owner, none of them are worth paying for. No board issues them, no state recognizes them, and no customer will ever ask. If you want one for a staff member, several of the free first-party courses hand out a certificate at the end, which costs you nothing but the time.

### Q. Can you get a job in AI with a certificate?

A.  A certificate alone rarely gets anyone hired, because employers hire for demonstrated work. It can help a resume get read alongside real projects. That is a job-seeker question, and it has little to do with whether a course is worth an owner’s money and an evening away from the business.

### Q. What certifications make 100k a year?

A.  No certification causes a salary. Pay follows the work someone can prove they do, the field they do it in, and where they live. Any course marketing a specific income figure to you is making a promise it has no way to keep, which is exactly the red flag to walk away from.

### Q. What is the 30% rule in AI?

A.  There is no standard 30% rule. The phrase floats around blogs with at least three meanings: that roughly a third of tasks in a job can be automated, that AI-written text should stay under 30% of a school assignment, and that 30% of an AI budget belongs to data cleanup. No standards body defines any of them.

### Q. Does AI training actually pay?

A.  It pays when you can point at a task that takes less time than it did a month ago. Measure hours on one named job, not revenue, because revenue moves for reasons you will never trace back to a class. If the hours have not moved after four weeks, the training did not work for you.

## The AI Rules People Quote, and Whether Any of Them Hold Up
Source: https://stlouismissourinearme.com/blog/the-ai-rules-people-quote-and-whether-they-hold

Imagine it’s a Tuesday morning, the coffee is doing its work, and you’re half-scrolling LinkedIn before the first call of the day. A post slides by with fourteen hundred reactions. It says only 10% of AI success is the algorithm and 70% is your people, and it calls this the 10/20/70 rule. Two posts later somebody explains the 30% rule. Somebody else lays out the four stages of AI adoption. A commenter drops the three laws of AI underneath, and forty people nod along.

By the time you set the phone down you’ve absorbed four apparent laws of nature about a technology most of us have had for about three years. An office manager in Ladue forwards one of them to her boss with a note that says we should talk about this. A shop owner in Jennings screenshots another. A contractor in Highland reads a third at a red light and decides, quietly, that he’s behind.

None of that is anybody’s fault. This subject is genuinely confusing, the vendor noise is deafening, and a tidy number feels like a handrail in the dark. So here is each of those rules traced back as far as it actually goes: who said it first, what kind of claim it is, and in two cases, the plain admission that the trail runs cold.

### What is the 10/20-70 rule for AI?

It’s a resource-allocation principle from Boston Consulting Group: put roughly 10% of your effort into algorithms, 20% into technology and data, and 70% into people and process. BCG presents it as a pattern drawn from its own client engagements, not as a measured research result. That distinction is the whole ballgame, and it disappears the moment the number reaches social media.

The framework runs through BCG’s generative AI writing, including work authored by Nicolas de Bellefonds, Sylvain Duranton and Vladimir Lukic, and it reappears in the firm’s 2025 report on the gap between AI spending and AI profit. Forbes contributor Joe McKendrick wrote it up on January 26, 2026 as a BCG principle, which is roughly the moment it started showing up in every third post on your feed.

The idea underneath it is worth hearing. Businesses that treat an AI rollout as a software purchase tend to end up with software nobody opens. The tool arrives, two people try it, the trial lapses, and everyone agrees AI didn’t work here. Anyone who has watched a point-of-sale migration go sideways already knows this in their bones. So the rule is pointing at something true.

It is still a rule of thumb wearing a lab coat.

### Is the 10/20-70 split a research finding or a consulting framework?

A framework. BCG’s own framing is that the split reflects what it has seen across case work involving hundreds of companies — a consultancy describing the shape of its own engagements. Publishing that is perfectly legitimate and genuinely useful. It is not a study. Nobody assigned firms at random to a 10/20/70 budget, held everything else steady, and measured what came out the other end.

Why should you care about the difference? Because a finding tells you what is true and a framework tells you where to look. If your actual bottleneck is that your customer records live in three places and none of them agree, the 70% figure is wrong for your situation and following it will waste your year. Frameworks are lenses. Lenses are for pointing, not for obeying.

One more tangle worth undoing. There is an older 70-20-10 model in workplace learning — 70% of development from doing the job, 20% from other people, 10% from formal courses — developed in the 1980s by Morgan McCall, Michael Lombardo and Robert Eichinger in connection with the Center for Creative Leadership and popularized in their 1996 book The Career Architect Development Planner. Its evidence base has been argued over for years, because it grew out of roughly 200 managers recalling how they learned. Same digits, different field, unrelated claim. When you see the numbers reversed in an AI post, that is usually where the confusion started.

### So where did the 30% rule come from?

I could not source it, and I want to be direct about that. There are at least two different rules sharing that number, neither carries a named author, a paper, a firm or a date, and the explainer articles circulating about it cannot source it either. This one is folklore, and it deserves to be labeled as folklore rather than quietly given a pedigree it never had.

Version one is a workflow split: let AI handle about 70% of a repetitive, data-heavy task and keep the remaining 30% — the judgment, the ethics, the creative call, the part where somebody is accountable — with a human. Version two comes out of schools, and says no more than about 30% of what you hand in should be AI-generated.

When BGR published an explainer on June 9, 2026, writer Joshua Hawkins reached for the same hedge anyone honest reaches for: according to some online reports, the idea may have originated in education, where Turnitin is used to assess how much of a submission looks AI-written. Note the hedging. Note also that Turnitin does not set a 30% threshold. The number looks like individual instructor practice that hardened, through repetition, into a rumored platform policy.

So the honest summary is this. The 30% rule circulates widely, it is quoted with real confidence, and I could not find its origin. That does not make the underlying advice bad — keep a person on the half that requires judgment is decent guidance in most trades. It means that if somebody quotes 30% at you as an established standard, they cannot tell you who established it, because nobody can.

### Are the three laws of AI real laws?

No. They are Isaac Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics, and they first appeared in full in a short story called Runaround, published in the March 1942 issue of Astounding Science Fiction. That is fiction, written by a young biochemistry student to give his robot stories something to break against. Asimov credited the magazine’s editor, John W. Campbell Jr., with helping formulate them during a conversation in December 1940; the first law alone had appeared in his story Liar! in May 1941.

They are elegant, and that elegance is exactly why they keep getting mistaken for policy. A robot may not harm a human or, through inaction, allow a human to come to harm. A robot must obey human orders unless doing so conflicts with the first law. A robot must protect itself unless that conflicts with the first two.

Here is the part almost nobody mentions when they quote them: most of Asimov’s robot stories are about the laws failing. The whole point of the device is that three tidy rules cannot survive contact with a messy situation. He built them so they would crack, then wrote the cracks.

No statute contains them. No AI product implements them. No regulator anywhere cites them. If you want to know what an AI system is actually forbidden from doing, you have to read law, and we get to that below.

### What about the four stages of AI adoption?

There is no canonical four-stage model, and that is the answer rather than a dodge. Searching for the original turns up several unrelated four-stage lists published by different organizations with different stage names. Innovate UK Business Connect publishes an Adoption Stages Framework built on Strategy, Data, Build and Implement. Other consultancies publish four stages running from resistant through exploring and implementing to optimized. Others publish five stages and call those canonical too.

They are not versions of one underlying model. They are separate maps drawn by separate firms, usually to sit at the front of a service offering, and each one is arranged so that the reader lands somewhere in the middle and needs help getting to the end. That is not a scandal. It is just what a maturity model is for.

So when a post asks what the four stages of AI adoption are, the accurate response is: whose four? Any of these can be a useful way to organize a conversation. None of them is a measurement of where you actually are.

Wildly off-topic — but St. Louis antique dealers know about old rules.

### Why does everyone say 95% of AI projects fail?

Because of one report. In August 2025, a group at the MIT Media Lab’s Project NANDA circulated a paper titled The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025, reporting that roughly 95% of enterprise generative AI pilots produced no measurable profit-and-loss impact. Fortune covered it on August 18, 2025, AI-exposed stocks wobbled, and the figure has been quoted daily ever since.

What it actually rests on: about 150 interviews with business leaders, roughly 350 employee survey responses, and analysis of around 300 publicly described deployments. It was circulated as a report rather than published through peer review. And the thing it counted was measurable impact on the profit line, not whether the software functioned. A pilot that worked fine and simply was never measured lands in the 95% alongside a pilot that collapsed.

It is also about enterprises. The subject was corporate pilots with real budgets, not a two-truck HVAC outfit using a chatbot to write follow-up emails. The report’s own conclusion was that the divide came down to approach rather than model quality — which, notice, is the same claim BCG’s 70% is making from a completely different direction. Two independent sources arriving at similar conclusions is the strongest thing in this whole article, and it is nobody’s favorite statistic.

### Did Stephen Hawking really warn us about AI?

Yes, and unlike most of the material in this article, the quote is real and precisely sourceable. In a BBC interview published December 2, 2014, Stephen Hawking told technology correspondent Rory Cellan-Jones that the development of full artificial intelligence could spell the end of the human race. He went on to say such a system would redesign itself at an ever-increasing rate, while humans, limited by slow biological evolution, could not compete.

Two pieces of context change how that lands. The interview was pegged to a new communication system built for Hawking with help from Intel and a predictive-text company — he was, at that moment, an enthusiastic user of the technology he was warning about. And the phrase he used was full artificial intelligence: a hypothetical system that improves itself without us. That is a real debate among serious people.

It is not a comment on whether a salon in the metro should let software draft appointment reminders. When the quote gets pasted under a post about business tools, it borrows the weight of a very different argument. Hawking earned his warning. It just was not about your invoicing.

### Which AI rules are actually written down?

The only place a genuine list of forbidden AI uses exists is statute, and the most complete one is European. Article 5 of the EU AI Act sets out eight prohibited practices — among them social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases, and emotion recognition in workplaces and schools. Those prohibitions became applicable February 2, 2025, and penalties became enforceable August 2, 2025, at up to 35 million euros or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

In the United States there is no comprehensive federal AI statute. So the rules that reach a business here are state rules, and in this metro they change when you cross the river.

Illinois has been writing AI law for years. The Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act took effect January 1, 2020, and requires an employer to give notice, explain how the system works, and get consent before AI analyzes a candidate’s video interview. House Bill 3773 amends the Illinois Human Rights Act effective January 1, 2026, barring the use of AI that has a discriminatory effect in employment decisions, requiring notice, and specifically prohibiting zip code as a proxy for a protected class. And the Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act, announced by the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation on August 4, 2025, bars using AI to deliver therapy or make mental health treatment decisions, while still allowing licensed clinicians to use it for administrative work.

Missouri has no AI-specific statute. More than a dozen AI bills were filed in the 2026 legislative session and every one of them died before the session ended, as KFVS reported on May 25, 2026. The next chance for state lawmakers is the session that opens in January 2027.

The practical version: an employer in Highland screening applicants with an AI hiring tool carries notice and non-discrimination obligations that an employer twenty-five minutes away in Missouri does not. That is a real, checkable difference, and it is worth more to you than any of the numbered rules above.

### What this looks like from behind the counter

If you run a small local service business, the constraint is not your software budget. It’s your own hours. You are the estimator, the dispatcher, the person who answers at 7:40 on a Wednesday night, and the one reconciling receipts on Sunday. Margin lives in scheduling density and in the callback you didn’t have to make, and a good chunk of the year gets decided in two or three brutal weeks when everybody calls at once. What owners complain to each other about is not falling behind on AI. It’s the estimate that sat in a truck three days and lost the job to whoever answered first.

That is why these rules land strangely. They were written for a company with a change-management line item. Your version of the 70% is you, on a Sunday, deciding whether a tool is worth learning. And that estimate only matters because somebody went looking for your trade in your town first — which is what being listed and complete on St Louis Near Me Directory is for.

### What actually decides whether AI helps a small business

After taking apart the folklore, it would be cheap to hand you another invented rule. So here is only what the evidence and plain observation will support, offered as questions rather than laws.

Is it one named task? Not AI for the business — the follow-up email after an estimate, the weekly schedule, the first draft of a job description. Every source above that says anything credible says the same thing from a different angle: the approach decides the outcome, and a vague approach has no outcome to measure.

Does the output have a defined shape somebody checks before a customer sees it? This is the one that quietly matters most, because in a lot of small businesses the staff are already using these tools whether or not the owner knows, which is its own shadow AI problem worth understanding.

Does it give you back your hours specifically? Not a staff member’s slack time. Yours. And would you notice within a week if it stopped working? If you can’t say what breaks when you switch it off, it was never doing anything.

One last piece of reassurance, with real numbers attached. Census Bureau data published May 26, 2026, covering December 14, 2025 through May 3, 2026, found under 20% of firms with four or fewer employees using AI, compared with 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees and 37% of those with 250 or more. A Federal Reserve note dated April 3, 2026 put overall use at about 18% of firms as of the end of 2025. Both are government figures, not vendor surveys, and they say the same thing: the smallest businesses are the least likely to have adopted anything.

One caution on those numbers. The Census Bureau changed its AI question in November 2025, from asking whether a firm uses AI to produce goods or services to asking whether it uses AI in any business function, and reported rates jumped between 47% and 159% depending on industry. Any trend line drawn across that date is measuring the question, not the behavior. If you want that pulled apart properly, the companion piece on what percent of small businesses actually use AI does it in detail, and the broader overview of AI for St. Louis businesses covers where to start.

If you would rather work through one real task with other owners in the room than read another numbered rule, that is more or less the premise of the AI workshops for metro business owners. And if you want to see how a specific tool behaves before you trust it with anything, start by reading up on Google AI Mode in plain language, since it is the one most of your customers will meet first.
